GATE is a well validated Monte Carlo simulation toolkit for a variety of medical imaging and dosimetry applications. However, there is a very limited usage of GATE in mammography, digital breast tomosynthesis, breast computed tomography and X-ray, as well as in breast dosimetry applications. In the present study, a set of breast imaging and dosimetry simulations have been modelled in GATE and compared with previously published data of Agata, XRMC and gCTD Monte Carlo codes. The validation test simulations included geometrical objects as well as anthropomorphic computational breast phantoms. Different simulations were applied with previously validated clinical CT spectra of 80 kVp and 100 kVp. For fast execution of the highly demanding simulations, in terms of computational time, high performance computing resources were used

articleTitle: The ETROC2 prototype for CMS MTD Endcap Timing Layer (ETL) upgrade
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: The Endcap Timing ReadOut Chip (ETROC) is designed to process LGAD signals with time resolution down to about 40-50ps per hit. The ETROC2 is the first full size (16x16) prototype design with the front-end based on and scaled up from the ETROC1 (4x4). The readout designs at pixel and global level and the system interfaces are all new and are compatible with the final chip specifications in terms of functionality. The ETROC2 is intended as a learning chip, as a stepstone to the ETROC3 which is intended as the pre-production design. The ETROC2 design and test results will be presented.

articleTitle: Impact of the ADC Nonlinearities on X-ray Spectral Analysis and Correction Techniques
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Analog-to-digital conversion (ADC) is a key element in spectroscopic systems with low-noise and high dynamic range and the impact of ADC non-linearities must be carefully estimated. Aim of this work is to study the impact of the ADC non-linearity errors and the benefit of suitable correction to experimental X-ray spectra. A simulative study was first conducted on the impact on centroid determination and on the discrimination of two X-ray lines. Correction techniques were applied to experimental X-ray spectra acquired by a ladder (512 x 128 pixels) of the Mini-SDD X-ray imager, featuring a fast 8-bit ADC integrated in the hexagonal pixel (136 μm side) and noise performance down to 40 electrons rms. We measured the individual ADC bin-edges with the 13-bit DAC available at the periphery of the readout ASIC. Fitting the ADC output vs. the DAC code with multiple error-function model returns the bin edges, the sigma of the bin transitions and the goodness-of-fit parameters. The global ADC staircase showed a relative bin-width non-uniformity (mostly differential non-linearity, DNL) in the range 10-50%. The relative bin-width non-uniformity across a full-size sensor (256 x 128) was found about 10% rms in the periphery of the sensor and 3-4 times larger in the internal rows. This spatial pattern had been already observed, e.g. in gain and noise measurements, confirming the relevance of DNL errors.X-ray spectra of Cu target have been compared before and after correction of the ADC bin widths. Both the pedestal and Cu Ka peak as well as the low-energy continuum visually recover a smoother trend. The root-mean-square error (RMSE) of the Cu Ka peak fit shows a marked reduction by a factor 3 after DNL correction. This is also reflected in the marked drop from 4% to 0.5% of the standard error of gain, directly linked to the improved peak fitting, which shows the significant benefit of the correction.

articleTitle: Atomistic analysis of DNA strand breaks in tritiated water by using Geant4-DNA simulation with knowledge from quantum chemical calculation
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: The strand breaks of a double strand B-form DNA in tritiated water were studied by using the Geant4-DNA. Previously, we reported that the reactivity of hydroxyl radicals on abstraction of a deoxyribose hydrogen in the indirect effect can be estimated by introducing the effective atomistic volume of moiety associated with the hydrogen site in the Geant4-DNA [1]. The result was consistent with the measured reactivity and the accessibility of hydroxyl radicals to the deoxyribose’s hydrogens calculated by using the quantum molecular dynamics simulation[2]. In this paper, firstly, we studied the hydrogen abstraction of deoxyribose by hydroxyl radicals in terms of the activation energy by using a semi-empirical quantum chemistry program, MOPAC. The reactivity is expressed by the chemical reaction rate and the accessibility between hydroxyl radicals and hydrogens in deoxyribose. The calculated activation energies were small and below 8 kcal/mol for all hydrogens through 1’ to 5’’. The result indicates that the reactivity is more dependent on the accessibility rather than the chemical reaction rate. Secondly, we studied the variation of fraction of the indirect effect in strand breaks by changing criterion of energy threshold for the direct effect. The fractions in the 2.5 keV electron beam simulation were approximately 30% and 90% for the energy threshold of 10.79 eV[3] and 17.5 eV[4], respectively. Since it is known that the indirect effect is dominant in strand breaks for low energy beta-rays, the 17.5 eV energy threshold is suitable. Thirdly, we started to study the influence of target oxygenation, which generates the other reactive oxygen species such as the superoxide anion and its protonated form other than hydroxyl radicals. The Geant4-DNA simulation was performed for water target with various concentration of dissolved oxygen. We also discuss the influence on strand breaks in this paper.

articleTitle: AstroPix: A Pixelated HVCMOS Silicon Sensor for Astrophysics and Nuclear Physics
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Addressing the "MeV gap" in astrophysical sensitivity with a singular instrument is challenging - the system must be sensitive to photons over four decades of energy interacting through three unique energy-dependent mechanisms. In order to accurately measure and reconstruct medium-energy gamma rays in this band, a particle tracking system with a low noise floor of 5 keV and precise energy resolution of 9.7% FWHM at 122 keV is required. The component must also draw relatively low power (<1mW/cm^2) to effectively scale into a large instrument. AstroPix is a CMOS monolithic active pixel silicon (APS) sensor being designed for such use in space-based gamma-ray telescopes. A high voltage applied individually to all pixels will allow for depletion into the bulk up to 500um, enabling a dynamic range of 25-700 keV per 500x500um pixel. Drawing from heritage in high-energy particle physics, AstroPix can be implemented in a range of instruments from future gamma-ray telescopes to nuclear physics experiments. This talk will outline the scientific drivers from gamma-ray astronomy that shape AstroPix’s benchmark characteristics and overview its development process. Special attention will be paid to the first flight version of AstroPix, version 3, to be flown in late 2024 and future implementations in nuclear physics.

articleTitle: High-Q Plasmonic Resonance Modes for Purcell Enhanced Scintillation
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: We performed finite-difference time-domain electromagnetic simulations of a hybrid plasmonic-photonic crystal for Purcell enhanced scintillation. The Purcell effect can be explained by cavity quantum electrodynamics and can be calculated from Maxwell's equations. Fermi's Golden Rule states that the radiative rate of a quantum emitter is proportional to the local density of optical states of a medium. We have designed a nanocomposite structure that is a Purcell enhanced "superscintillator" and can be fabricated by interspersing metallic nanoparticles with scintillating cube-shaped nanoparticles that we have previously developed and synthesized. The resulting nanocomposite structure creates an optimal spatial overlap between the optical resonance modes and localized surface plasmon resonance (LSPR) of the metallic nanoparticles. From simulations assuming aluminum plasmonic nanoparticles in unit cells that are 150 nanometers thick, we demonstrate a peak Purcell factor of over 300 at the peak emission frequency (350 nm) of our cerium-doped SrLuF nanoparticles. This much higher resulting radiative decay rate of this metamaterial scintillator design enables 300-fold higher light yield and shorter decay times, which if successfully scaled up in dimensions, would be a promising advance for the next generation time-of-flight positron emission tomography detectors.

articleTitle: Image Reconstruction Using Deep Image Prior in Projection Domain for Limited-Angle Problem
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: It has been studied that the image reconstruction method used for sparse projection data. The limited-angle and few-views are included in the sparse projection data. The incomplete tomography is reconstructed, since the insufficient data are used. In limited-angle problem, various reconstruction methods has been proposed, however, none of the methods have been able to completely reconstruct the image. In the image reconstruction, the deep learning technique has been widely studied and already implemented in clinical machine. The supervised deep learning technique is general and need huge data for training and validation of neural network. The deep image prior (DIP) is one of the unsupervised deep learning technique, so the training and validation data are not needed. The DIP can restore the data that cannot be acquired by a machine, and be proposed for denoising, super resolution and inpainting. The DIP processing in the image and the projection domain has been proposed. In this study, the novel DIP processing in he projection domain was applied for limited-angle problem. We performed a numerical simulation to valify whether the limited-angle problem can be solved by proposed method, some physical factors were not considered. The proposed DIP was able to reconstruct the image more accurately than the other comparative methods. In the image contrast, the proposed DIP was better than the others. In the root mean squared error (RMSE), the image reconstructed by FBP, ML-EM, and proposed method are 0.160, 0.023, and 0.014, respectively

articleTitle: Characterisation of the pFREYA16 ASIC for low-noise ptychography applications
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: The pFREYA16 ASIC is an 8 x 2 prototype pixellated matrix developed to comply with the stringent requirements on both noise performance and frame acquisition speed imposed by recent x-ray ptychography applications. Namely, each pixel in the matrix was designed focusing mainly on single photon detection at 5 keV, 9 keV and 25 keV photon energies, with an equivalent noise charge of 250 e-rms obtained in post-layout simulations in the nominal case, and 1 MHz conversion rate, comprising integration by means of a charge sensitive amplifier, signal shaping through an RC-CR stage, discrimination of interesting signals and analog to digital conversion. The whole chain is integrated in each pixel. pFREYA16 is the first step to validate the architecture of a future 128-by-128 matrix. The channel power consumption is 220 μW in post-layout simulations in the nominal case and the elementary cell area occupation is 150 μm x 150 μm. The ASIC, together with a test structure matrix, has been submitted in Q4 2022, is currently in the assembly house for bonding and will be received by the end of Q2 2023. This summary will focus on the pFREYA16 design and development, while the conference presentation will also showcase the results from the characterisation of the produced chips.

articleTitle: Simulation evaluation of uncertainty of estimated ranges for therapeutic carbon-ion beams bymeasuring secondary electron bremsstrahlung
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Range estimation of carbon-ion beams is important to prevent deviation of the irradiated area in carbon-ion therapy. Recently, a range-estimation method by measuring secondary electron bremsstrahlung with a pinhole X-ray camera was proposed and reported. The estimated ranges with this method achieved millimeter-order uncertainty for monochromatic carbon-ion beams. However, this method has not been evaluated at clinical dose level beams. The purpose of this study is to evaluate the uncertainty at clinical dose levels by Monte Carlo simulation. Simulations were performed on a supercomputer system using the simulation code PHITS. An acrylic target was placed 340 mm apart from a 10-mm-diameter pinhole collimator of an X-ray camera. As a result, the proposed method was able to estimate the range with uncertainty of millimeter order for clinical doses. We found that the uncertainty of the estimated ranges kept acceptable values even for clinical dose levels.

articleTitle: Improving TOF-PET performance by exploiting photon wavelength classification
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Time-of-flight positron emission tomography (TOF-PET) relies on excellent timing and energy resolutions, but improvement of both at the same time as proven challenging. In this study, we explore the possibility of exploiting both Cherenkov and scintillation at the same time and by separate in TOF-PET in order to reach new limits for timing and energy resolution. This separation could allow for optimization of time and energy resolution separately for each type of signal, resulting in an improved performance. Our study case material is bismuth germanium oxide (BGO) due to its relatively high Cherenkov emission. BGO has been revived as a TOF-PET scintillator candidate due to its excellent coincidence time resolution (CTR) and relatively low cost, but the presence of slower scintillation light is hindering its use in TOF-PET, hence we hypothesis that BGO could benefit from separation between Cherenkov and scintillation. We are exploring dichroic filters as a way to categorize photons by wavelength with a negligible photon loss. We have demonstrated the capability of Cherenkov and scintillation separation in simulations, and we will present some results with our TOF-PET coincidence prototype featuring dichroic filters.

articleTitle: HYPR4D Kernel Method with an Unsupervised 2.5SD+0.5TD Deep Learning Assisted Kernel Matrix
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: We describe a deep learning (DL) assisted HYPR4D kernelized reconstruction which produces nearly noise-free voxel level time-activity-curves (TACs) while preserving quantification within small structures as well as consistent spatiotemporal patterns/features within measured data. A series of iteration specific unsupervised DL networks was trained to minimize the inconsistency between the 4D kernelized OSEM subset estimates so that the network output would contain the most consistent features over the subsets for single subject training. We then construct the proposed DL HYPR4D kernel matrix based on the 4D high frequency features extracted from the network output for each reconstruction iteration. Moreover, inspired by the standard 2.5D de-noising models which use 3 slice input, we further include the corresponding slices one time frame before and after the frame of interest to provide spatiotemporal noise reduction (i.e. 2.5SD+0.5TD). Finally, we introduce a final tuning step within the reconstruction to mitigate the typical over-smoothing observed from the network output to preserve the quantification within small target structures. Contrast phantom and human [<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">18</sup>F]FDG data acquired on GE SIGNA PET/MR were used for evaluation. The proposed DL HYPR4D kernel method outperformed the standard HYPR4D kernel method as well as TOF-OSEM and TOF-BSREM (Q.Clear) in terms contrast recovery vs noise. The proposed final tuning reduced the underestimation bias due to over-smoothing within a 4mm target structure from ~15% to < 2% while maintaining nearly noise-free voxel level TACs. In addition, the proposed unsupervised DL assisted reconstruction also outperformed the supervised DL version in terms of minimizing biased patterns along the TACs.

articleTitle: Blurring correction for calculating functional images using an energy resolving photon counting detector
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Energy Resolving Photon Counting Detectors (ERPCD) can measure individual X-ray photons with energy discrimination. By analyzing multiple energy images, it can generate functional images that can obtain material information. At the edge of an object image blurring occurs which is caused by the point spread function. Image blurring interferes with the quantification of the object edge in the process of functional image calculation. The purpose of this study is to develop a novel blurring correction method to quantitatively analyze the object edge in functional images. In our correction method, the blurring is determined in a mask area of 5 × 5 pixels. First, in the highenergy image, only the blurred pixels are extracted and corrected by estimating the true value from the mask area. Then, the corresponding pixels in the low-energy image are corrected in the same way. As a result, the blurring is corrected in all pixels of both energy images. To perform theoretical verification of our correction method, a simulation study was conducted. Low- and high-energy images were generated using an aluminum bar phantom having a size of 1 mm × 1 mm and thicknesses of 1 mm to 10 mm taking into consideration detector response, charge sharing, and image blurring. Then, effective atomic number (Z<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">eff</inf>) images were calculated by analyzing the energy images. When an aluminum bar (Z<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">eff</inf> = 13) was affected by blurring, proper Z<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">eff</inf> could not be calculated in the blurred area. However, when applying our method to the blurred image, the blurring was properly corrected at the object edge, which shows the correct value of Z<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">eff</inf> =13. In addition, we performed experiments using a prototype ERPCD and obtained a similar correction result for a comb-shaped phantom made of aluminum and polymethylmethacrylate. In conclusion, we developed a novel blurring correction method for the quantitative analysis of multiple images.

articleTitle: Hybrid scanning technique for dose reduction and image quality improvement in CT system
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Purpose: Dose reduction techniques have been a main interest in radiation-based medical applications. In this study, we focused on Region of interest (ROI) based imaging technique for dose reduction. We tried to solve limitations and problems of conventional ROI imaging technique by suggesting a new novel method, hybrid scanning technique.Materials and Methods: A prototype of the computed tomography (CT) system (TVX-IL1500H, GERI, Korea) and the RSD anthropomorphic head phantom were used to obtain the reconstructed image by two types of hybrid scanning techniques. The source-to-detector distance was 1178 mm and the source-to-center of rotation distance was 905 mm. Hybrid CT images are reconstructed with a combination of truncated and nontruncated projections by the filtered back projection (FBP) reconstruction algorithm. The proposed hybrid CT scanning is divided into alternating and half scan. To optimize hybrid CT scanning, an acquisition parameter value called hybrid scanning weighting factor (HSWF) was proposed, and image quality was evaluated by acquiring images according to each HSWF value. We used the image restoration method based on a projection onto convex sets (POCS) algorithm. The reconstructed image quality was analyzed by the structural similarity index (SSIM), contrast to noise ratio (CNR) and figure of merit (FOM) value.Results: For dose reduction in CT system, we proposed the hybrid scanning technique. To verify the image quality, hybrid CT images were obtained through the prototype CT system. Alternating scan reduced the area dose by 81%, and half scan reduced the area dose by 88% compared with conventional full view scan.Conclusions: The hybrid scanning technique contributes the image quality improvement and the dose reduction. And we derived the appropriate acquisition parameter based on HSWF for proposed hybrid scanning technique. We believe that these advantages may be considered to an alternative option for a low dose CT imaging system.

articleTitle: Impact of environmental conditions on Low Gain Avalanche Diode response
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Low Gain Avalanche Diodes (LGADs) have demonstrated excellent timing resolution thanks to their characteristic internal gain. Detectors based on LGAD technology play a crucial role in High Energy and Nuclear Physics experiments, among other applications. However, their performance is strongly affected by environmental factors such as temperature, humidity, and storage conditions. A systematic evaluation of the response of LGAD sensors as a function of these environmental parameters is therefore of essential importance when accounting for any application. LGAD sensors fabricated at the Brookhaven National Laboratory (BNL, US) are characterized at the Silicon Lab at BNL and at the RD50 facility at CERN, where they are stress-tested against various operating conditions.

articleTitle: Identification of Multiple Radionuclides Based on Principal Component Analysis and Convolutional Neural Network
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Real-time radionuclides monitoring systems require algorithms to accurately identify the presence of sources. In this study, we developed a radionuclides identification algorithm that can be used in a drone-based gamma ray imaging system. The proposed algorithm aims at identifying multiple radionuclides in situations where the number of detected gamma rays is low. The types and magnitudes of photo peaks appearing on the spectra vary depending on the situation, and high-frequency noise is often present on the spectrum when measured over a short time period. It is necessary to remove high-frequency noise, to extract features from the spectrum, and to estimate what radionuclides exist. We removed high-frequency noise from the acquired low-count spectra using the maximal overlap discrete wavelet transform and extracted dominant component using principal component analysis. Finally, we estimated which source caused the extracted features and spectra using convolutional neural network. To evaluate the proposed algorithm, Co-57(9 µCi), Ba-133(51 µCi), Na-22(90.55 µCi), and Cs-137(9.56 µCi). were used. The results of the study showed high sensitivity and specificity for various forms of data, demonstrating the proposed algorithm’s robustness with minimal influence from factors such as source activity, type, and distance from detector.

articleTitle: Self-Powered Perovskite Photon Counting Detectors with Extremely Low Dark Count Rate at High Temperatures
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Here we show that polycrystalline perovskite photodetectors can count photons under zero bias at room or higher temperature with performance rivaling the commercial silicon photomultipliers (SiPMs) operating at a much higher bias. Different from perovskite solar cells, the photon counting capability of perovskite photon-counting detectors (PCDs) is mainly determined by shallow charge traps, despite that deep charge traps also limit charge collection efficiency. One main shallow defect level with energy depth of 5.8±0.8 millielectronvolt (meV) is identified in polycrystalline perovskites formed by one-step method, causing a high dark count rate (DCR) of >20,000 per second per square millimeter (cps/mm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sup>) at room temperature. Perovskite films formed by two-step process with larger grain size have the 57.2±0.1 meV shallow traps which mainly locate at the film surface. We show that these very shallow traps can also be reduced by surface passivation using diphenyl sulfide, which dramatically suppresses DCR to 2 cps/mm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sup>, 1000 times better than SiPMs, and enables much better response linearity of perovskite PCDs to weak light. The superior photon-counting capability allows perovskite PCDs to collect gamma-ray spectra with better energy resolution than SiPMs. The perovskite PCDs can operate at high temperature of 85 ℃ without losing performance because of barely changed DCR at higher temperature, while SiPMs become much worse at higher temperature.

articleTitle: Computational Efficient Brain PET Image Denoising by Diffusion Probabilistic Models
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Given the accomplishments of Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models (DDPMs) in a diverse range of generative artificial intelligence applications, including those related to medical imaging, their limited training and inference efficiency remain critical shortcomings. To address this issue, we propose an effective approach for generating high-quality, full-dose (FD) Positron Emission Tomography (PET) images from low-resolution, noisy low-dose (LD) PET images. Instead of initiating the denoising process by sampling from a Gaussian distribution, as in conventional DDPMs, our method commences with the output of a trained Variational Autoencoder (VAE) model, thereby enhancing computational efficiency. To assess the efficacy of our approach, we employed a dataset consisting of 75 <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">18</sup>F-Flutemetamol PET raw data from patients diagnosed with neurodegenerative diseases. We reconstructed FD images and corresponding LD images, which contained only 5% of the total events. Subsequently, we conducted a quantitative analysis using well-established metrics, including peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR), structural similarity index metric (SSIM), and root mean square error (RMSE). Our results revealed that the proposed DDPM-based denoising model can enhance SSIM and PSNR values up to 26% and 31%, respectively. This approach facilitates a reduction in the injection dose administered to patients by up to 95% while simultaneously improving quantitative and qualitative factors.

articleTitle: Development of a SiPM based Detector Array and Data Acquisition System for the Muon Spectrometer ‘Super-MuSR’
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Super-MuSR is the first of the next generation of muon spin spectrometers and is currently being built at the ISIS pulsed source, UK. Funded via the ‘Endeavour Programme’, Super-MuSR is a six million pound development which will provide novel muon techniques at transformational counting rates. The expected counting rate is an order of magnitude greater than the existing instrument, exceeding 10^<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">9</sup>•counts•hr<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">-1</sup>. The improved count rate capability comes from the use of silicon photomultipliers (SiPM) to build a high density detector array and the implementation of a new digital signal processing pipeline. The array will exceed 700 independent detector channels in a barrel geometry, roughly 1 m in length and 0.35 m in diameter. Each SiPM is coupled to a plastic scintillator using wavelength shifting fibers. Encapsulation of the ‘tile’ assembly is required for light collection and optical isolation from the environment. Comparison of encapsulation methods, including spray-coatings are reported. Signal digitisation, processing and streaming are provided by Nuclear Instruments DAQ 121, which uses a Xilinx Zynq<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">®</sup> UltraScale<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">+TM</sup> ‘system on a chip’ with ADCs capable of 1 GHz sampling. Super-MuSR’s count-rate stability specification, a 0.032% variation, translate into a demanding thermal stability requirement. To hold the array at a fixed temperature a novel temperature control system has been developed. A resistive heater has been embedded inside the readout PCB in a ‘serpentine’ pattern, capable of delivering 400 mW of power, heating the SiPM to ≈45 °C.

articleTitle: Fast, Dense Lu-Y mixed Oxide Ceramic Scintillators
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Dense inorganic scintillators that can be scaled up to large sizes are required for future colliders. These scintillators are expected to have a fast scintillation decay profile to mitigate pileup at high event rates and show radiation hardness up to tens of Mrad to withstand the high fluxes. There are only few scintillation mechanisms that provide ultrafast scintillation – one of them being the charge transfer transitions (CTT), in which the emission comes from an ion (e.g., Yb) changing its charge state.The Lu<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf>O<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</inf> doped with Yb has been identified as a very promising scintillator due to its fast charge transfer transitions. Lu<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf>O<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</inf> is also one of the densest hosts at 9.4 g/cm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</sup>, which makes it very attractive for HEP applications. Since, the melting point of Lu<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf>O<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</inf> is very high (> 2,000°C) and its structure is cubic, the optically transparent material is manufactured using ceramic process.Samples of Lu<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf>O<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</inf> and (Lu,Y)<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf>O<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</inf> doped with Yb were manufactured at RMD and evaluated at both RMD and Caltech. The samples of Lu<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf>O<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</inf> doped with Yb show light yield as high as 500 ph/MeV and X-ray excited luminescence peaks around 370 nm. The Y mixed samples show light yield as high as 1,500 ph/MeV and their emission peaks around 420 nm. The scintillation decay time measured with a fast photomultiplier tube is around 1.2 ns for Lu<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf>O<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</inf> samples, while the mixed samples show additional slower component (< 20 ns). The intensity of the slower component depends on the Yb concentration. With their high density and ultrafast decay, Lu and Y mixed oxide ceramics are promising for future HEP calorimetry, time of fight (TOF) applications, and high energy resolved radiography. Optical and scintillation properties and radiation hardness studies for both small and large size samples will be presented.

articleTitle: Joint PET/CT Reconstruction Using a Double Variational Autoencoder
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: We propose in this work a framework for synergistic PET/CT reconstruction using a joint generative model as a penalty. We use a synergistic penalty function that promotes PET/CT pairs that are likely to occur together. The synergistic penalty function is based on a generative model, namely β-VAE. The model generates a PET/CT image pair from the same latent variable which contains the information that is shared between the two modalities. This sharing of intermodal information between images can help reduce noise during reconstruction. Our result shows that our method was able to utilize the information between two modalities to reconstruct better images compared to individually reconstructed images in terms of PSNR.

articleTitle: Development of a PET subsystem for next generation preclinical PET/EPR for studying tumor hypoxia
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Previously, we reported a PET/EPR hybrid imaging system aiming to study and improve the efficacy of PET hypoxic tumor imaging using EPR oxygen imaging as a ground truth. Encouraged by the successful results with this exploratory system, we launched a PET subsystem development for the next generation PET/EPR scanner that has more suitable features for small animal imaging. The distinctive features of the new PET system include an ~4 times larger axial field-of-view (~106 mm) to allow whole body imaging of rodents, and a potentially sub-millimeter resolution by use of ~1 mm width LYSO scintillators. We devised a new signal multiplexing method to efficiently handle the significantly increased number of silicon photomultiplier outputs of this new system. The design of the detector module (DM) of the system has undergone several iterations. In the final design, the DM consists of 8 detector units (DU) on a 175mm x 20 mm printed circuit board, and each DU is made of a 12x12 LYSO crystals (1x1x10 mm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</sup>) coupled to a Hamamatsu 14161-3050HS-04 MPPC array (4x4 3.2 mm pitch). The new signal multiplexing method produces only 6 outputs for each DM: two outputs for coincidence time and DU identification, and four outputs for pixel crystal identification within a DU. Fourteen (14) DMs have been developed and successfully assembled into a PET ring whose inner and outer diameters are 60 mm and 115 mm, respectively. Evaluation tests were conducted by using a Brightonix BASP-10011 data acquisition board that provides high-throughput 16 12-bit 80 MSPS analog-to-digital converter (ADC) and 16 time-to-digital converter (TDC) channels. The initial results indicate that when using the BASP-10011 resulting DM performance properties were as good as those obtained by using the CAEN 5742 waveform sampler operating at 0.7 GSPS. At the meeting, we will present the development of the PET system employing the BASP-10011 DAQ and its performance measurement result.

articleTitle: Thick Gas Electron Multiplication (THGEM) Boards: Modeling the Hole Story
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: This summary describes a method for simulating the impact of mechanical tolerances on signal amplitude and collection efficiency for Thick Gas Electron Multiplication (THGEM) boards. Modeling THGEM board performance has a well defined workflow for the idealized case. This standard workflow defines a unit cell to simplify the model and reduce the computational requirements for the simulating the electron transport and ionizing collisions in Garfield++. However, the standard unit cell does not include an important aspect of THGEM manufacturing, the mechanical tolerances. Simulating how mechanical tolerances affect electron propagation in the gas is time intensive. An initial electron under our sensor’s ideal conditions creates more than 10,000 electrons at readout. Tracking that many electrons takes hours to days in Garfield++ when the electric field is complex. Since Garfield++ scales almost 1:1 with the number of available CPUs, we develop an architecture using Amazon Web Services (AWS) Elastic Compute Cloud (EC2). Using this architecture, we model a variety of configurations with high statistical fidelity. The results from 1000 simulations per configuration show concentricity of the insulator and metallized THGEM hole has a substantial impact on the simulated performance of a THGEM’s gain and efficiency. Both the gain and efficiency of the THGEM reduce from their optimal value in concentric holes as the distance from nominal increases. A greater than 40% loss in simulated gain and a greater than 16% loss in simulated efficiency materialize by 0.03mm from nominal. In addition, the range of simulated gain broadens, which implies a degradation in sensor energy resolution. As such, experimental analysis of THGEM gain and efficiencies should define the allowed or measured tolerances of hole concentricity when matching experimental and simulated gain values.

articleTitle: Experimental Evaluation of Spectral-Temporal-Double-Coincidence-Enhanced Preclinical SPECT Imaging of Low-Dose Therapeutic Radionuclides
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: We proposed the spectral-temporal double coincidence (STDC) technique to enhance SPECT imaging of therapeutic radionuclides emitting cascade photons, such as Lu-177, Ac-225, and In-111. The preliminary simulation study explored the potential that STDC could reject >99.9% of down-scattering contamination with a high timing resolution system. To experimentally evaluate the technique, a prototype STDC-SPECT system was constructed using 3D CZT detectors. The reconstructed images of a line-source demonstrated the dramatic enhancement of the image quality with STDC-SPECT compared to conventional SPECT data acquisition. These results have demonstrated the potential of STDC-enhanced SPECT imaging for low-dose therapeutic radionuclides in small animals.

articleTitle: A Bayesian Neural Network-Based Method For The Extraction Of A Metabolite Corrected Arterial Input Function From Dynamic [11C]PBR28 PET
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: In PET, arterial sampling and metabolite correction are prerequisites for the gold-standard measurement of values like the volume of distribution (V<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">T</inf>), often necessary for the full quantification of radioligand binding. However, the invasiveness and technical demands of these procedures limit their application in both research and clinical PET studies. Machine learning approaches have been explored to predict V<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">T</inf> from PET images, but their integration in clinical routine is limited by their lack of transparency or thorough evaluation. Here we propose a Bayesian Neural Network to estimate the arterial input function (AIF), while also outputting its prediction uncertainty, 1) directly from the entire dynamic PET images (NN-AEIF), 2) from an image-derived input function (IDIF)(NN-IDIF) and, as a sensitivity measure, 3) from the un-corrected plasma curve (NN-AIF). All methods, applied on [<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">11</sup>C]PBR28 PET data, were compared to the metabolite-corrected AIF in terms of V<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">T</inf>, and the prediction uncertainty was assessed in terms of normalised coefficient of variance (nCV). Overall, both NN-AEIF and NN-AIF were able to accurately predict V<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">T</inf>, outperforming the other methods, with NN-AEIF showing the lowest nCV.

articleTitle: A radiation tolerant read-out link and control Daughterboard for the upgrade the of the ATLAS Hadronic Calorimeter
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: This paper summarizes the design strategies and results of the radiation studies of the ATLAS Tile Calorimeter (TileCal) read-out link and control Daughterboard for the High Luminosity Large Hadron Collider (LHC). A total of 896 Daughterboards will interface the on- and off-detector electronics through 5376 optical multi-Gbps links powered by CERN radiation hard GBTx ASICs, Microsemi ProASIC FPGAs and Xilinx Kintex Ultrascale FPGAs. Each Daughterboard receives configuration commands, while recovering and phase adjusting LHC synchronized clocks that drive multiple sampling ADCs in the front-end. Simultaneously, continuous high-speed readout of digitized PMT samples, slow control and monitoring data is sent to the off-detector. Different variants of commercial off-the-shelf components have been studied under radiation to be qualified for the radiation levels simulated for the entire HL-LHC lifetime. Additionally, the design minimizes possible single points of failure induced by sensitivity to radiation damage by employing a double-redundant scheme, implementing Triple Mode Redundancy in the firmware designs, enabling the Xilinx Soft Error Mitigation solution in the Kintex FPGAs, and using Forward Error Correction (FEC) in all the links.

articleTitle: Radiation Damage Effects in X-ray SOI Pixel Sensors with Pinned Depleted Diode Structure
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: We have been developing the X-ray SOI pixel sensor named "XRPIX" for future X-ray astronomical satellites. XRPIX is a monolithic active pixel sensor composed of a high-resistivity Si sensor, thin SiO<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf> insulator, and CMOS pixel circuits by utilizing the silicon-on-insulator (SOI) technology. Since XRPIX is capable of event-driven readout, it can achieve a high timing resolution better than 10 μs, which enables an extremely low background observation by adopting the anticoincidence technique. However, it had a major issue with its radiation tolerance to the total ionizing dose (TID) effect because of its thick buried oxide layer due to the SOI structure. To improve radiation tolerance, we introduce a new device structure with pinned depleted diode (PDD). Thus, in this presentation, we report on the improvement of the radiation tolerance of the XRPIX with PDD structure based on proton-irradiation experiments. Even after the irradiation of 40 krad, the gain decreased only by about 1%, and the energy resolution at 5.9 keV in FWHM was still as good as 260 eV. In addition, we focus on the slight residual radiation effects seen even in the new XRPIX, and investigate its degradation mechanism utilizing device simulations. In particular, mechanisms of increase in readout noise and decrease in gain are investigated, taking into account the positive charge accumulation in the oxide layer. As a result, it is found that the increase in the sense-node capacitance plays an important role in the degradation of readout noise and gain.

articleTitle: Enhancing Performance and Resource Usage of a Multi-Channel FPGA Digitizer for BGO-Based Time-of-Flight (TOF) PET
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Bismuth germanate (BGO) shows great promise for cost-effective time-of-flight positron emission tomography (TOF PET) detectors by utilizing Cerenkov photons for timing measurement and scintillation photons for energy measurement. In this study, we present the development and evaluation of the updated version of our multi-channel field programmable gate array (FPGA) digitizer for a BGO-based TOF PET scanner (BGO-TOF digitizer). Our previous BGO-TOF digitizer showed a coincidence timing resolution (CTR) of ~450 ps using two 3 × 3 × 5 mm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</sup> BGO pixels. However, the previous digitizer exhibited worse timing performance compared to that measured with an oscilloscope. We have conducted extensive investigations to identify primary obstacles impeding superior timing performance and incorporated identified solutions into the new BGO-TOF digitizer, effectively reducing the time discrepancy with oscilloscope data. Furthermore, we have upgraded the time-to-digital converter (TDC) with a resource-efficient monitoring TDC scheme, maintaining similar performance. The new BGO-TOF digitizer was implemented on the same FPGA Virtex-7 (VC707, XC7VX485T-2FFG1761CES, Xilinx) and demonstrated a CTR of 515 ps in preliminary tests using 3 × 3 × 20 mm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</sup> BGOs coupled to NUV-HD silicon photomultipliers (SiPMs) from Fondazione Bruno Kessler (FBK) without an offset correction for timing signals.

articleTitle: Effect of depth of interaction resolution on the performance of SIAT aPET
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Depth encoding detectors are required to simultaneously achieve high sensitivity and uniform high spatial resolution for small animal PET scanners. As compared to other depth encoding PET detectors, dual-ended readout detectors can achieve much higher depth of interaction (DOI) resolution. In this work, the effects of DOI resolution on the spatial resolution of SIAT aPET that has a 111 mm detector ring diameter and uses crystals of 1x1x20 mm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</sup> were investigated by imaging a point source and a Derenzo phantom. The detectors of SIAT aPET achieved a DOI resolution of ~2 mm. The DOI information of the list-mode data were rebinned to 1, 2, 4, 8, and 16 DOI bins to simulate different DOI resolutions of the detectors. The images were reconstructed by using an ordered subsets expectation maximization (OSEM) algorithm with point spread function (PSF) modeling using spatial variant PSF parameters. First, the spatial resolution was evaluated by using a Na-22 point source placed at center axial field of view (FOV) with different radial offsets. Then, the imaging resolution of the scanner was evaluated by using a Derenzo phantom placed at the center and 15 mm off radial center FOV. The radial spatial resolution at large radial offsets were significantly affected and the axial spatial resolution was also moderately affected by the DOI effect if the DOI was not measured. A number of DOI bins of 8 or more was required to achieve a uniform high spatial resolution in the center 60 mm FOV for the SIAT aPET scanner.

articleTitle: Development of a fully-integrated gamma camera and ultrasound (γ-US) imaging probe
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Accurate detection of lesions, such as tumors, is crucial for diagnosis and surgery. Among various medical imaging equipment used for this purpose, nuclear medicine devices can quantitatively image functional and molecular information. However, they cannot obtain anatomical information. On the other hand, ultrasonic probes can provide real-time anatomical information. We previously developed a single-channel integrated γ-US probe that combines an ultrasonic transducer and gamma ray detector. In this study, we extended this design to an array by integrating a gamma camera and 1D ultrasonic array probe, as well as a gamma collimator that also serves as a backing layer (BL) for the ultrasonic array. We validated that the integrated γ-US array probe has little performance degradation compared to individual probes. Finally, we acquired a nuclear medicine-ultrasound (NM-US) hybrid image that can accurately locate the position of radiation source target.

articleTitle: Data Augmentation and Feature Engineering for Machine Learning in Neutron Activation Analysis
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Neutron activation analysis (NAA) is a widely used technique for detecting trace elements in various materials. In recent years, machine learning (ML) algorithms have shown great potential for improving the accuracy and efficiency of NAA. In this paper, to achieve optimal results, data augmentation and feature engineering techniques are applied to NAA datasets to improve the quality and quantity of data available for training ML models. We will investigate the effectiveness of various data augmentation and feature engineering techniques in improving the performance of ML models for NAA. We will explore techniques such as noise addition, feature selection and combination, temporal averaging, and evaluate their impact on the accuracy of NAA models. The results of this study will provide valuable insights into the optimal strategies for data augmentation and feature engineering in NAA, and could potentially lead to more accurate and efficient NAA systems in the future.

articleTitle: Timing limits of ultrafast cross-luminescence emission in CsZnCl-based crystals for TOF-PET, HEP and TOF-CT
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Cross-luminescence (CL) has been shown to be one of the promising scintillation mechanisms to overcome timing limitations in TOF-PET, TOF-CT or high energy physics. However, well-known CL-emitters (e.g. BaF<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf>) have so far not been established in practice due to their disadvantages, mainly the emission in the deep-UV, calling for the need to develop new CL-emitting scintillators. One promising candidate is CsZnCl-based materials with a decay time ~1-2ns and light emission ~300nm. In this work, Cs<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf>ZnCl<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">4</inf> and Cs<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</inf>ZnCl<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">5</inf> are examined regarding their scintillation emission time profile and coincidence time resolution (CTR) read out with commercially available and research SiPMs. With 2x2x3mm³ crystals and a time-correlated single-photon counting (TCSPC) setup decay times of 1.79ns for Cs<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf>ZnCl<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">4</inf> and 1.03ns for Cs<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</inf>ZnCl<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">5</inf> were measured with no long tails in the scintillation emission time profiles, validating previously published measurements. Additionally, a prompt emission with significant abundance of 5% and 6% was discovered. Assuming a light yield of 1980ph/MeV for Cs<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf>ZnCl<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">4</inf> and 1460ph/MeV for Cs<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</inf>ZnCl<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">5</inf>, this relates to 122 (Cs<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf>ZnCl<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">4</inf>) and 73 (Cs<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</inf>ZnCl<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">5</inf>) ph/MeV energy deposit. CTR measurements with a high-frequency setup reached 60ps (FWHM) using Cs<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf>ZnCl<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">4</inf> coupled to FBK VUV SiPMs with silicon oil (Dow Corning 200), which is on par with state-of-the-art LYSO:Ce,Ca glue-coupled to NUV-MT SiPMs at 58ps. We find that the CTR of Cs<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf>ZnCl<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">4</inf>, air-coupled to VUV SiPMs, at 78ps (FWHM) is comparable to BaF<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf> at 75ps (FWHM). With their fast decay time and high CTR, these crystals seem to be perfectly suitable for high-rate time-of-flight applications further supported by the non-hygroscopicity for Cs<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf>ZnCl<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">4</inf> and only slight hygroscopicity for Cs<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</inf>ZnCl<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">5</inf>. Further measurements and simulations are planned to explore the prompt emission and to investigate light transport and sensitivity.

articleTitle: Installation and Time Resolved Measurements of Accelerated Electron Beam Halo Using Diamond Detector at FACET
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: In this report we describe a novel installation of the Time Resolved Beam Halo Monitor (TRBHM) system, integrating a diamond detector and high-speed waveform digitizer, at the Facility for Advanced Accelerator Experimental Tests (FACET) at the SLAC National Accelerator Laboratory. This work will result in the measurement and characterization of high-energy electron accelerator beam halo both spatially and temporally. This measurement is done by utilizing on-detector electrode lithography and the resulting impulsive current pulses are read out by system-on-chip (SoC) high density waveform digitizers developed by Nalu Scientific LLC (NSL). The theory, detection methodology, and instrumentation will be discussed, as well the installation and initial measurements from the FACET beamline.

articleTitle: Contrast improvement of X-ray CT reconstructed images using photon energy
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Our research has been focusing on X-ray imagers that directly convert highly crystalline semiconductors such as CdTe, CdZnTe, and TlBr to obtain higher energy resolution than indirect conversion detectors that use scintillators. X-ray spectroscopic imaging has the advantages over X-ray imaging without spectroscopic imaging that beam hardening effect tends to be smaller. In this research, contrast adjustment using energy bands in transmission images has attempted. The shot noise generated in each energy band was focused, its coefficient was automatically determined, and corrected to equalize the signal-to-noise ratio. These methods were used to improve the image quality of reconstructed images in X-ray CT and corrected the images focusing on the shot noise in the same way. The effect of the correction on the reconstructed images was verified. The results showed that the image quality was also improved in the reconstructed X-ray CT images.

articleTitle: Development of Hybrid Pixel Array Detector Aiming for Time Resolved Soft X-ray Measurements
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Due to limitations of the fabrication process, most HPADs (Hybrid Pixel Array Detectors) are made with monolithic sensor and tiled readout ICs. In conventional HPAD, there were so-called "inter-chip pixels" on the edges of readout ICs. These inter-chip pixels have 1.5 times or wider width and/or height than non-inter-chip pixels. This means, we are losing position information of a hit of photons on those pixels.We have successfully dealt with this inter-chip pixel problem by use of re-distribution layer on the sensor. So, in our new detector, non-uniformity in a single sensor module is eliminated.This new detector is designed based on UFXC32k IC [1] designed by AGH University of Science and Technology and named XSPA-500k [2]. XSPA-500k detector consists of 16 UHXC chips tiled and 1024 x 512 76 um sq. pixels per module. No inter-chip pixels in between ROICs which terribly suffer the image quality.XSPA-500k is aiming not only for X-ray imaging but also for time-resolved X-ray measurements. Dealing with "inter-chip pixels" is our main feature for imaging, and for time-resolved measurements we understand that frame rate is as important as the size of the pixels and the area of the detector. Thanks to UFXC32k IC’s high count-rate and fast operation capability, combined with our high data throughput backend circuits, XSPA-500k is capable of more than 50,000 fps with full-frame readout and 100,000 fps with 100 lines ROI in the center of the modules with continuous exposure (zero-deadtime mode operation with 2-bit counter/pixel.) If the non-continuous exposure (burst-mode operation [3]) is allowed, it can achieve over 970,000 fps with approximately 2 % duty ratio.

articleTitle: Bench-to-Clinical Transfer of OpenPET: First In-Beam Test in a HIMAC Treatment Room
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: In-beam PET is recognized as the most practical method for range verification in particle therapy. Positron emitters produced through fragmentation reactions are visualized. In addition to the range verification, tumor diagnosis without using radiopharmaceuticals might be possible by analyzing the biological washout of positron emitters. However, previous in-beam PET systems have been based on a dual-head geometry, which tends to cause artifacts in 3D imaging. Therefore, we have developed OpenPET for artifact-free 3D in-beam PET. The OpenPET is based on a full-ring detector geometry, but the edges of the cylinder are cut by two aslant planes to pass through a treatment beam. A human-sized OpenPET system has been developed and tested for carbon and oxygen beams using physics experiment rooms in the HIMAC. In this study, we aimed to install the OpenPET system in a treatment room at HIMAC, equipped with two fixed beam ports for scanning carbon beam irradiation. Retractable straight rails were developed for the repeatability of accurate positioning of the OpenPET to the isocenter for the in-beam measurement after finishing patient positioning by adjusting the patient couch on a robotic arm. The developed system was tested for a realistic human head phantom with a procedure similar to that for head and neck cancer treatment; a treatment plan (TP) was made based on CT images, calibrated to carbon therapy, by using a clinical TP system, and PET measurements were started at the beginning of the beam irradiation and continued for 39 min after the irradiation of about 1 min (4 GyE). In a planned clinical study, PET measurement time after finishing the irradiation will be reduced to 10 min. In conclusion, PET images were successfully obtained for the beam irradiation based on a clinically realistic scenario, and the bench-to-clinical transfer of the developed OpenPET system was completed.

Index Terms: Head And Neck Squamous Cell Carcinoma

articleTitle: Coincidence Timing Resolution of a Pixelated CZT Detector System
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Two 3x3 arrays of 2x2x1.5cm^3 CZT modules are irradiated by a Na-22 source to investigate the coincidence timing resolution capabilities of these CZT detectors. Pixelated CZT systems have demonstrated a timing resolution of <10ns using GHz sampling systems. In this study, coincidence data is recorded using sampling frequencies of 20, 40, and 80MHz. The coincidence timing resolution is measured using a simple linear fitting procedure, and a best timing resolution of 35ns is obtained on this two-array system.

articleTitle: Cluster-Based Alpha-Analysis using a Timepix3 with a 5 mm Thick CdTe Sensor
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: In the field of decommissioning nuclear facilities and radiation safety, knowledge of the presence of alpha emitters is important in deciding whether a material can be released or has to be treated as radioactive waste. Yet, the real-time measurement of materials with a low activity of alpha emitters is difficult because of the varying background of natural alpha emitters from Radon and its progenies. Therefore, samples of the material usually have to be taken and analyzed by radio analytics in a laboratory to decide whether a material can be released or has to be treated as radioactive waste. This procedure makes the release process very time-consuming.For this reason, it was investigated whether a more efficient release process without sampling would be possible by the use of a Timepix3 detector with a 5 mm thick CdTe sensor.The Timepix3 readout chip is currently being further developed by the "Medipix4 Collaboration" at CERN. It offers 256 x 256 pixels with a native pixel pitch of 55 x 55 μm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sup> and can be bump bonded to different semiconductor sensor materials such as Si, GaAs, CdTe, and CdZnTe. The Timepix3 detector features energy and time-of-arrival information for each incident. Due to charge sharing, thicker sensors feature a lower spatial resolution than thinner sensors when photons are counted without a correction for charge sharing. However, if a correction for charge sharing is applied by cluster analysis, both a higher spatial resolution and better energy information can be achieved than when using thin sensors.To investigate whether a spectroscopic distinction between Radon and its progenies and other relevant alpha nuclides is possible, a cluster-based per-pixel calibration of the detector was developed. The analysis of the alpha spectra will be presented here as well as its use for the release process in nuclear decommissioning and radiation protection.

articleTitle: Development of Integrated Corner Retroreflectors for Monolithic PET Detector
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: We propose to improve spatial resolution, light collection, and depth of interaction capabilities of monolithic PET detectors by using corner reflectors machined directly into the front face of the scintillator (termed integrated corner reflectors, or ICR). Using GATE simulations, we compare the performance of a 20 mm thick ICR detector to previous monolithic approaches including fully absorptive black walls and optical coupling of a separate reflective material to the front face of the scintillator, which can result in undesirable absorption and reflections due to the multiple interfaces between materials with differing indices of refraction. The use of ICR improves light collection in the primary photosensors while preserving the light distribution and maximizing light collection within the cone defined by the indices of refraction of the photosensor coupling grease and LYSO. The increased photon statistics aid in improving both transverse and depth resolution by 30% when compared to the use of fully absorptive black and a flat specular reflector. Additionally, when compared to a coupled RR, improvements in transverse and depth resolution are also observed. Using a larger ICR structure (9 mm vs 1mm) improves transverse resolution by 15% but only improves depth resolution by 5% in the center 10 mm of the monolith. We have also assembled an experimental setup to measure actual detector performance, focusing initially on determining an appropriate surface treatment for the ICR.

articleTitle: Design of A Picosecond Resolution Control Loop for Fine TDC Based on 0.11 μm CMOS Process
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Our group has developed a multi-voltage threshold (MVT) digitizer implemented on the application-specific integrated circuit (MVT ASIC). This new digital converter offers the advantages of low power consumption, high efficiency, and small size. In addition, it also improves the time resolution. To further enhance the performance of the MVT ASIC and silicon photomultiplier (SiPM), we propose to implement the MVT ASIC based on the 0.11 µm CMOS process. Because of the inherent delay limit of ~50 ps in this process, designing a time-to-digital converter (TDC) with 20 ps resolution is a challenge. Therefore, we propose a resolution control loop based on a two-stage phase-locked and vernier delay line structure to overcome this limitation. Through simulation, we have shown that the proposed method can achieve a ~20 ps time resolution based on a 0.11 µm process.

articleTitle: Performance of a PET Detector Based on Multi-resolution SiPM Array
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: High-resolution positron emission tomography (PET) detectors often have crystal array pitches smaller than the photodetector array pitch, making it difficult to resolve the edge crystals due to limited light sharing. In this paper, we proposed a multi-resolution SiPM array design to better resolve the edge crystals. This design uses a mix of SiPMs with different sizes and arranges smaller SiPMs around larger SiPMs. A pseudo 9 × 9 multi-resolution SiPM array, consisting of 6.47 × 6.47 mm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sup> SiPMs, 6.47 × 3.07 mm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sup>, and 3.07 × 3.07 mm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sup> SiPMs, was implemented on a 16 × 16 array of MicroFJ-30035 SiPMs with a pitch size of 3.4 mm. Similarly, an 8 × 8 SiPM array with a pitch size of 6.8 mm was mimicked by merging 2 × 2 groups. The flood histograms and energy resolution of detectors based on these three SiPM arrays were compared using a 36 × 36 lutetium yttrium orthosilicate (LYSO) array with a pitch of 1.5 mm and a thickness of 10 mm. The results show that the flood histogram obtained using the 16 × 16 SiPM array is the best, and the flood histogram obtained using the 9 x 9 multi-resolution SiPM array is much better than that obtained using the 8 × 8 SiPM array. The energy resolutions obtained using the three SiPM arrays are similar, and around 10%.

articleTitle: Linearity and aftersignal of High-Flux CdZnTe with optimized electrodes for X-ray detectors
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: In this follow up characterization study of Redlen High-Flux Cadmium Zinc Telluride (HF-CZT), carried out as a collaboration between IMEM-CNR and the ESRF, we demonstrate the linearity of the photocurrent with incident X-ray flux up to 6×10<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">+11</sup> photons.mm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">-2</sup>.s<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">-1</sup>. We also carry out an in depth study of the aftersignal as a function of incident X-ray flux as well as irradiation duration, with a microsecond time resolution. From this study we demonstrate that the aftersignal has a characteristic undershoot, the amplitude of which is linear with both the incident X-ray flux and the irradiation duration. However, the ratio between instantaneous aftersignal and corresponding photocurrent decreases with incident X-ray flux from 3% at the lowest flux, to 0.05%, at the highest flux. The aftersignal is demonstrated to go back to the baseline in the seconds time range. This paves the way for the use of HF-CZT in new generation of detectors for 4<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">th</sup> generation synchrotrons.

articleTitle: Novel arrangement of pinhole clusters for high-energy preclinical SPECT
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Interest in SPECT and PET imaging of isotopes emitting high energy gammas is increasing as it can be valuable in e.g. theragnostic applications, simultaneous multi-isotope PET and PET/SPECT and positron range-free PET. At these energies ranging from 250 keV to above 1 MeV, traditional multi-pinhole SPECT suffers from severe pinhole edge penetration which degrades image resolution. To alleviate this issue, clustered pinholes (CP) with smaller opening angles were proposed and are currently applied in a commercial preclinical scanner (VECTor, MILabs B.V.). Here we investigate, via Monte Carlo simulations, if a novel twisted clustered pinhole (TCP) geometry with clusters twisted around their axis can further improve images. To this end, the sensitivity and Derenzo resolution images of the new TCP collimator and VECTor’s current CP collimator were compared for high-energy prompt gamma imaging of Zr-89 (909 keV). To grant a fair comparison, data for both collimators were acquired while maintaining equal calculated system resolution. The new TCP collimator improved sensitivity and ratio of direct photons respectively by a factor ~1.3 and ~2.0 over currently used CP collimator. The reconstructed resolution phantoms show that at low activity (12 MBq/ml), CP and TCP could distinguish 0.90 mm and 0.80 mm diameter rods respectively. At high activity (190 MBq/ml), the same rod sections of 0.65 mm were distinguishable. The presented results show that the novel TCP collimator design outperforms current CP both in terms of sensitivity and resolution.

articleTitle: Pilot Study on PET-to-SPECT Image Synthesis for PSMA-targeted Theranostics
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Accurate generation of post-injection SPECT images through pre-treatment PET imaging enables the prediction of patient response to conventional FAA dosimetry. This, in turn, allow physicians to optimize the dosage of injected radioactive ligand, facilitating patient patient-specific dosimetry. Furthermore, in order to obtain multiple post-treatment SPECT images at various time points (typically 24, 72, and 144 hours after drug uptake), patients are required to remain in the hospital and undergo frequent SPECT imaging sessions. This not only places a burden on the hospital but also on the patients themselves. However, if pretreatment PET could be utilized to anticipate post-treatment SPECT results and replace some of the actual SPECT images, it would effectively reduce the length of the patient's hospital stay and alleviate the burden on the imaging room. Image synthesis, in particular the use of magnetic resonance imaging to generate synthetic computed tomography images, has been an area of active research. However, to date, no previous studies have explored PET-to-SPECT synthesis.In this pilot study, we investigated the potential of utilizing Deep Learning models to generate synthetic post-injection SPECT images from pre-treatment PET scans. We evaluated two generative models and determined that the Pix2Pix model was capable of producing visually appealing 2D synthetic SPECT images. We believe that this study could establish a foundation for PET-to-SPECT synthesis and stimulate further research in this area.

articleTitle: Masking for DDG in SPECT Reduces Influence of Motion Artifacts
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Respiratory motion in Single Photon Emission Computed Tomography (SPECT) is typically corrected using a 1D respiratory estimate to correct for the most dominant head-to-foot motion in the data. Estimation of this respiratory surrogate signal is typically done based on all of the data measured on the detector, but there might not only be one correct 1D respiratory motion contained for a given projection dataset. Using a large set of simulated water cylinder phantoms with moving spheres, we probe the influence of different kinds of motion artifacts on Principal Component Analysis (PCA), Center of Light (COL), Isometric Feature Mapping (ISOMAP), and Laplacian Eigenmaps (LE) for Data Driven Gating (DDG) when used in combination with projection domain masking. We demonstrate that using masking for DDG improves accuracy for all methods when a motion artifact is present in the data. Overall the LE methods performed the most robust across all simulations.

articleTitle: Deep Learning Dose Reduction Strategies for Attenuation Correction in PET Imaging
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Current PET attenuation correction (AC) approaches mostly rely on the acquisition of a CT scan, which besides the additional radiation burden frequently induces artefacts due to spatial mismatch between PET and CT. Deep learning (DL) methods have demonstrated promising results to enable CT-less AC in PET imaging. However, one of the challenges is to implement a solution that works for whole-body acquisitions, and long axial field-of-view scanners, while being tracer-independent. In this abstract, we outline three DL approaches to create transmission images using scout images, non-AC PET images or both as input.
