In each case, the predicted DL-Tr image is utilized to derive the attenuation map for PET image reconstruction. We ultimately aim to develop a DL framework that allows for CT-less whole-body PET AC of multiple tracer studies, while emphasizing quantitative accuracy in PET.

articleTitle: An attenuation model-based dual-energy calibration method for dual-energy luggage inspection system
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: We propose an attenuation model-based dual-energy calibration (AMDC) method for material decomposition in X-ray radiographic inspection. AMDC uses polynomial terms to the power of real numbers less than one in its calibration process, in order to reduce the influence of beam-hardening effect to material decomposition in radiography. Application of AMDC to dual-energy X-ray images acquired using GATE simulation showed significant improvement in the performance of material decomposition in radiography.

articleTitle: Clinical application of a newly-developed, motion-correction brain PET system
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: We have developed a brain PET scanner HIAS-29000 with a head motion correction system, which requires no head restraint. We obtained regulatory approval for use of this PET system in Japan. Four retroreflective markers attached to the subject's face are irradiated by near-infrared light from within the gantry hall, and the reflected light is detected three-dimensionally with two CMOS cameras installed in the gantry hall as well. This composition allows to record the spatial position coordinates of the four points. The PET scan is measured in list mode, the movement of four spatial position coordinates is reflected for each coincidence counting event, and the head position is corrected to the initial setting by quaternion calculation. Good images were obtained in 3D brain Hoffman phantom experiments, and good images were also obtained in a clinical study for 18F-BCPP-EF PET brain images of a dementia patient with his head moving frequently. By combining high-speed position information from a CMOS camera and PET list data, this method enables correction for each coincidence count, and can correct head movements with high accuracy. This system allows to visualize brain physiology and brain pathophysiology more naturally under no restraint.

articleTitle: High-resolution Positronium Lifetime Imaging of Extended Heterogeneous Biological Samples
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: About 40% of positrons form positroniums in human tissue prior to annihilation. The lifetime of ortho-positroniums (oPs) is sensitive to the tissue microenvironment and can potentially provide valuable information for monitoring disease progression and treatment response. To obtain lifetime images using currently available positron emission tomography (PET) scanners, several statistical image reconstruction methods have been proposed but were only validated by imaging well-separated point sources. In this study, we design an experimental method to perform high-resolution positronium lifetime imaging of an extended heterogenous biological sample. A Na-22 source was employed to irradiate the ex vivo tissue sample with free positrons. The prompt gammas and annihilation photons were detected to reconstruct a positron lifetime image on the tissue surface. The annihilation activity image showed that a significant quantity of positrons annihilated in the tissue of interest after passing through the air, providing positronium lifetime events carrying the lifetime information in the tissue. The reconstructed lifetime image by our previously developed SIMPLE method showed clear separation between the muscle and fat regions with much better spatial resolution and lifetime contrast than those obtained by the direct TOF backprojection method.

articleTitle: Transformer-based Architecture for Assisting Title and Abstract Screening of a Systematic Review
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Systematic literature reviews are crucial for decision-making across various fields. Typically, these reviews are carried out using laborious manual methods that rely on, e.g. keyword searches, title, and text analysis. Their outcome is a thematic classification of papers. To alleviate the burden on scientists, several natural language processing-based approaches have been developed to facilitate the screening of papers.Our approach employs pre-trained transformer models, such as Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers (BERT), LITMC-BERT and PubMedBERT, for papers about artificial intelligence research on COVID-19 for the purposes of detection, diagnosis, and prediction. This subject has been growing rapidly over the past three years, thereby making it challenging to be up-to-date with the latest information pertaining to the virus. Furthermore, with the COVID-19 situation appearing to have become more stable, scientists are focusing on investigating the underlying factors that caused the outbreak of the contagion.Our models find relevant documents and categorize them according to their information on COVID-19, such as diseases, treatments, and vaccinations. The proposed models have been evaluated for screening performance using a test set that comprises articles retrieved from the searches of three independent reviewers, who have assessed the eligibility of each paper. Our approach has achieved promising results for researchers and demonstrated its ability to be generalized.

articleTitle: Neural Network Based Methods for the Survival Analysis of Idiopathic Pulmonary Fibrosis Patients from a Baseline CT Acquisition
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis is an interstitial lung disease that causes scarring of the lungs, leading to a decline in lung function and eventually death. Because this disease has a heterogeneous disease progression, predictive models could guide clinicians in making decisions about disease management. Some survival analysis methods, such as Cox, seek to rank participants based on their predicted survivability. However, Cox cannot directly output a survival time. DeepHit is a neural network based survival analysis method which predicts the most likely histogram bin of survival time. A disadvantage of DeepHit is that, when training, an error of one year is equivalent to an error of one hundred years. A common problem encountered is that training data is often censored, where the exact time of death is unknown except that it is past a censoring time. Here, a comparison of neural network approaches utilising five different losses is presented. Compared are; ranking based approaches (such as Cox or Cox with a memory bank of previous predictions) and death distribution based approaches (such as DeepHit and likelihood with a uniform or Gaussian distribution to sample censoring times). The input to each model is a single computed tomography volume (plus optionally clinical features) and the output is a survival time. Improvements over previous work includes; a larger model with a learned downsampling, a parameterised activation (which starts linear and becomes non-linear), a softplus output, orthogonal initialisation, an optimiser integrating weight decay, gradient accumulation, and an annealed learning rate. Evaluations used include; mean and relative absolute error, the concordance index, the Brier score, and a visual analysis of Grad-CAM results. Overall, the likelihood models performed the best, with DeepHit a close second and both Cox models a distant last. The uniform likelihood model performed marginally better than the alternative.

articleTitle: Advancement on Combined SPECT and PET Imaging With 3-D Position-Sensitive CdZnTe
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: This work employs 3-D position-sensitive CdZnTe to conduct single photon emission computed tomography (SPECT) via multi-pinhole imaging and positron emission tomography (PET) via line-of-response imaging simultaneously on small animals. The advantages of using CdZnTe detectors over the current instruments for PET and SPECT detectors include the ability to image gamma rays from multiple isotopes simultaneously, can achieve both high detection efficiency and high image resolution in PET modality, and has a high position resolution of about 300 µm in all three dimensions. This energy discrimination capability allows the imager to detect 511 keV coincidence gamma rays used in PET imaging and lower energy gamma rays used in SPECT imaging simultaneously and bin them appropriately. Partial energy depositions from Compton scattering can also be used in PET mode to increase the detection efficiency. This work demonstrates the successful implementation of these methods to reconstruct both PET and SPECT images. Some improvements are still needed to improve image quality.

articleTitle: Effect of Data Mashing on Energy-based Scatter Correction
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: In order to achieve quantitatively reliable images from Positron Emission Tomography (PET), scatter correction is necessary. By studying the energy measured for each event, useful information about the energy spectrum of the events is obtained. This information can be used for scatter correction. Efthimiou et al [1] proposed a method based on energy spectrum of scatter and a moments method to estimate scatter. In this study, we checked the effects of mashing data on scatter estimation based on this model. Mashing is the combination of multiple lines of response into a single one, to reduce the noise. Efthimiou et al. used the Delayed Window method to perform random corrections. In our study, the energy spectrum of random events was estimated experimentally. Our results indicate that mashing was useful for estimating the scatter contribution accurately.

articleTitle: Unsupervised Deep Learning with Self-Validation in Dynamic PET Dose Reduction
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Dose reduction in dynamic PET imaging confers less radiation exposure however increases noise in reconstructed time frames, which leads to higher noise and possible bias in estimated parametric images. Our aim is to develop self-validated unsupervised deep image prior (DIP) denoising techniques, which do not require vast numbers of well-paired images as the training data, for reduced-dose dynamic PET. We propose two methods with the single-frame (SF-DIP) method processing the dynamic images frame by frame and the all-frame (AF-DIP) method denoising all the frames simultaneously to benefit kinetic modeling. Spatiotemporal information of dynamic imaging is incorporated by using the time-weighted composite image as the DIP input. To benefit from the DIP's capability of capturing image features from corrupted images, the 1/10- dose frames are fed into the network as the target. Setting a hard threshold to optimize the DIP may not work well especially in dynamic PET where the uptake pattern of radiotracers and the noise level of frames change considerably during a scan. Here we adopt a self-validation strategy to ensure the robust performance of DIP. The proposed methods are evaluated using dynamic brain SV2A PET imaging data acquired with <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">11</sup>C-UCB-J. Averaged over thirteen FreeSurfer defined regions, the SF-DIP achieves a noise reduction of 69% relative to the reduced-dose data and a bias of 0.1% with respect to the full-count data. The noise reduction and bias for the AF-DIP method are 72% and -1.6%, respectively. Such a noise reduction (bias) translates into 51% (-2.3%) in BP<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">ND</inf> images after kinetic modeling for the SF-DIP and 57% (-0.6%) for the AF-DIP. To conclude, the proposed unsupervised-learning based denoising methods demonstrate better performance in noise reduction while keeping bias smaller compared with other denoising methods. Processing all time frames simultaneously further improves the performance of the unsupervised method in kinetic modeling analysis.

articleTitle: Timing optimization and timing resolution for the AARDVARC chips
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: In this article we describe a series of novel measurements and timing calibrations we performed on the Advanced ASoC Rapid Digitizer, Variable Readout Chip (AARDVARC), a waveform digitizer designed for the readout of signals with very high timing resolution. In the course of the analysis we will demonstrate how a proper timing calibration methodology can provide resolutions below 10ps.

articleTitle: Analytical modeling of the sensitivity of cylindrical PET systems based on bulk materials and metascintillators
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Positron emission tomography scanners are commonly characterized by their photon sensitivity. Scanner design often requires Monte Carlo simulations to probe different geometries and materials. However, the computational load of such simulations can be significant and costly. Furthermore, the applicability of the Monte Carlo approach in optimization loops is limited as each instance, such as source position or scanner dimensions, has to be simulated independently. In this work, Monte Carlo results have been accurately replicated by an analytical model that uses characteristics of the foreseen cylindrical scanner and returns the sensitivity profile following NEMA guidelines. BGO and LYSO bulk materials and several metascintillator scenarios have been used. The mean absolute error (MAE), mean absolute percentage error (MAPE) and standard deviation of the error (SDE) are as low as 0.49%, 2.22% and 0.26% when no energy window is used, respectively. With an energy window applied, the analytical model presents the lowest values of MAE and SDE, with MAPE value being 8.19%. A normalization factor has been used to compensate for the scattered events included in the 350-650 keV window. This work facilitates significantly the development of cylindrical scanners, allowing direct probing of their axial sensitivity profiles.

articleTitle: Deep Learning Model Observers Trained with Human Observer Data from Two-Alternative Forced Choice (2AFC) Trials
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: A model observer, designed to predict human observer responses in a detection task, is an efficient tool to characterize the task-based image quality, and is also useful for designing a system, a protocol, and an image reconstruction algorithm to optimize the detection performance. Conventionally, linear model observers such as channelized Hotelling observer (CHO) have been widely used. Recently, as a new type of model observers, neural networks have been trained to predict human responses in a detection task. Often, two-alternative forced choice (2AFC) experiments are performed, which have a useful property that the percent correct of 2AFC trials is equivalent to the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve under mild conditions. However, it is not straightforward to optimally train a neural network using 2AFC human observer data. In this study, we present a training scheme for a deep learning model observer (DLMO) directly using 2AFC data, where two neural networks with shared weights are trained. We evaluate the training scheme using 2AFC data from 8 human observers including 4 radiologists with PET images generated using simulated lesions with clinical backgrounds. This study shows the DLMO trained directly using the 2AFC data can predict human observer responses more accurately than the other model observers including CHO and a DLMO trained indirectly using the 2AFC data.

articleTitle: Comparison of timing and DOI performance of light-sharing TOF-PET modules with different readout electronics
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Time resolution plays a key role in positron emission tomography (PET) by enhancing the signal-to-noise ratio and ultimately improving the quality of the image. In previous studies, an array of 16 LYSO crystals (measuring 3.1x3.1x15 mm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</sup>) coupled to Hamamatsu S13361-3050AE-04 SiPMs and readout by a custom-made NINO board achieved a coincidence time resolution (CTR) below 160 ps. However, the spatial resolution of the array was affected by parallax error due to the unknown depth of interaction (DOI) of the incident gamma-ray photon. The DOI information was successfully extracted with 3 mm resolution using a light-sharing mechanism and the NINO board. Nevertheless, the board is not commercially available and cannot be scaled to a full PET detector. To address this limitation, this study examines the commercially available TOFPET2 ASIC (application specific integrated circuits) from PETsys Electronics S.A. using light-sharing DOI-capable modules and compares it to the custom-made NINO board. The SiPM array coupled to the matrix of 16 LYSO crystals using TOFPET2 PETsys demonstrates a DOI resolution of 3.6 ± 0.3 mm and a CTR value of 224 ± 3 ps. This approach is scalable to a full PET detector. Finally, potential paths to further improve DOI resolution and CTR are discussed.

articleTitle: TauPETGen: Text-Conditional Tau PET Image Synthesis Based on Latent Diffusion Models
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: In this work, we developed a novel text-guided image synthesis technique that could generate realistic tau PET images from textual descriptions and the subject's MR image. The generated tau PET images have the potential to be used in examining relations between different measures and also increasing the public availability of tau PET datasets. The method was based on latent diffusion models. Both textual descriptions and the subject's MR prior image were utilized as conditions during image generation. The subject's MR image can provide anatomical details, while the text descriptions, such as gender, scan time, cognitive test scores, and amyloid status, can provide further guidance regarding where the tau neurofibrillary tangles might be deposited. Preliminary experimental results based on clinical [18F]MK-6240 datasets demonstrate the feasibility of the proposed method in generating realistic tau PET images at different clinical stages.

articleTitle: Characterization of a 5mm thick CdTe photon-counting detector: Advancing nuclear decommissioning with Compton camera technology
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Following the 2011 Fukushima nuclear disaster, countries such as Switzerland, Spain, and Japan have limited the construction of new nuclear power plants. Nations like Germany are actively phasing out nuclear energy in pursuit of safer alternatives, necessitating innovative nuclear waste management methods. While high-level radioactive waste disposal is heavily regulated, managing low-level radioactive material remains challenging, since its identification and differentiation from non-radioactive material are crucial for recycling and repurposing in other industries. Existing radiation measurement methods, like Geiger-Muller counters, require close proximity to samples, increasing radiative exposure. Also, coded-aperture gamma cameras have limited field-of-view and energy sensitivity, with extended exposure times. Thus, Compton scattering-based systems offer a better alternative for precisely identifying radiation sources and radio nuclei. Pixelated photoncounting detectors, such as the Timepix or Medipix3, are presented on the market. These detectors allowed single event analysis only for low photon fluxes, and also limited time and energy information, making them unsuitable for its use as a single layer Compton system. The new Timepix3 detector allows for studying single events at high fluxes (38Mhits/cm2/s) due to its data-driven output. It also measures the energy and time-of-arrival for each event, providing the required information for reconstructing the location of the source of radiation, based on Compton scattering kinematics, as well as its energy spectrum. This work investigates the usage of a Timepix3 photon-counting detector, bump bonded with a 5mm CdTe sensor, in a single-layer Compton camera configuration. The general characterization of the ensemble is presented, including voltage-leakage current response, bias voltage response, and general imaging, as well as the first images of localization of radioactive sources in a controlled environment.

articleTitle: Improved quantification in end-to-end deep learning PET reconstruction using multi-view attenuation histo-images
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: End-to-end deep learning PET reconstruction is fast and could, in the future, surpass iterative reconstructions in specific cases, such as low-dose imaging. A breakthrough was reached in 2021 using histo-images instead of sinograms as the network input. Histo-images are an alternative format to sinograms that contain the same information but with the geometry of the image, making them much easier to handle by a convolutional neural network. The network input typically consists of a (multi-view) histo-image PET data patch and another attenuation map patch. However, inconsistent bias has been observed in the image and remains unsolved until now. In this work, we show that the leading cause of this bias is the lack of information provided to the network regarding the attenuation of regions outside the patch. This information is indeed necessary for a correct quantification. We propose to replace the attenuation map with a multi-view histo-image of the attenuation correction factors, similar to what is done in the iterative DIRECT framework. Such a histo-image contains the attenuation of each voxel in each direction in the entire lines of response. We propose to use the same angular sampling for the attenuation information and the PET data, as would be done in iterative reconstruction. We achieved a significant improvement in image quantification, with less than 7.7 % relative difference from MLEM in 75 % of slices, compared to 33 % with the previous approach. Our technique also removes some artifacts in the image. The remaining inconsistencies in the quantification could be due to an early stop in the training process and an inaccurate scatter estimation.

articleTitle: Detection of Neutrons in Wide Energy Range with Enhanced Discrimination with the Pixel Detector Timepix3 equipped with Si and SiC sensors
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: We present a practical method based on simplified instrumentation to detect neutrons in wide energy range, from thermal and epithermal energies up to fast neutrons in the ten of MeV range, with high selectivity. We use the hybrid semiconductor pixel detectors Timepix3 equipped with silicon and SiC sensors together with a thermal and fast neutron mask. We exploit the detector high granularity, per-pixel spectral response and high-resolution particle tracking response to analyze and characterize the micro-scale spectral tracks of single particles produced in the detector. This allows to resolve and examine detection channels of neutron inducted interactions with discrimination of background and unwanted events such as electron and gamma ray events. Together with extensive calibrations including other radiations (X rays, gamma ray, electrons) the resolving power of neutron induced tracks can be enhanced. Response matrices of the detector were derived from calibrations in well-defined neutron fields of varying energy including mono-energetic neutrons of tunable energy in several spectral regions produced at the Van-de-Graaff accelerator of the IEAP CTU Prague. The use of different sensors, namely Si and SiC, bump-bonded on the Timepix3 ASIC chip, enable to examine and selectively identify neutron induced interactions and detection channels in the detector. Results will be shown including detection efficiency, which is overall below 1 %, at selected neutron energies. The goal and advantage is to provide a compact neutron detector of enhanced selectivity, operated at room temperature and readout by integrated electronics of the MiniPIX-Timepix3 radiation camera (mass < 100 g, size < 10 cm, power consumption < 2 W).

articleTitle: Towards a standard for PET raw data
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: As the capabilities of computer hardware and software progresses, the importance of standardized data is becoming more relevant. While DICOM is widely used as a standard for PET images, no agreed format exists for PET raw data. In addition, all current vendor formats differ, to accommodate different architectures and processing strategies.An international working group comprised of PET imaging experts from academia and industry was formed in 2022 to propose a new standard format. Efforts include establishing the key informational elements to include in the standard, data container formats, and integration initiatives. An important feature of the proposal is the use of a meta-language (called Yardl) for defining data structure and protocols for accessing, transferring, and storing data, allowing logical separation of data elements and container formats. All portions of the format, tools for accessing the data in the standardized format, and example data will be made open source and publicly available.In this work, we will provide a status report of the progress of the working group. The effort is ongoing, and we welcome interest, feedback, and support from the greater community. We hope that this standard will facilitate a new paradigm for PET innovation, including new opportunities for inter-scanner and inter-vendor harmonization and AI applications, and aide in the advancement of novel PET applications and analysis tools.

articleTitle: First steps towards in-system applicability of a novel PET timing calibration method reaching sub-200 ps CTR
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: TOF-PET is an active research area affecting nearly all parts of a PET system, from detector developments to novel reconstruction algorithms. However, to profit from the TOF information in the PET image, sufficient good Coincidence Time Resolution (CTR) must be achieved on detector level. In recent works, we developed and proposed a calibration method to improve PET detectors’ timing capabilities by using a residual physics-inspired machine learning approach. By moving a <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">22</sup>Na source to several positions between two facing detectors and collecting coincidences, we introduce TOF domain knowledge to the model due to the physics-guided data generation. After rough data corrections, the model can be trained on the residual timing data. In our proof-of-concept study, we used a fine spatial sampling which would result in longish calibration times for complete PET systems. In this work, we demonstrate that the procedure can be accelerated by up to a factor of four without worsening the achievable performance and still obeying physical principles. In our measurement, we used two clinically relevant PET detectors with a height of 19 mm coupled to a digital SiPM-tile. One detector is based on a semi-monolithic design comprising eight LYSO slabs, each with a base area of 3.9 mm × 31.9 mm. The other detector used a one-to-one coupled design, with each of the 8 × 8 segments having a pitch of 4 mm. In our experiment we achieved up to 198 ps (185 ps) CTR for an energy range of 300 keV to 700 keV (450 keV to 550 keV) without applying any filter on the light distribution.

articleTitle: Advances in Calibration and Data-Processing for a clinical semi-monolithic DOI-capable PET Detector reaching sub-200 ps Timing Resolution
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Total- and Whole-Body-PET scanners utilize numerous detectors introducing further challenges besides spatial, energy, and time resolution, such as fast calibration and cost-efficiency. Semi-monolithic detectors (called slabs) combine the advantages of pixelated and monolithic scintillators, providing intrinsic depth-of-interaction (DOI) capabilities, high density of optical photons as well as reduced dead time at a competitive cost compared to classical segmented arrays. Here, we present recent advances made in the different aspects of detector calibration and data processing. An array of 8 monolithic LYSO slabs of dimensions 3.9 x 32 x 19 mm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</sup> was coupled to a 64-channel photosensor array based on digital SiPMs (DPC 3200-22-44). Positioning calibration was performed using the supervised ML algorithm gradient tree boosting (GTB) and a fan beam collimator with multiple simultaneous irradiations allowing for fast calibration routines. The timing calibration includes an analytical correction of the detector time skews following GTB-based improvements. We achieved a spatial resolution in terms of mean absolute error (MAE) of 1.22 mm in planar and 1.86 mm in DOI direction, a coincidence resolution time (CRT) of 186 ps, and an energy resolution of 11.3%. The performance is better than or comparable to currently established clinical detectors following a segmented design concept. We put a special focus on the easy and fast applicability of the calibration methods to demonstrate a pathway for the broad translation of slab-based detectors into clinical PET systems.

articleTitle: Design and Development of the Human Dynamic NeuroChemical Connectome Scanner
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: The Human Dynamic NeuroChemical Connectome will consist of a High Spatio-Temporal Resolution brain-dedicated PET (HSTR-BrainPET) scanner integrated with a 7T MRI system. The primary goal is to build a PET camera with an order of magnitude higher sensitivity than existing MR-compatible PET devices to allow investigators to merge seamlessly the dynamic functional capabilities of both PET and functional MRI on a comparable time scale. The HSTR-BrainPET will maximize geometric efficiency (~70% solid-angle coverage) by arranging 872 detector modules around a sphere with 32 cm inner diameter. Each module will consist of a 10×10 array of 1.6×1.6×26 mm LSO crystals coupled to a 4×4 multi-photon pixel-counter with 4×4 mm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sup> pixels. A 380µm light guide applied to the entry face will allow depth-dependent light sharing. The readout electronics consist of customized ASIC signal processing boards (218) and MR-side HUB boards (28) positioned in the MR scanner and PC-side HUB boards (28) located in the equipment room and connected through optical fibers. Here, we describe the results of Monte Carlo simulations that showed the sensitivity will be ~25% (before accounting for the TOF sensitivity amplifier effect) and the count rate performance will be excellent. We also provide an update on the design and development of all the components of the HSTR-BrainPET, including the detector modules, readout electronics, multi-functional gantry that will house the LSO crystal arrays and electronics, distribute the cooling channels and provide electromagnetic shielding.

articleTitle: ReconU-Net: Direct PET Image Reconstruction Using Back Projection-induced Skip Connection
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Direct positron emission tomography (PET) image reconstruction methods using convolutional neural networks (CNNs) have attracted increasing attention for the next generation of PET image reconstruction. These CNN-based direct reconstruction methods generate good reconstructed images from sinograms. However, it is difficult to obtain an accurate inverse transformation from sinograms to reconstructed images using a data-driven approach, and these direct reconstruction methods may produce finer "false" PET images with different structures from the ground truth. In this study, we propose a novel back projection-induced U-Net shape architecture, called ReconU-Net, for direct PET image reconstruction. The ReconU-Net guides the connections of the features from the encoder, expressed in sinogram space, to the decoder, expressed in the reconstructed image space by back-projection operations in the skip connection. Hence, the proposed ReconU-Net architecture can retain accurate spatial information from the input sinograms, according to the physical model. We generated and trained the proposed ReconU-Net with Monte Carlo simulation data from the BrainWeb phantom and tested it using simulation data and real brain PET data. Compared with the maximum likelihood expectation maximization and the DeepPET, the proposed ReconU-Net method outperforms the reconstruction performance in peak signal-to-noise ratio and can generate finer "true" PET images. In addition, the proposed ReconU-Net method successfully reconstructed the real brain PET data. Therefore, we concluded that the proposed ReconU-Net architecture is a practical solution for CNN-based direct PET image reconstruction.

articleTitle: Unpaired PET image enhancement using an improved cycle consistent adversarial network
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: With the improvement of hardware technology, novel scanners such as uEXPLORER obtain significantly higher image quality than conventional scanners, but they have yet to be widespread. In addition, due to the limitations of scanning time and radiotracer dose, the PET images obtained in primary hospitals usually contains a lot of noise, which has an impact on quantitative medical analysis and diagnostic accuracy. It is of great interest to use image enhancement methods to enable primary hospitals to obtain PET images of comparable quality to the novel scanners. Obviously, in this task, we are unable to construct paired training sets, which makes common deep-learning-based methods inapplicable.To overcome this challenge, we propose to use a cycle consistent generative adversarial network (CycleGAN) that does not require paired data to achieve PET image enhancement. In addition, we add correlation coefficient loss and image prior loss to the original CycleGAN model to directly constrain the structural consistency between the generated and input images. When using the proposed model for PET image enhancement, the high-quality image dataset acquired from the novel scanners is fixed as the basic high-quality training set. Since the low-and high-quality images can be unpaired, any low-quality PET images from different institutions that require enhancement can be input into the network as the low-quality set. After training, the generator can convert low-quality images into PET images with comparable image quality to that of the novel scanners. The results show that the proposed method outperforms NLM, BM3D, and DIP. Moreover, the proposed method performs better than the supervised RED-CNN and CycleGAN when implemented on a local hospital dataset.

articleTitle: Development of SiC-based Neutron Detector Heads for High Radiation Environments
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: The development of SiC-based neutron detector heads are designed for high radiation environments, such as the Primary Containment Vessels (PCVs) at the Fukushima Daichi Nuclear Power Plant. The detectors utilise enriched B10 as a conversion layer, with Geant4 simulations used to optimise the efficiency for neutron capture and reduce self-attenuation losses. The SiC diodes are electrically thinned for excellent gamma rejection. Each detector head contains up to two hundred eighty-eight sensors in various geometric configurations for maximum detection area. The modular construction allows for reconfiguration for deployment in a range of mixed neutron gamma fields. Preamplifier and amplifier circuits were designed for minimal noise and charge pile-up; the readout chain combines signals from multiple sensors for transmission via a single long coaxial cable. Testing demonstrated reliable detection of neutrons (<10nv) in gamma environments higher than sixty sieverts per hour, indicating SiC diodes as suitable detectors for neutron radiation in high gamma radiation backgrounds.

articleTitle: 2D Cylindrical Time-Encoded Imager Design
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Cylindrical time-encoded imaging allows for a non-pixelated detector to achieve imaging capabilities by surrounding it with a rotating coded aperture mask. The design of a 2D cylindrical time-encoded imager requires extensive simulation. An input-generating code for MCNP was written to simulate cylindrical coded aperture masks. Simulations of 1D time-encoded coded aperture masks are utilized for parameter selection and applied to a 2D imager. Design parameters are investigated for the trade-offs of geometric angular resolution, collimation, and weight. Pixel pitch, one of the parameters of focus, uses a different coded aperture mask pattern for each pitch. The Great Deluge Algorithm ensures each of these mask patterns has good imaging capability. MCNP6.2 simulations of a 35 x 1 uniformly redundant array and a 41 x 1 modified uniformly redundant array validate the geometry generating code’s ability to produce accurate input geometries for both 1D and subsequently 2D cylindrical time-encoded imaging simulations.

articleTitle: Towards an Analog Neural Network ASIC (ANNA) for Position Reconstruction in Anger Cameras
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: We present an analog ASIC implementing a neural network (NN) in charge domain for estimating the position of interaction of gamma rays in Anger Cameras. The multiplyand-accumulate (MAC) operations are performed by means of programmable switched-capacitor crossbar arrays. The analog NN consists of 64 input nodes receiving the SiPM signals, two hidden layers of 20 neurons each, and two outputs nodes corresponding to the inference of the x and y position of interaction. The network parameters (weights and biases) are obtained with an off-line training, using a reference dataset for which the 2D position of interaction of the events is known. To estimate the performance of the ASIC, which is currently in the final design phase and will be soon submitted for production, its positioning capabilities were tested using two different datasets. In both cases, the network parameters are quantized with 5-bit precision to emulate computations in a CMOS process. The first test was performed using the data obtained with a Monte Carlo simulation of a 51 mm×51 mm×10 mm LYSO scintillator read out by an 8×8 array of SiPMs: from high-level MATLAB simulations, consistent with ASIC topology and operations, the NN achieves a spatial resolution of 1.22 mm FWHM/1.66 mm MAE. The second test was performed using experimental data obtained with a PET detector based on 32 mm×32 mm×22 mm LYSO:Ce scintillator. For this detector, we report a comparison of the achieved spatial resolution with respect to a k nearest neighbour (k-NN) method, which shows that the NN achieves comparable results.

articleTitle: Deep Learning Image Denoising in PET: Quantitative Impact on Kinetic Modeling and Clinical Metrics
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: The increased sensitivity exhibited by long axial field-of-view (LAFOV) PET systems allows measurement of tracer kinetics across multiple organs and lesions at reduced doses and/or scan times. This flexibility has been utilized to perform dual-tracer imaging which in oncology offers complementary quantification about metabolic tumor processes. Yet to make dual-tracer studies more suitable for clinical practice, these scan protocols should be pushed towards lower injection doses and shorter scan times, but reduced count statistics inherently result in noisier PET images. Many have previously shown promising denoising performance of deep learning (DL) methods for low count PET images acquired at a single (static) late time point. However, only a few studies have investigated the use of DL to denoise dynamic PET data and the impact on kinetic modeling of parametric estimates. We first trained a DL algorithm (U-Net) with low-to-high count static <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">18</sup>F-FDG datasets and evaluated its performance using noise and clinical metrics. We next assessed the transferability of this pre-trained DL model for frame-by-frame image denoising of dynamic <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">18</sup>F-FGln and looked at the effect of such DL-based denoising on estimations of the volume of distribution of <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">18</sup>F-FGln (kinetic parameter to quantify glutamine pool size). This work provides the foundation for our next investigations into the use of DL for optimizing scan protocols to make dual-tracer studies more practical, and more accurate.

articleTitle: Excess noise and spectra distortion in pulsed-reset charge sensitive amplifiers due to non-stationary gain: analytical model and Monte Carlo simulations
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: An analytical model is developed to quantitatively account for non-stationary gain effects [1] present in energy-resolved detector readout systems using charge sensitive amplifiers (CSA) [2] with pulsed-reset architecture [3]. The model is derived starting from a piece wise linear (PWL) approximation of the gain error distribution within the CSA output voltage swing, and it is validated both by Monte Carlo simulations and experimental measurements on high energy-resolution spectroscopic systems employing Silicon Drift Detectors (SDDs) and pulsed-reset low noise CSAs. The proposed model can be easily generalized to provide front-end designers a precise estimation of the CSA response within its output voltage swing or, in turn, to asses the most appropriate reset threshold for high energy-resolution detector readout.

articleTitle: New SDD arrays for the SIDDHARTA-2 experiment
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: This paper reports on the development of novel 2×4 monolithic Silicon Drift Detector (SDD) arrays with a thickness of 1 mm, carried out in the context of the SIDDHARTA-2 experiment, representing an advancement in terms of detection efficiency over the presently adopted 450 μm thick detectors. The chip contains eight square SDD cells with an active area of 8 × 8 mm2 each and has a total dimension of 20 mm × 36 mm. Besides an optimization of the sensor design for the thicker substrate, this new version of the SDD array is characterized by the introduction of an additional electrode on the entrance window, which should reduce the charge sharing between pixels. The paper also describes the development of a detection module based on a stacked structure involving two SDDs placed atop each other. This solution aims to further increase the detection efficiency of the system without acting on the substrate thickness of the SDD. The results from the spectroscopic characterization of these new detectors, and the implementation and characterization of the stacked SDDs module will be presented at the conference.

articleTitle: Development of CoRDIA: An Imaging Detector for Next-Generation Synchrotron Rings and Free Electron Lasers
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: The current or planned upgrades of most radiation sources – for synchrotron rings towards the diffraction limit, and for Free Electron Lasers towards faster continuous operation at a few 100 kHz, require a new generation of detectors to profit from this step.The acronym CoRDIA stands for Continuous Readout Digitising Imager Array, and is a hybrid pixel detector development targeted on these next-generation synchrotron sources and Free Electron Lasers. Serving the latter it builds upon the concept of the AGIPD detector, employing a charge sensitive preamplifier with adaptive gain switching. The further signal path comprises of a Correlated Double Sampling stage and an Analogue to Digital Converter (ADC) with 11 bit resolution, serving a sub array of 16 pixels. 128 ADCs connect to a multi-gigabit serial link to drive the images off chip. For this part CoRDIA adopts the implementation on the Timepix4 chip by Nikhef. An Application Specific Integrated Circuit with 128 x 128 pixels will implement 8 of the previously described blocks. Since the links conform to industry standards (IEEE 802.3ae), the subsequent data acquisition can be based on commercial components (e.g. Field Programmable Gate Array cards connected via multi-fibre optical links).Performance targets are a continuous frame rate of ≈150 kHz, and singe-photon sensitivity at ≪12 keV, and a dynamic range of >10<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">4</sup> photons (@ 12 keV) with a silicon sensor, which could be extended using active sensors or sensors from "high-Z" materials.

articleTitle: TlBr Films for Hard X-Ray Imaging
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Semiconductor X-ray detector technology currently relies on the use of a silicon wafer, or a relatively thin CdTe crystal, bump bonded to their respective readout platform. Although the use of CdTe extends the energy range of these detectors beyond that of silicon, a further increase in energy performance is highly desirable. In this paper, we present preliminary results on thallium bromide (TlBr) films coupled to two readout chips, or application-specific integrated circuits (ASICs). TlBr is an attractive material for hard X-ray imaging due to its high atomic number and high density. Additionally, TlBr has a relatively low melting point (460 °C), melts congruently, and has a simple cubic crystal structure.

articleTitle: Preliminary results of the performance characteristics for the new digital uMI Panorama GS PET/CT system
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: The new digital uMI Panorama GS PET/CT system, which is designed with the uMI Panorama platform, consists of three independent detector units and each unit is equipped with 34×21 uExcel UDP(ultra dynamic platform) detector modules. The 21 modules along axial direction covers ~150cm FOV, forming a long axial field-of-view (LAFOV) scanner. The compact detector design with dedicated multi-channel ASIC, the full coincidence acquision and steady water cooling system guarantees the outstanding system performances. In this study, the system was evaluated based on the NEMA NU 2-2018 standard. The results demonstrates that the system has a spatial resolution of ~2.9 mm full width at half maximum (FWHM) at 1 cm offset of the transaxial center for both the 1/8 and 1/2 axial FOV. Moreover, the sensitivity of the 70cm and 200cm lines sources at the transaxial FOV were measured to be ~180 kcps/MBq and ~90 kcps/MBq, respectively. A peak NECR of 3075.24 kcps at 53.76 kBq/ml with scatter fraction of around 30% was observed, and a maximum relative count rate error among all slices was less than 4.5% at the activity concentration below NECR peak activity. Regarding the NEMA IQ phantom with 4:1 sphere-to-background ratio, the image contrast recovery ranges from 70.27% to 94.46% and background variability varies form 1.82% to 1.55% for the six hot spheres. Meanwhile, the phantom with higher sphere-to-background ratio (8:1) achieves higher CRC, ranging from 83.66% to 99.87%. Two mini-Deluxe phantom images were shown and the 1.4 mm rods, which approaches the theoretically resolution limit, was able to be partially disentangled, revealing excellent lesion detectability.

articleTitle: A New Dual-Injection Protocol for Reduced Scanning-Time in Dynamic Whole-Body PET
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: We previously presented a dual injection protocol for dynamic whole-body (DWB) PET using multi-bed multi-pass acquisition. The purpose was to allow for a reduced scanning time, while still providing accurate parametric images for irreversible tracers, such as [<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">18</sup>F]-FDG. The protocol consisted of a DWB scan with a delayed start, followed by a standard SUV scan. A 2<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">nd</sup> injection (~10% of the dose) was given during the dynamic scan for estimating the initial part of the input function. However, this protocol caused complications to the kinetic modelling as well as possible effects of the 2<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">nd</sup> injection on the SUV scan. We therefore now propose an alternative protocol, with the 2<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">nd</sup> injection after the SUV scan. PET data were simulated based on the XCAT phantom, Poisson noise was added, and images were reconstructed with OSEM. The input function was obtained from the LV of the heart and fitted with an analytical function. The area under the curve (AUC, 0-60 min) was calculated and the effect of different injection fractions and scan start-times were investigated. A patient study was also performed, with data acquisition from 0 to 75 min p.i. A 2<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">nd</sup> injection (9%) was given after 70 min. The input function was estimated using different data sub-sets and the AUC was compared with the gold standard. The simulation results showed that a 2<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">nd</sup> injection fraction of 10% and a scan start-time of 30 min gave accurate results, while smaller fraction or later start gave increased bias and variance. The results of the patient study were in general agreement with the simulation results, with a bias of ~2.7% for scan start times of 13-43 min and 5.1% at 50 min p.i. In conclusion, we found that a scanning protocol with a late start and a second injection at the end is a practical way to obtain accurate whole-body parametric PET images with a reduced scanning time.

articleTitle: Characterization of a state-of-the-art clinical detector block with TOFPET2 ASIC readout
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: The Biograph Vision, developed by Siemens Healthineers, is regarded as the gold standard for time-of-flight (TOF) performance in clinical positron emission tomography (PET) imaging. When comparing new multi-channel readout circuits, it is essential to account for potential disparities in material and assembly of custom detector blocks. This ensures that the sole influence of readout electronics on timing performance can be accurately assessed. In this context, we evaluate the TOFPET2 ASIC, designed by PETsys Electronics S.A., in conjunction with a Biograph Vision detector block. We examine the coincidence time resolution (CTR) and energy resolution. Furthermore we evaluated the scintillator for DOI capabailities, not available in the clinical product, using the channel-individual readout capabilities.

articleTitle: Implementation and Evaluation of a 3D-dependend Energy-Calibration Algorithm, including Interpolation Methods for missing read-out Channels
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: In PET, a clear discrimination of scattered events to non-scattered events is crucial to reconstruct an image with high signal to noise ratio. Therefore, a precise energy estimation for all detected gamma interactions is necessary. In particular, light sharing detectors profit from 3D-dependend energy calibration. This work presents a generic position-dependent energy calibration algorithm exemplary for light sharing detector composed out of eight monolithic LYSO slabs read out by digital SiPMs (DPC 3200-22, PDPC). The algorithm splits the whole scintillation volume into virtual sub-volumes (voxel) and performs an energy calibration for each voxel individually. All 16 DPCs are self-triggering, so it is possible for one gamma interaction to not trigger all DPC located beneath the hit slab. The calibration step only considers events that had a full readout. For events with missing channel information, the missing energy contribution needs to be accounted for. This work presents approaches based on an analytical average light distribution and k-Nearest-Neighbor (kNN) to impute these on voxel level. The overall energy resolution of the uncalibrated photon-spectrum was 13.5%, the presented algorithm improves that to close to 11% in the energy spectrum by applying an 8x13x5 voxelization and using the kNN-interpolation method on the 5% of gamma interactions that have partially missing channel information.

articleTitle: Microliter in vivo Brain PET Imaging with the Ultra-High Resolution (UHR) Scanner
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Brain PET imaging has proven useful for the characterization and diagnosis of various neurological diseases, but its potential has yet to be fully realized due to the typical poor spatial resolution of current PET scanners. To overcome this limitation, we developed the Ultra-High Resolution (UHR) brain PET scanner achieving 2 µL volumetric spatial resolution, a remarkable feature promising visualization and quantification of small brain structures such as the brainstem nuclei, which previously could hardly be resolved. Hence, the purpose of this study was to assess the capabilities of the UHR scanner to detect and accurately quantify radiotracer uptake in these important small structures of the human brain. Patients prescribed with a <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">18</sup>F-FDG PET scan underwent their medical examination on a Discovery MI clinical scanner followed by a brain scan on the UHR. Images from both scanners were compared based on relative SUV values, structures delineation and overall image quality. Striking differences were observed as millimetric-sized structures like brainstem nuclei and cortical gyri and sulci were clearly distinguishable on the UHR image and barely visible with the Discovery MI. These results indicate that the UHR scanner is a cutting-edge tool for brain imaging achieving a spatial resolution comparable to top-of-the-line preclinical scanners.

articleTitle: Simulation study on functional images to optimize radiographic condition using energy resolving photon counting detector
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Energy Resolving Photon Counting Detectors (ERPCD) are attracting attention as novel detectors having the potential to generate functional images. Since ERPCD can detect individual X-ray photons with energy discrimination, the differences in attenuations due to different X-ray energies can be analyzed. In previous studies, algorithms for determining effective atomic number (Z<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">eff</inf>), soft-tissue and bone images were developed. A current research topic related to deriving accurate functional images is optimizing imaging conditions. The purpose of this study is to derive the optimal imaging conditions to improve the performance of ERPCD. In this study, we proposed the availability of high tube voltage imaging based on the simulation study. First, we developed an in-house program to process X-ray images using Mathematica programming software. Second, using our program, the optimal imaging conditions were determined. Then, a demonstration of X-ray images using a digital phantom of the lumber spine was performed to mimic clinical conditions. In our program, the following calculations were taken into consideration: (1) attenuation in objects, (2) actual detector response, and (3) statistical fluctuation. The virtual phantoms of aluminum and polymethylmethacrylate (PMMA) had mass thicknesses of 0.1–80 g/cm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sup>. The total number of photons was set to correspond to an entrance surface dose of 0.4 mGy, which is the diagnostic reference level (DRL). Under higher tube voltage conditions such as 120 kV, Z<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">eff</inf> values were derived in a wide range of thicknesses, and good-quality functional images could be obtained. We believe that our Z<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">eff</inf> algorithm can be applied to diagnostic imaging such as jawbone and lumber spine. It is expected that functional images using ERPCD will add value to medical diagnosis.

articleTitle: Novel designs of ZnS:Ag/6LiF Wavelength Shifting Fibre Neutron Detectors for neutron reflectometers and diffractometers
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Scintillator detectors using ZnS:Ag/<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">6</sup>LiF coupled to wavelength shifting fibre (WLSF) are employed at several neutron scattering facilities, including J-PARC, SNS, ISIS and CSNS. Despite their historically excellent performance, several advancements can be made to suit current and future scientific requirements. ISIS is currently developing ZnS:Ag/<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">6</sup>LiF WLSF scintillator detectors for various neutron scattering applications by exploiting the flexibility, scalability, high performance, and cost effectiveness of these detectors.Two different detectors will be presented in this work for two neutron scattering techniques: neutron reflectometry and single crystal diffraction. The design improvements will be described, highlighting the difference between the two and how they address the requirements set by the two applications. Results of neutron measurements performed with an Am/Be source and on ISIS beam lines will be discussed for both detectors.To take advantage of the increased flux expected at ISIS reflectometers, a modular, position sensitive detector was developed using ZnS:Ag/<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">6</sup>LiF scintillator and a unique fibre coding method . Sub-millimetre position sensitivity, high counting rate capability (on the order of kHz per detector pixel) and large area coverage were achieved.A 2-dimensional detector with double scintillator-fibre layer was developed for single crystal neutron diffraction. Each layer consists of two orthogonal fibre planes placed between two scintillator sheets. The new design leads to about a factor 5 increase in detection efficiency with respect to the current clear fibre detectors installed on the SXD single crystal diffractometer at ISIS. The instrument will be upgraded by replacing all modules with the new double layer ZnS:Ag/<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">6</sup>LiF detectors.The improved performance of these detectors will extend the capability of the science programme and paves the way to future instrument upgrades at ISIS.

articleTitle: Joint Estimation of Motion and Image Data for Motion Correction in PET-MRI
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Respiratory motion correction of MR and PET is a topic of active research. For motion compensation of MR as well as PET data, MR data-driven motion estimation has been proven very useful.Depending on the protocol used and acquisition time available, MR data may suffer from undersampling artifacts that may hamper with the quality of the estimated motion. In this work, we present a method for joint reconstruction and motion estimation of gated MR data based on the alternating direction method of multipliers. The method is evaluated based on reconstruction of simulated data using the XCAT phantom showing that the proposed method yields good motion-corrected results and motion estimates on real-istic simulated MR data - even for high levels of undersampling.

articleTitle: Maximum-likelihood estimation of scatter scaling for PET-enabled dual-energy CT
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: PET-enabled dual-energy (DE) CT was recently proposed to enable integrated PET and DECT imaging on conventional PET/CT scanners without requiring a second x-ray CT scan. In this method, a 511 keV gamma-ray CT is reconstructed from time-of-flight PET emission data. Joint estimation methods such as the maximum-likelihood attenuation and activity (MLAA) or kernel MLAA algorithms can be applied for this purpose. The gamma-ray CT image is then combined with x-ray CT to obtain a DECT image pair. Quantitative reconstruction of gamma-ray CT image requires accurate correction of scatter events in measured emission data. Commonly used scatter correction methods require the determination of a multiplicative scaling factor. Existing methods for scatter scaling are mainly developed for reconstruction of PET activity images. In this work, we develop scatter scaling for improving PET-enabled DECT. We extended the kernel MLAA algorithm to jointly estimate the scatter scaling from the emission data. Simulation results indicate the proposed method can improve image quality of multi-material decomposition in PET-enabled DECT imaging.

articleTitle: Microchannel Plates with Quad Timepix3 Detector (MCP/TPX3) for Time-of-Flight Neutron Imaging
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Microchannel plates (MCPs) with a quad Timepix3 readout have emerged as a promising neutron imaging camera for neutron imaging with time-of-flight (TOF) capability. The detector comprises a pair of chevron-stacked MCPs coupled to a quad Timepix3 readout in a vacuum enclosure. To make the detector neutron-sensitive, one of the MCPs is doped with neutron absorbers such as <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">10</sup>B and <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">nat</sup>Gd. The Timepix3 readout is data-driven and zero-suppressed readout. Each Timepix3 chip has 256 × 256 pixels, and each pixel size is 55 × 55 μm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sup>. It can record the time-of-arrival and time-over-threshold information of every hit in a pixel simultaneously, up to 80 Mhits/s per chip. The timestamping of each hit enables the detector to do TOF imaging, which offers significant advantages over traditional neutron imaging. The ToF capability allows the detector to perform more advanced energy- resolved neutron imaging techniques. In this work, we present a neutron imaging camera capable of TOF imaging with a sub-55 μm spatial resolution and high rate capability. The detector demonstrated a rate capability of ≤ 120 Mhits/s, a neutron efficiency of ≥ 30% at 4.2A°,sub-μs time resolution for thermal and cold neutrons, a gamma sensitivity of ≤ 10<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">−2</sup> and an active area of 28.2 × 28.2 mm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sup>. The result of a Bragg-edge imaging using nickel powder is presented.

articleTitle: Exploration of X-ray Fluorescence Emission Tomography for Imaging Micro-Scintillators used in Remote Optogenetics Application
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Optogenetics is a biological technique which aims to modulate the neuronal activities of target cells through activation of light-sensitive proteins. X-ray induced optogenetics is an approach to generate visible light in deep tissues using radioluminescence of scintillating micro-particles through x-ray irradiation. The increase in the penetration depth, reduction in tissue heating, and absence of invasive surgical procedure are the major advantages of x-ray induced optogenetic approach. Previous studies have shown that Ce:GAGG (Ce: Gd<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</inf>Al<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf>Ga<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</inf>O<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">12</inf>) scintillating particles/crystals are biocompatible and non-cytotoxic with one of the brightest light yield which makes them a suitable candidate for X-Optogenetics. In this study, we demonstrate the feasibility of imaging Ce:GAGG micro-scintillating particles in mouse brain and gut region using our full-ring benchtop x-ray fluorescence emission tomography (XFET) system. Our preliminary experimental studies with pulverized Ce:GAGG micro-particles demonstrate an excellent detection limit of 14 mg in a small animal-sized phantom. We would further explore the improvement in signal-to-noise ratio and detection limit for remote optogenetic application by preparing a GEANT4 model of the multi-slit XFET system and simulating for different source configurations and detection angles.

articleTitle: FastIC ASIC readout performance for Cherenkov based TOF-PET imaging
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: The emerging field of ultra-fast timing has enormous potential in high-energy physics, nuclear medicine, and imaging, and is driving advances in detector and readout electronics. To achieve improved time resolution, significant efforts have been devoted to this field, resulting in impressive coincidence time resolution (CTR) values for silicon photomultiplier (SiPM) and scintillator crystals using state-of-the-art high-frequency (HF) readout. However, scaling this readout method for system-level applications is not yet feasible, hence requiring dedicated application-specific integrated circuits (ASICs). In this study, we evaluate the performance of the FastIC, an 8-channel readout ASIC suitable for TOP-PET application, in terms of CTR. The study employs Cherenkov photons produced in bismuth germanium oxide (BGO) scintillator crystals and novel SiPMs with metal-trenching. We obtain CTR values of 257±5 ps and 152±4 ps, respectively, for 2x2x20mm³ and 2x2x3mm³ BGO crystals using HF readout as a reference, with minimal electronic interference, by exploiting the full potential of SiPMs with metal trenching. In comparison, the CTR values obtained using the FastIC for the same crystals were 490±3 ps and 330±4 ps, respectively. We also assess the limits of the FastIC and suggest areas for further improvements.

articleTitle: Design and Development of AC-LGAD Detectors for Electron-Ion Collider
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: AC-coupled Low-Gain Avalanche Diode (AC-LGAD) is a new type of silicon sensors that can simultaneously provide precision timing and spatial measurements for charged particles. Its first large scale application will be at the Electron Ion Collider (EIC), a new flagship facility for nuclear physics studies to be built at Brookhaven National Laboratory (BNL) before 2032. The key components of AC-LGAD detector systems including AC-LGAD sensors, front-end readout ASICs, and low mass supporting structures are under development to meet the stringent requirements by the EIC program including a 20-30 ps timing resolution and 20-30 μm spatial resolution, as well as a low material budget of 1-4% radiation length per detector layer. We will present the design and development of key components of the AC-LGAD detectors for the EIC experiment. The results and experience can help guide future work on AC-LGAD detectors at other accelerator facilities, e.g., the High Luminosity Large Hadron Collider (HL-LHC) and the Future Circular Collider (FCC).

articleTitle: Investigating the benefit of scattering in 2D-3D rigid registration using a single proton radiography
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: The aim of the study is to explore whether proton scattering can aid to compensate rigid deformations of the treatment planning image (moving) by utilizing a single in-room proton radiograph (pRad; static) in a 2D-3D registration framework. A clinical head and neck x-ray CT is embedded in Monte Carlo (MC) to simulate pRads based on integration mode and single particle tracking detectors. We also consider the ideal projections in list mode where the MC data are replaced with forward projection along the most likely path of the proton trajectory.Misalignments were randomly sampled (1000-fold) to study the accuracy of the single view rigid registration. The statistical analysis shows that list mode outperforms integration mode especially when compensating the motion along the projection direction. Thereby, proton scattering does provide additional information, however only for ideal projections. To achieve the same for more realistic noisy data, more accurate assessment of scattering as well as dedicated data selection is necessary to achieve the required accuracy for clinical applications.

articleTitle: Physical Properties and Detector Response of (Cd,Mn)Te and (Cd,Mn)(Te,Se) Crystals
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: The use of semi-insulating compounds based on (Cd,Mn)Te with and without Se as materials for room temperature X-ray and gamma-ray detectors was investigated. These two Bridgman-grown compounds were compared for their crystal structure, mechanical and optical properties and ability to detect X and gamma radiation. The influence of annealing in Cd or Se vapors on crystal properties was also examined. The addition of selenium to (Cd,Mn)Te has been shown to increase the hardness of the compound. Low-temperature photoluminescence studies revealed the presence of defect states, with both materials exhibiting two donor-acceptor pair transitions (DAP) at different energy levels. The (Cd,Mn)Te detector was found to have a better response than the (Cd,Mn)(Te,Se) detector. The latter one exhibited poor response, probably due to the presence of a deep trap involved in the luminescence of DAP<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">d</sup>, which cannot be eliminated by annealing. This study shows that (Cd,Mn)Te is a more promising material for use in X-ray and gamma-ray detectors.

articleTitle: Deep learning-based automated segmentation of liver and tumors on CT arterial portography and hepatic arteriography for Y-90 radioembolization
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Y-90 radioembolization (RE) is an effective treatment for inoperable liver tumors. Pre-treatment planning using Tc-99m MAA requires segmentation of normal liver (NL), lungs and tumors. Deep learning (DL)-based automatic segmentations have been developed for liver tumor segmentation usually based on the portal phase contrast CT. However, CT arterial portography (CTAP) and CT hepatic arteriography (CTHA) are essential for RE to provide more structural and blood supply information of tumors. This study aims to develop a DL-based method for automatic NL and tumor segmentation using both CTAP and CTHA images for Y-90 RE treatment planning. Tc-99m-MAA SPECT/CT, CTAP and CTHA images of 48 patients were retrospectively collected. NL and tumor maps were provided as the gold standard. A self-adapting framework, nnU-Net, with 6-fold cross-validation was performed to evaluate 4 training strategies: (1) Att-nnUNet<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">CTAP+CTHA</inf>: nnU-Net with attention-gate trained on CTAP and CTHA; (2) nnUNet<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">CTAP+CTHA</inf>: nnU-Net trained on CTAP and CTHA; (3) Att-nnUNet<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">CTAP</inf>: nnU-Net with attention-gate trained on CTAP; and (4) nnUNet<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">CTAP</inf>: nnUNet trained on CTAP. The segmentation performance was evaluated using Dice. The DL-segmented tumor and NL maps were applied to the corresponding SPECT for calculating the tumor-to-NL ratio (TNR), and absorbed dose of NL, D<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">NL</inf>, and tumor, D<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">T</inf>. All training strategies achieved a mean Dice >0.93 for NL. Att-nnUNet<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">CTAP+CTHA</inf> had the best Dice with 0.83±0.12 followed by nnUNet<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">CTAP+CTHA</inf> with 0.82±0.11, while network trained by only CTAP achieved mean Dice <0.73 for tumor.
