Att-nnUNet<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">CTAP+CTHA</inf> had the least mean absolute error of TNR (13.03%±17.73%), D<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">NL</inf> (7.09%±11.50%) and D<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">T</inf> (8.41%±12.85%). DL-training on both CTAP and CTHA can achieve better segmentation performance compared with CTAP alone. The attention module can further improve segmentation accuracy.

articleTitle: Real-time highly-parallel tracking processing with FPGA at LHCb
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: For the future high luminosity LHC runs, it is expected to reconstruct events more complex than the actual ones. in view of this need, the LHCb Collaboration has established a testbed for heterogeneous computing equipment to develop solutions for real-time event reconstruction integrated with the LHCb DAQ infrastructure. The most advanced one is a highly-parallelized tracking processor, based on the "Artificial Retina", which uses a set of FPGA, to which the data are distributed using a custom optical mesh with high speed links. The aim at the testbed is to implement a demonstrator for the tracking of pixel detectors, able to manage the data of a sector of a detector. The scalability to a full size processor will be discussed, as well as the DAQ integration issues for a system running on real data.

articleTitle: openSSS: an open-source implementation of scatter estimation for 3D TOF-PET
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)

authors.preferredName: H. W. A. M. de Jong

abstract: Scatter correction is essential for quantitative and accurate time-of-flight (TOF) PET imaging. However, scatter estimation algorithms for TOF and custom geometries are not available in open-source reconstruction libraries. To this end, we have developed an open-source implementation of the TOF-aware single-scatter-simulation (SSS) [1] algorithm (openSSS). It is validated on NEMA phantoms and patient data, for two PET geometries, compared to Monte-Carlo simulations and two vendor-specific reconstruction platforms. The reconstructed images with openSSS scatter correction are visually similar with comparable contrast recovery. The estimated scatter distribution also shows good agreement with clinical software on clinical data. In conclusion, we have developed and validated an open-source implementation of the TOF-aware SSS for use in conjunction with reconstruction frameworks such as CASToR [2]. openSSS is available publicly for download here [3].

articleTitle: Increasing the resolution of clinical PET systems by the principle of structured illumination microscopy
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: We investigate applying the theory of super-resolution (SR) structured illumination microscopy (SIM) for increasing the resolution of clinical positron emission tomography (PET) imaging. The theory of SIM is based on modulating the image field to encode its high-frequency content above the bandwidth of the imaging device, and hence unobservable, into lower-frequency, detectable signals. Subsequently, high-resolution images are produced from a number of resolution-limited images that however encode the high-frequency content of the image field under examination by computationally restoring signals to their correct frequencies. In this work, we propose using a partially attenuating rotating ring, referred to as the modulator, in front of a stationary PET detector ring to create intensity modulation of the coincidence photons before detection. Using computer simulation data, we demonstrate a proof-of-concept for this SIM-inspired SR PET: We show that images reconstructed from multiple noise-free projection data obtained with the modulator at various rotational positions and a PET system made of 576 4.2 mm-width crystals can resolve 0.9 mm diameter sources. In practice, the characteristics of PET imaging physics and data noise will limit resolution recovery, but we also obtain promising initial results when using the ordered-subset expectation-maximization algorithm that is known to be relatively susceptible to noise. Further systematic studies are needed to better understand the theoretical aspects of the proposed method but we believe it can be practical after optimization of the design of the modulator and reconstruction method.

articleTitle: Kinetic Model-Informed Deep Learning for Multiplexed PET Image Separation
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Multiplexed positron emission tomography (PET) imaging observes multiple targets of interest for different tracers simultaneously in a single scan. The separation of the multiplexed PET signals within a single PET scan is challenging due to the fact that each tracer gives rise to indistinguishable 511 keV photon pair, and thus no unique energy information for differentiating the source of each photon pairs. Recently, many applications of deep learning for multiplexed signal separation have been concentrated on pure data-driven methods, e.g. training a neural network on separating multiplexed/multi-tracer images into single-tracer dynamic/static images. These methods use overparameterised networks with only a very weak inductive prior. In this work, we improve the inductive prior of the deep network by embedding a general kinetic model, enabling fewer learned parameters and ensuring network outputs are consistent with known kinetic models. In particular, we incorporate the spectral analysis model into a neural network by unrolling a regularised implementation of an image-space version of a fully 4D reconstruction algorithm. We evaluate the proposed model based separation method on 2D PET simulations. The results obtained suggest that incorporating the kinetic-model with deep learning leads to better separation performance, and less training data is required compared to the pure data-driven separation. Future work will focus on investigating the impacts of the time interval between tracer injections and the number of blocks in the unrolled image-space separation algorithm.

articleTitle: Advances in 3D Printed Apertures for FF-XRFImaging Spectrometers based on MPGDs
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: The use of 3D printing technologies for the design and fabrication of imaging apertures has revolutionized the production of X-ray collimators, especially those made of high-density materials. This approach provides a cost-effective way to manufacture optical components that can be used in X-ray imaging systems, including Energy Dispersive X-ray Fluorescence Imaging (EDXRFI) applications, where pinhole apertures are traditionally used, despite their limitations in terms of sensitivity, that lead to long acquisition times. To address this issue, alternative optical components, such as parallel multi-hole collimators, can be used.This research investigates the potential of Additive Manufacturing (AM) for creating imaging apertures that can enhance the performance of X-ray imaging systems, specifically Full Field X-ray Fluorescence (FF-XRF) spectrometers based on MicroPattern Gas Detectors (MPGD). In this study, different 3D printed multi-hole collimators, with varying geometries, material compositions and production methods, were produced and tested. The imaging system's performance, including relative sensitivity and position resolution were studied and compared with those obtained with pinhole-based setups.

articleTitle: Evaluation of a new type of semi-monolithic DOI detector with different surface treatments
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: A new type of semi-monolithic detector design, comprised of rows of pixelated crystals coupled to monolithic slabs using optical adhesive, is proposed. The semi-monolithic detector presents several advantages, including high precision in three-dimensional event localization, high detection efficiency, and simplified calibration. Moreover, this design has simple manufacturing process and low cost.To identify the optimal surface treatments for achieving high-quality flood images and high DOI resolution, the performance of five semi-monolithic detectors with different surface treatments were evaluated. Each prototype detector consists of two layers, and each layer consists of a 1 × 16 array of 1.53 × 1.03 × 0 mm3 LYSO crystals (1.61 mm pitch) and a monolithic slab of 5.84 × 0.5 × 0 mm3. The detectors were fabricated with either polished or unpolished crystal surfaces, and using different inter-crystal reflectors and optical adhesive of different refractive indexes (RI). Preliminary experimental studies in this work show that when the two optical coupling surfaces of the detector are unpolished and high-refractive optical adhesive is used, accurate two-dimensional position resolution and high DOI resolution can be obtained. The crystals in the prototype detectors can be clearly resolved except for the edge area. The optimal average DOI resolution and energy resolution are 6 mm and 11.5% FWHM, respectively.In conclusion, the experimental results demonstrated the potential of the prototype semi-monolithic DOI detector for high spatial resolution PET imaging.

articleTitle: Design Study of a Monolithic PET Detector for Scintillation Photon Counting
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: We conducted a comprehensive design study of a new scintillation photon counting concept which can significantly improve the performance of clinical positron emission tomography (PET) detectors. Our approach involves spreading scintillation lights through a monolithic crystal and reading it out using analog silicon photomultipliers (SiPMs) to leverage unique spatiotemporal information of detected photons. Single photons are converted into digital photon "bitstreams" in each channel by low-noise high-frequency electronics and fast comparators, processed by gigabit transceivers for acquisition. To model the concept and study performance tradeoffs, we built a realistic simulation framework using Geant4 and postprocessing based on empirically derived parameters and experimentally validated it against coincidence time resolution (CTR) measurements. Candidate combinations of SiPM channel width (3, 4, and 6 mm), channel density (6×6 ̶ 12×12), and crystal width (36 ̶ 48 mm with fixed 20-mm thick LGSO) were then evaluated. Preliminary metrics were chosen as the CTR, positioning mean absolute error (MAE), and scintillation photon sparsity for 511-keV events. A simple timing estimator that averages the first photon at each pixel yielded 118 to 126 ps of CTRs without any corrections. Overall, a smaller channel yielded worse CTR but better MAE. When using 4 mm SiPMs, MAEs were better for smaller crystals, with the 9×9 array yielding 1.78 and 2.94 mm for XY and Z, respectively. The percentage of uniquely resolved photons ranged from 52% to 66% depending on configuration. So far, simulations demonstrate that 120 ps CTR and sub-3mm MAE are achievable with the 20-mm thick photon counting detector. More advanced estimators that also provide corrections for 3D position and scintillation transit time jitter will be developed using the framework set up in this study. These studies guide the construction of a prototype module to experimentally demonstrate this concept.

articleTitle: Translation Between Amyloid and Tau Tracer Images for Alzheimer's Disease Using Deep Learning
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: We present a generative adversarial neural network (GAN) model to produce a predicted image of one tracer from a different tracer to improve the diagnosis of Alzheimer's disease (AD). AD is a progressive neurodegenerative disease where early diagnosis allows for new therapeutical intervention to slow cognitive decline. Using multiple biomarkers in PET imaging would give a complete picture of the disease biology of a patient, allowing better treatment and management. However, currently conducting simultaneous dual-tracer PET scans is not feasible, and performing multiple PET scans on a single patient is highly impractical due to the double increased radiation dose and costs. We retrospectively collected 67 PET scans of the AD patients using beta-amyloid (florbetaben) and tau-specific radioligands (PI-2620), two common radiopharmaceuticals used for the diagnosis of AD. Two generator and discriminator models were trained cyclically, each on one radiopharmaceutical PET scan, and attempted to predict the other radiopharmaceutical PET scan. We used Cycle-consistent generative adversarial network (CycleGAN) model architecture. We quantitatively evaluated the quality of the synthetic cross-tracer images using the pseudo-PET images and the acquired ones. The Peak Signal-to-Noise Ratio (PSNR), Structural Similarity Index Measure (SSIM), and Mean Squared Error (MSE) values obtained for translating from tau to amyloid were 22.84 ± 3.3, 0.82 ± 0.05, and 0.026 ± 0.01, respectively. Similarly, the corresponding values for translating amyloid to tau were 22.47±3.4, 0.81±0.06, and 0.030±0.02, respectively. Our findings suggest that image translation from tau radiopharmaceutical PET imaging to amyloid using generative models can provide comprehensive disease information without requiring two separate scans.

articleTitle: Modelling a Compact Compton Camera from HEXITEC Detectors for Radiation Therapy Applications
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: The detection of prompt gamma particles produced inside the patient’s body during radiation treatments (proton beam therapy, boron neutron capture therapy, among others) has been recognised as a promising tool for performing in-vivo verification studies. To achieve this, it is essential to obtain information about the production origin of such particles within the patient, as they are released from de-excitation processes in tissue nuclei during treatment. Compton cameras have the potential for accurate directional radiation detection with high count rates as no physical collimation is needed. However, current Compton camera models face challenges regarding both hardware in terms of portability and software in terms of useful event selection for noise reduction. The present work studies the feasibility of the High Energy X-ray Imaging Technology (HEXITEC) detector, which has a pixellated, energy resolved Cadmium Zinc Telluride sensor, as the elementary unit of a Compton camera. The study sets out to determine if the increased spectral and spatial information of the sensor can be exploited for this application, while maintaining a compact, portable detection system. This involves building a flexible Geant4 model where multiple HEXITEC modules are aligned pointing towards a prompt gamma source. The optimal geometric parameters including sensor placements, thicknesses and inter-layer spacing will be presented and discussed for experimental trials, along with an analysis on the effects of the back layers of the detector and the performance of the Stochastic Origin Ensemble as the reconstruction algorithm. Overall, this study represents a significant step towards a novel application of the HEXITEC detector for the development of a highly optimised, compact Compton camera system.

articleTitle: A new device of low-cost and transportable for detecting nuclear materials with a neutron source
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: The active neutron method is a highly effective approach for nuclear security, enabling the detection of nuclear materials by irradiating the object with neutrons and measuring the fission neutrons. This method has proven particularly effective for detecting highly enriched uranium, which is challenging to identify with passive neutron and gamma methods. However, distinguishing between irradiated neutrons and fission neutrons requires a special technique, such as using pulsed neutron irradiation. The DDA method and FNDI method are well-known for active neutron techniques using pulsed neutrons. However, those methods have the drawback of relying on expensive accelerators. Besides devices using accelerators have a disadvantage of the rather massive. Since those disadvantages prevent the devices’ widespread use, we have been developing a new method and device, which satisfies low-cost and transportable, for nuclear security. To address these challenges, we have developed a novel technique called the active rotation method, which utilizes a rotating neutron source near the object being measured to detect nuclear materials. The device to rotate a neutron source can be produced at low-cost and it is compact. A neutron source is rotated with several thousand rpm at measuring, and it is possible to detect nuclear materials by confirming the deformation of the time-distribution spectrum obtained by a neutron detector. In addition to the rotation device, we have also developed a low-cost neutron detector utilizing water Cherenkov radiation. Our presentation will introduce this newly developed a rotation device and demonstrate its nuclear material detection capabilities.

articleTitle: Periodic radiation mapping of contaminated wetlands
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: We present preliminary results from a 2023 radioactive contamination mapping campaign at the Savannah River Site (SRS) F-Area wetlands, and draw comparisons against our 2022 datasets from the same area. We discuss the implementation of a more robust LiDAR ground segmentation algorithm, and its effects on reconstruction artefacts. We also discuss efforts to accurately georeference and align measurements across the 2022 and 2023 campaigns. We discuss qualitative comparisons between reconstructed contamination distribution results where possible. Future work will involve returning to SRS in 2024 to continue looking for periodic changes in contamination distributions and to perform more focused surveys of specific hotspots.

articleTitle: 3D position determination in LaBr3 monolithic crystals with convolutional neural networks
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Convolutional neural networks have been used to determine the positions of photon interactions in a monolithic crystal. Data for the model training process was generated through Gate 8.2 simulations. Realistic simulations of a collimated source of 511 keV photons impinging a LaBr<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</inf> crystal coupled to a silicon photomultiplier array were carried out. The light collected by the pixels of the photomultiplier array was recorded to generate images employed to train and test the model. The optimal architecture was found using the Weights & Biases platform tools. The model's predictions were evaluated by analyzing the FWHM, euclidean distance and mean absolute error. Once an optimal model was found for predicting x and y coordinates, the DOI was estimated using the same model. Results were compared with previously published works, and the model performed well both in the 2D and 3D studies. This method shows promise for determining photon interaction positions in medical imaging applications.

articleTitle: High-Performance CsPbBr3 Perovskite Gamma Detectors
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Lead halide perovskites have garnered extensive attention in photovoltaics, light emitting devices (LEDs), lasers, as well as radiation detection. Cesium lead bromide (CsPbBr<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</inf>) based semiconductor radiation detector that has the potential to match the gamma detection properties of the leading edge RTSDs such as cadmium zinc telluride (CZT) and thallium bromide (TlBr). The high attenuation coefficient of CsPbBr3, owing to the presence of lead, along with its long carrier lifetime and high mobility, have made it a perfect candidate for use in the detection of gamma radiation. In this work, we report the fabrication of CsPbBr<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</inf> detectors with an uncorrected energy resolution of <2% at 662 keV with high photopeak-to-Compton ratios and hole mobility-lifetime products. We will also discuss the polarization processes and their effect on charge transport properties and energy spectra of the devices.

articleTitle: A Deep Learning Approach for Separating Gamma-Ultrasound Signals using Autoencoder
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Recently, the development of Gamma-Ultrasound (γ-US) probes has gained significant attention for their potential to simultaneously acquire anatomical and molecular information. However, separating gamma and ultrasound signals acquired in one readout channel has been a challenging task, mainly due to the limitation in signal bandwidth. To address this issue, we propose a deep learning-based Autoencoder model that can distinguish between gamma and ultrasound signals regardless of their frequency bands. We evaluated our proposed method and compared it with the Finite Impulse Response (FIR) filter method by varying the frequency of the gamma signal and US signal. The FIR filter method caused a significant reduction (up to 48.76%) in the peak voltage of the gamma signal as the signal length decreased, while our Autoencoder model showed similar performance to the original signal with only a negligible decrease (0.17%). Our findings demonstrate the potential of the proposed Autoencoder method to overcome the limitations of FIR filters and enable the application of Gamma-Ultrasound probes in various fields.

articleTitle: High temporal and spatial resolution upright Motion-tracked Immersive functional PET for behavioral neuroscience
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Functional [F18]-fluorodeoxyglucose positron emission tomography (FDG-fPET) is a promising new approach for measuring the dynamic functional changes in the brain related to stimulus and tasks during the scan. However, the fPET has yet to make a significant impact in neuroimaging due to PET’s limited photon detection sensitivity, poor spatial resolution, and subject motion during the task. To fully exploit the benefits of fPET and mitigate its limitations, we propose an ultra-high sensitivity, ultra-high resolution, motion-compensated, portable, and upright Prism-PET brain scanner. This proposed scanner will enable fPET imaging in the sitting position with immersive virtual reality (VR) headsets that can provide enhanced behavioral and visual stimulations. In this study, we designed a synthetic experiment that includes the GATE Zubal brain phantom simulation of brain activations due to visual stimulations. Bolus, constant infusion, and hybrid bolus-infusion injections were simulated, with the gray and white matter uptake modeled using a two-compartment model. A k3 increment was applied to the occipital lobe during the stimulation period and the occipital activity uptake at the end of the experiment is 20% higher than the average gray uptake. We also simulated different frame durations of 1, 5, 15, 30, and 60 seconds. Each frame's image was reconstructed individually using LM-OSEM with DOI-rebinning. The time-to-activity curve of each image voxel was determined and fitted using a general linear model (GLM) with two ground truth task regressors. The activation maps were converted into parametric z-maps, and the sensitivity and specificity of the activated region were calculated. Our simulation results demonstrated that the Prism-PET upright fPET scanner achieved high sensitivity (> 80%) and high specificity (>90%), enabling functional PET imaging with high temporal and spatial resolution.

articleTitle: Design and first performance tests of the SAFIR-II PET-MR Scanner
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: SAFIR-II is a high-performance Positron Emission Tomography (PET) insert designed for a Bruker BioSpin 70/30 magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scanner. It was designed to acquire images for mice and rats within 5 s. This is achieved by minimizing dead-time effects and widening bandwidth limitations, enabling image acquisition at high source activities of up to 500 MBq. Following the "Dual Ring Prototype" and SAFIR-I, SAFIR-II presents the finalized detector design. It employs 11.520 Lutetium-Yttrium oxyorthosilicate (LYSO) crystals (2.0 × 2.0 × 13 mm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</sup>) coupled one-to-one to Hamamatsu MPPC S13361-2050 silicon photomultiplier arrays (crystal pitch: 2.0 × 2.0 mm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sup>) to cover an axial field of view of 144.3 mm. The SiPM’s analog signals are digitized using PETA8 Application Specific Integrated Circuits (ASICs), and then read out and transmitted to a DAQ-Computer using an FPGA (Xilinx Kintex7) and an optical 10 GBit Ethernet Link. MR-compatible DC-DC converters and low dropout voltage regulators are used to condition all internal low-voltages. The total power consumption is 558 W.In this work, we present an initial performance evaluation of the PET insert using low and high activity measurements. A point-source measurement at 2.6 MBq yielded a coincidence timing resolution of 217 ps (full width at half maximum (FWHM)) and a coincidence energy resolution of 11.8 % (FWHM, from Gaussian fit). Measuring a line-source phantom at 500 MBq showed a coincidence timing resolution of 277 ps and a coincidence energy resolution of 12.3 %.

articleTitle: Monte Carlo simulations of in-vivo carbon-ion treatment monitoring with charged nuclear fragments
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Carbon-ion radiotherapy (CIRT) is a highly conformal form of radiotherapy that offers precise dose distributions for cancer treatment. On the other hand, CIRT is sensitive to morphological changes in the patient anatomy, such as swelling, tumor size variation, or cavity filling. Our research group at the German Cancer Research Center has been developing a method for monitoring such changes along the course of the treatment by tracking nuclear charged fragments that emerge from irradiated patients. A non-invasive in-vivo detection system with seven mini-trackers composed of 28 Timepix3 pixel detectors was developed. The detection system is used in the ongoing In-Vivo Monitoring (InViMo) clinical trial at the Heidelberg Ion-Beam Therapy Center. FLUKA Monte Carlo (MC) simulations were developed to support the clinical measurements and link specific anatomical changes to observed differences in the fragment emission profiles. In this work, the performance of the developed FLUKA MC simulation is reported and compared to the result of the first measurements performed with the detection system prototype are presented.

articleTitle: Preliminary Evaluation of the Detector for the Human Dynamic Neurochemical Connectome Scanner
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: The Human Dynamic Neurochemical Connectome Scanner is a high spatio-temporal resolution brain PET insert integrated with a 7T MR scanner. Long and thin scintillation crystals were chosen to maximize detection efficiency without sacrificing spatial resolution. To address the parallax error, our group develops a high-performance PET detector capable of depth of interaction (DOI). The detector is based on the C13500 TOF-PET modules (Hamamatsu), with modifications for MRI compatibility and a light sharing approach for the customized configuration of a 10×10 1.6×1.6×26mm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</sup> LSO crystal block and 4×4 4×4mm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sup> 50µm pixel multi-pixel photon counter (MPPC). DOI capability is provided by a 380µm light guide positioned on top of the crystal block enabling a depth-dependent light spread. Different bias voltage and parameter settings of the ASIC affecting gain, bandwidth and signal shaping were evaluated. DOI performance was assessed by side irradiation at different depths with a collimated F-18 source. A setup involving a beam-splitter and a 405 nm laser was used to assess MPPC and time to digital converter timing capability and for calibration. By using a customized firmware for light sharing as well as event post-processing, good performance was achieved in terms of crystal identification accuracy while initial results indicate an energy resolution of 18.7%. First results indicate a correct DOI identification for 97% (3mm) and 86% (23mm) with an ample energy window of ±15% even with 26mm long crystals. A coincidence time resolution of 57ps was achieved for 1.5V overvoltage for a pulsed laser beam between MPPCs (no scintillator crystal) even without significant fine timing correction. Despite challenges posed by long, thin crystals with a top light guide, the DOI-capable PET detector demonstrated good preliminary performance. Ongoing optimization of operation conditions, parameter settings, and implementation of DOI-based corrections will improve the performance of the detector.

articleTitle: Characterization of Thallium Bromide Gamma-Ray Detectors for Boron Neutron Capture Therapy
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: For Boron Neutron Capture Therapy (BNCT), the detection of prompt gamma rays of 478 keV emitted from <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">10</sup>B atoms reacted with thermal neutrons is useful to obtain the <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">10</sup>B distribution in the patient. High energy resolutions and high peak efficiencies are required for the prompt gammaray detectors. Thallium bromide (TlBr) is one of the promising materials for the fabrication of semiconductor detectors for the BNCT applications. TlBr exhibits high photon stopping power due to its high atomic numbers (81 and 35) and high density (7.56 g/cm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</sup>). The wide bandgap energy of 2.68 eV allows TlBr detectors to operate with low noise at room temperature. Zone-purified TlBr crystals exhibit good charge transport properties, resulting in the high energy resolutions of the detectors. In this study, the detection of 478 keV prompt gamma rays was performed with TlBr detectors. A TlBr detector with a planar cathode, and a pixel anode (1.5 mm × 1.5 mm) surrounded by a guard electrode was fabricated from the crystal grown by the traveling molten zone method using a zone-purified material. The detector thickness was approximately 3 mm. Charge-sensitive preamplifiers were connected to the cathode and anode. The output pulse waveforms were recorded with a 2-channel digitizer. The neutron radiography testing beam line at the Aomori Prefecture Quantum Science Center was used to irradiate a boron-containing polyethylene block with thermal neutrons to induce 478 keV prompt gamma rays. During the neutron irradiation, the gamma-ray spectrum was acquired with the TlBr detector. A clear 478 keV full-energy peak was obtained from the detector with an energy resolution of 4.0% full-width at half maximum with depth correction and selection based on the cathode to anode signal ratio.

articleTitle: Investigation of the SOI microdosimeter for high LET ion measurements
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: In this work, a 3D silicon-on-insulator (SOI) microdosimeter was investigated during high LET ion irradiation using a 24 MeV carbon ion microbeam and a 500 MeV/u argon ion therapeutic beam. The results demonstrate the performance of the SOI microdosimeter when measuring high LET particles, with some attributing low energy events observed in the extremely low energy region. However these events did not substantially affect the microdosimetric spectra nor the yD values. This demonstrates that the SOI microdosimeter is suitable for high LET ion QA applications.

articleTitle: Growth and Characterization of High Performance CsPbBr3 Crystals for γ-ray Detection Applications
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: The use of halide perovskite materials as radiation detectors has shown great promise due to their high yield, low cost, and high detection sensitivity. The crystal growth of CsPbBr<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</inf> was investigated through the Bridgman method, and detector fabrication was carried out at Argonne National Laboratory as part of this study.The results revealed that the crystals had an impressive mobility lifetime product for holes, close to 1 x 10<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">-3</sup> cm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sup>/V, indicating excellent charge carrier properties. Moreover, when subjected to <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">137</sup>Cs irradiation, a planar detector made from a crystal with 1 mm thickness demonstrated an energy resolution as low as 1.4% without any data corrections. This study also presents the crystal growth, detector fabrication, and spectral response of 10 mm thick CsPbBr<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</inf> crystals on <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">57</sup>Co and <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">137</sup>Cs irradiation. These findings suggest that CsPbBr<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</inf> is a promising material for radiation detection, as it displayed high performance in terms of charge carrier properties and energy resolution. Overall, this study offers valuable insights into the potential applications of CsPbBr<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</inf> as a radiation detector, suggesting that it could be a promising candidate for the development of cost-effective and highly sensitive radiation detection technologies.

articleTitle: High throughput X-ray Polarimetry with a new custom ASIC coupled to an electron multiplier of novel type
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: While the successful launch and operation in space of the Gas Pixel Detectors onboard the PolarLight cubesat and the Imaging X-ray Polarimetry Explorer demonstrate the viability and the technical soundness of this class of detectors for astronomical X-ray polarimetry, substantial improvements in some of the overall detector response quality factors are still possible, addressing the limitations posed by the readout ASIC and by the electrons multiplier stage. We report on the design and tests of a new generation Gas Pixel Detector made up of a new custom readout ASIC, dubbed XPOL-III, specifically designed to meet more challenging data rates requirements, and a new electron multiplier stage based on a thin, weakly resistive 60um pitch Capillary Plate, substituting the more standard high resistivity Gas Electron Multiplier aiming to improve both detector response stability and polarization measurement accuracy.

articleTitle: Absolute light yield measurement of various NaI:Tl crystal scintillators
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: We report on investigating the absolute light yield of various NaI:Tl crystals, which have been used for a variety of applications such as medical imaging, homeland security, and pure science research due to their high light yield, low cost, and crystal growth advantages. Even if it was known that the absolute light yield is known to be approximately 40,000 photons/MeV, the absolute light yields of these crystals have varied widely from typical values. We focus on using the PMT single photoelectron technique to measure the absolute light yield of many NaI:Tl crystals of various sizes, including high-quality crystals grown by laboratory and commercial companies. We also investigate the PMT optic using theoretical estimation and GEANT4 optical simulation to correct overrated light yield values. The results show the essential role of PMT optic correction in obtaining accurate absolute light yield values. We also compare the single photoelectron technique using different PMT to the method using a photodiode and avalanche photodiode and find a 10% systematic error. Our study shows that light yield varies from 30,000 photons/MeV – 60,000 photons which is close to the theoretical predicted light yield of around 70,000 ph/MeV. Overall, our study provides valuable insights into the absolute light yield of NaI:Tl crystals and the importance of correcting for the PMT optic to obtain accurate absolute light yield.

articleTitle: FELIX-MROD, FELIX-based readout of the ATLAS Muon Drift Tubes
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: The ATLAS Muon Drift Tube (MDT) ReadOut Drivers (MROD) have been in operation for more than 15 years and are expected to remain in operation until about 2026. In the event of extensive failures the number of spare modules may be insufficient. This project therefore proposes using the Front-End LInk eXchange (FELIX) system, a new component of the ATLAS data acquisition (DAQ) infrastructure, to overcome a potential MROD failure. The presentation will describe the FELIX-MROD’s design as well as tests of its functionality. The latest results of testing its integration into the ATLAS DAQ will be reported.

articleTitle: Advanced Sinogram Reconstruction via Fourier Neural Operators for High-Quality SPECT Imaging
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: This study introduces an innovative sinogram reconstruction technique employing Fourier neural operators (FNOs) for single-photon emission computed tomography (SPECT) imaging. The proposed method accepts a limited number of sinogram projections and directly reconstructs a superior image without intermediate steps. The approach is trained on a dataset of high-quality SPECT images using FNOs, a category of neural networks capable of learning linear operators through Fourier analysis. The method is assessed using software-generated phantoms via GATE and compared against the standard ordered subsets expectation maximization (OSEM) reconstruction method. The results demonstrate that the proposed method considerably enhances reconstruction quality and surpasses state-of-the-art compressed sensing techniques. The presented method holds the potential to decrease radiation exposure and scanning time required for SPECT imaging, rendering it a valuable asset in clinical practice. Future research could investigate the application of this method to other imaging modalities and advanced neural network architectures.

articleTitle: Testing of a line driver with configurable pre-emphasis on lossy transmission lines
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Rare-event physics experiments such as the Deep Underground Neutrino Experiment (DUNE) or the Enriched Xenon Observatory experiment (nEXO) require rare, low-energy events to be detected by sensitive detectors immersed in a cryogenic noble liquid (e.g., liquid xenon). Readout electronics used within such detectors must consume minimal power while operating reliably in cryogenic environments. Furthermore, maximizing the radiopurity of the environment is vital to minimize background event rates, in turn placing strict limits on the volume of dielectric materials and leading to high-loss data cables spanning distances up to 12~m. Such high transmission losses cause high attenuation and inter-symbol interference (ISI), resulting in a high bit-error rate (BER). These issues were addressed by developing a line driver with configurable pre-emphasis in 65~nm CMOS. The pre-emphasis parameters can be programmed to minimize BER for specific cables and data rates under power constraints. The driver was tested at room temperature on a 15~m twinax cable for a data rate of 0.6~Gb/s. The received waveforms were analyzed to define a suitable performance figure-of-merit (FoM), and pre-emphasis settings for improving this FoM were experimentally determined.

articleTitle: Image corrections software using emission data only for full and partial ring PET scanners
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: The PETITION (PET for InTensive Care units and Innovative protON therapy) project has successfully developed two new bedside Positron Emission Tomography (PET) scanners for Intensive Care Units (ICU) and proton beam therapy (PBT) applications. While the ICU device is a conventional full ring PET scanner, the PBT system has a U-shape design ensuring a suitable opening for proton irradiation.The iterative ordered subset expectation maximisation, including image corrections, is a well-known algorithm for PET image reconstruction. External information is commonly used for scatter and attenuation estimates. While transmission-less method is already used with full ring PET scanners, it is usually not used with partial ring devices. This document presents preliminary results of image reconstruction where scatter and attenuation estimators are fully computed from emission data for both full and partial ring PET scanners.

articleTitle: An Adaptive Approach to Spectroscopic Anomaly Detection and Isotope Identification
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Non-negative matrix factorization (NMF)-based algorithms have been shown to be highly effective for detecting anomalies and identifying isotopes in gamma-ray spectra. However, the conventional implementation of these approaches requires the lengthy pre-computation of various algorithm components. This represents a potential barrier to widespread adoption for real-time use in the field. We propose a new NMF-based algorithm which adapts to changing conditions such as the underlying background model, energy calibration, integration time, and detection thresholds without user intervention. The algorithm includes computational improvements to conventional NMF and a novel method for filtering spectral anomalies, enabling real-time analysis of data. This paper will discuss the use of NMF for radiological detection, and the necessity of an adaptive approach, and describe our algorithm and its performance.

articleTitle: Automatic Renal Cortical Defect Detection in Tc-99 DMSA Scintigraphy using Multi-view Deep Learning
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Renal dysfunction can arise from various factors, and detecting renal scarring (RS) is essential to prevent long-term consequences. DMSA scintigraphy is useful in detecting cortical anomalies and is considered the gold standard for diagnosing RS. Deep Learning (DL) has shown promising results in medical imaging, especially with multi-view input DL. This work aimed to develop a deep learning model that can automatically detect cortical defects in the kidney by analyzing multiple views of DMSA images. This study included 747 patients with DMSA images and eight different views to detect kidney cortical defects using deep learning. The ResNet152V2 model was applied to each view separately, followed by the Attention Augmented (AA) method. The model developed in this study showed promising results in detecting a cortical defect in DMSA scans with AUC=0.76, Sensitivity=0.84, and Specificity=0.63, which can be challenging for physicians. Furthermore, our model has shown promising results in automatically detecting cortical defects in the kidneys using DMSA images with multi-view input. This suggests that developing similar models could save time to physicians and be used as reliable assistants in diagnosing renal dysfunction.

articleTitle: Explainable AI and Transfer Learning in the Classification of PET Cardiac Perfusion Polar Maps
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: This study explores the application of transfer learning and explainable artificial intelligence for the classification of cardiac perfusion polar maps. The dataset consisted of 138 polar maps from 15O-H2O positron emission tomography (PET) myocardial perfusion imaging (MPI). A test accuracy of 0.869 was achieved with partially fine-tuned VGG19. Gradient-weighted class activation mapping (Grad-CAM) provided insight into the model's decision-making process. The results showed that while some predictions were based on clinically relevant features, others were based on irrelevant features, rendering them clinically invalid. These findings emphasize the need for further investigation into the validation of deep learning predictions for clinical use.

articleTitle: The Evolution of ArduSiPM technology : A Compact, Versatile, and Cost-effective Detector Platform for Radiation and Photon Flux Measurements
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: The INFN Rome group has been developing the ArduSiPM technology since 2012, which is an allin-one detector that uses SiPM, analog electronics, and SoC to count events and measure SiPM signal amplitude and time-of-arrival. The first-generation ArduSiPM was powered by the Arduino Due processor, an 84 MHz SAM3X8E Cortex-M3 RISC, and was highly flexible, allowing for continuous firmware updates and optimal resource usage. With the improvements in SoCs and SiPMs, second and third-generation detectors were constructed, providing enhanced precision and space efficiency.The new internal analog design of the SoCs and higher clock frequencies enabled a half-photon threshold and a time-of-arrival measurement precision of 6 ns. These detectors are perfect for onfield and space applications due to their small size, low weight, and low power consumption. The second-generation Cosmo ArduSIPM detectors have two SAMV71 Cortex-M7 RISC 300 MHz processors integrated into a 10x10 cm2 CubeSat form factor on a two-channel board weighing just 40 grams. The third generation, called Nano ArduSiPM, is under development to benefit from new TFPGA packages, which reduce the weight and size of the electronics, building a single-channel module with a form factor of picosatellites measuring just 5x5 cm2.This paper aims to demonstrate the performance of the new-generation detectors and compare them to the first-generation detectors. The analog and digital parts of the detectors have been optimized to enhance signals with a few photons, and edge computing processes are utilized to minimize data throughput to external communication devices, which is vital where throughput must be optimized, like space application.

articleTitle: A CubeSat-Sized Airborne Gamma-Ray Spectrometer for In-Flow Radioactivity Monitoring of Particulate Matter
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: We present a microcontroller-based in-flow airborne spectrometer to quantify the presence and activity of radioactive isotopes in particulate matter (PM). It is based on a hollow CsI(Tl) scintillator inside which air flows, thanks to a fan, and PM is captured by a micrometric filter placed in the middle, thus allowing full solid angle capture of gamma rays. The instrument is very compact, fitting in a 10 cm cube and thus being compatible with several unmanned flying vehicles, including an experimental rocket inside which it will be launched as scientific payload to evaluate the robustness of its design. Here we report the mechanical and electronics (for SiPM readout) design, as well as a preliminary characterization. Simulations have allowed to find the optimal compromise in the number and position of SiPM with an expected energy resolution better than 7% at 662 keV.

articleTitle: Introduction and Welcome
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: On behalf of the RTSD Scientific Advisory Committee, I am pleased to welcome you to the 30<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">th</sup> International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Radiation Detectors.The focus for this RTSD spans from scientific underpinnings in crystal growth to materials characterization, detector fabrication, device testing, feedback to growth and processing procedures, electronic readout development, novel instrumentation, and field uses. This vertical integration from understanding the starting materials to challenges in manufacturing instruments is very unusual, but our approach accelerates the maturity of our field. Now, you are here, and it is up to you to build on the commonality of your work, to share your data, energy, and experience with your colleagues, as we explore new ways to cooperate and collaborate in a mutually beneficial manner. By working together, we will be able to solve problems more effectively, plan better, get results more rapidly, maximize our opportunities, and achieve our vision of wide-scale deployment of room-temperature semiconductor detector technology in healthcare, security, astrophysics, environmental, mineral/oil exploration, materials sorting, among many other applications.Before beginning our technical program, I would like to shift my comments to a few announcements about the 2023 RTSD.

articleTitle: Polarized Probabilistic Compton Scattering Sequencing Method
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: This work describes a probabilistic method of sequence reconstruction for Compton scattering events, which includes the polarized Klein-Nishina formula. The change in degree of polarization as 511 keV photons scatter in a Cadmium Zinc Telluride (CZT) detector, for an initially linearly polarized and initially unpolarized radioactive source, is simulated in GEometry ANd Tracking 4 (GEANT4). Event sequencing is conducted on simulated data to compare the performance of the current unpolarized Klein-Nishina method and the proposed polarized Klein-Nishina method. For an initially unpolarized source, the polarized Klein-Nishina method shows a 16.89% improvement in sequencing for 3-interaction full-energy events and a 16.31% improvement in sequencing for 4-interaction full-energy events. It also shows a 14.84% improvement in sequencing for 3-interaction full-energy events and a 16.12% improvement in sequencing for 4-interaction full-energy events, for an initially linearly polarized source. Future work consists of implementing this method of sequence reconstruction in experiment, where the azimuthal scattering angle cannot be directly calculated.

articleTitle: Stoichiometric Variations and Impurity Distributions in CsPbBr3 Single Crystals Grown via Different Methods
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: The all-inorganic semiconducting perovskite cesium lead bromide, CsPbBr<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</inf>, exhibits promising properties for ionizing radiation detection applications. This work focuses on the comparative study of stoichiometric variations and impurity distributions in CsPbBr<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</inf> single crystals obtained from different crystal growth approaches. Single crystals of CsPbBr<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</inf> were grown from room-temperature solution methods, modified high temperature zone-refining methods as well as from Bridgman–Stockbarger methods. The bulk material purity was confirmed by X-ray diffraction method, while wavelength-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy was used to probe the local stoichiometry of the crystal. Laser ablation ICP-MS was employed to study the impurity distributions within crystal ingots. Photo-luminescence data was collected to identify the electrically active defect states. The observed intrinsic stoichiometric variations and extrinsic impurities were linked to the active defects identified by photo-luminescence spectroscopy. Finally, these material characterization results were correlated to the photo-electrical properties of the single crystal devices and the pulse height spectroscopy performances of the fabricated radiation detectors.

Index Terms: Laser Ablation Inductively Coupled Plasma Mass Spectrometry

articleTitle: Multiplexed PET Imaging Based on Multiple Coincidences and Deep-Learning
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Standard PET imaging cannot differentiate between radionuclides in multi-tracer acquisitions due to annihilation photons having the same energy (511 keV). PET-compatible radionuclides emitting prompt-gamma rays right after the positron emission may enable their differentiation, allowing simultaneous multi-tracer imaging without kinetic modeling or staggering injections. However, conventional PET scanners often have limited energy windows or lack sufficient energy information to differentiate prompt-gamma from annihilation gamma rays, making it difficult to reconstruct coincidences of more than 2 gamma rays. In previous works, we presented mPET, which does not require good energy resolution or specific detectors, to perform dual-tracer PET studies without hardware or firmware modifications. It uses an iterative reconstruction algorithm that allows multiple LORs (MLOR) for forward and backward projection of each coincidence. Data corrections such as scatter and prompt-gamma background, and sensitivity maps are obtained using the fast and realistic Monte Carlo simulator MCGPU-PET. mPET has been successfully applied to multiple studies with different combinations of radionuclides such as I-124, Y-86, Zr-89, F-18 and Ga-68 with both preclinical and clinical scanners. However, it still faces some challenges such as the different positron range of each radionuclide and the low sensitivity for triple coincidences. In this work, we have developed deep-learning models to reduce the bias and noise of the separated reconstructed images of each radiotracer. The performance of the methods was evaluated with multiple dual-tracer studies. The results show that the noise and the bias in some dual-isotope acquisition can be reduced by up to 30%, improving the overall quantitative accuracy of the activity distribution of each separated radiotracer.

articleTitle: Zynq SoM Readout for PET Imaging, for HEP Data Acquisition, and for Prototype PCBs
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: We describe our experience using several commerical system-on-module (SoM) daughter boards (MicroZed, Z-turn, Mercury XU5), based on the Zynq system-on-chip platform, for control and readout of 8 custom Printed Circuit Board (PCB) designs, both for Time-of-Flight Positron Emission Tomography (TOF-PET) and for High Energy Physics (HEP). SoMs are a convenient and powerful solution to interface custom PCBs to gigabit Ethernet for data acquisition. We use this approach for 3 PET-readout PCBs (MRB2, MCU, ROCSTAR, for readout of TOF-PET whole-body and dedicated breast scanners) and for 5 HEP designs (OCB, TP, PTC, AMAC tester, Q-Pix ASIC tester), which we briefly describe.The Zynq's hybrid nature (FPGA fabic woven to ARM CPU) facilitates a wide range of readout tasks. The SoMs offer 100+ FPGA-driven I/O pins for interfacing one's custom PCB, and integrate FPGA logic, CPU, 1GB+ SDRAM, gigabit Ethernet, DC/DC converters, and flash memory for power-on configuration. For small projects, such as our MCU and various ASIC-testing boards, the SoM eliminates the PCB engineering effort to integrate an FPGA and its power network. For larger projects, such as our ROCSTAR and MRB2, the SoM configures, controls, and intelligently networks our custom PCB's larger FPGA. In our experience, the SoM's embedded Linux environment straightforwardly facilitates power-up, configuration, firmware/software updates, networked register-file access, basic readout, and highly convenient remote control via Jupyter notebooks. Sustained gigabit readout via Direct Memory Access (DMA) has required more effort. With a fully-user-space approach (no device driver), we have sustained ~ 300 Mbit/s readout from FPGA to network. We describe both the unconventional user-space approach and a more conventional approach using a DMA device driver. We provide a pedagogical example of high-speed readout, both to stimulate discussion and to facilitate future applications.

articleTitle: Silicon Carbide Detector in Microbeam and Broad Beam Synchrotron Radiation Fields
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: We assess the performance of a CMRP designed epitaxial Schottky Silicon Carbide (SiC) detector, produced by SINTEF (Norway), for Microbeam Radiation Therapy (MRT). For dosimetry, ideally the detector should have a response similar to that of human tissue, should have micron-scale spatial resolution and accurately determine the dose that the microbeams deliver in the Synchrotron X-Ray radiation field. The average measured width of the microbeams (defined by 50 μm wide slots in a multislit collimator) was 54 ± 1 μm. The percentage depth dose (PDD) curve measured using the SiC detector in solid water, in the centre of a 20 mm x 20 mm uniform irradiation field, was also obtained. The PDD from depths ranging from 5 mm to 60 mm for two different X-ray beam filtration conditions are compared to equivalent GEANT4 simulations. The average experiment-simulation difference for all depths studied was ±5.1 % for copper-copper filtration and ±2.1 % for aluminium-copper filtration. The results obtained for the SiC detector to accurately resolve microbeams, as well as measuring the PDD, is very encouraging, in these intense synchrotron microbeam fields.

articleTitle: Prediction of brain metastases from nonsmall cell lung cancer using multimodal radiomics and deep learning based on 18FPET/CT images
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Brain metastasis (BM) is one of the most common malignant forms of non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) and has a poor prognosis. Additionally, there is only 3-5 months of median progressionfree survival after BM. Therefore. Early detection and treatment of NSCLC brain metastasis would help to develop more personalized treatment projects and improve patient survival rates. This study aims to investigate the feasibility of a multimodal radiomics-based method using 3D neural networks to predict the occurrence of BM in NSCLC patients based on <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">18</sup>F-FDG PET/CT images. We collected 229 NSCLC patients who underwent both <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">18</sup>F-FDG PET/CT scans, including lung and brain parts. Shallow lung tumor features and deep brain features were extracted using the python package PyRadiomics and a 3D neural network, respectively. Least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO) regression was conducted to select related radiomics signatures, and a support vector machine (SVM) was used to predict whether NSCLC patients would develop BM. Our results showed that the fused lung shallow and brain deep radiomics features demonstrated superior predictive performance with an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.95±0.01. In summary, our findings suggested that fused lung-brain features may significantly enhance predictive performance in recognizing whether NSCLC patients would develop BM, with potential clinical applications.

articleTitle: Discrimination of233U and235U by Delayed Neutron Signatures for Nondestructive Assay
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Many advanced nuclear reactor designs utilize a fuel cycle based on the conversion of <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">232</sup>Th to <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">233</sup>U, where the latter is used to drive the fission chain reaction. While this fuel cycle has many benefits over traditional fuel cycles, it presents a challenge for nuclear safeguards applied under the Non-Proliferation Treaty (NPT). In particular, there is a lack of mature techniques for the non-destructive assay (NDA) of <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">233</sup>U which must be addressed before thorium fuel cycles come online in states subject to international safeguards. This is further complicated by the fact that in most thorium reactor designs, <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">233</sup>U is collocated with <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">235</sup>U, both of which must be individually accounted for. In this work, a technique is demonstrated to utilize the β-delayed fission neutron decay time profiles to quantify the ratio of <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">233</sup>U to <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">235</sup>U in mixed-isotope items. An experiment was performed to measure the delayed neutron time profiles of <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">233</sup>U, <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">235</sup>U, and mixtures thereof using a modified active well coincidence counter (AWCC), in which the AmLi neutron source was replaced with a deuterium-deuterium neutron generator. The shape of the resultant delayed neutron decay time profiles shows a clear dependence on the relative abundance of each isotope. The measured profile shapes are quantified using a double-integration technique and are consistent with values obtained from an analytical model using the tabular six-group delayed neutron yield parameters. This technique represents the first proposed neutron-based method to discriminate between <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">233</sup>U and <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">235</sup>U.

articleTitle: Inter-crystal optical crosstalk: modeling in GATE and experimental validation
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: High resolution radiation detectors involves using small scintillating crystals optically isolated between each-other. To optimize detectors for avoiding spatial and energy performance detriment, the understanding of inter-crystal crosstalk is of great interest. Accurate optical Monte Carlo simulation plays a crucial role in this context. In this work we focused on inter-crystal optical photon crosstalk. We optimized the validated look-up table Davis Model to accurately simulate optical photons refraction at crystal interfaces using the toolkit GATE, with the goal of including accurate inter-crystal optical crosstalk in detector optimization. The crystal interfaces and bulk and optical properties of the materials were accurately modeled. Illustrative results showed an optical crosstalk of less then 1.35% when using two coupled 3 × 3 × 15 mm3 bismuth germanate crystals. The transmission model will be validated against experimental measurements and made available to GATE users. Complete simulations will be performed and will include the modeling of optical photons transport, reflection, refraction and detection using the software GATE, as well as a complete simulation of SiPMs at micro-cell level.

articleTitle: K-nearest neighbors for the automatic discrimination of alpha, beta and gamma rays in a phoswich detector
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: The paper discusses the development of a phoswich detector that can discriminate between alpha, beta, and gamma radiation using pulse shape discrimination technology. The detector has two layers of scintillators, a stilbene scintillator for detecting alpha and beta particles and a GAGG scintillator for detecting gamma rays. The study aims to apply machine learning techniques to radiation measurement using data from the phoswich detector. The K-nearest neighbors algorithm was used to classify the different types of radiation. The results showed that increasing the number of neighbors improved accuracy, and a value of 20 was chosen for radiation classification. The study demonstrates the effectiveness of machine learning in efficient and automatic alpha/beta/gamma ray discrimination and radionuclide identification, which can help workers with little experience in radiation to work in the field.

articleTitle: Multilayer perceptron-based body weight prediction using CT
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Body weight (BW) is an important normalization factor for calculating standardized uptake value (SUV) in PET/CT studies. Clinically, mainly due to human errors, erroneous BW information is often used, which leads to incorrect SUV measurement. For some patients, e.g., cognitive unconscious, it is challenging to measure the BW via a weight scale. Therefore, it can be useful if BW can be estimated using PET/CT images. Previous methods [1-3] have been proposed to estimate BW using CT or CT scout images, while the prediction accuracy was limited. With the knowledge of that physical density of tissue is proportional to the absorption/attenuation of the X-ray beam, BW estimation through HU-to-Density Mapping (HUDM) is available but only for total body CT images. To accommodate the scenarios for CT images of partial body or special cases, e.g., truncation artifacts, we propose a multilayer perceptron-based weight regression (MLPWR), based on the CT HU histogram. The proposed method demonstrated its predication accuracy for both total-body (MAE = 0.98kg) and whole-body (neck-to-thigh, MAE = 2.33kg) CT images. For the total-body CT, MLPWR yielded more accurate and robust weight prediction performance on special cases, especially for infants (MAE=0.33kg), than HUDM, which is not applicable for whole-body data predication. The results show that MLPWR can be used in the clinic for weight estimation and can provide weight QC for SUV calculation in the PET/CT studies. We thank Dr. Ben Spencer and Dr. Ramsey Badawi of UC Davis for providing a high BMI dataset.

articleTitle: Front-end ASIC spectral and timing performance on a high purity germanium strip detector
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: We present the characteristics and performance of an application specific integrated circuit (ASIC) designed to read out high-purity germanium (HPGe) strip detectors. The ASIC has 32 channels, each of which contains two shaping circuits to allow for high-resolution measurements of both energy and timing; from the timing measurements, the depth of interaction in a detector can be determined. The ASIC will be used as the front- end readout for the HPGe double-sided strip detectors flown aboard the Compton Spectrometer and Imager (COSI) NASA Small Explorer mission, and much of the ASIC development has been funded by the COSI project and by NASA APRA. While the ASIC was designed for HPGe strip detectors, it has also been used to read out silicon strip detectors, CZT detectors, and even silicon photomultipliers optically coupled to scintillators. We evaluated the ASIC on the bench with 30 pF input capacitance to simulate a detector and with a HPGe double-sided strip detector. Here we describe the initial results of these experiments. In particular, we present a measured full width at half maximum of 2.2 keV at 59.5 keV on a HPGe detector similar to the COSI detectors, showing that we are able to maintain the energy resolution required for the COSI mission using the ASIC as the front-end readout.

articleTitle: A System for Elemental Analysis of Aluminum Chips, based on Neutron Activation Analysis
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: The performance of the demonstrator of the system for elemental analysis of aluminum chips is presented. The system is based on neutron activation analysis and isotopic neutron source of PuBe emitting 2x10^6 n/s. The detection system comprises of large 3.5x8 inch LaBr scintillators with an option of easy change to 5x10 inch NaI(Tl) or 5x5 inch BGO. The industrial samples under study are constantly moving through a vertical pipe in a closed loop system which mimics the industrial conditions at aluminum refinery. The system performance is presented in relation to the recorded gamma spectra and gamma lines characteristic for the following chemical elements: Al, Cr, Cu, Fe, Mg, Mn, Ni, Pb, Si, Ti, Zn. The efficiency of gamma spectra detection in the proposed setup is also discussed in relation to the applied detectors and physical limits of neutron activation methods. The results are compared to the standard industrial analysis based on spark optical emission spectroscopy and multiple sample collection.

articleTitle: A-STEP: The AstroPix Sounding Rocket Technology Demonstration Payload
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Wide-field telescopes capable of detecting seconds-long transient astrophysical phenomena and localizing their origin in the sky within ~10 degrees are an important tool for supporting the growing fields of time domain astronomy and multi-messenger astrophysics. AstroPix is a monolithic CMOS active pixel sensor that enables high spatial (250 um) and spectral resolution (<9.7% FWHM at 122 keV) tracking of charged particle interactions within the detector medium. Layered AstroPix sensors can reconstruct the trajectories and energies of incident 25-700 keV gamma rays over large fields of view. A prototype multi-layered AstroPix instrument, called the AstroPix Sounding Rocket Technology Demonstration Payload (A-STEP), will provide a testbed for three layers of 4 x 4 cm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sup> "quad chips". These quad chips, 2 x 2 undiced AstroPix detectors, form the building block of future large area AstroPix detector arrays. This payload will be the first suborbital demonstration of AstroPix’s technological readiness for use in next-generation gamma-ray astrophysical observatories and nuclear physics applications. In this presentation we overview the design and state of development of the first AstroPix multi-layer payload. We anticipate measuring 1000 cosmic ray events within a 5-minute sounding rocket flight window, and will attempt to reconstruct particle tracks through three payload layers.

articleTitle: Positronium Lifetime Measurements using 82Rb in a Long-Axial FOV PET/CT Scanner
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: This work details results from two positronium (Ps) lifetime measurements performed in a long-axial FOV PET/CT scanner using <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">82</sup>Rb. Ps lifetime measurements are of interest for PET because they can yield additional diagnostic information. The first measurement placed drops of a <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">82</sup>Rb solution in between aluminum disks, quartz disks, and into a gelatin mixture. The extracted ortho-Ps (o-Ps) lifetime for the quartz sample was measured to be 1.53+/-0.04 ns, which agrees well with the previously published value of 1.56+/-0.08 ns. The lifetime of the aluminum is also compared with previous results, however, the lifetime exhibits a longer o-Ps lifetime due to positrons leaking into the surrounding plastic holder. The second measurement performed assessed the uniformity of the extracted lifetimes across a uniform cylinder (20φ×30 cm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</sup>) filled with water and an activity of approximately 73.3 MBq. The resulting histo-image was sliced into 1.25 cm thick cross sections, which resulted in lifetime distributions containing on average 1.98×10<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">5</sup>+/-1.06×10<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">4</sup> counts. These lifetime distributions were integral normalized and compared to an averaged lifetime across the uniform cylinder. Overall average deviation in the lifetime measured across the cylinder was determined to be -0.015+/-1.53 %.

articleTitle: Reducing edge effectsin semi-monolithicPET detectorsusing optical barriers: a simulation study
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Clinical Positron EmissionTomography (PET) scanners are based on pixelated detectors and hence their spatial resolution is limited to the pixel size.
