Also, retrieving Depth of Interaction (DOI) information is challenging and parallax error correction is not always available.Monolithic scintillators have been proposed as an alternative to pixelated ones but, achieving usable timing information on the photo n arrival time to the detectors is not easy and also, the events impacting towards the edges of the detector suffer from edge effects which degrades the spatial resolution. Recently, it has been proposed implementing semi-monolithic detectors which provide DOI information and acceptable Detector Time Resolution. Yet, the edge effect in the monolithic direction is still present.In this work, we study reducing edge effects by introducing Optical Barriers (OBs) within the slabs to slightly modify the Light Distribution and then, use Neuronal Networks (NN) for impact position estimation. Simulations of different OBs configurations were carried out. Our preliminary results are promising and demonstrate that OBs can improve the NN predictions at the scintillator edges. The MAE<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">X</inf> and MAE<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">DOI</inf> show an improvement of approximately 17% and 30 % when including OBs, respectively.

articleTitle: CT-less deep learning-based parametric imaging with image-derived input function
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Various approaches for CT-less PET acquisition have been proposed and evaluated in the standalone PET scanners or low-dose clinical applications. CT-less parametric imaging has yet been investigated and poses challenges in terms of both attenuation correction and estimation of image-derived input function (IDIF). In this work, we proposed a CT-less deep learning-based solution of parametric imaging with IDIF. A synthesized attenuation map from non-attenuation-corrected (NAC) PET was used for the dynamic PET image reconstruction, as well as the segmentation of aorta mask and estimation of IDIF. Clinical static <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">18</sup>F-FDG PET/CT data were acquired for the training and evaluation of the synthesis network and the segmentation network, and dynamic whole-body <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">18</sup>F-FDG scans were used to test the proposed method. High quantitative accuracy was found in the synthesized attenuation maps, segmented aorta masks, and estimated IDIFs. Small difference was observed in the subsequent Patlak parametric images as compared to the conventional CT-based results. The proposed CT-less solution was demonstrated feasible and accurate in the parametric imaging.

articleTitle: Performance of Black Silicon Photodiodes
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: We successfully fabricated black-Silicon (b-Si) photodiodes by modifying an n-type silicon photodiode with nanostructures for improved photon detection. The quantum efficiency of this induced-junction b-Si photodiode approaches 100% across a wide spectral range. We are now moving to the fabrication of a photodiode having an avalanche gain (b-Si avalanche photodiode - b-Si APD). The final goal of this project is to implement these techniques on a silicon photomultiplier (SiPM) which will ultimately allow us to realize a near 100% quantum efficiency b-SiPMs. This will have applications in nonproliferation and safeguards, ultra-low intensity light detection in various scientific applications, including quantum sensing, noble gas and liquid scintillating detectors.

articleTitle: Simulation Study of Channel Reduction in Side-readout Slab-based Monolithic Crystals used in PET Detector Modules
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: In positron emission tomography (PET), monolithic crystals have been used as an alternative to the conventional pixelated design to maintain high spatial resolution and improve energy/timing resolutions. Recent studies have proposed an approach using layers of thin crystal slabs with 4-side photosensor readout to address the challenges in thick monolithic crystals. This approach reduces the complex 3D calibration to 2D and maintains spatial resolution when total crystal thickness increases by having separate readouts for each layer.This approach is promising, with prototype detectors demonstrating high spatial, energy, and timing resolutions. However, the need to fully cover four sides of the crystal slabs with photosensors or not remains to be investigated. To address this concern, in this study, we explore alternative designs that use larger-pitch sensor arrays or more distant individual sensors while still maintaining sufficient resolutions. We used the GATE simulation toolkit to study the effect of different configurations, e.g., crystal sizes, sensor sizes, and sensor density, on the resolutions of a single crystal slab. Our simulation results suggest that spatial resolution is scalable with crystal width, enabling the estimation of spatial resolutions for different crystal sizes. Additionally, reducing the number of sensors using a larger-pitch sensor array still maintained spatial resolution, making it possible to propose more efficient sensor sizes and quantities to facilitate the implementation of this approach in actual PET scanners.

articleTitle: Image-Domain Material Decomposition and Beam Hardening Correction for Photon-Counting CT
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Photon Counting Detector (PCD) of a photon counting CT (PCCT) can directly measure each x-ray photon energy, enabling the material decomposition and tissue differentiation. Compared to the detector domain material decomposition, the imaging domain material decomposition is compatible with the traditional CT imaging reconstruction frame work and has much better computing efficiency, while it could amplifier the noise and suffers from beam hardness effects. In this paper, we propose a new algorithm fully utilizing the spectral information of photon counting detectors to effectively resolve beam hardening artifacts.

articleTitle: A modular approach to building high-performance curved detectors for neutron scattering
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: We present a modular design for large-area, curved, thermal neutron detectors motivated by the requirements of the next generation of neutron-scattering instruments for efficient use of beamtime and high throughput. The base unit of the detector is a <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</sup>He-filled, multi-wire proportional chamber (MWPC) with an individual readout of all cathodes. Mounting multiple of these MWPC segments together inside a common pressure vessel permits the creation of a single, seamless detection area offering simultaneous measurement across a wide angular range and with uniform performance and characteristics. A two-segment prototype detector was built as a proof of principle and successfully tested at the TREFF beamline at FRM II. Subsequently two nine-segment detectors have been produced for the diffractometers ERWIN at FRM II and DMC at PSI. These detectors provide 130° horizontal and 14° vertical coverage (30° and 14° for the prototype) at a sample distance of 800 mm, have position resolution of 1.6 mm in both x and y, corresponding to ~0.1°, and have an efficiency of 75% at 1.8 Å. Event positions are reconstructed from the raw cathode signals in real time by the front-end electronics with a counting rate capability of 200 kHz per segment and event timestamping with 100-ns precision. The detector at DMC has been in user mode since September 2022 and early scattering data will be presented. Finally, we will discuss a planned future development of a vertically orientated detector for the instrument STRESS-SPEC.

articleTitle: Deep learning-based Radionuclide Identification for high temperature applications
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: We propose a deep learning-based radionuclide identification algorithm capable of accurately identifying nuclear isotopes even with temperature fluctuations. To detect radiation at high temperatures, we fabricated a radiation detector using a ruggedized PMT and Ce:GPS scintillator, which demonstrates promising performance in high temperature conditions. Our proposed deep learning architecture comprises five hidden layers and one fully connected layer. The accuracy of the proposed radionuclide identification algorithm was verified using radiation sources of <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">137</sup>Cs, <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">57</sup>Co, and <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">133</sup>Ba. The trained deep learning model could identify all classes with a high accuracy of almost 100% from spectra obtained at 25 ℃, 50 ℃, 100 ℃, and 150 ℃. Furthermore, the model demonstrated a relatively high classification performance of 96% and 85.2% in identifying radionuclides from spectra obtained at 75 ℃ and 125 ℃, respectively, which were not included in the training data. This finding validates that our suggested deep learning model can accurately identify nuclides, regardless of temperature fluctuations.

articleTitle: Sensitivity Measurement for Long Axial Field-of-View PET by Continuously Moving Acquisition
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Sensitivity is a key feature of a positron emission tomographic (PET) scanner which evaluate the rate of detected coincidence events from a radiation source inside the field-of-view (FOV). According to the traditional standards, a 70 cm line source with metal sleeves or a 70 cm IEC scatter phantom which covers the whole axial FOV of the scanner, is employed to perform the sensitivity measurements. To date, with the appearance of long axial FOV PET scanner, usually longer than 1 m, the 70 cm line source is incapable to fulfill the whole LAFOV. However, using a line source and metal sleeves with lengths comparable to the scanner length brings difficulties in the manufacture of experiment tools and experiment operations. To solve this problem, we propose a new method of sensitivity measurement for long axial FOV PET scanner by continuously moving acquisition with short phantom. Both short line source with metal sleeves and scatter phantom are tested, the initial result show that the sensitivity with moving phantom is comparable to the 2-meter line source.

articleTitle: Explore the Use of Nuclear Voltaic Batteries as Power Supplies for Monitoring Nuclear Fuel Cycles
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Nuclear batteries have the potential to be a unique power source in various industrial applications, such as space exploration, remote devices, IoT, and monitoring the nuclear fuel cycle. Voltaic batteries harness radiation energy by directly collecting charges from ionization in semiconductors, instead of converting decay heat to electricity through radioisotope thermoelectric generators. A significant challenge for voltaic batteries is the need for a large amount of radioisotope. However, this is not a problem in spent fuel storage applications where there is an abundance of radiation. This excess radiation energy can be used to power monitoring devices. We conducted research to explore the potential of harvesting radiation energy inside dry storage canisters using wide band gap (WBG) SiC energy transducers. We fabricated and assembled SiC energy transducers, and tested their power output in an intensive gamma-ray field. We also used Geant 4 simulation to predict the final power output at a scaled-up dimension and total weight. Our results show that it is possible to provide mW-level power through a credit-card-sized device.

articleTitle: Development of Red-Light Oxide-Scintillators and Evaluation of the Dose Rate Monitoring System for the Decommissioning
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: For the decommissioning of Nuclear Plants, the realtime dose-rate monitor under the high doserate situation is required to remove the debris. A dose rate monitor consisting of a scintillator, optical fiber and CCD spectrometer has been proposed, and scintillation photons are read with the CCD spectrometer under the lower dose condition. Since longer emission wavelength (goal: 650-1000 nm) and higher light output are required for this application, we focused on Nd-doped Y<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</inf>Al<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">5</inf>O<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">12</inf> (Nd:YAG) scintillator, which is known as a laser material with infra-red emission. Scintillation properties for Tb co-doped Nd:YAG crystals were investigated as well as Nd:YAG, because we expected Tb-codoped samples (Nd/Tb:YAG) to have higher light outputs compared to Nd:YAG. The emission wavelength of peak intensity was approximately 885 nm by X-ray excitation, and 0.05%Tb-doped samples showed higher intensity. After confirmation of the emission wavelength, we operated a demonstration of the monitoring system with Nd/Tb:YAG scintillator. The relation between signal intensity of the emission spectrum and dose rate for each sample was able to be fitted to a power function. We evaluated the lower limit of the dynamic range of dose rate, and the lowest one was 0.6%Nd0.05%Tb:YAG with a lower limit of approximately 0.2 Gy/h. Nd/Tb:YAG was found to be applied to the monitoring system.

articleTitle: CNN-based retrieval of x-ray phase-contrast images from experimental data
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Speckle-based x-ray phase-contrast imaging (XPCI) offers enhanced sensitivity towards weakly-attenuating materials – such as human tissue – and overcomes limitations of typical phase-contrast imaging systems due to less stringent requirements for setup geometry, coherence, and propagation distances. However, obtaining high-quality phase-contrast images requires accurate tracking of the near-field speckles generated by a random diffuser. A recently proposed speckle tracking method, convolutional-neural-network-based analysis (CADE), offers superior tracking performance, reduced computational times, and robustness to noise when compared to previous state-of-the-art methods but has only been validated on simulated displacements. In this study, we validated CADE on a simulated sine wave sample and experimental XPCI images of a plastic ball. CADE achieved good accuracy in displacement estimation with a simulated sample and further successfully extracted phase contrast signals from experimental imaging data. This brings the implementation of CADE in XPCI one step closer, broadening the potential of XPCI by introducing a novel, improved speckle tracking method.

articleTitle: 6LiInSe2 and 6LiIn0.5Ga0.5Se2 Semiconductor Thermal Neutron Detectors
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Semiconductor crystals of <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">6</sup>LiInSe<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf> and <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">6</sup>LiIn<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">0.5</inf>Ga<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">0.5</inf>Se<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf> were grown through Vertical Bridgman (VB) technique using enriched lithium (<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">6</sup>Li). The materials were characterized for electronic and optical properties. Thermal neutron detectors were fabricated and characterized. Pulse height spectra were collected from an <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">241</sup>AmBe neutron source and a <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">60</sup>Co gamma-ray source. The measured resistivity, bandgap and mobility lifetime product of the samples are reported and compared. The thermal neutron detection efficiency of the <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">6</sup>LiInSe<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf>, , and <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">6</sup>LiGaInSe<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf> were also estimated and reported using Geant4 simulation and was compared with the fundamental calculation. Furthermore, the devices performance at elevated temperature (~50 °C) and room-temperature (RT) were also experimentally investigated and the results were compared.

articleTitle: Development of a High Count-Rate X-ray Detector with Backscattering Geometry for Synchrotron Applications
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: We present the development of a new 16-channel SDD-based X-ray detector with a backscattering geometry, called ASCANIO, designed for experiments in synchrotron beamlines.The main objective of this research project, supported by DESY (Germany), is to improve the quality of X-ray Fluorescence Microscopy (XFM) experiments providing a larger throughput of events. The detection module consists of four monolithic SDDs, each with four channels, and a thickness of 1 mm to provide a high absorption efficiency of 65% at 20 keV. ASCANIO is optimised to maximise photon collection by having a solid angle of 1 sr with 8 mm between the sample and the window. To ensure count-rate capabilities higher than 20 Mcps, it implements an innovative tilted SDD geometry that provides a uniform distribution of fluorescence light among channels. The low-noise analog read-out assures good energy resolution of 129 eV with 2 μs peaking time and 175 eV with 32 ns peaking time. The development of ASCANIO will contribute to the enhancement of XFM experiments by making sample analysis more detailed and faster.

articleTitle: Validation and application of markerless head motion tracking for a next-generation brain PET scanner
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Head motion during brain PET imaging can introduce significant artifacts, reducing image resolution and affecting tracer distribution estimation. To address this issue, real-time head motion tracking and correction have become essential. In this study, we validate the United Imaging Healthcare markerless motion tracking system (UMT) embedded in the next-generation ultra-high performance brain PET scanner, NeuroEXPLORER (NX), using a phantom study and a human FDG study. We apply event-by-event and frame-based motion correction methods to reduce motion blurring and compare the UMT tracking result with the ground truth. Our results show that UMT achieves precise and real-time motion correction for rigid movements, with an error of 0.05 ± 0.04 mm and 0.02 ± 0.02°. The FWHM result demonstrates that employing UMT for motion tracking can improve spatial resolution. Human study results suggest that UMT-based motion correction has the potential to improve clinical applicability by ameliorating PET motion blurring. This study highlights the importance of real-time motion tracking and correction in achieving ideal spatial resolution and improving the clinical value of brain PET imaging. Future studies will focus on real-time motion correction in clinical studies and further evaluation of the UMT-based motion correction in NX.

articleTitle: Effect of Low Temperature on Charge Collection in 3D CdZnTe Detectors
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: The effect of temperature on detector properties and performance may vary detector-by-detector. In this work, four 2.2×2.2×1.0 cm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</sup> pixelated CdZnTe detectors were tested at 20°C and -10°C to study changes in detector efficiency below room-temperature. At -10°C, the overall photopeak efficiency decreased, and the change in efficiency varied on a pixel-by-pixel basis. It was found that at -10°C, increasing the detector bias voltage worsens the efficiency loss, whereas decreasing the bias can help improve charge collection. Collimator measurements showed that there is non-uniformity in the electron drift path, and that the distribution of charge collected can vary on a subpixel scale when temperature and bias are altered.

articleTitle: Comparing Transport Properties of Large-Volume CZT Bar Detectors in Using Different Material Producers
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: The transport properties of Large-Volume CZT Bar Detectors in using different material producers are compared in this paper. These gamma-ray detectors can achieve excellent energy resolution approaching the statistical limit provided that high-quality crystals with a low content of defects are used. To reduce the high cost of large-volume high quality CZT material, arrays of small cross section (~ 5x5 mm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sup>) were introduced in the form of 15 to 30 mm long bar detectors with high aspect ratio. The geometry of such bars is convenient to assemble them into a matrix arranged as virtual Frisch-grid detectors. An important task in any CZT detector design is how to minimize the effect of carrier trapping. Investigation and improvement of the transport properties represent a significant contribution to the optimization of the detection performance. We tested two crystals grown by high-pressure Bridgman (A bar- 6×6×19.5 mm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</sup>) and traveling heater method (B bar - 6×6×19.3 mm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</sup>) with Au/Au semi-transparent electrical contacts. Both CZT materials were obtained from an older production of the manufacturers. We characterized the transport properties by Laser-Induced Transient Currents (L-TCT). A continuous DC electric field up to 1 kV/cm was applied to record a bias-dependent set of electron current waveforms (CWF) for the cathode illumination of both detectors. The corresponding electric field profile is also shown. Significant polarization was found in both detectors. Bias pulsing was applied to suppress space charge formation and to measure the space charge dynamics. Depolarized CWFs up to 600 V were measured for both detectors in this setup. This approach allows us precise evaluation of mobility and lifetime of charge carriers.

articleTitle: Perovskite-based scintillators for time-of-flight PET
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Lead halide perovskite-based scintillators are attractive to develop fast timing detectors due to their high light output and fast response. In this study, we have synthesized perovskite nanoparticles with emission wavelengths ranging from 400 to 520 nm and integrated them into organic scintillators alone or together with other dopants. The light readout was accomplished using silicon photomultipliers with different peak wavelength efficiency. The detectors were characterized in terms of light output, luminescence and time response. Their use for the development of time of flight PET scanners are under study.

articleTitle: Versatile XLM72S logic module for real-time event filtering in multi-detector systems: Implementation in Compton-suppressed gamma-ray spectroscopy
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: The strong interaction, one of the four fundamental interactions governing the universe, does not directly act upon nucleons and nuclei but rather on their constituent quarks. As a result, understanding how the strong interaction manifests itself at nuclear length and energy scales is a complicated process. One manner used to study this so-called nuclear interaction is to detect emitted radiation from various nuclear processes such as radioactive decay. The energy and other observables such as angular momentum of emitted radiation can provide insight into the nuclear interaction itself. Multi-detector systems increase the range of studies that can be performed both by increasing the overall efficiency and by using time-correlated measurement techniques. With multi-detector systems, however, comes an increase in complexity, size, power consumption, and cost for data acquisition systems which can process and perform logical operations on raw signals. To combat this in the Nuclear Science Laboratory at Simon Fraser University, real-time event filtering has been implemented using a user programmable logic module called XLM72S. The logic module provides 72 emitter-coupled logic ports, configurable quartet-wise as inputs or outputs, an on-board 80 MHz clock, four digital clock managers capable of synthesizing additional clock frequencies, and two serial peripheral interface memories. In the current setup, the XLM72S allows for simultaneous and computer controlled logic to be performed on up to 20 Compton Suppressed Spectrometers used for the detection of gamma rays from nuclear decays, as well as up to 4 auxiliary signals used for filtering events which have coincident particle emission. The XLM72S module has been implemented and tested for a system containing five Compton Suppressed Spectrometers and a charged particle detector, demonstrating it's effectiveness at performing logic in real time for anti-coincident Compton Suppression and coincidence multi-fold events.

articleTitle: Joint Temporal and Multi-energy Processing for Photon-Counting Fluoroscopy
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Spectral imaging is being increasingly explored for interventional applications, but noise amplification resulting from material decomposition has traditionally impeded clinical adoption. To address this problem, we propose a novel joint processing strategy that utilizes both the pre- and post-contrast acquisitions in angiography applications. By acquiring spectral measurements in both images and jointly process them in a model-based material decomposition approach, we may simultaneously leverage temporal and spectral information to improve imaging performance beyond what is achievable through conventional approaches either information by itself - e.g., temporal subtraction, or spectral imaging using just the post-contrast measurements. Furthermore, the proposed strategy enables three material decomposition to be performed using just two spectral channels, allowing the separation of soft tissue, calcium, and exogenous contrast agent that is not possible using, for example, conventional digital subtraction angiography. We demonstrate the theoretical noise advantage of the joint processing strategy in simulation studies, and show initial experimental results of three material decomposition on a benchtop system with a photon counting detector.

articleTitle: Eclectic Process Modelling
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Modelling and documenting the processes involved in the lifecycle of scientific projects has become a key requirement for many funding agencies. Nevertheless, concepts, methods and tools available for this purpose, usually developed for industrial production processes, are often poorly suited to scientific research and may involve a heavy-weight bureaucratic burden. This presentation illustrates the strategy developed over the years by our research team to effectively address process modelling in computational physics projects, which has contributed to cope efficiently with pathbreaking topics, tight resources and ambitious schedules. Cowboy programming has been a widely popular software development practice for decades in particle and nuclear physics, and related fields. On the other extreme, cumbersome project and process management obligations are often imposed on physics research projects by funding agencies and institutional authorities, which are seldom perceived as beneficial to the achievement of scientific results. We have found our way between these extreme by devising an effective approach to model and document processes in computational physics research projects: it takes advantage of multiple modelling techniques - UML (Unified Modeling Language), BPMN (Business Process Model and Notation) and ArchiMate, which are combined to support different views of the project. This eclectic approach places special emphasis on ease of communication, so that even collaborators with minimal software engineering literacy can benefit from it. We illustrate and discuss some process modelling applications in real-life experimental projects. We report an archetypal case, associated with an initiative originated at IEEE NSS 2022, where the neglect of process modelling has resulted in comedic contradictions and, ultimately, in waste of resources and the failure of relevant research.

articleTitle: Crystal quality evaluation of a large TlBr crystal using neutron Bragg-dip imaging
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Thallium bromide (TlBr) is a compound semiconductor attractive for gamma-ray spectrometers. TlBr detectors have shown excellent energy resolution, however, these results were obtained from relatively small crystal detectors. The next phase of TlBr development is to increase the detector size and improve the yield rate of detector production. So far, we have evaluated crystal quality of TlBr by using the neutron Bragg-dip imaging, which is one of the neutron diffraction techniques. In this study, we prepared a large TlBr crystal wafer with a diameter and thickness of 50 mm and 12 mm, respectively. We evaluated the quality of the large crystal by the neutron Bragg-dip imaging. The center region of the large TlBr crystal confirmed to be uniform and well-aligned. As a future work, we will evaluate the electric properties, such as the mobility-lifetime product, at various positions in this large crystal.

articleTitle: Preliminary field measurements with the MuPIC detector for portable muon tomography
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: The Muon Portable Imager for Counter-terrorism (MuPIC) detector is a compact plastic scintillator-based portable muon tomography system for field use that is currently undergoing testing and development at the Canadian Nuclear Laboratories (CNL). Imaging algorithms for muon scattering tomography and attenuation-based muon computed tomography were developed and adapted for use with MuPIC, along with a nonparametric dense-object detection algorithm. A series of experiments and field measurements were executed to evaluate the performance of the MuPIC detector in conjunction with these algorithms.

articleTitle: Initial Results of a Prototype AWSM-PET Device for Augmented Whole-body PET Imaging
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: The Augmented Whole-body Scanning via Magnifying PET (AWSM-PET) is a technology designed to enhance the diagnostic accuracy of whole-body (WB) PET/CT imaging for the detection of small lesions. We recently constructed the first prototype AWSM-PET device that consists of two panels of high-resolution time-of-flight (TOF) PET detectors (using ~1mm pitched LSO crystals), integrated with the standard readout electronics and event processing architecture of the Siemens Biograph Vision scanner. The system exhibits excellent spatial, energy and timing resolution, with an average coincidence resolving time of ~183 ps FWHM and an average energy resolution of ~11% FWHM at 511 keV. Custom firmware and software have been developed to encode the large number of detector elements and to enable coincidence detection between the AWSM-PET detectors and the Biograph Vision scanner.Initial tests of the AWSM-PET device show the image resolution of the Biograph Vision scanner is improved from the original >3mm to ~2mm FWHM. A GPU-based list-mode image reconstruction framework has been expanded to incorporate the point-spread function (PSF) of the native scanner and the AWSM-PET detectors to optimize the spatial resolution and improve image quality.Standard step-and-shoot and continuous-bed motion imaging protocols are supported for the AWSM-PET operation and are being evaluated for the reconstructed image resolution and the uniformity of the overall system sensitivity across a long axial FOV. Extensive phantom imaging studies are ongoing to evaluate the system's performance. Initial human imaging studies will be presented in the upcoming 2023 Medical Imaging Conference.

articleTitle: Fine-tuned BERT Language Model for Efficient Nuclear Medicine Data Retrieval
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Efficient data retrieval is crucial in medical databases, where quick access to relevant patient information can significantly impact data management. In this work, we propose an Natural language processing (NLP)-based approach for predicting the type of scan from nuclear medicine reports to enable efficient data retrieval. We utilized a deep learning approach, using the fine-tuned BERT model, to classify the scan type based on the finding. The scan types we predicted include 51 different classes, such as MPI SPECT, Whole-Body Bone Scans, Thyroid Scans, and Lung Perfusion. To train and evaluate the model, we used a 75/10/15 split for the training, evaluation, and test phases, respectively. The radiology reports were generated by different nuclear medicine physicians with varying years of experience, ensuring a high variability of the dataset. We evaluated our model on various types of scans and achieved an accuracy of 98% on a dataset consisting of 36,000 nuclear medicine reports from different centers. Our proposed approach has the potential to significantly improve the efficiency of data retrieval from medical databases by automating the process of extracting scan names from radiology reports. This will enable faster and more accurate retrieval of relevant information for medical professionals, thus improving the quality of patient care.

articleTitle: Imaging Studies of PETcoil: a Second-Generation RF-Penetrable Brain TOF-PET Insert for Simultaneous PET/MRI
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Simultaneous positron emission tomography/magnetic resonance imaging (PET/MRI) has unique advantages in providing complementary, concurrent information about anatomic, functional, and molecular changes in diseases. We are developing an MR-compatible RF-penetrable brain time-of-flight (TOF)-PET insert with a smaller scintillation crystal size and smaller PET ring diameter compared to clinical whole-body PET scanners, resulting in higher spatial resolution and sensitivity. This paper reports the phantom studies of our second-generation RF-penetrable PET insert with the full system assembled. In the resolution phantom study, the system resolved all 2.8 mm diameter rods and showed a 1.34 SNR gain after applying TOF information. The Hoffman phantom study showed a high-quality 3D reconstructed image even without attenuation and scatter correction. We plan to report MR compatibility evaluation of the full 16-detector ring PET insert in the near future.

articleTitle: Proton-Induced Radiation Damage in Twenty cm Long LYSO:Ce and BaF2:Y Crystals
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Inorganic scintillators are widely used in high-energy physics (HEP) experiments. Bright and fast cerium doped lutetium yttrium oxyorthosilicate (Lu<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2(1−x)</inf>Y<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2x</inf>SiO<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">5</inf>:Ce or LYSO:Ce) crystals have been chosen to construct the CMS barrel timing layer (BTL) detector at the high luminosity large hadron collider (HL-LHC), where up to 2.5 Mrad ionization dose, 1.7 × 10<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">13</sup> charged hadrons/cm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sup> and 2 × 10<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">14</sup> n<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">eq</inf>/cm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sup> are expected. With an ultrafast scintillation of less than 0.6 ns decay time and a suppressed slow component yttrium doped BaF<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf> (BaF<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf>:Y) crystal is a promising ultrafast inorganic scintillator for future HEP time of flight and calorimeter applications at the energy and intensity frontiers. Twenty cm long LYSO:Ce and BaF<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf>:Y crystals were irradiated by 800 MeV proton beam at the blue room of Los Alamos Neutron Science Center (LANSCE) up to 7.5 × 10<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">15</sup> p/cm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sup>. We report degradation of their optical and scintillation properties.

articleTitle: Advancements in TOF-PET using DOI Capable Modules and Low-Noise High-Frequency Readout
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Achieving good time resolution has become a prerequisite in positron emission tomography (PET) to improve the signal-to-noise ratio and thus the quality of the reconstructed image. A particularly attractive solution for the electronic readout is using low-noise high-frequency circuits (HF), which have demonstrated excellent timing performance in time-of-flight (TOF)-PET applications. With improvements in the achievable coincidence time resolution (CTR), the effect of light transport and gamma-ray depth of interaction (DOI) along the crystal axis becomes a dominant contribution that must be mitigated. To address this issue, a light-sharing mechanism using a matrix of scintillators coupled to an array of SiPMs can be employed to identify the DOI and correct for the induced bias. For the light-sharing method to work, readout integration in a multi-channel scheme is required. The use of HF circuits allows to lower the leading edge detection threshold, enabling the use of the fastest photons produced in the crystals and thereby overcoming the limitation of the NINO amplifier-discriminator chip. Previous studies have shown that the Hamamatsu S13361-3050AE-04 SiPM array and NINO amplifier-discriminator chip-based readout electronics achieved CTR values of 160 ps FWHM using an array of 16 LYSO crystals measuring 3.1x3.1x15 mm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</sup>. In this study, we present the performance improvement achieved by integrating this detector prototype into a 16-channel HF readout board. We outline the current limitations and solutions to overcome them.

articleTitle: Low-dose cerebral perfusion CT imaging based on a kinetic induced voxel-clustering filter (KVCF)
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Cerebral perfusion CT (PCT) is an effective imaging technique for the clinical diagnosis and therapy guidance of many kinds of cerebrovascular diseases (CVDs), but the large radiation dose imposed on a patient during repeated CT scans greatly limits its clinical applications. Low-dose PCT imaging is meaningful and, however, has long been challenging. In this work, we propose a kinetic-induced voxel-clustering filter (KVCF), based on which low-dose PCT images can be effectively denoised and corrected via repeated filtering operations. In our experiments, simulated PCT data were used to evaluate the KVCF method. Quantitative metrics, such as the peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR) and feature similarity (FSIM), are applied to measure the imaging accuracy and noise reduction effect of the KVCF. The KVCF method is compared to the well-known NLM and HYPR methods in our experiments, and the results show that the proposed KVCF method yields the best imaging results: the best visual effects as well as the highest framewise PSNR and FSIM values are provided by KVCF. The KVCF method is an effective PCT image postprocessing algorithm with high interpretability, which is likely to help promote the application of the PCT technique in clinical CVD diagnosis.

articleTitle: Efficacy of MOSkins in BreastCT Dosimetry
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: MOSkin is a radiation detector that is equipped to output the dose at the surface of the skin during radiography and radiotherapy procedures. With the commencement of the clinical trials using Synchrotron based computed tomography (CT) imaging for the breast, MOSkins are characterised for their energy dependence with Synchrotron mono-energetic beams, calibrated respective to PTW ionisation chambers. MOSkins are energy dependent at energies <100keV and requires energy correction of the calibration factor (Gy/V). For a synchrotron CT, using an ellipsoid gelatin breast phantom, MOSkin results show a 3x more dose delivered at the entry of the breast compared to the centre, with a decrease in entry dose once as the energy increases once normalised to the centre dose in the breast. Simulation results generated from GEANT4 using Livermore Physics present us with the same trends and results within error. MOSkins can be used to determine breast imaging doses with an energy-calibrated correction factor. Correct entry dose measurements for imaging beams and synchrotron CT beams ensure dose-tissue tolerances are met for radiosensitive breast tissue in clinical trials.

articleTitle: Study on the Energy Resolution Degradation at Low Cathode Bias for the Pixelated CdZnTe Detectors
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: For CdZnTe detectors, the energy resolution usually improves at a higher cathode bias. However, there are many practical benefits to operate pixelated CdZnTe detectors at lower cathode biases. This study explores the factors limiting the energy resolution at lower cathode bias. Measurements using the digital ASICs are presented and discussed. Effects of trapping, material defects, shaping and data sampling are investigated. Methods to mitigate the energy resolution degradation are proposed.

articleTitle: AI-Driven Approach for Accurate Gamma-Ray energy deposition Localization in Pixelated Scintillators
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Energy deposition location of gamma-ray interactions in pixelated scintillators using multiplexed electronic readout is commonly determined through classical centroiding based on Anger Logic. However, this methods are strongly susceptible to effects that cause a worsening of their performance along the peripheries of the readout pixels. We propose the use of neural network-based positioning algorithms that can be directly applied in the front-end pulse processing electronics pipeline, enabling faster and more precise positioning identification. As an exploratory alternative, it was also considered an ensemble of bagged decision trees. For the experiments, a Na<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">22</sup> positron source was used to generate 511 keV annihilation gamma rays, whose capture and measurement were conducted in two channels with a LYSO scintillator connected to one of 16 positions at a time in a multiplexed array of SiPMs. The present research involved a thorough investigation of various neural network approaches and architectures to classify our data. In addition to multiclass neural networks, we explored the potential of 16 binary and 16 neighbour neural networks. The resulting analysis provided a comprehensive understanding that these methods are advantageous compared to the conventional method, enabling to identify the energy deposition location more effectively. For the multiclass classification, it was obtained an average accuracy and a gain of well-classified events over the Anger Logic algorithm of 89,44% and 32,51%, respectively. For the binary approach, 88,83% and 30,05%, respectively. Furthermore, the first-near neighbour approach reached 89,96% and 34,93%, respectively. On the other hand, the ensemble bagged decision trees approach got up to 90,49% and 37,38%, respectively. These results showcase the potential of our proposed approach to streamline the energy deposition location determination process.

articleTitle: Adaptive CNN Models for X-ray Scatter Correction in CBCT: A Transfer Learning Strategy
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: In recent years, convolutional neural networks (CNN) have demonstrated potential to perform xray scatter corrections, but there are still challenges to effectively use CNN: first, deep learning models benefit from large volumes of data. Second, it is not clear how generalizable these models are. In this work, a framework to address the previously described challenges by means of transfer learning (TL) and data simulation is proposed. The use of TL allowed adapting a pretrained CNN to specialized tasks, with relatively small volumes of data and in a fast manner. A data simulation approach enabled to easily generate tailored training datasets for given acquisition settings and anatomical regions. The pretraining was performed using geometric phantom data, while TL was achieved using anthropomorphic data. For the pretraining stage, it was observed that scatter ratio (SR) predictions were accurate (SSIM~0.8). This was further improved after TL, with a relatively short retraining time (~13 times faster than pretraining) and using considerably fewer samples compared to the pretraining dataset (~5 times smaller). In conclusion, a fast and low-cost methodology to generate task-specific CNN for scatter correction in CBCT was developed. CNN models trained with the proposed methodology were successful to correct x-ray scatter in anthropomorphic structures, unknown to the network, for simulated data.

articleTitle: Deep Patient Motion Estimation: Pretraining, Overfitting, or Pretraining and Overfitting?
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: When a patient moves during a CBCT scan, for instance by breathing, the resulting reconstruction is likely to show motion artifacts, e.g. blurring. If the internal motion of the patient is known, it becomes possible to compensate for the motion during reconstruction and produce a volume with little to no motion artifacts. Many methods exist to determine a vector field that deforms a source volume to appear like a destination volume. A known neural network approach to this problem is called VoxelMorph. It is trained in an unsupervised manner to produce a deformation vector field that minimizes the difference between the transformed source and the destination. A network trained in such a manner may be trained on the data it will be applied to, removing the need for pretraining the network on other data. This process is often referred to as overfitting. This study examines if a similar approach works for estimating breathing motion from CBCT scans and the effects pretraining and overfitting have on a similar neural network to register a target source onto a destination, and whether this is advantageous.

articleTitle: Lesion Detectability and Image Quality Evaluation for High-Sensitivity Digital-BGO PET/CT System
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Lesion detectability in PET/CT is often challenging in clinical scenarios that includes high attenuation, scatter and randoms. We studied the impact of sensitivity on small lesion detectability and image quality in Omni Legend 32 system (GE HealthCare), compared to Discovery MI 25 cm (GE HealthCare), with TOF performance of 385 psec and NEMA sensitivity of 21 cps/kBq. Omni Legend 32 cm is based on 4×4×30 mm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</sup> bismuth germanate crystals coupled to silicon photomultipliers (digital-BGO). This scanner features ultra-high NEMA sensitivity of 46 cps/kBq, as well as high spatial resolution of 3.6 mm (2.5 mm for BSREM reconstruction), and energy resolution on 9.8%.For small lesion detectability evaluation, uniformly filled IEC phantom was scanned; then synthetic spherical lesions with a diameter as small as 4 mm and lesion to background ratio of 3:1 were digitally inserted. Independent and identically distributed noise realizations were replayed at activity concentrations of 5.2-3.4 kBq/ml and reconstructed using OSEM, OSEM-PSF and BSREM. Reconstructed images were analyzed using channelized Hotelling model observer.<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">[1]</sup> It was found that Omni Legend 32 cm increases small lesion detectability by 16% on average and up to 20%, compared to the Discovery MI 25 cm TOF PET/CT with matched scan time/injected dose.For clinically-relevant image quality assessment, and the enhancement gained by the deep learning-based TOF reconstruction (Precision DL),<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">[2]</sup> a phantom study was performed using Oval PET phantom with small spheres<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">[3]</sup> ranging from 8 mm to 13 mm. The phantom was filled with FDG, maintaining a sphere to background ratio of 4:1. To reach high count rates, the background activity at scan start was 14.2 kBq/ml, and decayed to clinically relevant activities ~4 kBq/ml. The impact on image enhancement was evaluated using contrast recovery, background variability and contrast to noise ratio calculated for various activities, noise equivalent count and scan times.

articleTitle: Novel Mixed-Field Neutron-Gamma Borehole Detectors for Deuterium-Tritium Pulsed Neutron Well-Logging
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: This work reports simulated results and detector designs for a novel borehole detector consisting of cylindrically coupled custom-made plastic scintillator and BN:ZnS(Ag) thermal neutron converter foils. A monolithic detector was simulated within a mock borehole configuration under a 14 MeV pulsed neutron flux to test detector response to induced radiation from test materials. A data set was built up from simulations of 500 different test materials containing varying quantities of Carbon, Hydrogen, and Oxygen, and used to train several models to make predictions of Hydrogen content. Detector heatmaps (position and time-after-pulse) were used as training data. An example detector with 12 z-bins predicted H-content to within +/-1% in 58% of cases using random forests. Results showed that higher segmentation offers no significant advantage over conventional dual-binned detectors. This work will also report on manufacture and testing of custom-made plastic scintillator which will be coupled to BN:ZnS(Ag) thermal neutron converter foils as part of isolated detector modules.

articleTitle: Design and First Measurement Results for the Revision 4 of AARDVARC Waveform Sampling System On Chip
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: In this article we describe the design and initial measurement results of revision 4 "rev4" of the Advanced ASoC Rapid Digitizer, Variable Readout Chip (AARDVARC). AARDVARC is a 8-channel waveform digitizing and processing Application Specific Integrated Circuit (ASIC) front-end. We will report on the diverse improvements from the previous design and detail the performance in comparison to the previous revision.

articleTitle: Fully FPGA-based Compact Pulse-Width-Modulated Tunable Threshold Comparator Circuit for Time-to-Digital Converters
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Recent developments in nuclear electronics have resulted in significant progress in time interval measurements. Detectors can now achieve timing performance in the order of tens of ps, requiring Time-to-Digital Converters (TDCs) that provide not only high-precision matching the detector’s jitter but also a large number of channels for parallel data acquisition. Designers are increasingly turning to fully-digital solutions, such as Field-Programmable Gate Arrays (FPGAs), due to its ability to offer flexibility in measurement setup and fast-prototyping. Proper discrimination of the analog signal output from detectors is crucial for accurately acquiring temporal information. The most suitable circuit for this task is the tunable Threshold Comparator (TC), due to its compactness. Various TC circuits can be found in the literature, whose threshold is generated using a Digital-to-Amplitude Converter (DAC) and the discrimination is performed by a ultra-fast comparator guaranteeing a jitter lower than few ps. However, in this solution the presence of the DAC significantly increases the circuit’s area occupancy, while the use of an ultra-fast comparator can dramatically increase power dissipation (up to tens of mW per channel). In this paper, we propose a fully FPGA-based architecture for a TC and TDC, targeting Xilinx 28-nm 7-Series FPGAs. Our design eliminates the need for an external comparator and replaces the DAC with a compact external Low-Pass Filter (LPF); additionally, we employ a Pulse-Width Modulator (PWM) implemented in firmware to achieve the desired threshold level. The proposed approach leads to a noteworthy reduction in power consumption (tens of mW) and hardware resources, while providing a comparable jitter performance worsen only by a factor 5 with respect a classical state-of-the-art TC circuit. Finally, the presented TC is interfaced with a compact multi-channels (up to 103) TDC with hundreds of picoseconds resolution (up to 156 ps) in a Axtix-7.

articleTitle: Assessment of new, photon counting specific triggering schemes to mitigate spectral distortion
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Photon counting (PC) techniques are central to the next generation of x-ray imaging systems. The interaction of an x-ray with a semiconductor sensor causes a transient rise in the voltage associated with the sensor output. In the standard (STD) approach to PC, a counter is incremented each time the sensor output voltage rises above a given threshold, thus counting the number of photons that are detected. By using multiple, different thresholds, the STD approach can be extended to provide x-ray photon counting spectral imaging (x-CSI). Using Monte Carlo and Finite Element tools, we demonstrate that the STD approach in x-CSI can give rise to spectral distortions which differ from those seen in other spectroscopic modalities, even resulting in negative number of photons being counted. These results are shown to hold over a wide range of sensor thicknesses (1 – 3 mm), pixel pitches (100 – 600 µm) and number of energy thresholds (3 – 130), though they depend heavily on the x-ray flux (fluxes of 10<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">6</sup>–10<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">9</sup> photons mm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">−2</sup> s<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">−1</sup> were modelled). Crucially, we demonstrate that these distortions are often mistaken for other sources of noise and that may be present under medically relevant conditions. We proposed a range of alternatives to the STD counting scheme, designed to minimise negative count based distortions. Count rate and spectral efficiency for each proposed scheme were compared with both an ideal system and the STD approach. Current results indicate spectral distortion can be reduced significantly (by up to 62%) at medically relevant fluxes by choosing one of the best performing counting schemes. Detailed analysis of how performance varies with all simulated variables will be presented at the conference.

articleTitle: A Pulse Processing Method for Well Logging Based on MVT
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: As a direct digitized scintillation pulse sampling method, the multi-voltage threshold (MVT) method has gained widespread attention due to its full digitized, accurate sampling advantage, and has proven its excellent performance and application potential in PET. This article applies the MVT method to the field of well logging, which requires us to achieve real-time acquisition of gamma energy spectra with wide amplitude range, high counting rate, and high energy resolution. In this scenario, the speed and accuracy of MVT calculation of scintillation pulse energy are closely related to the pulse model selection and fitting implementation method. This article chooses the Gaussian function as the pulse model to take advantage of its simple circuit structure and easy back-end processing, samples Gaussian-shaped pulses with amplitude distribution ranging from 200mV to 2000mV, and then uses linear least square fitting to obtain pulse energy information. Finally, without widening the original pulse, the extraction of pulse energy has been completed. The energy resolution of the characteristic peaks of Na-22 and Cs-137 obtained under LaBr<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</inf> / PMT detection are 7.79% and 6.79%, respectively.

articleTitle: Fiber-coupled GAGG scintillators for real-time small-field dosimetry in FLASH proton therapy
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: FLASH radiation therapy (RT) has been recently proposed as a novel modality that features reduced toxicity to healthy tissue while maintaining the same antitumor efficacy as conventional radiotherapy. FLASH-RT is characterized by the delivery of ultra-high dose rates (> 40 Gy/s) in sub-second treatment times. Real-time beam monitoring and dosimetry for FLASH are challenging and new approaches have been proposed to address this issue. Along this line, novel detectors based on fiber-coupled scintillators are under development at the University of Bern. This work reports on the characterization of a detector prototype made of a sample of Cerium-doped Gadolinium Aluminum Gallium Garnet (Ce:GAGG) of size (0.5×0.5×2) mm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</sup> coupled to an optical fiber. The scintillation light pulses are driven to a single photon detector and to a multi-channel scaler operated at 10 kHz sampling rate. Functional tests have been performed at the Francis H. Burr Proton Therapy Center at the Massachusetts General Hospital (Boston, MA) with 227.5 MeV proton beams. The detector response was found to be linear in the range 4-120 Gy/s (maximum dose rate available). We compared the GAGG depth dose curve with that of a reference ion chamber and of a rectifier diode. We observed a reduction of the GAGG signal which is likely due to quenching effects and loss of in-scattering contribution in the sub-millimeter volume of the scintillator, and is currently under investigation. Overall, the proposed system has been found to be suitable for real-time ultra-high dose rate small field dosimetry and it is promising for quality assurance, beam monitoring and in-vivo dosimetry for FLASH therapy.

articleTitle: Performance Evaluation of the Detector Blocks used in the IMAS Total-Body
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Positron Emission Tomography (PET) is a non-invasive imaging modality used to provide information on the internal function of the human or animal body. Recent tendency has been to increase the axial Field of View (FOV) coverage of scanners as a means to increase signal-to-noise ratio (SNR). This has led to the development of total body (TB) PET systems. Further increase in SNR can also be achieved by including time-of-flight (TOF) capabilities. Moreover, retrieving photon depth of interaction (DOI) information allows one to reduce parallax error and obtain a homogeneous FOV spatial resolution.Despite being a challenge, constructing detectors able to simultaneously provide TOF and DOI information results in an increased manufacturing cost due to the large volumes of scintillators and photosensors but also, to the huge number of channels to be digitized. This fact makes TB-PET devices inaccessible for most clinical facilities. To alleviate this problem, the IMAS project focuses on building cost-effective TB-PET technology.In this work, we show the performance of the detectors implemented for the IMAS TB-PET, which is currently being installed at the hospital La Fe in Valencia (Spain). The read-out electronics comprises a highly multiplexed circuitry able to reduce the number of channels by a factor of 4 while maintaining temporal performance in the range of 350 ps, as well as DOI capabilities using thick LYSO scintillator crystals in a semi-monolithic geometry.

articleTitle: Cost-effective Total-Body PET with Axial and Transverse Gaps
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: With significantly higher sensitivity compared to conventional PET, total-body PET offers improvements in image quality and quantification to enable faster scan times, lower dose, and new applications with novel tracers. However, the higher system cost hinders wide application of total-body PET technology in the clinic. Cost-effective total-body PET designs using fewer detectors in sparse configurations can be a potential solution. This paper aims to design sparse PET systems with both axial and transverse gaps, acquire and reconstruct patient images with no artifacts, and evaluate lesion quantification and detectability in these systems by leveraging the advantages of time-of-flight (TOF) technology. Taking PennPET Explorer as a template, two sparse configurations maintaining the same long axial field of view (LAFOV) of 142 cm were designed with the same total detector saving of 43% (around 1/3 of all line of response (LORs) remain). One design, called Sparse PET MT, includes more transverse gaps, while the second design with more axial gaps is called Sparse PET MA. We acquired patient data on the PennPET Explorer and generated data from Sparse PET MT and MA by discarding missing LORs. We embedded lesion data with varying uptake levels in lung and liver regions of measured patient FDG data. Images were analyzed using bias and precision metrics in measured lesion uptake as well using generalized scan statistics methodology to estimate lesion detectability. Our results show that the two sparse PET designs provide comparable lesion uptake measurement to the PennPET Explorer with no visual artifacts in a 1 min scan. Detailed evaluation will be performed for lesion quantitation and detectability measurements as a function of varying lesion uptake values.

articleTitle: Long range imaging of alpha emitters using alpha induced radio-luminescence
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Heavy nuclides like uranium and their decay products are commonly found in nuclear industries and can pose a significant health risk to humans due to their alpha-emitting properties. Traditional alpha detectors require direct contact with the contaminated surface, which can be time-consuming, labor-intensive, and puts personnel at risk. In this study, we propose a novel technique called alpha-induced radio-luminescence that uses the emission of photons by excited nitrogen molecules to detect alpha emitters at long distances, from meters to tens of meters away. We were able to detect a 3MBq Am241 source at a distance of 30 meter in 5 minutes, both in room light environment and inside a glovebox. This technology can greatly enhance remote alpha monitoring, nuclear forensics, and contamination limiting during decommissioning. By detecting the photons emitted by excited nitrogen molecules, we can locate alpha emitters without the need for direct contact, reducing the risks associated with conventional detection methods. Our findings demonstrate the feasibility of this technique and its potential for widespread application in nuclear industries, providing a safer and more efficient approach to detect and monitor alpha emitters.

articleTitle: ViSERA: Visualized & Standardized Environment for Radiomics Analysis - A Shareable, Executable, and Reproducible Workflow Generator
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Medical image computing software development is essential for discovering novel image biomarkers in clinical research, which can improve patient outcomes by enabling more effective diagnosis and treatment strategies. However, a lack of standardized and user-friendly software environments has impeded their widespread adoption. This study presents the Visualized & Standardized Environment for Radiomics Analysis (ViSERA) software to address this challenge. The modular software provides a flexible platform for reliable and easy-to-use image reading from different modalities and formats, image registration, image fusion, image processing, image visualization, image segmentation, radiomics feature extraction, and machine learning model development. ViSERA offers a modular approach to medical image analysis, allowing users with different expertise levels to execute each module independently or combine them with other components. The output of one module can be fed as input to another module, enabling users to create custom, executable, and reproducible workflows with multiple steps. Further, the results of each module execution can be viewed directly in the visualization window, providing immediate feedback on the accuracy and effectiveness of each step. This modular approach offers flexibility and customization options to researchers and clinicians, making it easier to perform reliable and reproducible radiomics research in clinical practice settings. Furthermore, ViSERA offers a convenient way to save and share customized workflows with other users, promoting reproducibility, reusability, and transparency in medical image analysis. This feature is particularly useful for collaborative research projects and for ensuring consistency across different studies. This key feature and user-friendliness make it accessible for researchers at different skill levels, including radiation oncologists, radiologists, physicists, and data scientists.

articleTitle: Investigating Intensity Normalisation for PET Reconstruction with Supervised Deep Learning
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Deep learning methods have shown great promise in the field of Positron Emission Tomography (PET) reconstruction, but the successful application of these methods depends heavily on the intensity scale of the images. Normalisation is a crucial step that aims to adjust the intensity of network inputs to make them more uniform and comparable across samples, acquisition times, and activity levels. In this work, we study the influence of different linear intensity normalisation approaches. We focus on two popular deep learning based image reconstruction methods: an unrolled algorithm (Learned Primal-Dual) and a post-processing method (OSEMConvNet). Results on the out-of-distribution test dataset demonstrate that the choice of intensity normalisation significantly impacts on generalisability of these methods. Normalisation using the mean of acquisition data or corrected acquisition data led to improved peak-signal-to-noise-ratio (PSNR) and data-consistency (KLDIV). Through evaluation of lesion-specific metrics of contrast recovery coefficients (CRC) and standard deviation (STD) an increase in CRC and STD is observed. These findings highlight the importance of carefully selecting an appropriate normalisation method for supervised deep learning-based PET reconstruction applications.

articleTitle: Reconstruction of Sub-Pixel Interaction Locations using Principal Component Analysis
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Pixelated CdZnTe gamma-ray detectors have proven to be versatile tools for characterization of radiation fields in unknown spaces. This is due in part to their fine spatial resolution, allowing for high fidelity radiation images. The position of radiation interactions can be determined to subpixel precision by analyzing non-collecting pixel signals. Recent electronics allow for the recording of full event waveforms from these non-collecting pixels, offering an improvement in position resolution compared to traditional analog processing electronic chains. However, the relationship between signal waveform and subpixel position is complicated and it is challenging to design an algorithm that makes the best use of the available information to reconstruct the position. We demonstrate a position reconstruction technique based on principal component analysis of the signal waveforms. A calibration method is presented and discussed, and an improvement over the traditional neighbor-ratio based techniques is demonstrated in experiment using a Cs-137 source. The position resolution with a coarse-level implementation is improved by 25 µm relative to the classic techniques.

articleTitle: Utilising machine learning techniques for analysis, generation and compression of data for a single photon counting detector
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: This research details approaches to training neural networks with a hybrid approach of using empirical and generative data from trained variational auto-encoders (VAE), which aim to generate realistic single photon events. Using machine learning techniques to traverse the latent space within the VAE allows generation of novel training samples as experimental set up is no longer a constraint. Furthermore, this permits for calculation of statistical guarantees of the robustness of the model, which will be detailed within the paper.In this work, machine learning (ML) is being explored as a potential solution for performing real time data processing and imaging of single photon events. Photek's development of a 256 Micro-Channel Plate Photo-Multiplier Tube (MCP-PMT) to further increase the spatial resolution while maintaining single photon timing resolution using charge sharing techniques would enable a novel commercial camera system. This would be designed so that each channel is an independent photon detector allowing for single photon counting possibilities which would advance fields such as particle physics. However electronic capabilities to measure increasing photon rates have introduced a bottleneck in the path of real time data processing using current algorithmic software. Hence, the objective of this investigation is to utilise ML techniques to reconstruct the photon event in both spatial and temporal coordinates with a time constraint 10mus per single photon event. The results demonstrate the ML model's success in reconstructing photon events, further work discusses the performance of the reconstructive model comparatively trained and tested with both empirical and generative data. Concluding remarks in the work discuss the viability in using auto-encoders for data compression, in fields whereby data rates are unmanageable.

articleTitle: Cadmium Zinc Telluride (CZT)-Based PET Scanner for Plant Rhizosphere Imaging
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: The soil interacts with the plant’s roots in the rhizosphere, altering its physical, chemical, and biological processes. Understanding and simulating the behavior of the soil-root interface (Rhizosphere) will help us understand the limitations of the existing Earth System Model (ESM), which make it difficult to predict climate change with sufficient accuracy under different conditions. We are currently developing a cadmium zinc telluride (CZT) based high resolution positron emission tomography (PET) scanner for plant rhizosphere imaging. In this paper, we report the preliminary imaging performance of a two panel CZT-PET scanner. In this phantom study, the roots of the plant were represented by a custom manufactured container that houses 5-capillary tubes with inner diameter ~1.3 mm placed at various distances from the center.
