Two cases were investigated. 1), F-18 filled capillaries in air with no soil; 2) F-18 filled capillaries with organic soil present to simulate the root system of a plant. All 5 capillary rods could be resolved in both cases with 2.04 ± 0.18 mm and 2.29 ± 0.24 mm FWHM resolution measured from a line profile taken through the capillaries in the tomographic images in the x and y directions (i.e., x and y form a plane orthogonal to the capillary tube direction). Deconvolving the X.Y mm capillary inner diameter yields 1.85 ±0.29 and 1.57±-.23 mm FWHM, respectively, indicating excellent resolution required for resolving biological information in individual root structures. In our next experiment, this two-panel system will be utilized to collect images of a real plant rhizosphere.

articleTitle: Deep learning-based dynamic parametric image generation with static perfusion computed tomography
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Myocardial blood flow can reflect the hemodynamic status of the myocardium and play a crucial role in the diagnosis of myocardial ischemia. However, the derivation of myocardial blood flow requires a series of dynamic-computed tomography perfusion scans, which lead to high radiation exposure. We explore a convolutional neural network-based parametric image generation method for accessing parametric images without dynamic scans. With a simulated static computed tomography perfusion scan as the input, the network can generate corresponding myocardial blood flow. With the assistance of bolus triggering, this method can realize accessibility of myocardial blood flow even without dynamic computed tomography perfusion, therefore reducing the radiation dosage in radiology examination and significantly boosting the duration of postprocessing. First, we pretrained the network with the averaged dynamic computed tomography perfusion scans for better default parameters. Fine-tuning with the simulated static computed tomography perfusion scans was then implemented for desired end-to-end image translation. The performance of the issued image translation method was evaluated by using the usual image rating criteria and a clinical functional assessment. The results illustrated that the synthetic image quality is fine and that the clinical functionality of the synthetic myocardial blood flow is satisfactory. The proposed method showed great potential in dose reduction; the effective dosage was reduced by 90% in our cases and the postprocessing time was shortened from 19 minutes to approximately 10 seconds.

articleTitle: Simultaneous Perfusion-Metabolism Imaging with 18F-FDG Positron Emission Tomography
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Perfusion-glucose metabolism imaging with positron emission tomography (PET) has utility in cancer among other diseases in identifying a mismatch between vascular delivery of glucose and its utilization in tissue. PET perfusion-metabolism requires serial imaging with a flow radiotracer and <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">18</sup>F-fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG), which is resource intensive. We hypothesized that perfusion and glucose metabolism can be simultaneously estimated with a flow-modified two-tissue compartment kinetic model (F2TCM) applied to FDG-PET studies. The F2TCM is a time-domain approximation to a distributed parameter (DP) model without a closed-form time domain solution. A basis function and exponential spectral analysis-based method were used to estimate the seven F2TCM parameters. We validated the F2TCM by estimating parameters from synthetic tissue time-activity curves generated with the DP model over 1024 trials of PET-like noise simulations. The mean ± standard deviation bias in estimated perfusion versus the ground truth over 1024 noise trials and ten DP parameter sets was -6.1 ± 5.7% with an average coefficient of variation of 24.6%. Bias and variation were likely from differences between the F2TCM and the DP model and lower signal-to-noise ratio, the latter which is partially mitigated in patient studies as dynamic images and maps are strongly filtered. Applying the F2TCM to a total body FDG-PET study of a patient with metastatic lung cancer, we observed a lung tumor with reduced perfusion and increased net uptake rate (K<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">i</inf>), indicating a mismatch between vascular delivery of glucose via perfusion versus its utilization and tumor energy demand. Parameter decrease was unique to perfusion as blood volume and K<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">1</inf> (perfusion surrogates) were normal or elevated. Our novel contribution was to demonstrate the feasibility of perfusion-metabolism imaging from a single FDG-PET study.

articleTitle: Thermal Tomography for Medical Applications
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: We report results supporting that Thermal Tomography may be feasible as a medical diagnostic tool. Tomographic images from investigations using software and hardware phantoms and the Athens Model Analysis Independent Scheme (AMIAS) analysis package show that it is feasible to detect in tomographic images low temperature (1-4 °C) hotspots at depths reaching 1,5 cm below the skin. These results indicate that identification and description of hotspots in this temperature range within the human body is possible, thereby allowing for the development of diagnostic capabilities for a number of diseases, such as rheumatoid arthritis and cancer where the tumor is situated in proximity to the skin surface.

articleTitle: Development and initial evaluation of 3D-printed ultra-high resolution brain phantoms
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: In brain imaging, phantoms that accurately represent the human brain are needed for a precise investigation of scanner performance. Therefore, we designed a phantom dedicated to brain imaging using 3D-printing technology. Using surface data of cortical gray matter and white matter from the BigBrain atlas, gray matter (GM) phantoms were created. We also developed reliable and efficient methods based for filling these phantoms. The GM phantom was filled with a radioactive solution and scanned on the NeuroEXPLORER dedicated brain PET/CT (NX, United Imaging Healthcare), Focus 220 small animal PET (Siemens), High Resolution Research Tomograph brain PET (HRRT, Siemens), and Biograph Vision whole-body PET/CT (Siemens). The NX data was reconstructed with 7 and 20 iterations and 20 iterations showed higher spatial resolution. Among the PET images from the four different scanners, the NX and Focus 220 demonstrated better spatial resolution when compared to the HRRT and Vision, with the NX images comparable to the Focus 220 images. 3D-printing technologies can produce high-resolution models with complex geometries, and we successfully created a phantom representing the structure of the human brain, gray matter, with the thickness as thin as 1 mm. The phantoms with　fine brain structure will be used to evaluate and validate the performance of different PET scanners and reconstruction algorithms on human brain images.

articleTitle: Portable Calibration Device for X-ray Detector Array
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: A portable device for calibrating an array of X-ray detectors has been developed. It uses a handheld X-ray generator operated remotely to reduce personnel radiation exposure. A rotating-wheel cassette consisting of ten slots are deployed for loading metal filters. The initial test observed cross talk between the detector under test and the neighboring detectors owing to photon scattering. Geant4 simulations show that by adding a tungsten collimator at the exit of the generator and a tungsten barrel below the cassette would substantially reduce cross talk arisen from photon scattering. A revision of the device is in progress.

articleTitle: Investigation of a Next Generation Medical Imaging SiPM Technology
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Scintillation detectors based on silicon photomulitpliers (SiPM) have led to performance advances in both medical imaging and high energy physics applications. The performance of SiPM devices is of particular interest in the field of positron emission tomography (PET) where time-of-flight (TOF) information can be used to improve PET reconstruction image signal-to-noise ratio. Key to TOF performance is the coincidence time resolution (CTR), which for a PET system is determined by several factors including the properties of the scintillation crystals, the speed, noise and photon detection efficiency (PDE) of the SiPM device, as well as the readout electronics. Additionally, better energy resolution improves timing measurements as well as the system’s ability to reject scattered photons. This report characterizes the CTR and energy resolution of cutting-edge SiPM technology. Coincidence measurements were taken from a <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">22</sup>Na source using two detectors comprising 3×3×3 mm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</sup> LYSO crystals wrapped in Teflon reflector tape and coupled via optical grease to pairs of new SiPM devices of varying properties. From the measurements taken, the best CTR for the next generation SiPM devices is 95.3 ps (± 1.5 ps standard error), which is a significant improvement over comparable J-series devices that measured 105.2 ps (± 1.6 ps standard error). Additionally, the energy resolution at 511 keV was measured to be 11.7% (± 0.8%) for the next generation SiPM devices as compared to 13.4% (± 0.8%) for the J-series device.

articleTitle: Simulation of Cherenkov Light by Prompt-Gammas in Pure Cherenkov Emitters for Proton Range Verification
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Live assessment of the proton range in proton radiotherapy is an outstanding problem. Proton range verification (PRV) by means of prompt-gammas is a promising approach provided their prompt time properties and characteristic energies when compared to other radiation byproducts of the proton beam. In this work, we study the Cherenkov light created by such prompt-gammas in pure Cherenkov emitters with the aim of using it as an effective discriminator and achieve high count rates. Crystals of TlBr, TlCl and PbF2 with dimensions of 1×1×1 cm3 and 1×1×2 cm3 coupled to a 1×1 mm2 photodetector on one of their faces were simulated. The interaction processes and energy deposited in the crystal showed a strong relation with the generation and detection of Cherenkov photons, thus shaping the yield distributions and, consequently, impacting the average yield results. Pair production was the process that contributed the most to high yield events and was more present with increasing prompt-gamma energies, while Compton scattering dominated at lower energies. Cherenkov light detection yield was studied for different photodetector scenarios. Among materials, TlCl achieved the highest Cherenkov yield results across all energies, detector dimensions, and photodetector efficiency modeling. Crystals with 2 cm thickness showed a greater number of total detected events than 1 cm-thick ones. However, the average Cherenkov yield per event was the same for each material regardless of crystal length. The next step of this study is to model a prototype consisting of an array of such detectors.

articleTitle: Data Acquisition Methods with Off- and Half-step for Few-view SPECT in Triple Detector Systems
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Single photon emission computed tomography (SPECT) is an important imaging modality in clinical practice, but obtaining high quality images can be time-consuming and susceptible to motion artifacts. The off-set acquisition method is one approach to reduce the number of projections need for image acquisition, but it is not widely used in clinical settings. In this study, we proposed two new acquisition methods for triple detector system: the off-step and half-step methods, which are developed from the off-set method. The off-step method changes the step angle in certain steps, while the step angle of the half-step method is half of that of the on-set method. We used a brain phantom and generated projection data using Monte Carlo simulation code that accounts for attenuation, scattering, and collimator aperture. We reconstructed images using the TV-EM method and evaluated the accuracy using normalized root mean square error (NRMSE). Our results showed that the reconstructed images using the off-step and half-step methods with 6 projections were better than the on-set acquisition method, while using 9 projections, the on-set method performed better. When the number of projections was small, on-set method from an odd number of projections and off-step method from an even number of projections were better than the others. These results suggested that the proposed off-step and half-step acquisition methods were efficient and useful for few-view SPECT.

articleTitle: Acquisition Time Reduction in Pediatric PET Imaging using Unsupervised Convolution Neural Networks
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: The deep image prior (DIP) method, based on unsupervised training of convolutional neural networks, has demonstrated the potential of using neural networks as a constraint in image denoising. An appropriate stop criterion for the DIP method is crucial to avoiding insufficient training or overfitting. We propose a DIP-based image denoising method for PET images corresponding to 1/3 of the clinical standard 90 sec/bed acquisition time using auto-stop criteria. PET/CT data from 7 patients under age 12 were used in this study. For each patient, we trained a U-Net with his/her whole-body CT image as the input and the 30 sec/bed PET image reconstructed by the TOF Q.Clear with a regularization parameter (RP) of 700 as the label. To properly train the U-Net, we adopted self-validation based on the low-frequency information of the input and the label. The training iteration was stopped automatically when the validation loss began to increase or converge. We compared the DIP outputs with the Gaussian filtered 30 sec/bed images (RP = 700) and the 30 sec/bed images reconstructed with the RP of 1300, with the clinical 90 sec/bed images (RP = 700) as references. The DIP-generated images displayed lower noise and were visually closer to the reference images. The average normalized mean squared error values (×10<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">-5</sup>) were 5.9 ± 1.5 for the DIP-generated images, 17.6 ± 3.0 for the 30 sec/bed (RP = 700) images, 10.6 ± 1.9 for the Gaussian filtered images, and 8.7 ± 1.2 for the 30 sec/bed (RP = 1300) images. With the 90 sec/bed images as references, the average SUV<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">mean</inf>, SUV<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">max</inf>, and SUV<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">standard</inf> <inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">deviation</inf> <inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">(SD)</inf>/SUV<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">mean</inf> differences decreased by 10%, 84%, and 80% after the DIP enhancement. Quantitative results showed that the DIP method with auto-stop criteria improved the image similarity and quantitative accuracy of images from shortened acquisition time with respect to the clinical standard images, demonstrating its potential in reducing acquisition time for pediatric PET imaging.

articleTitle: A Novel Energy Estimation Method for PET Detectors Composed of Multiple Scintillators
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: In this study, we propose a novel technique for estimating energy in PET detectors composed of multiple scintillators. We mixed waveforms from two detectors, each containing BGO, GAGG, or LGSO scintillators, and trained a model using artificial neural networks to distinguish the energy of each waveform. We compared the accuracy of using amplitude and integration values as labels for energy estimation, using R<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sup> values as a metric. When applying the neural network-based energy estimator to the mixed waveforms of BGO and GAGG detectors, the R<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sup> values were (0.88, 0.99) for amplitude-based training and (0.95, 0.99) for integration-based training. In BGO and LGSO, the R<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sup> values were (0.94, 0.99) for amplitude-based training and (0.99, 0.99) for integration-based training. In GAGG and LGSO, the R<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sup> values were (0.99, 0.98) for amplitude-based training and (0.99, 0.98) for integration-based training. By utilizing this method, we could estimate energy in radiation detectors that combine scintillators with different properties, including phoswich detectors and meta-scintillators.

articleTitle: Pixelated CsPbBr3 Semiconductor Gamma Spectrometers
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: CsPbBr<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</inf> is a promising material for alternative room-temperature semiconductor gamma-ray spectrometers, for its demonstrated good energy resolution of ~1.0% FWHM at 662 keV with the detector thickness up to 12 mm, high stopping power and inexpensive material cost. In addition to required good gamma-ray spectroscopic performance and high detection efficiency, detector stability over long time operation is also critical. This work reports observed polarization phenomenon (detector performance changes over time) on CsPbBr<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</inf> detectors having pixelated electrodes, and observed characteristics. The dark current versus bias voltage (I-V), frequency property of the dark current at operating bias voltages, gamma-ray energy spectra with low and high energy photons, charge drift and collection characteristics, have been measured over time. These diagnostic measurements will help identify the possible causes of polarization, to improve stability of CsPbBr<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</inf> gamma-ray detectors for practical applications.

articleTitle: Feasibility Study on Direction-Sensitive Dark Matter Search using Tungstate Crystals irradiated with Several Particles
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: One of the candidates for the Dark Matters are weakly interacting massive particles (WIMPs) which are expected to form a halo around our Galaxy. Our Solar System is rotating around the center of the Galaxy, and we expect that the Earth should experience a "wind" (named 'WIMP wind') against the direction of the rotation, where is the direction to Cygnus. When a direction sensitive detector is realized, sensitivity can be higher. Some team reports that ZnWO<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">4</inf> can detect the direction of incident particles due to anisotropic. However, the mechanism has been not revealed. A Mg-admix ZnWO<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">4</inf> crystal is expected to have a different lattice constant from a normal ZnWO<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">4</inf>, and anisotropic properties can be changed. Thus, we compared scintillation and anisotropic properties for ZnWO<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">4</inf> and Mg-admix ZnWO<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">4.</inf> Both ZnWO<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">4</inf> and Mg-admix ZnWO<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">4</inf> were irradiated with gamma rays and alpha particles, the light output ratios (a /g ratio), defined as peak channel of 5.5-MeV alpha-ray absorption peak over that of 59.5-keV X-ray, were evaluated. B-surfaces, (010) orientations, had different α/γ ratios compared to the other surface for both ZnWO<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">4</inf> and Mg-admix ZnWO<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">4</inf>. Moreover, we tested the scintillation properties and anisotropic effect for PbWO<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">4</inf>, and PbWO<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">4</inf> was found to have the different light output and α/γ ratios in each surface as well as ZnWO<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">4</inf> had. Additionally, we measured the ZnWO<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">4</inf> irradiated with electrons and protons, and proton irradiation showed the anisotropic effect.

articleTitle: FPGA-based TDC for alpha particle measurements using a silicon strip detector
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: We present a prototype time-to-digital converter (TDC) for measuring the time of arrival of signals generated by interactions between an alpha source and a silicon strip sensor. The generated charge, in a form of small current pulses, is amplified and shaped by an ASIC that generates differential analog waveforms. An Artix7 FPGA is used to interface with 22 channels carrying these waveforms. The analog voltages are directly connected to FPGA inputs configured in LVDS (Low-Voltage Differential Signaling) mode. The FPGA input is configured as an DDR (Double Data Rate) buffer to operate in the oversampling mode, resulting in a sampling rate of 2.4 GS/s. As the FPGA inputs are analog, the 0→1 and 1→0 transitions suffers from bounce due to switching noise. Accurate extraction of the transition time thus requires an appropriate digital filter. Several filter designs are presented, along with their performance on real signals. The time resolution of the resulting TDC alone is approximately 200 ps rms. System-level measurements that include a 100 pF capacitance at the ASIC inputs reveal an increased timing variance of 520 ps rms.

articleTitle: A standalone Monte Carlo simulation toolkit at the micro-cell level to mimic SiPMs signals
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Recently, a SiPM digitizer has been implemented in GATE version 8.2 and has been made available as open source code. A standalone version of this experimentally-validated digitizer is presented here, which allows to simulate a SiPM offline or with data not specifically generated with GATE. It is composed of a C++ class with a default implemention including several functions modeling the SiPM detection efficiency, geometry, noise properties (crosstalk, afterpulse), timing response (SPTR and micro-cell signal shape generation). All parameters can be modified by the user to match with a desired experimental or simulated setup. The SiPM class allows Mont Carlo simulation at the micro-cell scale and is based on the generation of a signal for each impinging photon (also called pulse) onto a micro-cell.

articleTitle: Considering anatomical priors for total-body positron emission tomography attenuation correction through deep learning
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: During positron emission tomography (PET) scanning, additional computed tomography (CT) imaging is utilized to provide attenuation coefficient maps to achieve more precise quantification on PET images. But this not only exposes patients to extra doses of ionizing radiation but also makes attenuation correction (AC) difficult for PET/MRI or PET-only scanners. Recently, many efforts have been applied to address this issue and have achieved satisfactory performance. However, the majority of these methods have been implemented on specific anatomical tissue, ignoring the structural differences among various human body sites. Moreover, identical body sites across individuals shared similar anatomical information. Considering these anatomical disparities, we utilized the Cycle Consistent Generative Adversarial Network (Cycle GAN) as a foundation and modified its discriminator to differentiate between the authenticity of the input and its corresponding anatomy. In addition, the training process included the integration of a discriminative loss that relied on anatomical structures to enhance the quality of the generated AC PET images. Experiments demonstrate that our method yields superior quantification outcomes with a peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR) of 38.02 ± 5.52 dB and a structural similarity index (SSIM) of 0.96 ± 0.05. Compared to non-attenuation-corrected PET (NAC PET) images, our method resulted in a 14% increase in both PSNR and SSIM, indicating its effectiveness in converting NAC PET images into AC PET images.

articleTitle: In-situ Measurements of Activity in Microliter Droplets
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Imaging of tracers labeled with positron emitters is a powerful tool that enables understanding the initiation and progression of disease and the creation of novel therapeutics. Development and validation of new PET tracers takes years of research, in part due to the complexity, cost and limited throughput of conventional radiochemistry. To address this limitation, we are constructing a high-throughput radiochemistry system for the rapid development of radio-tracers for molecular imaging. The core of the system is a silicon wafer "chip" that contains a 4x4 array of 3mm diameter microdroplet reaction sites that allow performing simultaneous droplet-based radiosynthesis. A critical requirement for these systems is that the activity of the microliter droplets must be repeatedly and accurately measured to monitor the efficacy of each radiosynthesis step. To perform rapid and non-destructive in situ measurements of radioactivity at each droplet reaction site, two optical methods based on imaging via an overhead camera are considered: (a) measuring the intrinsic but weak Cerenkov light produced by positrons (<1 ph/e+) inside droplets and (b) measuring the much stronger (~103 ph/e+) scintillation light generated above the reaction sites from positrons that exit the droplets and interact in an organic scintillator. Absolute quantification of radioactivity in droplets is complicated by variations in overall positron energy deposition depending on the stage of synthesis, including the volume (and thus "thickness") of the droplet. We sought to determine the sensitivity of these methods to droplet geometry via Monte Carlo simulations of radiation emanating from arrays of droplets. We examined which of the imaging methods would provide better signal-to-noise, minimum crosstalk between droplets, minimum impact of background radiation and more consistent measurements for different experimental conditions.

articleTitle: Production, quality control and performance studies of the small-diameter Muon Drift Tube Detectors for the Phase-2 Upgrade of the ATLAS muon spectrometer
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: In the next long shutdown for the Phase-2 Upgrade of the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) in 2026–2028, the 96 new integrated muon tracking and trigger modules will be installed at the ends of the toroid magnet coils in the small azimuthal sectors of the inner barrel layer (BIS1-6) of the ATLAS muon spectrometer in order to increase the trigger efficiency in the barrel region and to improve the rate capability of the muon chambers in the regions of high background rate corresponding to the High Luminosity-LHC project. The new muon module consists of the smallDiameter Muon Drift Tube (sMDT) chamber with a 15 mm tube diameter and thin-gap Resistive Plate Chamber (RPC) triplet with 1 mm gas gap thickness. Due to the narrow available space, the BIS1-6 project foresees to replace the all-existing Monitored Drift Tubes, used for the precise position measurement in this area, with muon stations formed by sMDT and RPC, capable of withstanding the higher rates and provide a robust standalone muon confirmation. Moreover, the advantages of sMDT technology are not only to make room for the new trigger chambers, but it has already demonstrated their excellent precise tracking measurement over large areas at high background rates. In the next few years, ATLAS MDT group of the Max Planck Institute for Physics (MPI) in Munich will produce the 48 sMDT detectors with a total number of the drift tube of about 27000. For this reason, the detailed common assembly protocol and quality control procedures have been established, with the ambitious goal to ensure standardization of the performance of the constructed detectors and their components. In this contribution, we present the final results of the QC tests performed on the 48 BIS1-6 sMDT chambers assembled by the MPI Munich production site following the well-defined specification parameters.

articleTitle: On-beam Qualification of the First Depfet Ladder of the DSSC X-ray Imager
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: The first ladder (512 x 128) of the DEPFET Sensor with Signal Compression (DSSC), under development for ultra-fast imaging of soft X-rays at the European XFEL, is instrumented and the key features have been qualified in a dedicated beam time. Pixel readout is based on a Depleted P-Channel Field Effect Transistor (DEPFET) with non-linear response designed to jointly provide low noise and high dynamic range. The XFEL beam hits an Aluminium (Al) target and the DEPFET ladder is mounted perpendicular to the XFEL beam to collect Al Ka fluorescence photons. Low-intensity X-ray spectra of Al Ka photons (< 1 ph/pulse/pixel) were acquired to study noise and gain versus integration time and temperature. The best obtained Equivalent Noise Charge is 8 electrons rms. Combined with a high gain value of 40 eV/ADU, we could achieve the impressive discrimination of the Al Ka peak with signal-to-noise ratio of 50:1.The qualification of the pixel non-linear response up to several MeV/pixel was obtained by increasing the beam intensity on the target with fine steps. Different techniques to precisely calibrate the pulse energy deposited into individual pixels have been investigated and will be discussed in detail. In particular, the linear range of the DSSC pixel response was extended more than a factor x1000 by covering selected regions of the detector with Al filters of increasing attenuation.A key improvement was the correction of the signal-dependent shift of the pedestal value, non-negligible at high illumination intensities, due to the power distribution scheme of individual ASIC columns. This was accomplished with a custom mask that allowed measurement of model parameters over the whole intensity range. The non-linear curves of all pixels have been collected and the major features of compression will be discussed in detail. These results validate the expected performance and the employed techniques for the final qualification of the 1 Mpixel DSSC camera.

articleTitle: Benchtop cone-beam X-ray fluorescence CT system with high sensitivity and high spatial resolution
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: X-ray fluorescence computed tomography (XFCT) is a promising imaging modality that enables quantification of the distribution of high-Z elements, such as gold, gadolinium, and iodine, in diverse biomedical applications, by specifically detecting the X-ray fluorescence (XRF) emitted from the target element. XFCT experiments were initially performed at synchrotron facilities, but recent advances in benchtop XFCT systems using conventional polychromatic X-ray sources have accelerated its application in biomedical imaging. However, achieving a balance between imaging sensitivity, spatial resolution, and imaging time remains a challenge for benchtop XFCT. In this work, we present an upgrade to the cone beam XFCT imaging system that utilizes high energy resolution photon counting detectors (PCD) and fluorescence signal extraction methods based on net fluorescence spectrum and scatter spectrum fitting. A PMMA phantom filled with Gadolinium (Gd) saline solutions in concentrations ranging from 0 to 1.2mg/ml was used for the XFCT sensitivity experiment and a phantom with smaller inserts was used for spatial resolution verification. Furthermore, the study also includes imaging experiments on tumor bearing mice that received an injection of a Gd solution. Our phantom experiments demonstrate a minimal detection limit of 0.28 mg/mL and a spatial resolution of 1.4 mm. Additionally, our pilot experiment on mice highlights the potential of XFCT/CBCT dual modality imaging for high-sensitivity and high-resolution imaging of high-Z element particles in more biomedical applications. Our findings suggest that the XFCT/CBCT imaging system holds great promise for improving preclinical study of tumor diagnosis and treatment using high-Z elements nanoparticles.

articleTitle: Development of Novel Red and Infrared Emitting Scintillation Materials and Dose-Rate Monitoring System with an Optical Fiber
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Real dose monitors under the high dose-rate condition are required to remove the debris in the Fukushima Daiichi Nuclear Power Plant as the decommissioning step. We have proposed a dose-rate monitor consisting of a scintillator, optical fiber and photodetector, and scintillation materials are required to have the long-emission-wavelength (550 - 1000 nm) and high light output. We have developed several novel materials such as Cs<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf>HfI<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">6</inf> and Rb<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf>HfI<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">6</inf> for gamma-ray detection, and Li<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf>HfBr<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">6</inf> had sensitive to both gamma rays and neutrons. These scintillators had light outputs of up to 70,000 photons/MeV, and emission wavelengths of 600 to 750 nm. Using such scintillators, we succeeded in the demonstration of the dose-rate monitoring system with a <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">60</sup>Co source with an activity of around 100 TBq. Here, the measurement time of the one spot was less than 3 sec and the diameter of the fiber core was 0.6 mm. The dose-rate dynamic range was from 10 mGy to over 1 kGy, and our system was found to evaluate the wide dose-rate range in real-time.

articleTitle: Metal oxide nanoparticle-loaded plastic scintillator using fluorophore PTP+POPOP for high energy X-ray detection
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: We have developed heavy-metal-oxide nanoparticle loaded plastic scintillators (High-Z PLSs) for high energy X-ray detection. The High-Z PLS loaded with the surface-modified ZrO<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf>, HfO<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf> and Bi<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf>O<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</inf> nanoparticles is useful for high-energy X-ray measurements of up to a high count-rate > 10<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">7</sup> s<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">-1</sup> with an improved detection efficiency. Here we present test results on the High-Z PLSs with a two-component fluorophore of p-terphenyl (PTP) and 1,4-Bis[2-(5-phenyloxazolyl)]benzene (POPOP). The fluorophore has a maximum emission wavelength of ~420 nm and is suitable for common photomultipliers. The High-Z PLSs successfully maintained transparency, after polymerization by mixing monomers, consisting mainly of vinyltoluene. Test samples of the High-Z PLSs (8 mm in diameter, 3 mm thick) were prepared for 10 wt% and 20 wt% Zr, Hf and Bi elements. Properties of each sample were investigated using 67.41 keV synchrotron X-ray beam at beamline BL-14A of the Photon Factory (PF), KEK. The detection efficiency reached 48.6 ± 0.5% for a Hf 20 wt% loaded PLS. We will present the results for count-rate measurement using an X-ray scintillation detector with Hf 28 wt% loaded PLS (25 mm in diameter, 5 mm thick) and a common photomultiplier at 60.00 keV.

articleTitle: Enhancing Timing Performance of Heterostructures with Double-Sided Readout
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Heterostructured scintillators are gaining ground as a possible solution to the trade-off between the high sensitivity and fast timing of detectors for time-of-flight positron emission tomography (TOF-PET). They consist of stacks of alternating layers of two materials with complementary properties: high stopping power and ultrafast timing. The fast emitter improves the timing performance of the detector. However, layering is a limiting factor for the best achievable time resolution, as it worsens light transport. This effect can be mitigated by increasing light collection and retrieving the depth-of-interaction (DOI) information. The double-sided readout can meet both requirements.In this work, we use high-frequency electronics in a double-sided readout configuration with a 3x3x20mm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</sup> BGO&EJ232 heterostructure. By selecting the photopeak events, we were able to achieve a DOI resolution of 6.4±0.5mm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</sup>. The improvement in coincidence time resolution (CTR), compared to the single-sided readout, is 18% for all photopeak events (from 256±8 to 211±6ps) and 36% when considering only photopeak events that share the energy between the two materials (from 200±6 to 128±4ps).

articleTitle: Improved Performance of a Dual-Headed Molecular Breast Imaging system by Detector Angulation
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: We are developing a stationary tomographic molecular breast imaging system consisting of two planar CZT detectors and multi-pinhole collimators. One downside is that the limited angular sampling results in a limited spatial resolution perpendicular to the detectors. Here we investigate the potential to improve both resolution and sensitivity over a reduced field-of-view (FOV) by introducing some flexibility in the detector orientation. By tilting the external parts of the detector arrays towards the centre, the angular sampling and sensitivity could be improved in the central FOV. The system would still be stationary during acquisition. We performed computer simulations, assuming 198 mm wide detector arrays, divided into 3 sections, such that the first and last one could be tilted by different angles. The activity distribution consisted of an elliptical cylinder containing three line-sources on the mid-plane between the detectors at different horizontal distances from the centre (0, 25 and 50 mm). On average for the three sources, the resolution was improved (reduced FWHM) by factors of 0.92, 0.81, and 0.76 in the x-direction and 0.88, 0.72 and 0.64 in the y-direction for detector tilt angles of 10°, 20° and 30°, respectively. The sensitivity was increased by factors of 1.19, 1.45 and 1.72, respectively, for the same angles. The improvements are due to both increased angular sampling and reduced detector distance. Our simulations show that, by introducing some flexibility in the detector configuration, it is possible to improve both spatial resolution and sensitivity by sacrificing part of the FOV. However, as the standard configuration of two opposing parallel planar detectors could be easier to integrate in a clinical system, we will explore different pinhole configurations as an alternative.

Index Terms: Center Of The Field Of View

articleTitle: Iodine-131 whole gamma imaging outperforms clinical SPECT
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Whole gamma imaging (WGI), which is a novel combination of PET and Compton imaging, may have a potential to replace conventional single photon emission computed tomography (SPECT) by Compton imaging, but nobody has ever demonstrated it. As the first trial, this work aimed at imaging <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">131</sup>I. <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">131</sup>I is a theranostic radioisotope which emits β-particles and γ-rays. Although in vivo imaging is possible by a clinical gamma camera, the spatial resolution and the sensitivity are limited due to the high energy (364 keV) of the γ-rays. On the other hand, Compton imaging has the potential to become a novel imaging modality in nuclear medicine because it can visualize γ-rays with a wide energy range. In this study, we used a WGI prototype system consisting of a dual ring of GSOZ scintillation detectors. In addition, we compared the imaging performance with that of a clinical gamma camera. Using a stereolithography-type 3D printer, we developed two phantoms having outer diameters of 76 mm. A multi-rod phantom (rod diameters: 3, 4, 5, 8 and 10 mm) was developed for spatial resolution evaluation. A multi-contrast phantom was developed for image contrast evaluation. Two 20 mm rod regions were placed inside the phantom. The phantoms were filled with <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">131</sup>I solutions and then were measured by the WGI prototype system and the clinical gamma camera (30-min measurement each). The 5 mm rods were resolved in the <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">131</sup>I Compton images, while the clinical gamma camera could not resolve them. Hot and cold 20 mm rods were clearly visualized in the <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">131</sup>I Compton images of the multi-contrast phantom. The spatial resolution, hot rod contrast and cold rod contrast of the <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">131</sup>I Compton images were better than those of the <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">131</sup>I SPECT images. These results suggest that WGI may be useful for <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">131</sup>I imaging and dosimetry.

articleTitle: Data acquisition setup comparison for fast timing ToF-PET applications/systems
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: The choice of readout technology can impact a scanner's timing and energy resolution, which affects image quality in Photon Emission Tomography (PET). Achieving optimal timing information is imperative for Time-of-Flight (ToF) systems.This study presents a comparison of different data acquisition technologies ranging between custom-made high-frequency electronics (CM-HF) and commercial systems, like PETsys. Different scenarios were compared using 3x3x5 mm$^3$ LYSO:Ce,Ca scintillator crystal pixels from SIPAT. Also, a timing comparison between two SiPMs from different manufacturers (Fondazione Bruno Kessler, Hamamatsu) has been performed. To achieve the best timing and energy results, a voltage bias scan has been performed using a longer pixel.The study evaluates each readout's timing and energy resolution and discusses the possible alternatives available to implement novel data acquisition chains. Results show energy resolutions very close for each scenario (between 7-10 %), while the CTRs differ from the best result for CM-HF (82 ps) and the worst one for PETsys (160 ps) readouts.

articleTitle: Measurement of beta, gamma, and neutron radiation using an alpha imager based on a CCD camera and discrimination from alpha particles
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: This study reports the effects of different types of radiation on a high-resolution alpha imager, developed using an Electron Multiplying Charge-Coupled Device (EMCCD) camera. The imager was originally designed to visualize Pu oxide particles in decommissioning sites, where other types of radiation such as beta particles, gamma-rays, and neutrons are also present. The study aims to confirm the effects of these radiations on the imager and to develop a discrimination method between alpha particles and other radiations. The measurement of alpha particles, beta particles, gamma-rays, and neutrons were performed. The discrimination method was based on the characteristics of the image distribution, where the image values were binarized and a Gaussian filter was applied to count the number of alpha particle spots. The results show that it is possible to discriminate between alpha and gamma (neutron) rays using the difference in intensity. The study provides important information for the development of radiation detection techniques in decommissioning sites.

articleTitle: Micro-scale particle tracking with hybrid detectors
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Positron emission particle tracking (PEPT) is a tracer-based measurement technique used in the non-invasive study of dynamic and flowing systems. PEPT relies on positron imaging principles; using coincident detection of annihilation photons to determine the instantaneous 3D position of positron emitting tracers. Successful applications include laboratory scale systems across engineering disciplines, achieving millimetre spatial resolution and tracking speeds up to 10 m/s. On smaller scales with reduced radiotracer activity, performance is limited by the efficiency of conventional fixed geometry detectors. To investigate micro-scale phenomena a modular hybrid system consisting of pixelated scintillator and semiconductor detectors has been constructed. 1024 BGO scintillator crystals (of mixed dimensions <6.75 x <6.25 x 30 mm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</sup>) form a field of view 120 x 196 x 101 mm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</sup> with a pair of pixelated CZT room temperature semiconductors (9680 pixels of 1.8 x 1.8 x 0.5 mm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</sup>) covering the central 62 x 42 x 20 mm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</sup> region at high spatial resolution. Detection geometry was optimised through numerical modelling by maximising the absolute efficiency with high solid angle coverage of the scintillators, while enhancing the spatial resolution with the high pixelization of the semiconductors. At 511 keV, intrinsic efficiencies of 60% and 15%, and energy resolutions of 30.5% and 1.15%, were measured for the scintillators and semiconductors respectively. The combined high efficiency and high energy resolution enable precision windowing on detected events to discriminate noise. The timing resolution of both arrays was measured to be 12.7 ns and 268 ns respectively, allowing optimisation of coincidence gates. Sensitivity profile measurements were performed with a novel positioning stage benchmarked against modelling and demonstrating significant improvement in PEPT spatial resolution. Results indicate the potential study of micro-scale flows for the first time.

articleTitle: Secure Blockchain Encryption of Homeland Security Reachback Data for Spectroscopic Radiation Measurements
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: A blockchain algorithm approach is shown that hashes the original data and stores the hash information as part of the spectrum file. The procedure is based on the spectroscopic information, mathematical transformations and even additional information from the detector itself. The resulting N42.42 compatible file remains in its standardised form and is readable at all times. It keeps a record of binary information to allow posterior analysis, in case a cyberattack was detected. Then, the procedure also allows to reconstruct the original data again.Spectroscopic equipment is the basis for many homeland security applications that deal with radiation analysis. Those instruments measure gamma ray spectra, which are used for subsequent analysis, often by nuclear security experts. The data must be easy to transfer, free of manipulations and secure. A common threat of cyberattacks targets those data, especially concerning autonomous installation such as portals. But even handheld equipment can suffer attacks on its data, if it transfers it for reachback purposes. Here, it has to get network access and the data is transmitted via common web technology.A demonstrator of the technique is shown to work with homeland security spectrum data. With a series of exemplary attacks on the data, the demonstrator is tested and the detection capabilities analysed. Randomisation of encryption keys is based on inherent radiation detector parameters like the high voltage at the time of measurement or the ambient temperature.

articleTitle: Radiation Tolerant Multi-Gigabit Serializer for data readout in High Energy Physics experiments
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: This paper describes the SER28_V1 circuit: including thea prototype of an 8 Gbps 20-bit Serializer developed in a commercial CMOS 28nm technology. The circuit is designed to be radiation-tolerant up to a Total Ionizing Dose (TID) of 10 MGy Grad in view of applications in the readout of future High Energy Physics experiments. It will be used as building block of a Double-Data-Rate 16 Gbps Serializer that will be integrated in the demonstrator of a 64 Gbps optical data link based on Ring-Resonators and radiation-tolerant electronics. The circuit includes a radiation-tolerant Built-In-Self-Test module and LVDS and CML differential drivers and receivers. Results of test and characterization of SER28_V1 prototypes are presented.

articleTitle: Region-of-Interest and Handcrafted vs. Deep Radiomics Feature Comparisons for Survival Outcome Prediction: Application to Lung PET/CT Imaging
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Although many studies have focused on handcrafted radiomics features (RF), a much more indepth study, as follows in this study, is necessary to explore usage of deep RFs extracted from deep learning (DL) algorithms to assess survival analysis. We enrolled 215 lung cancer patients with PET, CT, and clinical data from The Cancer Imaging Archive and the Vancouver General Hospital. This study aims to assess 3 approaches, including comparison of i) PET vs. CT images; ii) different region of interests (ROI) used for deep RF extraction; and iii) deep vs. handcrafted RFs in prediction of overall survival (OS; regression task to predict exact time-to-death and survival probability) by hybrid machine learning systems (HMLS), including Analysis of Variance (ANOVA) and principal component analysis (PCA) linked with regression algorithms (RA). Subsequently, 256 deep RFs were extracted from 3 ROIs on both images by a 3D auto-encoder. The 3 ROIs included i) a segmented lung tumor; ii) a 3D bounding box (36x48x46 millimeter) including the lung tumor area; and iii) entire image. Further, 215 handcrafted RFs were extracted from each segmented tumor on both images through the standardized ViSERA-radiomics package. In OS prediction, i) PET-based HMLSs outperformed CT-based HMLSs, ii) deep RFs extracted from the cropped images outperformed deep RFs extracted from other ROIs, receiving the highest mean absolute error (MAE) of 595±126 [range 36-5596 days] by ANOVA+support vector regression, and iii) deep RFs significantly outperformed handcrafted RFs. In survival probability prediction, i) PET-based HMLSs outperformed CT based HMLSs, ii) PET-based deep RFs extracted from the entire image outperformed deep RFs extracted from other ROIs, having the highest c-index of 0.65±0.05 through PCA+Random Survival Forest, and iii) deep RFs outperformed handcrafted RFs.

articleTitle: Absolute measurement of bone mineral density in general radiography using energy-resolving photon-counting detector
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Energy-Resolving Photon-Counting Detector (ERPCD), which can acquire X-ray energy information, has the potential for quantitative analysis of objects. In previous research, algorithms to determine the effective atomic number (Z<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">eff</inf>) image have been proposed. Although these methods have been found to be ideally usable for determining the properties of materials, it remains to be clarified their applicability and impact on clinical diagnosis. The aim of our study is to demonstrate the effectiveness of the functional images and to propose an absolute measurement of Bone Mineral Density (BMD). Our algorithms can realize an ideal analysis in which polychromatic X-rays measured with the ERPCD can be treated as monochromatic X-rays by using Z<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">eff</inf> information. Then each mass thickness (ρt) can be determined by assuming that the object consists of soft tissue and bone elements. For assuming each element, the following two different systems were used: system A in which mass attenuation coefficients of Z<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">eff</inf> = 6.5 (acrylic) and 13 (aluminum) were applied, and system B in which those of Z<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">eff</inf> = 6 (resin) and 16 (hydroxyapatite) were used. To demonstrate our method, dental samples of the mandible and teeth and BMD calibrators (0–0.8 g/cm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sup>) were measured using a prototype ERPCD system by mimicking actual dental radiography. In the ρt images, each element can be extracted completely even in areas where bone and/or teeth overlap with acrylic (soft-tissue), which demonstrates the possibility of accurately analyzing each element itself. When analyzing these values, there is a linearity in the relationship between measured BMD and predetermined one for systems A and B, which means that BMD can be measured using the ERPCD. Furthermore, for system B, the measured BMD was in good agreement with the predetermined one. It was found that absolute BMD measurement can be performed without using a BMD calibrator.

articleTitle: Measurements on HDSoCv1 performance and rate handling for acquiring fast silicon photomultiplier signals
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: We present preliminary results on the timing performance, data throughput and the trigger rate of HDSoC Version 1, a 32-channel digitizer, sampling at 1 Giga Samples per second (GSa/s). In this paper, we discuss the intra-channel timing between pulses and fast data acquisition using Gigabit Ethernet to improve the pulse acquisition rate.

articleTitle: The Tiny Triplet Finder as a Versatile Track Segment Seeding Engine for Trigger Systems
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: In high energy physics experiment trigger systems, track segment seeding is a resource consuming function and the primary reason is the computing complexity of the segment finding process. As the Moore’s' Law is reaching its physical limit, reducing computing complexity should be carefully considered, rather than keep piling up silicon resources. The Tiny Triplet Finder is a scheme that reduces the computing complexity of the segment seeding. As a proof of concept, a 3D track segment seeding engine core based on the Tiny Triplet Finder has been implemented and tested in a low-cost FPGA device. The seeding engine is designed to preselect and group hits (stubs) from detector layers to feed subsequent track fitting stage. The seeding engine consists of a Hough transform space for r-z view and a Tiny Triplet Finder for r-phi view to implement 3D constraints. The seeding engine is organized as a pipeline so that each hit is processed in a single clock cycle. The Tiny Triplet Finder is also a generic coincidence finding scheme that can be used for many tasks. As a versatility demonstration, track segment finding performances for two distinctive detector geometries are tested in our seeding engine. In a collider barrel-layer geometry, the fake segment rates are studied for 3D (i.e., both r-phi and r-z views) and 2D (i.e., rphi or r-z view only) configurations for high hit multiplicity events (>4000 hits/layer in the barrel region). Another detector geometry contains strip plane layers with timing information. The numbers of coincidences, both real or fake, with or without timing ("3D" or "2D") information at various hit multiplicities are studied.

articleTitle: Perpendicular photonic crystal slabs integrated in metascintillators
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Metascintillators have shown their advantages in achieving superior timing in Time-of-flight PET by combining different scintillation materials providing both fast emission and high stopping power. In this work, we try to further improve their timing performance by integrating thin-layer two-dimensional photonic crystal devices into the detector. This kind of nano-photonic devices, named after photonic crystal slabs, inserted between different scintillation material layers of a metascintillator are expected to first couple the energy of optical photons isotropically radiated out-of-plane into its in-plane propagating modes. Then the energy is guided with directivity toward photon detection surfaces. We demonstrate that photonic crystal slabs tailored for metascintillators have the potential to improve light collection efficiency and also reduce light transport time.

articleTitle: Passive Radiological Inspection of Shipping Containers at Seaports using UAV-based Detectors with the Method of Spectral Comparison Ratios
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Radiation detectors mounted on unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) can be utilised to screen freight passing through a seaport for radioactive material that could be used in radiological dispersal devices (RDDs) or improvised nuclear explosive devices. Payload and battery life restrictions limit the size of the sensor package that can be deployed on a UAV and as a result a low-cost system is likely to deploy small and lightweight detectors that produce count-starved spectra. The method of spectral comparison ratios (SCRs) is a well-studied approach to processing such data and is used in this work to process measurements obtained with a 3.8×3.8×2.5 cm CsI(Tl) scintillator mounted on a UAV. An aerial survey of an outdoor facility housing several shipping containers is carried out to obtain a "benign source population" which characterises variation and features in background radiation at the site. The benign source population is then used in combination with laboratory measurements to determine optimum bins for the detection of <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">137</sup>Cs and <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">60</sup>Co - two commercially available sources that could be used in an RDD. To account for the shielding effect of shipping container cargo on concealed sources, measurements of <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">137</sup>Cs and <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">60</sup>Co with different thicknesses of attenuating material are obtained. It is shown that the optimal bins required to detect these isotopes using the SCR method are dependent the amount of shielding present. With the optimal bins determined the SCR method is then used to process a combination of experimental data from sources concealed in shipping containers and modelled data, where source profiles are artificially injected into measurements.

articleTitle: Study of 13N High Purity Germanium Detectors with amorphous-Ge Contacts
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Compared with traditional "Li diffusion and B implantation" high-purity germanium detector electrode preparation process, the use of amorphous semiconductor electrical contacts has many advantages such as ease of electrode segmentation, low dependency on equipment, as well as simplicity for manufacturing, making this preparation method practical for mass production of high performance HPGe detector. Vital (www.vitalchem.com) use in-house grown 13N high-purity germanium crystals, and RF sputtering to deposit amorphous germanium (a-Ge). A number of detectors prepared with a-Ge contact, under different processing conditions, have been prepared and investigated, mainly on device reliability and associated leakage current. Detector stability and typical energy resolution of 0.23% at 1.27 Mev from 22Na source have been observed and will be reported in this work.

articleTitle: Gamma Camera with Self-collimation and Compton Imaging
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Self-collimation is a novel approach in gamma imaging that employs the detector itself to play the role of collimation, enabling high resolution and sensitivity. However, for high-energy gamma rays (e.g., 511 keV), inter-scintillator scattering becomes more pronounced and reduces imaging performance. Compton imaging is a well-established approach that has advantages in imaging high-energy gamma rays, albeit with limited spatial resolution. In this work, we present a proof-of-concept study for a gamma camera that combines the principles of self-collimation and Compton imaging. The camera consists of 1) interspaced mosaic scintillator bars with dual-end SiPM readouts for self-collimation imaging, and 2) a mechanism to incorporate Compton coincidence events for image formation. Monte Carlo simulations demonstrate that incorporating Compton imaging leads to improved performance in terms of reducing noise-induced artifacts and enhancing spatial resolution. We believe that integrating self-collimation and Compton imaging can facilitate the application of high-energy gamma ray imaging in SPECT and expand the range of available radiopharmaceuticals.

articleTitle: Ultralow Dose Small Animal SPECT reconstruction for Alpha-Emitter Radiopharmaceutical Therapy
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Alpha-emitter radiopharmaceutical therapy (αRPT) becomes a promising cancer treatment, which harnesses the high linear energy transfer (LET) and short range of α-particles to deliver targeted destruction of cancer cells. However, the application of alpha-emitters in Targeted Alpha Therapies (TATs) may lead to the release of daughter products, which can migrate away from the tumor site and cause toxicity in nearby tissues and organs. To identify the biodistribution of primary α-emitters and their daughters, SPECT scanner with superior energy resolution is crucial to differentiate specific gamma-rays from different isotopes and distinguish the primary signal from scattering noise events. Because TAT imaging typically utilizes very low concentrations of alpha-particle emitters less than 1 μCi, the image reconstruction with denoising is necessary. Recently, we have developed an innovative preclinical SPECT system at UIUC featuring smallpixel CdTe detectors, which provides ultra-high energy resolution and exceptional spatial resolution for small-animal αRPT imaging applications. In this study, we focused on low count SPECT reconstruction, which involves 1) constructing a system matrix using voxel-driven forward/backward projectors, and 2) implementing a penalized SPECT reconstruction method utilizing the forward-backward splitting approach. We evaluated our approach using a resolution phantom filled with diagnostic isotope Tc-99m (1.5 mCi). Our results demonstrate that our system achieved a spatial resolution of approximately 0.75 mm and was capable of detecting and imaging low-activity sources with reduced artifact. In our future studies, the imaging of a mouse with sub 1-μCi Ac-225 will be particularly challenging.

articleTitle: Proton therapy treatment verification: a spatio-temporal emission reconstruction with experimental data
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Many efforts have been made to fully exploit charged particles' specific features in terms of dose delivered to the target and sparing of healthy tissues. Although the dose maximum, defined by the Bragg peak, can be well characterized for materials of known composition and physical properties, uncertainties in its determination are encountered in the clinical practice. To mitigate these uncertainties, treatment verification techniques based on the detection of secondaries have gained importance, but a clinical device integrated in the patient routine is yet to be available. We present here the first experimental results of the spatio-temporal emission reconstruction for treatment verification in proton therapy. With a multi-detector prompt-gamma timing system, we are able to simultaneously reconstruct the spatial and temporal distribution of the emitted prompt photons. This distribution is correlated to both the primary particle range and their motion inside the target. A detector prototype comprising two LaBr3:Ce-based detectors and an Ultra Fast Silicon detector was developed within the MERLINO (Measurement of the EneRgy Loss for IN-vivo Optimization in particle therapy) project for the technique proof-of-concept. Experimental measurements of a 227 MeV proton beam impinging on an homogeneous phantom were taken at the National Center for Oncological Hadrontherapy in Italy. First comparisons between data and simulation show excellent agreement, with a 98% average correlation of the prompt gamma timing distributions. A preliminary reconstruction of the prompt photons spatio-temporal emission is here reported for the first time for experimental data. The corresponding simulation was carried out with the FLUKA Monte Carlo tool. The results shown here represent the first step towards the experimental validation of the technique.

articleTitle: Deep-Learning for Reduction of Deformations from Dual-Panel Breast-PET System
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Dedicated dual-panel Breast-PET (B-PET) scanners have many benefits for specific breast imaging in diagnosis and treatment applications, due to their higher sensitivity, improved resolution, and lower costs compared to the whole body PET scanners. However, images from dual-panel PET systems are affected by the limited-angle artifacts due to the data angular truncations and depth-of-interaction effects for oblique lines of response (especially for objects placed close to the detector panels), leading to strong isotropic, asymmetric, and spatially variant image deformations. In this work, we investigate deep-learning based post-reconstruction deformation reduction for dual-panel TOF based B-PET imaging. While the idea presented is relevant to other neural networks as well, in this work we investigated an U-Net based architecture for artifact reduction. The network was trained on a simulated synthetic data sets providing ground truth for objects resembling experimentally acquired phantoms on which the network deformation corrections were then tested. The synthetic training data, as well as testing experimental phantom data were reconstructed using RAMLA-DIRECT reconstructions without resolution modeling, which were used as the network inputs. We demonstrate that Deep-Learning (DL) can significantly eliminate deformations of limited angle systems and improve the quantitative image quality for the B-PET system.

articleTitle: Optimizing FPGA-based Sparse Coding for Real-time Processing in X-ray Instrumentation
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: As detectors improve, large physics experiments generate more data. However, real-time raw data processing near the sensors can be challenging due to the high data velocity and the resource-constrained location. A practical solution involves using low-latency data reduction to lower the incoming throughput. Sparse representations and machine learning are popular methods for data reduction, with the Learned Iterative Shrinkage-Thresholding Algorithm, dubbed LISTA, combining both techniques to produce fast approximations of sparse coding. In previous work, we proposed a multi-stage strategy to compress the data at the edge. We targeted the billion-pixel X-ray camera, an X-ray imaging system with a data rate of 10 TB/s. The compression leverages a LISTA-like architecture followed by quantization and entropy coding, achieving a 100:1 compression ratio with minimal image artifacts. Using high-level synthesis, we fitted the fully connected LISTA on an FPGA. Although the inference time was around 1 μs, the number of parameters per layer of the network was limited, imposing a low input size and restricting the FPGA throughput. In this work, we explore and compare solutions for a larger input size that maintain similar performance. We studied splitting the initial linear layers into smaller ones using low-rank matrix factorization. Preliminary results indicate that the factorization can achieve a 77% increase in the input size, with increased throughput at the cost of added resources. Finally, we discuss the current limitations of the compression strategy and potential improvements moving forward.

articleTitle: Development of 7-channel germanium detector for X-ray Absorption Fine Structure
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: There is a strong need for spectroscopy detector for high-energy X-ray application where silicon, the material of choice for direct detection becomes X-ray transparent. Current effort for high-Z materials for high-energy X-ray application is limited to imaging applications. In this work we have fabricated a custom 7-channel germanium pixel detector and instrumented using a low-noise commercial charge sensitive pre-amplifier. The sensor is cooled at about 100K with a commercial closed cycle system, while the in vacuum readout board is thermally isolated from the cold finger. Details of the sensor characteristics and detector performances will be discussed.

articleTitle: Deep Learning-based Scatter Correction of kV and MV CBCT images: A CT number evaluation
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: A deep learning-based model was trained to identify and suppress the scatter contributions in Cone Beam Computed Tomography (CBCT) images. The model was trained with CBCT projections generated by a validated Monte Carlo (MC) model of the kV and MV imaging system of the TrueBeam STx Linac. Several loss functions and convolutional neural network (CNN) architectures were tested in order to select the appropriate parameters for the optimal performance of the model. The model's performance was evaluated through the percentage error in corrected projections and the accuracy of CT number, evaluated in the reconstructed images. For CT number evaluation, the trained deep learning-based model was used to correct a complete set of CBCT projections of a cylindrical phantom of water with inserts of several materials. The CT number of the materials in the reconstructed image was compared with the expected values for a reconstruction with projections generated only with primary radiation, according to MC-based methods. A CBCT study can be corrected for scatter radiation in approximately three seconds with a trained UNet, which is around five orders of magnitude faster than MC-based methods.

articleTitle: First application of sparse-view reconstruction method to in-vivo imaging for SiPM-based photon-counting CT
