publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Photon-counting computed tomography (PC-CT) is a next-generation X-ray CT system for medical applications. It enables quantitative evaluation, such as concentration estimation, which is impossible with conventional CT systems. Utilizing this property to estimate the concentration of contrast agents injected into the body is expected to expand the possibilities of novel diagnostics, such as drug delivery systems. Therefore, we have established the silicon photomultiplier (SiPM)-based PC-CT system combined with fast scintillators and have evaluated its imaging performance with contrast agents injected into small animals. However, to estimate the concentration of contrast agents flowing inside small animals more accurately, the temporal resolution of CT imaging needs to be improved. In such a situation, the sparse-view CT technique is an attractive method that enables CT imaging with a shorter duration without degrading image quality. In this study, we reported the initial results of an image quality evaluation of sparse-view CT images obtained with our SiPM-based PC-CT system. We used static phantoms equivalent to an iodine contrast agent and a mouse injected with iodine contrast agents as the subjects. We then applied the image reconstruction method based on total variation minimization to the sparsely view-sample sinogram with the number of projections reduced to 1/5 of the measured projection data. Consequently, we successfully reconstructed sparse-view CT images with 34.0% less image noise than the original, implying that the total imaging time could be reduced to 1/5 while improving image quality. In addition, it also showed great potential for reducing the X-ray dose to 1/5, and there are high expectations for the clinical application of SiPM-based PC-CT with sparse-view reconstruction.

articleTitle: Directional radiation monitoring system using ANN-based algorithm
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: A radiation detector capable to determine the direction of a radioactive source is necessary to minimize radiation exposure to the general public in the event of a radiation accident. In this study, a directional radiation monitoring system consisting of four NaI(Tl) detector modules arranged in a rectangular shape and externally attached wall-type collimators was designed. The field of view of each detector module varies with the source direction due to the geometry of wall collimators, so the measured counts of each module are different for one source. The directional information of the source can be extracted by analyzing the count difference between modules using an artificial neural network (ANN) based algorithm. GATE simulations were performed to build datasets for machine learning by moving the <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">60</sup>Co source from 0 to 90 degrees at 5-degree intervals, and the distances between the source and system were set at 50 m, 100 m, 200 m, and 400 m, respectively. The ANN algorithm consists of four input-layer nodes, one hidden layer, and one output-layer node, and the activation function of the hidden layer was set to a sine function. A total of 600 datasets were generated and divided into training, validation, and test datasets, with ratio of 40%, 40%, and 20%, respectively. As a result of training and validation, the mean squared error (MSE) converged to 0.5 from epoch 14, and the prediction accuracy of the source angle was 2.37%. The results show that the proposed directional radiation monitoring system is feasible.

articleTitle: Optimization of Electrical contacts for Solution Grown Single Crystal CsPbBr3 Radiation Detectors
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: CsPbBr<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</inf> radiation detectors are a potential low-cost alternative to the leading room-temperature detector material, Cadmium Zinc Telluride (CZT). However, the leading method for growing CsPbBr<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</inf> uses expensive starting materials that do not offer major cost reductions compared to other detector materials. This work focuses on optimizing the electrical contacts for CsPbBr<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</inf> detectors grown from cheaper starting materials of lower purity. In order to grow high purity crystals from lower purity starting material, a modified growth method was used to segregate impurities during growth. The unique growing condition for these crystals necessitates tailored optimization of electrical contacts in order to handle their charge carrier transport behaviour. Asymmetrical devices with a high work function metal contact (Au) and a lower work function metal contact (In) were fabricated in order to have low leakage current under a specific polarity. Pure In contacts have not been extensively studied compared to other metals. The In contacts were not stable when left directly exposed to air, so these contacts were covered with a semitransparent layer of Au (40 nm). Devices made with this configuration were able to resolve the energy spectrum of alpha particles a <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">241</sup>Am source. We have yet to resolve gamma radiation with our solution grown detectors, though the Au/In/CsPbBr<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</inf>/Au configuration has been able to resolve the gamma spectrum of a <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">137</sup>Cs source using a detector grown from the more typical pure binaries method. This aim of this work and future work is to continue to reduce the differences in detector performance between our growth method and the standard method.

articleTitle: Characterization of a Long Axial Field of View PET Scanner
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: The current NEMA NU-2 2018 protocol for characterizing positron emission tomography scanners is inadequate for performance measurements of long axial field of view (LAFOV) scanners with an axial FOV of 1 m. or more. Additionally, the method is very simplied and may not be suitable for clinically relevant situations. In the current work, we present noise equivalent count rate (NECR) measurements of a Siemens Vision Quadra system with an axial FOV of 1.06 m. in a multiphantom setup. Additionally, we have characterized the resolution of the scanner as a function of both axial position, transaxial displacement and using different maximum ring difference reconstructions. In brief, several phantoms were used representing the brain, lungs, heart, liver, lesions and bladder. The individual phantom compartments were filled with realistic concentration ratios and had a start actvity of > 2 GBq, i.e. above count rate saturation. Scans were acquired for 5 min. initially every 20 min., subsequently every 30 min. or 60 min. For resolution measurement a <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">22</sup>Na source was placed on an acrylic ruler to minimize the influence of attenuation. Data was collected from middle to the edge of the axial FOV in radial displacements of 1 cm. and 20 cm. For the phantom measurements peak NECR was 1.02 Mcps@17.3 kBq/ml and seems to be determined by a coincidence bottleneck rather than detector deadtime or correction effects. At peak NECR the curve is almost constant suggesting little image quality gain with increased acitvity concentration. In our measurments a reduction from 3 MBq/kg to 0.3 MBq/kg can be compensated by a increase in scan time by a factor of 7. Resolution measurements showed a nearly constant resolution as function of both the axial FOV and transaxial displacement when using point spread function correction. A minor resolution loss was observed for large MRD reconstructions due to the oblique angle line of responses.

articleTitle: Synthesis and scintillation properties of metal cation doped (C6H5C2H4NH3)2PbBr4
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: In this study, (C<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">6</inf>H<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">5</inf>C<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf>H<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">4</inf>NH<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</inf>)<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf>Pb<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">0.9</inf>M<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">0.1</inf>Br<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">4</inf> (M = Fe, Co, Ni, Cu, Zn, Cd, Hg, Sn) single crystals were synthesized by the poor solvent diffusion method. After the crystal growth, photoluminescence and scintillation properties of these crystals were compared. In photoluminescence, all the samples showed two emission peaks at ~410 and ~440 nm. Photoluminescence quantum yield of the current samples resulted few%, and Ni, Zn and Cd doped ones exhibited the highest value of ~5%. The emission origins of the former and latter ones were ascribed to free excitons and trapped excitons, respectively. Photoluminescence decay curves were well approximated by a sum of three exponential functions, and typical decay times were ~10, ~30, and ~200 ns. The origin of the fastest one (~10 ns) was considered to be the free exciton while that of the other two components would be blamed for the trapped exciton. When X-rays were irradiated to the samples, intense emission peak was observed at ~440 nm since ~410 nm emission was self-absorbed in transmission-type measurement geometry. Scintillation decay times were also similar with photoluminescence. After these characterizations, pulse height spectra were measured to determine the scintillation light yield. Under irradiation of 662 keV g-rays from <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">137</sup>Cs, Zn and Cd doped ones showed the highest scintillation light yield of 18000 ph/MeV with a very fast decay time of ~10 ns.

articleTitle: RTSD Scientist Award
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: This is not a technical presentation; it is an introduction of the 2023 RTSD Scientist Award recipient. [If a review is required, please give the abstract an average grade.]This presentation recognizes an individual who has made high-impact contributions to the development of room-temperature semiconductor detector technology. The RTSD Steering Committee begins the selection process by nominating worthy individuals, followed by identifying the finalists and casting votes for them.The first RTSD Scientist Award recipient was in 2001, and the award has been given at each RTSD Symposium since then. Past awardees included, in order of receipt: Paul Siffert, Ralph James, Michael Schieber, Arnold Burger, Michael Fiederle, Csaba Szeles, Zhong He, Henry Chen, Aleksey Bolotnikov, Larry Franks, Jan Iwanczyk, Andrea Zappettini, Krishna Mandal, Giuseppe Bertuccio, Kanai Shah, Beatrice Fraboni and Jan Franc.Please join us to recognize the 2023 RTSD Scientist Award recipient.

articleTitle: MexSIC, a Data Acquisition Channel for SiPMs
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: This work presents a data acquisition channel for SiPMs, called MexSIC, composed of a mixed-mode ASIC front-end and an FPGA-based processing stage. The ASIC provides a 1-bit modulated version of the SiPM current, a flag indicating the start/end of the SiPM pulse, and a clock reference generated by an internal Phase Locked-Loop (PLL). The FPGA gathers the signals from the ASIC and performs a decimation process to complete data recovery. To provide the digital information, the SiPM current is converted to voltage by a 1.2 GHz bandwidth transimpedance amplifier whose gain can be switched between 30x and 800x, allowing a 0.1-10mA dynamic input-range. After that, this voltage signal is applied to a Trigger Unit (TU) and to a 1-bit quantizer second-order sigma-delta modulator (ΣΔ-M) that provides an Equivalent Number Of Bits (ENOB) of 6.24. This type of modulator was selected to have a single line instead of a bus with many lines, this is important in applications where the number of sensors is very large. The TU circuit sends a start/end bit flag by comparing the SiPM voltage signal with an 8-bit programmable voltage reference. The 10 MHz bandwidth ΣΔ-M uses an Over Sampling Ratio (OSR) of 50 and a 1 GHz sampling clock that is generated by a PLL using an off-chip 100 MHz reference. Due to its high decimation rates, the decimator uses a Cascade Integrator Comb (CIC) filter that is adequate to process sigma-delta modulated signals. The recovered signal is visualized in Matlab environment. The ASIC was designed in a 180 nm CMOS standard process using Cadence<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">©</sup> software and the processing stage was implemented in a Kintex-7 FPGA.

articleTitle: A Boosted Active Quenching Circuit with Detector Capacitance Compensation
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: The detector capacitance compensation (DCC) technique which achieves double active quenching of single-photon avalanche diode (SPAD) is presented in this paper. A well-defined active quenching circuit has the advantages of a higher maximum photon-counting rate and lower afterpulsing probability. Quenching time and area are important criteria when implementing an active quenching circuit. The proposed novel active quenching circuit employing the DCC technique achieves 2.5 times better quenching time than the conventional one, with an area increase of just 23%. The schematic and simulation results are shown in this paper. Designed circuits are fabricated and simulated in 180 nm CMOS technology.

articleTitle: Data-driven respiratory signal detection of infants and toddlers in total-body PET/CT
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: PET/CT plays an important role in tumor staging and treatment evaluation, but pediatric patients encounter many challenges, e.g., dose and patient motion, in performing PET/CT scans. Total-body PET/CT, given its excellent sensitivity, enables dose reduction and shorter scan times for pediatric oncology imaging. However, respiratory motion can still lead to image artifacts and inaccurate lesion quantification in total-body PET/CT. To track the respiratory motion, hardware-based approaches and data-driven respiratory motion detection methods are often used. So far, there has been no dedicated external devices designed for pediatric patients, especially for infants and toddlers. In this work, we proposed to apply an optimized data-driven respiratory signal extraction method to the pediatric patients and to evaluate the respiratory signal quality. Specifically, we retrospectively analyzed N=126 PET/CT studies of infants and toddlers under three years old on the total-body PET/CT. Preliminary statistics show that the proposed method increases the respiratory signal-to-noise ratio by over 8 folds as compared to the conventional method for the infant and toddlers population, which indicates that sufficient quality of the respiratory signal can be generated using a data-driven method for any pediatric population. In the future, we will evaluate respiratory gating and motion correction using these respiratory signals.

articleTitle: Development and Performance Evaluation of an Ultra-High-Resolution Self-Collimation SPECT System for Small Animal Imaging
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: We have recently introduced a novel self-collimation (SC) concept for SPECT imaging, which utilizes detectors also as collimators to overcome the resolution-sensitivity trade-off innate to mechanical collimators. In this work, we report a prototype SC-SPECT system dedicated for high-resolution small animal imaging.The prototype consists of four concentric detector rings with spatially separated scintillators and a high-aperture-ratio tungsten ring, where each detector ring is collimated by other inner detector rings and the tungsten ring. The four detector rings have inner diameters of 260 mm, 390 mm, 520 mm, and 650 mm, and consist of 480, 720, 960, and 1,200 GAGG(Ce) scintillators, respectively. The scintillators are 0.84 mm (tangential) × 6 mm (radial) × 20 mm (axial) in size, evenly separated by a 0.84 mm gap in the tangential direction. The four detector rings are constructed with 40 detector modules, each covering a 9° angular region and comprising 42 detector units. In each detector unit, two scintillators are optically coupled to four SiPMs on the axial ends to determine photons’ axial interaction position with the depth-of-interaction technique; the decay time constants of the two scintillators are 90 ns and 200 ns, respectively, allowing for crystal identification with pulse shape discrimination. The tungsten ring has an inner diameter of 75 mm, an axial length of 290 mm, and a thickness of 2.5 mm, with 200 circular apertures (D = 0.4 mm) evenly distributed on the central transverse plane with a center-to-center distance of 1.2 mm.Preliminary results show that the prototype has a sensitivity of 0.064% at the center of the field-of-view. In the transverse plane, it can clearly resolve 5 × 5 point sources with a diameter of 0.36 mm and a center-to-center distance of 0.36 mm. Axially, it can clearly resolve point sources with a diameter of 0.4 mm and a center-to-center distance of 0.6 mm. A comprehensive performance evaluation is currently underway.

articleTitle: High-speed clock sequencing module implementation of high precision time digital converter for brain PET
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: High-precision Time Digital Converter (TDC), a time measuring tool, can measure time periods to achieve picosecond accuracy. At present, it is widely used in satellite navigation, radar positioning, medical imaging, high energy physics and other cutting-edge scientific research fields. With the rapid development of semiconductor technology, the way of realizing TDC by analogue method has gradually withdrawn from the historical stage. The digital method based on FPGA (Field Programable Gate Array) has become the mainstream direction of high-precision time measurement technology due to its high flexibility, low-cost and short development cycle. In this paper, we improve a new NUMP TDC phase shift clock sequencing scheme and designed a high-speed clock sequencing scheme based on FPGA hard line logic resources. Through board-level verification analysis, it is found that the high-speed hardware sequencing scheme is feasible, which significantly reduces the time of clock sequencing, thus promoting the application of multichannel TDC and the study of high-precision brain PET time measurement.

articleTitle: A Compact Anti-Coincidence Detector Based on BGO Scintillator and SiPM
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: This paper presents a compact anti-coincidence detector (ACD) based on BGO scintillator and silicon photomultiplier (SiPM) for a CubeSat mission named MASS-Cube. The ACD is a highly compact and delicated detector, utilizing two printed circuit boards (PCBs) within an area of less than 5.5 square centimeters. The ACD features a highly modular design, allowing it to function as an independent detection unit. Simple temperature compensation techniques were implemented to achieve good gain stability in the 20-30°C range. This paper describes the design process and calibration results of the ACD

articleTitle: Simplifying Dosimetry by Voxel-wise Activity Prediction with Regularized nCDE Encoder-nODE Decoder
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Object: In this study, we propose a new approach that utilizes nCDE and nODE as encoder and decoder, respectively, to predict the voxel-wise activity of late time points from acquired SPECT images at early time points to simplify the imaging process required for dosimetry.Method: We used <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">177</sup>Lu-DOTATATE SPECT dataset acquired in Sunway Medical Centre (SMC, Selangor, Malaysia). The nCDE encoder-nODE decoder framework was constructed for voxel-wise activity prediction. We fed 3D patches randomly extracted from early sequential SPECT images (i.e. x<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">0.5h</inf>, x<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">4h</inf>, x<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">24h</inf>) to the network. Then, the predicted voxel-wise activity is generated (x<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">48h</inf>) through the encoder and decoder. Runge-Kutta method was applied for nCDE encoder and nODE decoder. The 17 SPECT datasets were divided into 12:3:2 for training, evaluation, and testing data sets respectively.Result: The voxel-wise activity levels of kidneys and tumor regions predicted by the network were more similar to the real SPECT image. The network yielded relatively smaller mean differences of region-specific activity compared to the Mono-exp regardless of regions. The network showed a better voxel-wise correlation with true SPECT<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">48h</inf> than Mono-exp regardless of the regions. The tendency of estimated TIA and corresponding differences was similar but the differences were larger than those of predicted region-specific activities.Conclusion: We confirmed the potential to predict the voxel-wise activity of later time point from the early acquired SPECT images using the nCDE-nODE framework for the first time. This framework would be beneficial to simplify the sequential imaging required for voxel-based dosimetry.

articleTitle: MRI-styled PET: Dual-modality Fusion for PET Image Enhancement
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: This study introduces a novel image modality, named MRI-styled PET, which aims to enhance local structural details in FDG-PET images using T1-weighted MRI, with minimal distortion in SUVr. The proposed model involves a UNet++ network with a fusion strategy block in the bottleneck layer to combine multi-scale features from PET and MRI. Three fusion strategies, namely spatial-channel attention, self-attention, and cross-attention, have been proposed. The effectiveness of the fusion models was evaluated based on quantitative metrics, regional SUVr consistency, and visual realism. The results showed that spatial-channel attention with only the gray matter portion of MRI as input is the optimal fusion model. These preliminary results demonstrate the potential of MRI-styled PET images as a PET enhancement method with clinical utility.

articleTitle: Development of the GRAiNITA prototype with ZnWO4 and BGO crystal grains
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: We will present the development of two medium-size prototypes of GRAiNITA, a next-generation shashlik calorimeter, based on the use of ZnWO<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">4</inf> and BGO crystal grains, respectively, soaked in a high-density and high-refractive index liquid. As in the LiquidO detection technique[1], due to the presence of the grains, the scintillation light remains stochastically confined in the area of production; for this reason, it can be collected and transferred towards the photodetectors by the use of wavelength shifting fibers evenly distributed in the detection volume, similarly as in a conventional shashlik calorimeter.GRAiNITA represents a very appealing electromagnetic calorimeter candidate for high energy physics experiments for future electron-positron colliders. Indeed, due to the extreme fine sampling, GRAiNITA has the potential to reach a photon energy resolution of R~2%/sqrt(E) [2], thus increasing the precision of flavor physics with rare decays to photons or neutral pions. In this communication, we will present the outcomes of the study that led us to the choice of the best suited fibers for ZnWO<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">4</inf> and BGO, respectively, and we will present the effect observed on the light propagation, when adding isopropanol in the detection volume (as a first approximation of future liquids), to fill the space between the crystal grains. Finally, we will discuss the development and characterization of the prototypes, presenting either the mechanical and the electronic design.

articleTitle: Gamma Ray-Induced Radiation Damage in Ultrafast Lu2O3:Yb Ceramic Scintillators
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Activated by charge transfer luminescence ytterbium doped lutetium oxide (Lu<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf>O<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</inf>:Yb) is an ultrafast scintillator. Combined with its high density (9.4 g/cm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</sup>), it is a promising ultrafast inorganic scintillator for breaking the picosecond (ps) timing barrier for future high energy physics (HEP) time of flight (TOF) and ultrafast calorimetry applications. We report gamma rayinduced radiation damage in Lu<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf>O<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</inf>:Yb and Lu<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2x</inf>Y<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2(1-x)</inf>O<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</inf>:Yb ceramic samples fabricated in Radiation Monitoring Devices Inc. All samples show X-ray excited luminescence peaked at 370 nm with an ultrafast decay time of one ns observed by using a microchannel plate-photomultiplier tube-based test bench. Pulse height spectra and light output as a function of integration time were measured before and after irradiation up to 20 Mrad. This is a part of an on-going investigation for developing ultrafast inorganic scintillators for future HEP experiments.

articleTitle: Towards Safe Operation of Liquid TriMethyl Bismuth for Use in a Drift Detector
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: TriMethyl Bismuth (TMBi) has been proposed as a detector medium with charge and Cherenkov photon readout for positron emission tomography. Bold-PET pursues the idea of a drift detector based on TMBi, a heavy metal-organic liquid, to read out both the charge and the light generated in the liquid. The high atomic number (Z<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">Bi</inf> = 83) effectively converts TMBi 511 keV photons through the photoelectric effect (47% photo fraction). In addition, high optical density for visible wavelengths enables the emission of Cherenkov radiation generated by relativistic electrons in TMBi.In this work, we present studies on handling TMBi at different electric fields and under different environmental conditions to find suitable configurations to suppress electrical breakdown in TMBi at room temperature. A two-electrode glass cell filled with TMBi was constructed, and the breakdown behavior was tested under different operating conditions. At the vapor pressure of TMBi at room temperature of about 40 mbar and electric fields up to 20 kV/cm in the presence of low oxygen contamination, we found the formation of a discharge channel in the liquid and a steady increase in current. Further pressure reduction led to boiling of the TMBi and spontaneous ignition.We conclude from our experiments that TMBi remains stable against electric breakdown at room temperature in a pure argon atmosphere of 1 bar, at least up to electric field strengths of 20 kV/cm, presumably because the formation of gaseous TMBi was prevented.

articleTitle: Experimental Evaluation of Maximum-Likelihood-Based Data Preconditioning for DE-SPECT: A Clinical SPECT System Constructed with CZT Imaging Detectors
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: We present a maximum-likelihood (ML) -based data preconditioning method for a 3-D position sensitive CZT detector used in the DE-SPECT imaging system, a clinical SPECT system dedicated for imaging the peripheral vascular diseases (PVD) in lower extremities. The 3-D CZT detectors offer subpixel resolution of <0.5 mm FWHM in X-Y-Z directions and an ultrahigh energy resolution of 3 keV at 200 keV, 4.5 keV at 450 keV, and 5.4 keV at 511 keV. Due to pixel edge effects and distortion issues, we utilized sheet beam scanning to measure the detector response, and then used an ML-based algorithm to reconstruct the projection, which effectively deconvolve the distortions in detector linear responses. As we showed in the experimental results, this technique produces corrected positions of interactions. Additionally, we anticipate that this approach can be applied to other solid-state and scintillation detectors with known distortion due to imperfections in detectors and electronics. Future work includes phantom studies to evaluate the effect of the data preconditioning approach on experimental SPECT imaging studies.

articleTitle: GATE Optical Simulation of U-Shaped DOI Detectors for Optimal Crystal Surface Roughness
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: For brain dedicated positron emission tomography (PET), depth-of-interaction (DOI) information is essential to minimize the parallax error at the periphery of the PET field-of-view, where the human cortex is located. In this work, therefore, we propose a new U-shaped light sharing crystal design that has a tapered geometry to achieve good DOI resolution in the single-ended readout scheme. We investigated the optimal crystal surface roughness of the new DOI detector using GATE optical simulation in terms of DOI resolution. In addition, the DOI resolution of the proposed design was compared with previous U-shaped detectors, the crosshair light sharing (CLS) detector, and the Prism detector. The proposed crystal geometry had dimensions of 3.0×6.2×15 mm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</sup>, in which the central part has a 0.2 mm slit with a 12 mm in length, thereby yielding a 3 mm optical window at the crystal top region. The bottom of the crystal was optically coupled to two SiPM channels (each with sensitive area of 3×3 mm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sup>) by one-to-one coupling. The emission spectrum of the LYSO crystal and the photon detection efficiency of the SiPM were considered in the optical simulation. To evaluate DOI resolution, collimated 511 keV radiations were irradiated into different crystal depths (2.5, 5.0, 7.5, 10.0, 12.5, 13.5, and 14.5 mm). Three different surface roughness of 0.5º (mechanical polishing), 10º (roughened), and 26º (as-cut) were investigated. The proposed detector with the as-cut surface finish provided the best DOI resolution (1.5±0.1 mm), which outperformed those (as-cut) of the CLS detector (1.8±0.2 mm) and Prism detector (1.9±0.2 mm). By the time of the conference, the GATE optical simulation results will be compared with experimental results for validation of the simulation as well as for investigation of the effect on timing resolution.

articleTitle: Imaging simulation of "Scratch-PET": an intraoperative PET with a hand-held detector
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: In cancer surgery, excessive resection of biological tissues leads to the functional loss of the organ and the increase of physical burden for patients. However, it is difficult to identify precise resection regions intraoperatively. PET is often used for cancer diagnosis, but its intraoperative use has been prevented; massive equipment like a detector ring may interfere with the surgical process. Therefore, we aimed at developing an intraoperative PET system with a hand-held probe-type detector, called "Scratch-PET." The system allows the surgeon to scan a target region using a hand-held detector. PET images appear like on a scratch card. In this work, we proposed an image reconstruction framework to achieve real-time image reconstruction even under the condition that the geometry changes by moving a hand-held detector. We used GPU-based list-mode time-of-flight (TOF) row-action maximum likelihood algorithm (RAMLA) reconstruction, and the reconstructed image is displayed every 10 s. We also implemented a fast calculation method for the global sensitivity image that is required in the Scratch-PET image reconstruction. We demonstrated the feasibility of the proposed method through computer simulation. We modeled the small geometry of Scratch-PET and simulated a 2 min measurement of a tumor phantom with a practical activity concentration. The tumor phantom consisted of the elliptical background and four spherical sources of 10, 8, 6 and 4 mm diameter, each with 1:8 contrast. As a result, we were able to visualize a spherical source of 6mm diameter. Our proposed image reconstruction framework ran without delay, which supported the feasibility of the Scratch-PET concept.

articleTitle: Characterisation of the PETITION ICU System
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: The PETITION (PET for InTensive care units and Innovative protON therapy) collaboration has developed two Positron Emission Tomography (PET) systems to enable novel clinical applications for this imaging modality. Both PET scanners are brain systems featuring a bore diameter of 300 mm and an axial field of view length of 179 mm. One of the PET system is a mobile beside PET scanner that can be employed in the intensive care unit (ICU) to image vulnerable patients, who cannot be moved into regular PET scanners. The second system is designed for applications in proton beam therapy and therefore has an opening to allow for simultaneous irradiation and imaging.In this work we focus on the characterisation of the first system, called ICU system. On the hardware side, we use Lutetium-yttrium oxyorthosilicate crystals (2.74 × 2.74 × 15 mm3 ) together with sparse silicon photomultiplier arrays and custom readout electronics to capture the gamma rays from the tracer decay. A 400 keV − 600 keV energy window together with a 2 ns coincidence timing window are used and list mode files containing all coincidences are generated. With a 22 Na point source, we measure a coincidence energy resolution of 11.8 % (FWHM) at the photo peak and a coincidence timing resolution of 560 ps (FWHM). Using the same source, we obtain a spatial resolution between 2.2 mm (FWHM) and 3.3 mm (FWHM) after iterative image reconstruction, depending on the source position.

articleTitle: From MACACOp to FALCON, characterization and in-beam tests
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: The IRIS group of IFIC-Valencia has developed and characterized a Compton camera, MACACOp , for in-vivo proton beam range verification. The prototype is composed of monolithic LaBr3 scintillation crystals coupled to SiPMs and uses the TOFPET2 ASIC as readout electronics. The prototype was successfully tested with a cyclotron at a proton therapy center. With the purpose of testing MACACOp in a state-of-the-art accelerator, measurements were performed with a superconducting synchrocyclotron (IBA S2C2). The obtained results show MACACOp 's potential to reconstruct images using advanced clinical proton beams. An upgraded prototype, FALCON, was developed with the aim of improving the system's efficiency and capability. FALCON was characterized in the laboratory and will soon be tested in-beam.

articleTitle: Experimental characterization of asimultaneous photoncounting and energy integrating detector for X-ray imaging applications
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: This paper presents the experimental test results of the X-ray detectors based on our simultaneous photon counting and energy integrating readout ASIC. The readout ASIC consists of 128 signal processing channels. Each signal processing channel contains a photon counting channel and an energy integrating channel. The detector module consists of 8 readout ASICs, a CdTe sensor and a fan-out PCB that connects the ASICs and the sensor. The detector performance was then characterized using X-ray tubes. The energy responses of the detectors were measured using the characteristic X-ray of the target materials. The non-uniformity of both the charge-voltage gain and energy threshold among channels was measured and then compensated by tuning the local DACs. The polarization effects of both energy integrating and photon counting channels under different photon fluxes were studied. The detailed test results will be presented on the conference.

articleTitle: X-ray Radiolysis of CsI:Tl Scintillator Films and the Release of I2
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Among the various types of scintillators, vapor-deposited films of CsI:Tl have been widely used in X-ray imaging, mainly for medical and industrial applications. As for its mechanism of radiation damage, the creation of color centers is a well-known fact. However, several previous studies have exemplified radiolysis into colloids of alkali metal and clusters of halogen molecules for some fcc alkali halides, while there have been few reports about CsI, which has a bcc structure. In this study we confirmed for the first time the release of I<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf> from CsI:TI columnar films induced by 60 kV X-rays at room temperature using DART-MS and ion chromatography analysis. We also revealed that the amount of released I<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf> decreases logarithmically with an increase in the concentration of Tl. Furthermore, we investigated how much this phenomenon affects the optical performance of the scintillator. Spectroscopic analysis demonstrated that it degrades the transmittance at around a certain wavelength, 440 nm. In addition, we visually presented the correlation between Tl concentration and the intensity of absorption peaks induced by X-rays.

articleTitle: Performance of custom fine-pitch SiPM-scintillator based photon counting detectors
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Photon Counting X-ray detectors attract great interest recently, which requires very high operating count rate up to 10<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">8</sup> photons/s/mm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sup>. Pixelated energy resolving detectors are necessary and greatly in interest for the use in X-ray photon-counting computed tomography (PCCT) systems. Direct detectors, such as CdTe or CdZnTe, have been successfully studied and used in clinical PCCT scanner. On the other hand, the possibility of indirect fast scintillation detectors coupled with photo-sensors has been proposed and investigated, however, the realistic fine-pitch (a few hundred micrometers pixel) SiPM-scintillator array are not demonstrated yet. In this study, we have fabricated a new custom-silicon photomultiplier (SiPM) array with the pixel size of 250 µm array (10 × 10 elements) one-to-one coupled with fine-pitch GFAG/GAGG arrays to achieve a good energy resolution and counting rate. The energy resolution shows 16.2 % at 122 keV with GAGG single pixel (20 µm device) and 18 % at 122 keV with GAGG arrays (15 µm device). GAGG shows better energy resolution than GFAG, but GFAG is promising in terms of faster response time ( <= 40 ns). Those results show the great feasibility of the indirect SiPM-scintillator based detectors for the use of X-ray PCCT. The more detail analysis and first image will be shown in the presentation.

articleTitle: A high spatial resolution small animal PET-Insert system compatible with 9.4T MRI based on a dual-ended readout method
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: A high spatial resolution small animal PET-Insert system with DOI capability based-on Dual Readout, compatible with the United Imaging Healthcare (UIH) 9.4T small animal MRI system, is presented. The PET-Insert can be easily installed MRI scanner or used as a stand-alone PET system. Due to the limited space of the small animal MRI system, the PET-Insert detector has a flat design with a total thickness of 22.5mm. Each detector module has 6 SiPM array boards (dual-ended readout) and 1 control board, with 224 SiPM channels on each SiPM array board. The SiPM signals are connected to control board by a Flexible Print Circuit (FPC). All analog SiPM signals are digitized by UIH Monaco ASIC, using SensL 3 x 3mm² microFJ60035 SiPMs. The detector is based on 3 units, with each unit containing 448 SiPMs (dual-ended), and an AFOV is 178mm. The 8x8 crystal arrays are read out from both ends with 2x2 SiPMs array. The crystal size is 0.8x0.8x12mm³ of LYSO. The system is composed of 8 detectors with a TFOV of 105mm. The experimental evaluation of the PET system shows that the DOI resolution of the system is 1.97mm, the spatial resolution of the Derenzo model by 3D-OSEM reconstruction is 0.7mm, and the energy resolution with scatter recovery is 14.18%. Experiments in 9.4T MRI system are currently in progress.

articleTitle: On-chip artificial neural network for PET source position reconstruction
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: This work presents the characterization results and methods used to determine the reconstruction of a <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">22</sup>Na point source placed in a coincidence setup. For this purpose, a novel, fully-integrated, reconfigurable feed-forward artificial neural network was implemented in a 16-nm FinFET CMOS technology node. The artificial neural network uses timestamps obtained from 10 on-chip time-to-digital converters. The network topology can be reconfigured at any time within design limits. After appropriate training, the artificial neural network successfully distinguished six different radioactive source positions placed between the two photodetectors along the X axis that fed the time-to-digital converters. Thanks to its ability to filter frames without any coincidence and to increase the overall sensitivity, the on-chip approach significantly reduces both system complexity and data throughput.

articleTitle: Advanced Empiricial Dual Energy Calibration
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: In dual energy computed tomography (DECT) the task of material decomposition remains a challenging task [1]. One established method due to its simple implementation is the empirical dual-energy calibration (EDEC) [2]. In this research, the EDEC method is expanded by incorporating prior knowledge through the addition of further calibration materials. This involves including a new set of dual energy data for the new materials and incorporating these into the proposed optimization data term. Thus, an enlarged system of equations is created in which the equations of the standard method are coupled by a linear combination using the knowledge of the theoretical monoenergetic attenuation values. The proposed calibration technique was performed on two measured data sets of standardized phantoms for which the exact material compositions are known. The precision of the virtual monoenergetic images' (VMIs) [3] attenuation values obtained from a separate evaluation data set was calculated in terms of mean-squared error over all considered energies. The results show a systematic reduction in the deviation from the expected attenuation values. The proposed extension can be easily implemented in current dual energy CT (DECT) protocols. In conclusion, without restricting the simplicity of conventional EDEC application, the diagnostic value of the computed VMIs can be improved through the proposed advanced calibration process.

articleTitle: Characterization of ePixUHR-35kHz: a 13.8 Gb/s full-frame X-ray imaging readout ASIC for the LCLS-II upgrade
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: ePixUHR-35kHz is a novel readout ASIC designed and optimized for the high dynamic range, high spatial resolution and demanding high repetition rate requirements of the newer generation of Free Electron Lasers (FELs).The ePixUHR-35kHz ASIC is composed by 192 (H) × 168 (V) pixels, organized in clusters of 6 (H) ×12 (V) pixels each. Every cluster contains its own digitizer, for a total of 448 integrated SAR ADCs operating concurrently. When running at its target frequency, 35.71 kHz, the ASIC will generate about 13.8 Gb/s of data. In order to manage the ASIC, monitor the system and stream the acquired data, a specialized detector camera system called ePixHR is used. The camera is composed of two separate PCBs: the Analog card and the Digital card. It uses a Kintex Ultrascale FPGA and implements 4 parallel and independent fiber optic links, with each link running at a speed of 6.25 Gbps.In the following, characterization and analysis of the ePixUHR-35kHz ASIC, along with the description of the camera system, are discussed.

articleTitle: Adding Position-Sensitive Functionality to a Forceps-Type Mini-PET Prototype
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Optimizing the extent of lymph node (LN) dissection in surgical cancer treatment is expected to minimize the postoperative complication rate. Our previous clinical study reported that <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">18</sup>F-fluoro-2-deoxy-D-glucose (FDG) could be a biomarker for intraoperative LN metastasis diagnosis. To realize an intraoperative LN diagnosis with FDG, we are developing a forceps-type mini-PET as an intraoperative device. With a pair of small scintillation detectors mounted on the forceps head, the device can detect annihilation radiations from FDG by pinching a target LN individually. However, the radiation-detection efficiency strongly depends on the position of the radioactivity source in the field-of-view (FOV) between paired detectors, which may cause false judgment in LN diagnosis. To correct the efficiency variation, the positional information of the radioactivity distribution is necessary. Therefore, in this work, we proposed to add a position-sensitive functionality to the forceps-type mini PET. The basic concept is to divide each monolithic scintillator into a 2×2 matrix (consisting of four crystals). The center position of the 18F distribution can be estimated from 4×4 signals by applying a simple neural network (NN), which was proven in our previous simulation study. In this study, we developed the prototype device having the 2×2 matrix and evaluated the source position estimation performance. The NN was tuned by using Geant4 simulation data. The energy resolution was 27 % at 511keV, and the coincidence timing resolution was 9.24 ns. The proposed method for source position estimation using the NN worked well, and the accuracy of the z position was within the error of 2 mm.

articleTitle: Positron Annihilation Lifetime Spectroscopy and GEANT4 Simulation of Positronium (Ps) Lifetime in Soft Tissues
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: In Positron Emission Tomography (PET), the positron-emitting radiotracer is administered to the patient’s body, and the annihilation photons are used to create an image map of the spatial distribution of the radiotracer uptake. However, a positron can also combine with an electron in the surrounding lattice, forming para-positronium (p-Ps) or ortho-positronium (o-Ps). The decay of positronium, as compared to "pick-off" from the tissue can potentially provide additional information about the material and improve image contrast. In this study, we experimentally demonstrated the dependence of positronium lifetime on the tissue type using the positron annihilation lifetime spectroscopy (PALS) technique. We extracted the three components of positron lifetime corresponding to the positron free annihilation lifetime, p-PS lifetime, and o-Ps lifetime for three types of bovine, non-fixated soft tissues: adipose, hepatic, and muscle. The o-Ps lifetime in adipose tissue (2.53±0.01ns) was found to be approximately 25% longer than in hepatic (2.03±0.02ns) and muscle tissues (2.00±0.01ns). Our measurements also confirmed that the probability of positron and p-Ps annihilation in soft tissues increases with the electron density of the tissue. The relative contrast of adipose tissue is larger compared to X-ray phase-contrast imaging, the current state-of-the-art for soft tissue imaging and analysis. Furthermore, we developed a physics-based Geant4 model of positron decay in tissue. We used the model to reconstruct a positronium lifetime image, based on the annihilation events, emitting two gamma rays back-to-back, and the o-Ps decay, emitting three gamma rays simultaneously. We aim to further validate the Geant4 model by simulating the PALS setup and reproducing the experimental results.

articleTitle: The PISA concept: Photon Induced Scintillation Amplifier as an innovative high-gain photonmultiplier with Imaging capability
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: The current generation of noble liquid DM detectors is limited by the radioactivity from the detector materials, mostly from the specially radio-clean photomultiplier tubes (PMT), contributing to the background at ~ 80% level. We propose a simple concept, the Photon Induced Scintillation Amplifier (PISA), for ionization signal amplification. The PISA is a true photon-multiplier, where the secondary scintillation produced in the charge avalanches inside the holes of the micropattern electron multiplier is read out by suitable photosensors, such as SiPM.We have shown that a very large number of photons are produced in micropattern electron multipliers. One electron may produce about 10^5 and 10^4 photons in the THGEM avalanches in xenon and argon, respectively. A MHSP etched on Kapton for radiopurity sake, can be used instead of the GEM or THGEM cascade, since the former presents higher photon output. A large photon output in the final charge avalanche ensures the capability for single-photon sensitivity. The PISA will be cost-effective in comparison with the vacuum PMT and will allow for area coverage above 80%. The SiPM can be distributed in a 2D array with a pitch suitable for the imaging capabilities of the PISA.The PISA provides a breakthrough in radiopurity, due to reduced radioactivity levels of Kapton foils, SiPM, fused silica window, metal case and the feasibility to deploy remote "hot" electronics, since the large gains achieved in SiPMs allow for signal transmission over large distances without significant degradation.

articleTitle: FFFI: A Full-Field X-ray Fluorescence Imaging System
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: A full field X-ray fluorescence imaging system requires two major subsystems: an optical system which provides suitable magnification of the emissions to provide the required spatial resolution while remaining achromatic, and a detector capable of spectral resolution in each pixel. In this work, we will present two examples of full-field imaging optics that satisfy this requirement. The first is a tapered polycapillary optic, the second is a Modified Uniform Redundant Array (MURA) coded aperture. Polycapillary optics have the advantage of giving direct imaging of a sample but are not strictly achromatic. We will show fluorescence slice tomography data from samples using a tapered polycapillary optic with a 5:1 taper. MURAs use the concept of coded aperture arrays which have the attraction of having higher efficiency with 50% open area. Our arrays have 7 µm openings and are truly achromatic in our energy regime (2-14 keV) but require computation to form an image. Using our silicon laboratory at Brookhaven National Laboratory we have produced various orders of MURAs made from gold on a 1 µm thick silicon nitride membrane. A custom detector is being designed for this project. That design is being presented separately at this conference. It will offer 128 x 128 pixels, each 100 µm square, and will provide spectra with around 200eV resolution at 5.9keV. Readout will be sparsified to minimize the required readout bandwidth.

articleTitle: Timepix3 detector: Performance of thick CdTe sensors for spectral X-ray imaging in industrial applications
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: This study presents the initial imaging performance results of a 5 mm thick CdTe Timepix3 ASIC for high-energy photon detection and imaging, continuation of previous work done with a 2 mm CZT sensor, which demonstrated enhanced material contrast by using sub-pixel imaging and spectroscopically-enhanced imaging. The increased sensor thickness has a few immediate implications. On one hand, it increases radiation attenuation and thus radiation detection efficiency. On the other hand, a thicker sensible volume increases charge-sharing between neighboring pixels, which at the same time can potentially increase spatial resolution through sub-pixel imaging. Yet, by leveraging the ASIC's spectral analysis capabilities, such as Time-over-Threshold (ToT) and Time-of-Arrival (ToA), event information can be used to improve the image formation process beyond untreated datasets, by using techniques such as event clustering. Additional material calibration measurements allow the use of energy-weighted imaging that increase the Contrast-to-Noise ratio of specific materials, allowing for material highlighting, separation and identification in real-life samples. The 5 mm thickness, was subjected to a general device characterization. While the use of detectors with sensor thicknesses beyond 2 mm is rare, achieving good imaging performance with thick detectors can open new application possibilities e.g. non-destructive testing in production sectors, radiotherapy or nuclear medicine. Thus, this work highlights the potential of the 5 mm CdTe Timepix3 detector in material visibility enhancement, showcasing its potential in a range of industrial applications for Spectroscopic Photon Counting Detectors SPCDs.

articleTitle: The new Matterhorn detector for 4th generation synchrotrons
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: The new fourth-generation storage rings (diffraction-limited storage rings, e.g., MAXIV, ESRF EBS, SLS2.0) will have a much higher brilliance than the third-generation sources increasing the photon flux at the pixel level. This will exceed the count rate capabilities of many of the single photon-counting detectors currently used, making them unsuitable to be used in future experiments at these machines. Matterhorn is a 2-D hybrid pixel detector developed by the PSD detector group of the Paul Scherrer Institut (PSI, Switzerland) to be used at SLS2.0. The main goal of this detector is to extend the count rate capability (target 20 Mcounts/pixel/s) by means of multi-threshold circuitry in the pixels.The final Matterhorn ASIC will have 256 x 256 pixels with 75 μm pitch, will be designed in UMC 110nm technology, and will be highly configurable. Each pixel will have a charge-sensitive amplifier and a shaper connected to four comparators. Each comparator will have an adjustable threshold that can be set to a value higher than the photon energy allowing to extend the count rate capability. Each comparator is connected to a 16-bit independently gateable counter. The target frame rate for reading out one 16-bit counter of all pixels is 10 kHz. Therefore, each ASIC will be equipped with four serial links operating at the clock frequency of 3.125 GHz provided by an on-chip PLL.The first prototype of the ASIC with 48 x 48 pixels was submitted in January 2023 and is expected back by June 2023. The pixels already include the four comparators and counters. In the periphery, two serial links working at a clock frequency of 1.6 GHz provided by an on-chip PLL are included. Moreover, the digital periphery can be configured to read one (selectable), two, three, or all the counters.In this contribution, we will show the working principle of this detector and all its foreseen functionalities. Moreover, the experimental results of the first prototype will also be shown.

articleTitle: Deep Learning Framework for the Synthesis of Rest Phase from Stress Phase in Positron Emission Tomography Myocardial Perfusion Imaging
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Positron Emission Tomography Myocardial Perfusion Imaging (PET-MPI) is non-invasive and gold standard for diagnosis of coronary artery disease. MPI using [<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">13</sup>N]NH3 is a Rest-Stress process and involves acquiring myocardial images at two different phases of the cardiac cycle. However, the procedure involves two phases that can present challenges in terms of patient comfort, radiation dose, and workload for healthcare facilities. Recent advances in deep learning (DL) have shown promising results in various medical imaging tasks, such as prediction, translation, and synthesis. In this study, we explore the potential of DL in synthesizing the rest phase of PET-MPI scans using stress phase images. To achieve this goal, we developed a DL model using U-Net architecture equipped with self-attention layers that capture long-range dependencies between feature maps and focus on more relevant regions of the image. We further augmented this model with ResNet and trained two separate models on the dataset of 200 patients. We qualitatively and quantitatively evaluated our method. There was a good visual agreement between the synthesized and ground truth images. The quantitative metrics were calculated including peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR), structural similarity index (SSIM), and normalized mean square error (NMSE) values to quantify the distortion level of the synthesized images and similarity between the ground truth and synthesized images. Our models demonstrated high-quality image reconstruction with an average PSNR of 32.44, a high degree of structural similarity with an average SSIM of 0.96, and high accuracy with an average NMSE of 0.05. In conclusion, our study highlights the potential of DL in improving the accuracy and efficiency of PET-MPI scans, which can have significant clinical implications. Our proposed approach could potentially reduce the need for patients to undergo additional imaging scans, leading to improved patient outcomes and reduced healthcare costs.

articleTitle: Fundamental Study on Image Improvement of X-ray Fluorescence Computed Tomography by Deep Image Prior
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: We are developing an X-ray fluorescence computed tomography (XFCT) system using nonradioactive contrast agents (e.g. iodine compounds) for preclinical studies as a new modality that provides biological function images like positron emission tomography (PET) and single photon emission computed tomography (SPECT). To perform in vivo imaging of small animals with XFCT, it is necessary to improve the image quality and detection limit. The aim of this study is to improve image quality of XFCT by applying deep image prior (DIP), a type of convolutional neural network, to image reconstruction. DIP can restore image with only the target image acquired by XFCT. Projection images were processed with DIP for noise reduction after scatter correction. Reconstructed images were generated by ML-EM method for multi-pinhole XFCT. To evaluate the image improvement effect, physical phantom experiments were performed using synchrotron monochromatic X-rays as excitation light. The contrast-to-noise ratio of the reconstructed image was greatly improved by 4.6 times in the 0.3 mg/ml iodine solution region, and the detection limit improved from 0.069 mg/ml to 0.035 mg/ml. This study demonstrated that reconstruction using DIP could greatly improve the image quality and detection limit of XFCT without degrading the spatial resolution.

articleTitle: Feasibility study of positronium imaging with Biograph Vision Quadra and Modular J-PET
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Positronium Imaging is gaining interest as a new promising method that may improve the diagnostic specificity of Positron Emission Tomography. Recently, the first ex-vivo and in-vivo positronium lifetime images were demonstrated by means of the dedicated multi-photon J-PET system. The latest upgrades of the Biograph Vision Quadra (Siemens Healthineers) to the singles mode acquisition open the possibility of multi-photon imaging. In this simulation-based work, sensitivity of both systems has been assessed as a function of the energy window applied for registration of the prompt photon. The research was conducted using four radioisotopes: <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">124</sup>I, <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">68</sup>Ga, <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">44</sup>Sc, <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">22</sup>Na, which were chosen due to their medical or laboratory utilization. Simulations were performed with the GATE software. The result indicates that Biograph Vision Quadra provides about 400 times higher sensitivity with respect to the modular J-PET prototype used to demonstrate the first positronium images, assuming full energy acquisition of the prompt photon.

articleTitle: Self-Supervised learning framework to generate preclinical Standard-Count PET from Low-Count PET and multi-objective task-based performance evaluation
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Low-Count preclinical PET (LC-PET) imaging has numerous benefits in improving animal logistics, increasing scanner throughput and preserving integrity in longitudinal studies. However, LC-PET suffers from poor signal-to-noise ratio (SNR), quantification uncertainties and segmentation difficulties. Supervised learning techniques are effective at generating Standard-Count PET (SC-PET) images from LC-PET but require large datasets for training. To address these challenges, we developed a self-supervised learning framework to generate SC-PET from LC-PET and evaluated the performance of the framework using fidelity-based, task-based segmentation and quantification metrics for different LC-PET realizations. We developed the Multi-Block Residual Network (MBR-Net) for implementing the Noise-to-Noise (N2N) self-supervised learning principle. Multiple residual units are implemented to facilitate large-scale feature compression for faster propagation and convergence across the network. The performance of N2N MBR-Net generated SC-PET images were benchmarked against supervised DL based methods including Residual UNet (RU-Net) and Dilated Network (D-Net) and non-DL denoisers like Non-Local Means (NLM) and Block Matching and 3D Filtering (BM3D). The N2N MBR-Net generated SC-PET images exhibited significantly (p<0.05) improved image quality expressed in terms of SSIM and NRMSE compared to non-DL approaches and is comparable to supervised DL methods. Tumor segmentation performance for N2N MBR-Net evaluated using Dice score exhibited similar performance to supervised DL methods and better performance than non-DL methods. In terms of SUV<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">MEAN</inf> bias, N2N MBR-Net exhibited a median bias of 0.7%, 1.2% and 2.8% for 19.8M (~10% of SC-PET), 9.9M (~5% of SC-PET) and 1.6M (~0.8% of SC-PET) photon count level consistent to supervised DL methods and better than non-DL approaches. The N2N MBR-Net successfully generated quantitatively accurate SC-PET images using self-supervised learning.

articleTitle: Characterizing the Performance of Spectroscopic Anomaly Detection and Identification Algorithms with a Synthetic Urban Search Dataset
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: The ability to characterize the performance of an anomaly detection/isotope identification algorithm is contingent on the diversity of scenarios present in the training, validation, and testing datasets. However, it is often infeasible to collect enough data to get good performance at operationally relevant false alarm rates. Instead, we can use Monte Carlo simulations to generate realistic synthetic data. Doing so allows us control over the source of radiation, its strength, its mass, and its shielding; the detector type, its energy resolution, and its location; and other environmental factors such as the ambient radioactivity from structures and materials present in urban scenes and environmental attenuation. As part of the Radiological Anomaly Detection And Identification (RADAI) and RADAI-extended (REX) projects, we have developed such a dataset with which we can characterize the performance of different approaches to spectroscopic anomaly detection and isotope identification. This paper will discuss the use of template matching algorithms (non-negative matrix factorization and multiplexed censored energy window) and more complex algorithms which exploit the time-series nature of the data (transformer-based neural networks) as benchmarks for characterizing the difficulty of the dataset. We show that the initial dataset was found to be too difficult for some sources and too easy for others, and we are currently using this feedback to improve the design of the dataset.

articleTitle: High-energy-resolution CdZnTe linear array pixel detectors with fast and low noise readout electronics
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Radiation detectors based on Cadmium Zinc Telluride (CZT) compounds find many applications thanks to their high detection efficiency, room temperature operation, and to their reliability in compact detection systems for medical, astrophysical, or industrial applications. In this work, we present the latest results achieved in terms of energy resolution using SIRIO [1], a fast ultra low-noise charge sensitive amplifier, and two linear-array pixel detector, based on different CZT crystals. The first detector features a 0.25 mm pitch, 25 μm interpixel gap, 1-mm thick and was grown by IMEM/CNR using the boron oxide encapsulated vertical Bridgman (B-VB) technique. The second detector is based on a "High-Flux" material manufactured by Redlen grown by high-pressure Bridgman technique (HPB), with 0.5 mm pixel pitch, 50 μm interpixel gap and 1 mm thickness. The spectroscopic performances of the detection systems were characterized using 57Co, 241Am and 55Fe radioactive sources, showing an excellent energy-resolving capability in the lowenergy range, obtaining room-temperature spectra with a noise threshold below 1 keV and intrinsic noise levels down to 189 eV FWHM equivalent [2]. These activities where carried out in the framework of an Italian collaboration on the development of energy-resolved X-ray scanners for material recycling, medical applications, and non-destructive testing in the food industry.

articleTitle: On-the-fly 3D muon path estimation algorithm for muon imaging applications
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Muon tomography has gained attention for its potential use in critical national security applications, such as nuclear nonproliferation and safeguards verification, due to the unique properties of cosmic ray muons, including high energy and low attenuation even in dense materials. However, the resolution of muon image reconstruction is limited by multiple Coulomb scattering (MCS) within the target object. To improve and expand muon tomography, there is a need for efficient and flexible physics-based algorithms to model the MCS process accurately. In this study, we present a new algorithm based on Bayesian probability theory and a Gaussian approximation of MCS for estimating the most likely path of a cosmic ray muon as it traverses a uniform or nonuniform medium. Using GEANT4 simulations in a simple homogeneous 20 cm cube of low, medium, and high Z materials, we show that this algorithm can achieve reduced noise and better resolution for cosmic ray muons of various energies.

articleTitle: Characterization of a Low Noise and Low Background Charge Sensitive Amplifier for the Readout of Germanium Detectors
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: The observation of neutrinoless double beta decay would have major implications in the understanding of the origin of the matter in the universe. Given zero electric charge and no colour, they may be Majorana particles, i.e. their own antiparticles. The Large Enriched Germanium Experiment for Neutrinoless double beta Decay (LEGEND) is a ton-scale experimental program to search for the neutrinoless decay in the isotope 76Ge. In this framework, we have designed a new ASIC in the 0.35 μm CMOS technology, which will fulfill Ge-detector requirements. The ASIC has a key role in order to obtain a good energy resolution and a high radiopurity environment that are crucial conditions in neutrinoless double beta decay experiments. The ASIC has been designed featuring a low noise Charge Sensitive Amplifier (CSA) and an on-chip Low-DropOut regulator (LDO). Two different versions of the CSA has been implemented. One has a dedicated compensation network and implements an integrated large value resistor through an ICON cell. The other CSA works with a large external feedback resistor. The LDO allows the chip to be powered without by-pass capacitors which are not compliant with the radiopurity requirement. With a 50 pA leakage current and a detector capacitance of 4 pF, the ASIC aims to achieve a noise performance of 50 e<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">−</sup>rms. This work shows the results of the experimental characterization of the ASIC. We report the measured characteristic Output Voltage vs Input Voltage (external power supply) at room temperature of the LDO and the measured transient response of the CSA, showing characteristics in line with the predictions.

articleTitle: Precise and accurate coincidence processing for the BrainPET-7T with triple coincidences and randoms
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: The new BrainPET-7T is a high-performance PET insert for human neuroimaging compatible with UHF-MRI. Its high efficiency facilitates the detection of triple coincidences of the two annihilation photons and an additional prompt gamma from isotopes as Mn-52 and I-124 to enable dual-tracer PET. Additionally, aiming at a sensitivity of more than 12% and a quantitation accuracy of 99% we are striving for a correct treatment of triple random coincidences for pure positron PET radionuclides such as F-18, C-11, and O-15 which has a trade-off between a loss of sensitivity and inaccurate quantitation with current approaches. Therefore, an appropriate random estimation considering random triple coincidences is required. We estimate the number of random triple coincidences and reduce the variance of the estimations by means of multiple delayed windows. We have investigated the methods with the simulator PeneloPET for a point source and an extended homogeneous source. The studies reveal the importance of considering triples, since for the studied cases the ratio of triple coincidences to double coincidences is 10% for 40 MBq. The amount of random triples is estimated with a rel. error of less than 1% and less than 5% for triples of two and three different decays, respectively at 10 MBq. The results show how the variance of the random coincidence estimator is reduced by applying multiple delayed windows.

articleTitle: A Versatile Edge Machine Learning Test Bench for High Bandwidth Instrumentation
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: New scientific experiments and instruments generate large volumes of data that need to be transferred to storage or processing. Edge machine learning could allow us to reduce the amount of data before transmission, thus reducing the cost of experiments. Data compression can be done in various ways depending on the targeted experiment such as image compression or rejection of unwanted events using a veto system.
