The high throughput, complexity and operational costs of the instruments make debugging in the real system a difficult challenge. To facilitate debugging and caracterisation of edge machine learning systems, we developed a test bench that can be used for fast testing using both simulated and measured data. This paper details this test bench and the methodology used for caracterizing the performance of a real time data compression system based on an FPGA. In our current configuration, the test bench acquires 51.2 Gbps from a 6.4 GSps analog to digital converter and is designed to integrate data pre-processing and machine learning inside an FPGA. All elements are modular and this test bench could be used for analog or digital detectors but also time to digital converters based systems.

articleTitle: Pushing the Limit of BGO-based Dual-ended Cherenkov PET Detector Through Photon Transit Time Correction
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: The rising production costs of commonly used lutetium-based fast scintillators and the development of silicon photomultipliers technology have made BGO a promising candidate for time-of-flight positron emission tomography (TOF PET) detectors due to its ability to generate prompt Cherenkov photons. However, using BGO as a hybrid scintillator presents challenges due to low photon statistics and a distribution that does not conform well to a single Gaussian. To mitigate this, a proposal was made to increase the likelihood of detecting the first Cherenkov photons by positioning two photosensors in opposition at the entrance and exit faces of the scintillator [1]. In the other hand, compensating for the photon transit time spread is known to enhance the timing performance of the dual-ended BGO Cherenkov TOF PET detector [2]. A 3 × 3 × 15 mm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</sup> unpolished BGO sample was prepared and tested. The high-frequency dual-ended BGO detector was implemented and coincidence events were acquired against a 3 × 3 × 3 mm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</sup> LYSO:Ce:Mg reference detector. The timing performance of dual-ended BGO detectors were analyzed using bottom, top, meantime, and adaptive timestamp methods. Through a depth-of-interaction based (DOI-based) correction of photon transit time spread, we demonstrated a further improvement in timing resolution of dual-ended BGO-based Cherenkov TOF PET detector with adaptive arrival time pickoff. The use of a dual-ended configuration resulted in a significant improvement in timing resolution compared to a single-ended readout configuration, particularly in terms of FWTM value. Although polishing the crystal surface was still favorable in terms of FWHM value, compensating for photon travel time by taking advantage of DOI information from unpolished crystals with relatively higher light loss enabled further enhancement in timing performance the polished crystals.

articleTitle: Performance of the Area Radiation Gamma and Neutron Origin Telemetry (ARGANOT) Radiological Detection System
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: A single Area Radiation Gamma and Neutron Origin Telemetry (ARGANOT) System module utilizing both high efficiency Dual Sided Microstructured Semiconducting Neutron Detectors (DS-MSNDs) and a compact scintillator CsI gamma detector with energy resolution of 8% for a 2.34 cm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</sup> size crystal and the accompanying android application for data collection was flown on DJI Matrice 100 drone. The system demonstrated the ability to alert to, search, locate, and identify an unshielded 0.8 mCi Cs-137 through several detection scenarios when mapping the shield at an altitude of 3, 10, and 20ft and a drone speed of 3, 5, and 10 mph.

articleTitle: The Mobile Antineutrino Demonstrator Project
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: The Mobile Antineutrino Demonstrator project aims to construct a realistically deployable antineutrino detection system that can operate at essentially any reactor facility with no infrastructure support beyond electrical power. Through engagement with potential end-users and host facilities, this effort will advance the technical readiness of neutrino-based reactor monitoring concepts by enabling operationally relevant demonstrations. The project is motivated by recent technology development that enables antineutrino detectors to operate at the earth’s surface and the results of the Nu Tools study which provided new insight into the utility of antineutrino measurements for current and foreseen nuclear security problems. Specifically, a mobile demonstrator system has relevance to the most promising use cases identified in that study, Advanced Reactors and Future Nuclear Deals, and will incorporate recommendations regarding End-User Engagement and Technical Readiness in the system development process. In this presentation we will describe the mobile system design process, antineutrino detector technology options under development, and operational concepts for the mobile system.

articleTitle: Area Radiation Gamma and Neutron Origin Telemetry (ARGANOT) Radiological Detection System
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: The Area Radiation Gamma and Neutron Origin Telemetry (ARGANOT) System is encompassed by up to eight single modules. With each ARGANOT module (16 x 69 x 150 mm), nine high Dual-sided Microstructured Semiconductor Neutron Detector (DS-MSND) are arrayed together along with a single CsI or SrI<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf>(Eu) scintillator gamma detector. With an operating mission time of up to 18 hours, the system is able to provide the user on an android application livetime gamma and neutron count rate information along with an accumulative gamma spectrum every 10 seconds. Such capabilities have allowed for the implementation of functionalities such source directionality, isotope identification and gamma dose estimations through GADRAS software implementation, as well as user notifications in the form of alarms and warnings. The neutron sensitivity of the standalone module as well as the ARGANOT system worn in a vest has been characterized.

articleTitle: X-ray, Gamma and Neutron Diagnostics Requirements for Projectile Driven Inertial Confinement Fusion
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: First Light Fusion is researching inertial confinement fusion (ICF) with a one-sided pressure drive. To create the extreme temperatures and pressures required for fusion, we use unique targets: an ‘amplifier' boosts the pressure generated by the projectile impact and creates convergence, imploding the fuel capsule from many directions.Our experimental facilities include a two-stage light-gas gun (‘BFG') and a 140 kV, 9 MA electromagnetic pulsed-power driver (Machine 3 or M3). The company is also intensively working on designing the next generation pulsed power machine, the 100 MJ M4, to demonstrate ignition.In 2022 First Light Fusion validated neutron production from projectile-driven DD and DT fusion on the BFG [1], [2]. The first part of this contribution will focus on our current neutron and x-ray diagnostic capabilities. We fielded scintillation detectors at distances between 1-2 m from the fusion targets, which provides n-TOF and validates the energy of neutrons. Filtered Si PIN diodes are used as x-ray flux diagnostics to roughly estimate the electron temperature in the fuel. The temporal profile of the detected x-rays provides information about fuel compression.In the second part of this contribution, we will present an overview of the nuclear diagnostic requirements for the planned M4 machine. These requirements are driven by fusion products that need to be detected to gain understanding of the physics relevant to ignition [3], [4]. For example, our primary diagnostics goal is to be able to diagnose energetic DD and DT neutrons and a high energy x-rays and gammas that can escape from the extremely dense fuel without being attenuated by high-Z materials surrounding the fuel capsule. Physical quantities of interests are the total neutron yield which can be determined using activation foils, fuel ion temperature which can be inferred from n-TOF and burn duration from the fusion gamma intensity profiles.

articleTitle: Impact of energy sharing in heterostructured scintillators on image quality in time-of-flight PET
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Research for the improvement of Time of Flight (TOF) Positron Emission Tomography (PET) is giving rise to many new developments. One is the use of heterostructured scintillators, which consist of µm-scale layers of different materials with complementary properties (high stopping power and fast timing). The fundamental mechanism here is energy sharing with the fast scintillator. The incoming gamma ray is fully stopped in the high stopping power material, but the resulting photoelectron can than deposit its energy in both materials. The temporal resolution improves globally with the energy deposited in the fast scintillator [1], [2].In this contribution we present a classification of events depending on their shared energy and show the effects on the image quality of a PET scan. For this purpose, we use data from a Monte Carlo simulation and perform an image reconstruction with several TOF kernels, which are selected depending on the aforementioned classification. The image quality is assessed based on the contrast to noise ratio and the contrast recovery coefficient and background variability [2], [3]. This study will guide future work investigating the quantitative measurement of energy sharing in a heterostructured scintillator.

articleTitle: New generation of XFCT imaging Scanners based on Gaseous Detectors
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: X-ray Fluorescence Computed Tomography (XFCT) is a non-invasive and non-destructive imaging modality that merges X-ray fluorescence spectroscopy and tomographic methodologies. This technique permits the 3D elemental mapping of samples and has gained popularity as a molecular imaging technique for mapping different elements, such as metals or nanoparticle agents. Typically, conventional XFCT systems employ solid-state detectors, which are characterized by high costs and complexity.In this work, we proposed a novel, cost-effective benchtop XFCT system based on gaseous detectors. The proposed system offers the advantages of simplicity and affordability, and as a result, the proposed system provides an attractive alternative to existing XFCT systems, with potential applications in a broad range of fields, including biological imaging.

articleTitle: Qualification of a Smart Rad-Hard Fast Detection System for Radioactive Ion Beam Tagging and Diagnostics
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Radioactive Ion Beams (RIBs) are a unique tool to probe nuclear structure in uncharted territories of the nuclei chart, especially for nuclei located far from the stability valley. At the Laboratori Nazionali del Sud of INFN in Catania (Italy), the construction of a novel Radioactive Ion Beams (RIBs) facility FRAISE (FRAgment In-flight SEparator) is in advanced state of construction. FRAISE makes use of light and medium mass primary beams, having power up to ≈ 2–3 kW, leading to RIBs, with unprecedented intensities in the range of ≈ 10<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</sup>–10<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">7</sup> pps, for nuclei far from and close to the stability valley, respectively. FRAISE aims at providing high-intensity and high quality RIBs for nuclear physics experiments, also serving to interdisciplinary research areas, such as medical physics. Τhe operation in radioactively activated environments because of the expected 2 kW beam lost in the dipole after the production target, impose the use of rad-hard technologies for the detection system. We are developing a dedicated instrument for the diagnostics and the tagging of RIBs along the transport line based on an array of SiC diodes, readout by an optimized fast frontend electronics and ready to be coupled with a smart DAQ with Data Real-Time Management capabilities and a dedicated software layer implementing Artificial Intelligence and machine learning techniques. This contribution deals with the experimental qualification of a workhorse of the full detection system aimed at assessing the main properties of the individual components and at making sound the estimation of the whole system performance. A full set of measurements to assess the performance of the designed system will be presented and critically analysed and the design of the final tagging system will be presented.

articleTitle: Simulation results for limited-angle ultra-high time-of-flight resolution PET system
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Positron emission tomography (PET) has become standard practice in many clinical applications including oncology, cardiology and neurology. Recent developments in PET scanners have pushed the limits of these applications, thanks to long axial field of view scanners which can improve system sensitivity and the use of time-of-flight (TOF) information which can improve spatial resolution. However, the cost and space requirements for total-body PET systems has created a need for flexible, low-cost yet high-sensitivity systems with large axial field of view. Additionally, currently achievable TOF resolutions (around 200 ps for current clinical scanners) limit the gains in image resolution. In this work, we present the first reconstructions for a flexible two-panel ultra-high TOF resolution PET system expected to achieve 75 ps full-width at half maximum (FWHM). The scanner relies on pixelated L(Y)SO scintillators with novel detectors with dual readout measuring depth-of-interaction (DOI) information. The performance of the new system is demonstrated on Monte-Carlo simulations of an anthropomorphological numerical phantom reconstructed using a newly developed TOF+DOI-enabled reconstruction engine. The presented reconstructions exhibit high image quality, demonstrating the promise of the proposed PET system.

articleTitle: Partial volume correction for Lu-177-PSMA SPECT
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Lu-177 PSMA therapy of metastatic prostate cancer requires sequential SPECT/CT imaging for dosimetry. However, the limited spatial resolution in SPECT images leads to the severe partial volume effect. In this study, we aimed to quantitatively analyze the influence of PVE and effectiveness of a partial volume correction (PVC) method in Lu-177 PSMA SPECT images. A cylindrical phantom (diameter: 30 cm) with seven spheres (diameter from 10 to 50 mm, center-to-center distance of 48-60 mm, activity concentration of 2 MBq/mL), an XCAT phantom with 10 spherical lesions (diameter from 10 to 30 mm) located in various locations of the spine were modelled based on the activity distributions of clinical data. Sixty projections were simulated for a clinical dual-head SPECT/CT with medium energy general propose collimators using SIMIND Monte Carlo code and reconstructed with OS-EM algorithm with dual energy window scatter correction, attenuation correction and geometric collimator-detector-response correction. Sequential quantitative SPECT/CT imaging at 2, 20, 40 and 60 h of five patients treated with 6.0-7.4 GBq Lu-177-PSMA-617 were analyzed retrospectively. The reblurred Van-Cittert (RVC) iterative deconvolution PVC method was applied on the post-reconstructed simulated and clinical SPECT images. In the geometrical phantom, the quantification error decreased as the sphere size increased. PVC reduced the quantification error from 87.7% to 85.7% for the smallest sphere and from 14.8% to 4.9% for the largest one. For the XCAT phantom, PVC reduced the activity quantification error of bone lesions from 50.1%±2.5 to 42.5%±3.7 and kidneys from 41.6%±4.7 to 37.8%±16.7 respectively. For clinical data, the mean activity difference w/ and w/o PVC was 24.4%±11.9 for tumor and 10.7%±5.6 for kidneys at 60 h. RVC-based PVC improves quantification accuracy in Lu-177 PSMA SPECT.

articleTitle: A Modular Detection Module for Time-of-Flight Computed Tomography
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Integrating time-of-flight measurements in computed tomography has the potential to increase image quality and reduce the X-ray dose but poses several technological challenges. The past design of time-of-flight computed tomography systems focused on adding the time measurement but could not reach performances comparable to conventional computed tomography regarding spatial resolution and acquisition time. Thus, a new detection module aimed at proving the clinical viability of time-of-flight computed tomography is proposed here. This novel architecture offers sufficient modularity to explore multiple technological avenues regarding the timing resolution of X-ray detection. A tileable detection module comprised of 64 1 × 1 mm2 pixels, used with a pulsed X-ray source, shows the possibility of single-pixel count rates reaching 500 kcps. A synchronization resolution of 30 ps FWHM is obtained between the X-ray source and detectors, thus allowing for a theoretical system timing resolution below 300 ps FWHM, sufficient to obtain significant gains regarding image quality.

articleTitle: Modelling Polarization Effects in CdZnTe Sensor at Low Bias
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Semi-insulating CdTe and CdZnTe crystals fabricated into pixelated sensors and integrated into radiation detection modules have demonstrated great ability to operate under the rapidly changing X-ray irradiation environments. Such challenging conditions are required by all photon-counting-based applications including medical CT, airport scanners and non-destructive testing. High-flux sensors typically require operating bias of the order of 1000 V inducing in 2 mm thick detector the electric field 5 kV/cm or locally even higher in polarized detector. This high electric field might cause some long-term reliability concerns so it would be desirable to reduce its value. In addition, the requirement of generating high-voltage causes limitations for portable scanning equipment. It is therefore important to study what minimum electric field is required for proper counting operation.In this presentation, we investigate the possibility to pursue the detector at the high-flux up to 80 Mcps/mm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sup> X-ray irradiation at a low electric field satisfactory for maintaining good counting operation. We numerically simulate the high-flux-induced polarization in commercial 2 mm thick pixelated CdZnTe detector with 330 μm pixel pitch used in spectral Computed Tomography applications and define defect model that is consistent with the electric field profile visualized by Pockels effect. We find the low bias 300 V as acceptable for utilization the detector for photon counting and spectral sensing applications. We calculate collected charge and construct X-ray spectrum considering the processing of the signal by allied electronics. We identify a strong ballistic deficit arising from the extended charge collection time as the main reason for the spectrum distortion. Finally, we suggest possible optimization of the setup to improve the charge collection efficiency and present optimized spectrum.

articleTitle: A Modular Time Division Multiplexed Warm Readout System for CMB-S4
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: We present a new system for warm Time Division Multiplexed (TDM) readout of the CMB-S4 microwave background telescopes. The system consists of "Row Address" and "Column Readout" boards which can be grouped together in modular fashion for readout of each detector wafer. Each Row Address board is capable of addressing 32 signals used for flux-activated row select switches. Each Column Readout board provides bias, feedback and readout for 8 columns of Superconducting Quantum Interference Device (SQUID) amplifiers operating at 100 mK and 4 K temperature stages. It also provides bias for the 100-mK Transition Edge Sensors (TES) being amplified by each SQUID. A typical CMB-S4 group will consist of 2 Row Address and 3 Column Readout boards, for TDM readout of up to 24 columns and 64 rows. Firmware on the module implements a servo loop to bias the SQUIDS at the optimum operating point. A timing distribution and communications loop between all boards in a group allows one board to act as the "Coordinator", distributing timing and slow control to other boards in the group, and multiplexing readout data to the back-end DAQ system. The first prototypes have been developed and are fully functional and have been connected to a cryogenic readout chain at SLAC for testing and analysis.

articleTitle: The DE-SPECT System: A Hyperspectral SPECT System for in Vivo 3-D Gamma-Ray Spectrometry of Molecular Theranostics
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: The Dynamic Extremity SPECT (DE-SPECT) system is a hyperspectral organ-dedicated SPECT system based on 1-cm thick Cadmium Zinc Telluride (CZT) imaging spectrometers and dynamic dual-field-of-view (FOV) compound-eye collimators. The objective of the project is to develop a non-invasive imaging technique for comprehensive assessment of peripheral vascular disease (PVD) in lower extremities.The DE-SPECT system is a stationary and high-performance SPECT system that offers an excellent energy performance (2.6 keV FWHM at 220 keV, 3.3 keV at 440 keV) over a wide energy range up to 600 keV, an optimized imaging geometry with a numerically-controlled dual-FOV aperture (offering 28-cm diameter FOV for dual-leg imaging and 16-cm diameter FOV for focused high-resolution and high-sensitivity imaging), and a relatively high sensitivity for multi-tracer SPECT imaging in the lower extremities. The system offers an unmatched ability to perform in vivo voxel-by-voxel gamma-ray spectrometry to derive the concentrations of multiple commonly used radiotracers (Tl-201, Tc-99m, I-123, In-111, etc.) and therapeutic radionuclides (Ac-225, Ra-223, and Lu-177, etc.) in user-selected targeted regions. This capability makes it particularly attractive for molecularly-guided interventions.

articleTitle: Transmission Source Enhanced Attenuation Correction for High-Performance Brain PET
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Attenuation correction (AC) using the PET data alone is a promising option for accurate uptake quantification in standalone brain PET systems. However, current deep learning and joint reconstruction methods frequently exceed 5% uptake bias. Our objective is to optimize and evaluate an AC scheme for PET brain imaging that uses coincidences from a low-activity transmission source and the patient to reconstruct μ-maps from physics principles alone. We fabricated a sparse transmission source from a fillable tube (ID=1.6 mm) wrapped helically around the inside of a PET/CT bore. Our transmission aided maximum likelihood reconstruction of attenuation and activity (sTX-MLAA) includes a μ-map update that maximizes a log-likelihood of terms representing counts originating from all sources (i.e. external source and patient) and a hyperparameter weighted expression of counts segmented from the external source. Scatter is fully corrected from PET data alone. We evaluated performance of sTX-MLAA with a striatal brain phantom study on a time-of-flight PET/CT. The phantom was filled with <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">64</sup>Cu (12.7 hr half-life) to approximate patient uptake of a dopamine transporter tracer, the transmission source filled with <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">18</sup>F (1.8 hr half-life), and the phantom imaged for 30 min repeatedly over ~3 half-lives of <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">18</sup>F; enabling an evaluation of the impact of transmission activity on performance with relatively fixed subject uptake. Qualitatively, PET images generated with AC from sTX-MLAA had high agreement with CT-AC data. With as little as 5 MBq in the transmission source, bias in tracer uptake was <1.6% in the striata for sTX-MLAA, compared to up to 6.6% bias when using attenuation maps reconstructed with MLAA from counts largely originating from the patient. At this same activity, the increase in the PET image coefficient of variation for sTX-MLAA relative to CT-AC (from a large background VOI) was only 1.4%. Results suggest that sTX-MLAA will enable quantitative PET for neuroimaging.

articleTitle: Unsupervised Sinogram Denoising for Single Photon Emission Computed Tomography
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: This paper presents a novel methodology for denoising sinograms based on cycle-consistent adversarial networks, focusing on medical imaging applications. The proposed method is designed to denoise sinograms without requiring paired information of low to high levels of noise and uncertainty, which is often difficult to obtain in real-world scenarios. The method was trained on three two sets of projection data from randomly generated software phantoms, using GATE, with various levels of collections time. The denoised and high-collection-time sinograms were then reconstructed and compared using the Ordered Subset Expectation Maximization (OSEM) method, which showed that the proposed method significantly removes noise without impacting the quality of the sinograms and improving the reconstructions. Finally, the method was tested on dopamine transporter imaging with single-photon emission computed tomography (DAT-SPECT) sinograms to demonstrate its effectiveness and capability.

articleTitle: Applying Exponential Data Consistency Conditions in SPECT with Multiple Activity Regions
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: For conventional models of exponential SPECT (single photon emission computed tomography) projections, all the activity is required to be inside a convex region of homogeneous attenuation. In this work, we show that for certain applications, this restriction can be relaxed, while remaining mathematically correct. We point out that a subset of attenuated projections can be converted to exponential projections if different regions of activity can each be contained within different convex regions of homogeneous attenuation. Then, if the attenuated projection data have projection views where the different activity regions are separable, meaning there is no non-zero overlap in the two regions, the process of conversion to exponential projections can be applied separately to each. Thus, the combination by summation of each individual region converted into exponential projections gives the same result as converting those separable projections in the combined data set to exponential projections. Using an NCAT computer phantom, an activity distribution was set up simulating a heart with constant attenuation and a liver with constant attenuation, with no background activity, but with variable attenuation between the two regions due to the lungs. A set of attenuated parallel-hole projections were simulated including projection views where the heart activity sinogram and liver activity sinogram could be separated. Converting only the separable projection views to exponential projections, data consistency conditions on those exponential projections were applied to assess a data consistency-based attenuation map alignment method.

articleTitle: SparkPix-T: Spatial and Time Resolving Front-End ASIC with MHz-Rate Information Extraction for Momentum Spectroscopy at LCLS-II
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: SparkPix-T is a spatial and time resolving front-end ASIC capable of operation at up to 1 MHz repetition rate, developed to enable massive multi-particle coincidence experiments at the TMO instrument at LCLS-II. It has 100 μm x 100 μm pixels arranged in a 176 x 192 matrix configuration, capable of measuring charged particle time-of-arrival (TOA) with 100 ps resolution and 6.5 μs range. Signal energy is indirectly assessed through 8-bit time-over-threshold (TOT) measurements. A fast gating of the front-end preamplifier is implemented for rejection of photons produced by the LCLS pulse that could otherwise blind the detector to upcoming signal. A sparse readout information extraction scheme is implemented to allow for a trade-off between repetition rate and event occupancy (percentage of pixels with signal above threshold per repetition cycle). At 1 MHz rate the ASIC can sustain occupancy of 0.5% without data loss, at 100 kHz the occupancy can be 5%, while a full matrix readout (100% occupancy) is possible at 5 kHz. SparkPix-T has been fabricated in a 0.13 μm CMOS technology and its design and initial characterization will be reported.

articleTitle: The ScIDEP Project at the Egyptian Pyramid of Khafre
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: The ScIDEP (Scintillator Imaging Detector for the Egyptian Pyramids) Collaboration is constructing a scintillator-based muon telescope to investigate the internal structure of the Egyptian Pyramid of Khafre. This pyramid is only slightly smaller than the Great Pyramid, however its known internal structure seems much simpler compared to the latter and hence raises the question if there are any hidden rooms or structures that have yet to be discovered. The previous and very first muography campaign at this pyramid conducted by Alvarez et al. in the 1970s yielded no indications of any hidden structures.The current project aims to install a new muon telescope inside the king’s burial chamber which is located at the very bottom of the pyramid, slightly off-center from the central axis. The base detector that has been developed consists of two 61x61x2cm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</sup> plastic scintillator planes with wavelength shifting fibers embedded in orthogonal orientations in both faces of each scintillator, to retrieve 2D hit information from each plane for muon tracking. The scintillation light is read out by SiPMs connected to each individual fiber. The data-acquisition system is based on commercial CAEN Petiroc2A-ASIC based digitizer modules. The detector construction has recently been completed and commissioning of the setup in the lab is currently ongoing.In parallel to the detector commissioning, a detailed simulation package for the full setup is being developed. The cosmic ray spectrum is taken from the CRY generator, while the particle transport through the pyramid and the detector is modelled both in the Geant4 and MCNP packages.An overview of this project will be given, including the detector description and initial results, plus results from the simulation studies.

articleTitle: Growth and characterization of CsPbBr3 single crystals
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Metal halide perovskites with APbX<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</inf> crystal structure show rapidly increasing global interest as a new generation of radiation detection materials alternative to CdZnTe. In this work, we present our results of the multiple single crystals growth of all-inorganic perovskite CsPbBr<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</inf> using Bridgman method. Crystals were prepared directly from CsBr and PbBr<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf> starting materials mixed with a various mole ratio. Our optimized growth process produces crystals with diameter 15 mm and length over 50 mm. We found that the quality of grown single crystals strongly depends on the purity of the starting materials, dropping speed of the growth ampule and cooling rate after growth. For characterization of transport properties of as-grown samples, we used pulsed I-V characteristics, Laser-induced transient current technique (L-TCT) at pulsed DC bias or Time-correlated single photon counting (TCSPC). We compared crystallographic and the transport properties of grown crystals depending on the change in the mole ratio of the starting materials, the change in the purity of the starting materials, different degrees of overheating, and different dropping speed of growth ampoule. In case of 1:1 stoichiometric ratio, 40 K overheating and dropping speed of 0.5 mm h<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">-1</sup>, we have grown CsPbBr<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</inf> crystal with resistivity ρ=2.7•10<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">9</sup> Ωcm evaluated from pulsed I-V characteristics. Pulse-biased L-TCT current waveforms show shorter hole lifetime at the center of the wafer than close in its border. The TCSPC signal indicates non single exponential decay with average rapid component of 0.5 ns.

articleTitle: Integrated PET/MRI-based automatic brain structures segmentation through deep learning
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Brain structure segmentation is of great value in diagnosing brain disorders, allowing radiologists to quickly acquire regions of interest and assist in subsequent analyses, diagnoses, and treatment. However, most of the current methods for segmenting the brain are based on unimodal magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) but rarely combine structural and functional information. Therefore, we aimed to explore a deep learning method for joint segmentation based on dual-modality data. In this study, nnU-Net was employed to segment the whole brain into 45 structures with positron emission tomography (PET) and MRI images as parallel inputs. Meanwhile, fivefold cross-validation was applied to train and validate our method as well. Compared with several single-modality methods, our dual-modality method achieved superior results with an 86.37% Dice similarity coefficient (DSC), 77.86% Jaccard index (JAC), 86.68% recall, and 87.38% precision. Furthermore, the time required to segment whole-brain images from test datasets was decreased from over 7 hours using FreeSurfer software to approximately 2 minutes, greatly improving the efficiency of brain structure delineation. In conclusion, our method can incorporate multimodal information without the need for additional pre- or postprocessing, yielding better visualization and quantification results. For future work, we will attempt to transfer the proposed method to other multimodal tasks and clinical applications.

articleTitle: Design of a 100 Gb/s Ethernet Interface for a Silicon Photonics-based Data Acquisition System for Particle Physics Experiments
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Particle physics experiments, like nEXO and ARGO, require a large-scale data acquisition system capable of supporting high data rates. One can expect a total data rate of approximately 400 Gb/s for nEXO, whereas ARGO estimates are on a scale of Pb/s. To support those experiments, which require a low-power and high-bandwidth communication (≈1 Gb/s per link), a modular Silicon-Photonics (SiP) communication module is in development to connect the front-end electronics to the data acquisition system (DAQ). This research focuses on the interface between more than 100 optical transceivers and the DAQ. To eliminate the need for custom hardware in the servers of the DAQ, the system is compatible with a standard Ethernet network. Targetting an Ethernet interface allows the use of commodity off-the-shelf equipment to connect custom electronics to the DAQ and simplifies integration, deployment, and maintenance. This system is composed of a Zynq system-on-chip (SoC), where the FPGA receives data from a set of transceivers and wraps the frame received in UDP datagrams sent to the DAQ; the processor handles various configurations and commands. To match the requirements on data rates and modularity, this study proposes a proof of concept demonstrating a 100 Gb/s link using a FPGA to transfer the data from the custom SiP transceivers to a server running DAQ software, implemented using the MIDAS framework. Following this work, the implemented Ethernet link will constitute a system ready to integrate with the SiP communication module. This integration will provide a platform to deploy large-scale and high data-rate DAQs for the targeted experiments, namely nEXO and ARGO.

articleTitle: Investigating the effect of data streaming on CZT PET system bandwidth
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Positron emission tomography (PET) systems require a large number of readout channels in order to maintain the desired properties of the system. In addition to this large number of channels, large amounts of data are also processed to reconstruct the image. If events are dropped during the data acquisition chain, sensitivity and performance of the PET system will be decreased. This work investigates the effects of software changes to the bandwidth of a Cadmium Zinc Telluride (CZT) PET system that uses a cross-strip electrode configuration in a two-panel system with up to 300 CZT crystals.

articleTitle: Evaluation of Sintering Techniques for CsPbBr3 Polycrystalline X-ray Detectors
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Metal-halide perovskites have been the subject of fast moving research for use in solid-state X-ray detection. A wide range of materials synthesis and manufacturing techniques have been investigated for these material systems including solution precipitation, solid-state reaction, thin film deposition, melt-based crystal growth, and sintering. To date, however, there lacks a fundamental comparison of these various manufacturing technologies and description of their relative benefits and drawbacks when applied to metal-halide perovskite radiation detectors. In this work, we aim to begin developing these comparisons by evaluating the consolidation of CsPbBr<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</inf> polycrystalline devices via three sintering techniques, namely conventional sintering, cold sintering, and field assisted sintering. The resulting microstructures from each processing technique is evaluated with regards to density and grain size. These microstructural characteristics are linked to X-ray sensitivity performance. Initial results from conventionally sintered CsPbBr<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</inf> demonstrate X-ray sensitivity of $151\;\mu {\text{C}}/{\text{G}}{{\text{y}}_{{\text{air}}}}^{ - 1}{\text{c}}{{\text{m}}^{ - 2}}$ under 20 V bias. Further characterization, optimization and performance evaluation will be conducted on each of the sintering methods, enabling robust comparisons to be made.

articleTitle: An Interval-Based Data Consistency Condition for Two Exponential Fanbeam Projections
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Data consistency conditions (DCCs) allow the verification of whether tomographic data conforms with the mathematical model describing the underlying physical process. Such conditions describe the overlapping information in different projections, and particularly useful are conditions capable of finding inconsistencies from just two projections, which we refer to as pairwise data consistency conditions (PDCCs). While PDCCs are known for many projection operators (associated with different types of tomography), for the exponential fanbeam transform (associated with pinhole SPECT) no such conditions were known, and indeed, the authors recently mathematically proved them nonexistent. Nevertheless, identifying inconsistencies between two pinhole SPECT projections is of interest for practical purposes. To that end, we propose a novel type of consistency condition for pairs of exponential fanbeam projections created from non-negative activities. Unlike the classical PDCCs – for which certain functionals of the two projections must coincide – the proposed approach checks whether functionals of the respective projections fall into a predetermined range (an interval) of acceptable values. Such a condition is not as powerful as classical PDCCs, because it can find some inconsistencies, but might be inconclusive otherwise. Nonetheless, these conditions certainly have potential for applications, as we show via numerical simulations involving the NCAT phantom, allowing us to detect motion inconsistencies.

articleTitle: Advanced In-Flight Verification and New Detector Materials for Particle Detection as Tested for ESRA ECP
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: The Experiment for Space Radiation Analysis (ESRA) is a 12U CubeSat demonstration and validation mission from the Los Alamos National Laboratory. ESRA is scheduled to be placed in a geosynchronous transfer orbit to verify new technologies while providing measurements of the charged particle environment. The Energetic Charged Particle (ECP) instrument on board the ESRA CubeSat is a particle telescope which aims to measure protons from 100 keV to 1000 MeV, and electrons from 100 keV to 20 MeV. A standard collimator reduces impinging fluxes to manageable levels. The telescope itself consists of five detector layers. On-board analysis is done by direct-to-digital data processing FPGA code, developed in-house. A great deal of effort is dedicated to in-flight verification, which utilize a variety of in-flight debugging options. In addition to developing these capabilities, the ECP was designed as a test platform for new detector materials such as Cadmium Zinc Telluride and GAGG ($ Gd_{3}Al_{2}Ga_{3}O_{12}$). This paper will focus on the advancement of in-flight verification capabilities, and the obstacles which were met during development when utilizing these new detector materials for charged particle detection.

articleTitle: Identifying Signal-to-Noise Ratios Representative of Gamma Detector Response in Realistic Scenarios
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: The development of accurate analytical models for gamma-ray spectral analysis is critical for applications ranging from nuclear security to fundamental science. Depending on the machine learning model being trained and the complexity of the application space, a staggering amount of data could be necessary to accurately represent variations in the measurement geometry, source, detector, and environment. The accumulation of such datasets may be costly and resource intensive if acquired through an arduous measurement campaign, leaving analysts to turn towards nuclear transport codes to synthesize spectral data. The Python based Radioisotope Identification (PyRIID) software package provides utilities that support data generation through the GAmma Detector Response and Analysis Software (GADRAS). PyRIID uses sampling techniques to quickly generate large quantities of data. The objective of this work is to identify use-case scenarios that result in statistically viable spectra. This is achieved by comparing spectral seeds, or templates, using the Jensen Shannon Distance to identify statistically similar sampling parameters. The findings of this work will enable models that are better representatives of physical phenomena and hence, more useful in real world applications.

articleTitle: Head Motion Correction Validation Using Hoffman 3D Brain Phantom for Multiple PET/CT Systems
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: In clinical practice of brain PET imaging, head motion may introduce image artifacts, which lead to decreased image resolution and poor quantitative accuracy. In this study, we implemented a new head motion correction (HMC) algorithm for four PET/CT systems, which are uMI Vista (VI), uMI780 (780), uMI Panorama (PA) and NeuroEXPLORER (NX). Hoffman 3D brain phantom studies with and without manual motion were performed for HMC evaluation. The detailed structures of phantom were well recovered by HMC for all the scanners. Furthermore, the spatial resolution of NX in both no motion and HMC images has reached a comparable level of CT, reflecting the excellent resolution of NX and the excellent motion correction performance. Quantitatively, the VOI differences between HMC and no motion image of all scanners were less than 3%, 2% and 7% at hot, warm and cold regions, respectively for VI and 780; For PA and NX, the same differences were only 1%, 2% and 2%. The validation results demonstrate the effectiveness of the new HMC algorithm. Finally, we would like to point out that the detailed level of Hoffman brain phantom may no longer be enough to challenge the resolution limit of modern PET scanners. In the future, we will perform HMC studies with a phantom with more realistic and finer brain details.

articleTitle: A Comparison of Vertical and Lateral Devices for Transient Photocurrent Time of Flight in Amorphous Selenium and its Alloys
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Understanding the properties of semiconductors for photodetection, imaging, and sensing is of extreme importance in optimizing their performance. Amorphous selenium (a-Se) has been well studied over the last several decades and is of great interest in X-ray detection, particle physics, and memory applications. Many studies have been conducted on its alloys; however, some varieties can only be fabricated in thin film form, preventing the use of common techniques for extracting transport properties. In this work, we demonstrate that lateral devices employing optical slits may be used for transient photocurrent time of flight on thin films, allowing the calculation of mobility and opening the door for future studies of thin film selenium alloys.

articleTitle: Study of very high temporal resolution in clinical total body PET imaging
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: PET imaging is witnessing the development of new generations of detectors with less than 100ps CTR (Coincidence Time Resolution). Such a high CTR promises enhanced image quality. Another way to improve image quality is to use a total body (TB) geometry, increasing device sensitivity. Our work aims to quantify the expected improvements of TB geometry and high CTR detectors on clinical imaging and 4D pharmacokinetic studies. To do so, our first step is to model one of the gold-standard commercial devices, the GE SIGNA PET/MR, using the GATE Monte Carlo software. The simulation is validated against experimental data for sensitivity, Noise Equivalent Count Rate (NECR), spatial resolution, CTR and image analysis according to NEMA protocols. Results show good agreement for spatial resolution (3,1 vs 3,2 mm), sensitivity (23,6 vs 24,1 cps/kBq), NECR (peak at 221 vs 226,1 kcps respectively at 15,0 and 18,0 kBq/mL) and contrast recovery coefficients. For the performance illustration, <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">18</sup>F FDG brain exams are simulated with a 390 ps and a 100 ps CTR. For the same purpose, <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">18</sup>F FDG total body exams are also compared: an image reconstructed with three bed steps of the SIGNA with 390 ps CTR to one with a TB geometry, i.e. three times larger axial FOV with a 100 ps CTR. Images show expected contrast enhancement and background noise reduction in simulated clinical images. Future work is planned to be focused on the simulation of 4D exams and the quantification of these improvements in image quality.

articleTitle: A self-certifying FPGA based pixel readout chip test system for CMS ETL detector upgrade
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: This talk presents a flexible self-certifying FPGA-based pixel readout test system for testing the Endcap Timing Read-Out Chip (ETROC) being developed for the CMS MIP Timing Detector (MTD). The system includes an FPGA-based emulator and a test system. The test system can take data from emulator or up to four ETROC test boards in beam telescope mode and is compatible with both ETROC1 and ETROC2 boards. A python-based GUI simplifies configuration and calibration. The system provides an efficient and reliable solution for testing ETROC chips and can be extended to other readout chips with similar architecture.

articleTitle: A Novel Laser Guidance System for Calibrating the sPHENIX TPC
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: A time projection chamber (TPC) is the main tracking detector for the sPHENIX experiment, which recently completed installation at Brookhaven National Laboratory's Relativistic Heavy Ion Collider. The TPC is a high precision device that must rely on several independent calibration schemes to correct for significant modifications to particle tracks by non-uniformities in both the electric and magnetic fields in the drift region, including ExB effects. These complications typically arise from mechanical misalignments of the field cage and space charge build-up from ion back flow. To address these issues, one prong of the calibration strategy is to introduce multiple laser beams into the TPC active volume to establish lines of ionization that serve as absolute calibration references. Once collections of tracks in different regions are analyzed, a correction model may be established. Due to rate limitations, the system described here is specifically suited to address static or slowly evolving distortions, mostly associated with mechanical defects. We report on a novel laser beam guidance system that accomplishes this task by steering a single beam over a very large angular range within the TPC, without the need for establishing a complicated web of fixed beams, as has been done by other experiments. By utilizing four laser beams on each endcap, this system allows almost the full drift region to be sampled with multiple laser track crossings at each space point. At the conference the TPC Line Laser System will be described in detail and several key performance characteristics that are vital to operating the TPC will be presented.

articleTitle: Development of an ultrahigh resolution real time alpha particle imaging system for observing the trajectories in a scintillator and its applications
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: High-resolution imaging of alpha particles is required in the detection of alpha radionuclides in cells or small organs for the development of radio-compounds for targeted alpha-particle therapy or other purposes. We developed an ultrahigh resolution, real time alpha-particle imaging system for observing the trajectories of alpha particles in a scintillator. The developed system is based on a magnifying unit and a cooled electron multiplying charge-coupled device (EM-CCD) camera, combined with a 100-µm-thick Ce-doped Gd<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</inf>Al<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf>Ga<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</inf>O<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">12</inf> (GAGG) scintillator plate. Alpha particles from an Am-241 source were irradiated to the GAGG scintillator and imaged with the system. Using our system, we measured the trajectories of the alpha particles having different shapes in real time. In some of these measured trajectories, the line shapes of the alpha particles that flew in the GAGG scintillator were clearly observed. The lateral profiles of the alpha-particle trajectories were imaged with widths of less than 2 µm. We conclude that the developed imaging system is promising for research on targeted alpha-particle therapy or other alpha particle detections that require high spatial resolution. In the conference, we will also show the energy distributions, depth profiles and quenching measured by the developed system.

articleTitle: PET image segmentation based on geodetic prior
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: PET imaging is effective in aiding doctors in cancer diagnosis and treatment by reflecting the metabolic rate of glucose in the human body. However, PET segmentation remains a challenging task due to its typically low resolution. In this paper, we propose a geodesic prior adapted for PET to overcome the disadvantages of low resolution and blurred boundaries in PET images.Additionally, we design a dual-branch network framework that constructs an attention mechanism using the geodesic prior, effectively fusing the features of the geodesic prior and PET images. Furthermore, we introduce an active contour module for post-processingpostprocessing in the network, which can optimize parameters through the network. We apply the model to lung cancer segmentation and also apply the lung cancer trained model to test the breast cancer dataset. Compared to other models, our segmentation results have higher accuracy and some degree of generalization.

articleTitle: Automatic Scaphoid Fracture Detection in Radiography by aid of Interpretable Deep Learning
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Among carpal bones, the scaphoid is commonly reported using radiographs to be fractured. However, the invisibility of some fractures in radiographs makes it hard to physicians to accurately detect more than 75% of them. Hence, we aim to develop an interpretable deeplearning (DL) model to classify fractured and not fractured scaphoids in a shorter time with acceptable accuracy. To do so, 679 radiographs were included, of which 315 cases had fractured whereas 364 cases were fracture-free. The images were cropped, resized to 256 × 256, clipped between 1% and 99% before normalization, and normalized using the min-max method. Eight DL models were developed after data splitting to 60% training, 20% testing, and 20 % validation sets. Finally, we achieved AUC = 0.73, specificity = 0.74, and sensitivity = 0.64 as our best results using the DenseNet 121 network. This result shows that DL-based models can easily achieve human accuracy in fracture detection and also shows the important areas of DL model learns from using an attention map.

articleTitle: Performance Evaluation of Eight-Channels Picosecond Chip MVT22_8LF
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: MVT22_8LF is a new multi-voltage threshold (MVT) digitizer implementation. Compared to field-programmable gate array (FPGA) based approaches, application-specific integrated circuit (ASIC) technology can improve integration and resolution capabilities. It can also reduce power consumption. In this work, we comprehensively evaluate the performance of MVT22_8LF, showing a bin size of 19.5 ps, an RMS of 16.2 ps, and inter-channel time evaluation consistency under 1.9 ps. The transition of MVT digitizers from FPGA to ASIC implementation provides a unique opportunity to streamline PET detection systems.

articleTitle: SiPM readout of large-volume scintillator detectors for high-energy γ-rays
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Large-volume scintillator detector arrays are especially used in nuclear physics experiments with high-energy γ-rays. In the case of magnetic spectrometers or relativistic beams, reading the scintillation light via silicon photomultipliers usually provides better results compared to the magnetic-field-sensitive photomultiplier tubes.To solve this issue silicon photomultipliers could be a solution as a substitute for the photomultiplier tubes because they are not affected by the magnetic field and can offer position sensitivity.This paper compares the results obtained with various scintillator detectors (LaBr<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</inf>:Ce, phoswich of CeBr<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</inf>-NaI and CLYC) of different volumes (from 103 up to 394 cm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</sup>) coupled to large-area silicon photomultiplier matrixes and photomultiplier tubes, in terms of energy resolution, linearity (up to 9 MeV) and time resolution. The obtained results show that the two light readout solutions are generally comparable in terms of time resolution and slightly better for the SiPM-based readout for energy resolution, with more predictable and correctable non-linearity effects compared to phototubes.

articleTitle: Simulation Study of a 3-layer DOI-PET Detector Inserting Striped Glasses Between Crystal Layers and Employing Modified Resistive Charge Division Networks
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: This study introduces a DOI-PET detector employing 3-layer scintillation crystal structure in combination with the light-sharing approach and modified-resistive charge division (M-RCD) networks. Two striped glasses inserting between the crystal layers were placed orthogonally to each other, so that scintillation photons can travel only through the X-direction in the top-striped glass and then further spread through the Y-direction in the bottom-striped glass. The light distribution was additionally controlled in M-RCD networks by adding weighting factors for the reduction of identification error. A total of 3,200,000 γ-ray interactions were simulated. 100 different detector configurations having the 10 different thicknesses for each top- and bottom-striped glass were examined. The traced light was further processed for six-types of M-RCD. As the thickness of the striped glass increased from 0 to 10 mm, the average number of collected photons decreased from 4799 to 4547 for 1<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">st</sup>-layer, from 4737 to 4246 for 2<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">nd</sup>-layer and from 4720 to 4129 for 3<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">rd</sup>-layer. It was estimated that an average light loss dependency was ~0.84%∕mm. The 2-D flood histogram could be generated a unique distinguishable pattern according to each crystal position. Moreover, it was verified that the combined the striped glasses with a 4 mm thickness at both top and bottom, and M-RCD with weighting factor of × 3.5 at Rx2 & Ry2 position, could provide excellent identification accuracy (>98%). This study demonstrated that the proposed 3-layer DOI-PET detector can extract the 3-D γ-ray interaction position without considerable performance degradations from the 2-D flood histogram.

articleTitle: Deep learning limited angle artefact correction in the Walk-Through Total-Body PET system
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: This study discusses the limited angle artefact problem in the newly proposed walk-through total-body PET scanner and proposes a deep learning approach for artefact correction. The scanner consists of two vertically placed flat detector panels (74 cm x 106 cm in size, spaced 50 cm apart), between which the patient stands upright for a short 30 s to 1 min scan. The image reconstruction shows limited angle artefacts due to the large angular gap between both panels. We train a U-Net based neural network to produce artefact free images from the reconstructions. Training is performed based on GATE Monte Carlo simulations and subsequent image reconstructions of humanoid XCAT phantoms, where we use a rotating (and therefore artefact free) configuration of the scanner for generating training targets. The network can remove the artefacts without introducing irregularities, showing the potential for deep learning based limited angle artefact correction in the walk-through total-body PET system.

articleTitle: A Comparison of Voltage-Mode and Time-Based Timing and Energy Read-Out Circuits
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Modern applications like nuclear measurements, and energy discriminating detectors, to name a few of the most prevalent, have all witnessed a significant increase in timing measurements. For this purpose, high-performance Time-to-Digital Converters (TDCs) play an increasingly key role. However, in many setups, the measurement of occurrence time of an event is accompanied by the measurement of the energy associated with it. Therefore, the ideal would be to combine the measurements of the two parameters with the performance required by the specific experimental context. In literature, entirely time-based solutions are available, such as the Time-over-Threshold (ToT) technique, or mixed solutions in which the TDC, used for timing only, is coupled with a voltage-mode analog circuit for energy readout (a.k.a., amplitude of the signal), such as a PeakDetector (PD) or an integrator (INT) that interfaces via Analog-to-Digital Converter (ADC) to a digital system. This paper investigates the performance obtained in terms of energy (i.e., amplitude) and timing measurements, highlighting the strengths and weaknesses of the proposed approaches. Moreover, to minimize the impact of jitter, the ToT technique will also be validated using a Charge Readout (CR) circuit. The circuits were implemented on a Printed Circuit Board (PCB) and interfaced to a Xilinx 28-nm Artix-7 200T Field Programmable Gate Arrays (FPGA) housed in a Nexys Video. In the FPGA, in addition to the logic for interfacing with the ADC for amplitude read-out, a TDC with a precision of 12 ps r.m.s. is also included. The TDC is responsible not only for generating the timestamp for the PD and INT circuits but also for estimating the energy in the ToT with and without the CF. It can be observed that it is possible to detect amplitudes up to some volts with a precision of a few millivolts using both time-based and voltagemode approaches at rates of tens of Msps maintaining a temporal resolution of tens of picoseconds.

articleTitle: A 4 x 4 SiPM Sensor Array with Fast Preamplified Output Engineered for the PWO Detectors of the EIC EEEMCAL
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: The PbWO4 scintillation detectors for the Electron-Ion Collider Electron Endcap Electromagnetic Calorimeter (EEEMCAL) cannot use vacuum photomultipler tubes due to the high magnetic field environment. We are presenting a readout solution with a 4 x 4 SiPM array directly coupled to a preamplification and summing stage. A second amplification stage with variable gain and offset adjustments is also included in the compact electronics module. The integrated power supply feeds the signal processing chain and the adjustable bias control. The parameter settings are saved locally on a EEPROM and are adjustable via the integrated communication interface through USB or RS485. The design was optimized to maximize signal collection energy resolution, for fast timing and wide dynamic range while keeping a small footprint with low power consumption and heat dissipation. The output response is fast enough to meet the 100 – 200 ns digitization gate requirements for the detector. The electronics assembly requires no active cooling and includes a temperature sensor and a gain compensation of thermal variations which are important features for stable operation in large scale detector structures. A detector prototype was constructed with 20 mm x 20 mm x 200 mm PWO crystals affixed with individual SiPM array readouts and arranged in a 3 x 3 array. This detector was tested at the Thomas Jefferson National Accelerator Facility with 5GeV positrons. We will present the results of these detector characterization measurements.

articleTitle: Application of the Wasserstein Distance to identify inter-crystal scatter in a light-sharing depth-encoding PET detector
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: In finely-pixelated PET detectors, Compton-scatter of the incident annihilation photon generates a spatial blurring known as inter-crystal scatter (ICS). This blurring is particularly exacerbated in light-sharing depth-encoding detectors - a design that is otherwise an excellent candidate for cost-effective high-resolution imaging. Accurate identification of ICS in these detectors is crucial to establishing their viability as a high-performance imaging platform. We therefore developed a pair of data-driven ICS identification algorithms - a contour-based method that utilizes only the centroid position of the event and a Wasserstein distanced-based method that incorporates the full dimensionality of the detector response pattern. As a proof-of-concept, both algorithms were tested on experimental calibration data acquired from the Prism-PET brain scanner, and each event was classified as ICS or photoelectric (PE). Results of the classification were evaluated by inspecting distributions of the energy and the DOI estimation parameter (w) for both ICS and PE-classified events. Excellent classification performance was demonstrated by both methods via suppression of high-energy components of the energy distribution and shaping of the DOI-parameter distribution to align with expectations from the Beer-Lambert relation. However, the Wasserstein-based classification outperformed the contour method, indicating the importance of utilizing the full dimensionality of the input detector response data.

articleTitle: Simultaneous Counting and Integrating: A New Paradigm for Pulse Pileup Correction in Photon Counting CT
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: The pulse pileup problem is the fundamental technical challenge to adopting photon counting detectors (PCDs) in diagnostic CTs, where the input photon flux can be 3- to 6-orders of magnitude higher than in nuclear medicine imaging. Reducing pileup effects generally requires a higher power consumption or a smaller pixel area which increases charge-sharing effects. Software-based correction methods have found success in nonparalyzable PCDs but eventually encounter a degeneracy problem in paralyzable PCDs where a given recorded value of counts can correspond to two vastly different input photon numbers. In this work, we were inspired by the fact that energy-integrating detectors (EIDs) do not suffer from pulse pileups: for a given spectrum, the outputs of EIDs are linearly related to the input photon numbers and are independent of how close in time those photons arrive. Adding charge-integrating elements to the ASICs of PCDs is inexpensive—in fact, many state-of-the-art PCDs are already equipped with charge-summing nodes for each block of pixels, albeit they were used for a different purpose (charge sharing correction). To experimentally demonstrate the feasibility of simultaneous photon counting and charge integration and the benefits of using the collected total charge for PCD pileup correction, prototype electronics were constructed to collect time-integrated charge simultaneously with photon counts: a splitter was used to feed the electric signal from a CdTe diode detector in parallel to both a digital counter and a charge integrator. A lookup table was generated to map raw counts in the two energy bins and total charge to estimate pile-up-free true counts for each PCD energy bin. The experimental results demonstrate that with the proposed correction, paralyzable PCD counts became linear with tube current (mA) for both energy bins, and the CT sinogram data became accurate in terms of representing the true radiological path lengths of objects.

articleTitle: Prompt Gamma Timing for Proton Range Verification with Pure Cherenkov Emitters
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Proton range verification (PRV) through prompt gamma imaging (PGI) is a promising modality to assess the dose delivery in proton and heavy ion therapy. In AC-coupled cyclotrons, the periodicity of the proton bunches can be used as a tool to reject weakly time correlated background noise, thus increasing signal contrast, and to assess the Bragg peak position by means of the time-of-flight (TOF) information of the proton or heavy ion. In this work we study the prompt- gamma timing (PGT) signal from 3 crystals: a 3×3×20 mm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</sup> TlBr, a 12×12×12 mm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</sup> TlBr, and a 5×5×5 mm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</sup> TlCl. PGT data was acquired at the Crocker Nuclear Laboraotry (CNL) in the UC Davis campus. A detector consisting of a plastic scintillator and a photomulitplier was used as the time-of-flight reference. A PMMA target was exposed to a proton beam of 1 nA and 67.5 MeV of energy and it was shifted in 3 mm increments. The three detectors showed consistent shifts for the PGT distributions with the 3 mm positions of the PMMA target. Material choice and crystal dimensions did not seem to affect the outcome of the results. These results show the Cherenkov light generated by prompt-gammas in heavy materials is a robust signal for PGT. Future measurements will include an improvement of the reference detector and the acquisition of more data with detectors with different geometries.

articleTitle: Experimental Characterization of Adaptive Multi-pinhole Apertures
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: We characterize a dynamic, multiple pinhole, single photon emission computed tomography (SPECT) aperture structure. These apertures are developed for a dedicated brain imaging system whose primary purpose is to acquire data for pharmacokinetic analysis. The apertures are capable of dynamically changing between imaging configurations corresponding to several different resolutions and sensitivities. We report on testing of the aperture performance at different emission energies. We expect to have more leakage from higher energy sources. Aperture assembly reliability is being tested by repeatedly moving apertures between different configurations to simulate acquisition cycles. This data is evaluated for repeated precision of aperture positioning. Data will also help optimize motor speed versus re-calibration frequency to run the system at its highest performance.

articleTitle: A new HPGe detector with improved high count-rate capabilities for X-ray applications
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: In order to cope for the next generation of synchrotron facilities with higher brilliance and energies, X-ray detectors need to be improved to achieve best energy resolution at count-rate up to few million counts-per-second (cps). Silicon Drift Detectors (SDDs) are well suited for such application, therefore they focused developments over the last two decades up to the current level where the silicon material properties can become a limiting factor to improve resolving power. High Purity Germanium (HPGe) has intrinsic performances that can complete, compete or even exceed SDDs thanks to its higher stopping power and better ionization conversion. Latest major improvement of synchrotron based HPGe detectors was the successful coupling of HPGe diodes with new generation of CMOS preamplifier which was a breakthrough regarding performance improvement of such systems. This paper reports on the performances of a new HPGe detector meant for synchrotron application where the focus was made on the HPGe diode processing itself to get an input capacitance contact as low as an SDD. Preliminary measurements show extremely good performances with resolution FWHM at the 5.9 keV line from <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">55</sup>Fe of 97 eV at 1 kcps and 130 eV at 1 Mcps using analog shapers. This as a potential to be improved using up-to-date digital electronics. Such results are very promising and open one way towards a next generation HPGe detectors for X-ray applications with improved performances.

articleTitle: X-ray detection and tomography with Depleted Monolithic Active Pixel Sensors
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: X-ray detection for industrial and medical applications mostly focuses on the 10 keV (soft x-rays) to 300 keV (hard x-rays) energy range, where the spectrum of commercial x-ray tubes lies within. At these energies, high-Z materials are used as sensors, in combination with different detector technologies, to perform x-ray imaging and tomography.
