While employing high-Z materials is the standard when to maximize quantum efficiency, there are many applications where a lower sensor intrinsic efficiency may be compensated by other figures of merit (e.g. larger area, lower price, faster speed, higher spatial resolution, etc...) of the chosen detector.In particular, while Monolithic Active Pixel Sensor (MAPS) are rarely used for x-ray imaging, especially above 10 keV of energy, they offer critical performance advantages in therms of area, resolution, speed and cost when compared to the almost universally adopted high-Z hybrid detectors (sensor coupled to a separate readout chip).This contribution shows how Depleted MAPS (D-MAPS) of several hundreds micron thickness, where an electric field makes the whole silicon volume capable of collecting the photo-generated charge, are indeed suitable for x-ray detection in the full industrial/medical energy range. Furthermore, while a single sensor cannot match the performance of established high-Z technology, it is shown how a stack of D-MAPS may reach detection efficiencies comparable to the state-of-the-art, offering at the same time higher spatial resolution, higher speed, and significantly lower cost per unit of instrumented area.To demonstrate the potentiality of the idea, x-ray measures on working D-MAPS prototypes are illustrated and discussed, as well as quantitative simulations of the 3D reconstruction capabilities such an approach may led to, with detailed comparison of different tissues (bone, muscle, water, etc..) discerning capabilities in tomography applications.

articleTitle: Assessing lesion detectability of the Walk-Through Total Body PET scanner using XCAT anthropomorphic phantom
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: This study presents a cost-effective total-body PET scanner called the walk-through (WT) TB-PET system, consisting of two flat detector panels with intrinsic depth-of-interaction capabilities and high spatial resolution. The objective of this investigation is to assess the detectability of subcentimeter-grade lesions using simulation and image reconstruction of the XCAT phantom. Our results demonstrate that the WT TB-PET scanner can detect and visualize all investigated lesions with diameters of 5, 7, and 10 mm, positioning it as a capable tomograph for detecting early-stage lesions. These findings suggest that the WT TB-PET system could improve the sensitivity and specificity of early cancer detection, while also reducing patient dose and scan time.

articleTitle: High count rates using Timepix3 Detectors: Efficient Data Processing in spectroscopic CT
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: This work introduces a new approach to data processing and recording with photon-counting Timepix3 detectors, addressing challenges related to high count rates and large amounts of data when measuring in data-driven readout mode. The 12x1 Timepix3 detector array combined with a 1mm CdTe sensor allows an event-based, data-driven readout mode. The energy information, arrival time, and position of each registered photon are stored in the ASIC. This data-driven readout causes a challenging amount of data which requires new techniques to handle long-lasting scans performed with a fully spectroscopic working detection mode. Our strategy limits the number of collected photons per pixel based on a selectable signal-to-noise ratio. It applies a simple but effective clustering algorithm that pre-processes data before storing it on the hard drive. This approach significantly reduces the amount of data in two different steps, allowing the performance of fully spectroscopic CT scans using standard laboratory computer setups. To measure the absorption of an underlying object considering the active time of each pixel from the start of the recording until it reaches the total amount of desired counts, was introduced. The results reveal the potential of the Timepix3 detector array with CdTe sensors in performing spectroscopic CT scans and provide insights into future applications in materials science and other relevant fields.

articleTitle: Online Monitoring of Boron Concentration in Nuclear Reactors: A Comparative Study of Dual-Channel and Multi-Detection Designs by Monte-Carlo Simulation
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Boron Concentration Online Monitoring System (BCOMS), commonly referred to as "online boron meter", is used to continuously monitor boron concentration in Pressurized Water Reactors (PWRs). Due to its large neutron absorption cross section, boron-10 (<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">10</sup>B) is added as boric acid to the primary fluid to adjust the nuclear reactor's criticality during normal operation, operational transients and accidental events. It is crucial to continuously monitor boron concentration in order to ensure the reactor's safety and to avoid some accidental events that could lead rapidly to a reactivity excursion in the reactor's core. The physical principle of BCOMS is based on measuring the attenuation of a neutron flux generated by a neutron source. <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">10</sup>B, contained in the primary fluid, absorbs a fraction of neutrons following the <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">10</sup>B(n,α)<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">7</sup>Li reaction, while a specific neutron counter measures the remaining neutrons. Subsequently, calibration techniques enable to determine the most accurate fitting function, ensuring the conversion of each measured counting rate to a boron concentration. In the frame of this work, we study the measurement performance of non-intrusive BCOMS, mounted around the discharge line of the Chemical and Volume Control System (CVCS). First, we address the issues and challenges surrounding the measurement of boron concentration based on specifically defined performance criteria. Second, we assess the performance of two different measurement approaches: a dual-channel compared to a multi-detection based BCOMS. This performance study is carried out by Monte Carlo simulations, using the MCNP6.2 code. Finally, we discuss pros and cons for each measuring approach in contrast to design and safety requirements.

articleTitle: A convolutional neural network for respiratory motion correction in PET
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Breathing related patient motion is a serious source of image blurring in oncological PET. Respiratory gating allows to subdivide the acquisition data into temporal bins ("gates") depending on the breathing cycle which are basically motion-free but exhibit increased noise levels. Image registration of all gates to a reference gate and subsequent averaging is possible but traditional registration algorithms are frequently slow or of limited accuracy. Deep learning methods have recently attracted much interest and have been successfully applied to image registration tasks. Their flexibility and execution speed are especially attractive in the present context. We have therefore implemented and evaluated an unsupervised deep learning framework for the registration of gated PET images.Image volume pairs consisting of a fixed gate and a second moving gate serve as input to a U-Net convolutional neural network which predicts a deformation vector field (DVF) mapping the moving image to the fixed image. The network is trained unsupervised by optimizing a similarity metric between the registered image pairs as well as an additional regularization loss. Fifty-two gated PET scans (8 gates) were available for training (N=42; 2352 gate pairs) and testing (N=10). Normalized cross correlation (NCC) was used as a measure of registration accuracy. The motion corrected images were compared to the respective ungated image, single reference gate and a commercially available motion correction method (OncoFreeze™, Siemens). Lesion SUV<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">max</inf> and noise levels in the liver were determined.Our method achieved visually very satisfactory motion compensation and consequently improved NCC for all test scans (by 4.9% on average). Motion artifacts were substantially reduced while maintaining the noise level of the ungated images.The proposed framework is suitable for efficient reduction of motion artifacts in PET and is competitive to the OncoFreeze™ method.

articleTitle: Certification of industrial manufactures for thin-gap Resistive Plate Chambers
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Resistive plate chambers (RPCs) with electrodes of high-pressure phenolic laminate and small gas gap widths down to 1 mm provide large area tracking at relatively low cost in combination with high rate capability and fast response with excellent time resolution of better than 500 ps. They are perfectly suited for experiments requiring sub-nanosecond time resolution and spatial resolution on the order of a few millimeters over large areas. Thin-gap RPCs will therefore be used for the upgrade of the barrel muon system of the ATLAS experiment at HL-LHC and are candidates for the instrumentation of future collider detectors and experiments searching for long-lived particles in experiments like ANUBIS. RPCs are also frequently used in large area cosmic ray detectors. The large demand for RPCs exceeds the presently available production capacities. At the same time, the requirements on mechanical precision, reliability and reproducibility for collider detectors have increased, especially with the reduced gas gap widths. Additional suppliers with industry-style quality assurance are therefore urgently needed. We have established RPC production procedures compliant with industrial requirements and are in the process of certifying several companies for RPC production for the ATLAS upgrade for HL-LHC and beyond. We report about the technology transfer, the RPC prototype production at the selected companies and the results of the certification procedure, as well as their performance and stability measurements in laboratory tests and at CERN SPS X5 120GeV muon beams under high rate <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">137</sup>Cs irradiation.

articleTitle: Fast detector timing resolutions with GANs
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Researchers are working on improving radiation detector coincidence timing resolution to enhance time-of-flight positron emission tomography (PET) and improve image signal-to-noise ratio. Large system simulations are necessary for testing new radiation detector technologies in a scanner setting. As timing resolution strongly depends on optical transport in the detector, using detailed optical photon transport modeling in simulations might be necessary but it is time and memory-intensive, making it impractical for system-level studies. To address this, a conditional Wasserstein Generative Adversarial Network (GAN), called optiGAN, was developed to generate multidimensional optical photon distributions on the photodetector of a radiation detector without conducting individual photon tracking. The accuracy of the GAN-generated distributions has already been demonstrated by similarity values higher than 93.5% when compared to distributions obtained with traditional particle tracking simulation. This work includes the optical photon timing distribution at the photodetector face within the training dataset generated through accurate optical Monte Carlo simulations with GATE. This enables the generation of multidimensional distributions useful for studying radiation detector timing performance. The GAN-generated distributions have been used as input of an experimentally-verified SiPM model to produce detector electrical signals, allowing the estimation of the coincidence timing resolution from realistic simulation data. The optiGAN-generated time distributions show excellent agreement with the training dataset distributions, with similarity values higher than 92% for all different points where the distributions were generated, with a speed gain of up to two orders of magnitude. The SiPM signals from tracking simulations or GAN-generated distributions show very good agreement, demonstrating that GAN-generated distributions can be used to perform timing resolution studies.

articleTitle: Cloud-Based Serverless Computing Enables Accelerated Monte Carlo-Based Scatter Correction for Positron Emission Tomography
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: This study investigates the potential of cloud-based serverless computing to accelerate Monte Carlo (MC)-based scatter correction (SC) in positron emission tomography (PET) imaging. Especially with longer axial field of view, wider acceptance angles and increased number of lines-of-response, SC can pose high computational burden for image reconstruction methods – even when executed on a modern multi-core computing server. In this work we investigate the computational performance of a cloud-based serverless MC simulation using Amazon Web Service (AWS) Lambda and provide a comparison to the computational performance of modern on-premises multi-thread reconstruction server. We find that for our specific application cloud-based SC can outperform local server-based computations by more than an order of magnitude. Adopting cloud-based serverless computing in PET imaging facilities can significantly improve processing times and overall workflow efficiency, with future research exploring additional enhancements through optimized configurations and computational methods.

articleTitle: Performance Comparison of two Machine Learning Methods for Positioning in Analog and Digitally Read-out Slab-detectors
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: The development of Whole and Total-Body Positron Emission Tomography (PET) systems has increased over the last years. These systems aim to increase sensitivity while extending its use to other clinical areas. However, building such systems requires using large volumes of materials and complex signal multiplexing and data analysis processes.In this work, we focus on comparing two PET detector designs that may be part of the potential solution for constructing cost-effective clinical PET systems. Both detectors are based on semi-monolithic crystals and have been developed i3M in Valencia (analog SiPM read-out) and at PMI in Aachen, (digital SiPM read-out). We performed a direct comparison between them by implementing two calibration set-ups and two positioning methodologies based on Neural Networks (NN) and Gradient Tree Boosting (GTB).We report for each set-up the Mean Absolute Error (MAE), bias vector and FWHM of the Point Spread Function. Our results demonstrate that both detectors and positioning algorithms are highly comparable and, thus, potential candidates for being implemented in Whole- and Total-Body PET designs.

articleTitle: Improving the timing resolution of a time-of-flight and depth-of-interaction PET array detector
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Recently, silicon photomultiplier (SiPM) has emerged as the photodetectors of choice for PET, due to its small size and performance characteristics. A well-studied design for depth-of-interaction (DOI) and time-of-flight (TOF) capable PET detectors is the individual, double-ended light readout of small, pixelated scintillators. An NxN array detector of this kind has 2NxN SiPMs, which poses a challenge in readout. We previously proposed using a stripline (SL) for reading the front (back) SiPM array in row (column) and produce two outputs (four outputs total). We achieved accurate crystal identification, an average energy resolution (ER) of about 14%, a DOI resolution of about 2.7mm when applied to a 4x4 array of 3x3x20mm LYSO crystals, and a TOF resolution of about 391ps when measured in coincidence with a single-pixel reference detector. When increasing the array size to 8x8, these performance characteristics remained about the same but the TOF resolution degraded to 584ps. In this work, we identified the cause for the degradation as likely due to inter-crystal scattering (ICS). To mitigate its effect, we investigated the use of two SLs per SiPM array for reading alternating rows or columns. Although it doubles the number of detector outputs to eight, the readout is still highly multiplexing. In an initial experiment, we measured an average ER of about 20%, a DOI resolution of about 1.5mm, and a TOF resolution of about 456ps.

articleTitle: Development of a Clinical Self-Collimating Gamma Camera with high resolution and sensitivity
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Gamma cameras are essential components of nuclear medicine imaging, but their performance has long been limited by the resolution-noise trade-off imposed by mechanical collimators. To overcome this limitation, we have recently proposed the self-collimation concept, which utilizes active detectors as collimators for photon collimation. We have validated the feasibility of self-collimation using a multi-layer interspaced mosaic detectors (MATRICES) architecture. In this work, we present two versions of the self-collimating gamma camera (SCGC) with the MATRICES architecture, aimed at significantly improving resolution and signal-to-noise performance.SCGC version 1 consists of a coded-aperture plate and four detector layers. The first three detector layers consist of a 16x8 scintillator array with 3-mm intrinsic resolution arranged in a honeycomb-like pattern, while the fourth layer has a 32x32 GAGG(Ce) scintillator array with 2-mm intrinsic resolution. Experimental evaluations reveal that SCGC version 1 has a sensitivity of 0.05% (average) ± 0.005% (standard deviation) in a 10-cm-diameter field-of-view (FOV). It can localize a 10 μCi 99mTc source within 0.5 s at a source-to-camera distance of 10 cm and resolve 3-by-3 point array sources with a separation of 1.6 mm.SCGC version 2 has a detector area four times larger than SCGC version 1. Monte Carlo simulations show that SCGC version 2 can clearly resolve a hot-rod phantom with a minimal hotrod diameter of 1.6 mm. In a thyroid phantom with 15 MBq total activity, SCGC version 2 can clearly resolve 6-mm-diameter nodes in 1 min, providing accurate results with high resolution and high contrast.We are currently developing a realistic SCGC version 2 system and plan to characterize its imaging performance with experimental studies in the coming months.

articleTitle: Initial human evaluation of the performance of the NeuroEXPLORER, a next-generation ultra-high performance brain PET imager
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: The aim of this work was to evaluate the performance of the NeuroEXPLORER (NX) in comparison to the High-Resolution Research Tomography (HRRT) and Siemens Biograph Vision, based on the first human NX scan. The NX system has a 52.4 cm system diameter and a long axial field-of-view of 49.5 cm.. The detector micro-block consists of a 4x2 array of 1.56x3.07x20 mm LYSO crystals decoded by four 3-mm SiPMs, which utilize an optical bridge for light-sharing between axial crystal pairs to measure depth-of-interaction (DOI). The ultra-high resolution of the NX was demonstrated visually in comparison to the HRRT and Vision. Further, the exceptional contrast resolution of the NX compared to the Vision was demonstrated using line intensity profiles. Finally, a dramatic improvement in variation (72%) was exhibited by the NX compared to the HRRT, corresponding to an effective sensitivity increase of 13-fold. Future analyses will further characterize the performance of the NX using paired human scans on the NX, HRRT, and Vision, conducted under identical conditions.

articleTitle: A compact gamma-ray detector for SPECT systems applied to BNCT dose monitoring
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: We present a compact gamma-ray detector, combined with a dedicated collimator and an appropriate shielding case, as a single unit to be assembled for the realization of a SPECT apparatus dedicated to dose monitoring and verification during BNCT treatments. The detector, based on a LaBr<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</inf>(Ce+Sr) scintillator crystal readout by Silicon Photomultipliers (SiPMs) and compact electronics, features excellent energy resolution (<3% at 662 keV) and good detection efficiency (60% at 478 keV) that allow to detect the 478 keV gamma rays emitted by boron neutron capture reactions for real-time dose monitoring purposes. FLUKA simulations have been used to analyze the background signal nearby the BNCT photopeak induced by the neutron activation of the detector itself, a key issue in this application. The predominant contribution is due to the PCBs of the electronics readout. A dedicated cadmium shielding has been designed in order to improve the detector's sensitivity and reliability, while maintaining compact size, lower than 15×15×12 cm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</sup>, in view of the final ring configuration where many modules are required. The effectiveness of the shielding material, together with the capability of the detector to identify and resolve the BNCT signal, have been confirmed with experimental measurements at the TRIGA MARK II reactor of Pavia University.

articleTitle: 3-D Reconstruction of Extended Sources During Dispersal Trial with a Compton Imager
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: We present a real-time tomographic reconstruction of an extended radioactive distribution composed of two large regions of different La-140 concentrations. During the trial, a Compton imager took back-projection images at different points outside of the perimeter. Both the location of the radioactive material on the ground and the relative intensity of the two regions are reconstructed. A post-processed image reconstruction that makes use of the known detector response (determined via Monte-Carlo simulations) and employs a Chi-square minimization will also be shown. These imaging techniques have direct applications for use in emergency response, nuclear security and international treaty verification.

articleTitle: High level performance of the RICH detector of the NA62 experiment at CERN during run 2 data taking
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: After the run 1 data taking of NA62 (2014-2018), the RICH detector has been successfully operated during the beginning of run 2 in 2021 and 2022, being essential in most of the NA62 analyses. The main design aspects and operational characteristics of the detector will be described and a detailed report of its high level performance concerning the $\pi / \mu$ separation, directly measured with the data collected in 2022, will be presented in comparison to the run 1 results, in order to asses the effect of the detector aging. To this purpose the time dependence of the basic performance of the RICH will also be presented. Furthermore, new analysis techniques, to improve the knowledge of the RICH behaviour (mirror reflectivity, PM efficiency), will be presented.

articleTitle: Combat strategies for charge sharing and pulse pileup with photon counting detectors
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: The first clinical photon counting detector computed tomography (PCD-CT) was cleared by FDA in 2021. Other CT vendors have developed prototype PCD-CT systems. These systems have demonstrated improved spatial resolution but limited improvement in spectral performance compared to existing dual-energy CT scanners. This is mainly due to spectral distortion via charge sharing and pulse pileup. Addressing both of them is an unmet clinical need for this much hyped CT technology. There have been a few PCD designs and strategies to combat these problems, but their strengths and weaknesses have not been studied and compared against each other systematically. The aim of this study was to conduct such a comparison study.In this work, we conducted a Monte Carlo simulation study to compare six PCD designs and strategies. The following specification was used as the default setting #1 (which is similar to the only clinical PCD-CT available today): 20-ns pulse duration, 1.6 mm-thick CdTe crystal, 250-µm PCD pixels, 2-dimensional anti-scatter grids outside 4x4 pixels, 2 energy bins (windows), and a standard threshold–subtract (TS) counting scheme to produce energy bins. The following designs and strategies were implemented and compared: #1) TS scheme with the default setting, #2) TS with 500-µm PCD pixels, #3) TS with 4 bins, #4) 500-µm pixels with 4 bins, #5) analog charge summing mode (CSM) with 4 bins, and #6) spectral, multi-energy inter-pixel coincidence counter (MEICC) with 4 bins. MEICC is a novel design which counts coincidence events via charge sharing but does not interfere with the primary counting process, which makes PCDs with MEICC as fast as those without MEICC.We present the simulation results and discuss pros and cons of these approaches.

articleTitle: Development of a hybrid amorphous Selenium/CMOS detector for the Selena Neutrino Experiment
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: The Selena Neutrino Experiment couples a <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">82</sup>Se enriched amorphous selenium (aSe) ionization target to a complimentary metal-oxide semiconductor (CMOS) active pixel array as an imaging detector for next generation neutrino physics. The high Q value of <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">82</sup>Se and the excellent event classification allows for a search for neutrinoless double beta decay free from environmental backgrounds. Furthermore, we can take advantage of the spatiotemporal resolution to perform high efficiency electron neutrino spectroscopy for solar neutrino studies and sterile neutrino searches. The Selena experiment will operate with a 10-ton target for a 100-ton year exposure. We are currently characterizing our first prototypes of the Selena detectors, which consist of 500um of aSe deposited on the Topmetal-II− CMOS pixel charge sensor. We present R&D results from our studies and show the induced beta and gamma tracks within our detector, as well as a noise performance of 23 electrons. We also present status on the development of the next version of the Selena detectors, which were fabricated using the open-source Skywater 130nm process..

articleTitle: A Deep Texture Metric for PET Image Quantification and Image Synthesis
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG) Positron Emission Tomography (PET) serves as a cornerstone in functional imaging. PET imaging reveals metabolic abnormalities before morphological alterations occur. The standardized uptake value is a common metric to semi-quantify PET images. Visual scoring of PET image heterogeneity has demonstrated correlations with tumour characteristics. Quantification of this spatial variation in FDG distribution via its shape and texture has proven to be a fertile area of research under the umbrella term "Radiomics." Deep learning with convolutional neural networks (CNN) serves as large feature extractors with proven ability in tumour type classification in PET imaging. Deep learning in PET imaging has also been utilized for image enhancement, reconstruction, segmentation and image synthesis. In this work, we quantify the feature distribution of neural activations of each layer in a CNN following propagation through the network of a PET image. The Gramian matrix of the activation functions quantifies the neural representation of the CNN and thus serves as a measure of visual perception. Image synthesis using gradient descent on the target PET image Gramian matrix allows visualization of the texture. This metric is tested in PET imaging data of a recently developed texture phantom and a single primary tumour from a non-small-cell lung cancer (NSCLC) patient. It is demonstrated that the summation of the Gramian decreases with decreasing homogeneity. The visual appearance of the synthesized PET images closely resembles that ground truth PET images, both in the texture phantom and clinical image.

articleTitle: Analysis of Recombination Kinetics of Electron-Hole Pairs in TlBr Crystals Using Pulsed Electron Beams of Different Intensities
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: TlBr has long been a candidate for ionizing radiation semiconductor detectors. Its large band gap energy is also favorable for use at room temperature. However, to obtain excellent energy resolution, semiconductor detector applications require single crystals of high purity and quality; thus far, issues such as crystal growth reproducibility have limited the development of such applications. TlBr crystal quality has been evaluated using many analysis methods. One well-studied method is optical characterization.We analyzed the transient absorption properties of TlBr crystals using pulsed electron beams as excitation sources. We observed the transient absorption spectra and temporal profiles on the pico-and nanosecond scales. The pulse intensity was changed, and the influence of the pulse intensity (dose) on the decay kinetics was analyzed in detail. In the picosecond scale, the transient absorbance decreased with time for the pulse dose of 49 Gy, whereas the decrease was not observed for the pulse dose of 20 Gy. This result indicates that, at low excitation density, the recombination is negligible up to several ns. The decay kinetics in the nanosecond scale were described as the second order decay, in which the decay rate is proportional to the square of the concentration of electron-hole pairs. On the basis of the analysis of the decay kinetics with the second order decay, we obtained the bimolecular recombination constant of around 2×10<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">8</sup> cm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</sup> s<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">-1</sup>. The decay kinetics were quite similar in the TlBr crystals at different positions in the grown crystalline boule.

articleTitle: Data Acquisition Methods for SiPM Characterization: Current Status of the VERA System at TRIUMF
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: This study will describe the design and continued development of readout software and instrumentation for the Vacuum Emission, Reflection, and Absorption (VERA) measurement apparatus at TRIUMF. The VERA apparatus is used to characterize Silicon Photomultiplier responses to vacuum-ultraviolet light at cryogenic temperatures, and contributes to selecting a SiPM for nEXO. VERA consists of a liquid nitrogen cooling system, programmable power supplies for SiPM bias, a lamp, and a vacuum chamber. Data collection and experiment monitoring software is built using the Maximum Integrated Data Acquisition System, developed jointly by TRIUMF and PSI. Current work is focused on expanding our data acquisition software to support new procedures and measurement equipment, reducing noise, and ensuring repeatable measurements.

articleTitle: An accurate and robust time calibration method for PET with high DOI resolution
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: PET time alignment refers to the process of correcting the time differences between the signals detected by different detectors in a PET scanner. The arrival times of the signals detected by each detector may differ due to various factors such as differences in cable length, signal processing delays, and temperature variations. This can result in errors in the reconstruction of the PET image, reducing its spatial and temporal resolution. To address this, PET scanners incorporate time alignment techniques to synchronize the signals detected by different detectors.DOI (Depth-of-Interaction) PET refers to a type of positron emission tomography (PET) scanner that is designed to improve the spatial resolution of PET images by allowing for the detection of the depth of interaction of the gamma photons within the scintillator crystals. We have designed and made a DOI PET scanner. The position of the interaction along the depth axis is calculated based on the ratio of the light produced in the sensors. It is possible to regard each small DOI segment as a small crystal.Time alignment on DOI PET is similar to that on traditional PET scanners, but with some additional considerations due to the use of segmented scintillator crystals. One of the main challenges of doing time alignment on DOI PET is the increased complexity of the detector system due to the segmentation of the scintillator crystals. With traditional PET scanners, the signals from all the crystals in a module are combined to form a coincidence event, and any time offsets between the crystals can be easily corrected for using a single time offset value. However, with DOI PET, the signals from each crystal segment must be separately timed and combined, which requires more advanced timing algorithms and huge data. In this work, we extend the time alignment method and designed a method that does not need that huge data, and could output accurate time offsets result.

articleTitle: Initial performance of an ultra-high resolution DOI/TOF PET scanner for small animal PET/CT imaging
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: This work introduces a small animal dedicated PET scanner with depth of interaction (DOI) and time of flight (TOF) capabilities, which adopts a build-in light guide crystal array, a dual-ended readout structure and a self-developed application-specific integrated circuit (ASIC) readout electronics design, achieving sub-millimeter spatial resolution and multi-layer DOI response capability. The system consists of 1344 micro-blocks forming a regular octagonal detector ring, each micro-block contains 64 crystal pixels of 0.8x0.8x12mm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</sup> and 4 SiPMs with dual-ended readout. The system has a long axial field of view of 177mm and a large scan aperture of 140mm, which can support dynamic whole-body scanning and multi-mouse co-bed imaging. The test results show that the system has an energy resolution of 13.16% and a time resolution of 482ps, and within the effective field of view, the system has a mean FBP spatial resolution of better than 1mm, and can resolve 0.6mm rods from the Mini-Derenzo phantom with iterative reconstruction. The system can meet the high-end needs of current preclinical research.

articleTitle: Experimental studies of ionization-induced modulation of optical properties in crystals using spectral encoding
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Improving the coincidence time resolution (CTR) to 10ps would greatly improve PET’s ability to visualize and quantify disease. One proposed method for achieving this is through the direct detection of modulation of optical properties caused by ionization-induced charge carriers that result from 511 keV interactions in crystal materials. To date, this method has primarily been investigated using synchronized sources. Previously, spectral encoding, which precisely encodes an ionizing interaction event time into a modulated wavelength of a probe pulse, was shown to be a state-of-the-art technique capable of achieving ultrafast temporal resolution using single-shot measurements of x-ray pulses.Here, we implemented the spectral encoding technique specifically designed to detect 511 keV photons. To achieve this, we increased the pulse duration of the supercontinuum probe to 4 ns, providing sufficient coverage for the entire charge carrier cascade time of 511 keV photon interactions. By also employing a high-repetition-rate laser and a high-frame-rate camera, we significantly increased the live-time coverage of the detection, which will address the asynchronous arrival times of the 511 keV photons.For proof-of-principle demonstration, we employed a synchronous IR excitation source to generate optical property modulations, which we detected after modifying the optical path of the IR beam relative to the visible probe beam. The delay stage position was adjusted in increments of 10 cm, ranging from 40 cm to 20 cm, corresponding to 330 picosecond delay steps. We observed shifts in spectral peaks corresponding to 12.5 pixels or 14.9 nm in wavelength using the spectral encoding method. In this initial setup, the mean temporal variance was 122.4 ± 22.3 ps.This work lays the groundwork for future research in the detection of asynchronous radiation particles with extremely low temporal variance for use in PET applications.

articleTitle: An integrated ionization chamber for intensity and position monitoring
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: We have developed an ionization chamber with fully integrated electronics. It features an extremely low noise charge digitizer, an embedded EPICS IOC and an integrated HV generator capable of providing up to 2000V. It requires only a 5V supply and an Ethernet connection for operation. Its construction uses standard PCB technology to form a rigid chamber with fringe-field correction side plates. Its aperture is 40 mm horizontally by 5 mm vertically, and it is 230 mm (9 inches) long. Its collection plate is split by a zig-zag break to provide approximately 5 mm of position indication in one dimension. When used as a position sensor it gives a position accuracy of 0.8 um standard deviation when operated at 15nA ion current.

articleTitle: Resolving 10 mmHg and 40 mmHg pO2 Samples by Positronium Lifetime in Clinical PET
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Positronium (Ps) imaging has been recently spotlighted for its potential applications in nuclear medicine. Among them, with an expectation that the Ps lifetime can be a biomarker for tumor hypoxia, we are aiming to achieve Ps lifetime imaging, Quantum PET (Q-PET), based on whole gamma imaging (WGI). Shibuya et al. have shown a linear correlation between the Ps lifetime and the oxygen partial pressure (pO<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf>) in water by using a bench-top detector system. However, nobody has ever demonstrated the possibility of distinguishing pO<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf> values of 10 mmHg and 40 mmHg, corresponding to hypoxic cancer cells and healthy tissue cells, respectively. Therefore, this study aimed at measuring the Ps lifetime of <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">22</sup>Na solutions each with such a tiny difference in the pO<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf> value. For possible extension toward imaging, a clinical brain-dedicated TOF PET system, VRAIN, which has a hemispherical detector arrangement and 229 ps TOF resolution, was used. The pO<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf> values of the <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">22</sup>Na solutions (200-370 kBq) were adjusted to 0, 10, 40, and 160 mmHg by adjusting the inflow of nitrogen gas. Each <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">22</sup>Na solution was placed near the center of the detector geometry, and measured for 48 hours. Three different energy windows (EWs) for 1275 keV gamma detection were compared (1100-1500 keV, 900-1500 keV, and 700-1500 keV). Due to the increased number of events, the error values (σ: standard deviation) of the calculated Ps lifetimes decreased as the energy window widened. The optimized EW was 700-1500 keV. The Ps lifetime values gradually became shorter as the pO<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf> values increased. The Ps lifetime values at 0 mmHg and 160 mmHg were 1.9389±0.0025 ns and 1.9251±0.0020 ns at the EW of 700-1500 keV. The difference was more than twice the errors (±2σ), and considered a statistically significant difference. The Ps lifetime values of 10 mmHg and 40 mmHg were 1.9360±0.0026 ns and 1.9291±0.0024 ns at the same condition, and the difference could be detected with an error value of more than ±1σ.

articleTitle: Attenuation estimation of a flexible body matrix coil in PET/MRI using MLAA and registration
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Attenuation of the PET signal by magnetic resonance (MR) hardware (HW) is currently ignored for flexible coils, which can lead to underestimation of activity in the patient. This study investigates the use of a maximum likelihood algorithm which updates activity and attenuation distributions simultaneously from acquired emission data (MLAA) and subsequent registration of pre-acquired CT-derived μMaps of the HW.NonTOF PET scans of a cylinder phantom where a flexible body coil was wrapped around were performed. This data was reconstructed using MLAA with known phantom-, but unknown HW attenuation. In addition, CT scans of the same body coil were performed with different bending and Hounsfield units were scaled to PET-energies. Those μMaps were then registered to the MLAA output and used in final ordered subset expectation maximisation (OSEM) reconstructions of the PET data.Rigid registration of a coil-image in the identical position as during PET acquisition moved the highly attenuating preamplifiers overall in the right position, although with a remaining gap transaxially. Non-rigid registration of a coil-image in a different deformation moved the preamplifiers in the right position, however the structures were distorted. In all cases, the activity images reconstructed with the obtained μMaps show a smaller error with respect to the ground truth compared to the uncorrected case.

articleTitle: DIGILOG: A digital-analog SiPM towards 10 ps prompt-photon tagging in TOF-PET
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Functional imaging techniques like positron emission tomography (PET) are an essential tool in an aging society. Despite impressive advances in microelectronics, photodetectors and scintillation materials, PET is still awaiting a breakthrough in terms of reduced cost and increased performance. Large potential is seen in ultraprecise time-of-flight (TOF), aiming at coincidence time resolutions (CTRs) better than 30 ps. However, state-of-the-art TOF-PET systems are still far away from this goal, achieving typical CTRs of 214 ps (FWHM). Several proposals have been put forth, whereas the most promising is to use prompt photon emission, e.g. Cherenkov radiation in BGO crystals, which are cheap to produce, thus contributing to drastic cost cutting. However, Cherenkov detection is challenging due to its limited photon yield, which in turn requires a very high photon detection efficiency (PDE), low dark count rate (DCR) and extremely fast and innovative electronic readout schemes. Recent analog silicon photomultipliers (aSiPMs) meet the first two targets, but not the latter.In the Digilog project we envisage to unite the best of these two worlds, combining high PDE, low DCR and an exceptional SPTR. To reach this goal, we will segment state-of-the-art aSiPMs into smaller clusters, called µSiPMs. A balanced segmentation of the electronic readout will make it possible to efficiently detect the first scintillation and Cherenkov photons, with a manageable granularity at system level. The µSiPM signals will feature photon-density time walk correction and photon counting. We envision to create 3D-stacked sensors where the electronics will be housed in a CMOS bottom-tier and the µSiPMs in the top-tier chip. Preliminary measurements on first µSiPM test-structures already reached PDE and DCR close to their commercial counterparts, while an SPTR of 25 ps FWHM, close to our sub-20 ps goal, has been achieved.

articleTitle: Investigation of gamma-ray detection with an opaque liquid scintillator
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Opaque scintillators are highly scattering such that scintillation photons are probabilistically confined to a small sub-region of the detector. The light is then transported out of the detector via wavelength-shifting fibers. We present the experimental results with a prototype detector that is 1 liter in volume and has 32 wavelength-shifting fibers, each connected to a pixel of a multi-anode photomultiplier tube and read out by a separate digitizer channel. The detection medium is linear-alkylbenze with wavelength shifting fluors and paraffin wax to induce opacity. We compare the spectra of gamma rays from two radioisotopes to show they are differentiable. We show the capability of the detector for source localization through observation of the spatial distribution of light. Lastly, we investigate the resolution in reconstructing the event position in a direction transverse to optical fibers.

articleTitle: A Design of MVT Thresholds Using a Geometric Sequence Relative to the First Threshold
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: The multi-threshold voltage(MVT) method is gaining attention as a digitalization method for scintillation pulses, with potential for wide energy applications. However, a uniform threshold setting scheme requires numerous channel voltage thresholds, decreasing integration and increasing power consumption.This paper introduces several voltage threshold setting methods and evaluates them using an R<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sup> parameter. A threshold design scheme is proposed that achieves results similar to using 63 voltage thresholds, compared to the first threshold using a geometric series design.The proposed method reduces the required voltage thresholds while maintaining high accuracy in the MVT method, improving integration and reducing power consumption in wide energy range applications.

articleTitle: Test-Time Augmentation Towards Improved Cross-Center PET/CT Segmentations by the Swin UNETR
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: In this study, we performed lymphoma lesion segmentation and make a dual contribution. First, we evaluate the impact of Test-Time Augmentation (TTA) on segmentation performance of the Swin UNEt TRansformer (UNETR). Secondly, we assess the effectiveness of TTA on a model trained with data from two different centers and on different lymphoma subtypes. Our results show that TTA significantly improves the segmentation performance of the Swin UNETR model (with an average Dice of 0.70 on the test data of center I and II) from Dice=0.55±0.09 to 0.61±0.17 (p-value<0.001) on the external unseen data from center III. Moreover, we also showed that TTA improves the generalizability of the model, enabling it to perform well on data from different centers and lymphoma types. We found the weights of the transformation for TTA by random serach. These findings have important implications for improving the accuracy and robustness of lymphoma lesion segmentation in clinical practice.

articleTitle: Preliminary investigation of image reconstruction from sparse data in spectra-spatial electron paramagnetic resonance imaging
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: In electron paramagnetic resonance imaging (EPRI), the commonly used continuous wave (CW) scanning scheme with Zeeman modulation (ZM) requires dense samplings, leading to long scan times. Conventional FBP algorithm often results in significant image-quality degradation when reconstructing images from sparse-view data. Thus, there is great interest in developing advanced reconstruction algorithms for speeding up EPRI by collecting data over reduced projection views while maintaining image quality. In this study, we tailored the recently developed DTV algorithm to investigate accurate image reconstruction from sparse-view data in CW-ZM EPRI. Our results demonstrate that the DTV algorithm yields image reconstructions from sparse-view data with quality comparable to those obtained from full data in EPRI. These findings suggest the potential for developing algorithms to enable sparse-view scanning configurations in spectral-spatial EPRI, thereby reducing imaging time.

articleTitle: Geant4 Silver Anniversary: Science Production with a Simulation System
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: 2023 is the 25th anniversary of Geant4's public release and the 20th anniversary of the publication of its first reference paper (S. Agostinelli et al., Geant4 - a simulation toolkit, NIM A 506 (2003) 250–303), which is the most cited publication in Particle and Fields Physics, Nuclear Science and Technology, and Instruments and Instrumentation journals. This presentation reviews Geant4's lifetime from a scientometric perspective through the analysis of the scientific production it has enabled. The scientometric data, collected from the Web of Science (Clarivate Analytics), are evaluated with rigorous statistical methods; the analysis highlights characteristics as diversity, inequality and trends in the scientific, geographic and institutional distribution of the literature associated with Geant4. The results make up a picture of the evolution of the role of Geant4's use in particle and nuclear physics, astrophysics and medical physics research, and in related fields over the past 25 years. This overview is complemented by some comparative assessment of the role played by other major Monte Carlo particle transport codes.

articleTitle: µRWELL-PICOSEC: The Development of Fast Timing Resistive Micro-WELL Detector Technology
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: We present the development of a new concept of fast timing gaseous detector, the µRWELLPICOSEC detector based on Resistive Micro-Well (µRWELL) technology to provide timing resolution in the tens of picosecond range for application as time-of-flight (TOF) technology in the particle physics and medical instrumentation fields. The µRWELL-PICOSEC technology combined a Cerenkov radiator for the generation of Cerenkov photons from high energy charged particles, a photocathode for the conversion of the produced photons into primary electrons and the µRWELL foil for the multiplication of the electron to produce large signal on pad segmentation readout. The proof of concept of µRWELL-PICOSEC is demonstrated with a small single-channel prototype and preliminary timing performance of 90 ps has been measured. Optimization study the amplification structure of µRWELL-PICOSEC for the improvement of timing resolution is discussed and results on timing performance studies in beam at CERN are presented. The development of large area (100 mm × 100 mm) µRWELL-PICOSEC and associated multichannel fast readout electronics and data acquisition system are also reported.

articleTitle: A Novel Readout Approach with Multiplexed Timing for High Timing Resolution TOF-PET Detector
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: It is challenging to read out the tens of thousands of signal channels in a TOF-PET system based on SiPMs. To reduce the complexity and meanwhile achieve the high timing resolution, we developed a scalable readout scheme that multiplexes timing signals of multiple SiPMs into one channel using a summing circuit and performs the one-to-one readout of energy signals by a Sigma-Delta circuit. When tested on a piece of 3×3×3 mm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</sup> LYSO crystal, the proposed scheme achieved a high coincidence timing resolution (CTR) of 109.45±1.24 ps FWHM with 9 SiPMs multiplexed (corresponding to a total effective detection area of 331.60 mm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sup>). The degradation in CTR was only 22.06 ps from the single SiPM readout scheme. CTRs measured at different multiplexing ratios indicate our readout scheme is promising in effectively simplifying the readout electronics while providing excellent coincidence timing performance.

articleTitle: Synchronising A High Speed Dynamic Collimator and a 6-Axis Robot For Synchrotron Radiotherapy Treatments
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Research utilizing synchrotron radiation for radiotherapy applications is becoming increasingly complex as it pushes towards canine clinical trials [1]–[3]. Recently, several beamline developments at the Imaging and Medical Beamline (IMBL) have taken place towards supporting the forthcoming canine clinical trials. A high speed dynamic collimator has been developed and tested on IMBL for shaping the synchrotron beam as a target is moved through the beam. A 6-Axis Kuka robot has also been configured to allow a target to be positioned and treated with respect to the synchrotron beam. In this work, we describe the synchronisation of these two systems when combined to deliver conformal radiotherapy treatments on IMBL for large animals. A proof-of-concept treatment is demonstrated whereby a medical physics phantom (ball bearings encased in an acryllic cube) is aligned and treated with the robot and dynamic collimator. A full characterisation of the systems capabilities is to follow such that appropriate treatment margins can be generated when using this configuration. More importantly, the ability to dynamically deliver conformal fields on the synchrotron beamline for large animals will ensure that the canine clinical trails can utilise conformal fields for the treatment of cancers whilst avoiding nearby critical structures.

articleTitle: Attenuation correction for PET imaging using conditional denoising diffusion probabilistic model
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: During PET acquisition, attenuation correction is an indispensable procedure in which computed tomography (CT) image is usually regarded as the standard. However, attenuation correction in PET/MR systems is challenging because magnetic resonance (MR) images lack information on the attenuation coefficients. To address this issue, we propose a novel method to synthesize attenuation coefficients (CT) images from MR images using a conditional diffusion probabilistic model (con-DDPM). To enhance the constraint on generated images based on MR images, we introduce a condition encoder into the original diffusion model to extract features from MR images. And then, corresponding low-level features from the condition encoder and diffusion encoder are fused together. Results demonstrate that our proposed method can achieve more accurate attenuation coefficient synthesis than UNet and Generative Adversarial Network (GAN) models.

articleTitle: Development of a beta-probe based on scintillation fibers and silicon photomultipliers.
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Beta radiation (electrons and positrons) coming from radiotracers of interest in nuclear medicine have generally a short range of a few mm in tissues. Beta-probes are appropriate for the detection of surface radiation which can be used in clinical and preclinical applications. We have developed a beta-probe based on scintillation fibers and silicon photomultipliers. Scintillation fibers with different size, geometry and cladding configuration were compared in terms of beta particle detection efficiency and light collection. Silicon photomultipliers of different sizes and sensitivities were tested with an in-house developed readout electronics.

articleTitle: An LYSO and BGO checkerboard pattern detector with inter-crystal scatter identification capability
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Inter-crystal scatter (ICS) events cause inaccurate assignment of photon interaction position and degrade spatial resolution. It is more challenging to identify ICS in light sharing detectors with smaller crystals.In this work, a checkerboard pattern detector composed of two types of scintillators (LYSO and BGO) is proposed. Each crystal within an array is surrounded on four lateral sides by crystals of different type. Two detectors with different crystal sizes were developed. The detector #1 is an 8×8 array of 1.51×1.51×15 mm3 crystals. The detector #2 is a 8× 8 array of 0.38×0.38×4 mm3 crystals. A 2 mm thick glass light guide were placed between the scintillator array and a 64-channel Hamamatsu MPPC. A PETsys TOFPET2 ASIC records both integrated charge (QDC) and time over threshold (ToT) for each MPPC channel to discriminate the LYSO, BGO and ICS events. The identified ICS events (ICS-LB) correspond to the events that interact with both LYSO and BGO crystals.Flood images and energy spectra were measured using a 22-Na point source. Majority of the crystals (including the 0.38 mm BGO) were clearly resolved. The fraction of the identified ICS events in detector #2 (43.8%) is higher than that in #1 (23.0%), due to its smaller crystal size. The average energy resolution are 22.8±3.4% (LYSO) and 37.8±5.1% (BGO) in detector #1, and are 18.8±7.2% (LYSO) and 26.9±5.2% (BGO) in detector #2.GATE simulation was used to investigate the fraction of the ICS events. Without simulating the process of electron ionization and deexcitation, the fraction of the ICS-LB events are 19.8% and 16.4% for the detector #1 and #2. With the process simulated, the ICS-LB fraction increase to 37.1% (#1) and 71.0% (#2). The ICS-LB in detector #2 (smaller crystal size) increases more (16.4% to 71.0%), since secondary particles are easier to escape from the crystal of first interaction.

articleTitle: Creation of a Head Tracking Dataset for Motion Correction in High Resolution Brain PET Imaging
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Head motion is a source of spatial blurring in brain PET imaging that is becoming increasingly important with the renewed interest in the development of dedicated ultra-high resolution PET scanners. External head tracking can provide accurate position correction, but is cumbersome and difficult to implement on a regular basis in the clinical setting. Data-driven head motion detection can also be used, but its accuracy is currently limited. Deep-learning based data-driven motion tracking can potentially provide suitable correction for patient movements. A large dataset of accurate motion-encoded PET data would be required for training a neural network, which would be difficult to build from PET imaging of human subjects. As a surrogate of PET data, we propose to build a dataset of typical head motion in the brain PET imaging context using an external motion tracking system. The goal of this dataset will be to enable the simulation of realistic motion-plagued brain PET acquisitions which would then be used to develop regularization methods for data-driven motion tracking and correction. This paper describes the proposed methodology to create this dataset. During the investigation, we discovered that the external tracking system suffers from a significant loss of accuracy when tracking relative to a reference fiducial. A solution based on the filtering of the reference fiducial orientation vector is demonstrated to mitigate this loss.

articleTitle: Commissioning a cost-effective TB-PET with TOF and DOI: the IMAS project
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Total-Body Positron Emission Tomography (TB-PET) technology and designs have become very popular in recent years. The advantages of these systems are many, pinpointing the high sensitivity achieved by their long axial FOV and eventually TOF, and the capabilities to simultaneously study the kinetics of multiple organs. Most of TB-PET designs and implementations are based on LYSO crystal pixels without DOI. In this work we present a TB-PET system based on semi-monolithic crystals and, therefore, simultaneously enabling TOF and depth of interaction capabilities. Furthermore, the design named IMAS, makes use of a reduction of signals without compromising performance. We have completed exhaustive simulation studies of the final system geometry, based on 5 rings of 10 cm in the axial direction each, and gaps of about 5 cm, with a total axial length of 71.4 cm. These studies confirm the good performance of the system in terms of spatial resolution, sensitivity and other relevant parameters. Moreover, these days, the full system is being installed at the largest hospital in our region. Very preliminary experimental tests at the lab with the first ring, already predict a spatial resolution of 2.9 mm at the cFOV. We aim to report a full characterization of the scanner during the conference.

articleTitle: Parallax-free Total-Body PET using Monolithic Flat-Panel Detectors
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Parallax error, caused by incorrect registration of lines of response (LORs) for oblique incidences, is an important factor limiting the spatial resolution of current (Total-Body) PET systems. We propose a novel concept for cost-effective, high-throughput and high-resolution Total-Body (TB-) PET: Walk-Through (WT) TB-PET. In this study, we investigate to what extent the parallax effect is present in the WT-PET, whose monolithic detector modules have intrinsic depth-of-interaction (DOI) decoding capabilities, allowing more accurate estimation of the LORs. To this end, the spatial resolution is evaluated and compared to that of the Biograph Vision Quadra, a non-DOI-capable clinical TB-PET device. Data is obtained in GATE by Monte Carlo simulation of point sources positioned along specific axes for both scanners. The WT-TB-PET shows approximately Gaussian behavior with equally narrow peaks (FWHM less than 2 mm) at all positions, proving that the device is (almost) unaffected by the parallax effect. The performance of the WT-TB-PET is superior compared to the Quadra, whose line profiles in the radial direction clearly show fingerprints of the parallax effect, characterized by broadening of the peaks and loss of Gaussian shape with increasing radial offsets. Cutting the maximal ring difference from 322 to 85 slightly improves the axial resolution. However, it does not reduce the radial parallax effect and leads to significant sensitivity losses (a factor 2.1).

articleTitle: Active Interrogation Using Extant Radiography Equipment
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Active interrogation (AI) is a technique which utilises an external source of radiation to induce a signal in a fissionable sample of interest. Current available technology focusses on the use of high energy (approx. 9MeV and higher) photon sources or neutron sources, due to the favourable cross-sections, to induce a fission signal which can then be detected. Many systems in development or already available are costly and produce high levels of radiation which make them less appealing for deployment. This work is focused on using extant equipment to extract photofission signals that are already being produced in situations such as cargo radiography. In such cases, x-ray systems with end-point energies which are higher than 6MeV are considered. In addition, currently available or deployed detector units are being evaluated for their ability to extract the photofission signals of interest in conjunction with the x-ray sources. This paper discusses results from a set of experiments conducted where a Depleted Uranium (DU), or U-238 plate was irradiated by two bremsstrahlung x-ray sources with 6MeV and 7.5 MeV endpoint energies. Results from an electro-mechanically cooled High Purity Germanium (HPGe) detector are presented and show that while this detector type suffers significant dead time when operated with such x-ray sources, a small quantity of delayed gammas from photofission can be extracted if the dead time is known.

articleTitle: NASA-gamma: a Python-based open source GUI for gamma ray spectroscopy
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: NASA-gamma is a Python-based open source analysis software toolkit designed for gamma ray spectroscopy. Some of its features include advanced peak fitting and error estimation, energy calibration, efficiency calibration, peak finding, peak identification with specialized databases, and advanced visualization. NASA-gamma was originally developed to support neutroninduced gamma ray analysis in the context of planetary science. However, it can be used in many applications that make use of gamma ray spectroscopy. We present here its overall functionality and advanced features so that researchers and students around the globe can make use of it. Its Graphical Unit Interface (GUI) allows the community to make use of its many features without any programming knowledge.

articleTitle: Pulse Shape Discrimination in Nanoparticle ZnS:Ag Scintillators
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Neutron detectors with pulse shape discrimination (PSD) are needed in a wide variety of industries including nuclear security, nuclear energy, and neutron scattering for material science research. ZnS:Ag has been the scintillator of choice for neutron detectors at several scattering facilities for many years, due to its numerous desirable properties - including high light output, good PSD capability, stability and affordability. These characteristics enable detectors with large areas or specific geometries to be produced. The main disadvantage of the scintillator is its inherently long afterglow that, coupled with the large dynamic range of light output, fundamentally limits the count rate capability. Recently, nanoparticles of ZnS:Ag have demonstrated minimal afterglow and scintillation decay ~20 times faster than standard micro powder ZnS:Ag, making them an interesting candidate for future high rate capability neutron detectors.In this work nanoparticles of ZnS:Ag have been developed into a neutron detector prototype for the first time through the incorporation of <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">6</sup>LiF powder. The viability of nanoparticle ZnS:Ag scintillators for use in a realistic neutron detector is investigated here, with a focus on the capability for PSD. We have identified pulse shape differences between neutron and gamma signals and exploited these differences with simple signal processing to achieve very good gamma sensitivities, <10<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">-5</sup>. This PSD technique can be implemented at high incident neutron rates and therefore is suitable for use in high rate capability nanoparticle ZnS:Ag detectors. The current performance of these detectors on a beamline at ISIS will be presented, including challenges which result from the comparatively low light output. While there are currently limitations, the present work shows promise for the development of nanoparticle ZnS:Ag into future high rate capability neutron detectors with gamma rejection suitable for use in high gamma background environments.

articleTitle: Ventilation Segmentation Accuracy Enhancement using Kirsch Operator in Pulmonary MRI
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Hyperpolarized (HP) noble gas magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and inert fluorinated gas MRI are the main pulmonary functional imaging modalities capable of regional ventilation assessment. To quantify pulmonary ventilation, K-means-based segmentation of ventilation images is usually performed. K-means clustering, however, performs poorly on images with relatively low SNR and cannot effectively distinguish background noise from low-ventilated areas. Here, we demonstrate a novel ventilation segmentation approach based on the subsequent implementation of lung edge detection using the Kirsch Compass operator followed by K-means segmentation. Our segmentation algorithm resulted in significantly higher accuracy of ventilation defect volume (VDV) assessment compared to a conventional ventilation segmentation algorithm. There were no significant changes in ventilation volume (VV) between our segmentation approach and conventional K-means segmentation. These indicate that implementation of digital lung edge detection prior to K-means segmentation substantially decreases segmentation sensitivity to background noise and allows a much more accurate assessment of low-ventilated regions of the lungs.

articleTitle: The CsI calorimeter for AMEGO-X
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Astronomical observations with gamma rays in the range of several hundred keV to hundreds of MeV represent an under-explored region of the electromagnetic spectrum. To help increase the sensitivity for measurements in this so-called "MeV gap", a mission concept known as the All-sky Medium-Energy Gamma-ray Observatory eXplorer (AMEGO-X) is in development, led by NASA Goddard Space Flight Center (GSFC). One of the main instrument subsystems for AMEGO-X is a calorimeter based on hodoscopically arranged CsI:Tl bars readout on each end by dual-gain SiPMs, led by the U.S. Naval Research Laboratory (NRL). NRL designed and built a prototype CsI:Tl calorimeter instrument using a commercial-off-the-shelf (COTS) silicon photomultipliers (SiPMs) and front-end to assess the performance and dynamic energy range. Per log, we observed significant non-linearities in the energy response and limited dynamic range using COTS SiPMs, well below the four orders of magnitude in energy required for the instrument. To mitigate this issue, we developed dual-gain SiPM boards with two SiPM geometries, read out separately, to increase the dynamic energy range of the readout and improve non-linearity across that range. SiPMs that utilize 40 μm microcell pitch for both SiPM geometries demonstrate the desired response when tested with high-energy beams. The approximate energy range of the calorimeter is 0.25 − 400 MeV with overlap in the different SiPM groups of around 2.5−30 MeV. NRL is currently working with FBK to develop custom SiPM readout and constructing a prototype calorimeter for the AMEGO-X instrument.

articleTitle: Dose estimation from in-beam PET imaging of 11C and 15O beams
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Monitoring the stopping position of primary ions in a tumor is desirable for effective tumor treatment by ensuring tumor coverage and preventing overdose exposure to normal tissues in ion therapy. The use of positron-emitting ion beams, such as <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">11</sup>C and <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">15</sup>O, has been suggested for range verification in ion therapy exploiting in-beam positron emission tomography (PET) imaging, where the ion stopping position is visualized with a high signal-to-noise ratio. We have previously demonstrated the feasibility of in-beam PET imaging for range verification of <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">11</sup>C and <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">15</sup>O ion beams. In this study, we investigate a method for prediction of dose profiles from PET images for both <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">11</sup>C and <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">15</sup>O ion beams for the first time. The depth dose was measured in water for both ion beams with momentum acceptance (MA) of 0.5% and 5%. The PET images were obtained for an irradiated polymethyl methacrylate (PMMA) phantom with both beams under the same MA conditions. The beams with smaller MA were considered as mono-energetic beams and were used to obtain the best energy weights for reproducing the measured PET activity of the beams with MA of 5%. Then the obtained optimum energy weights were used for prediction of dose profiles for the beams with MA of 5%. The predicted dose profiles were in overall good agreement with the measured ones and the distal fall-off positions at 80% of the Bragg peaks were also predicted within 0.2 mm for both <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">11</sup>C and <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">15</sup>O ion beams.

articleTitle: Non-iterative Compensation for Patient Motion in Dental CBCT Imaging
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Cone Beam Computed Tomography is widely used in dentistry for diagnosis and treatment planning. However, it is susceptible to artifacts caused by patient movement during scanning. Manufacturers of cone beam CT systems have added mechanical fixations to prevent patient movement, but these are not completely rigid and still allow some movement.
