Researchers have tried to solve this problem with motion compensation algorithms. However, these solutions are often time consuming and only partially address the problem. This paper proposes a novel motion compensation approach based on a motion detection strategy to extract a motion-free subset of the scanned projections. A short-scan reconstruction is performed from the motion-free subset, which is used as a reference for the compensation algorithm, eliminating the need for multiple full-scan reconstructions at this stage. Motion compensation is performed by optimizing the motion parameters with a regularized 3D-2D image registration. The results show that the proposed algorithm can be used effectively to compensate for large and long-duration motions.

articleTitle: Feasibility Assessment of a 3D Radiomicroscope for Charged Particles by Monte Carlo Simulation
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: In this paper, we propose the new concept of 3D lensless radiomicrosope for charged particle by simulation. Applying the principle of lensless imaging and thin phosphor films as scintillator with directional guide, this imaging technique enables information of position and energy in optical pixel array. 2D autoradiograph images including this information were acquired at specific angles. Two beta emission sources are placed in different part of tissue, and these two sources are distinguished by intensity of pixels. In addition, the intensity difference between two sources discriminates as the placement of optical interface differs. Effects of directional information given by two phosphor films has also been verified by measuring of gaussian fitting curve of events on phosphor film compositions. In perspective of optical sensor application in real, fluorine-18 source activity was calculated by short video and estimated the exponential decay curve. The curve showed similar tendency with reference F-18 source. The results reveal that 3D lensless radiomicroscope method can work as another method to capture the beta emission information by utilizing simple optical source. The simulation result demonstrates that this method is practically feasible.

articleTitle: Preliminary Design of Readout Electronics for DCLS Gas Monitor Detectors
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: This paper presents the preliminary design and test of readout electronics for DCLS (Dalian Coherent Light Source) GMDs (Gas Monitor Detectors). DCLS is an FEL (Free-Electron Laser) at EUV (Extreme Ultraviolet) and operates at a maximum repetition frequency of 50 Hz. There are two beamlines and each one has been installed with two GMDs. GMDs are deployed to monitor the intensity of the EUV pulse by pulse from 0.1 μJ to 1 mJ online. The readout electronics consist of a self-designed preamplifier, an adapter board with a high-voltage filter, and a digitizer (1-GSPS oscilloscope). The preamplifier is near the detector plate and has two-stage amplifiers: a TIA (Trans-Impedance Amplifier) and a ratio phase amplifier. First-stage outputs for 10 μJ to 1 mJ FEL detection and second-stage for 0.1 μJ to 10 μJ, which makes digitizers work on high resolution. Preliminary results show that this readout electronics works properly. This paper can provide design references on other gas detectors’signal readouts.

articleTitle: Spatiotemporal PET reconstruction with attenuation and motion correction
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: The diagnostic power of Positron Emission Tomography for early stage lung cancer is challenging since the lesion dimensions are comparable with the spatial resolution of modern clinical scanners and their contrast is decreased by respiratory motion. Moreover, strong artifacts in reconstructed images are introduced by attenuation, resulting in depression of activity in the middle of the image. In this paper we propose a modified version of Maximum Likelihood Activity and Attenuation (MLAA) algorithm, the Morphed-MLAA (M-MLAA), which, given gated data, jointly corrects for patient motion during the acquisition by composing the forward and backward operators with the registration fields between the different gates. The registration fields are evaluated with the deep-learning model Synthmorph. The main advantage of the proposed algorithm is that it makes use of the entire projection data set, thus improving the lesion signal-to-noise ratio, compared to the case in which images are reconstructed from a subset of the data. Our proposed algorithm has been tested on the XCAT phantom with some added lung lesions and shows improved performance for the detection and reconstruction of some of them; this improved performance is corroborated by the evaluation of two figures of merit (PSNR and RC). Our results show the potential of M-MLAA algorithm, but, at the same time, also that there is still space for improvements, since some lesions are better detected by the other more classical approaches, as MLAA single or total gates reconstructions.

articleTitle: In-orbit operation and spectrum analysis of the GRID-02 CubeSat detector
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: The Gamma-Ray Integrated Detectors (GRID) mission is a space science project that uses multiple CubeSats carrying scintillation detector payloads based on silicon photomultipliers (SiPMs) to detect gamma-ray bursts (GRBs) associated with high-energy astrophysical transients. In this paper, we present the in-orbit observation strategy and spectrum analysis of GRID-02, the second detector of GRID mission, and verify the working status of the detector. We set bias voltages of SiPMs to a constant value and record necessary housekeeping data during the detector's operation in order to correct the signal amplitudes to a standard condition. We use both the on-ground calibration results and in-orbit data to reconstruct detected energies from original data. We analyze the spectrum of GRB 210121A observed by GRID-02 with the response matrix generated from Monte Carlo simulation, and the fitting result is consistent with the joint analysis result of other instruments including Fermi/GBM, HXMT and GECAM. This result proves that GRID-02 detector performs well and that GRID can produce valuable data for high-energy astrophysical transients' research.

articleTitle: Evaluation of 10 × 10 mm2 Linearly Graded SiPMs for High-resolution Small-animal PET
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Position-sensitive SiPMs (PS-SiPMs) are promising photodetectors for high-resolution small animal positron emission tomography (PET) scanners. With the ultimate goal of developing a 0.5 mm resolution small-animal PET scanner, we developed 10 x 10 mm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sup> linearly graded SiPMs (LG-SiPMs), a type of PS-SiPMs. In this paper, the performance of depth-of-interaction encoding dual-ended readout detectors based on these LG-SiPMs and LYSO arrays with a pitch of 0.5 mm and a thickness of 20 mm were evaluated. The flood histogram shows the crystal elements were clearly resolved. The average energy resolution and timing resolution across the LYSO array are 22.3 ± 9.4% and 0.99 ± 0.02 ns, respectively.

articleTitle: Melting and crystallization peculiarities of CsPbBr2I perovskite
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: CsPbBr<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf>I halide perovskite showed great potential in applications for sensing, generation and emission of single photons, solar cells, and light-emitting diodes (LEDs). However, currently, there is no information about the regularities of melting and crystallization, as well as the influence of the growth rate of crystals on their quality. The thermal properties of this halide perovskite were studied by differential thermal analysis method. Samples of CsPbBr<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf>I were obtained by melting equimolar amounts of CsI and PbBr<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf>. It was established that the complete melting of the CsPbBr<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf>I alloy and its transition into the equilibrium liquid state occurs when the sample is heated to temperatures not lower than 768 K. When the CsPbBr<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf>I alloy is kept in the temperature range of 748-768 K, its melt crystallizes without supercooling, and at temperatures higher than 768 K - with supercooling in comparing to the temperature at which the alloy starts melting. Both in the case of melt crystallization of CsPbBr<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf>I with supercooling, and in the case of melt crystallization without supercooling, there is a tendency to decrease the rate of melt crystallization with an increase in its crystallization temperature.

articleTitle: Investigation of photocurrent relaxation in MAPbBr3 perovskites with Cr/SnO2/, Cr/ contacts
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Investigation of photocurrent relaxations in MAPbBr<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</inf> reveals an unusual increase of current after the bias polarity switch. Observed transient effect show bias dependence similar to that of hole waveforms measured by the laser-induced transient current technique. The combination of these results points to a barrier-induced accumulation of holes beneath the cathode. Accumulated holes relax with a characteristic time 1ms, regardless of contact material.

articleTitle: Development of HRPPDs for RICH Detectors at the EIC
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: High Resolution Picosecond Photon Detectors (HRPPDs) are large area Microchannel Plate (MCP) detectors that can provide ultrafast timing and detect single photons with high efficiency and good spatial resolution. This makes them an excellent choice for use in Ring Imaging Cherenkov (RICH) detectors that can be used for particle identification in high energy particle collisions. These devices are being considered for several RICH detectors for the ePIC Experiment at the future Electron Ion Collider (EIC) at Brookhaven National Lab. An effort is currently under way to improve the properties of HRPPDs for RICH applications and to optimize their performance for use at the EIC. This contribution will report on the latest developments with HRPPDs for their use with various types of RICH detectors, and also discuss some of the RICH detector designs for the future ePIC experiment at the EIC.

articleTitle: Effect of inter-crystal scattering events on the performance of dual-ended readout PET detectors
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: In PET imaging, there are significant amount of inter-crystal scattering (ICS) events that degrade the contrast and spatial resolution of PET images. In this work, the effect of ICS events on the performance of detectors consisting of LYSO crystal arrays dual-ended read out by SiPM arrays was evaluated. The first two detectors are 8×8 LYSO arrays with crystal sizes of 3.12×3.12×20 mm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</sup> using ESR and BaSO<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">4</inf> reflectors, respectively. The third detector is a 13×13 LYSO array with crystal size of 1.88×1.88×20 mm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</sup> and BaSO<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">4</inf> reflector. 8×8 SiPM arrays with a 3×3 mm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sup> pixel area was used. Two novel methods were proposed to classify the ICS and single interaction events. The probabilities of ICS events were 31.7%, 30.7% and 44.9% for the three detectors. The intrinsic spatial resolutions of single interaction events were ~ 10% better than these of all events. The timing resolutions of the ICS events were ~30% worse than these of the single interaction events since the energies of ICS events are deposited in two or more crystals and the signal-to-noise ratio of the SiPM with the maximum signal amplitude is small. In the future, the effect of ICS events on energy and depth of interaction resolutions will be measured. The two ICS events classification methods will be compared.

articleTitle: Head motion estimation using simulated dynamic PET frames
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Patient motion is a common issue in dynamic positron emission tomography (PET) imaging of the head, due to the long acquisition times (up to several hours). Estimating this motion without causing additional discomfort to the patient or changing the scan protocol requires the use of data-driven methods. Registration-based approaches are commonly used, but are not always reliable in dynamic scans due to the changing tracer distributions. The success of registration-based motion estimation for dynamic scans can be improved by incorporating information from tracer kinetics and changes in tracer distribution. Therefore, we have developed a framework that can perform multiple frame alignment (MFA) with simulated time-accurate PET frames as a reference, and evaluated its performance compared to regular MFA on 6 <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">18</sup>F-SynVesT-1 brain scans. Both methods produced a similar motion estimate from 30s after injection to the end of the scan.

articleTitle: Characterization of a Novel Gamma-Ray Detection System for Tomographic, In-Situ Proton Therapy Quality Assurance
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: In the field of hadron therapy, quality assurance is vital to ensure the accurate delivery of radiation to the target while minimizing the dose to healthy tissue. In this work, we present the characterization of a novel gamma-ray detection system developed by Terapet SA for in-situ quality assurance in proton therapy. The detector is intended for use with either phantoms or anatomical targets, and operates by reconstruction of the PET activity induced in the target by proton irradiation. The detector is composed of scintillator-based detection modules, each with an area of 60 mm by 60 mm, a spatial resolution for 511 keV gamma ray interactions of approximately 1 mm and depth of interaction resolution of 1.2 mm. The field of view is extended by rotation and displacement of the detector about the target. The proposed use cases for the device are to detect changes in beam delivery or target positioning, and to assess the accuracy of target modelling by the treatment planning system. The results presented assess the performance of the device and its ability to fulfill the stated quality assurance use cases.

articleTitle: Development of a Radioxenon Beta Cell based on Organic Glass Scintillator
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Radioxenon detection is one of the four technologies used in the International Monitoring System to monitor for nuclear explosions around the globe. Currently deployed radioxenon detection systems detect the correlated beta and gamma-ray emissions from radioxenon isotopes using a hollow cell of plastic scintillator (so-called "beta cell") inside a well of sodium-iodide scintillator. Newly developed organic glass scintillators possess several properties that make them attractive for beta cells in radioxenon detectors, most notably good energy resolution, which would improve the sensitivity of systems deployed in the field. In this work we are developing an organic glass beta cell using a custom-built mold; we have developed CAD models for both the square- and rounded-cylinder designs, which will be cast and characterized to determine the energy resolution compared to the plastic scintillator that is currently used in the field. In the full paper, we will present the final beta cell prototype and results for its performance characterization, including light output and energy resolution.

articleTitle: Design and Implementation of a Peak Picking System for MVT Digitizer
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Multi-Voltage Threshold (MVT) digitizer is a well-known integrated digital signal processing method for new radiation detection technology in Positron Emission Tomography (PET) imaging. However, MVT may face challenges in selecting appropriate threshold voltages for scintillation pulses with a wide range of energy spans, which can limit the PET signal reconstruction performance in terms of energy and time. To address this issue, we propose incorporating peak information into the MVT method. Traditional methods of obtaining peaks using discrete components result in unacceptable high costs and power consumption, particularly in practical PET multi-channel applications. In this paper, we propose a novel 36-channel peak acquisition system chip for MVT digitizers using multi-channel multiplexing technology. We also preliminarily evaluate the multiplexed Analog to Digital Converter (ADC) performance of our design. This provides a basis for the implementation of Peak Picking-MVT in clinical PET detectors. This is expected to have a positive impact on other scintillator-based applications.

articleTitle: Normalization and scatter corrections for the J-PET scanner
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: The Jagiellonian PET scanner is a cost-effective large axial FOV Positron Emission Tomography technology that enables multi-photon imaging and is currently under development at the Jagiellonian University. The current 50 cm prototype, named "Modular J-PET", is being investigated for various applications. It is well known that PET data can be affected by several effects during acquisition, such as scattered gamma photons or variations in detection efficiency. Consequently, achieving the reconstruction of images of satisfactory quality requires a set of corrections to be applied to each line-of-response. This summary discusses the implementation and performance of scatter and normalization corrections for the Modular J-PET, and their extension prior to the assembly of a total-body Jagiellonian PET scanner. Normalization correction is achieved using component-based normalization, a method particularly suitable for large scanners with a high number of lines-of-response. Scatter correction is achieved using an extension of the single scatter simulation technique that incorporates time-of-flight information. Reconstruction of reference phantoms based on Monte Carlo simulations highlight improvements in image quality. The application of normalization reduces the non-uniformity in the reconstructed image by a factor of 10 in the axial direction and 2 in the radial direction.

articleTitle: High resolution brain PET image reconstruction with deep progressive learning
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Positron emission tomography (PET) can be used for the diagnosis and therapeutic monitoring of brain tumors and neurodegenerative diseases. However, brain PET images typically require high resolution and high image quality to obtain sufficient diagnostic value due to the complex and delicate anatomical structure of the brain. It further limits the use of low-dose and fast acquisition schemes on conventional PET systems. In this work, we proposed a deep progressive learning based super-resolution reconstruction (DPR) method for brain PET imaging. Specifically, a denoising network and an enhanced super-resolution network were designed and used in the reconstruction. The algorithm was evaluated using an XCAT digital brain phantom based on GATE simulation, and compared to OSEM with different pixel sizes. The evaluation results indicate that DPR achieves the best performance in metrics as SSMI, PSNR, Contrast, and background COV, especially under low count conditions. In conclusion, the proposed DPR algorithm makes it possible to obtain high-resolution and high-quality brain PET images under low-dose and/or fast scanning conditions.

articleTitle: Acceleration of Monte Carlo Simulation based Scatter Correction for PET Imaging with Rigid Motion
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Unsatisfactory image quality in PET scans is frequently caused by motion. Multiple-frame reconstrucitons and registrations are required for an accurate motion correction. Consequently, frame based scatter correction (SC) are needed. Moreover, the continuous moving source method is commonly used for physical corrections in long-axis systems. However, SC of finely divided frames would be significantly time-consuming. To address this issue, this article proposes an accelerated Monte Carlo simulation (MCS) based SC algorithm for rigid-motion utilizing flexibility and reusability of simulated photons in MCS. The proposed method was validated by 1) simulation of NEMA IEC body phatom with multi-frame motion and 2) experimental measurement of a moving Germanium cylinder phantom in the uMI Panorama GS system. The results show that the accelerated SC has a NRMSE < 1% compared to the original version, and that it accerlates a 3-frame SC with motion by 58.82%.

articleTitle: A Dynamic Prior Constrained Limited-angle 4DCT Reconstruction Method
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: This paper proposes a new scanning model and a novel 4DCT reconstruction algorithm for the challenging task of obtaining high-temporal-resolution 3D images of the rapidly beating heart. The proposed scanning model allows for limited-angle projections in each cardiac phase by scanning only one single beat, while the 4DCT reconstruction algorithm alternates between iterative reconstruction, deformable image registration, and prior constraints. This approach combines the advantages of iterative reconstruction, motion-compensated reconstruction, and regularization constraint reconstruction, yielding superior reconstruction quality with minimal radiation dose and high temporal resolution.

articleTitle: Automatic determination algorithm of intrinsic parameters on response function of energy-resolving photon counting imaging detector
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: In medical X-ray diagnosis, the Energy-Resolving Photon Counting Detector (ERPCD) technology has focused on deriving quantitative information of objects. For the quantitative analysis using polychromatic X-rays, the effects of beam hardening and the detector response should be corrected. To estimate the response function accurately, it is necessary to determine the optimal combination of the two parameters related to energy resolution (peak broadening) and charge-sharing effect (peak efficiency), which are the intrinsic characteristics of each detector module. However, to manually tune the parameters of modules takes a lot of time and therefore it is impractical. This study aims to develop an automatic determination algorithm for intrinsic parameters. We focus on the fact that the measured X-ray attenuation rates (µt values) of objects reflect the parameters of the detector module. In our algorithm, the proper parameters can be determined so as to reproduce the experimental µt values among the simulated µt values considered various parameters. Experimental values were measured using an aluminum step phantom with 1–30 mm thicknesses and our ERPCD system, which consists of CZT multi-pixel detector with a pixel size of 200 µm × 200 µm and three energy bins. For each parameter, we evaluated the differences between the experimental and theoretical µt values for three energy bins: 20–32–40–56 keV for 60 kV radiographic system. The algorithm was verified by deriving the effective atomic number (Z<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">eff</inf>) image of the aluminum step phantom and evaluating the accuracy. As a result, the accuracy of Z<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">eff</inf> values was approximately ±1.0, suggesting that our algorithm can be used to tune an imaging detector for quantitative analysis in radiography. The developed algorithm is expected to make it possible to quickly and automatically determine the response function parameters unique to each module.

articleTitle: VPG4, Versatile Parallelizable Geant4 Interface: A Novel Platform for Modeling Complex Nuclear Medicine Imaging Scanners
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: In this work, we present a new Geant4-based simulation modeling platform for complex nuclear medicine imaging scanners that uses computer-aided design (CAD) tools and parallelization on both CPU and GPU to accelerate the Monte Carlo simulation and reduce computational cost. The application combines the newly developed open-source GDML package and the new version of open-source Opticks code to create simulation models for complex structures. We demonstrate that the application is suitable for imaging scanners with complex structures, and we show that the computational cost is significantly decreased. Our results show the computational efficiency enhanced over two orders of magnitudes using both GPU and CPU. Our application has the potential to make the simulation of complex imaging systems more accessible and efficient for new users of nuclear Monte Carlo codes. Also, we plan to extend this work to include other modalities and to examine the performance of more complex structures.

articleTitle: Design and Assembly of High Resolution Fast-Neutron Radiography Panel
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Although large industrial x-ray flat panel imagers are readily available off-the-shelf, a flat panel imager for fast neutron radiography does not exist. A high-resolution fast-neutron flat panel radiography system was designed and fabricated to produce images utilizing a 6x6 array of ROSSPAD modules. Each module utilizes an IDEAS ROSSPAD with an 8×8 array of SensL MICROFJ-60035-TSV SiPMs coupled to a 3 mm thick acrylic light spreader and 3 mm thick sheet of EJ-200. The resulting imager can produce high-resolution, high-energy neutron radiographs in a portable flat panel form factor.

articleTitle: An analytical model for comparing the effective sensitivity of different PET systems
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: There is a large variability in the features of existing (and future) positron emission tomography (PET) systems. This complicates comparison of the performance of different systems for different tasks. We propose a mathematical model that estimates the relative performance of a PET system for imaging a uniform cylinder of a particular diameter, attenuation and length, and producing a reconstructed image with a particular spatial resolution. The PET system is assumed to be (approximately) cylindrical. The model computes an "effective sensitivity", taking into account the solid angle covered by the detectors, the detector stopping power, the time-of-flight resolution, the scatter fraction and the spatial resolution of the system, the attenuation and diameter of the cylinder and the desired spatial resolution of the reconstructed image. This effective sensitivity can be calibrated based on the NEMA line source sensitivity. The PET systems are compared at matched scantime. Systems with the same effective sensitivity are predicted to produce reconstructed images with the same pixel variance. As performance metric for scanning long objects, the minimum sensitivity achieved over the object is computed, with an optimal number of bed positions and optimal overlap between them. The influence of the spatial and TOF resolution on the effective sensitivity is verified with simulations.

articleTitle: ALICE ITS3 Detector Overview and Performance of the Prototype Monolithic Stitched Sensor MOSS
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: The innermost three layers of the inner tracker currently installed in ALICE will be replaced by the new Inner Tracking System (ITS3) during the Long Shutdown 3 (LS3) of the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) starting 2026. The ITS3 is based on three layers of wafer-scale, cylindrically bent Monolithic Active Pixel Sensors (MAPS) with a thickness below 50 μm. Stitching is used to manufacture sensors of up to 26 x 9.4 cm size in 65 nm CMOS technology. The ITS3 will be constructed as two halves with three sensors each, at radii of 18, 24, 30 mm from the beam axis, respectively. The air-cooled sensors are held in place with carbon foam. This allows for an extremely low material budget with an unprecedented 0.05% X<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">0</inf> per layer, increasing the pointing resolution by a factor of two, and the tracking efficiency at momenta below 0.3 GeV/c. To demonstrate the feasibility of the stitching process, a prototype MOnolithic Stitched Sensor (MOSS) chip has been designed. A single MOSS chip has dimensions of 14 x 259 mm and 6.72 million pixels.To characterize the MOSS chip, a dedicated test system has been developed. Studied performance parameters include manufacturing yield, power distribution, data rates, noise, and power consumption. After an ITS3 overview, the MOSS chip and test system will be introduced, and results of the MOSS measurement campaign will be presented in this contribution.

articleTitle: Evaluation of easyPET for Quality Assessment in Proton Therapy: a promising approach
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Proton therapy is a highly conformal radiation therapy technique that delivers a precise radiation dose to tumors, leading to better treatment outcomes and higher survival rates. However, the depth-dose profile (Bragg-Peak) is a major concern for clinical usage, as even slight spatial uncertainties can result in high unwanted doses to healthy tissues. To address this issue, imaging techniques based on detecting secondary particles generated by beam-tissue interactions have been proposed. PET imaging is being widely studied for real-time assessment of beam interaction in the body during proton therapy procedures and for quality assurance. In this study, the suitability of the easyPET.3D for proton therapy quality assessment is evaluated through Monte Carlo simulations. The focus of the work lay in predicting accurately the distribution of positron emitters produced in a phantom after proton beam irradiation, and in determining the quality of the PET signal near the Bragg peak, crucial to the success of using the easyPET system for proton beam’s quality control.

articleTitle: GPU-accelerated Monte Carlo Simulation for PET imaging (Part II): Patient Motion and Dynamic Imaging Simulation
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Monte Carlo Simulation (MCS) is a fundamental tool for PET research and applications, which aims to generate near-realistic PET data based on a known ground truth. Most existing MCS methods, such as GATE, are accurate in terms of physical processes, however, suffers from two drawbacks: 1) excessive computational resource and time demands 2) lack of simulation for biological processes.In this work, we propose a GPU-accelerated MCS framework for PET imaging that supports not only static phantom simulations, but also simulations tracer dynamics and patient motion. The detailed algorithm design and implementation are presented. Three individual simulation studies were performed and reconstructed with 1) rigid head motion, 2) non-rigid respiratory motion and 3) dynamics and a rigid body motion. The modelling and implementation of physical processes are presented through a separate submission.

articleTitle: In-Beam PET Monitoring of Carbon Ion Radiotherapy Using a Dual-Panel PET System: A Case Study of Liver Cancer Treatment
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: This study aims to explore the application of In-beam PET technology based on GATE in carbon ion radiotherapy for liver cancer treatment. The treatment plan for primary liver cancer patients involved a single-field irradiation with the PTV receiving a single dose of 4 Gy. The Carbon ion therapy was administered using a fixed vertical therapy head at 0° gantry angle while the patient lay flat on the treatment table. A spread-out process delivery technique was utilized <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">12</sup>C beam with 28 energy layers ranging from 141.4 to 284.81 MeV/u. A dual-panel PET with an imaging area of 40×40 cm² and a 2.5 mm crystal pitch was used to monitor the carbon ion beam in real-time during the patient's treatment. This in-beam PET allows for timely adjustments of the treatment dose to improve treatment effectiveness and reduce unnecessary radiation damage to the patient. The results showed that the In-beam PET technology can provide effective assurance for the precision and safety of carbon ion radiotherapy. This study provides a new approach for the application of carbon ion radiotherapy in liver cancer treatment.

articleTitle: Preliminary Performance Evaluation of a Hand-Held Magic-Cube Spectral Intraoperative Gamma Camera
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Portable gamma cameras are valuable tools for intraoperative imaging guidance. However, existing intraoperative cameras primarily rely on mechanical collimation, resulting in limited clinical impact and sensitivity, particularly during real-time or short-time-framed imaging. Additionally, imaging high-energy radionuclides is often necessary for certain applications, but the stronger collimator penetration results in degraded imaging performance.In this work, we develop a novel gamma camera prototype that consists of a magic-cube detector composed of scintillator, optical glass, and metal elements. The geometrical configuration and composition of the detector enable the application of a hybrid collimation concept, that is, mixing collimations formed by the inter-layer scintillator, optical glass, and metal, to achieve high sensitivity and resolution simultaneously, overcoming the intrinsic limitation of mechanical collimation. The prototype magic-cube assembly has a size of 67.2 mm × 67.2 mm × 20.0 mm, weighs 0.7 kg, and records detected gamma events with spatial and energy information.We conducted imaging experiments on the prototype using <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">99m</sup>Tc and <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">18</sup>F point sources. The energy resolution of the camera as a single detector is 13.5% and 24.5% for 511 keV and 140 keV gamma rays, respectively. The average sensitivity is 1700 cps/MBq and 703 cps/MBq for <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">99m</sup>Tc and <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">18</sup>F point sources, respectively, at a distance of 15 cm from the camera. The spatial resolutions (FWHM) are less than 9.4 mm and 14.8 mm, respectively, when measured with a 20 μCi <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">99m</sup>Tc and 1 mCi <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">18</sup>F source at 15 cm from the detector for 1 s. The camera clearly resolves a 3 × 3 <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">99m</sup>Tc point source array (each point source 4.3 mCi, 10 s) with a 2-cm point-to-point separation and a 2 × 2 <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">18</sup>F point source array (each point source 1.5 mCi, 10 s) with a 4-cm separation. The prototype’s high sensitivity and hybrid collimation concept offer significant potential for practical intraoperative applications.

articleTitle: Evaluation of Image Degradation Factors and Correction Methods in DAT SPECT Using a Digital Population of Phantoms
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Dopamine transporter (DAT) SPECT is a competent diagnostic tool for Parkinson’s disease (PD). However, image degradation factors like attenuation, scatter and penetration affect its image quality and quantitative accuracy. We aim to evaluate these factors and their correction methods for 2 common DAT SPECT tracers, i.e., <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">99m</sup>Tc-TRODAT (<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">99m</sup>Tc) and <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">123</sup>I-ioflupane (<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">123</sup>I), using the SIMIND MC tool and a population of digital brain phantoms. We generated 40 phantoms based on clinical brain MRI data to model anatomical variations of striatum, brain background and head size. Striatal binding ratios (SBR) were varied according to different PD stages for 2 tracers (up to 6 for <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">99m</sup>Tc and up to 12 for <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">123</sup>I). We generated 120 noisy projections with 1.5 M counts for <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">123</sup>I and 3 M counts for <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">99m</sup>Tc based on a dual-head clinical SPECT scanner with low-energy high-resolution parallel-hole collimators. Projection count for all interactions (T), attenuation (A), scatter (S), penetration (P), and ideal situation with no scatter and attenuation modeled (AIR) were compared for both tracers. Projections were reconstructed with OS-EM algorithm (4 subsets and 8 iterations) with (i) CT-based attenuation correction (AC) and Dual Energy Window (DEW) scatter correction (AC+SC), (ii) with AC only, (iii) with SC only, and (iv) without AC and SC (NC). Mean square error (MSE), structural similarity index (SSIM), SBR and image profiles were evaluated. Projection count ratios of AIR:T:A:S:P were 231:100:77:17:5 for <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">99m</sup>Tc and 225:100:75:16:7 for <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">123</sup>I respectively. MSE, SSIM, SBR and profiles all showed that AC+SC substantially improved quantitative accuracy, followed by AC only, NC and SC only for both tracers. Attenuation impacted DAT SPECT the most, followed by scatter and penetration. CT-based AC and DEW are effective corrections for DAT SPECT.

articleTitle: Development of a transportable neutron spectro-imager using a pixelated plastic scintillator
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Fast neutron imaging spectrometry is an effective way for locating and identifying neutron sources in the nuclear industry field. To achieve this goal, a compact neutron imager was developed specifically for this purpose, using a pixelated plastic scintillator coupled with a SiPM (Silicon Photomultiplier) and a MURA (Modified Uniformly Redundant Array) coded mask. The imager's sensitivity was confirmed by obtaining a neutron image of a Cf-252 neutron source emitting 1.12 × 10<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">5</sup> neutrons.s<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">-1</sup>, placed 30 cm away from the detector for 4.5 hours. Additionally, a neutron image was taken for 40 minutes in front of a mono-energetic neutron beam (5 × 10<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">5</sup> neutrons.s<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">-1</sup> with energy of 2.4 MeV) at the Amande facility of the IRSN Cadarache. In addition, we have demonstrated the preliminary results of neutron spectrometry by showing the simulated proton recoil spectra obtained with the neutron spectro-imager prototype.

articleTitle: Self super resolution for hepatic vessel CT segmentation
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Accurate hepatic vessel segmentation from abdominal CT images is a major requirement for hepatic diagnosis and surgery. However, it is a very complex task due to the intricate nature of the vascular anatomy and the limitations of CT imaging. A growing number of work advocate for the critical importance of pre-processing in the success of deep supervised image segmentation techniques. For instance, abdominal CT images are often reconstructed into anisotropic voxelized volumes with a typical ratio of 2 to 5 between in-plane and through-plane voxel sampling, which hampers analysis and vessel detection in the low resolution plane. In this work, we study whether self super resolution (i.e. learning-based super resolution relying on the anisotropic volume only) could be used to improve liver vessel segmentation performance in abdominal CT images. This way, we avoid resorting to curated super resolution training sets that are difficult / impossible to collect in practice. We leverage a self super resolution approach previously proposed for brain MR images, SMORE, and demonstrate its interest for fine vessel reconstruction. In particular, we show that reporting segmentation results in terms of global overlap metrics such as Dice cannot faithfully account for segmentation performance improvements with this type of data. For this reason, we also consider the recently proposed clDice metric accounting for the connectedness of the segmentation output. Using a nn-UNet segmentation benchmark, we show that we significantly improve on average segmentation results using the proposed self super resolution stage, both qualitatively and quantitatively.

articleTitle: Prototype Testing of a Novel High Performance Spread Field Imaging Collimator for SPECT
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Spread field imaging-narrow angle (SFI-NA) collimation is a novel design that uses long and narrow holes arranged in a pattern placed away from detector to offer high-sensitivity, high-resolution imaging in single photon emission computed tomography (SPECT). In this article, a prototype SFI-NA collimator was built and mounted on a clinical dual-head SPECT system, and experiments were conducted using common phantoms to evaluate and compare its performance relative to parallel-hole low energy ultra-high resolution (LEUHR) collimators. The holes in the SFI collimator are almost twice the size (in linear dimension) and 20% shorter compared with holes in the LEUHR collimator, and the sensitivity of the SFI collimator was measured to be 3 times higher. Results from an experiment using a Jaszczak phantom showed that the SFI collimator yielded better resolution compared with the LEUHR collimator despite using much bigger and shorter holes, validating the SFI imaging theory. Results from imaging a body phantom with hot spheres demonstrated that better lesion detectability as defined by contrast-noise ratio was achieved in a 2-minute scan using the SFI collimator compared with that in an 8-minute scan using LEUHR collimators, suggesting that scan time reduction up to 75% may be possible. These results demonstrate that the SFI collimators are applicable to conventional SPECT systems but offer remarkable improvement on both resolution and sensitivity, and potential time reduction may be a game-changer in many applications such as pediatrics and oncology where long scan time is a great limitation. Further performance boost is possible with better system integration, manufacturing improvements and application-specific optimization.

articleTitle: Test Beam Results on 3D Pixel Sensors for the CMS Tracker Upgrade at the High-Luminosity LHC
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: The High Luminosity upgrade of the CERN Large Hadron Collider (HL-LHC) will require new high-radiation tolerant silicon pixel sensors for the innermost layer of the CMS experiment tracking detector. The innermost part of the tracker will be exposed to fluences up to 2.3E16 neq/cm2. A wide program aiming at 3D pixel sensors in the framework of the CMS tracker R&D activities has been carried out, and an overview of the results obtained in beam test experiments will be reported in this talk. The 3D pixel sensors were made in the FBK (Trento, Italy) and CNM (Barcelona, Spain) foundries. They are interconnected with the CROC which is the readout chip that will be mounted on the final detector. The modules have been tested on beam at CERN, before and after irradiation up to an equivalent fluence of about 1E16 neq/cm2. Analysis of collected data shows great performance, with hit detection efficiencies around 98% measured after irradiation. Studies on spatial resolution will also be presented. New irradiation campaigns are foreseen to go beyond the above fluence and the preliminary results will be shown.

articleTitle: Strategies to improve the detective quantum efficiency of silicon photon counting detectors
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Silicon (Si) is an attractive material for photon counting detectors (PCDs) in CT applications for its electrical properties and its widespread availability, but its x-ray attenuation properties are poor. We sought to characterize possible strategies for improving detection in Si PCDs as well as assess their ultimate limits using Monte Carlo simulations. A variety of Si PCDs were modeled in GEANT4 and irradiated by a 120 kV spectrum filtered by 30 cm of water. The figure of merit was the detective quantum efficiency at zero frequency, DQE(0), analyzed with a single energy threshold. This corresponds to a non-spectral detection task. While spectral performance is also an important figure of merit, it is outside the scope of this work. The baseline Si PCD included tungsten foils 0.02 mm thick between silicon wafers 0.48 mm thick, was 60 mm thick (deep), and used a lowest energy threshold of 8 keV (corresponding to a reported electronic noise of 1.6 keV, using five standard deviations to avoid dark counts). This achieved a DQE(0) of 0.60. From here, we tested several individual improvements: (1) increasing the PCD thickness to 600 mm, to fully compensate for the low stopping power of Si, improved the DQE(0) to 0.63; (2) using perfect anti-coincidence logic, eliminating any double counting effects, improved the DQE(0) to 0.65; (3) decreasing the lowest energy threshold to 1 keV, enabling better detection of Compton events, improved the DQE(0) to 74; (4) implementing all of the above simultaneously improved the DQE(0) to 0.87. The final losses in DQE occur primarily from Rayleigh scattering (~10%) and the dead space from the tungsten foil (4%). We conclude that decreasing the electronic noise of the Si PCD could be the best immediate path to improving DQE(0). Rayleigh scattering presents an ultimate limit to dose efficiency because photons that undergo Rayleigh scattering and are subsequently absorbed by the tungsten foil leave no evidence and cannot be counted.

articleTitle: Image Intensity Normalization Benefits Deep Learning Brain PET Motion Correction
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Machine learning algorithms are now widely used to perform various tasks in medical imaging research, and some studies have shown that such methods are sensitive to input data normalization. While this pre-processing step has been investigated on other imaging modalities, few studies are available on PET images intensity normalization as neural network inputs. In this work, we explore different normalization strategies on input data used to train a Deep Learning Head Motion Correction (DL-HMC) method that we previously proposed. Qualitative and quantitative analysis on testing subjects show that motion prediction benefits from normalization. Our results demonstrate that normalizing images with the intensity of the earliest frame significantly decreases motion prediction error on testing subjects compared to data that are not normalized or normalized using other strategies. Reconstructions and Standard Uptake Value analysis further confirm this observation. We validate the proposed method on data from two tracers.

articleTitle: Development of the 4th Whole Gamma Imaging Prototype for 89Zr Mouse Imaging Demonstration
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Whole gamma imaging (WGI) is a novel concept combining PET and Compton imaging. Inserting an additional detector ring inside a PET ring allows detection of single gamma rays by the Compton imaging method. Motivated by many promising nuclear medicine applications, we have the final goal of developing a clinical WGI system. So far, three prototype systems have been developed for a proof-of-concept of WGI in small animals. This work aimed at developing innovative detector technologies to push the PET resolution limit by WGI Compton imaging with <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">89</sup>Zr (909 keV γ-rays). Compton imaging, which is not influenced by the long positron range of <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">89</sup>Zr, may have a chance to outperform PET. However, better energy resolution and better spatial resolution are required for inner scatterer detectors. Therefore, we developed a detector based on the crosshair light sharing (CLS) configuration by using a modified GAGG scintillator (1.45×1.45×15 mm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</sup>), for which the Ga:Al ratio (band gap control) was optimized for acquiring better energy resolution and Mg was co-doped (control of energy transfer) for acquiring a shorter decay time. Then we developed the WGI 4<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">th</sup> prototype for a technological demonstration in <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">89</sup>Zr mouse imaging. The outer (absorber) detectors were composed of 3.1×3.1×20 mm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</sup> fast-LGSO crystals. To confirm the PET imaging performance of the outer ring, we measured the <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">22</sup>Na ultra-micro hot phantom. The outer rings successfully visualized the 1.7 mm rods, which was a reasonable result for the crystal pitch of 3.1 mm. Then, we evaluated the basic performance (2D position map and energy resolution) of the scatterer detector. We confirmed the expected DOI identification capability. The energy resolution was 8.3% at 662 keV, which was better than that of previous WGI prototype systems. System designing and initial detector performance evaluation have been completed, and the WGI 4<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">th</sup> prototype system is now ready to proceed with the Compton imaging demonstration.

articleTitle: Scintillation Properties of an Ag-doped ZnS Translucent Ceramic by the Spark Plasma Sintering Method
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Scintillation detectors for α-ray detections have been widely used in nuclear fuel facilities because there exist the α-rays emitters including <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">238</sup>Pu, <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">239</sup>Pu, and <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">240</sup>Pu isotopes. Since Ag-doped ZnS (Ag:ZnS) has a medium Z<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">eff</inf> (~27), high light yield, and high stability, Ag:ZnS-based scintillation detectors have been used for a long time decades. However, their poor energy resolution is unsuitable for separating the signals of different isotopes because Ag:ZnS polycrystalline powder is quite opaque. To improve the energy resolution, it is necessary to use the transparent scintillators. So far, the material form of the most scintillators selected the single crystals because of high optical quality. In contrast, Ag:ZnS is very difficult to synthesize the single crystal from the melt because ZnS undergoes a phase transition to the high temperature at 1020°C. To solve this problem, one of the effective approaches is the use of translucent ceramics in the material forms. In recent years, the translucent ceramics of non-doped ZnS for infrared optical material were synthesized by the chemical vapor deposition, hot-press sintering, and spark plasma sintering (SPS) methods. However, most of the researches were carried out on non-doped ZnS translucent ceramics for infrared lenses, there are no reports on the scintillation properties of Ag:ZnS translucent ceramics. In this study, we have developed an Ag:ZnS translucent ceramic by the SPS method, their optical and scintillation properties were investigated. In the optical properties, the transmittance of the Ag-doped ZnS was ~50% in the visible ranges. Under the <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">241</sup>Am α-ray source, a broad emission peak around 450 nm was confirmed in the translucent ceramic, and the origin would be the donor-acceptor pair recombination. In the pulse height spectrum, a full absorption peak was observed in the Ag-doped ZnS. The calculated light yield and energy resolution were 15,000 photons/ 5.5 MeV α-ray and 40%, respectively.

articleTitle: Impact of acquisition speed in spatial resolution and detection efficiency on a preclinical PET scanner
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: The present work aims to evaluate the impact of the acquisition speed in the spatial resolution and detection efficiency of the easyPET.3D scanner, a compact high-resolution Positron Emission Tomography (PET) scanner for mice imaging. All measurement data were performed and analyzed based on the National Electrical Manufacturers Association (NEMA) NU 4-2008 standard. Both resolution (1.03 mm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</sup> vs 0.87 mm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</sup>) and sensitivity (doubled) improved by decreasing the acquisition speed from 200 steps/s to 20 steps/s without increasing the acquisition time for in vivo experiments. The results were also validated through image quality parameters assessed using the NEMA NU-4 image quality phantom.

articleTitle: Respiratory motion estimation and compensation using fineley sampled patient projection data in pediatric Tc-99m labeled dimercaptosuccinic acid (DMSA) SPECT imaging
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: We recently implemented the center-of-mass (COM) methodology to sense the axial motion of the kidneys using finely sampled simulated Tc-99m labeled dimercaptosuccinic acid (DMSA) SPECT projections of the XCAT phantom.The objective of this study was to extend the COM estimation of the respiratory signal and consequent respiratory motion estimation and compensation to pediatric DMSA patients with finely sampled projection data acquired at Boston Children’s Hospital.Acquisitions were performed 3-4 hours after injecting between 0.5 mCi and 3.0 mCi Tc-99m DMSA depending on patient weight. Thus far we successfully acquired 15 patients (10 female) ranging in age from less than a year old to 20.Respiratory estimates for the 15 patients vary from 1.5 mm to 13.9 mm with an average of 5.4 mm ± 3.5 mm in the axial direction when all the data (both detectors rotating through 360-degrees) are considered. Measurable respiration was observed in the anterior-posterior direction varying from 1.3 mm to 4.3 mm with an average of 2.6 mm ± 1.0 mm, while side-to-side respiratory estimates vary from 0.3 mm to 2.6 mm with an average of 1.3 mm ± 0.6 mm.Similar trends as that observed during cardiac perfusion SPECT respiratory motion estimation from projection data are emerging in this work, except for the influence of high background activity. Therefore, total counts in the kidneys, respiratory amplitude, and respiratory frequency all contribute, with the limited counts an anticipated severe challenge when reducing dose are considered

articleTitle: Generation of multi-tracer PET attenuation maps using zero-shot learning
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Attenuation correction is crucial for achieving high accuracy in PET images. Unfortunately, attenuation correction cannot be performed on PET images when transmission or CT data is unavailable. In such cases, an attenuation map is obtained by utilizing additional anatomical or morphological images. In previous studies, specific models for each tracer in PET images were trained to generate attenuation maps. However, this approach is associated with two major limitations. First, computational resources are greatly increased as each tracer requires a separate network for training. Second, PET images with less commonly used tracers usually have a shortage of data, making it challenging to train a network. To address these limitations, we propose a zero-shot learning method for generating CT-derived attenuation maps (µ-CT) from MLAA-derived attenuation maps (µ-MLAA) using only <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">18</sup>F-FDG images. Unlike tracer-specific methods which require a separate network for each tracer, this method utilizes a single generator network that encodes the structural features of the input image and the style of the reference µCT to generate the attenuation map. We evaluated our method using clinical brain PET/CT scan datasets of three different tracers, which are <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">18</sup>F-FDG, <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">18</sup>F-Florbetaben, and <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">18</sup>F-FP-CIT. The proposed method which was exclusively trained on <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">18</sup>F-FDG performs better than tracer-specific networks trained on the same tracer across all evaluation metrics. Moreover, the proposed method generates predictions for the tracers <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">18</sup>F-Florbetaben and <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">18</sup>F-FP-CIT, which were not included in the training data, that are either highly comparable or not significantly different from those produced by the tracer-specific networks trained on the corresponding tracer data. The results demonstrate the effectiveness of our zero-shot learning approach in generating multi-tracer PET attenuation maps with only <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">18</sup>F-FDG.

articleTitle: Personalized PBPK modeling can reduce uncertainty of the dose prediction in radiopharmaceutical therapy (RPT): a simulation study
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Physiologically based pharmacokinetic modeling plays a crucial role in optimizing dosimetry estimates for radiopharmaceutical therapy (RPT) on cancer patients. Presently, PBPK applications in RPT predominantly depend on population-level parameters, leading to large uncertainties on the dose prediction. These uncertainties can result in sub-optimal therapeutic effects, increase toxicity, and compromise treatment planning. In this study, we developed a whole body PBPK model, incorporating a Tumor compartment, to predict the dose in different organs. By personalizing certain anatomical and physiological parameters that could be potentially derived from pre-treatment PET/CT and blood test, we observed a substantial decrease in the uncertainty of dose prediction when utilizing personalized PBPK modeling.

articleTitle: Estimation of the PET Sensitivity and Spatial Resolution of the Human Dynamic NeuroChemical Connectome Scanner
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Recent technological advances have led to high-sensitivity PET scanners, with increased fields of view, thousands of detectors, and billions of lines of response (LORs). The high sensitivity can be used to decrease radiotracer dose and/or acquisition time. Alternatively, it enables dynamic studies with unprecedented temporal precision. To preserve high spatial resolution, small section crystals and depth of interaction (DOI) corrections are mandatory, which increases by orders of magnitude the number of LORs. Cylindrical geometries chosen for high sensitivity whole-body scanners are suboptimal for dedicated brain PET scanners, for which spherical geometries would confer important advantages. Sensitivity can be further increased by proper consideration of triple (and beyond) coincidences, coming from photons which interact in more than one detector (inter-detector scatter). The Human Dynamic NeuroChemical Connectome scanner that will consist of a high spatio-temporal resolution (HSTR) BrainPET insert with a spherical geometry integrated with a 7T MRI scanner is currently being developed. Here, we present the results of Monte Carlo (MC) simulations aimed at assessing the HSTR-BrainPET scanner sensitivity before and after including triple-coincidences as well as phantom images reconstructed from simulated data using analytical and iterative approaches. The latter used a GPU-based iterative reconstruction algorithm capable of processing large datasets in either list mode or LOR-histograms. Resolution modeling was incorporated by means of a spatially variant point spread function, which was computed from realistic MC simulations considering DOI and other relevant effects. Our implementation enables high-resolution reconstructions within a few minutes, and demonstrates an achievable resolution better than 1.5 mm and sensitivity values higher than 25% in most of the relevant brain areas.

articleTitle: An AI-Based CT Truncation Artifact Reduction Method for Improving PET Attenuation Correction
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: In PET/CT, many CT systems integrated into PET/CT systems have a smaller scan field of view (SFOV) than the PET SFOV, leading to truncation artifacts (TA) in the CT images, especially in regions outside the CT SFOV (but within PET SFOV), when scanning obese patients or with body parts extending beyond the SFOV. With TA contaminated CT images used for attenuation correction (AC) in PET reconstruction, PET uptake mis-estimation occurs and the error level depends on where anatomically TA occurs. In this study, we proposed a new method that combines extrapolation in the projection domain with AI-based image processing in the image domain to reduce the TA in CT and improve HU accuracy outside the CT SFOV. The proposed method was validated via simulated studies and was evaluated using real PET/CT datasets. We compared the proposed method with two conventional extended field of view (EFOV) methods. Simulation studies validated the proposed method and demonstrated its superiority in TA reduction as compared to two conventional EFOV methods. Clinical PET/CT showed 9-16% differences in lesion SUVmean between using the proposed method and the conventional methods.

articleTitle: Evaluation of the Maximum Throughput of ARDESIA-16 with Different Digital Pulse Processors
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: We present an evaluation of the maximum throughput of ARDESIA-16 at varying Input Count Rates using three different Digital Pulse Processors: XGLab's DANTE, XIA LLC's FalconX8, and a modified version of CAEN S.p.A.'s DT5560SE digitizer. We will cover performance metrics such as Output Count Rate and energy resolution, defined as the FWHM of the Mn-Kα peak. These measurements are specifically optimized to achieve a reasonable compromise between a satisfactory energy resolution and a high count rate with low dead time.The aim of this work is to study the performance of ARDESIA-16 with various Digital Pulse Processors at high input rates in order to cope with the quest for ultra-high-rate detectors required by next-generations synchrotron beamlines.

articleTitle: Performance evaluation of a large-area layered structure PET detector module
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: In previous studies, we demonstrated that the layer structure PET detector with side readout can provide high performance using crystal slabs with relatively small aspect ratio. To study the effect of aspect ratio of the crystal slab on the detector performance, we built a detector module using a LYSO crystal slab with a larger aspect ratio of 40×40×3.72 mm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</sup>, and evaluated its performance in terms of energy/spatial/timing resolution. All six surfaces of the crystal were polished, the top and bottom surfaces were covered with enhanced specular reflector (ESR) - the other four sides were coupled with four arrays of 8×1 Broadcom AFBR-S4N44C013 SiPMs. The 32 analog signals of the SiPMs from detecting the scintillation light were digitized individually in the TOFPET-2 FEM128 system from PETsys. A convolutional neural network (CNN) was trained to decode the one-to-one relationship between the gamma ray interaction position and the scintillation light distribution pattern on the 32 SiPMs. The average energy resolution after SiPM saturation correction for the entire detector was 11.9%; the average spatial resolution for the entire detector was 1.56/1.53 mm FWHM along x/y directions; the average timing resolution for the entire detector was 563.6 ps FWHM.

articleTitle: Population-based Deep Image Prior for Dynamic PET Denoising
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: We proposed a novel denoising technique called Population-based Deep Image Prior (PDIP) to reduce the noise in dynamic PET images and substantially improve the image quality of K<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">i</inf> images. PDIP integrates population-based prior information through supervised learning into the optimization process of Deep Image Prior (DIP).The population-based prior image was generated from a supervised denoising model that was trained on a noise-level-matched static dataset, comprising 100 clinical studies. We evaluated the efficacy of PDIP for reducing noise in 25%-count and 100%-count dynamic PET images from 23 patients by comparing its performance with two other techniques: a supervised model and a conditional DIP (CDIP) model that employed the mean static PET image as the prior. In addition to measuring the effectiveness of each technique for noise reduction, we also assessed their ability to accurately predict lesion K<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">i</inf> values. To implement these techniques, we employed a 3D U-Net architecture for both the supervised model and the DIP optimization process.The supervised model and CDIP showed effective noise reduction but resulted in smoothing and removal of small lesions. The similarity across CDIP dynamic frames resulted in decreased K<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">i</inf> values, as well as the incorrect K<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">i</inf> estimation in the descending aorta, suggesting that utilizing one single prior image for DIP in the context of dynamic PET denoising may not be optimal. The proposed PDIP had comparable noise reduction with the supervised model and CDIP but enhanced lesion K<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">i</inf> predictions.In conclusion, we developed a PDIP model that effectively reduces noise from dynamic PET images at 25%-count and 100%-count. The model utilized intrinsic image features from the dynamic dataset and a large clinical static dataset, resulting in superior performance compared to the supervised model and CDIP.

articleTitle: Radiation Source Quantification from 3D Simultaneous Localization and Mapping and an Imaging Spectrometer
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: A quantitative study on how Simultaneous Localization and Mapping and 3D Radiation Imaging affects source activity estimates. This work compares a commercially available SLAM system with an imaging spectrometer to evaluate the influences of path error, imaging uncertainty, and source distribution on quantification estimates. This work leverages an optical tracking system to evaluate SLAM error. Both Coded Aperture Imaging and Compton Imaging are considered to evaluate the influence on radiation image position estimate error against true source position.

articleTitle: A Method to Detect Charge Sharing Using Pulse Shape of CdTe Detector
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: X-ray spectral information is important for X-ray imaging. However, under high dose such as medical CT, pile-up is a problem and correct measurement is difficult. One effective measure is to reduce the detector area, but as the electrodes become smaller, charge-sharing becomes a problem. Different charge-sharing measures are taken by different methods depending on the electrode structure. If only the measurement of the X-ray spectrum at a single point, for example, a detector with a structure of a single pixel and an auxiliary electrode for charge-sharing correction around it can be considered. Such a simple structure allows independent measurement and analysis of output waveforms at all electrodes. When there is a large difference in the mobility of electron and hole such as in Cadmium Telluride (CdTe), pulses that are positively or negatively different from the normal waveform (negative pulses) may be generated depending on the position where the electron-hole pairs occur in the detector. This event includes a charge-sharing event. Therefore, detecting and removing this event can reduce the effects of charge-sharing. Two electrodes of the same size (3mm*1.45mm) were mounted on CdTe for confirmation, and spectrum and signals were measured with a digital MCA and an oscilloscope. As a result, it was confirmed that negative pulses sometimes occur at the same time as normal signals and that the energy resolution of the spectrum can be improved by removing events that occur at the same time as the negative pulses.

articleTitle: Toward Three-Particle Imaging with Polysiloxane-based Scintillators
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: In recent years, new scintillator materials have been developed to address long-standing radiation detection challenges, such as imaging of thermal and fast neutrons in the presence of gammas. Polysiloxane-based scintillators have demonstrated good pulse shape discrimination (PSD) between fast neutrons and gammas with figures of merit (FOMs) exceeding the 1.27 threshold for efficient discrimination. Recently, by incorporating boron-10 enriched molecules into these scintillators, thermal neutron sensitivity was demonstrated while retaining good discrimination between fast neutrons and gammas. In this work, a set of the polysiloxane scintillators were doped with the tolyl-B10 molecule, which least impacted PSD, and assembled into an array to test three particle imaging (thermal neutron, fast neutron, and gammas) using machine learning methods to discriminate thermal neutron interactions.

articleTitle: An Improved Low Dose Simulation Method for CT
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: We present a new low dose simulation method in the projection space of CT data which allows any general electronic noise model.
