In particular, the model for electronic noise is not restricted to have zero mean. Poisson and Gaussian noise are added to higher dose projection data in such a way as to properly account for the mean and variance of the resulting lower dose signal. The accuracy of the simulation in the very low dose limit is restricted only by the accuracy of the electronic noise model used. The method is well defined over the full dose ratio range 0 ≤ r ≤ 1. Results are demonstrated by comparing real and simulated water equivalent phantom data.

articleTitle: Improving Sparse-view CT Image Quality using fractal images with deep learning
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Computed tomography (CT) has brought tremendous benefits to medicine, but it has also increased medical radiation exposure. Sparse-view CT, which reduces the number of projections, is one way to reduce radiation exposure. However, reducing the number of projections causes streak-like artifacts in the reconstructed image. Studies of sparse-view CT using deep learning have reported higher image quality than conventional reconstruction methods. In general, deep learning requires many real images, which can be difficult to collect for medical images due to legal and ethical issues. The purpose of this study is to investigate whether fractal images can be used to improve image quality even when the number of real images is reduced. Fractal images were generated using IFS in Python, and the CT images were abdominal CT images obtained from the CHAOS dataset. They were collected 180° with parallel beams to obtain 36-projection sinograms. Input images (sparse-view images) were then generated by FBP reconstruction. The number of CT images was varied from 10 to 1000 and compared using three different networks: FBPConvNet, W-Net, and W-Net with pre-training. The peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR) and the structural similarity index (SSIM) were used to evaluate the accuracy of the reconstructed images. The use of fractal images was found to provide better image quality than training from CT images alone. W-Net with pre-training had the best results, suggesting that the number of real images can be reduced.

articleTitle: A Multichannel 14-Bit, 3-Msps/channel, Event-Driven Hybrid ADC with SAR/SS/TDC Architecture for Dark Matter Detection
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: In the next-generation dark matter detection misssion, energy-efficient front-end electronics plays an importan role to construct space-bone radiation detector systems. A multichannel analog-to-digital converter (ADC) is required to digitize the analog signals from readout channels which is employed to read out the charges from a PMT detector with the plastic scintillator. The requirements of the ADC are listed below: the resolution of 14 bits; the sampling rate of larger than 3 Msps per channel, and the channel number of 16 (or more). In this paper, a novel hybrid ADC, which combines the techniques of successive approximate register (SAR) ADC, single-slope (SS) ramp ADC and time-to-digital converter (TDC) based on delay-locked loop (DLL), is proposed to meet the above performance constrains. A 5-bit SAR ADC, a 4-bit SS ADC and a 5-bit TDC are finally selected to construct a 14-bit converter under the tradeoff of resolution, speed and power dissipation. The advantage of this architecture lies in that it is easy to extended to multiple channels by the increase small power and area overhead in each channel. Both event-driven mode and continuous-conversion mode are realized for timing controlling and data readout. A four-channel prototype chip has been designed and fabricated in 0.18 μm CMOS process with 1.8/3.3 V power supply. A sampling rate of ~ 3.3 MS/s is achieved at the clock frequency of 100 MHz. Under the power consumption of 4 mW/channel, the differential nonlinearity (DNL) and the integral nonlinearity (INL) are simulated as -1/+0.7 LSB and -3 LSB/+2.8 LSB, respectively. The effective-number-of-bits (ENOB) is 12.7 bits and the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) is 85.9 dB. The figure-of-merit (FOM) of 192.9 f J /conv.-step has been achieved.

articleTitle: A Depth-encoding Technique for the Biograph Vision PET/CT Scanner
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Detectors of the Siemens Biograph Vision PET scanner do not provide depth-of-interaction (DOI) information. The lack of DOI causes image resolution degradation at large radial offsets due to parallax error. In the current work, we explore an artificial intelligence-based method that can enable DOI without any hardware changes to the detectors. To detect DOI information from the single-ended readout detectors, a long short-term memory (LSTM) network was trained using energy signals from the SiPM channels digitized at 60 MHz. The training dataset was collected using a bench detector identical to the detector block of the Biograph Vision (5 × 5 array of LSO crystals with size 3.2 × 3.2 × 20 mm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</sup>) at known interaction depths every 2 mm. The trained network was evaluated using a separate test dataset. Also, to show the effects of DOI on the image quality of the Biograph Vision PET scanner, a Monte Carlo simulation study was done. Assuming ideal DOI accuracy, photon interaction positions were used to extract DOI information given 2-layer discrete DOI detectors with an equal layer thickness of 10 mm. A Derenzo-like phantom with rods of diameter 4.6 to 19.0 mm positioned at a transaxial offset of 13 cm along both the x- and y-axes was scanned. Simulated data were histogrammed into two sets of sinograms with and without DOI and were reconstructed using the time-of-flight OS-EM reconstruction algorithm. Analysis of the test data acquired on a bench detector showed that the proposed DOI approach has an accuracy of up to 91% in classifying events into their correct DOI. The average accuracy was measured to be around 76% across all studied interaction depths. Profiles across the set of three smallest rods on images with and without DOI were drawn to study the potential gain from DOI. Reconstructed images with and without DOI suggest that a dual layer DOI detector improves the peak-to-valley ratio of the 6.4 mm rods by about 44% at a radial offset of 18 cm.

articleTitle: Radiation-Induced Cystitis Perediction in Prostate Cancer due to IMRT based on 3D CT Radiomics and Dosiomics
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Radiation-induced hemorrhagic cystitis (RIHC) is a common side effect in prostate cancer patients. In this study, we aim to investigate the feasibility of using radiomics and dosiomics from CT and 3D Dose distribution data to predict RIHC in patients with prostate cancer undergoing pelvic radiation therapy. We used 59 patients with CT and Dose images and follow-up. First, radiomic and dosimic features were extracted from the bladder. Following, we proceeded with various feature selection (FS) and classifier algorithms on the training dataset and evaluated on test dataset with Specificity (SPE), Sensitivity (SEN), and Balance Accuracy (BAC) metrics. For CT radiomic features, the Boruta+XGB model performed best with BAC=0.75, SEN=0.80, and SPE=0.70; while in the Dose dataset, the RFE+DT model had the highest performance with BAC=0.71, SEN=0.85, and SPE=0.57. Finally, by combining CT and Dose datasets, we obtained BAC=0.67, SEN=0.6, and SPE=0.75. The findings of our study suggest the potential for using radiomic and dosomic features could predict acute RIHC in prostate cancer patients.

articleTitle: Estimating Arterial Input Function for Dynamic PET via Deep Regression
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Imaging-based estimation of arterial input functions (AIFs) from dynamic positron emission tomography (PET) images offers an alternative to invasive and laborious arterial sampling. However, accurate AIF estimation is contingent on precise blood pool segmentation in these dynamic PET images, which may be compromised by limited accuracy due to the partial volume effect and noise. Here, we present a deep regression framework for direct metabolite-corrected AIF estimation from dynamic PET, obviating the need for image segmentation and mitigating potential errors in imaging-based AIF estimation. Our approach first employs a variational autoencoder in a self-supervised learning task to reconstruct the input dynamic PET. We then extract features from the bottleneck layers, which serve as compact latent representations of the 3D dynamic PET images. These latent representations are combined along the temporal axis and inputted into a deep regression network to predict the AIF. We applied the proposed method to clinical data and assessed its performance using a weighted relative error (WRE) weighted by the sensitivity of kinetic modeling. The model achieved a small WRE of 1.2±0.56%, highlighting the effectiveness of the proposed model for AIF estimation and its potential for clinical application.

articleTitle: Optimization and Calibration of the Single Photon Avalanche Diode (SPAD) for Integrated On-Chip Sensor Interface in Common CMOS Process
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: In this work, we present a single photon avalanche diode (SPAD) fabricated using a standard 180 nm CMOS process, which allows for straightforward integration with diverse circuit logic. This is achieved through the optimization and calibration of the SPAD cell, a necessary progression in designing CMOS-based integrated sensor interface. Our proposed SPAD was designed to be exploited as a radiation detector of the sensor network interface in nuclear power plants (NPP) in the event of severe accidents, considering its low operating voltage and small size. The designed SPAD with two types of different junctions, shallow and deep, which were applied to compare the dark count rate (DCR) and photon detection probability (PDP). The shallow trench isolation (STI) guard ring (GR) is placed only to prevent the premature edge breakdown (PEB) in the deep junction devices. All the devices were measured to calibrate key parameters corresponding to breakdown voltage, DCR, and PDP. The primarily proposed model 3 achieved with a DCR of 286.3 Hz per unit area and a PDP of 24.48 % at low operating voltage, which is around a breakdown voltage of about 10.75 V.

articleTitle: Multiparticle Imaging of Plutonium Using Varying Organic Scintillator Materials
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Work at the University of Michigan towards a compact dual-particle imager design has resulted in the development of two separate versions composed of trans-stilbene and organic glass. Trans-stilbene crystals have traditionally been valued for having superior particle discrimination capabilities among scintillators. The organic glass composition used in this work was developed by Sandia National Laboratories and offers reduced discrimination capabilities in exchange for good light output and timing properties. In this work, an initial comparison between the two systems was performed by measuring a plutonium source under identical experimental conditions. Gamma-ray images indicate that the trans-stilbene imager may be more efficient when gating on 646 ± 36 keV keV. Fast-neutron images suggest that the organic glass imager is more precise in localizing the source. In the final paper, we will investigate how the comparison changes when applying equivalent energy thresholds, imageable event statistics, and measurement times.

articleTitle: Next generation PET imager
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: The shift towards early diagnosis and prevention in medicine necessitates high-performing PET imaging systems with improved sensitivity and specificity. To achieve this, additional time-of-flight measurements in PET enhance the signal-to-noise ratio and enable the construction of better-performing systems. However, the timing resolution of PET systems is limited by several factors, such as slow scintillation response time, optical photon travel time spread, number of detected scintillation photons, and timing precision of the photo-sensor and fast readout electronics. Although there have been efforts to develop new scintillators for PET, this contribution focuses on optimizing photo sensors and readout electronics. The authors integrated high-performing HD-NUV-MT silicon photomultipliers from FBK with novel low-power FastIC ASICs for fast-timing applications. They constructed a pair of 16-channel gamma detector modules and placed them in a coincidence setup, demonstrating very high coincidence timing resolution below 100 ps FWHM. This achievement enables the construction of high-performing PET detectors with incomplete sampling and simplified systems consisting of flat panel detectors that can be easily combined in larger systems. The authors simulated the performance of an imager comprising two 120 cm × 60 cm panels of segmented 20 mm thick LYSO crystal arrays read by dual-sided readout with fast timing and imaged a human XCAT phantom. They demonstrated that such a system, consisting of much less scintillator material compared to a total body PET imager with a standard opening, exhibits excellent performance. Overall, this approach provides a promising path toward developing highly sensitive and specific PET imaging systems that can aid in early disease diagnosis and prevention.

articleTitle: Novel LGAD structure for 4D tracking
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Low-Gain Avalanche Diodes are widely studied silicon sensors which are characterized by an internal moderate gain that enhances the signal amplitude induced by mips and by fast signals: because of these two properties LGADs have excellent timing performance. However, to overcome their poor spatial resolution, the AC-coupled LGAD approach was introduced, and other LGAD-based sensors are under development, towards detectors with 100% fill factor that can simultaneously provide excellent timing and spatial resolution. We are developing a novel device based on the LGAD concept, which overcomes some limitations of the AC-LGADs and can therefore be of interest for some future tracking systems. As the AC-LGAD, it features 100% fill factor, good spatial and timing resolution, while potentially having a simplified fabrication process in clean room.

articleTitle: Validation of a model of the Symbia Intevo Bold SPECT scanner for Monte Carlo simulations
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: In nuclear medicine, Monte Carlo (MC) simulation is a powerful technique to model the stochastic nature of radiation, e.g. radiation detection in single photon emission computed tomography (SPECT). The aim of this study was to validate a MC model of the Symbia Intevo Bold SPECT scanner. To this end, we conducted two experiments with Tc-99m: 1) planar imaging with a point-like source to evaluate the detector response in terms of intrinsic energy resolution, spatial resolution, and detector efficiency and 2) tomographic imaging with a NEMA IEC body phantom to evaluate the image quality in terms of activity recovery coefficient. The experimental results were then compared with the MC simulations performed in the same configuration and with the reference values provided by the manufacturer. The spatial resolution showed good agreement among all three values at 10 cm but had slight deviations (below 1.2 mm) at further distances. Detector efficiency measured from simulation and experiment was slightly higher than the manufacturer value with a relative difference below 7.1%. The activity recovery coefficients were comparable between the simulation and the experiment and reached a maximum value of 0.9 when both attenuation and scatter were corrected. The studied MC model has shown its potential to simulate the Symbia Intevo Bold SPECT scanner.

articleTitle: Simulation of He-3 Neutron Detectors with DRiFT, a Detector Response Function Toolkit
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Gas detectors, particularly those that utilize helium-3, are important tools for the detection of neutrons across a number of applications. The MCNP<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">®</sup> Monte Carlo transport code has the capacity to model neutrons’ transport to and interaction in such a gas detector, but it has no capability to simulate a detector’s response to that radiation. DRiFT, a Detector Response Function Toolkit, post-processes the output of MCNP<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">®</sup> to simulate a realistic gas detector response. Using DRiFT, individual detection events are simulated to determine the contributions of wall effects, where the resultant protons and tritons from the neutron capture reaction deposit energy in the detector wall rather than the active volume, and the effects of end-tube inactive regions, where the detector is insensitive to energy deposition. This allows a realistic detector response to be calculated, and representative pulse shapes and detector energy spectra to be generated. Measurements of a californium source were taken in the Epithermal Neutron Multiplicity Detector (ENMC) to serve as a point of comparison for MCNP<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">®</sup> simulations with and without DRiFT. The neutron count rate was measured with the source at different vertical positions throughout the ENMC instrument well, corresponding to different locations along the He-3 detectors’ active volumes. MCNP<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">®</sup> and DRiFT were then utilized to simulate the detector’s response. Using DRiFT with MCNP<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">®</sup> increased the fidelity of the simulations over MCNP<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">®</sup> alone by allowing for a more realistic treatment of the end regions of the He-3 tubes. This demonstrates the value of DRiFT as a tool for high fidelity modelling of gas detector response to neutrons.

articleTitle: Evaluation of a Neutron Resonance Capture Analysis Signal in a Field-Portable System
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: The re-emergence of thorium as a potential fuel for nuclear energy introduces the requirement for the non-destructive assay (NDA) of <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">232</sup>Th and <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">238</sup>U in varied chemical and physical arrangements. The thorium fuel cycle presents several safeguards challenges, among them the ability to differentiate between <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">232</sup>Th and <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">238</sup>U in mixed samples. NDA methods currently deployed for safeguards uses have poor differentiation between <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">238</sup>U and <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">232</sup>Th in mixed materials. We describe the initial efforts in the experimental evaluation of a portable Neutron Resonance Capture Analysis (NRCA) system, which leverages neutron resonances occurring in the epithermal (1-100 eV) range for certain isotopes. NRCA has been demonstrated at large beam facilities to have good isotopic sensitivity based on neutron time-of-flight correlation with unique resonances. We propose and evaluate the miniaturization of the technique using moderated neutrons from a compact deuterium-tritium neutron generator. This work seeks to determine the feasibility of NRCA for practical in-field isotopic characterization, both as a stand-alone technique and when used in concert with a compact Neutron Resonance Transmission Analysis (NRTA) system. Initial results suggest the viability of the technique to correlate time-based γ-rays with isotopic resonance structure, however the time resolution must continue to be improved to apply it to discrimination of materials with closely-spaced resonances.

articleTitle: Deep Learning Based Scatter Correction for TOF-PET
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Most of the scatter correction studies employing deep learning method have been performed using the data such as images, sinograms, and profiles, however this method suffers from long computation time and consumes a lot of computing resources. To overcome this problem, a deep learning-based scatter correction (DSC) method using list-mode data was developed in this study.A multi-layer perceptron model (MLP) that classifies true and scatter events among prompt events was implemented to verify the usefulness of DSC method. The weights of network were initialized using the Xavier initialization method and updated using the Adam optimizer and binary cross entropy loss. To obtain training and test dataset, a TOF brain PET with an axial length of 111 mm and a ring diameter of 257 mm was simulated using GATE. One-hundred million coincidence list mode data for a uniform phantom were collected and the position, energy, time, and additional information of the collected data were used as an input for training of the MLP. For the test of the MLP, 70 million coincidence list mode data of the same phantom was collected by additional simulation. Tomographic images were reconstructed using original data including true and scatter events (OD), true event data (TD), and corrected data by the DSC (C-DSC) method. To estimate the performance of the DSC method, the accuracy of model was assessed and the profiles of tomographic images of uniform phantom were drawn.The number of scatter events among the prompt events were decreased from 30.0% to 10.6% by classifying scatter events using the DSC method. The profile of reconstructed image using C-DSC was similar to that of the image reconstructed using TD.The results of this study indicated that the DSC method was useful in providing scatter-corrected images of high-quality only with reduced computational time and computing resources.

articleTitle: Transformer-based Reconstruction Method for Near-Field Coded Aperture Imaging with Sparse Projection Data
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Single photon emission computerized tomography (SPECT) has been widely used in clinical diagnosis as a nuclear medical imaging technique. SPECT imaging relies on mechanical collimation, such as parallel-hole, fan-beam, multi-pinhole. These types of collimators suffer from low sensitivity, while coded aperture (CA) collimator has the advantage of being efficient and has been used in SPECT imaging to improve sensitivity. However, objects are close to the mask in SPECT imaging, resulting in severe near-field artifacts. Besides, improving the efficiency of SPECT can reduce radiation risk, which means reducing imaging time and reconstructing images with sparse projection data. However, it is difficult for conventional reconstruction methods, such as the correlation analysis algorithm and iterative algorithms, to reconstruct high quality images with sparse projection data under near-field conditions. In the past decade, deep learning (DL) has made significant progress in image processing. In recent years, a deep learning framework, Transformer, has been widely used in image processing with impressive results. We proposed a Transformer-based method to reconstruct high quality images with sparse projected data under near-field conditions. We compared our method with correlation analysis method and maximum likelihood expectation maximization (MLEM) method with data obtained by Monte Carlo simulation. The simulation results show that the Transformer-based method can reduce background noise and restore low radioactive sources clearer. Besides, the Transformer-based method has average PSNR gains of 7.23dB over the MLEM method with only 0.02s inference time of one image.

articleTitle: Multi-Angle Image Reconstruction Method for a Planar Organ-Targeted PET Detector
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Organ-targeted PET detectors with a pair of planar detectors optimized to sustain a large solid angle around an organ of interest offer versatility in imaging applications not achievable with ring detectors. However, this versatility comes with a trade-off of a lower axial spatial resolution compared to the transaxial spatial resolution, which hinders the ability to perform certain image processing tasks such as multi-modal image fusion, image segmentation, and feature extraction. To address these limitations, a method was developed for generating a higher axial spatial resolution composite image by fusing images acquired from multiple angles. Here we present a workflow of a multi-angle maximum likelihood expectation maximization (MLEM) algorithm, which reconstructs multiple datasets acquired from different angles using two planar detector heads. To demonstrate the feasibility of this method, acquisitions were performed using a planar organ-targeted PET detector oriented at 0° and 90°, and composite images were reconstructed using the multi-angle MLEM on (1) multi-angle datasets from four spheres (ranging in size from 12.4 mm, 7.9 mm, 6.2 mm, 5 mm) and (2) a NEMA NU4-2008 image quality (IQ) phantom filled with [¹⁸F]Fluorodeoxyglucose. The composite images indicate qualitative improvement in overall image quality and quantitative improvement in spatial resolution. For example, in the composite images of the 12.4 mm sphere, the Full-Width Half-Maximum (FWHM) of the line profiles along the axial plane was improved by ~5.63 mm. Also, composite images from the IQ phantom demonstrate more accurate representations of the hot rods and cold chambers along the axial plane vs. images reconstructed without fusion. The presented multi-angle reconstruction may provide a practical means to improve the 3D images reconstructed using data from planar organ-targeted PET detectors.

articleTitle: A study on characteristics of u-shaped single-ended readout DOI TOF-PET detector
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: We propose a novel U-shaped single-ended readout PET detector with depth of interaction (DOI) and time of flight (TOF) capabilities. We analyze the main factors affecting the performance of the U-shaped crystals by experimental comparison, and discuss their application prospects in different PET scenarios. The U-shaped crystal consists of a pair of crystals connected by a bridge at the top, which distributes the scintillation light within the crystal pair. The output ratio information of the U-shaped crystal contains both the crystal position and DOI information, and two-dimensional flood map for multiple groups of U-shaped crystals can be achieved by built-in light guide structure. The experimental results show that the detector can achieve 2.21 mm DOI, 172.3 ps TOF, 10.25% energy resolution (ER) and 2.76 mm intrinsic spatial resolution (SR) for clinical PET applications; it can achieve 2.8 mm DOI, 207 ps TOF, 11.3% ER and 1.64/3.21 mm intrinsic SR for local imaging PET applications; and it can achieve a smaller intrinsic SR for preclinical large animal PET applications. Therefore, we regard the U-shaped structure as a simple and feasible, easy-to-promote, cost-effective solution for DOI TOF-PET detector, which has great potential to play a huge advantage in high-performance PET imaging.

articleTitle: Brain MRI Synthesis using Enhanced Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models from Brain PET and CT scans
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Denoising diffusion probabilistic models (DDPM) has shown superior performance in image synthesis for various fields. In this study, we propose an enhanced DDPM framework with the joint probability for synthesizing brain MRI from brain PET/CT. Although PET/MRI scans provide high-resolution structural information for partial evaluation and image reconstruction, it is costly and time-consuming compared to PET/CT. Also, synthesizing MRI from PET/CT including anatomical details has not been extensively studied. We achieved significant performance of proposed network compared with U-Net and cGAN in various input.

articleTitle: A novel few-shot segmentation framework for computed tomography images
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Recently, segmentation based on deep learning has become popular in the medical image domain. However, these deep-learning-based segmentation methods rely heavily on an extremely large number of manual labels and lack the requisite interpretation in mathematical theory. In this paper, we propose a few-shot segmentation framework coupling a deep neural network with active contour models for lung nodules. The advantages of the proposed framework are summarized into 3 categories: 1) The proposed framework requires only few-shot manually labeled samples during network training, which reduces the reliance on data samples and increases the theoretical interpretation with a mathematical model. 2) The initial contours provided by a coarse segmentation network are refined through an optimized active contour model, which offers an automatic process for traditional active contour models without manual setting of initial contours. 3) The proposed framework is easy to extend to other tasks, and the deep learning components are substitutable for plug-and-play presegmented models. In the experiments, the proposed method is evaluated on clinical CT images with lung nodules from a hospital. The results show that the proposed method is effective and robust for improving segmentation accuracy.

articleTitle: One-millimeter resolution hemispherical brain PET: a simulation study
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: The photon non-collinearity effect is one of the factors that limit spatial resolution in positron emission tomography (PET), and therefore a smaller detector ring may result in better spatial resolution. In brain imaging, a hemispherical detector geometry can minimize the detector-to-detector distance. Therefore, we have developed the world's first hemispherical brain PET, VRAIN. Clear visualization of small nuclei in the deep brain have been achieved with the help of 229 ps time-of-flight (TOF) resolution, even though the crystal pitch in the detector was 4.2 mm, which is coarse for a brain PET system. In this work, we aimed at achieving 1 mm resolution, which should be the theoretical limit of resolution in brain PET. We simulated our original crosshair light sharing (CLS) detector with 1.45×1.45×15 mm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</sup> fast-LGSO crystals, which can measure both TOF and depth-of-interaction (DOI) information. The detector geometry size was the same as that of the VRAIN (bottom ring diameter=28 cm), and in the simulation, the proposed new system (DOI/TOF brain PET) was compared with VRAIN. An ultra-micro hot phantom was used for spatial resolution evaluation, and the hemispherical Hoffman 3D brain phantom was used for evaluation of the contrast between gray and white matters. With an iterative reconstruction, the DOI/TOF brain PET could separate 0.75 mm rods clearly, and achieved higher gray-to-white matter contrast than VRAIN did. In conclusion, we showed the feasibility of 1 mm resolution brain PET with the hemispherical arrangement of the DOI/TOF detectors.

articleTitle: A Monte Carlo scattering correction method for Lu-176 induced background radiation
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Maximum likelihood activity and attenuation estimation, maximum likelihood activity and attenuation correction factors estimation algorithm were developed to reconstruct the activity image in CT-less PET scans. Additional attenuation information can be obtained through the analysis of background radiation from Lu-176 in LYSO/LSO crystals. In this study, we developed a fast GPU-based Monte Carlo scattering correction method for background radiation to achieve more accurate attenuation factors. Background data was acquired on the uMI Panorama GS platform to evaluate the effectiveness of the scattering correction method. There have been two scans performed, one with an empty field of view and the other with a NEMA IQ phantom inside. Reconstructed results of the test phantom's linear attenuation coefficient (mu, denoted as μ) image by the MLTR algorithm showed that the scattering correction method can effectively improve the accuracy of attenuation information introduced by background radiation, where the bias of water’s mu value was reduced from 10%-20% to less than 5%.

articleTitle: Development of Optical Signal Transmission Devices for Two-Dimensional Neutron Detector
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Optical signal transmission devices were developed for a two-dimensional neutron detector system. The devices are used for long-distance signal transmission between the detector head installed in the measurement room and the data acquisition equipment installed in the data acquisition room. The devices consist of an optical signal transmitting board, an optical fiber, and an optical signal receiving module. The optical transmitting board receives digital signals from application-specific integrated circuits and outputs position data as an optical signal. The optical receiving module receives the signal from the optical fiber and converts it into a data format compatible with data acquisition equipment. The developed devices were tested using detector-simulating signals, double pulses of various time intervals, and continuous pulses of various frequencies. The results showed that the devices can transmit two-dimensional neutron data with a counting rate linearity of more than 1.3 MHz and a pulse-pair resolution of less than 0.4 μs. Using optical fiber for signal transmission is advantageous due to its compactness, light weight, low transmission loss, and immunity to electrical noise. These features make it suitable for long-distance signal transmission in large-scale experimental facilities.

articleTitle: Sub-150 ps CTR Obtained with Hamamatsu S14-Series SiPMs for a 20-mm Long Fast- LGSO Crystal
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Coincidence timing resolution (CTR) is one of the important parameters in state-of-the-art clinical positron emission tomography (PET) scanners to increase the signal-to-noise ratio of reconstructed PET images by using time-of-flight (TOF) information. For TOF detectors, selection of a silicon photomultiplier (SiPM) model is one of the important parameters to obtain good CTR. The aim of this study was to investigate the CTR of various SiPMs, from Hamamatsu Photonics to achieve sub-150 ps. The TOF-PET detector we used consisted of a fast LGSO scintillation crystal (3.0 × 3.0 × 20 mm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</sup>, OXIDE Japan) and an SiPM. Four different types of SiPMs (S13160-3050CS, S14160-3050HS, S14160-4050HS, and S14160-4075HS, Hamamatsu Photonics, K.K., Japan) were used to find the optimal SiPM model in terms of CTR. The timing and energy signals were extracted by using a high-frequency SiPM readout circuit and then were digitized by using a CAMAC DAQ system. The SiPM over-voltage and leading edge discriminator threshold were optimized for each SiPM model. Front irradiation was used without any depth-of-interaction correction. For the SiPMs with a sensitive area of 3 × 3 mm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sup>, the S14160-3050HS (149 ± 6 ps) resulted in a 5 ps better CTR than that of S13160-3050HS (154 ± 2 ps). The SiPMs with a sensitive area of 4 × 4 mm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sup> (S14160-4050HS and S14160-4075HS), provided about 12 ps better CTR than the SiPMs with a sensitive area of 3 × 3 mm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sup>, as the edge region was not covered by the crystal. In the S14 series, the micropixel size of 75 μm showed not significant difference in CTR compared to that of 50 μm. In conclusion, the S14 series would be the best choice for TOF-PET to achieve sub-150 ps CTR in the one-to-one coupling readout scheme.

articleTitle: The Effect of Vertebral Bone Attenuation on Measured Spinal Cord Activity in PET/MRI
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Vertebral bone attenuation is typically ignored in image reconstruction for PET/MRI, but there is a risk that this biases the measured tracer uptake in the spinal cord. The aim of this study is to investigate this issue using patient data and simulations in an anthropomorphic phantom. Data in 2 patients administered 200MBq [18F]FDG were acquired on GE Signa PET/MR scanner to a 2 bed position static PET acquisition protocol with simultaneous MRI. Patient images were reconstructed with a Time of Flight OSEM Algorithm (2 iterations, 28 subsets, 2.3x2.3x2.78mm voxel size). Simulated data was created with the XCAT phantom representing the physiological [18F]FDG uptake of the neck and thorax. Simulated sinogram data were reconstructed in SIRF using an OSEM algorithm (10 iterations, 28 subsets, 2x2x2.78mm voxel size) with an accurate reference attenuation map and again using an attenuation map modified to assign tissue values to all bones. Data in both patients showed a sharp and consistent 46%-53% decline in activity at the transition from the cervical to the thoracic spine. This effect was not observed in simulated data with correct bone densities. When bone was incorrectly assigned tissue densities, a similar drop in the uptake was observed, but at 8.1% for mean uptake (20.1% for maximum uptake) this was substantially weaker than in the patient data. We conclude that while the spinal cord clearly shows an unphysiological decline in uptake values when acquired in PET/MRI, this can only partly be explained by ignoring attenuation in bone.

articleTitle: In vivo simultaneous imaging of 18F-FDG and Na131I with Compton PET system
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Single Photon Emission Computed Tomography (SPECT) and Positron Emission Tomography (PET) are two modalities used for molecular imaging the most. We have developed Compton-PET system that can take images of single photon emitters whose energies are from a few hundred keV to more than 1 MeV and PET tracers simultaneously. Single photon emitters are imaged with Compton camera and PET tracers are imaged with both Compton camera and PET. The system consisted of eight Compton camera modules composing an octagon. In this study, in-vivo images of two isotopes <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">18</sup>F and <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">131</sup>I in mice were acquired simultaneously. This isotope combination has particular importance in <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">131</sup>I radiation therapy to evaluate refractory tumors. <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">18</sup>F-FDG and Na<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">131</sup>I were administered to mice and the two tracers were imaged successfully. <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">18</sup>F-FDG was imaged with PET and Compton camera and Na<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">131</sup>I was imaged with Compton camera. <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">18</sup>F-FDG accumulated mostly in brown fat and brain and <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">131</sup>I accumulated mostly in thyroid. Additionally, performance evaluation with point source and five rods phantom were conducted. This study shows feasibility of pre-clinical <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">18</sup>F and <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">131</sup>I simultaneous imaging and considerable potential of <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">18</sup>F and <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">131</sup>I simultaneous imaging for therapeutic purposes.

articleTitle: New spectrometer dedicated to metrological characterization of radionuclide-based neutron sources
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: This work presents a new system dedicated to the measurement of energy spectra from radionuclide-based neutrons sources (ex. AmBe, PuBe, <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">252</sup>Cf). The experimental device consists of a large-volume polyethylene container that is equipped with a central channel accommodating the source to be measured and 12-measurement channels (in a spiral formation) around the source, into which detectors can be placed. The container is filled with water in order to moderate neutrons emitted from the source and to reduce the sensitivity of the detectors to the external environment. Measurements have been performed with <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">6</sup>Li-doped plastic scintillators (PS) developed in-house and optimized for the simultaneous detection of fast neutrons, thermal neutrons, and gamma rays, through signal processing based on Pulse Shape Discrimination (PSD). This novel approach solves the underdetermined problem as observed in the case of classical neutron spectrometers (ex. Bonner sphere systems with limited experimental data). Through the use of <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">6</sup>Li-doped PS information, the increased experimental data enable the spectrum of interest to be recreated without the need to introduce a "default spectrum" in the unfolding process. The reconstruction is performed with an iterative Maximum-Likelihood Expectation–Maximization algorithm (ML-EM) throughout the detector's responses matrix calculated with the MCNP6 code. An optimized version of this ML-EM algorithm with a regularization step has been also tested. The design, methodology and preliminary results are presented. Different types of neutron sources were measured and results are consistent, with a clear benefit when using experimental data taking into account the measured fast neutron component instead of using only thermal neutron counting.

articleTitle: Characterization of a prototype detector unit for fast neutron imaging and spectrometry
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Neutron scatter camera, having wide field of view and spectral sensitivity, has been recent research efforts regarding passive fast neutron imaging technique. However, limited the sensitivity to special nuclear material (SUM) prevents it from practical applications. Recently reported Single Volume Scatter Camera (SVSC) [1-5] developed by Sandia National Laboratory demonstrated an order of magnitude increase in detection efficiency. We present a new design of single volume neutron scatter camera in order to improve the position resolution of n-p elastic scatters inside detector unit. The camera composes by ten layers of optically segmented plastic scintillator sheet. Each scintillator sheet consists of a plastic scintillator sheet of 10 cm × 10 cm × 1 cm dimensions and two groups (6×2) of wavelength-shifting fibers with orthogonal directions embedded into grooves on two opposite scintillator surfaces. Fiber scintillation signals were read out by silicon photomultipliers (SiPMs). A prototype detector unit has been characterized experimentally. Light output of the unidimensional six fiber channels from one side of the detector unit was calibrated to be 14.45 photoelectrons per MeVee. Position resolution of the detector unit was measured to be 0.35–0.44 times fiber pitch, corresponding to 5.48 mm for proton recoil energy interval of 1.63–2.60 MeV, and 4.60 mm for proton recoil energy interval of 4.82–5.50 MeV. Energy threshold for recoil proton localization was estimated to be 1.18 MeV. The potential performance optimization methods include reducing light signal loss by increasing the fiber diameter and decreasing the number of channels involved in position reconstruction by narrowing the scintillation signal distribution function of the detector unit.

articleTitle: Development of large area SOI pixel sensor "XRPIX-X" with pinned depleted diode structure
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: We have been developing a novel X-ray pixel sensor, called "XRPIX", based on silicon-on-insulator and complementary metal-oxide-semiconductor monolithic technologies for the next generation of X-ray astronomy satellites. XRPIX is equipped with "Event-driven readout mode" that can read out only X-ray hit pixel using a trigger output function, which archives a better time resolution (≤~10 μs) than that of charge-coupled devices (~1–10 s) and enables coincidence extraction with other devices. For the improvement of energy resolution and sensitive X-ray detection area, we have developed a large area XRPIX-X with a pinned depleted diode structure. The active area of fabricated XRPIX-X is 21.9 mm × 13.2 mm, where 608 × 368 pixels are arranged with a pixel size of 36 μm × 36 μm. The thickness of Si sensor layer is approximately 300 μm. In this study, we evaluated the basic performance of XRPIX-X, a large area PDD SOI-CMOS monolithic sensor. Although the spectral performance in the area far from power pads significantly degraded, the pixel area near power pads showed improved energy spectra with preliminary results of resolutions of 914 eV and 898 eV (FWHM) at 13.9 keV and 14.4 keV in 7 × 8 pixels, respectively, compared to that of the previous large area double SOI sensor XRPIX7. We will report on the full characterization of XRPIX-X device.

articleTitle: Experimental Evaluation of Novel a 4π Field of View Gamma-ray Imaging Method
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: In the present study, we devised a new gamma-ray imaging technique (Three-Dimentional Shadow Method: TDSM) that uses three-dimensional shadows of gamma rays. This technique is based on the fact that the three-dimensional shading of gamma-ray flux, which is uniquely determined by the direction of gamma-ray irradiation, is generated by randomly arranging shields in space. In this study, we developed a new prototype gamma-ray imager (Coded Cube Camera for Gamma-ray: C3G) and performed 4π gamma-ray imaging experiments targeting a <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">137</sup>Cs source. C3G is a gamma-ray imager designed to apply TDSM, consisting of 8 GAGG (Ce) scintillator cubes, 18 lead cubes, and one empty cube randomly arranged in a Rubik's cube configuration. The size of each cube is 10 mm * 10 mm * 10 mm; the entire C3G is 86 mm * 86 mm * 86 mm and weighs about 600 g. The experiments were conducted indoors and outdoors under the condition that the 10 MBq <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">137</sup>Cs source was placed at a 3 m from the C3G. As a result, it was experimentally confirmed that 4π imaging could be performed by the C3G with an angular resolution of approximately 10 degrees. This result suggests that the performance of our proposed method is equivalent to or better than that of the existing imaging methods. Further development of this technique is expected to significantly contribute to decommissioning, decontamination, nuclear medicine, astronomy, etc.

articleTitle: PEA2PbBr4 perovskite as the fast material in semi-monolithic metascintillators, leading to <90 ps CTR
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Metascintillators take advantage of the range of recoil electrons after absorption of a gamma photon from a material, allowing scintillators placed close together to share the energy of interaction. This solution allows combining superb timing with improved stopping power. PEA<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf>PbBr<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">4</inf> perovskite has shown great promise for time-of-flight applications, due to fast decay times (~10 ns) and a high light yield (~50k photons/MeV). However, stopping power is relatively low. In this work, we benchmark the integration of PEA<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf>PbBr<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">4</inf> in a metascintillator with LYSO:Ce. Our Monte-Carlo simulation leads to realistic timing characteristics for system level timing, based on commercially available SiPM and DaQ systems. This leads to an overall CTR of 89 ps, with 22% of the events at 42 ps, after 3 mm depth-of-interaction correction. This metascintillator improves the stopping power to medically applicable scenarios, combining it with unprecedented timing for a portion of the events.

articleTitle: First Images from MERMAID, a Small Aquatic Animal PET Scanner Prototype
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: MERMAID-v1 is a positron emission tomography (PET) scanner prototype aimed to support biomedical research involving adult zebrafish and other small aquatic animals. It consists of 4 modules, two in each detector head, facing each other. To acquire a full dataset, the head rotate around the object.The current setup has been calibrated and scans of various phantoms have been performed. After energy calibration and threshold optimization, the average energy resolution is about 19% @ 511 keV. The scintillation light from the crystal matrix with a Na-22 point source placed behind was directly measured with an optical camera. Results suggest some light crosstalk; other causes like positron range or insufficient optical shielding will be further investigated. For image reconstruction, a maximum-a-posteriori (MAP) one-step-late (OSL) with a TV prior with depth of interaction (DOI) modeling was used; no attenuation or efficiency correction has been applied yet. The reconstructed image of two 1-mm Na-22 point sources (distance 5 mm) showed an average spatial resolution of 0.8 mm (FWHM). Scans of a 18-F-FDG filled cylindrical phantom acquired with various rotation steps show similar image quality. A 3D printed 18-F-FDG 50% downscaled micro-PET IQ phantom (NEMA-like) was measured. A small shrinkage in size was observed; it might be caused by the missing DOI information. Next steps include a more detailed characterisation, efficiency and attenuation correction in the reconstruction and imaging of animal-like phantoms.

articleTitle: Implementation of multi-GHz digital shaper for high-rate nuclear spectroscopy
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: In recent years, nuclear spectroscopy has benefited from advances in the field of high-speed digital signal processing (DSP), enabling improved detector response and reduced dead time. The trapezoidal shaper, has been widely used for pulse processing in nuclear spectroscopy applications. Trapezoidal allows to fine tune the energy resolution and sustainable rate by selecting the shaping time. The filter is typically implemented in FPGA using a recursive architecture. At the state of art, the recursive implementation of the trapezoidal filter allows to operate no more than 250-300 MHz on modern devices. However, with the advent of very fast detectors such as photomultiplier tubes (PMTs), diamond sensors, and fast silicon photomultipliers (SiPMs), the demand for even higher-speed implementations has grown.In this paper, we present a novel high-speed implementation of the trapezoidal shaping method that can operate at up to 5 GSPS for trapezoidal filters with a maximum length of 1024 samples and at 2.5 GSPS for filters with a maximum length of 8192 samples. This significant improvement in speed was achieved by parallelizing all digital blocks within the FPGA-based digital pulse processing architecture.

articleTitle: Current developments and upgrades of the Adaptive Gain Integrating Pixel Detector at the European XFEL
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Modern X-ray sources offer an opportunity for new techniques in photon science experiments and require detectors which can cope with their demanding constraints. The Adaptive Gain Integrating Pixel Detector (AGIPD) was developed in a collaboration of DESY, PSI and universities of Hamburg and Bonn as one of the main photon detectors for the experimental stations of the European X-Ray Free-Electron Laser (XFEL). AGIPD is a hybrid pixel detector with semiconductor sensor bump bonded to the front-end microelectronics capable of taking images in a burst mode with 4.5 MHz repetition rate providing a dynamic range up to 10<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">4</sup> 12.5 keV photons and single photon sensitivity. Two 1 Megapixel systems were delivered to SPB and MID instruments of the European XFEL in 2017 and 2019 respectively, they provide users with high quality scientific data. The operation experience revealed certain imperfections which led to hardware upgrades. AGIPD utilizes an adaptive gain technique which requires to store information about the gain that was selected during data acquisition. These data were compromised due to analogue memory cell initial design and required an upgrade of the Application-Specific Integrated Circuit (ASIC), which was done in a separate engineering run. A calibration complication in form of a signal baseline shift due to the inappropriate filtering in high voltage circuit led to a major intervention performed during a shutdown time. Along with upgrades, the next generation of detectors is being developed for the SFX and the HIBEF user consortia. It features more dense and compact back-end electronics design which also required different cooling concept. An intermediate 0.5 Megapixel prototype system is already being used at the HED instrument. Delivery of the 4 Megapixel detector (SFX instrument) and 1 Megapixel (HED instrument) is scheduled for the end of 2023.

articleTitle: Deep learning based Synthetic Magnetic Resonance Image Generation from Computed Tomography Imaging for Cerebral Ischemic Stroke Patient
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Cerebral ischemic stroke is a leading cause of death and disability worldwide, and timely diagnosis and treatment are crucial for improving patient outcomes. Computed tomography (CT) and magnetic resonance (MR) imaging are both widely used imaging modalities for diagnosing stroke. However, CT is often the first choice due to its accessibility and speed, while MR provides higher sensitivity and specificity. This study aims to investigate the feasibility of converting CT images of cerebral ischemic stroke patients to MR images using deep learning techniques. The proposed method utilizes a Generative Adversarial Network(GAN) to learn the mapping between the two modalities and generate synthetic MR images from CT scans. We have added a new attribute to the network, based on the observation that stroke lesions are highly discernible on MR images. The performance of the method is evaluated on a dataset of stroke patient images. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed approach can effectively generate high-quality MR images from CT scans, achieving a peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR) of 24.4 dB and a structural similarity index (SSIM) of 0.78. Furthermore, our method outperforms existing image-to-image translation methods in terms of visual quality and quantitative evaluation metrics.

articleTitle: FedFTN: Personalized Federated Learning with Deep Feature Transformation Network for Multi-institutional Low-count PET Denoising
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Low-count PET is an efficient way to reduce radiation and acquisition time, but the images often suffer from a low signal-to-noise ratio (SNR). Recent advances in deep learning have shown great potential in improving low-count PET image quality, but acquiring a large, centralized, and diverse dataset from multiple institutions for training a robust model is difficult due to privacy and security concerns of patient data. Moreover, low-count PET data at different institutions may have different data distributions, thus requiring personalized models. While previous federated learning (FL) algorithms enable multi-institution collaborative training without the need of aggregating local data, addressing the large domain shift in the application of multi-institutional low-count PET denoising remains a challenge and is still highly under-explored. In this work, we propose FedFTN, a personalized federated learning strategy that addresses these challenges. FedFTN uses a local deep feature transformation network (FTN) to modulate the feature outputs of a globally shared denoising network, enabling personalized low-count PET denoising for each institution. During the federated learning process, only the denoising network's weights are communicated and aggregated, while the FTN remains at the local institutions for feature transformation. We evaluated our method using a large-scale dataset of multi-institutional low-count PET imaging data from three medical centers located across three continents and showed that FedFTN provides high-quality low-count PET images, outperforming previous baseline FL reconstruction methods across all low-count levels at all three institutions.

articleTitle: Anatomical brain regions segmentation from MR images using global and local deep learning networks
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: The examination of brain regions, including white matter and hippocampus, is critical in monitoring, evaluating, and diagnosing neurodegenerative diseases, such as Alzheimer's. Though various conventional algorithms were devised for brain image segmentation from MRI, deep learning-based networks play a pivotal role in brain segmentation owing to their promising outcomes. Deep learning networks were employed in numerous studies to segment distinct brain regions from a diverse range of MR brain datasets, the segmentation of brain images remains a considerable challenge. In this study, we focus on a 3D brain image segmentation from MRI to achieve better performance compared to other segmentation techniques using global and local deep learning models. To this end, MR volumes from the Open Access Series of Imaging Studies (OASIS-3) were employed and a global deep learning architecture (3D U-Net) trained to segment thirteen brain regions including white matter, brain stem, cerebellum, brain ventricles, and gray matter. To improve the segmentation of eight regions (including the background), wherein the global network exhibited suboptimal performance, a local deep learning network (SegResNet) was exploited. The performance of the proposed approach was assessed using the Dice similarity coefficient. The outcomes of both networks, trained by minimizing soft Dice loss, were quantitatively analyzed. The global network achieved a mean Dice index of 0.9062 ± 0.0530 for thirteen brain regions. Moreover, the local model achieved superior results for segmentation of the eight regions with a mean Dice coefficient of 0.9061 ± 0.0481 compared with 0.8879 ± 0.0569 achieved by the global model. The local network performance exhibited significantly superior performance for seven regions over the global network as demonstrated by the results of statistical analysis (ρ-value<0.0001). In conclusion, this approach is recommended for accurate MRI brain segmentation.

articleTitle: 3D image reconstruction for Compton camera utilizing a transformer-based neural network
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: We introduce a novel approach for direct 3D image reconstruction in a two-Compton-Camera system utilizing a transformer-based segmentation neural network known as UNETR. Our proposed method aims to reconstruct the distribution of sources within a 32mm*32mm*32mm image space with pixel size of 1mm*1mm*1mm. The network operates on the results of a simple back projection method from two visual angles, which preserves the information of Compton kinematics and detector uncertainties while effectively canceling the impact of z-dimension error. We present the training of the network and the reconstruction results of both single-source and multiple-source scenarios using GATE simulated data. Additionally, we provide a comparison of our proposed methodology with a single Compton Camera setting and a simple UNET architecture. Our proposed approach achieves a spatial resolution of 1mm and an average Mean Squared Error (MSE) loss of 0.0010 for sparse multiple-source cases. Lastly, we discuss potential future advancements in this field of research.

articleTitle: Direct Detection of keV-scale Electrons in Single-Photon Avalanche Diode-Based Detectors
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Photomultiplier tubes (PMTs), despite being almost a century old, are still the most suitable photodetector for many astroparticle physics experiments, such as neutrino telescopes. One example of such a project is the Pacific Ocean Neutrino Experiment (P-ONE), a proposed deep-ocean neutrino telescope to be deployed off the coast of Canada that will monitor a few cubic kilometers of sea water with thousands of photodetectors. While the baseline design uses PMTs, incorporating single-photon avalanche diodes (SPADs), with their precise photon counting and sub-nanosecond time resolution, could greatly improve the detector pointing resolution. However, the requirements of large photosensitive areas with low single-photon noise levels limits their use. A proposed solution is to use a hybrid photomultiplier tube instead: a PMT where the dynode chain is substituted by a SPAD array. Used in this configuration, SPADs need to directly detect electrons with O(100 eV - 10 keV) energies. Here we present a systematic study of direct electron detection in a prototype SPAD and a commercially available array to guide the design of a SPAD tailored for a hybrid photodetector.

articleTitle: Convergence of Pixel-Driven Discretizations of Projection Operators
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Using numerical methods in tomography naturally requires the discretization of projection operators describing the underlying physical measurement process. Over the years, multiple discretization approaches based on different heuristics were developed, each supposedly particularly apt at handling specific situations. For instance, the ray-driven approach is said to discretize the forward projection properly but yields a poor approximation of the backprojection. In contrast, the pixel-driven approach is the standard discretization for backprojections but known to create strong oscillations in some cases when used for the forward operator. Thus, it is common practice to use discretization approaches from different heuristics for the forward and backprojections featured in most reconstruction algorithms. Those two operators are adjoint; a property not shared by the discretizations unless derived from the same heuristics. Adjointness of discretizations is relevant for the convergence properties of iterative solvers, and particularly more complex optimization algorithms’ convergence might slow down when lacking adjointness. Curiously, there is hardly any rigorous analysis discussing the approximation properties of these discretizations; rather, said notions of being apt or poor approximations are mostly anecdotal. To that end, we present a rigorous analysis of pixel-driven approaches, discussing convergence properties for both forward and backprojections, and finding that these discretizations approximate arbitrarily well under suitable assumptions. These assumptions are not standard, which might explain the anecdotal poor approximation of pixel-driven forward projections as caused by inadequate discretization parameters. Numerical simulations confirm these findings.

articleTitle: GPU-accelerated Monte Carlo Simulation for PET Imaging (Part I): Validation of Imaging Physics Simulation
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Monte Carlo simulation (MCS) is essential for nuclear medicine research. MCS tools have been developed for general purposes or specifically for nuclear medical imaging, such as GEANT4 and GATE. However, most of these tools are time-consuming and inconvenient to simulate patient motion and radio-tracer dynamics. We propose a new GPU-accelerated MCS toolkit, which is dedicated to efficient and user-friendly simulations of United-Imaging Healthcare (UIH) PET systems and is included in the UIH PET Reconstruction Toolbox (URT). Its speed is approximately three orders of magnitude faster than a CPU-based GATE simulation. This work illustrates the basic software architecture of URT-MCS and compares it with GATE in various phantom simulations to validate: 1) positron range and non-collinearity, 2) depositions in crystals, 3) central sensitivity, 4) detector responses, 5) scatter fractions in different materials and 6) simulation of complex voxelized phantoms. All comparisons show consistent simulation results with a relative difference or NRMSE <4.5%. The implementations of patient motion and tracer dynamic simulation are presented in a separate submission by Sun et al. [9].

articleTitle: Contact and material properties of (Cd,Mn)Te and (Cd,Mn)(Te,Se)
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: We made Schottky contacts for materials with a resistivity of about 10<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">9</sup> - 10<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">10</sup> Ωcm. We achieve this type of contact by selecting appropriate contact materials that act as a barrier for injecting electrons from one side and holes from the other side of the detector and creating a depletion layer in the sample by applying voltage increases in the signal produced by charge carriers generated by radiation.In this work, we present such contacts made on (Cd,Mn)Te and (Cd,Mn)(Te,Se) crystals doped with V, In, or co-doped with V and In. We measured I-V characteristics, Time of Flight (TOF), and photocurrent as a function of the applied field (PC-V) for selected samples. We collect data as a function of temperature in the range of 0 to 70°C. The measurements allowed us to obtain electron mobility values ( ≈ 880-980 cm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sup>V<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">-1</sup>s<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">-1</sup>) and holes ( ≈ 30-50 cm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sup>V<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">-1</sup>s<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">-1</sup>). From measurements of parameter μτ ( μ<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">e</inf>τ<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">e</inf> ≈ 1•10<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">-3</sup> cmV<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">1</sup>), we calculated an electron lifetime of the order of 10<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">-6</sup> s. TOF measurements allow for the estimation of trapping and de-trapping processes. The I-V vs. T data lets us determine barrier heights at the junction and the activation energies of shallow states in the material's energy gap.

articleTitle: Classifying chronic pain conditions using deep learning and resting-state fMRI
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Introduction: Due to its comorbidities with other symptoms and lack of effective treatments, chronic pain is considered a complex disease. At the same time, advancements in brain imaging, the spread of machine learning methods, and the creation of new diagnostic tools based on these technologies have demonstrated that these tools may be an option for assisting healthcare professionals in making decisions. However, a growing body of research in neuroimaging suggests that functional networks show dynamic changes in connection strength as well as variable phase difference (nonzero time-lag) between regions. Our goal is to compare performances in developing and evaluating deep learning (DL) and traditional machine learnings (MLs) in predicting chronic pain.Methods: A resting state functional MRI (rsfMRI) data with pain status were obtained from UK BioBank (UKBB) 6500 dataset. We computed functional brain activity to evaluate how well the 6 ML models (i.e., K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN), Logistic Regression (LR), Random Forest (RF), XGBoost (XGB), AdaBoost (Ada), LightGBM (GBM) and convolutional neural network (CNN), categorized chronic pain patients and pain-free controls in this study. They were compared using Area Under the Curve (AUC).Results: Training a CNN with preprocessed images produced the best results. CNN has an AUC of 0.69 compared to KNN (AUC = 0.52), LR (AUC = 0.55), RF (AUC = 0.54), XGB (AUC = 0.54), Ada (AUC = 0.52), and GBM (AUC = 0.54).Conclusion: The idea that resting-state fMRI data could be used as a biomarker for chronic pain conditions is supported by these findings.

articleTitle: A CMOS Implementation of a Switched Capacitor Analog Neural Network ASIC (ANNA)
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: We present an implementation of an analog Neural Network (NN) ASIC designed on a CMOS 0.35 μm process node, to be embedded in detector readout with ADC-less and FPGA-less processing.Computations are performed with 5-bit precision in charge domain, by means of charge sharing on programmable switched-capacitors crossbar arrays (which also implements network weights) and charge integration on low-power high-gain operational amplifiers. The NN memory is implemented with SRAM cells, programmed with SPI protocol, and timing events are synchronized with programmable on-chip ring counters driven by an external arbitrary clock. Full circuit simulation has been carried out to evaluate the ASIC performances. The estimated energy consumption to perform an inference is 12 nJ, considering the contribution of components involved in the operations (i.e. capacitors and amplifiers), and the expected energy efficiency is ∼296 GOPs/W. The ASIC is currently in the final design phase and will be soon submitted for fabrication.

articleTitle: Treatment verification by Prompt Gamma-Ray Timing on an anthropomorphic head phantom under pre-clinical conditions
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Range verification is essential to develop the full potential of proton therapy. The prompt gamma-ray timing method [1]-[2] is a promising candidate for its clinical realization, since it is a light-weight system with small footprint, which can be easily integrated into existing treatment facilities.To verify the clinical applicability of this system, range deviations were introduced on a realistic head phantom using plastic plates of up to 7 mm thickness. The produced prompt gamma radiation was detected simultaneously by eight CeBr\textsubscript{3} detectors. Several improvements to the detector hardware and setup made it possible to reliably detect the introduced range deviations.Thus, this study demonstrates for the first time that the prompt gamma-ray timing system can resolve range deviations of a few millimeters at clinically realistic pencil beam spot intensities, making it a strong option for on-line treatment verification.

articleTitle: Brain tissue perfusion assessment without using a CT system
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Real-time perfusion imaging is highly desirable for effectively using endovascular thrombectomy in treating ischemic stroke; the current standard of care is hindered by the lack of intra-operative perfusion imaging. We propose an Intra-intervention perfusion with no C-arm rotation (IPEN)-based method using X-ray angiographic images in the interventional suite. This approach aims to provide a volumetric brain perfusion assessment.
