IPEN is built on tomographic theory; wherein if an object consists of homogenous regions-of-interest (ROIs) with known shapes then N x-ray beams in a single projection are sufficient to estimate values of the N ROIs. IPEN for brain perfusion assessment aims to estimate the dynamic time-enhancement curve of each homogeneous ROI in the brain. The proposed algorithm was evaluated using XCAT phantoms updated for dynamic CT perfusion. Eight ischemic stroke cases were simulated. Using intra-arterial contrast-enhanced bi-plane XA images for each case, IPEN was performed to estimate the TEC values. Quantitatively, the estimated TECs had an excellent agreement with the true TECs. The normalized weighted root mean square error was 14.5% ± 1.7%, and the linear correlation coefficient values (R) ranged 0.85–0.95 (P < 0.01) for 8 cases.

articleTitle: Exploring the Feasibility of Implementation of a Whole TOF-CT System with Current Technology
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Recently, Time-of-Flight (ToF) X-ray imaging gained attention as an approach to negate the adverse effects of scattered photons as well as increase the CNR of the images. The principle is based on the analysis of each individual photon to identify and eliminate those with a longer time of flight than expected for ballistic photons. This technology is based on a pulsed X-ray source synchronized with an array of time-accurate detectors. Currently, Université de Sherbrooke is developing this new technology and aims to design the first scanner able to produce ToF radiography and CT images. The next step toward clinical use of this technology is the design of a fan-beam scanner based on 100 mm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sup> detector circuits distributed on a rotating ring. We are designing a new ASIC to integrate all the front-end electronics for this scanner which is able to timestamp X-ray photons with better than 300~ps~FWHM resolution. In this paper, the first digital architecture based on time histogramming and distributed signal processing in ASICs and FPGAs is proposed. Also, a model based on the aforementioned specifications is simulated to further study the requirements for the front-end electronics. These simulations, along with the physical constraints, provide insights into validating the proposed digital architecture and estimating the data rates at different stages of the signal processing and system. These estimations and calculations showed a good agreement with the feasibility of implementing time-of-flight computed tomography with existing technology.

articleTitle: Characterizing a Research Reactor Based Fast Neutron Beam with Organic Scintillators
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Organic scintillators remain underexplored and underutilized in high radiation field characterization and monitoring experiments, with no recent examples found in literature. Nuclear reactor monitoring, nuclear safeguards, and other nonproliferation activities may benefit from the dual particle detection capabilities of organic scintillators. To address this knowledge gap, we recently performed experiments in the fast neutron beam of the Ohio State University Research Reactor (OSURR), a light water moderated 500 kWth materials testing reactor. This work is a new experiment providing new results. We used two types of detectors, namely organic glass scintillators (OGS) and stilbenes, to investigate their performance for pulse shape discrimination (PSD), efficiency, and gamma-ray versus neutron pulse integral distributions. We further compared different detector sizes, specifically a 50.8 mm diameter stilbene, a 25.4 mm diameter OGS, and 6 mm edge stilbene and OGS cubes. We show that the gamma pulse integral distributions show distinct Compton edges that may correspond to gamma-ray emission lines from the reactor, for example H(n,g).

articleTitle: Acceleration of Sensitivity Image Computation in PET Motion Corrected Reconstruction
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Methods for motion correction in PET reconstruction have advanced in recent decades, especially for the brain due to the head’s approximately rigid nature. One challenge for clinical adoption of event-based motion correction is the computational cost of the time-averaged sensitivity image that is necessary for iterative reconstruction with maximum likelihood methods. Mathematically, the ideal solution requires a full back projection of the multiplicative corrections for every motion state, but this is very computationally expensive. A previously described acceleration approach involves a single back projection and then image-space modeling of motion; however, this involves an image noise penalty due to the required pre-correction of attenuation. In this work, we propose a method that provides the same acceleration, but with a smaller image quality penalty. We include a stationary approximation of patient attenuation in a single back projection for the sensitivity image creation, followed by image space motion modeling. The actual attenuation of each event's line-of-response is calculated, and the "residual" difference from the stationary approximation is accounted for as a pre-correction. With this approach, the image noise penalty is reduced since the residual pre-correction is much smaller in magnitude as compared to full precorrection. We present the detailed methodology and an evaluation of results at varying count density levels.

articleTitle: Effects of Various Additives on Cs2AgBiBr6 Double Perovskite Single Crystals for Radiation Detector Applications
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: This study investigates the influence of various additives, including sodium chloride, potassium acetate, toluol, ethyl acetate, thiourea, and sodium acetate, on the growth, size, material structure, and performance of all-inorganic Cs<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf>AgBiBr<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">6</inf> double perovskite single crystals for radiation detectors. A detailed experimental setup and analysis are employed, resulting in the growth of higher quality red, semi-transparent single crystals with a pseudocubo octahedral form and smoother pseudohexagonal crystal faces. The results show that the selection of additives significantly affects the properties of the growing crystals, potentially improving detector performance for a variety of applications. This work the effects of different additives on the size, crystal structure, and charge carrier transport properties of all-inorganic Cs2AgBiBr6 double perovskite single crystals. During crystal growth using the solution-based method, sodium chloride, potassium acetate, toluol, ethyl acetate, thiourea, and sodium acetate were added. SEM was used to measure the size and shape of the resultant crystals, and X-ray diffraction was applied to determine structural properties of the crystals. The performance of the crystals was evaluated by measuring their photocurrent response to radiation. The findings suggest that the choice of additive has a significant impact on the crystal size, morphology, and structure, as well as the detector performance. These results provide insights for the development of high-performance radiation detectors based on all-inorganic Cs2AgBiBr6 double perovskite single crystals.

articleTitle: Deep Learning-Based Outcome Prediction Using Harmonized CT Images for Head and Neck Cancer Patients: A Novel Approach with Attention and DeepHitSingle
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: This study presents a novel approach for predicting progression-free survival (PFS) in head and neck cancer patients, emphasizing on the importance of image harmonization and missing values imputation. We used the HECKTOR 2021 Challenge dataset containing 325 PET/CT scans (224 patients for training, 101 for testing) from six clinical centers, along with clinical data and contours of tumors. Previous studies achieved concordance index (C-index) scores between 0.61 and 0.72, but none explicitly harmonized multicentric images. Our two-module pipeline outperformed these previous results. The first module pre-processes the CT component of PET/CT images, addressing inter-scanner variability through a deep learning-based image harmonization model using a Multi-Scale Convolutional Neural Network (MCNN) with channel-wise and spatial attention mechanisms. The harmonized CT images were combined with clinical variables for which missing values were imputed using Multiple Correspondence Analysis (MCA) into our second module for PFS prediction relying on a MultiLayer Perceptron (MLP) NN integrated into a DeepHitSingle-based model. Our approach achieved a C-index of 0.75 using raw clinical features. With MCA, the C-index increased to 0.80. Ablation studies confirmed the effectiveness of MCNN for image harmonization and the DeepHit survival model. The addition of a fusion layer, combining channel-wise and spatial attention layers, further improved the C-index to 0.86 ± 0.035. Future work will focus on adding PET image harmonization to investigate the added value of combined PET/CT and evaluating our approach on the 2022 dataset (880 patients across 9 centers).

Index Terms: Head And Neck Squamous Cell Carcinoma

articleTitle: Experimental results from the characterization of a 32-channels mixed-signal processor for the GAPS experiment
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: This work describes the experimental results obtained from the characterization of a 32-channels readout ASIC that is the core of a module composed by 4 Lithium-drifted Silicon, Si(Li), detectors. The module is the building block of a tracker in an upcoming balloon experiment. The activity is carried out within the General AntiParticle Spectrometer (GAPS) international collaboration, whose objective is the indirect detection of dark matter through the detection of antiparticles present in cosmic rays at low energies. The balloon flight is foreseen in 2024 from the McMurdo station in Antarctica. The ASIC is designed in a 180 nm CMOS technology and has 32 low-noise analog readout channels featuring a dynamic compression of the signal, an 11-bit SAR ADC, and a digital back-end section responsible for channel setting and for sending digital information to the data acquisition system of the tracker. This work has a twofold goal: it intends on the one hand to verify the performance of the circuit, on the other to select at least 300 good samples to be used for the assembly of the GAPS Si(Li) tracker.

articleTitle: Bone metastasis automatic segmentation from [18F]NaF whole-body PET using a convolutional neural network
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Whole-body [<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">18</sup>F]NaF positron emission tomography has attracted growing attention for its extremely sensitive bone imaging performance and outstanding diagnostic efficacy in identifying bone metastases during both the staging and restaging processes for patients with high-risk cancer. However, segmentation for whole-body imaging data is heavy and time-consuming work for radiologists and manual segmentation can leave out suspicious metastatic lesions. To utilize the automatic segmentation of suspicious bone metastatic lesions from [<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">18</sup>F]NaF positron emission tomography, we explore convolutional neural network-based deep learning techniques to achieve an end-to-end segmentation method. The network was trained from the input [<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">18</sup>F]NaF positron emission tomography standard uptake value image to produce a corresponding segmentation mask. The performance of the issued segmentation method was evaluated by typical segmentation criteria including precision, recall, F1-score and intersection over union. The quality of neural network-produced segmentation masks is good in general, and it showed the potential to assist clinicians and radiologists and simplify the process of segmentation substantially.

articleTitle: Development of Spectroscopic Polymer Organic Glass Scintillators for Radiation Portal Monitors
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Multi-mode radiation detectors capable of gamma-ray spectroscopy are needed as the next generation of radiation portal monitors (RPMs) at ports of entry along the nation’s borders. Inorganic scintillators are difficult to procure in large volumes needed for portal monitoring and their cost can be prohibitive. Plastic scintillators that are currently used in RPMs can be produced in very large volumes at low cost, but due to their low density and low effective atomic number (Zeff), are limited to gross gamma-ray counting. To meet the performance and size requirements needed for RPMs, RMD and SNL are developing metal-loaded Polymer Organic Glass Scintillators (POGS). In this work we show progress in the formulation chemistry of metal-loaded POGS. We have fabricated high quality samples of tin-loaded POGS up to 2" diameter sizes resulting in light yields >10,000 photons/MeV and energy resolutions <10 % @ 662 keV. We have performed successful fusing of individual tin-POGS elements, performed accelerated aging studies, and GEANT4 simulations to establish a working model of tin-POGS, and compared gamma-ray and neutron efficiencies of OGS, tin-loaded POGS and EJ-200.

articleTitle: A 32-channel high-sampling-rate electronic system for compact neutron cameras
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Neutron measurement is essential across several scientific fields, e.g. nuclear physics, materials science, and engineering. Neutron detection allows the exploration of neutron behavior in various materials, verifies the occurrence of nuclear reactions and radiation, and enables nuclear power plant monitoring. This paper presents a compact camera designed for neutron imaging. We developed an electronic system consisting of 32 channels with high sampling rates for this neutron imaging camera. The electronic system is suitable for applications requiring low cost and low power consumption. The system is based on the Domino Ring Sampler 4 (DRS4) chip capable of high-speed sampling of up to 5.12 GSPS to digitize pulses from neutron detectors. The electronic system is capable of pulse shape discrimination (PSD). Additionally, a real-time algorithm for neutron-gamma discrimination was implemented directly in the field-programmable gate array (FPGA). Finally, this paper presents the results of neutron-gamma discrimination with different sampling rate (1GSPS and 2GSOS), as well as the reconstructed images of a single 241Am-Be neutron source.

articleTitle: Alpha-SPECT-mini: A Preclinical SPECT system Using Ultrahigh Energy Resolution CdTe detectors for Low-Dose Alpha Emitter Radiopharmaceutical Therapy Imaging
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: In this work, we have developed the CdTe detector-based alpha-SPECT-mini system for preclinical studies. The system is designed to have ultrahigh energy resolution <3keV on average and sensitivity to accommodate the low dose of the targeted alpha therapy applications in mice studies. Machine learning charge sharing reconstruction algorithms are used to achieve the best energy resolution and sensitivity simultaneously. We have performed the Derenzo resolution and Image Quality phantom studies with Tc-99m to evaluate the intrinsic resolution <0.75mm and with Ac-225 to evaluate the multi-isotope imaging capabilities (Ac-225, Fr-221, Bi-213, Tl-209) of the system. Soon, we will also perform the in vivo mice imaging study to further evaluate the system performance for low dose imaging and to study the biological reaction of mice to Ac-225 and toxicity effects on surrounding healthy tissues.

articleTitle: Gibbs Artifacts Removal with a Nonlinear Method
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Gibbs artifacts are a common issue in image processing, appearing as oscillations or ringing around sharp edges or boundaries. They arise when the image’s frequency components are adjusted, such as in image deblurring and sharpening. Linear methods are ineffective in reducing Gibbs artifacts, so nonlinear methods may be more effective. One such nonlinear method is the use of neural networks. In this paper, we apply a simple convolutional neural network to an image sharpening task and observe the effect on Gibbs artifacts. For a simple, unrealistic case study, the Gibbs artifacts are completely removed. However, it’s worth noting that this task can be achieved without using a neural network.

articleTitle: SACI: A Serial Interface for ASIC Configuration
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: We present a new protocol, the SLAC ASIC Configuration Interface (SACI), which has been developed to fit the command and configuration requirements of the ePix line of ASICs and X-ray cameras developed for LCLS at SLAC. SACI is a serial protocol very similar to SPI, with adaptations to allow for backpressure. The protocol has an open source VHDL implementation, and has been successfully implemented in over 15 different ASICs developed by SLAC.

articleTitle: MAPSSIC, a beta+ implantable microprobe for neuroimaging of awake and freely moving rats: first sensor characterization and in vivo imaging simulations
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: The correlation of molecular neuroimaging and behavior studies in the preclinical field is of major interest to unlock progress in the understanding of brain processes and assess the validity of preclinical studies in drug development. However, fully achieving this ambition requires to perform molecular images of awake and freely moving animals, whereas most of the preclinical imaging procedures are currently performed under anesthesia. To achieve such a combination, the MAPSSIC project aims to develop a pixelated intracerebral probe based on the MAPS technology to be implanted on awake freely moving rats. Thanks to its in situ position, the probe is able to directly detect short range positrons of β<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">+</sup> radioisotopes whereas micro-PET devices use the coincident γ-rays from annihilation as a relevant signal. In this paper, we discuss the first characterization of the new probe’s sensors and present the results from Monte Carlo simulations of a typical animal experiment using a commonly used β<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">+</sup> radiotracer to confirm the relevance of this imaging device. First measurements show an energy threshold lower than 1 keV allowing the detection of β<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">+</sup> particles as well as a background sensitivity of 1.7 × 10<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">−3</sup> cps. Simulations confirm the ability of the probe to record a local information, with more than 93 % of the detected particles being emitted within the first 2 mm surrounding the probe, that allows to perform kinetic studies on brain structures such as the striatum.

articleTitle: Perovskite CsPbBr3: Material Purity, Crystal Defects, and Detector Performance
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: The perovskite CsPbBr<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</inf> is a new generation semiconductor in the field of X-ray and g-ray detection. The fundamental physical properties of CsPbBr<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</inf> well meet the requirements for high energy detector applications, with direct band gap (orange color, 2.25 eV), high density (4.85 g/cm3), attenuation coefficient comparable to CZT, and high resistivity (10<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">9</sup>-10<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">10</sup> W• cm) and carrier mobility-lifetime product (10<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">-3</sup> - 10<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">-4</sup> cm2/V). We developed a new chemical process for inexpensive material production with an excellent purity (>99.999%) and quantitative (>95%) yield. Large crystals of CsPbBr<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</inf> grown by the Bridgman method show high transparency (85% transmission in FT-IR spectroscopy) and well resolved characteristic peaks in g-ray spectroscopy with <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">241</sup>Am, <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">57</sup>Co, and <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">137</sup>Cs and high flux X-rays as radiation sources. The energy resolution of the planar detector has reached the value close to 1% from the <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">137</sup>Cs g-ray irradiation. One of the major challenges currently lying in practical applications of this material is the crystal defects including domain and twin boundaries and the charge carrier trap states present in the material, all of which should be minimized to maximize the detector sensitivity. This presentation will give an overview of the process of synthesis, crystal growth and optimization efforts to mitigate the issues above to enhance crystal quality and detector performance of CsPbBr<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</inf>.

articleTitle: First results of the 4D-PET brain system
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Positron EmissionTomography (PET) constitutes the molecular imaging technique of choice for the diagnosis, treatment follow-up, and understanding of several diseases, including many neurological conditions. Focusing on its application in neurology, dedicated PET systems aim to increase both clinical and physical sensitivity.This abstract presents the geometrical design and preliminary results of the novel 4D-PET, a high-sensitivity organ-specific PET system dedicated to studying the human brain. The 4D-PET system will allow accurate imaging for brain studies due to its expected high sensitivity, high 3D spatial resolution by implementing a Neural Network architecture for the 3D photon impact position estimation- and boosted signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) -enabled by including precise photon time of flight (TOF) information-. We report the preliminary performance results obtained at super-module level (experimental validation) and system level (simulated data), demonstrating the superior performance of the 4D-PET. The experimental results yielded a spatial resolution (FWHM) in the pixelated axis of approximately ½ the slab thickness ~0.8 mm. Regarding the monolithic and DOI axis, the Neural Network prediction reported average FWHM values of 2.1±1.0 mm and 3.4±1.8 mm, respectively. The timing measurements reported an average CTR value of 359±7 ps. Regarding the simulations results, a sensitivity of >15% at the center of the field of view was obtained. Reconstructed phantom images show good image quality and spatial resolution. Similarly. the calculated Contrast Recovery Coefficient (CRC) values improved when using TOF information compared to the non-TOF case.These results demonstrate that, the unique 4D-PET configuration allows for a simultaneous 3D-impact positioning of the gamma-ray and its arrival time estimation thus, making it possible to visualize small critical structures of the brain for neurophysiology and neuropsychiatry applications.

articleTitle: Performance evaluation of an electromagnetic motion tracking system for PET/CT head motion correction
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Patient motion has limited the PET image quality and quantification accuracy. For high resolution PET imaging of a rigid human brain, both the position and orientation of the head must be precisely estimated in real time. A wearable electromagnetic motion tracking system has been carefully designed to achieve submillimeter motion tracking in our previous study. In this work, we evaluate the systematic performance of PET/CT head motion correction using the electromagnetic motion tracking system, and propose an automatic intersystem calibration method to simplify the coordinate system calibration between the motion tracking and PET scanner systems.

articleTitle: An adaptive 3D denoising network for low dose PET/MR imaging using spatial brain transform
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: The PET/MR system provides both anatomical and functional information, which offers much sensitivity and accuracy for clinical imaging and research. This may lead to certain health risks of radiation exposure and the cost of radiopharmaceuticals for patients, which results in low-dose PET imaging reducing the radiation dose and recovering noisy images. Considering the profitable anatomical information of MR images, we introduce spatial brain anatomical alignment information for PET/MR images to solve the denoising tasks of low-dose PET imaging. In this paper, a novel 3D denoising network model equipped with spatial brain transform is proposed. Experiments are conducted on 100 patient datasets, and 10 test datasets are utilized to evaluate the performance of our proposed method. Visual results and quantitative results illustrate the effectiveness of the proposed methods compared with several deep learning methods. Making full use of MR's spatial anatomy information will result in significant performance gains. In future works, the proposed method could be applied to other multimodal systems, such as PET/CT.

articleTitle: Digital Pulse Processing and Pile-up Correction in NaI(Tl) for Neutron Active Interrogation
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Neutron active interrogation (NAI) is a valuable technique for detecting specific elements in materials to monitor hazardous or potentially threatening substances. This study proposes a pulsed fast neutron analysis (PFNA) method using a NaI(Tl) detector with digital processing and pile-up correction. By measuring the event time distribution during the operation of a deuterium-tritium (DT) neutron generator, time gating is applied, while modified phase-only correlation (MPOC) and maximum likelihood estimation (MLE) methods are used for pile-up correction. The pile-up corrected spectrum is compared with a conventional pulse-integrated spectrum. Application of time gating and pile-up correction techniques to gamma-ray spectroscopy in PFNA leads to an increased signal-to-background ratio in detecting specific gamma-ray lines. Different target materials are tested to distinguish the amount of carbon and observe the evidence of nitrogen presence.

articleTitle: Feasibility Study of Drift Detector Structures in Amorphous Selenium Detectors
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: This paper introduces amorphous Selenium (a-Se) drift detectors with uniform drift field as a promising alternative to Silicon drift detectors in high-energy applications. A 3D model was created with a finite element method to simulate the electric field and potential for two detector designs that utilize microstrips and resistive collecting electrodes to increase spatial and energy resolution without increasing readout channels. The charge division readout technique is employed for 3D position sensing. The a-Se drift detector enables unipolar charge sensing for higher mobility carriers, resulting in higher temporal and energy resolution. Additionally, this detector design increases the detection area ratio and reduces the electronics noise, making it a cost-effective alternative with high energy resolution for large-area high-energy applications.

articleTitle: Performance of a Large-area GEM Detector with Low Mass for EIC
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: We present the tracking performance of a large low-mass Triple-GEM detector prototype in a 120 GeV proton beam. The trapezoidal detector covers an azimuthal angle of 30.1 degrees and a radial range of 8-90 cm. This detector has been developed as a prototype for tracking with MPGDs at the future Electron-Ion Collider. In this environment, such a detector would mainly support the pattern recognition for tracking in the forward and backward directions. Because multiple scattering of tracks must be minimized, the material budget for the forward and backward tracking detectors is critical. Consequently, this detector implements drift and readout electrodes on large foils instead of on standard PCBs. All five foils including the three GEM foils are mechanically stretched in a single stack adapting an assembly technique pioneered by CMS for the muon endcap GEM upgrade. This results in total detector material of only 0.6% radiation lengths in the active area. Outer frames custom-made from stiff carbon-fiber composite material are employed to take up the large tension from the stretched foil stack and to provide detector rigidity while keeping the detector mass low. We describe the mitigation of insufficient rigidity of the initial design and of HV instabilities that arise from using conductive carbon fiber material. The signal is read out with one-dimensional radial zigzag strips that reduce the number of electronics channels and cost associated with that while maintaining good spatial resolution. We present performance results including a measurement of the spatial resolution of the detector obtained in a beam test at the Fermilab test beam facility.

articleTitle: A discrete charge-to-time converter based on a saturated MOSFET
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: In the context of preclinical tomographic imaging, the readout electronics of radiation detectors measures the charge and time of signals. An interesting electronic architecture is the cascade of charge-to-time converters (QTC) with time-to-digital converters (TDC). We propose a non-gated QTC circuit with the fewest standard discrete components known in the literature. The proposed converter only consists in one amplifier and one MOSFET transistor wired in negative feedback while providing a Time-over-Threshold (ToT) response to the input charge. For negative or positive detector output current, the MOSFET is a n-channel or a p-channel respectively. The transistor in saturation regime operates simultaneously a charge integration with its intrinsic capacitance and a constant current discharge. An additional capacitor in parallel of the MOSFET can extend the functional charge range. A n-MOSFET QTC prototype board was designed and tested with both a digital detector emulator and a detector irradiated with a <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">99m</sup>Tc source. Preliminary results of ToT in function of charges show a relative error less than 3.5 % with linear fit, on the range from 0.9 pC to 21.9 pC. Future work will focus on using a Field-Programmable-Gate-Array (FPGA) which will include the TDC function but also the discriminator function using a single-ended voltage-referenced input receiver.

articleTitle: Simulation study on GAGG and BGO crystals for enhanced light extraction using Nano pattern coating
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: PET detectors commonly use inorganic scintillator, and their performance strongly relies on scintillator properties, particularly light yield. However, a significant number of photons are lost at the scintillator-photosensor boundary due to the mismatched refractive index (RI) of scintillator and photosensor. Furthermore, using long and narrow crystals in PET detectors increases the number of photons that escape the crystal.To address this problem, a simulation study was conducted to investigate the use of a nano-pattern coating on the crystal surface to improve light extraction. The finite difference time domain simulation was used to evaluate photon propagation within the nano structures. Two scintillators, high-performance GAGG crystal and cost-effective BGO crystal, coated with hole-type nano pattern were simulated to enhance the light extraction. Various nano pattern properties, including hole diameter (D), height (H), pattern period ratio (L/D), and RI, were tested to determine the optimal value for light extraction. Reference data set was obtained for the comparison which consists of 26 μm-thick-grease instead of the nano pattern. Photon transmittance was obtained from the simulation and light extraction gain was calculated by normalizing total photon transmittance to that of reference data.Based on simulation results, we observed that applying nano pattern coating leads to an improvement in photon transmittance for all photon incident angles, particularly for angles larger than the critical angle. GAGG crystal, the light extraction gain increased by x1.54 with D=500 nm, H=100 nm, L/D=4, and RI=1.7. BGO crystal light extraction gain increased by x1.50 with D=600 nm, H=100 nm, L/D=4, and RI=1.8. Here, we observed the potential of using a nano-pattern coating on crystals to improve the light extraction of PET detectors, which will lead to improved PET system performance.

articleTitle: Temperature Drift Correction for FPGA-Based Time Measurement Systems
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: A field programmable gate array (FPGA) based time measurement system has been developed for measuring signal arrival time at the picosecond level. However, it has been found that ambient temperature can significantly affect the timing precision of the system. This paper presents an analysis of the temperature effects on each part of the time measurement system, which draws the conclusion that the temperature effect mainly comes from the used switch boxes on the pathway of routing. To understand this temperature effect, the behavior of the switch boxes on their delay time varying with the temperature is investigated, which gives us a simple idea for temperature drift correction. Using single-photon signals from Microchannel Plate Photomultiplier Tubes (MCP-PMTs), the delay temperature coefficients of 128 channels of the system can be easily obtained, which will be used for final temperature-related calibration. After the correction in the temperature range of 35°C to 65°C, the single-photon time resolution of the system is improved from 33-50 ps to 32-37 ps, which demonstrates that the temperature effect in FPGA-based time measurement systems can be almost fully corrected.

articleTitle: Development of a new ground level cosmic ray neutron monitor
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: We report on the ongoing development of a new ground level neutron monitor to be put in operation a UK meteorological station as part of the growing interest in predicting extreme space weather events. The monitor has a modular design offering flexibility of sensitivity with the first production unit intended to have a counting rate similar to that of a 6-NM-64 but with a smaller and lighter footprint. The design adopts proven sensor and electronic components because high reliability, exceptional stability, and a long-service life are critical. The neutronic design relied heavily on Monte Carlo simulations which were validated in various ways. In this paper we describe one such benchmark experiment designed to explore the ability of the simulation tool to predict the response of thermal neutron detectors embedded in a polyethylene-lead-polyethylene-lead-polyethylene assembly when exposed to an accelerator-produced high-energy spallation neutron beam representative of secondary cosmic-ray nucleons.

articleTitle: Impact of image constraints on DECT reconstruction with limited-angular-range data
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: There exists interest in DECT with limited-angular- range (LAR) data for meeting unique workflow needs in practical imaging applications. Optimization-based, one-step algorithm can lead to quantitatively accurate image reconstruction in DECT with advanced LAR scanning configurations where data are col- lected with non-overlapping LAR scans. The aim of this work is to investigate and evaluate the impact of different image constraint designs in the optimization program on the reconstructed images qualitatively and quantitatively. We investigate and prototype optimization programs that incorporate two different designs of image constraints on the directional-total variation (DTV) of either basis images or monochromatic images. We then efficiently derive algorithms for numerically solving these optimization programs, thanks to the primal-dual-based algorithm framework. Results from both simulated and real data collected using a two-orthogonal-arc scanning configuration suggest that one-step algorithms may be designed that can reconstruct images with minimal artifacts from LAR data. Furthermore, the image constraint on the DTVs of monochromatic images may yield images that are visually closer to the reference images from FAR data, while the constraint on the DTVs of basis images may yield improved accuracy of iodine concentration estimation. The methods and results in the work may engender insights into the design of practical reconstruction procedures for DECT with LAR data of potential application significance.

articleTitle: Auto-PET-IQA: A Fully Automated Region-Specific PET Image Quality Assessment Tool
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Incorporating fully automated human perception-driven PET image quality assessment (IQA) measures into the scanning routine is beneficial due to: (1) it could be useful in a clinical setting to instantly identify the need for reperformed acquisition or image reconstruction; (2) by delivering high-quality scans, it alleviates radiologists’ daily workload and expedites the diagnosis and monitoring procedure; and (3) low image quality is a primary limitation in the development of different artificial intelligence (AI)-based models for PET processing and analysis, and an automated PET IQA model can serve as a useful tool to organize and refine input data towards AI-based models for PET analysis. In this study, we developed fully automated AI-based region-specific [<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">18</sup>F]FDG-PET IQA models. The IQ of 174 <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">18</sup>F-PET/CT scans (acquired on two scanners) were rated by two nuclear medicine physicians and binarized to low- and high-quality. Region identification (head and neck, chest, chest-abdomen interval, abdomen, and pelvis) and body contouring (BC) (excluding the arms) were automatically performed utilizing deep learning (DL) models on CT images and then edited/verified by the physicians. For radiomics-machine learning (R-ML) models, IBSI-based features were fed into multiple feature selection and ML algorithms. DL model was developed using the SEResNet50 architecture. All R-ML and DL models were evaluated using AUC, accuracy, sensitivity, and specificity. Most effected features selected in radiomics models are reported. Except for the chest-abdomen region, DL model performance was superior to R-ML models. Region-wise AUCs of DL vs. best R-ML model were: head - 0.91 vs. 0.85, chest - 0.82 vs. 0.79, chest-abdomen - 0.7 vs. 0.77, abdomen - 0.8 vs. 0.79, and pelvis - 0.91 vs. 0.75, respectively.

articleTitle: Utilizing THz Radiation for In Vivo Medical Imaging
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: THz radiation is rapidly becoming suitable as an in vivo biomedical imaging modality for cancer [2] and a number of other proposed applications[3] [5]. The MacPherson THz group is currently conducting a number of pilot clinical studies using a unique portable THz scanner.Characterisation of patient invariant factors, and of the THz scanner itself, have been carried out through in vivo measurements of healthy volunteers.

articleTitle: Toward a second generation of Metascintillators using the Purcell effect
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: We are developing a new scintillation concept, which will become part of the second generation of metascintillators. The first generation approached 100 ps equivalent coincidence time resolution (CTR) in a PET scanner configuration with LYSO/plastic and LYSO/BaF<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf> designs, and reached 200 ps with much cheaper BGO/plastic and BGO/BaF<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf> heterostructures. Some of these designs allowed the determination of the depth of interaction (DOI). In the second generation of metascintillators, the fast scintillator (plastic or BaF<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf>) will be replaced by even faster, denser and more compact nanophotonic features.We report here on the first very encouraging results obtained in the lab on a multilayer system exploiting the Purcell effect, with the double effect of 1) strongly enhancing the coupling of the electromagnetic wave associated with the incident g-ray to the optical states of the material and 2) restricting the angular distribution of the scintillation light to a small cone in the direction of the photodetector.These encouraging results make us confident that the implementation of such features in a second generation of metacintillators will bring significant benefits in terms of detection efficiency and timing resolution.

articleTitle: Developing 4D Tracking Technology Using Centimeter-Scale AC-LGAD Sensors and the FCFD ASIC
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: We present the results of studies aimed at developing 4D tracking technology for a wide range of physics experiments, including the Electron Ion Collider (EIC) and future Lepton Colliders. The studies focused on evaluating the performance of centimeter-scale AC-LGAD (AC-Low Gain Avalanche Detector) sensors and a new ASIC (Application-Specific Integrated Circuit) called the Fermilab Constant Fraction Discriminator (FCFD). For the AC-LGADs, we present the resolutions obtained with several prototypes, which reach simultaneous resolutions of 18 microns and 32 ps from strips of 1 cm length and 500 micron pitch. Regarding the FCFD, the mean time response for a wide range of signal amplitudes has been measured to be no more than 15 ps. This is orders of magnitude more precise than an uncorrected leading-edge discriminator-based measurement and effectively eliminates the need for a signal amplitude-based correction. Furthermore, the measured contribution to the time resolution from the FCFD ASIC is found to be 10 ps for signals with charges above 20 fC.

articleTitle: VRAIN-M: Monkey brain PET developed based on clinical PET with hemispherical geometry
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Brain PET imaging of nonhuman primates such as monkeys plays an essential role in research and development of new treatments and prevention methods for human brain diseases. Smooth translation of results in nonhuman primates to clinical application is important, and sharing the same detector technology among primates and clinical studies is ideal in terms of data comparability. Therefore, in this work, we aimed to realize monkey PET based on VRAIN (ATOX Co. Ltd., Japan), which is a recently-commercialized clinical brain-dedicated PET system with a hemispherical geometry. To allow monkey brain imaging in a sitting position, the monkey chair was placed in front of the gantry and the standard gantry angle was changed to 90° (horizontal to the ground) from the original 45°. A previous monkey PET system, SHR-7700 (Hamamatsu Photonics, K.K., Japan), which had been used for a long time in our institution, was replaced by the developed system (VRAIN-M). Then, imaging performance was evaluated based on the NEMA NU 4 standards; the image quality, the count rate characteristics, the TOF resolution and the small lesion detectability were assessed. VRAIN-M showed better contrasts of hot and cold regions with lower noise levels than SHR-7700. The peak NECR of VRAIN-M was 61 kcps and the TOF resolution was 234 ps at the 42 kBq/mL. A 4 mm hot sphere attached to a brain-sized cylindrical phantom could be visualized and a 1 mm rod could be identified in the condition without background activity. The first monkey brain imaging with <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">18</sup>F-FDG was conducted under anesthesia; brain cortex, caudate and putamen were clearly visualized. In conclusion, a high-performance monkey PET was realized based on well-proven technologies of the state-of-the-art clinical brain-dedicated PET, VRAIN.

articleTitle: Large Single-Crystalline Radiation-HardHigh Light Yield β-Ga2O3 Scintillators
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Despite years of research on materials, there is still a limited supply of suitable scintillators that can withstand intense radiation, have ultrafast decay times (around 10 nanoseconds), and produce high light yields (over 2000 photons per MeV). The baseline technology for most radiation intense Electron-Ion Collider Electromagnetic Calorimetry (EIC) EMCal uses the well-established and well-understood (but costly) lead tungstate (PbWO<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">4</inf>) crystal calorimetry. However, this material has shown significant radiation damage resulting in loss of collected signal. In this study, we show that scintillators based on gallium oxide (β-Ga<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf>O<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</inf>) have great potential for high count rate applications. We used the optical float zone (OFZ) technique to grow low-cost β-Ga<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf>O<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</inf> scintillators and tested several dopants and growth atmospheres to achieve a balance between fast primary decay time and light yield. We have obtained the highest light yields of 6476 ± 719 photons per MeV and decay times as fast as 12 nanoseconds. Additionally, we obtained an excellent energy resolution of 7% for 662 keV gamma rays using β-Ga<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf>O<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</inf>:Ce crystals. Interestingly, the gamma radiation resistance of β-Ga<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf>O<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</inf> crystals was better than that of the leading radiation-hard lead tungstate (PbWO<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">4</inf>) crystals. To test the radiation hardness of the scintillators, we subjected twenty-six scintillators made from the grown β-Ga<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf>O<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</inf> crystals to a <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">60</sup>Co gamma irradiation rate of 14 krad/h, with a total radiation dose of 2 Mrad, and found that their scintillation properties remained unchanged. These FZ-grown low-cost, non-hygroscopic, and high-density β-Ga<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf>O<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</inf> scintillators have the potential to replace existing scintillators in many applications, including nuclear and high energy physics experiments, as well as nuclear security.

articleTitle: Regularisation of the Origin-Ensemble algorithm with a "Beam Prior" for Particle-Range Verification
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: In particle therapy, potential range uncertainties prevent the full exploitation of ion-beam dose distribution in matter. Tomographic imaging methods such as in-beam PET or Compton-cameras (CC) have been proposed to infer range deviations through the detection of secondary radiation. However, very low counts, data truncation and strong background noise usually distort the reconstructed images. To mitigate these effects when using the Origin Ensemble (OE) reconstruction algorithm, we propose here to regularize OE using a priori information about the beam direction. We derive a prior term from a beam model and test the approach using Monte-Carlo simulations of therapeutic proton beams and a Compton camera. This regularisation term could be adapted to in-beam PET. We have simulated two water-filled phantoms with GATE, the second of which also contained an air cavity to induce a range shift. We reconstructed the images in 3D with various regularisation levels. The beam width required by the prior was first extracted from a reconstruction with few iterations and no regularisation. This gave results comparable to taking the ground-truth beam width. The distal edge shifts were quantified as the differences between the position of the inflection points from a sigmoid fit. First results show that OE with the beam prior can notably enhance image quality and improve the identification of the distal edge position. The outcomes were very sensitive to the regularization parameter. Medium regularization reduced the relative error of the shift from 51.7% without prior to 1.7%, but high regularisation increased the relative error again to 31.7%. Still, regularized OE outperformed conventional OE in most cases. Further studies are planned to characterize the dependencies of the results on the regularization parameter.

articleTitle: Positron Enhanced Prompt Gamma Imaging with a Modular CdZnTe Compton Camera
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: This paper introduces a Positron Enhanced Prompt Gamma Imaging (PEPGI) technique to improve the image reconstruction from a CdZnTe Compton Camera for use in dose reconstruction during proton therapy. PEPGI uses coincidence 511 keV gamma rays emitted from a target to locate the proton beam line using a Positron Emission Particle Tracking (PEPT) style algorithm, which is then used to improve Compton Camera Prompt Gamma Imaging (PGI) through Distance of Closest Approach (DCA) filtering. This filter eliminates noisy data by removing reconstructed gamma ray events that do not originate close to the proton beam line. The proposed method consists of three CdZnTe detectors configured to combine a dual head Compton Camera with a face to face detector setup in order to detect back-to-back 511 keV gamma ray pairs produced during positron annihilation. In this study, Monte-Carlo simulations, using the Geant4 toolkit, were used to verify the PEPGI process for proton therapy scenarios, in preparation for forthcoming measurements. This method should make image reconstruction more efficient and will require less data to produce.

articleTitle: Impact of Subsets and Iterations on PET Image Quality in TOF-OSEM Reconstruction
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: The use of ordered subsets to accelerate the convergence of expectation maximization led to the clinically feasible OSEM iterative reconstruction algorithm for PET imaging. While the use of subsets decreases image reconstruction time roughly proportional to the number of subsets, it is known to produce images that differ from reconstructions using no subsets. In this study, we modify the ASIM analytic simulator to provide noise-free time-of-fight emission sinograms. We reconstruct phantom images for varying noise levels and coincidence timing resolutions. Representative clinical reconstructions using 2 iterations and 34 subsets are compared to our test images, which have 16 iterations and 2 subsets. While the test images take much longer to compute, they show improved noise properties, evident in their visual appearance as well as their reduced variability of region-of-interest measurements and increased sensitivity index d’, which is computed using the mean and variance of lesion and background signal values.

articleTitle: Accelerated Deep Image Prior-based PET Image Reconstruction Using Two-Step Optimization
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) are a powerful tool for deep learning-based positron emission tomography (PET) image reconstruction to enhance PET image quality. Recent unsupervised learning-based PET image reconstruction methods have shown a better generalization performance with different PET tracers because they do not need to use any training dataset, such as pairs of high- and low-quality PET images. However, these reconstruction methods require very time consuming calculations. In this work, we proposed an accelerated deep image prior (DIP)-based unsupervised PET image reconstruction using two-step optimization to improve the computational speed as well as the reconstruction performance. The proposed reconstruction method consists of two steps: a pre-training step and a reconstruction step. In the pre-training step, the pre-training is performed using the magnetic resonance image as input data and the reconstructed image from measured PET data as target data. In the reconstruction step, the CNN weights are transferred from the first step network. And then, we adjust (or fine-tune) the network weights using measured data, and get the final reconstructed image in a few iterations. The proposed reconstruction method was evaluated using Monte Carlo simulation data of a human brain [<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">18</sup>F]FDG PET, and its results were compared with those of the maximum likelihood expectation maximization and the other DIP-based one-step reconstruction method. The simulation results showed that the proposed two-step reconstruction method has a faster computational time than the previous one-step method by substantially reducing the number of iterations while enhancing the reconstruction performance. Therefore, we concluded that our proposed two-step reconstruction method is a practical algorithm for DIP-based PET image reconstruction.

articleTitle: Development of a Diode-based Symmetric Charge Division Circuit for Brain-dedicated PET with High-Resolution Detector
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Positron emission tomography (PET) imaging has emerged as a valuable tool for diagnosing neurodegenerative diseases. However brain imaging with a conventional PET has limitations including high cost, limited spatial resolution, and insufficient sensitivity. Recently, brain-dedicated PET systems have been actively developed to achieve high performance for brain imaging.A detector module consisted of 14 × 14 array of 1.75 × 1.75 × 16 mm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</sup> LYSO, 8 × 8 array of 3 × 3 mm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sup> SiPM and light guide of 0.5 mm thickness was designed for high-resolution brain-PET. Optical glue was used to assemble the detector module. Application specific integrated circuits (ASICs) were used to process the signals of the detector module. A diode based symmetric charge division circuit reducing the 64 SiPM channels to 16 output channels was developed to simplify the signal processing circuits and to reduce the development costs. The performance of multiplexing circuit was evaluated by comparing that of the individual readout scheme of ASICs. The charge to digital convertor (QDC) integrator gain of ASIC was adjusted to higher than default value for energy restoration of multiplexed output signals. Flood histogram, energy resolution and photopeak positions were evaluated according to the bias voltage of SiPM.All the crystal pixels were clearly resolved and the flood histogram acquired using the multiplexing circuit was qualitatively similar to that acquired using the individual readout scheme. Average energy resolution was 8.4±1.3% which was better than that of the individual readout scheme, 9.8±1.7%. The average photopeak position was also higher with the multiplexing circuit than with the individual readout scheme. The results demonstrated that the proposed multiplexing circuit could provide high spatial resolution using light sharing scheme with reduced electronic cost. The results of coincidence timing resolution (CTR) and additional optimizations will be presented at the conference.

articleTitle: Head Motion Correction with Deep Learning-based Reconstruction Algorithm on uMI Panorama
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Head motion (HM) leads to a degradation in PET image quality and inaccurate quantification, which affects the results of clinical diagnosis. To solve this problem, both image-based and rawdata-based correction methods have been proposed. Image based-method is easy to implement, but it has two main drawbacks. Firstly, due to the uncertainty of motion, some very noisy frames will inevitably be discarded, which means that only a portion of all counts can be used during motion correction. Secondly, if the motion is frequent and irregular, HM correction is time-consuming because many motion-free frames must be reconstructed before motion correction. In the past few years, researchers have proposed various deep learning-based image enhancement/reconstruction methods, which can obtain good brain images even at low counts. In this work, we introduced a deep learning-based reconstruction method for HM correction. The ROI-based quantitative results demonstrated that the proposed method could get better signal-tonoise ratio and contrast without introducing quantification bias.

articleTitle: 3D Measurement of RI Distribution by 3-Row Multi-Pinhole Collimator Camera
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: We have focused on a multi-pinhole gamma camera to develop a device that, when combined with laparoscopic surgery, will allow rapid measurement of radiopharmaceutical distribution during surgery. For the development of this inspection device, we conducted an experimental evaluation of the feasibility of measuring the three-dimensional distribution of RI using three single-column pinhole collimator cameras. In this study, the ML-EM method was employed and the inspection area was set to be a cubic region of 50 mm x 50 mm x 50 mm. The region was divided into voxels with a position resolution of 10 mm and 5 mm, and the response was calculated assuming that each voxel was a source position. A collimator with four pinholes in a row and an image detector behind the collimator were used as the detector. Two geometrical arrangement of three detectors were considered, one parallel to the x-axis and the other in the xyz 3-axis. In addition, an experimental detector response was obtained using a <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">57</sup>Co source with a multi-pinhole collimator and a PP behind it. In the 3-axis case, the calculated values were used as input data for reconstruction, and convergence to the same position as the calculated results was obtained. The cause of the misalignment of the reconstructed positions in the parallel arrangement can be attributed to the geometrical configuration system of the three detectors. The results of these reconstructions of the experimental data confirm that it is possible to reconstruct the position of the source in three dimensions. From these results, it was confirmed that, as a measurement system, the xyz-axis type arrangement of the detectors provides more accurate results compared to the parallel arrangement.

articleTitle: Normalization approach for long axial field-of-view PET system
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: For PET system, it is necessary to update normalization factor regularly to keep latest estimates of sensitivity of each line of response (LOR). Conventional component-based normalization method need to scan the rotating rod source and a static cylindrical source which cover the whole axial field-of-view (FOV) of system to generate the all normalization factors. For PET system with a long axial FOV, it is unrealizable to update the normalization factor as normal. Therefore, we firstly proposed a complete set of schemes for long axial FOV system to generate all components of normalization. In our method, the geometry components were generated by scanning a short rod source, which rotating around the transverse center at one edge of axial FOV, an additional scale factor generated from simulation data was used to aliment the short rod data as long rod data. For detector efficiency components, a continually moving cylinder source was used instead of long axial cylinder. This method was performed on uMI Panorama GS. We also evaluated the uniformity of a long axial cylinder image, which has similar result with conventional way. The results show that our method greatly simplify the procedure of normalization calibration for long axial FOV PET system.

articleTitle: Pushing the Limits: Single Electron-Hole Pair Detection with an Ultra-Low Threshold Germanium Detector
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: This paper presents a novel germanium detector with an extremely low energy threshold and the capability of detecting a single electron-hole pair, making it suitable for exploring new physics such as low-mass dark matter searches and new properties of neutrinos. The detector utilizes phonon excitation of dipole and cluster dipole states when operated at liquid helium temperature at which residual impurities in the germanium detector undergo freeze-out from the conduction or valence band, creating localized states that form thermally stable dipole and cluster dipole states. These states have binding energies below 10 meV for both p-type and n-type germanium detectors. This low binding energy corresponds to about 2 THz of phonon frequency, making it suitable for infrared radiation detection. The detector generates single electron-hole pairs when the trapped charge carriers are released through deformation of dipole or cluster dipole states. These carriers are drifted under an electric field toward a point contact, where the highest electric field strength is established. Depending on the bias voltage, the amplification gain factor can be controlled from a factor of 100 to 1000 or higher, enabling the detector to overcome electronic noise. This detector can be sensitive to low-mass dark matter down to 1 keV/c<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sup> and low-energy neutrinos such as solar neutrinos and reactor neutrinos for coherent elastic neutrino-nucleus scattering. Additionally, the detector can provide finger fingerings for materials as an instrumentation tracker.

articleTitle: Simulation Study of Fast, High-Z, High-Transparency Nanocomposite Organic Scintillators for use in Timing Radiation Detectors
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Organic scintillators traditionally had limited use for x-ray and gamma ray detection because of their low stopping power. In addition, because of the near absence of photoelectric interactions they lack spectroscopy capabilities. Recent advances in material engineering have made it possible to efficiently embed high atomic number elements within plastic while retaining high transparency to light. These nanocomposite materials hold the promise of combining the fast rise and decay times of organic scintillators with the higher density, efficiency and photofraction of traditional inorganic scintillators. Furthermore, such nanocomposites are easily scalable to significant volumes without the difficulties involved with growing large inorganic crystals. Here we examine in simulation the expected response to gamma radiation of several new nanocomposite scintillators under development at UCLA. Three high-Z composites are studied: CdxZn1-xS/ZnS (CZS) which is a self-luminescent quantum dot (QD) and HfO2 and YbF3 which are non-luminescent high-Z compounds. The response of these nanocomposites loaded in plastic at several weight percentages are compared to common organic and inorganic scintillators: NE102 and LYSO. The coincidence timing response (CTR) will depend on the measured rise (τr) and decay (τd) times of these scintillators as well as the light yield (LY) and collection efficiency (ε) of a photo detector. Here we report on the photofraction and efficiency as determined through simulation and discuss our plan to measure CTR for these scintillators.

articleTitle: Comparative Analysis of Three Generations of LYSO:Ce Crystals for Medical Imaging Applications
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: The identification of new, high-performing scintillator compounds is critical to the advancement of time of flight positron emission tomography (TOF-PET). Here, we characterize 2nd, 4th, and 5th generation cerium-doped lutetium–yttrium oxyorthosilicate (LYSO:Ce) crystals developed and supplied by Luxium Solutions in terms of light yield and decay time using a photomultiplier tube and a Hamamatsu N5084 X-ray tube, respectively. Additionally, the coincidence resolving time (CRT) of the crystals is measured using Philips digital photon counter (DPC) 3200-22-44 detector modules at −25°C. The 4th and 5th generation crystals are shown to have similar light yields and decay times at room temperature, and outperform the 2nd generation crystals in all characteristics. The 5th generation crystal pairs had markedly better CRT values than their 4th generation counterparts. It remains to be investigated whether this is due to differing luminosity-temperature relationships, or the better matching of the emission spectrum to the wavelength-dependent photodetection efficiency (PDE) of the DPC with the 5th generation crystals. A determination of the contribution of the different factors to the observed CRT values using Cramer-Rao lower bound analysis is planned.

articleTitle: Photoelectric event discrimination with neural networks in metascintillators, beyond energy resolution concepts
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Energy resolution is a handy, dimensionless metric presenting the quality of energy conversions in a radiation detector. In novel systems such as the metascintillator-based ones, with variable light yield per event, this concept is inapplicable.In this work, we present the theoretical concept and simulation-based neural network application on the reconstruction of event interaction. We show the ability of neural networks to significantly improve the classification of event interaction as photoelectric or scattered, when more than two independent information channels (e.g. multiple SiPMs) are used. In this pilot work, we show the application of this concept for a 3x25.1x24 mm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</sup> semi-monolithic design using BGO-EJ232 and LYSO:Ce-EJ232Q as meta-scintillators. Regardless of the difference in light yield between the constituting components, ranging from the same to one order of magnitude, the neural network achieves above 95% precision in identifying photoelectric interactions. This is a significant improvement to the standard, energy spectrum based approach.

articleTitle: Performance studies of pixelated HPGe detectors for synchrotron applications
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: X-ray Absorption Fine Structure experiments conducted at synchrotron facilities are currently limited by the performance of the current generation of Silicon and Germanium detectors. In order to mitigate this limitation, the detector consortium of the European project LEAPS-INNOV has undertaken an ambitious R&D program devoted to develop a new generation of multi-element monolithic Germanium detectors for X-ray detection. Two detector prototypes are currently being developed and are expected to be commissioned end of 2024. After a brief introduction to the project, the paper will focus on the efforts to evaluate and optimize the performance of the prototypes using a full simulation chain developed within the framework of the LEAPS-INNOV project. These evaluations demonstrate that by combining a collimator, with cross-talk corrections and charge sharing rejection in the digital pulse processor, a signal-to-background ratio greater than 1000 could be attained in the energy range of interest from 5 keV to 100 keV.

articleTitle: The NOVO project - hybrid neutron/gamma-ray imaging for range verification in particle therapy
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Particle therapy has proven highly sensitive range uncertainties, making online range verification essential. Here we present a status update on work by the NOVO collaboration investigating range verification through simultaneous imaging of prompt gamma-rays and fast neutrons. The proposed system is designed to offer high detection sensitivity to range shifts with a smaller footprint and cost than current state-of-the art systems, where the proton range can be calculated by imaging elastically scattered neutrons and gamma-rays emitted from patient tissues during treatment. Both the detector design and feasibility of the NOVO concept were investigated using Monte Carlo particle transport simulations, supported by an experimental characterization of candidate scintillator materials. The detector design was chosen to maximize the number of image-able detected events under clinical treatment conditions. The feasibility of the method was demonstrated using a real patient case chosen from the Cancer Imaging Archive. Results show that a range-shift sensitivity of 1 mm per spot is attainable for clinical proton intensities with detector resolution effects included. Our findings demonstrate the potential of particle treatment verification through simultaneous fast neutron and prompt gamma-ray imaging, present a design for such a system, and reinforce its suitability in clinical application.

articleTitle: Deep Learning Aided Motion Correction for Low-Dose Brain PET
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: We have previously developed a deep learning (DL) aided PET motion correction method which successfully detected and corrected for head motion in the situation of a rapidly changing tracer distribution such as the initial tracer uptake period – immediately after injection. Here we extend this data driven method to a general low-dose scenario where tracer distribution is relatively constant but available counts are very low, such as for low-dose imaging. Data from four tracers were used ([<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">11</sup>C]-RAC, [<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">18</sup>F]-FDG, [<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">11</sup>C]-PBR, and [<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">11</sup>C]-DTBZ) to form a representative dataset for training and testing of a model capable of mapping low-count, high temporal resolution frames (acquired during a low-count period of the scan), to higher-count frames containing better structural features than the original low-count frames. The ability to recover a known motion trace that was artificially injected into low-count subject data was tested. The use of the DL model reduced the standard deviation of the motion estimation error from 0.5 mm and 0.8 degrees (when registration was performed without the aid of DL) to 0.3 mm and 0.5 degrees. These results were then validated with real human motion using the estimated motion from simultaneous fMRI acquisition as the ground truth.

articleTitle: Design and Characterization of HERMES a Discrete-time Electronics CMOS Sensor Prototype in 110 nm for Timing Applications
