publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: This article presents the design and characterization of a fully depleted CMOS sensor optimized for timing applications, focusing on the discrete-time and low-power discriminator. The prototype has been designed within the ARCADIA collaboration, and fabricated in a standard 110-nm CMOS process, with 1.2 V and 3.3 V transistors. Sensor and electronics share the same high-resistivity n-type substrate, which is post-processed at the foundry using a dedicated mask set for the implementation of the backside structures. This proprietary technique allows for the depletion of substrate volumes ranging from 50 and up to 500 $\mu m$ thick sensors. Each channel reads eight 50 x 50 $\mu m^2$ diodes grouped together, and consists of a charge sensitive amplifier and a CMOS inverter-based discriminator with a self-compensation of the offset. Measurements of the time over the threshold are supported for time-walk correction and achieved by a linear discharge of the discriminator's input node. Process variations have been reduced by adding degeneration transistors in the linear region to the stage. The discriminator occupies a small area and can be implemented in the deep p-well regions around the sensor electrode. The estimated power consumption of the stage is 12 $\mu W$, making it a suitable solution for monolithic pixel sensors with fast timing and low-power. Characterization of the electronics shows that the discriminator concept works and preliminary tests with a laser pulse generator demonstrate that the prototype can achieve a timing resolution better than 100 ps. We will present the results of a complete test campaign with laser and radioactive sources.

articleTitle: Soft X-ray MCP/Timepix Photon Counting Detectors for Synchrotron and FEL Applications
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Detection of soft X-ray photons requires some signal multiplication as charge produced by one photon is not sufficient enough for photon counting. Microchannel Plates (MCPs) can provide that multiplication with a factor up to several millions, enabling efficient thresholding of electronic noise in the readout. Various types of readouts can be used to decode the output signal from the MCP(s), among them Timepix Readout-Specific Integrated Circuit (ROIC) placed directly below MCP in the vacuum. The capability of these readouts to detect many simultaneous events substantially increases the count rate capabilities of these devices to GHz levels, with the detector still operating in a photon counting mode. In this paper, we present the results obtained with an MCP detector coupled to a quad Timepix and Timepix3 readout, forming a 512x512 matrix of 55 μm pixels. The spatial resolution of this detector is determined by the size of the MCP pore (5 μm on 6 μm centers for the current commercially available MCP technology). This high resolution is achieved in real time through the event cenrtoiding applied to each registered cluster on the Timepix readout. A couple of application examples of these detectors at Resonance Inelastic X-ray Scattering (RIXS) and X-ray Photon Correlation Spectroscopy demonstrate the unique capabilities of such devices for certain synchrotron-based experimental studies. Same MCP/Timepix detectors can be very attractive for the applications where the photon/electron/ion/neutron counting with high spatial and temporal resolution is required, such as Time of Flight experiments in energy-resolving neutron imaging at spallation neutron sources, fluorescence lifetime imaging and, if adapted for the electron detection, experiments on photoelectron spectroscopy.

articleTitle: Real-Time Feature Extraction for Readout ASICs: Algorithms and On-Chip Implementations
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Recent work has proposed the integration of machine learning (ML) algorithms within the front-end ASICs used for charge detection and readout in high-energy and nuclear physics experiments. The main goal is to alleviate data transfer bottlenecks to back-end FPGAs by only transmitting higher-level signal features. The latter may either be continuous-valued (e.g., amplitude, time constant, time of arrival) or discrete (e.g., particle ID). Several types of artificial neural networks (ANNs), such as multi-layer perceptrons (MLPs) and convolutional NNs (CNNs), have been optimized for this purpose. However, the performance of such networks on noisy data has not been compared with either fundamental accuracy limits (from estimation theory) or more conventional algorithms.This paper seeks to fill the gap by 1) deriving theoretical performance bounds; 2) comparing the performance of a variety of algorithms against these bounds; and 3) implementing the selected algorithms on-chip using high-level synthesis (HLS) tools. To this end, the paper derives theoretical error bounds for estimation of higher-level features from digitized waveform data. The performance of several algorithms, including matched filters, nonlinear recursive filters (NRF), nonlinear least squares (NLS), and ANNs, is compared with these bounds for an amplitude estimation task. Additional algorithms are developed and evaluated for 1) estimation of pulse shape parameters, and 2) pulse shape classification. An automated design flow is developed for implementing hardware-optimized versions of the algorithms in real-time on front-end ASICs starting from high-level code in MATLAB. Synthesis results in 65 nm CMOS technology are also presented.

articleTitle: Radiobiological-guided radiopharmaceutical therapy: Radiopharmacokinetic parameter optimization using PBPK modeling
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: We developed a whole-body physiologically based pharmacokinetic (PBPK) model to simulate and predict the distribution and uptake of PSMA-targeted radiopharmaceuticals in the tumor and normal tissues. Using this model, we evaluated different theoretical ranges of pharmacokinetic parameters, including association rate, serum flow density, half-life, internalization rate, ligand amount, surface permeability, receptor density, release rate, and serum protein binding rate. The resulting time-activity curves were used to calculate the biologically effective dose (BED) for the tumor, salivary gland, and kidney. We performed sensitivity analysis and observed that changing the parameters had varied effects on the BED values. We found that tumor volume, followed by ligand amount and tumor receptor density, are the most important factors in BED. Furthermore, radiopharmaceuticals therapy (RPT) using long half-life radionuclides will increase the BED in tumors and organs-at-risk (OARs). Similarly, changes in the pharmacokinetic parameters had varying impacts on the figure-of-merit BED (fBED), which we calculated as the ratio of the BEDs of OARs to tumor. Our results showed that changes the tumor receptor density had the most significant impact on fBED values, up to 30-40-fold, while changes in the association rate had the least impact limited to few percents. These findings highlight the importance of considering the effects of pharmacokinetic parameters when evaluating the efficacy of radiopharmaceuticals in targeted radiation therapy.

articleTitle: Overview and First Results of the EUSO-SPB2
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: The Extreme Universe Space Observatory on a Super Pressure Balloon II (EUSO-SPB2) has been built to PeV energy neutrinos from steady-state and transient astrophysical sources and will measure PeV and EeV cosmic rays. Observing ultra-high energy cosmic rays and very high energy neutrinos from space is a promising way to measure their extremely low fluxes by significantly increasing the observed volume.To reach its goals, the pioneering EUSO-SPB2 payload will fly two telescopes optimized for different observations. A Fluorescence Telescope (FT) with a PMT camera pointed in nadir will collect fluorescence light from cosmic ray extensive air shower (EAS) above 1 EeV. A Cherenkov telescope will point toward the earth’s limb. It can be tilted a few degrees above the limb to observe Cherenkov emission from PeV energy cosmic rays or tilted below the limb to search for Cherenkov emission from air showers induced through neutrino interactions in the earth’s limb. Since the CT is a novel instrument, optical background measurements for space neutrino observation are an important goal of the mission.Presently, the payload is in preparation for launch at the NASA balloon launch site in Wanaka NZ. The expected launch date is May 2023. Any data collected during the mission will influence and improve the development of a space-based multi-messenger observatory such as the Probe of Extreme Multi-Messenger Astrophysics (POEMMA). This contribution will present an overview of EUSO-SPB2 and its science goals and summarize all results as available, from the 2023 flight.

articleTitle: X-ray Irradiance Distribution for an Interferometer with a Curved Biprism Array
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: The development of interferometry-based X-ray phase contrast imaging systems that provide highly resolved X-rays with spatially-modulated intensity is enabling the full potential of X-ray optics to image phase, attenuation, and small angle scatter properties of soft tissue. In this work we present analytical formulations of a new hardware concept for X-ray phase contrast imaging wherein the phase grating is replaced with an array of Fresnel biprisms. We derive expressions for the irradiance distribution pattern of a biprism interferometer composed of a curved biprism array with multiple biprisms and multiple point sources. These expressions are used to plot fringe patterns for X-ray design parameters, including 1) size, number, and period of X-ray point sources; 2) biprism parameters of material composition, angle, number, and period; and 3) biprism array to X-ray source and detector distances. Analytical results show that the biprism interferometer provides a longitudinally-nonperiodic pattern of spatially modulated intensity different from the Talbot longitudinally-periodic pattern common in grating interferometry. The curvature of the biprism array brings a sharper longitudinal fringe pattern. Experiments are being performed to verify the analytical calculations for a biprism plastic material of SU-8 using a synchrotron source. X-ray biprism material has widely varied indexes of refraction relative to wavelength and thus the separation of the virtual sources and resulting interference fringe period also varies with X-ray wavelength. Our aim is to develop biprism interferometry imaging systems with excellent polychromatic performance that produce high-contrast fringes with spatially incoherent X-ray illumination. Biprism interferometry will potentially provide higher fringe visibility with better image quality to that of diffraction grating interferometry.

articleTitle: Continuous single-ended DOI measurement using highly (64:4) multiplexed signals
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: This study aims to investigate the feasibility of applying a multiplexing method that uses a high-pass filter and an artificial neural network proposed by the authors to a system. The accuracy of the proposed method was measured for four sampling rates ranging from 125MHz to 1GHz and three crystal configurations, including one-to-one coupling, light-sharing, and cDOI configuration. The accuracy was compared using the R<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sup> value between the true amplitude and estimated amplitude of the signal, and it was confirmed that the proposed method achieved an accuracy of 0.97 or higher in all situations. Furthermore, when measuring the DOI resolution using the cDOI configuration, the proposed method exhibited an accuracy of 0.97 or higher even under side irradiation conditions and achieved a DOI accurcacy of 74.4%. Therefore, it was confirmed that a sufficient DOI resolution could be obtained for an 8 × 8 SiPM array with a 3mm pitch attached with a 12 × 12 LSO array with a 2mm pitch using only four multiplexed readouts. This method guarantees high accuracy, sufficient multiplexing ratio, and operation at a suitable sampling rate for the system.

articleTitle: MR compatibility assesment of the edgeless preclinical PET insert: ScintoTube
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: The combination of Positron Emission Tomography (PET) with Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) constitutes a promising hybrid molecular imaging modality as it takes advantage of both the high sensitivity of PET for metabolic processes with the detailed anatomical and functional information from MRI.Simultaneous PET/MRI became a reality during the last decade and has already impacted the preclinical (small animal) field. This hybrid modality allows acquisition of perfectly registered images from both systems in a single session and thus, enables one to study different conditions and to develop accurate disease models that may help answering relevant question in the medical area. Yet, further improvements in the detector technology are still needed to completely exploit the advantages provided by these hybrid systems.Seeking the next generation of preclinical PET/MRI, we have proposed a novel PET insert design (ScintoTube) based on a single scintillator annulus to avoid gaps between detectors and thus, promote sensitivity while enhancing image resolution. We have already constructed the ScintoTube and it demonstrates excellent imaging capabilities.In this work we focus on the assessment of its MR-compatibility and on its validation to serve as an insert. The system has been evaluated inside both 7T and 9.4T Bruker MRI systems. The reported results demonstrate that there are no interferences between the systems. Hence, the ScintoTube is an attractive option for the next generation of preclinical PET/MRI.

articleTitle: An automated, efficient energy calibration procedure for detector arrays
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Energy calibration procedures are always required to retrieve the precise amount of energy released within any radiation detector in physics data acquisition mode. Using calibration sources emitting gamma rays of known energy, the underlying detector nonlinear calibration model can be tuned with respect to the position of the corresponding full-energy peaks in the energy spectrum. In between of the calibration energy values, however, the calibration curve highly depends on the assumed detector non-linearity model.This procedure for energy calibration of detector arrays is based on the previously mentioned procedure for single detector calibration, but takes into account not only the full-energy peak events with multiplicity one, but the entire set of interactions that release the full-energy lines of the calibration source into the detector array, regardless of their multiplicity level. As a result, i) the time required to collect the appropriate number of events is reduced, especially for high-energy calibration sources for which the full-energy peak efficiency of each single detector is typically low, and ii) the precision of the resulting calibration curves is improved due to the much greater variety of information collected. Once the full-energy peak positions are extracted from the multidimensional calibration spectra, the entire set of calibration curves can be automatically derived using a least mean square optimization procedure. The proposed method has been implemented and tested on a two-detector array with promising results. Further tests with state-of-the-art detector arrays in the field of nuclear physics are planned.

articleTitle: Preliminary evaluation of a compact, high sensitivity and high resolution small animal PET prototype
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: A compact, high sensitivity and high resolution small animal PET prototype was recently developed at Shenzhen Bay Laboratory (SZBL). This work aims to characterize the detector performance and preliminarily evaluate the system performance of the prototype PET scanner. Following the benchtop design idea, the overall size of the prototype was about twice the size of a commercial desktop PC case. The prototype consists of twenty detector modules arranged in two rings. The diameter is 80 mm and the axial FOV is 104.5 mm. Each detector module is comprised of a two-layer LYSO/BGO pixelated scintillator array, a 1 mm thick lightguide with oblique cuts, and two pieces of 8×8 Hamamatsu S14161-3050HS MPPCs. All MPPC channels were read out by PETsys TOFPET2 ASICs. The front layer (gamma ray entrance) is a 30×60 array of 0.79×0.79×5 mm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</sup> LYSO crystals. The back layer is a 20×40 array of 1.22×1.22×7.5 mm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</sup> BGO crystals. The complete detector module has overall dimensions of 26×52 mm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sup>.We used charge integration (QDC) and time-over-threshold (ToT) to discriminate the LYSO and BGO layers. All crystal pixels can be resolved thanks to the customized lightguide. The average energy resolution of the detector module was 11.5%± 2.9% for the LYSO layer events and 26.2%± 3.0% for the BGO layer events. With an energy window of 350–650 keV, the coincidence timing resolution (CTR) of the LYSO-LYSO, BGO-BGO and LYSO-BGO coincidences were 598 ps, 2.52 ns and 1.50 ns respectively, and the peak absolute sensitivity was 14.4% including the cross layer crystal scatter (CLCS) events and 11.2 % excluding CLCS events. The average spatial resolution in FWHM using OSEM reconstruction was 0.76 mm.

articleTitle: Novel Cascaded Ring Oscillator Vernier based TDC Architecture with a Feedthrough Reference Oscillator
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Time to digital converters (TDCs) are widely used in particle physics and medical imaging to determine the relative arrival time of photons and other particles. Vernier TDCs are one of the most attractive options due to their power consumption efficiency and their small footprint. We present our newly patented innovative architecture of cascaded-stage Vernier TDCs comprised of a feedthrough reference oscillator. This architecture lead to successive Vernier measurements that result in a lower number of cycles for the same dynamic range to resolution ratio (DRRR), leading to reduced conversion time and lower jitter. To validate this architecture, a test chip was designed in 0.18~μm TSMC technology, integrating four types of cascaded Vernier TDCs with an increasing number of stages. The performance of the chip was assessed using a modular test platform specifically designed for TDCs. For comparison purposes, all TDCs were tested with a LSB of 50~ps and a dynamic range of 20~ns. The experimental results demonstrate the highest gain in performance between 1 stage Vernier and 2 stage Vernier TDCs with the precision improved from 36~ps~rms to 21~ps~rms, the maximum number of turns from 110 to 25 counts and the dead time, from 266.4~ns to 76.5~ns, on average. Adding Vernier stages is only relevant for a higher DRRR. Therefore, the 3-stage and 4-stage Vernier TDCs also show performance gains, but improvements are limited.

articleTitle: Development of Coded Aperture Collimator for Drone - Based Radiation Imaging System
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Current process of deploying personnel in radiation accidents might result in casualties due to radiation exposure. Therefore, a drone-based radiation imaging system that can detect exposed radioactive isotopes in real-time from a remote location is necessary. The payload weight that can be carried by a drone is limited to only a few kilograms. In this study, we developed a lightweight and sensitive coded aperture collimator for gamma-ray detectors mounted on a drone. The pattern of the collimator was a mosaicked modified uniformly redundant array (MURA). To derive appropriate performance parameters for the detector, simulations were conducted. Ba-133 and Cs-137 sources were used to evaluate imaging capability for both low and high energy isotopes. Based on simulation results, experiments were conducted to compare the performance of collimator for Ba-133 and Cs-137 radiation sources. In the case of Ba-133, the use of an 8 mm-thick collimator resulted better than the 6 mm thickness collimator. Additionally, using the 8 mm thickness collimator, high-resolution gamma images with a 7-degree angular resolution could be obtained when imaging Ba-133 and Cs-137.

articleTitle: Conceptual Design of a Multi-Channel Distributed Receiver Electronics for Photomultipliers and Gas Detectors
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: In this paper, we present a new concept of ASIC-based receiver electronics, specifically designed for particle detectors with multiple analog channels. The electronics will include both analog and digital parts. The analog unit will contain a tunable low-noise transimpedance amplifier with variable input impedance (10 – 100 Ω) followed by a pipelined SAR ADC with programmable resolution (7 – 10 bit) and sampling rates (up to 1 GS/s), as well as a time-to-digital converter (target resolution ≤ 20 ps). The digital unit, will act as a data concentrator, and can interface up to 64 analog channels. It extracts various features from the digitized input signal (e.g. Time-over-Threshold, Time-of-Arrival, signal samples, wavelets, etc.), concentrates the data to reduce the bandwidth and stream the data to the central data unit. In this concept, two types of data interfaces are proposed for data streaming. Currently, 28 nm CMOS technology has been selected for prototyping, but other technology nodes might be used in the future.

articleTitle: 4D (X,Y,Z,E) Event Parameter Estimation in a Hybrid Modular Gamma Camera
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: We are developing a 4D maximum-likelihood gamma-ray parameter-estimation algorithm that will be used for the hybrid modular gamma cameras designed for AdaptiSPECT-C that use a combination of silicon photomultipliers (SiPMs) and photomultiplier tubes (PMTs) for optical readout. Energy estimation is usually based on the sum of the signals of the light sensors in the camera. This works when all of the light sensors are of the same size and shape. Due to the hybrid combination of light sensors in AdaptiSPECT-C, energy estimation based on the sum of the signals is no longer possible due to strong dependence on the position and depth-of-interaction (DOI). In this work, we show, using 3D simulated MDRFs at a reference energy, that energy estimation is dependent on 3D position estimation. Therefore, a fast and reliable maximum-likelihood x,y,z and energy parameter estimation algorithm is needed for these cameras. We investigate whether the energy should be estimated simultaneously with the 3D position in a 4D contracting grid or whether it is equally effective to alternate between contracting 3D position and 1D energy grids.

articleTitle: Development of a Portable Self-Collimation Gamma Camera for Super-Fast Intraoperative Imaging
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Gamma cameras have a growing presence in various intraoperative applications, but current designs often suffer from drawbacks such as weight and low imaging speed. These limitations stem from the mechanical collimator used for imaging, which adds significant weight and impedes sensitivity. To address these challenges, we recently proposed a novel gamma camera design featuring a 3-D mosaic patterned self-collimation imaging detector. In this work, we aim to develop a portable intraoperative gamma camera using this design and evaluate its performance in representative clinical scenarios.Our gamma camera consists of a 3-D mosaic patterned scintillator block sandwiched between two SiPM boards. The scintillator block contains 16 × 16 interspaced scintillator bars, each measuring 2.0 mm (x) × 2.0 mm (y) × 20.0 mm (z). Each scintillator bar contains 5 interspaced GAGG(Ce) scintillator and K9 glass elements, with each element measuring 2.0 mm (x) × 2.0 mm (y) × 2.0 mm (z). The scintillator block is coupled to 16 × 16 SiPM arrays on both ends, enabling 3-D event position determination through the readout signals of the two SiPMs on each end. The imaging detector is mounted in a hand-held optically shielded case that weighs only 1.0 kg.Our gamma camera demonstrates an average sensitivity of 1700 cps/MBq in a 10 cm × 10 cm field of view at a 10 cm distance. The camera can resolve two point sources spaced 7 – 9 mm apart throughout the entire field of view. In a phantom study mimicking sentinel lymph node localization, the camera accurately detected lymph nodes with 20 μCi activity in less than 2 s imaging time. Future work will involve pre-clinical experiments to further evaluate the camera's capabilities.

articleTitle: Single Event Effects and Total Ionizing Dose Sensitivity of a 0.15 µm Antifuse FPGA
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: This work includes measurements of the single event effects and cumulative effects induced in the antifuse FPGA by radiation. Several FPGAs were irradiated with 24 MeV protons and X-rays. During irradiations, the dose rate values were between 0.1 and 1 krad/s and the maximum value of the total ionization dose was 8 Mrad. For these dose rates, the radiation-induced leakage currents were observed in the FPGA power consumption. This induced leakage current was measured above a non-fixed threshold which depends on dose rate. At a very high dose rate of 1 krad/s, the threshold value is about 260 krad. We have also measured a very fast room-temperature annealing process. With the FPGA operating continuously after the beam exposure, the annealing process restored the core current in one FPGA from 470 mA to 60 mA in about 38 hours. During the first 3-4 months after irradiation, the core current continued the descending trend, and the relative difference with respect to the current before irradiation shrinks to 30%-50%. Using dedicated firmware, the FPGA logic resources (Flip-Flops, RAM Blocks, and I/O blocks) were monitored for single event effects. Only in the most extreme conditions tested, a low number of logic errors (3 errors) was found for a fluence of (2.5 ± 0.5) • 10<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">13</sup> protons/cm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sup>, hence the upper limit of the cross-section was computed to be 2.6 • 10<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">-13</sup> cm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sup>/DUT. The RAM resources were determined to be prone to single-event upsets, and the cross-section value was determined to be (3.72 ± 0.8) • 10<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">-14</sup> cm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sup>/bit. The FPGA will operate with no visible effects in a typical radiation environment from space or high-energy physics experiments. The expected dose rates for experiments are on order of 0.1 rads/s, and any effects will be mitigated through a rapid room-temperature annealing process.

articleTitle: Development of Pipe Wall Thinning Inspection Method by Energy Spectrum of Backscattered Gamma Rays
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Inspection of plant piping is important to ensure the integrity of the plant, and various types of inspections are performed. We propose a new inspection method by the energy spectrum of back-scattered gamma-rays when pipes are irradiated with gamma rays. Gamma-rays with energy around 1 MeV mainly cause Compton scattering when incident on an object, and produces scattered gamma-rays. The energy of the scattered gamma-ray is derived by the energy of the incident gamma-ray and the scattering angle. If the incident direction of the gamma-ray and the final scattering direction are fixed, the energy of the gamma ray scattered in the final scattering direction differs depending on the number of scattering. Since the probability of multiple scattering is determined by the geometry, especially thickness, of the scattering object. The thickness of the scatterer can be estimated by the ratio of one-time scattering to two-time scattering. This method does not need to peel off any insulation material, and has advantage of allowing greater flexibility in the installation of the inspection device. Gamma rays were irradiated to iron plates and pipes in the Cobalt 60 irradiation facility at Nagoya University, and energy spectra of scattered gamma rays in the 90-degree direction were acquired with a CdTe detector. The ratio of the counts corresponding to one-time scattering and two-time scattering was derived from obtained spectrum. In all results, the ratio values increased with increasing thickness. It was also observed that the change in the counting ratio tends to plateau when the thickness exceeds 10 mm. This suggests that pipe wall thinning inspection will be possible for plate thicknesses of around 10 mm by our proposed method.

articleTitle: Energy Sharing Estimation in Metascintillators with Neural Networks
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Energy sharing is at the core of the metascintillator detection approach which combines different scintillator types to provide both fast emission and good stopping power necessary for time-of-flight PET. Contrary to single bulk scintillators, the detection signals in metascintillators are imprinted with a more complex, yet information-rich set of features created by the stochastic nature of the energy sharing process between the scintillator types. This complexity raises the need of an accurate signal analysis to retrieve information about the interaction in the detector. In this work, we propose the first steps towards using neural networks (NN) to estimate the energy sharing in metascintillators. Using GATE Monte Carlo simulations, we assessed the energy sharing prediction accuracy with a NN for a BGO/EJ232 metascintillator. The NN was fed with either crossing times of simulated waveforms at various thresholds or with time-over-thresholds values. The NN is able to predict energy sharing with good accuracy with coefficients of determination (R<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sup>) against real energy sharing values in the range of ~0.8–0.9, even when simulating SiPM crosstalk, electronic noise and low-pass filtering. Two thresholds yielded good accuracy—without much improvement using more thresholds—which can facilitate hardware implementation. This study thus paves the way to better exploit time information in metascintillator signals to further push their performance.

articleTitle: Hyperspectral Imaging based Characterization and Identification of Sintered UO2 Fuel Pellets
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Hyperspectral Imaging (HSI) is a well-established technology able to capture the same spatial scene or image in hundreds of different wavelengths across the electromagnetic spectrum, covering not only the visible but also the shortwave infrared range (1000-2500nm), potentially revealing information otherwise invisible to the human eye. In this work, we explored whether HSI technology can be used for the fast-non-invasive characterization and identification of sintered UO<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf> fuel pellets. Preliminary experiments included the imaging of the pellets, revealing their spectral responses. These show promising features that could be used for their identification, where two different groups of pellets, pure and doped, seem to be easily recognized based on their spectral response. The experiments included a pixel-wise classification map generated via the Spectral Angle Mapper (SAM) technique in which the pure and doped pellets are successfully identified.

articleTitle: Coincidence window effects on the image quality of rotational PET systems
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: The accuracy of PET imaging heavily relies on the reconstructed image quality, which can be affected by several factors, including the coincidence time resolution (CTR) of the PET system. PET systems that use the patented dual rotation technology of easyPET, offer a cost-effective and portable solution with high resolution capabilities for preclinical and low activity applica- tions. Due to a reduced number of detectors, the system has a lower sensitivity which helps to reduce the effects of a large coincidence window for low activities.This study aimed to investigate the coincidence window effects on the image quality of this PET system, by comparing the performance of expensive commercial state-of-the-art electronics, which enables scans with CTR of 300 ps, with a slower but cheaper electronics, with a CTR of 40 ns. The simulation data shows that the number of events detected is 70% higher for the 40 ns coincidence window, when compared to the 300 ps, for a mean activity of 400 μCi.To evaluate the CTR effect on the image quality, a NEMA IQ 2008-NU-4 phantom was filled with 300 uCi of 18 F and simulated over a period of 7 hours (to compensate the system low sensitivity). The recovery coefficient(RC), uniformity and spilled ratio (SOR) were measured. The images were reconstructed with dedicated GPU LM-MLEM algorithm, with voxel volume of 0.57 mm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</sup> and 25 iterations. A energy window of 30% was applied at 511 keV and the listmode data was decay corrected and normalized. The image quality metrics did not show relevant difference between the 300 ps and 40 ns CTR.

articleTitle: Automated Diastolic Dysfunction Diagnosis in Gated Myocardial Perfusion Imaging SPECT using Deep Learning
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Cardiovascular diseases are a leading cause of death globally. Diastolic and systolic function are important indicators of the heart, with diastolic dysfunction being a common early sign of left ventricular dysfunction in many cardiac diseases. Early identification and appropriate treatment of diastolic dysfunction can prevent heart failure. While Doppler echocardiography is commonly used to assess diastolic function, recent studies have shown that GSPECT-MPI can also be used to assess both diastolic and systolic function and detect the presence and extent of coronary artery disease. This study aims to use deep learning algorithms to classify patients into normal and abnormal categories based on End-Systole (ES) and End-Diastole (ED) GSPECT-MPI images in single-view and multi-view modes to diagnose diastolic dysfunction. This study examined 266 individuals using GSPECT-MPI. The patients were divided into normal and abnormal groups based on the echocardiography results. The data was split into training (70%), validation (15%), and test (15%). Deep learning networks were used with ResNet152V2, and an aggregation Spatial Pyramid Pooling (SPP) method was used to integrate ED and ES images as inputs for the network. ResNet152V2-SPP was the best model (AUC: 0.73, sensitivity: 0.67, specificity: 0.79). The results showed that the ResNet152V2 model performed better when fed from the multi-view mode using SPP. The study suggests that ED and ES images may provide complementary information in assessing heart function. The model has the potential to reduce physician workload and save time.

articleTitle: Image Performance Evaluation of a Mobile DTS System Using a Uni-axially Moving Digital X-ray Source Array
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: In this study, we developed a mobile digital tomosynthesis(DTS) system composed of a moving carbon nanotube(CNT)-based digital X-ray source array and a fixed detector for extremity diagnosis such as hand, foot and knee. This novel design allows to reduce a source-to-detector distance(SDD) of only 400 mm in this study and to achieve a compact size of the system. This study aims to quantitatively and qualitatively evaluate the image performance of this system with the strengths of low dose and mobility. We measured the performance of reconstructed images according to EUREF's Digital Breast Tomosynthesis Image Performance Evaluation Protocol. In-plane MTF was evaluated using a 25 µm diameter tungsten wire placed between 10 mm and 5 mm PMMA phantoms, range from 1.59 to 2.29 of MTF<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">0.5</inf> frequency in the source array(x)-direction and between 0.84 and 2.55 in the array moving(y)-direction. Z-resolution was measured with 1 mm diameter tungsten balls in 5 mm thick PMMA phantom. The average z-resolution of 4.55 mm was calculated by FWHM of ball spread profile in the z-direction without any geometry distortion. In homogeneity evaluation with 45 mm thick PMMA phantom, maximum deviation of ROI_mean and ROI_SNR values are 2% and 9% of the average respectively, and both are within the limiting values of ± 15%. The maximum deviation of neighboring ROI_variance was 19% and smaller than the limiting value of 30%. The reconstructed images of hand, ankle and knee phantoms were evaluated qualitatively. We also measured entrance surface dose(ESD), which is the sum of dose received from individual projections using a dosemeter placed at the center of the detector. The ESDs for hand, foot and knee configurations were equivalent to ones of 2D radiography. The image evaluation results show that our DTS system has been successfully developed.

articleTitle: A 0.5 mm Resolution Mouse Brain PET for Simultaneous Two-Photon Excitation Fluoroscopy
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Simultaneous positron emission tomography (PET) and two-photon excitation fluorescence (TPEF) imaging has a potential to decode mouse brain function from molecular to cellular levels. In this study, we developed a third generation small animal PET scanner that can be combined with the TPEF microscope for simultaneous PET and TPEF imaging of mouse brain. This scanner has two open spaces, one is for mouse placing, and the other one is for inserting the TPEF microscope. The scanner has a 52.5 mm inner diameter and 24.5 mm axial FOV. The LYSO crystal array has the pixel pitch of 1 mm and total thickness of 15 mm. There are two detector rings each of which has 16 DOI detectors. Each DOI detector consists of a 3-layer staggered LYSO crystal array and 4×4 SiPM (Hamamatsu, S14161-3050HS-04, Japan) array with a pixel pitch of 3.2 mm. The SiPM anode signals are multiplexed using a resistive network and then digitized by a custom-made DAQ. The coincidence data are generated by using coincidence process software with a coincidence window of 10 ns. The measured spatial resolutions at the center and 5 mm radial offset are 0.89 mm and 0.87 mm for FBP, respectively. Using the OSEM, we are able to separate rods of 0.5 mm in diameter. The peak absolute sensitivity is 1.35% with an energy window of 400-600 keV. In conclusion, we successfully developed the small animal PET scanner that can be combined with a commercial TPEF microscope. We are ready to carry out the simultaneous PET and TPEF imaging of a mouse brain using hybrid radio-optical tracers.

articleTitle: Semiconductor sensor readout integrated circuit with in-pixel artificial neural network for pulse amplitude measurement
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: We present a novel pixel readout integrated circuit (IC) with an on-chip and in-pixel artificial neural network (ANN) for X-ray imaging applications. The IC is optimized for the silicon sensor response to X-ray photons in the 4 – 12 keV energy range. The analog front-end consists of a charge-sensitive amplifier and shaper with a target noise level of 60 el. rms. The signal is digitized by a 6-bit successive approximation analog-to-digital converter at a 5 MHz sampling rate. The digitized data is processed by a Multilayer Perceptron ANN with 5 layers and ~420 parameters, which achieves high measurement resolution and classification accuracy. The IC is designed in CMOS 28 nm technology and has a structure of 8 × 8 square-shaped pixels with 200 µm pitch. We verify the performance of the IC in hardware and demonstrate an error below 1% and a detection efficiency of 100%.

articleTitle: A Feasibility Study on Deep Learning Denoising for Standard-Dose Cardiac-Gated SPECT Images
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Cardiac-gated studies in myocardial perfusion imaging with SPECT are known to suffer from increased noise owing to lowered data counts within individual gate frames. In this work, we investigate the feasibility of applying a deep learning (DL) denoising network for noise suppression in cardiac-gated studies. With the lack of ground truth images in clinical cardiac-gated studies for DL network training, we employ a denoising network that were pre-trained instead on ungated imaging data in reduced-dose studies based on their equivalence in data counts. In the experiments we demonstrated this approach on a set of 50 clinical gated acquisitions. The quantitative results demonstrate that the proposed approach can effectively improve the uniformity of the left ventricular (LV) wall and suppress the frame-to-frame variations caused by imaging noise in gated images. Moreover, the DL processed images also yield volumetric measurements of the LV consistent with reconstruction with conventional Gaussian filtering

articleTitle: Deconvolution-based Image Recovery for Dynamic Study With Multi-pinhole SPECT System
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Single photon emission CT(SPECT) can visualize a function of organs with a radiopharmaceutical like a positron emission CT(PET). In the case of a PET system, many scintillation detector locate around a patient, and measure two 511 keV gamma rays which enter the detectors at the same time. On the other hand, conventional SPECT systems require detector rotation, which degrades the time information and prevents us from performing a dynamic study. To cope with this issue, we have studied a multi-gamma camera SPECT system attached with a multi-pinhole collimator. This system enables a stationary data acquisition, and a dynamic study can be realized. However, this system uses pinhole collimators, as a result of it, blurring occurs on the projection image depending on the size of a pinhole. To improve the resolution of a reconstructed image, we have proposed a deconvolution-based resolution recovery method in the previous paper. In this paper, we applied the method to the dynamic study with a SPECT system. The stationary SPECT system used in this study has eleven pinholes and the number of gamma-camera positions was six. The diameter of a pinhole was 5 mm. For simplicity, we used a phantom in which an activity in a small sphere inside a large sphere varied according to time. To evaluate the feasibility of our proposed method, we compared our method with the conventional resolution recovery method with 7rays and 21-rays methods. The performance of our proposed method was quantitatively evaluated with the contrast ratio defined with the activity of a target area and outside the target area. Simulation results showed the feasibility of our proposed method.

articleTitle: Growth and Performance of Co-Doped Tl2LiYCl6 Scintillator Crystals
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: We are reporting on the growth and performance of co-doped Tl<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf>LiYCl<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">6</inf> (TLYC) crystals grown by the Bridgman method at Fisk University. In recent years cerium doped TLYC has emerged as a promising dual-mode scintillation detector material for many defense and homeland security applications. For the past few years Fisk University has successfully grown and produced large diameter (≥ 1-inch diameter) TLYC:Ce crystals with consistent growth yield and scintillation performance. Good gamma-ray energy resolution as well as good neutron-gamma pulse height discrimination (PSD) are regularly obtained. We have recently started to grow co-doped TLYC crystals in an attempt to further improve growth and scintillation properties.16-mm diameter TLYC crystals co-doped with lanthanides and alkali metal halides have been grown and characterized. A sample sent to Radiation Monitoring Devices, Inc. for neutron-gamma PSD measurement results in a figure of merit better than that of TLYC:Ce. Characterization results from the growth of large diameter TLYC crystal co-doped with lanthanides and alkali metal halides, as well as radiation tolerance of packaged co-doped TLYC crystal, will be presented.

articleTitle: Fused multimodal radiomics with deep learning for predicting EGFR-sensitizing mutations based on 18F- PET/CT images
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) is one of the most common driver genes in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), including EGFR-resistance mutations and EGFR-sensitizing mutations. Meanwhile, only NSCLC patients with EGFR-sensitizing mutations exhibit a positive response to tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs). Radiomics-based deep learning methods provide noninvasive technologies for predicting EGFR-sensitizing mutations in NSCLC patients. In our work, we fused multimodal radiomics data from 18F-FDG PET/CT images with a deep learning algorithm to predict EGFR-sensitizing mutations in NSCLC patients. Specifically, 202 NSCLC patients scanned with 18F-FDG PET/CT were collected. Traditional radiomics features were extracted by PyRadiomics software, while deep features were extracted by a residual neural network from PET/CT images. We used the least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO) and support vector machine (SVM) to reduce redundant features and predict EGFR-sensitizing mutations. Additionally, we introduced different deep models and imaging modalities to compare the predictive performance. Our results showed that the fused ResNet-based deep and traditional features demonstrated excellent prediction performance. In addition, multimodal PET/CT radiomics-based methods might predict mutations better than CT-only and PET-only methods.

articleTitle: Monitoring of Scattered Photons in Radiotherapy for Cavity Movement Detection in Human Body
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Radiation therapy is one of the most commonly selected treatment for malignant tumors. Linac accelerator sends X-rays to cancerous tissue from outside of human body. However, the cancerous tissue changes its position in the body due to respiration, pulsation of the circulatory system, and movement of the intestinal tract. Thus, irradiation is performed while confirming the position of the tissues in the body. Although simple methods for monitoring the positional changes of cancer tissue due to the movement of the respiratory and circulatory systems have already been established, it is difficult to monitor the positional changes of cancer tissue due to the movement of the intestinal tract, especially the movement of the air cavity (void) in the intestinal tract without taking the CT. Therefore, we focused on scattered therapeutic X-rays and proposed an application of imaging with scattered X-rays to the detection of bowel movements. In our proposed method, the cancer tissue is regarded as the source of scattered X-rays because the therapeutic X-ray beam always penetrates through the cancer tissue, and a radiation detector is placed on the extension line connecting the cancer tissue and the intestinal void around the cancer tissue. To investigate the possibility of the above monitoring method, we irradiated a plastic phantom by a beam of gamma rays from cobalt-60 source. Spectrum of the scattered gamma rays was measured by a CdTe detector. We confirmed that the intensity of the scattered gamma rays changed by changing the position of the void at a depth of 0 cm to 5 cm from the phantom surface. This indicates that monitoring the intensity of scattered gamma rays can detect the movement of a 1 cm thick void in the phantom in this region. Next step of this study is to demonstrate the detection of void migration at deeper region using Linac X-rays, which are used in actual medical treatments.

articleTitle: Computing Null Space Hallucinations on Simulated SPECT Image Reconstructions
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Iterative reconstruction techniques have been integrated into clinical practice for emission tomography reconstruction. While these techniques have shown promising results in image reconstruction, there remains a lack of clarity regarding which parts of the image are reliably estimated and which are not. Currently, there is a missing measure to differentiate between epistemic and aleatoric errors. One approach to address this issue is to estimate the null space of the imaging model for a given object. In this study, we utilize a previously proposed adaptation of the Landweber iteration, known as the Wilson-Barret method, for calculating the null space of a noiseless reference phantom and for a corresponding reconstruction of a simulated phantom. Using the calculated null spaces we can apply a method for creating hallucination maps, that allow derivation of the epistemic error. Our findings suggest that the hallucinated components of the image are primarily attributable to the edges or high-frequency components of the phantom as well as the center of the phantom, which is consistent with expectations.

articleTitle: High-Z sensors for synchrotron sources and FELs
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: High-Z compound semiconductors aim to replace silicon as sensor material for X-ray energies above 15 keV thanks to their superior absorption efficiency. However, compared to silicon, high-Z sensors still lack in several aspects such as homogeneity, charge transport properties, charge trapping (leading to polarization and afterglow effects), long ranged fluorescence photons, and others.The aim of this study is to identify sensor materials that can widen the usable energy range of our detector systems at synchrotron sources and free electron lasers (FELs) towards higher photon energies. The main characterization tool was the 75 μm pitch JUNGFRAU charge integrating detector in combination with various high-Z sensors. As charge integrating detectors allow the direct measurement of the collected charge of every single photon with a high spatial resolution, these detectors offer interesting insights into temporal as well as spatial sensor effects which affect the charge collection.As one of the major challenges of the upcoming 4<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">th</sup> generation of synchrotrons or FELs are very intense and potentially pulsed photon beams, the sensors needs to be able to reliably measure highly intense signals and to have no afterglow phenomena after illumination. Measurements performed at the Material Science (MS) beamline of the SLS using photon fluxes up to 5×10<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">10</sup> ph/(mm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sup>• s) and at the FXE beamline of the EuXFEL focused on understanding the dynamic behavior (like signal stability, polarization and afterglow effects) of various high-Z sensor materials like GaAs:Cr (from different suppliers), as well as CdTe (Ohmic and Schottky type) and CdZnTe.The presentation will give an overview of the specific needs of the sensors for the different photon sources and will show how the results obtained fulfill these requirements.

articleTitle: Toward developing a gapless multi-layer PET scanner based on the semi-monolithic crystals
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Recent research into positron emission tomography (PET) scanner has put an emphasis on obtaining the best possible spatial resolution with high sensitivity. Our group has recently focused on developing a multi-layer semi-monolithic based detector module with side photodetector readout system, which can provide fine spatial resolution while preserving sensitivity. Another important issue for producing high quality images is to mitigate the degradation caused by dead space regions. Minimizing dead space not only can increase the detection efficiency, but can improve sampling of the object, improving the resolution of the images and reducing artifacts. Using semi-monolithic crystals can reduce the loss of sensitivity due to the dead space introduced by the reflectors between pixelated crystals. However, layered modules with the side readout technique need more space between crystal blocks, which may result in larger dead space. In this study, we introduce a novel configuration of a PET system based on the layer structure module that overcomes this challenge and can be considered as a gapless PET system. This configuration is designed based on the best possible distribution of the detector space by moving and rotating different layers relative to each other. Results from simulation of a cylindrical volume source in a PET system with 24 modules shows an increased ratio of 19% and 23% for the number of detected coincidences in the proposed gapless design compared to the normal configuration for crystal thicknesses of 3.72 and 6.00 mm, respectively. The proposed approach can be beneficial for PET scanners seeking high performance in spatial resolution and sensitivity simultaneously at the expense of the complexity of the detector module arrangement.

articleTitle: Effect of Polynomial Gain Correction on the MTF and NPS of an X-ray microtomography system
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: X-ray microtomography systems for small animal studies provide images with high spatial resolution, allowing fine details of small structures to be observed. In the Biomedical Imaging Laboratory of the Institute of Physics at UNAM, a rotating-base micro-CT system was developed, consisting of an Oxford Apogee Series 5000 X-ray tube and a Radicon Shad-o-box 2k flat panel detector using a Gd<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf>O<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf>S screen. In this work, the transfer functions of the detector and the system were analyzed, for which projections were obtained from an edge phantom, a spatial-resolution phantom and a uniform phantom. The projections were corrected by two methods: the standard flat field correction (FFC) and the less common polynomial gain correction (PGC), and from them tomographic reconstructions were obtained. Image quality was evaluated in terms of spatial resolution and noise, by calculating the modulation transfer function (MTF) and noise power spectrum (NPS) at both the system (tomographic) and detector (projection) levels. It was observed that the spatial resolution of the micro-CT system was 95 μm for FFC and 105 μm for PGC, at a magnification of 1.35, using the FDK reconstruction algorithm with a Hamming filter and 0.8 cut-off frequency. Correspondingly, the resolution of the flat panel detector was 53 μm for FFC and 60 μm for PGC. However, the PGC method allowed to significantly reduce the magnitude of statistical noise in the images throughout the range of spatial frequencies studied and presented good overall performance in terms of image quality, by considerably improving noise properties with a modest loss of spatial resolution. Further studies will include the analysis of a Hounsfield units calibration phantom and the effect of iterative reconstruction algorithms.

articleTitle: The Readout Electronics for the JUNO-TAO Central Detector
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: The TAO (Taishan Antineutrino Observatory) detector aims at a precise measurement of the reactor neutrino spectrum as a reference for JUNO. The needed high energy resolution is obtained exploiting high photon detection efficiency SiPMs for the readout of the liquid scintillator in the Central Detector. In this work we present the readout electronics based on low-noise, high-speed front-end boards (Front-End Boards, FEBs) for large area SiPMs developed for the JUNO-TAO experiment. The FEBs are able to manage the signals coming from a 25 cm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sup> SiPM tile, showing single photoelectron resolution better than 13% and dynamic range up to 250 p.e.. A total of 4024 boards, with two output each, are needed to instrument the TAO detector that has roughly 10m<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sup> of detection area. Due to the number of SiPM elements, to avoid an extremely high dark count ratio, the detector will work at -50° C inside a cryostat filled with LAB. The cryostat is equipped with 8 custom flanges allowing the entrance in the cryostat of the supply cables for the FEBs (for a total power of about 1.5 kW) and the exit of the 8048 output signal cables to be connected to the Front End Controllers (FECs) that are hosted on uTCA crates outside the criostat. Each FEC manages up to 128 ADC channels, each ADC has a maximum sampling rate of 250 MHz with 12-bit resolution, or 125 MHz with 16-bit, which are configurable. A dedicated trigger and DAQ system will filter and record occurring events, rejecting dark count events.

articleTitle: Prototype of the digital hardware trigger system for TAO central detector
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: The Taishan Antineutrino Observatory (TAO) is a high-resolution reactor neutrino experiment designed to measure the fine structure of the reactor neutrino energy spectrum. There are totally 4024 silicon photomultipliers (SiPM) sensor tiles used to detect the photons generated by nuclear reactions of neutrinos in gadolinium-doped liquid scintillator. The dark noise of SiPMs leads the total counting rate reaching up to 1GHz to the detector system, while the reactor neutrino experiment effective physical event rate is only about 520Hz. How to select the rare physics events among large amount of noises correctly and effectively in real time becomes a challenge for the trigger system design. In order to reduce unnecessary system resource consumption, a digital hardware trigger system based on the mTCA platform is proposed according to the data characteristics of TAO. A flexible and reconfigurable two-stage trigger processing architecture is adopted to realize the aggregation, caching, trigger selection, and data upload of the raw data from the TAO front-end electronics. Preliminary tests with configurable simulation data show that the trigger system can correctly extract the physical event data from the raw data, meeting the requirements of TAO.

articleTitle: A High-Resolution Semi-Monolithic Slab Detector tailored for Pre-Clinical PET
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Current pre-clinical positron emission tomography (PET) scanners are often based on monolithic detectors due to their high spatial resolution and intrinsic depth-of-interaction (DOI) capabilities to reduce parallax positioning errors. However, the broad light distributions of monolithic designs can lead to drawbacks in the sensor readout and in the processing chain, e.g., dead time as well as pile up. Semi-monolithic slab detectors represent an attractive alternative as they provide a higher optical photon density while allowing a DOI determination. The cost can be assumed competitive with monoliths. This work presents a semi-monolithic detector comprising 1 mm thin high-resolution LYSO slabs coupled to a 12 × 12 channel digital SiPM tile. Currently, a detector spatial resolution (SR) (FWHM of the PSF) of 1.2 / 2.3 mm and a mean absolute error (MAE) of 0.9 / 1.1 mm is achieved in planar-monolithic / DOI direction with a correct slab identification in the planar-segmented direction of 92 % considering a [435 - 585] keV energy window. An energy resolution of 15.2 % and 461 ps coincidence timing resolution (CTR) were obtained.

articleTitle: Modeling of Photonic Crystals into the GATE LUT Davis Model for Detector Simulation
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Positron Emission Tomography (PET) plays a pivotal role in clinical care and biomedical research. Improving PET timing and spatial resolution contributes to enhancing image quality. A PET scanner consists of multiple radiation detectors composed of a scintillator, photodetector, and readout circuit. Radiation detectors currently are limited by scintillator size, stopping power, etc. In addition, optical photons emitted by the scintillator may be trapped inside the scintillator and not be detected by the photodetector due to total internal reflection. Losing optical photons will degrade the detector energy and timing resolutions. Longer crystals increase the number of emitted optical photons, but the timing resolution may deteriorate. Photonic Crystals (PhC) are periodic nanostructures with a size comparable to optical photons’ wavelength that increase the number of collected optical photons by breaking the critical angle limit. Scintillator detector design software such as GATE currently cannot model PhC into scintillator detector simulation because optical photons are modeled as discrete particles, obeying geometric optics rules and not wave optics principles that optical photons transported in PhC must follow. To connect PhC with GATE optical photons simulation, we build a bridge between geometric optics and wave optics, using our previously developed framework of the LUT Davis model. The transmission pattern obtained from numerical modeling of PhC has good agreement with experiment results. We develop and incorporate new PhC LUT into the LUT Davis model. This novel strategy makes scintillation detector design work more versatile.

articleTitle: Double-sided silicon-strip detector for a scatterer in whole gamma imaging
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Whole gamma imaging (WGI) is our original concept to combine PET and Compton imaging. The WGI will be enabled by inserting a scatterer ring in a PET ring, which also works as an absorber in Compton imaging. Previously, we developed WGI prototypes using scintillators such as GSOZ and GAGG as the scatterer detector. However, such scintillators may have limitations for the use in WGI, in terms of energy resolution and Doppler broadening. Therefore, this work aimed at developing a Si detector, which would be a better choice for the scatterer, in particular, for low energy gamma rays because of its better energy resolution and higher Compton scattering efficiency than those of the scintillators. We constructed a prototype scatterer which consisted of a double-sided silicon strip detector (DSSD) and readout circuits with ASICs. The total chip size of the DSSD was 45.5 mm × 45.5 mm. The size of the active area was 43.2 mm × 43.2 mm. Strip pitch was 900 μm and the chip thickness was 600 μm. The number of strips was 48 channels for each side. The DSSD chip was connected to the readout circuit board with ASIC chips, which contained pre-amplifiers, shapers and analog-to-digital circuits. Digitalized data were collected and recorded with a FPGA board and a control PC. Performance evaluation of the Si scatterer was conducted for low-energy gamma rays and x-rays from Am-142, Ba-133 and Co-57 sources irradiated from ~10 cm above the DSSD. The x-ray energy peaks lower than 50 keV could be clearly recognized when the temperature was below -10 °C. The energy resolutions at -20 °C of 4.0%, 3.6% and 2.2% were obtained at 59.5 keV (Am-241), 81 keV (Ba-133) and 122 keV (Co-57), respectively.

articleTitle: Imaging Performance of the Fully Assembled Ultra-High Resolution (UHR) Brain PET scanner
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: High spatial resolution is needed to resolve small structures in the brain and to enable imaging of neurological pathways at the onset of diseases. The Ultra-High Resolution (UHR) brain PET scanner can be key in the quest for brain PET imaging with finer precision. We report the latest measurement results obtained with the now fully-assembled UHR scanner having an axial field-of-view of 235 mm. The UHR scanner is based on the LabPET II modular technology platform employing a truly pixelated detector readout scheme to achieve superior spatial resolution. Ultrahigh resolution is confirmed with 87% resolvability of 1 mm rods and fully resolved larger rods (≥1.35 mm) of the Ultra-Micro Hot Spot phantom. A lower partial volume effect with the UHR leads to good measured contrast recovery both for the NU 4 and NU 2 image quality phantoms as well as excellent image quality and substructure resolvability of the 3D Hoffman brain phantom. Peak noise-equivalent count rate of 10.3 kcps was measured at 21.6 kBq/ml. This set of measurements thus completes the physical and imaging characterization of the UHR scanner, showing possibilities towards the identification of small-scale structures implicated in brain disorders and neurodegenerative diseases.

articleTitle: Development of Continuous Krypton Sampling System in Cryogenic Environment
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: The radioactive krypton-85 (<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">85</sup>Kr) gas is a noble gas with little chemical reaction and accumulates in the atmosphere. The main sources of Kr gas are anthropogenic and it would be an important indicator of clandestine nuclear activity, such as nuclear weapon testing and nuclear fuel reprocessing. Therefore, Continuous <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">85</sup>Kr monitoring is required to obtain reliable global and local <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">85</sup>Kr radioactivity concentration. Considerable researches have been conducted for analyzing <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">85</sup>Kr in the atmosphere such as BfS-IAR system. It uses soda lime, silica gel, and liquid nitrogen (LN<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf>) that must be periodically exchanged or replenished. To reduce the periodic input of manpower for this, we have developed Kr adsorption system using a membrane- based impurity removal module, an electric cooling module, and a prototype automated LN<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf> supply module. In this study, cryogenic cooling simulations and experiments were conducted, and a buried adsorption module structure was designed to improve the limitation of condensation and LN<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf> vaporization in the existing prototype structure for an expanded continuous Kr sampling system. As an experimental result, the lowest temperature of about 80 K was maintained from 30 min after the start of the LN<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf> supply, and the amount of vaporization per hour is reduced by 15 % compared to the prototype system.

articleTitle: Joint Image Reconstruction of Activity and Attenuation with DOI for the NeuroEXPLORER
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: The NeuroEXPLORER (NX) is a next generation SiPM based dedicated brain PET scanner with ultra-high sensitivity and spatial resolution. To provide previously unachievable imaging performance, NX provides both time-of-flight (TOF) and depth-of-interaction (DOI) measurements. The NX has an excellent timing resolution of 236 ps. In this work, we investigate a joint reconstruction based on MLAA with autonomous scaling and joint scatter estimation for a TOF PET scanner with DOI measurements. We introduce a generalized scaling determination method based on our previous method using a selected volume of interest (VOI) in a reconstructed attenuation image with known attenuation. First, we construct a step attenuation medium based on the support of an imaging object or a patient. The scaling factor can then be determined from the difference between the reconstructed attenuation image and the known attenuation within the selected VOI compared with the step attenuation medium. We used DOI-rebinning method to incorporate the DOI information into the joint reconstruction. The proposed joint reconstruction algorithm includes 4steps in each iteration: 1) the activity is updated using TOF OSEM from DOIrebinned TOF list-mode data; 2) the attenuation image is updated using XMLTR (an extended MLTR) from non-TOF LOR sinograms; 3) a scaling factor is determined based on the selected VOI; 4) scatter is estimated using TOF single scatter simulation. The performance of joint reconstruction is studied using the experimental data of the first human FDG scan from the NX. We show that the proposed joint reconstruction with proper autonomous scaling provides an alternative method for attenuation correction when the CT attenuation is missing or incomplete.

articleTitle: A modular readout electronics for multi-wire proportional chambers with individual channel readout
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: We present a modular readout system for the new curved 3He-detectors built for the upcoming powder diffractometer ErwiN at the Forschungs-Neutronenquelle Heinz Maier-Leibnitz (FRM II), Germany and the upgrade of the cold powder diffractometer DMC at the Paul Scherrer Institut (PSI), Switzerland. These detectors are based on multi-wire proportional chambers (MWPC) with individual readout of all cathode wires and stripes. Nine individual curved MWPC segments are mounted inside a 3He-filled common pressure vessel to form a homogenous, seamless detection area. The modular design of the detector is mirrored by the architecture of the readout electronics. This permits to adapt the readout system to similar detector types with an arbitrary number of MWPC segments. The analog Front-end consists of charge sensitive preamplifiers with 350 ns peaking time followed by comparators to deliver a Time-over-Threshold (ToT) signal. The ToT-signals are encoded and timestamped at 80 MHz by an FPGA-based board directly mounted on top of each MWPC segment. The signal processing includes a cluster recognition in x- and y-position as well as in signal arrival time. The neutron impact position is then determined using a centre-of-gravity algorithm based on the ToT-information. A further FPGA-based board gathers and post-processes data from all the segments for reconstructing neutron events occurring at the boundary of two adjacent segments. Finally, the reconstructed events are delivered to the DAQ system with 10-bit position resolution, timestamping with 100 ns precision and total charge deposit with 8-bit resolution.

articleTitle: The Regenerative Current Mirror: A Very Low Power Front-End Amplifier for Silicon Pixel Detectors
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: In pixelized detectors, reducing power consumption in the front end ASIC chips becomes a crucial demand. Optimization based on mature pre-amplifier schemes today is unlikely to bring sufficient improvements. A new CMOS front-end gain stage topology with very low power consumption called regenerative current mirror is developed to fulfill the demand. The circuit takes advantage of high speed performance of current amplification while operating with relatively low bias current. The regenerative current mirror uses a NMOS current mirror and a PMOS current mirror, both with nominal gain of 1, to form a loop-back topology that provides a positive feedback. An NMOS FET with an external adjustable voltage applied to it gate terminal is used to limit open loop gain of the current mirrors to be slightly lower than 1. This yields a net gain of the positive feedback loop to be much larger than 1 while operating the current mirrors under relatively low bias currents. Simulation shows that in 65 nm fabrication process, the power consumption of the gain stages suitable for silicon pixel detectors can be controlled < 10 micro-Watts per channel. Another novel low-power circuit called Pseudo-Thyristor presented in another document will replace traditional discriminator and the Regenerative Current Mirror plus Pseudo-Thyristor will provide a full solution for the silicon pixel low-power frontend ASIC.

articleTitle: Analysis of Lesion Signals in Reduced-Dose Pediatric Tc-DMSA Renal SPECTImages with Deep Learning Denoising
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
