abstract: Recently we demonstrated the feasibility of applying a 3D convolutional autoencoder (CAE) network for suppressing the elevated imaging noise in reduced-dose renal studies with single photon emission computed tomography (SPECT) using 99mTc-labelled dimercaptosuccinic acid (DMSA). Built on this prior study, in this work we further investigate how the denoising performance by the 3D CAE network can impact on image features that are important for detection of cortical defects in reduced-dose DMSA renal SPECT images. For this purpose we analyzed the image contrast of a set of small to medium sized focal cortical lesions identified in clinical acquisitions. The quantitative results demonstrate that the denoising network can better preserve the image contrast of defect signals compared to conventional Gaussian filtering. Moreover, the denoising network can also reduce the image variability by 18.35% and 21.03% in defect and normal cortical regions (p-value < 0.05), respectively, in reduced-dose studies.

articleTitle: Direct Deep-Learned Kinetic Parametric Map Separation for Multiplexed PET
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Multiplexed positron emission tomography (PET) imaging combines information from multiple tracers to open up greater levels of relevant information for clinical decisionmaking in a single scan. Estimating kinetic parametric maps from multiplexed PET is challenging due to the high level of noise in the raw dual-tracer images obtained from the scanner, and an arterial input function needs to be provided. Deep learning now offers useful new tools for multiplexed signal separation without explicitly knowing the input functions and has been shown to implicitly denoise the separated dual-tracer images. In this work, we propose a deep learning framework for kinetic parametric map separation for multiplexed PET. In particular, we investigated the feasibility of using a trained neural network to separate dynamic [<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">18</sup>F]FDG and [<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">11</sup>C]MET dual-tracer images into single-tracer kinetic parametric maps when two tracers are injected in close succession. The kinetic parametric maps K<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">1</inf> and k<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf> are learned jointly using a 2D convolutional encoder-decoder with weighted mean square error loss. The results obtained suggest that the deep learning-based method leads to better separation performance compared to the classical compartment modelling-based method for parametric maps K<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">1</inf> and k<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf>. Future work will focus on including k<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</inf> and k<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">4</inf> in the separation task and investigating the weighting strategy in the loss function to further improve the separation performance.

articleTitle: Comparison of Neural Deblurring Methods for Improving SPECT Reconstruction Quality
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Single photon emission computed tomography (SPECT) is a nuclear imaging technique which has numerous applications in the clinical and medical research domain. However, SPECT images suffer from various types of image degradation which may directly influence the quality of the final resulting image. In recent years, due to the fast development of machine learning, many studies have emerged that utilize neural networks (NNs) to improve the image quality of SPECT. Yet, many of of these developing techniques require a significant amount of time and data to train the NN in order to achieve acceptable performance. In this work, we investigated several NN deblurring models which have been pretrained but were never previously trained for medical imaging tasks or with SPECT reconstruction. These methods provide a fast approach for deblurring since there is no extra training work required. Visually inspecting all the methods demonstrated each method's ability to effectively reduce the amount of blur. We also used a quantitative measurement called Blind/Referenceless Image Spatial Quality Evaluator (BRISQUE) to evaluate the output image quality of those four methods. The result shows all the neural deblurring methods such as SwinIR and ESRGAN are able to effectively produce a clearer and more readable image from the blurry SPECT reconstructions.

articleTitle: Partial Volume Correction for PET imaging based on Deep Image PriorPartial Volume Correction for PET imaging based on Deep Image Prior
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: PET imaging suffers from partial volume effect (PVE) due to the low spatial resolution inherent to the technique. Deep learning provides promise for conducting partial volume correction (PVC), but the limited available data poses a challenge for training neural networks. In this paper, we introduce an unsupervised deep learning framework for PVC that integrates various techniques based on deep image prior (DIP). DIP utilizes network architecture as prior information, allowing for smooth and noise-free output from a noisy input. We combine regulation of denoising (Red) and back projection (BP) fidelity term to further enhance image quality, and use conditional DIP with MR images for PVC guidance. We also employ populational pretraining and individual fine-tuning for improved training. We evaluated our approach on a dataset of degraded noisy PET images and corresponding ground-truth images on simulated and clinical datasets. Our methods achieves high PVC quality as measured by peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR) and structural similarity (SSIM). The experiments demonstrated that Red could effectively improve image quality, and BP could achieve good results when the system matrix was known. The pre-training strategy enabled the network to generate the approximate contour of the image early on under the guidance of MR images, which was advantageous for the subsequent iterative process.

articleTitle: Developments for the ATLAS Tile Calorimeter readout system for HL-LHC
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: The Large Hadron Collider (LHC) is undergoing a major upgrade towards the High Luminosity LHC (HL-LHC), which is set to deliver five times the nominal instantaneous luminosity of the LHC. This upgrade, scheduled for 2026-2028 during the Long Shutdown 3, includes the complete replacement of the on- and off-detector electronics of the ATLAS Tile Hadronic Calorimeter (TileCal) with a new read-out architecture. The TileCal PreProcessor (TilePPr) receives and processes the digitized signals from on-detector electronics and transmits them to the Front-End Link eXchange (FELIX) system, which serves as a data router for all sub-detectors and distributes Timing, Trigger and Control (TTC) signals to the TilePPr. The data is then forwarded by FELIX to the SoftWare Read-Out Driver (SWROD) computers, which perform detector-specific data processing. To evaluate the new readout architecture and component prototypes, TileCal developed prototype detector modules ("Demonstrators") and exposed them to different particle beams at varying energies at CERN facilities. The data acquisition and processing software was developed to ensure backward compatibility with the legacy system, while data is being read out via FELIX and SWROD in parallel. In this contribution, we present the developments for the new readout architecture as well as comparative results of the new readout schema with the legacy one during the data-taking period of the test beam.

articleTitle: Glass-free SiPMs with Through Silicon Vias for VUV/NUV light detection
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Glass-free Silicon Photomultipliers (SiPMs) optimized for Vacuum Ultraviolet (VUV) light detection have been developed and characterized at FBK, including Through Silicon Vias (TSVs) that bring the top contact to the backside of the device tier to be able to perform 3D integration with the readout electronics. R&D activity was carried out on SiPMs on Vacuum Ultraviolet-High Density (VUV-HD) SiPMs with a 1x1 cm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sup> active area and a Photon Detection Efficiency of about 23% at 175 nm. Two different TSV fabrication strategies have been developed: "Via-Mid", in which the TSV is formed during the processing of the frontside of the wafer, and "Via-Last", in which the TSV is fabricated with backside-only processing. Both approaches provided functional TSVs, showing good characteristics, such as high connection yield, good insulation from the substrate and no modification of the SiPM characteristics for the "Via-Last" approach. A notable feature of the TSVs fabricated at FBK and customized for the VUV-HD SiPMs is the absence of the glass support wafer, which allows preserving sensitivity to VUV light as well as a reduction of the external component of the optical crosstalk. In this work, we discuss the different microfabrication strategies and report on the detailed electro-optical characterization of 1x1 cm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sup> VUV-HD SiPMs with "Via-Last" TSVs.

articleTitle: Scalable Time Measurement System based on a Multi-FPGA Architecture
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Many modern applications in various scientific, industrial, and consumer sectors, such as Time-of-Flight Positron Emission Tomography and 3D imaging scanning in medicine, or Particle Identification in nuclear physics, require the measurement of time intervals with both high-precision (picoseconds) and extremely large number of channels (hundreds). Among the most established Time Interval Meters (TIMs), Time-to-Digital Converters (TDCs) are increasingly a very popular choice, especially thanks to their extremely high flexibility, in the version implemented in Field Programmable Gate Array (FPGA) devices. However, the number of channels is becoming so high in the most advanced applications, that a single FPGA device is not sufficient to host the necessary architecture and therefore the problem arises of realizing a multi-FPGA based TDCs, necessarily all perfectly synchronized with each other. Given the picoseconds-precision required, the problem of TDCs synchronization is a very significant issue that requires the development of methodologies and techniques designed and developed ad hoc. The proposed solution is a structure that meets these needs and is implemented using a "main board" that hosts a 16-nm Xilinx Zynq UltraScale+ XCZU9EG-2FFVB1156 Multi-Processor System-on-Chip (MPSoC). The main board coordinates up to 8 FPGA-based "satellite boards", each hosting a Xilinx 28-nm 7-Series Kintex-7 XC7K410T-2FFG676I FPGA, in which a 16-channel, 12-picoseconds precision FPGA-based TDC is implemented. In this way, it is possible to manage up to 128 channels with a precision of 12 ps r.m.s. The satellite boards are connected to the main board via the Aurora protocol on Gigabit Transceiver Hardmacro (GTH), making it possible to achieve a data collection rate of 250 Msps by the main board. The entire system is housed in a 4U, 460 x 305 mm, 4U rack.

articleTitle: Characterization of the 166-Pixel Monolithic SDD TRISTAN Detector with Photons and Electrons in the KATRIN Monitor Spectrometer
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: We report on the characterization of a monolithic array of 166 Silicon Drift Detectors (SDD) with integrated JFET. This high-density detection module (4 cm by 4 cm) was designed and assembled within the TRISTAN development of the KATRIN experiment for search of sterile neutrinos in the keV mass range by means of beta spectroscopy. The detector was commissioned in the KATRIN monitor spectrometer and was exposed both to X-ray photons (at 5.9 keV of Fe55) and electrons (at 32.2 keV energy of Kr83m) reaching state-of-the-art homogeneity and energy resolution: 157 eV and 352.8 eV FWHM respectively (with 2 us shaping time and -33°C cooling).

articleTitle: Calibration of the Background-Subtracting Gamma-Ray Spectrometer for the MAMBO CubeSat Mission
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: The origin of the cosmic diffuse gamma-ray (CDG) background in the 0.3 – 10 MeV energy range is a mystery that has persisted for over 40 years. The best existing measurements have large systematic uncertainties and sparse sky coverage. Intriguingly, the latest theoretical models based on emission from active galactic nuclei and supernovae differ significantly from these data below ~1.5 MeV. The Mini Astrophysical MeV Background Observatory (MAMBO) is a new CubeSat mission under development at Los Alamos National Laboratory with the goal of making high-quality measurements of the MeV CDG to help solve this puzzle. Scheduled for launch in early 2025, the concept is motivated by the fact that the sensitivity of space-based MeV gamma-ray instruments to the CDG is limited not by size, but by the locally generated instrumental background produced by interactions of energetic particles in spacecraft materials. Comparatively tiny CubeSat platforms provide a uniquely quiet environment relative to previous gamma-ray science missions. The MAMBO mission will provide the best measurement ever made of the MeV CDG spectrum and uniformity across the sky utilizing an innovative shielded spectrometer that simultaneously measures signal and background. Primary detector, background monitor, and active shield volumes made of bismuth germanate (BGO) scintillator are read out by custom silicon photomultiplier (SiPM) arrays to enable an efficient, compact instrument suitable for CubeSat deployment. A tagged calibration source maintains constant gain across detector elements despite expected temperature variations. We present detailed calibration measurements of the MAMBO instrument which verify the required energy range, energy resolution, and stable performance over the expected operating temperature range. These measurements also validate a detailed Monte Carlo simulation model, enabling prediction of detector counting rates and scientific performance in orbit.

articleTitle: Scatter and Beam Hardening Correction of Cone Beam CT with a Convolutional Neural Network
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: There are linear accelerators for the radiation therapy equipped with a cone beam CT (CBCT). The usage of this CBCT is for the confirmation of the position of an irradiation target and not for the planning of the radiation therapy. The reason is that measured CT data include lots of scattered photons due to the insufficient collimation of scattered photons. If we can use the CBCT for the treatment planning, we can make an adaptive therapy in which we make a modification of treatment plan according to the condition of a radiation target such as the size and position. The aim of this study is to remove the effect of scattered photons and beam hardening for the adaptive radiation therapy. To correct scattered photons and beam hardening effect, we used a convolutional neural network(CNN). The architecture of the CNN was the UNet++. To calculate cone-beam projection data of CT images, we conducted a Monte Carlo simulation with a cone-beam geometry and calculated projection data affected with scattered photons and beam hardening effect. These projection data were used for the input data of the CNN. To make training data without the effect of scattering and beam hardening, we calculated projection data with an average energy of x-rays. Simulation results showed that the image reconstructed with the projection data corrected by the CNN was close to the ideal image without scattering and beam hardening. These results showed the effectiveness of the proposed method.

articleTitle: Simulation of the Induced Signals in SiC Detectors for Radioactive Ion Beam Tagging
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: The design of detection systems for modern nuclear physics experiments have to face several challenges like i) the increase in beam intensity, ii) increase of the required angular resolution, iii) the request to lower the detection threshold and to identify even the reaction products stopping in one and only detection layer. The availability of versatile, fast and powerful simulation codes would be of great help to study signal formation due to an arbitrary ionization profile and evaluate any pulse-shape processing technique, especially in the case of different and novel materials and/or topologies. SiC technology feature superior performance in terms of radiation hardness but there is limited literature on the simulation of the induced signals in materials other than Si. In this contribution we present a simplified model for the computation of the signal induced at the electrodes potentially in any planar diode detector together with the extension of a fast semi-analytical 3D simulation code, originally conceived for Si detectors, to simulate SiC detectors. The poster will also discuss the results of the simulation of the signals induced at the electrodes in SiC detectors compared to the one achieved in detectors with the same geometry but in Si for different ions.

articleTitle: Iterative Image Reconstruction with Under- Sampled Data Assisted by a Neural Network
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Image reconstruction with under-sampled data is usually achieved by an iterative algorithm, which minimizes an objective function. The objective function commonly contains a data fidelity term and one or more Bayesian terms. This paper suggests that a neural network can be used for a Bayesian term to assist the iterative image reconstruction.

articleTitle: Neutron Positron Emission Portal Imaging (nPEPI): A Quality Assurance Tool for Intensity Modulated Neutron Therapy (IMNT)
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Our institution recently implemented IMNT, which reduces off-target dosing compared to 3D conformal treatment techniques. Because high LET neutrons are uniquely damaging to electronics, we constructed an in-house portal imaging system that operates outside the treatment room. For this system, a 20×20×0.6 cm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</sup> piece of polyethylene is irradiated by neutrons to create patient- and field-specific spatial patterns from <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">12</sup>C(n,2n)<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">11</sup>C reactions. The induced-activity distribution is then imaged on a nearby two-dimensional PET imager, the nPEPI system. nPEPI images are produced using focal plane tomography. Our pre-treatment PET QA is based on g-analysis (5%/5mm evaluation criterion) of Monte Carlo simulated and measured <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">11</sup>C activity maps. A modulation factor (MF), defined as the total number of monitor units (MU)/prescribed dose (cGy), is used to characterize the extent of IMNT field modulation.Using our current nPEPI system, IMNT treatments for large, irregularly shaped treatment volumes are more likely to fail patient QA when the MF exceeds 3 MU/cGy. To date all IMNT plans with an MF less than 3 MU/cGy passed QA testing. About 20% of plans with an MF > 3 MU/cGy needed re-optimization to reduce the MF and subsequently passed QA with no significant change in tumor coverage and organ-at-risk (OAR) dose. While re-optimized plans have all passed patient specific QA, they require extra personnel effort and about 2-days of computer simulation.In this work, we investigate how improving the imaging performance for the nPEPI system might improve the QA pass rate for highly modulated (MF > 3) IMNT fields. Specific performance parameters investigated are intrinsic spatial resolution, pixel size, detection efficiency, and planar imaging area. Our goal is to identify best-design parameters for a future second generation nPEPI system using more modern imaging technologies to enable QA of highly modulated IMNT fields that further spare OAR tissues without compromising tumor targets.

articleTitle: (BZA)2PbBr4: Ultrafast Scintillation Detector with Potential for Photon-Counting CT
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Photon-counting computed tomography (PCCT) is a rapidly emerging medical imaging technology. Several PCCT scanners have been developed in recent years, using finely pixelated room-temperature semiconductor detectors (RTSD) such as CdTe, Cd<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">(1-x)</inf>Zn<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">x</inf>Te (CZT), and Si. Whereas scintillation detectors were traditionally considered too slow to handle the X-ray fluence rates > 10<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">8</sup> photons s<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">-1</sup> mm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">-2</sup> encountered in clinical PCCT, we have recently demonstrated how the properties of modern scintillators and silicon photomultipliers (SiPMs) force us to rethink this paradigm. It appears that indirect detection using ultrafast scintillators and SiPMs may provide a robust, scalable, and cost-effective X-ray photon-counting technology. Here, we evaluate a new, solution-processable, two-dimensional (2D) perovskite scintillator, benzylamonium lead bromide or (BZA)<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf>PbBr<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">4</inf>, as a candidate material for PCCT. Experimental characterization of this material reveals an approximately 4 ns decay time constant under X-ray excitation at 300 K, combined with a light yield of 3.7 photons/keV and an energy resolution of 8% FWHM at 662 keV. The emission spectrum with its maximum at 432 nm matches well with the photodetection efficiency (PDE) curve of typical SiPMs. Pulses produced by a SiPM-based (BZA)<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf>PbBr<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">4</inf> detector were modeled using the simulation tool previously developed by Van der Sar et al. The ultrafast decay of (BZA)<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf>PbBr<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">4</inf> results in outstanding count-rate capability per detector pixel, outperforming that of CZT detectors described in literature. Combined with its cost-effective, solution-based synthesis, this makes (BZA)<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf>PbBr<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">4</inf> a promising indirect-conversion material for PCCT.

articleTitle: R&D of Passive Fast Neutron Multiplicity Counting System
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: A passive fast neutron multiplicity counting system has been developed in the School of Nuclear Science and Engineering, North China Electrical Power University, Beijing, China. The system mainly consists of 32 custom-made EJ-309 liquid scintillation detectors and a custom-made multichannel readout electronics. These detectors are symmetrically mounted on a patented spherical supporting structure. The simulation results show that the detection efficiency of the system is about 12% for <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">252</sup>Cf neutrons at an energy threshold of 100 keVee and not affected by the size and shape of the samples if their location and distribution within a radius of 10 cm in the system which is due to the symmetrical arrangement of these detectors. The experimental results further show that the system has a uniform detection efficiency of ~11% for <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">252</sup>Cf neutrons at an energy threshold of 100 keVee with a relative efficiency deviation of less than 5% as samples are located or distributed within a radius of 6 cm in the system. The readout electronics integrates two combined neutron-gamma discrimination circuits for the realization of pulse-shape and pulse-width discrimination algorithms and a FPGA(Field Programmable Gate Array)-based data acquisition system for picking out all neutron events and registering their global arriving time. By combining pulse-shape and pulse-width discrimination methods, the detection system can achieve a neutron-gamma discrimination performance with FOM>1 even at a lower energy threshold of 100 keVee. The spontaneous rates of seven different <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">252</sup>Cf sources measured with our system are within less than 5% of the results using a Plutonium Scrap Multiplicity Counter (PSMC). The system is going to be tested with Plutonium samples and the corresponding results will be reported on the conference.

articleTitle: Simulation study of the effect of TOF on a new Biplanar PET scanner
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Positron Emission Tomography (PET) provides functional information for the diagnosis and treatment monitoring of several diseases. Regarding the use of PET for guiding medical interventions, this work presents a biplanar PET scanner with an open geometry to allow the entrance of interventional instruments while acquiring data. We estimated the performance of this new PET scanner with Monte Carlo simulations using GATE v9.2. The two paddles are based on 2x2x12 mm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</sup> LYSO crystals. The MLEM reconstruction algorithm uses Time of Flight (TOF) information with a Coincidence Time Resolution (CTR) of 180 ps to improve the image quality. To illustrate the system performance, we have simulated the NEMA NU-4 2008 phantom and calculated the Contrast Recovery Coefficients (CRC) and the uniformity value following this protocol. We performed an analysis of the number of time bins needed to maximize the effect of TOF information in our reconstruction algorithm. In addition, we simulated a Derenzo phantom where all the rods above 1.6 mm are well resolved. Given the results, this new scanner may be suitable for organ exploration as brain or cardiac applications.

articleTitle: Development of Novel CsCl-based Ultrafast Scintillators
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: In this work, we explore scintillation properties and timing performance of novel core valence luminescence crystals. These materials may be promising for the heterostructure concept in time-of-flight PET, for photon counting CT, or in high energy physics experiments due to their ultrafast 1-2 ns single-component decay times, relatively high light outputs compared to BaF<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf>, and higher densities compared to fast plastic scintillators. Single crystals of Cs<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</inf>MgCl<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">5</inf>, Cs<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf>MgCl<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">4</inf>, and CsMgCl<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</inf> are grown, and scintillation is observed in Cs<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</inf>MgCl<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">5</inf> and Cs<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf>MgCl<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">4</inf> for the first time. The effects of doping crystals with 5 mol% Zn are also investigated for all three compounds, and light output is found to increase significantly without negatively impacting decay time. As a result, an improved coincidence time resolution (CTR) can be expected for the Zn-doped crystals. The best CTR of 98 ps FWHM has been measured with CsMgCl<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</inf>:Zn 5%.

articleTitle: A Reactor Noise Analysis Using Auto-Correlation Function with Time-stamping data
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: In the conventional study, neutron time series data required for reactor noise analysis have been measured using Single Channel Analyze (SCA) and Multi-Channel Scaler (MCS). However, those method provides only limited information. Currently, there is a new Multi-Channel Analyzer (MCA) with time-stamping capability which can be used to obtain more information. In this study, using the same neutron time-sequence data obtained from a new MCA, prompt neutron decay constants were determined by the conventional variance-to-mean ratio method and the auto correlation function method. The auto correlation function method was one of reactor noise technique and few experiments with the method have been conducted in the past. The experiments were conducted using the Kyoto University Critical Assembly (KUCA). As the results, the decay constants were agreement between the variance-to-mean method and the auto correlation function method within the error range. In addition, the obtained decay constant by the auto-correlation function method had not the detector position dependency.

articleTitle: The muEDM experiment and its subdetectors
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: The muEDM experiment aims at setting the ground for a new direct electric dipole moment search using muons (muon EDM). The experiment will perform this dedicated search using for the first time worldwide the frozen-spin technique for the muon EDM, improving the current sensitivity by more than three orders of magnitude to better than 6x 10−23 e cm, an astonishing jump. This search is a unique opportunity to probe previously uncharted territory and test theories of Behind Standard Model Physics. One key point of the experiment is to accumulate muons in the proper orbit and then measure the asymmetry of the positrons from the muon decays as a signature of a non-zero muon EDM. We will report in detail the experiment’s status, which merges several innovative techniques for nuclear and particle physics. In particular, we will focus on the so-called muon entrance detector system and its first prototype which has been built and tested for the first time along a muon beam and the positron detector, designed to measure the muon EDM signature.The first is based on very thin scintillating foil (100 um thick) coupled to silicon photomultiplier (SiPM), and the second to very thin scintillating fiber (250 um thick) coupled to SiPM. All results obtained along the beam will be discussed. The comparison between data and the Monte Carlo simulation will be also shown.

articleTitle: Comparison of Extracting Tissue- and Image-based Characteristic Features for Machine Learning Prediction of Colorectal Polyp Malignancy
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Detection and classification of precursor polyp via computed tomography colonography (CTC) has shown its significant clinical impact on management of colorectal cancer (CRC). In this study, we compared the classification performance of five machine learning (ML) models and one deep learning (DL) model. The five ML models utilized the Haralick feature (HF), Haralick measure (HM), extended Haralick feature (eHF), and extended Haralick measure (eHM), and one Affine tissue elastic feature with Karhunen-Loève (KL) Transformation on virtual monoenergetic images (Affine_KL VMI) that included 10 energies and were trained with a Random Forest classifier. The DL model was a 17-layer 3D convolutional neural network (3D_CNN) model including 3 instance normalization layers. The performance of the six models was evaluated using the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC).The AUC values for the six models ranged from 0.870 to 0.997 for 100 polyp masses with a diameter larger than 30mm, 0.711 to 0.985 for 182 polyp masses with a diameter between 10 to 30mm, 0.601 to 0.890 for 357 polyp masses with a diameter less than 10 mm, respectively. The Affine_KL VMI model consistently outperformed the other models, achieving the highest AUC values across all datasets, ranging from 0.890 to 0.997. This indicates that the Affine_KL VMI ML model is a promising approach for detecting and classifying precursor polyps in CTC images and may have significant clinical impact on the management of CRC.

articleTitle: Positron transmission imaging of histological slices
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: We propose positron transmission imaging as a novel concept of imaging modality that will use a uniform β<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">+</sup> source to illuminate a tissue sample with positrons in order to image the electronic density of histological tissues slices with a ~50μm resolution. This imaging modality will be implemented as part of a high resolution 2D τ<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">OPs</inf> imager to serve as reference anatomical image to a τ<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">OPs</inf> image. We will describe the imager layout, present the concept of the e<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">+</sup> transmission imaging modality, and the results of preliminary simulations evaluating the expected count rate for the various layers of the imager, the expected sensitivity and spatial resolution of the reconstructed image.

articleTitle: Feasibility study on detection and verification of minor actinides by NDA technique based on photonuclear reactions
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: The photon-induced multiple neutron generation reaction rate ratio (PMNRR) method is a novel active gamma-ray method that detects fissionable materials based on the photonuclear reaction rate ratio. In the present study, the feasibility of detection of <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">241</sup>Am by the PMNRR method was verified using numerical analysis simulations. As a result, the separated <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">241</sup>Am could be discriminated from <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">237</sup>Np, <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">235</sup>U and <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">238</sup>U using the PMNRR　with the optimal combination of incident photon energies, even if a 10% uncertainty was considered in the nuclear data of the (γ, fission/2n) reaction. In addition, the prospect of estimation of Am composition ratios in UO<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf> using PMNRR was also obtained.

articleTitle: A Trigger Primitive Generation System for the High-Granularity Calorimeter (HGCAL) of the CMS Phase-2 detector upgrade
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: The CMS collaboration is building the high-granularity calorimeter (HGCAL) for the endcap regions as part of its planned upgrade for the High-Luminosity LHC (HL-LHC). The calorimeter data will form part of the Level-1 trigger (L1T) of the CMS experiment, reducing the event rate from the nominal 40 MHz down to 750 kHz with a latency of 12.5 microseconds. Among the 6 million readout channel of this 5D imaging calorimeter, 1 million "trigger channels" are read at 40 MHz, presenting a significant challenge in terms of data processing for the back-end trigger primitive system. The amount of data produced scales up to 50 Tb/s, an order of magnitude above what is currently handled at CMS. The HGCAL trigger primitive generation (TPG) system is organized in 2 stages: the first stage receiving the front-end data and organizing them into a Time-Multiplexed fashion before transmitting them to the second processing stage, where the data associated with a 120-degree sector of the HGCAL are used to reconstruct particle associated showers in a full depth 3D view. The system is instrumented with 63 ATCA electronic boards equipped with Xilinx Ultrascale FPGAs and SoC controllers, as well as high-speed optical links (16 Gb/s). We present here the technological challenge of implementing such a system and designing the firmware used in reconstructing 3D clusters. Together with tracking information, which will also be available at L1T, particle-flow reconstruction techniques and other sophisticated machine learning approach can be contemplated. We present here the HGCAL TPG system architecture design and the ongoing developments, prototyping and testing. Outlook towards modern technological approach to large data volume processing will be discussed.

articleTitle: An alternating algorithm for Prompt Gamma Time Imaging with the TIARA project
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: In hadrontherapy, the precise tracking of the hadron during treatment and the real-time determination of its different characteristics (prompt gamma positions, velocity profile and energy loss) is highly recommended to detect any change or mismatch between the treatment planning and the conditions present at the time of the treatment.To the best of our knowledge, there is currently no automatic method proposed to meet this need and promptly alert or halt the treatment if there is a risk of over-irradiating healthy tissues.In the present work, we present a mathematical measurement model and an alternating strategy that ensure a joint estimation of the different properties of the hadron (the prompt gamma positions and the velocity profile allow us to determine the energy loss) throughout the measured times of flight. Our proposition is based on convergence guarantees.

articleTitle: Application of a performance evaluation standard for a GAGG-scintillator Compton camera
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: This study aimed at designing performance evaluation standards for clinical Compton imaging systems. We selected <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">57</sup>Co (122 keV), <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">133</sup>Ba (356 keV), and <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">22</sup>Na (511 and 1275 keV) as surrogate radioisotopes whose γ-ray energies are close to those of candidate radioisotopes for future clinical use (such as <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">99m</sup>Tc, <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">131</sup>I, <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">18</sup>F, <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">89</sup>Zr, and <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">44</sup>Sc). We proposed the use of a point source for measuring the sensitivity and the angular resolution measure (ARM) at some points of a field-of-view. A multi-rod phantom (rod diameters: 3, 4, 5, 8 and 10 mm) was designed to evaluate image spatial resolution and a multi-contrast phantom was designed to evaluate image quality (contrast, noise, and uniformity). In this study, based on the proposed evaluation standards, we evaluated a cost-effective Compton camera using GAGG scintillators and a positron emission tomography data acquisition system, which was developed for imaging of astatine-211 in targeted alpha therapy. The full width at half maximus of ARMs were 33°, and 29° for γ-rays of 356 keV and 511 keV, respectively. While no images were obtained for the 122 keV (<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">57</sup>Co) and 1275 keV (<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">22</sup>Na) γ rays due to the limited energy range to measure, the multi-rod and multi-contrast phantoms for 511 keV (<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">22</sup>Na) could be visualized. The proposed evaluation method enables us to characterize the performance of various Compton imaging systems in the same manner.

articleTitle: Performance evaluation of a smoothed total variation regularization algorithm
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Total variation (TV) regularization algorithm is effective in image noise reduction and lesion quantification accuracy improvement. However, TV reconstructed image tends to be patchy if the detected counts are low. Low-count scenarios are common for PET/MR imaging, since a large number of emitted counts are attenuated by MR coils. In this work, an improved regularization method with a new smoothed total variation (STV) prior was proposed. It was initialized by a few iterations of TV regularization reconstruction, and followed by STV regularization reconstruction until the image converges. OSEM, TV and TV-STV reconstruction algorithms were compared through phantom and clinical studies. A numerical observer was designed to evaluate the lesion detectability in the phantom study. TV-STV achieved the highest area under LROC curve in both 30 s and 60 s reconstructions, and had the highest contrast recovery coefficients for cold spheres. For the patient study, TV-STV generated images with reduced hot spots and improved lesion contrast. And the image texture was similar to that of OSEM images.

articleTitle: Simulation and verification of tri-modality CT imaging system containing X-ray transmission, fluorescence, and scattering
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: X-ray transmission computed tomography (XCT) utilizes the attenuation effect of X-ray for imaging and has been widely used in the medical field. X-ray fluorescence computed tomography (XFCT) could realize quantitative imaging of high Z elements and achieve functional imaging of specific tissues. Currently, dual-modality imaging of XFCT and XCT is being extensively studied, which has great potential in the field of medical diagnosis. In current studies, scattered photons collected by XFCT are regarded as noise, but in fact, these scattered photons contain extra electron density information. Electron density imaging could be realized through reconstructing the scattered signal collected by XFCT detector. At the same time, the linear attenuation coefficients under different energies could be calculated by using the electron density imaging, transmission imaging and fluorescence imaging results. And then we could perform attenuation correction for the fluorescence imaging and scattering imaging results. In this paper, tri-modality imaging system of X-ray transmission, scattering, and fluorescence computed tomography is proposed, and the feasibility of this system is verified by simulation experiments. We reconstruct the electron density successfully and realize the attenuation correction of electron density image and fluorescence image in simulation experiments.

articleTitle: Qualification of the Spectral Performance and Count Rate Capabilities of the new PILATUS4 Detector with Different Sensor Materials
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: The new PILATUS4 detector is the successor of the well known PILATUS3 family, based on the hybrid pixel photon counting technology. Main features of the detector include instant retrigger technology for high count rate capability, 4 selectable energy thresholds, a pixel size of 150 μm and a selectable holes or electrons readout mode, that allows compatibility with different sensor materials. This detector enables X-ray diffraction (XRD) experiments requiring a large active detector area and/or at high speed, like macromolecular criystallography, scanning powder XRD computed tomography, time-resolved XRD, as well as scanning XRD and SAXS applications. We present the characterization of the spectral performance and the count rate capability of PILATUS4 with two different sensor materials: silicon (Si) and cadmium telluride (CdTe). Silicon is suitable for low energies up to 40 keV(value), CdTe is used with hard X-rays up to about 100 keV(value). We present results from Tthe characterization of both the CdTe sensor that has been characterized at the high energy beamline BAMline at BESSY II Synchrotron (Berlin, DE), and, for the silicon sensor that a beamtime is foreseen to be characterized in June 2023 at the PXII beam line at the SLS synchrotron (Villigen, CH).

articleTitle: Efficient Method for Generating System Response Functions using Monte Carlo Simulations
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: We have developed and tested a new method for generating imaging system matrices using a GPU-based Monte Carlo (MC) simulation package. Traditional methods of generating a system response matrix involve measurement with small sources translated throughout the field of view (FOV), or simulations of the detector responses to the photons emitted at each location. GPU-based MC simulations have the advantage that they can simultaneously simulate millions of photons at a time. In terms of system-response generation, GPU-based simulation suffers because of the inefficiencies of the data transfers and the difficulties of determining when a simulation has progressed enough to move on to the next locations. In addition, when a system matrix with a different voxel resolution is needed, this typically requires an entirely new simulation as the previous results are not transferable.We have developed a new, efficient method for using GPU MC techniques to generate system response matrices where photons are uniformly sampled from within the entire FOV. During simulation, each photon is tagged with its point of origin, and list-mode data are generated and stored instead of binned images. These data files can be quickly processed at any voxelization as long as enough photons have been simulated. Additional runs only add to the fidelity of the system response and thus, there is no wasted simulation time. The cost of this method is large data files, but we have found that these are very manageable even with desktop computers. We demonstrate this technique using for a multiple-pinhole cardiac SPECT system being developed at Mass General Hospital. Example reconstructions are shown at various resolutions all derived from a set of list-mode calibration data. We will present how this method automatically accounts for sub-voxelization, aperture sub-sampling, and penetration through thin regions of the collimator. We will also discuss the photon number requirements.

articleTitle: Recent Results in CZT Detectors for PCCT
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Photon-counting computed tomography (PCCT) is an emerging technology displacing conventional energy-integrating CTs. In this presentation, the status of Redlen's PCCT detector, which is now in clinical trials, will be reviewed, and some recent work on spatial resolution, improved stability and the impact of nonuniformity in X-ray illumination will be reported.

articleTitle: Modeling and Testing a Time-of-Flight Neutron Emission Spectrometer for General Fusion
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: General Fusion is building a prototype fusion machine as part of the Fusion Demonstration Program (FDP) in Culham, U.K. using principles of magnetic target fusion. A primary goal of the FDP is to reach an ion temperature of 10 keV, and making a measurement of this temperature will be a technological challenge. The proposed solution to this measurement in a time-of-flight neutron emission spectrometer. Deuterium-deuterium fusion reaction produce monoenergetic 2.45 MeV neutrons, but the temperature of the plasma causes the energy in the lab frame to have a dispersion with standard deviation proportional to the square root of the temperature in keV. A neutron spectrometer built from two layers of plastic scintillator can measure neutron energies if the neutrons interact in both layers by recording the scattering angle and time of flight between the two interaction points. This spectrometer will be a challenge to design due to the low total neutron count and high rate, so extensive modelling and simulation of the neutron spectrometer’s response are essential to ensuring a precise enough measurement of the plasma temperature can be made. This poster will describe the design and testing plan of the neutron spectrometer.

articleTitle: Fast28 a low-power fast readout design for SiPMs in 28nm CMOS
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: The field of detector readout electronics for precise timing has experienced a remarkable surge of interest due to its diverse range of applications in nuclear medicine such as Positron Emission Tomography (PET), High Energy Physics (HEP), Time-of-Flight (ToF) mass spectrometry and many other fields. This growth can be attributed to rapid advancements in photodetectors, particularly the silicon photomultiplier (SiPM), which has demonstrated exceptional suitability for these applications, owing to its ability to generate signals with unprecedentedly fast rise times. This work presents a low-power and high timing resolution readout front-end design for SiPMs in 28nm CMOS technology. With a low input impedance of less than 20Ω and a current-based input stage, it is suitable for a wide range of SiPM types and sizes. The power consumption of one timing channel is less than 2mW, and it achieves a sub-20ps r.m.s timing jitter for a single photo-electron, considering parasitic capacitances and inductances, with a 3x3mm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sup> Hamamatsu SiPM S13360-3050CS at 4.5V over-voltage. These exceptional features make this front-end readout a promising candidate for numerous applications.

articleTitle: Enhancing Lithium-Ion Battery Tomosynthesis Reconstruction Images using a 3-D UNet
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: We propose a method for enhancing Lithium-Ion Battery (LIB) tomosynthesis reconstructed images using a 3-D UNet network by using tomosynthesis-CT image pairs. Our approach involves 3-D tomosynthesis reconstructed image as the input and corresponding CT reconstructed image as the output. To reduce the size of the input and output due to computing memory issues, we decreased the resolution in depth direction of LIB and used a rectangular patch instead of the conventional square shape patch to take more care of the y-directional information. In the network modeling part, we used an upsampling instead of convolution to remove checkerboard artifacts in the image. For the loss functions, in addition to the mean square error (MSE) loss, we used the y-directional gradient and structure similarity index measure (SSIM) loss to improve the structure similarity in the y-direction. Using a rectangular shape patch instead of a square patch helped to reduce the stitching artifacts as well. Our results demonstrate that the proposed method successfully improves the resolution in the depth direction and reduces stitching artifacts, making it a promising approach for enhancing image quality of tomosynthesis in LIB inspection.

articleTitle: Advanced Leading-edge Discrimination Methods for Cherenkov-radiator-integrated Microchannel Plate Photomultiplier Tubes
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Reconstruction-free direct positron emission imaging (dPEI) using two single-channel Cherenkov-radiator-integrated microchannel plate photomultiplier tubes (CRI-MCP-PMTs) was recently demonstrated. However, the 4-channel oscilloscope used in the demonstration study is not suitable for clinical systems using multichannel detector modules, therefore a dedicated multichannel data acquisition (DAQ) system with ultra-high timing resolution is required. Moreover, for developing a multi-channel ultrafast DAQ system, the leading-edge discrimination (LED) method is preferred to reduce resource usage and complexity compared to a constant-fraction discrimination method. In this study, we investigate the characteristics of CRI-MCP-PMT signals and introduce the current status of development in advanced LED methods for CRI-MCP-PMTs. Timing performance was compared at different bandwidths from 0.5 GHz to 12.5 GHz. Advanced LED methods with appropriate event classification based on the characteristics of the CRI-MCP-PMT improved timing performance. When rise time information was used for event classification, the best CTR of 28.6 ps FWHM was obtained using 10.8% of total events. In addition, a CTR of 31.3 ps FWHM was obtained with 17.3% of total events using signal fall time information for event classification.

articleTitle: Marker Line Identification in Special Nuclear Material using Physics-Informed Autoencoding
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Nuclide identification codes have been extensively tested for their performance regarding special nuclear material (SNM) in the past. A main focus was put on the identification quality for masking scenarios. Normally strong medical masks are mixed with weak traces of the SNM, to find the limiting ratio, at which the identification code can no longer find the SNM. In the present work this perspective is changed. The paper questions, whether algorithms are capable to identify marker isotopes in SNM. Markers are of interest, as they contain information about the nuclear facility that produced the material. They consequently allow to determine a country of origin for the threat material.For the algorithm this means, the SNM is present with a strong signature. It is covering different perturbing isotopes. Advantage of this situation is, that the SNM is already known prior to the identification. A solution based on an Autoencoder (AE) is presented. This is an autoregressive neural network, that belongs to the group of unsupervised machine learning technique. Autoencoders have proven successful in anomaly detection problems in the past, as they feature two unique modes for detecting deviations from trained data.An implementation of the AE in Tensorflow is demonstrated, that is trained with over 400 real-world spectra of high enriched uranium (HEU). This network learns the best nonlinear representation of HEU in the lower dimensional subspace of the latent layers within the AE. Deviations from pure HEU can be detected quickly and the residual parts of the markers can be extracted via the AE procedure. Results of those tests are shown with a marker substitute (Eu-152). The method was also tested on Weapon-Grade Plutonium and with real marker lines.

articleTitle: Self-supervised Noise-aware Network for Dynamic Rubidium-82 Cardiac PET Image Denoising
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: PET is a functional imaging modality widely used in different clinical settings. Since PET scans are accompanied by substantial radiation exposure, reducing the radiation dose in PET scans is important. However, low-dose PET scans usually result in high image noise, which can negatively affect image quality and diagnostic performance. In addition, tracer decay in dynamic PET images results in continuously changing noise levels across different dynamic frames, especially for fastdecaying tracers such as Rubidium-82. Recent advances in deep learning showed great potential for low-dose PET denoising. However, most previously-proposed supervised methods cannot be adapted for this case since it is not possible to obtain paired labels for every single dynamic frame. Also, previously-proposed unsupervised methods were only developed for single noise-level images, and therefore cannot be adapted for dynamic cardiac PET scans due to changing noise levels across different frames. To address these challenges, we propose a self-supervised noise-aware method for dynamic Rubidium-82 cardiac PET image denoising. Validated on 10 patient studies obtained on a Siemens Biograph mCT PET/CT system, the proposed method showed promising denoising performance across all the dynamic frames.

articleTitle: A digital real-time high-resolution imaging system to quantify and identify all emitted charged particles
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: This paper describes an instrumentation imaging system that provides, at real-time, localization, quantification and identification of a radioactive source with a precision up to 20μm. The localization of each decay position is obtained with using a parallel ionization multiplier gaseous detector and a reconstruction algorithm. The spatial identification of the composition of the radioactive source is performed by an original specific set of temporal and energy spectrometry techniques. The system allows with a single detector to combine the measurement of the spatial distribution with the ability to separate and quantify at real time each radionuclide. From an application point of view, this system opens up possibilities for theragnostic applications that typically use two radionuclides. Further upstream, it can optimize the production and distribution challenge of α radionuclides by allowing the identification and characterization of individual radionuclides in radionuclide chains such as <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">225</sup>Ac. Moreover, the measurement system and the associated method could strongly contribute to facilitate research on the biodistribution of α radionuclides that are by their nature difficult to characterize by standard methods.

articleTitle: Design evaluation of a self-collimation single-photon emission breast tomography
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Self-collimation is a concept that sensitive detectors carry out collimation for themselves. For example, in a detector constructed with multi-layers of sparsely distributed scintillators, the inner (closer to the object) layer scintillators form physical apertures, or collimation, for outer layer scintillators. This concept and its implementation address a significant drawback of absorption-based collimation and opens the possibility of improving resolution and detection efficiency simultaneously. The goal of this work is to study the design considerations of a self-collimation single-photon emission breast tomography (SC-SPEBT) system.The system takes the shape of a hexagon prism, each side of it is a detector panel, comprising modules stacked in the axial direction. Each module consists of a GAGG(Ce) scintillator assembly masked on its side facing the FOV by a perforated tungsten plate. Scintillators, except those on the outmost layer, are sparsely distributed over an 8×8 grid pattern in the transverse plane, the grid pitch size is 3.36 mm in both tangential and radial directions. The size of each scintillator is 3-mm × 2-mm × 20-mm. In this work, with a preselected base configuration of detector geometry, we study the impact of 1) the width and number of apertures on the tungsten plate, and 2) the impact of introducing object movement during acquisition on the system response characteristics and image quality. We assess the resolution-to-noise trade-off of each configuration using the contrast recovery coefficient to noise ratio as a figure of merit. The studies are carried out through analytical system modeling and with simulated hot-rod and a contrast phantom. We have obtained preliminary results on hot-rod and contrast phantoms. At the conference, we will present configuration optimization results by analyzing system response characteristics in terms of projection probability density function (PPDF) and evaluating the resolution to noise trade-off.

articleTitle: Simultaneous Radiological Spectral Decomposition and Source Mapping with a Single Detector
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: This study introduces a novel method for decomposing a series of time-integrated energy spectra collected from a single, free-moving detector into their constituent radiological components while also reconstructing source distribution images corresponding to the identified components. Initially, the problem is formulated as an energy-image integrated spectral deconvolution problem. Subsequently, we leverage the inherent low-dimensional structures in the problem to ensure computational feasibility and robustness. Although the problem is highly ill-posed, we demonstrate that by imposing Gaussian process priors (GPP), the proposed method can effectively reconstruct source images and components even in low signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) scenarios with fluctuating background contributions. Moreover, the proposed spectral decomposition method allows for a better understanding of the salient radiological source and background features present in the imaging space.

articleTitle: Accelerated Parametric Imaging of Dynamic PET using Fully Convolutional Neural Networks
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Dynamic positron emission tomography (PET) images are useful in clinical practice because they can be used to calculate the metabolic parameters (Ki) of tissues using graphical methods (such as Patlak plots). Ki is more stable than the standard uptake value (SUV) and has a good reference value for clinical diagnosis. However, the long scanning time required for obtaining dynamic PET images, usually an hour, makes this method less useful in some ways. There is a tradeoff between the scan durations and the signal-to-noise ratios (SNRs) of Ki images. The purpose of our study is to obtain approximately the same image as that produced by scanning for one hour in just half an hour, improving the SNRs of images obtained by scanning for 30 minutes and reducing the necessary 1-hour scanning time for acquiring dynamic PET images. In this paper, we present a new approach to parametric imaging in positron emission tomography (PET) using a fully convolutional neural network with a U-Net architecture. Our method significantly reduces scanning time, allowing for higher-quality parametric images to be obtained after scanning for only 30 minutes compared to the standard hour-long scanning time. We also introduce a novel kinetic model network for processing dynamic PET images. Our proposed approach improves the signal-to-noise ratio and is more robust than previous methods that use the Patlak plot for quantitative analysis. Our method also reduces the noise and generation time of parametric images, making them available for clinical use more quickly. We demonstrate the efficacy of our method with simulations and real patient data.

articleTitle: Comprehensive Study on Cherenkov Radiation for Ultrafast PET Detectors, Considering Refractive Index and Wavelength
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: This study aims to investigate the characteristics of Cherenkov radiation with respect to wavelength and refractive index. Refractive index is a function of wavelength, and when it changes, not only does the gain of Cherenkov radiation increase, but also the photon loss in the medium increases. Therefore, we examine how photons of different wavelengths behave under changing refractive index conditions. We adjust the refractive index to maintain a constant emission angle of Cherenkov radiation based on the deceleration rate of electrons moving in the medium. When electrons generating Cherenkov radiation move a total of 200 μm, both long-wavelength and short-wavelength photons are emitted at the initial stage; however, only short-wavelength photons are emitted at the late stage. Although the shorter-wavelength photons arrive first among the photons that reach the detector, the longer-wavelength photons are detected more, forming a significant peak, which is due to the fact that the former experience more absorption-based photon loss in the medium than the latter.

articleTitle: A Feasibility Study of Domain-aware Deep Learning Ideal Model Observer
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Assessment of medical image quality is a task historically performed by human experts, yet due to high cost and time constrains, algorithms called Model Observers (MO) have been developed to perform this task instead. Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) based MOs have previously been implemented for defect localization in medical images. Although effective, this approach lacks domain awareness - the ability to discern the unseen data types (i.e. different statistical characteristics) compared to the data it was trained on. In this paper, we are proposing an approach for defect localization which aims to achieve the accuracy of the ideal MO, as well as reconstruct the input image, for the purpose of achieving domain-awareness. By developing a domain-aware algorithm, we model a clinician's behavior, who can decide whether an image is familiar, and judge their own reliability in this context. Preliminary results show the algorithm's ability to successfully perform defect localization task alongside reconstructing the original input image. Additionally, we demonstrate a strong correlation between the defect localization accuracy and its mean squared error (MSE). These results reveal that a CNN based MO can be trained to perform both defect localization and image reconstruction simultaneously by minimizing two MSE functions - one for each task, instead of having to train two models which perform these tasks separately.

articleTitle: Accurate Range Shift Verification by Using a Dual-View LYSO-LaBr3 Compton Camera Prototype during Proton Beam Irradiation
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Compton-based prompt gamma imaging (PGI) is promising to realize a real-time range verification for in-vivo beams during proton therapy. However, the resolution of the real-world detectors and the detection efficiency under the clinical dose rate limit the actual application of the Compton camera (CC). Besides, the background noise caused by the secondary neutrons and protons further degrades the spatial resolution of the CC in the PGI. To meet the requirement of the high-resolution and low-background 3D PGI, we attempted the first-ever effort to develop a novel dual-view Compton camera prototype. The developed dual-view LYSO-LaBr<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</inf> CC utilized the projection data obtained by the different CC to extract feature information and eliminate the background noise. Meanwhile, the prototype overcomes the problem of distortion in the direction perpendicular to the detector plane during the 3D reconstruction of a single Compton camera. A 13 MeV proton beam with a cross-section of 1 mm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sup> irradiates a block of graphite, a block of polymethacrylates, and a block of fresh pork, respectively. A range shift varied from 1 mm to 5 mm of the proton beam is used to evaluate the performance of the prototype in PGI. The current intensity was about 640 nA. The pulse width and frequency were 100 μs and 1 Hz, respectively. The number of incident protons in each measurement was about 3.6×10<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">8</sup>. The developed CC prototype could distinguish the displacement of the Bragg peak in 2 mm (reaching 1 mm) at a distance of about 13 cm. The mean deviation of the reconstructed positions of the Bragg peak was 0.13 mm in the eighteen groups of experiments. The experiments demonstrate the feasibility of the developed dual-view LYSO-LaBr<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</inf> CC in realizing accurate range shift monitoring and show its potential in range verification during clinical proton therapy and high particle rate proton therapy (e.g. FLASH proton therapy).

articleTitle: A noise-adapted network for low-dose CT imaging
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Low-dose CT techniques attempt to minimize the radiation exposure of patients by estimating high-resolution normal-dose CT images to reduce the risk of radiation-induced cancer. In recent years, many deep learning methods have been proposed to solve this problem by building a mapping function between low-dose CT images and their high-dose counterparts. However, most of these methods ignore the effect of different radiation doses on the final CT images, which results in large differences in the intensity of the noise observable in CT images. Moreover, the noise intensity of low-dose CT images exhibits significant differences under different medical device manufacturers. In this paper, we propose a noise-adapted network to recover low-dose CT images under uncertain noise levels. Under two dose reduction strategies, experiments to evaluate the performance of the proposed method are conducted on two datasets, including the simulated clinical AAPM challenge datasets and commercial CT datasets from United Imaging Healthcare (UIH). The experimental results illustrate the effectiveness of our proposed method in terms of noise suppression and structural detail preservation compared with several other deep learning-based methods. Ablation studies validate the effectiveness of the individual components regarding the afforded performance improvement. Further research for practical clinical applications and other medical modalities is required in future works.

articleTitle: 3D Prompt Gamma Imaging in a Dual-head Multi-slit System for Proton Beam Range Monitoring
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Proton range online verification is of great importance in proton therapy due to range uncertainty. Prompt gamma imaging is a promising method for online range monitoring.In previous work, a dual-head system aiming at 3D prompt gamma imaging was already assembled and calibrated. Spatial resolution of the system is better than 2 mm and sensitivity at the center of the field of view (FOV) is 0.62%, according to results in <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">60</sup>Co point source experiment. In this work, the first system test under proton therapy equipment is reported. 100 MeV, 0.5 nA proton beam is used in the experiment. Prompt gamma generated by a polymethylmethacrylate (PMMA) phantom is collected by the system. A maximum-likelihood expectation-maximization (MLEM) algorithm is used for 3D prompt gamma image reconstruction.Range shift of 1 mm is able to be distinguished by calculating the most distal edge position (MDEP) of prompt gamma profile. MDEP accuracy evaluated through repeated experiments is 0.2 mm. Positioning accuracy of the prompt gamma distribution peak position in proton beam cross section is 0.2 mm. Range deviation accuracy calculated by prompt gamma image of 1×10<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">8</sup> protons is less than 1 mm.The dual-head imaging system provides excellent result when the Bragg peak of proton beam is located near the center of the FOV. Proton range resolving ability of the system in proton pencil beam scanning lattice will be evaluated in the future.

articleTitle: Simulation Based Feasibility Analysis of a new XFCT Imaging System based on Gaseous Detectors
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: X-ray fluorescence computed tomography (XFCT) enables to map three-dimensional distribution of elements present in a sample.
