Gaseous detectors are suitable for the purpose, mainly due to there characteristics, such as, low material budget, versatility, and lower complexity, which make them suitable to be applied in several imaging studies. In this work, we simulated the novel concept of XFCT imaging using GATE simulation software. Encouraging results were obtained, revealing the potential suitability of a gaseous detector-based XFCT imaging system for producing 3D elemental distribution of samples.

articleTitle: Lessons Learned from the SkinScan Project
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: The SkinScan project develops computational tools for a challenging radiotherapy technique -total skin irradiation with electrons for the treatment of cutaneous lymphomas. It addresses a complex problem domain, which still rests on a radiation therapy methodology developed in the 80's of the past century, by means of an innovative computational approach that involves a multidisciplinary team of physicists, medical experts, computer scientists and bioengineers. In addition to its intrinsic scientific difficulties, the project has suffered hardships associated with the computational environment, the software development process, the heterogeneous background of the team and unforeseeable external constraints, which have threatened its success. We review the obstacles encountered in the computational development and we analyze in retrospect the effectiveness of the steps taken to address them. We highlight how technical and methodological aspects are intertwined and show how issues in software engineering hindered the achievement of scientific results. The lessons learned from this project represent valuable food for thought for other computational developments. Finally, we present an overview of SkinScan scientific results and identify the key factors which enabled them.

articleTitle: In-beam whole gamma imaging of a 10C ion beam: a phantom study
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: For range verification in carbon therapy, in-beam positron emission tomography (PET) imaging of radioactive ion (RI) beams is ideal because the beam stopping position can be directly visualized. Among such RI beams, a <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">10</sup>C beam is appropriate because its short half-life (19.3 s) results in high signal to noise ratio even for an in-beam PET scan of about 1 min. <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">10</sup>C emits a 718 keV gamma ray almost simultaneously with the positron decay, and we have shown the feasibility of its direct localization based on the b<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">+</sup>-gamma coincidence (i.e., triple-gamma imaging) by our whole gamma imaging (WGI). The WGI system is realized as a dual-detector ring geometry, which can work in three modes of PET, Compton imaging and triple-gamma imaging. However, range verification performance for each of these three modes has not been assessed yet. In particular, the potential of Compton imaging, which is not influenced by the relatively long positron range of <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">10</sup>C, has not been shown. Therefore in this work, for the <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">10</sup>C beam range verification, we compared the performance of Compton imaging with those of PET and triple-gamma imaging using the WGI. First, a current WGI prototype was modeled by Geant4, and imaging performance was assessed for a <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">10</sup>C point source and a <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">10</sup>C pencil beam. Then, a polymethyl methacrylate (PMMA) phantom was irradiated with a <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">10</sup>C beam under in-beam WGI measurement in the carbon therapy facility of the Heavy Ion Medical Accelerator in Chiba, and the measured images were compared with the depth dose, which was measured in water. Small shifts (< 3 mm) of the Bragg peak position and the positions of the peaks for Compton, PET and triple-gamma imaging were observed, which confirm the feasibility of Compton imaging for range verification of a <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">10</sup>C beam. The worst shift was observed for the Compton imaging which may be explained by the energy resolution of the scatterer detectors. The availability of three imaging modalities may offer better range verification.

articleTitle: Development of an omnidirectional detector for beta and gamma-ray imaging with fractal geometry
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Radiation imaging is useful in various fields where the location of radiation sources needs to be identified. Especially in environments where radiation sources are distributed in three dimensions and difficult to locate, the development of a small imaging sensor that can detect radiation in the 4π direction will have a significant impact on the progress of work. We have developed a radiation detector with a fractal geometry. This is a unit of tetrahedral radiation sensors, 16 sensors are arranged in a Sierpinski tetrahedron shape, and the space between the sensors is filled with heavy metals. The count rates of the individual sensors make it possible to determine the direction of radiation incidence. Furthermore, since there is no external shielding, the distribution of charged particles, such as beta rays, can also be measured. We have analyzed the response of the Sierpinski radiation detector with respect to the incident direction of γ and β rays and compared it with experimental results to understand the sensitivity characteristics.

articleTitle: PET Imaging using Expanded Energy Window with Monte Carlo Simulation based Scatter Correction
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: PET systems with LYSO crystals generally has a low-level discriminator (LLD) around 430 keV, to seek the balance between sensitivity and noise equivalent count rate (NECR). A lower LLD could provide a higher sensitivity, but may cost of lower NECR and greater difficulties in scatter correction (SC). However, scans with expanded energy window (EEW) is a possible scenario for simultaneously collecting background radiation and annihilation photons. This work explores whether the increased events with EEW could be beneficial. Monte Carlo simulation (MCS) based-SC is used to handle the increased scatter events. Furthermore, we proposed two advanced methods, i.e. asymmetric energy window (AEW) and dual-energy-window reconstruction (DEWR), for better exploiting of data. The proposed method was evaluated by: 1) a NEMA NEC phantom for observing the variation in true, scatter, random counts, NEC and TOF resolution for different LLDs. 2) a modified IQ phantom with a 50:1 contrast lung insert for SC stress test, 3) a combination phantom, consisting of a Hoffman phantom, a NEMA IQ phantom and a uniform phantom, for image quality assessment. The results show that AEW provides up to 52.4% increase of sensitivity at 200-keV LLD with no decrease in NEC, that MCS-based SC is indeed capable of handling EEW reconstructions and that AEW+DEWR can be beneficial for image quality under certain settings.

articleTitle: Novel Compton SPECT Camera for Whole-Body Diagnostic and Targeted Radionuclide Therapy Applications
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: We present a collimator-less SPECT system using a Compton camera design with applications in whole-body imaging and targeted radionuclide therapy applications that enables multi-energy gamma photon detection with high efficiency compared to mechanically collimated SPECT systems. The system consists of one fixed, and one zooming scatterer/absorber detector pairs, providing an FOV adequate for whole-body imaging, while achieving high sensitivity and clinical useable imaging resolution within reasonable scanning time. The imaging performance is evaluated at two energy peaks simulated (440 keV, 218 keV), the two detectable gamma energies generated from Actinium-225, one of the radionuclides under investigation for targeted alpha therapy (TAT). Results show a 5.5 mm-8.0 mm resolution with sensitivity 0.2%-0.05% for whole-body imaging can be achieved.

articleTitle: Modular Compton Coincidence NaI Array for Scintillator Light Yield Non-Proportionality Characterisation
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: The Compton Coincidence Technique (CCT) is a well-established experiment to characterise the light yield non-proportionality of scintillator detectors. This project aims to resolve some of the impracticalities performing these measurements.First, a modular and scalable array of NaI(Tl) secondary detectors will allow for simultaneous measurements which speeds up the overall characterisation time. Second, this project introduces tungsten powder collimation and shielding with 3-D printed housing. The 3-D printed baseplates also allow for interchangeable scattering angle selection. These additions make the technique more flexible but maintains the precision and consistency required for the linearity characterisation measurements.This facility contributes to the existing detector characterisation capabilities at AWE for nuclear security research and development (R&D) under the UK Nuclear Threat Reduction (NTR) programme. Additionally, it adds value to our collaborative academic and industrial partner research efforts in the characterisation of novel scintillator materials.

articleTitle: Towards Efficient Data Processing on the Edge With Neuromorphic Computing for Instrumentation
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: With Moore's law coming to an end and the increasing computational complexity of deep neural network models, a noticeable gap is emerging between the limited computing power available at the edge and the potential of machine learning for instrumentation. Unlike classical deep neural networks, spiking neural networks utilize asynchronous computing and exhibit inherent low-power computing potential, making them ideal for processing large amounts of high-rate event-based data. To showcase this approach, we provide an initial proof of concept that focuses on the CookieBox - an angular streaking detector developed for LCLS-II placed upstream as an online beam diagnostic tool. We utilized a surrogate gradient learning approach to train a basic spiking neural network capable of characterizing individual X-ray pulse using the CookieBox data. The spiking neural network achieves an overall classification accuracy of 86 %, which is comparable to the accuracy achieved by the most recent convolutional neural network performing the same task. We also addressed key elements to enable spiking neural networks capabilities in terms of power and latency requirements for edge machine learning in science experiments. The proposed approach demonstrates and validates that a simple spiking neural network can compete with sophisticated deep neural network and has significant implications for the field of edge machine learning for scientific data acquisition.

articleTitle: Development of a mobile gamma-ray LaBr3:Ce detector system for in situ radionuclide analysis
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: The spillage of polluted process water from the Bosveld Phosphates mine adjacent to the Kruger National Park, South Africa during December 2013/January 2014, led to the investigation of possible radiation pollution in the Olifants River. The river runs directly into the park. An environmental impact study has been planned together with South Africa National Parks for in situ measurements, to evaluate the current situation in terms of pollution from a radiation and chemical perspective. The study will be extended upstream from the Olifants River to create a footprint of the current state of radiation contamination and the determination of disequilibrium by investigating the chemistry related to U, Th and the relevant gamma-ray emitting isotopes. A mobile gamma-ray detection unit equipped with a LaBr3:Ce detector has been designed and built in the form of a portable backpack that can be used for in situ measurement of radionuclide activity. Real-time activity data are collected and synchronised with GPS coordination. In addition to these measurements, grab samples are taken and analysed in the laboratory using a gamma-ray spectrometer equipped with an HPGe-detector.A comparison of in situ results obtained by the mobile device and the more sensitive laboratory spectrometer will allow the determination of the sensitivity, effectiveness and practicality of the mobile system. Grab samples will be analysed chemically to determine radioactive decay disequilibrium and fate and transport of radioactive elements. These results will be used for environmental impact study purposes in the designated areas affected by the mine spillage as mentioned earlier.Proof-of-principal of the measurement system was undertaken at iThemba LABS with radioactive sources and at the South African Nuclear Energy Corporation. In situ measurements at two sites in the Kruger National Park have been performed and preliminary results will be presented.

articleTitle: CT-less attenuation correction using the lutetium background radiation in the NeuroEXPLORER
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: The high sensitivity, increased volume of crystal material, and improved timing resolution in the current generation of PET scanners has led to increased interest in developing CT–less attenuation correction using the lutetium background radiation. In this work, the background radiation from the radionuclide <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">176</sup>Lu in the LYSO scintillators was used to estimate the attenuation map for PET attenuation correction (AC) in a recently-developed brain-dedicated PET scanner, the NeuroEXPLORER (NX). The proposed method was evaluated using a NEMA NU2 image quality (IQ) phantom dataset and a human subject scan performed on the NX. The lutetium-based AC from the cold IQ phantom was compared to the CT-based AC. Non-local means (NLM) filtering was also applied to improve the estimate of attenuation maps. The contrast of the six hot spheres and the centered cold volume were analyzed. Lutetium-based AC outperformed the non-AC images of the IQ phantom with 10% bias compared to CT-based AC. This bias is mostly due to the lack of scatter correction in the transmission reconstruction. The NLM smoothing provided higher contrast in the hot spheres and improved quantitation. Lutetium-based attenuation map of a human subject scan demonstrated good image quality in the soft tissue, skull, and air cavities in the nasal, paranasal, and tracheal regions. The results demonstrate the feasibility of using lutetium background radiation for CT-less AC in the NeuroEXPLORER.

articleTitle: High-spatial-resolution imaging of rhenium-186 produced by accelerator-based synthesis
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Rhenium radioisotopes are very attractive for targeted radionuclide therapy. <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">186</sup>Re has both beta particle emissions with properties suitable to perform targeted therapy and photon emissions, which can be used for diagnostic investigation by SPECT. Accelerator-based synthesis by proton-or deuteron-induced reaction on <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">186</sup>W can provide no-carrier-added <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">186</sup>Re, which is difficult to produce by a conventional method with nuclear reactors. However, in our previous study, the signals for imaging, 137 keV photons emitted from <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">186</sup>Re produced in the <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">186</sup>W(d,2n)<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">186</sup>Re reaction at the deuteron energy of 24 MeV, were prone to be contaminated by the continuum background constituted by scattering of high-energy gamma-rays caused by rhenium isotopes other than <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">186</sup>Re. In particular, the continuum background generated by the byproduct <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">184</sup>Re caused significant degradation in imaging quality. In this study, we produced <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">186</sup>Re in the <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">186</sup>W(p,n)<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">186</sup>Re reaction at the proton energy of 15 MeV using the RIKEN AVF cyclotron. The radionuclidic purity of <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">186</sup>Re was successfully improved from 94.43% to 99.56%. We demonstrated the effectiveness of high-purity <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">186</sup>Re for high-spatial-resolution imaging with an ultra-high resolution small animal SPECT (CdTe-DSD SPECT-I) recently developed by our team. We believe that such high-spatial-resolution imaging will contribute to drug delivery studies to improve precision in radionuclide therapy.

articleTitle: A time-based double-sided readout concept of LYSO:Ce,Ca and BGO fibers for future axial TOF-PET
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Improving time-of-flight (TOF) is an effective way to boost the signal-to-noise ratio in positron emission tomography (PET), however, the scanner sensitivity and resolution must be maintained. The use of axially aligned long LYSO:Ce,Ca or BGO fibers employing double-sided readout has the potential to reduce parallax errors through depth-of-interaction (DOI) estimation and to allow a reduction in the number of readout channels required, resulting in cost benefits. Due to orientation, these fibers may also facilitate the integration of TOF-PET with magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) in hybrid imaging systems.In a first step, we tested LYSO:Ce,Ca and BGO scintillation fibers of 3x3x20 mm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</sup> and 3x3x100 mm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</sup> to determine the best achievable DOI and coincidence time resolution (CTR). Using Broadcoam NUV-HD SiPMs of 3x3 mm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sup> size we measured for the 100 mm fiber an average CTR of (137±1) ps FWHM and an average DOI resolution within the fiber of (12.3±0.5) mm FWHM. The 3x3x20 mm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</sup> crystal showed a sub-100 ps CTR of (98±1) ps and a DOI resolution of (8.5±0.2) mm, whereas in both cases the spatial resolution is defined to 3 mm in all other directions. Newest SiPMs from Broadcom, with metal in trench technology (NUV-MT), further show to improve these values. Measuring with 3x3x20 mm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</sup> BGO we obtain (220±5) ps FWHM in standard single-sided readout, but observed a non-negligible influence of optical crosstalk in double-sided readout, caused by the opposing SiPM.This study indicates that long scintillation fibers can achieve excellent CTR and DOI resolution, almost independent on the fiber length, due to a time-based estimation. Using 100 mm long fibers, an electronic channel reduction of a factor 2.5 is achieved, which can lead to lower production costs and to advantages in building organ-dedicated or total-body/large-scale PET scanners.

articleTitle: Neural Architecture Search for Unsupervised PET Image Denoising
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Deep image prior (DIP) has been proven to be an effective method to improve the image quality of positron emission tomography (PET) images when large datasets are not available. However most DIP-type methods are based on 3D U-net, which may be not suitable for unsupervised PET image denoising. In this work, we developed a neural architecture search method to find a better neural architecture for unsupervised PET image denoising. The cell level architecture and the network level architecture are searched alternatively. In each searching step, we designed a super network as a full set of all possible networks. Then the high-count PET images were used to update architecture and the low-count PET images were used to update weights. The performance of the searched architecture was evaluated through phantom study. The results showed that the searched neural architecture can better preserve image details while maintaining a lower noise level.

articleTitle: Opportunities and limitations of pure Cherenkov TOF PET scanners
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: To detect annihilation photons, PET conventionally employs scintillation light detection, but an interesting alternative involves detecting Cherenkov photons. Dense Cherenkov radiators are highly efficient at stopping gammas and can offer exceptional coincidence time resolution (CTR). However, due to the limited number of detected Cherenkov photons, pure Cherenkov detectors provide very little energy information, leading to higher scatter fractions. This work explores the performance of scanners based on pure Cherenkov detectors using Monte Carlo simulations. The simulations are performed on a super-computing network using GATE software, and CASToR software is used for (TOF-OSEM) image reconstruction. The investigated detectors are based on 20 mm long PbF$_2$ crystals wrapped with a reflector and coupled to a SiPM. The geometry of Cherenkov scanners is based on clinical scanners with a regular and long axial field of view (LAFOV) - Siemens Biograph Vision (Quadra). The performance of Cherenkov PET scanners is evaluated and compared to the reference scanners, following the NEMA standard and also imaging a highly anatomically detailed phantom (XCAT). Special attention is dedicated to the dark count rate (DCR) of the SiPMs, which could notably affect the image quality. The DCR of SiPMs is characterized at cryogenic temperatures, and the degree of cooling is estimated to make the impact of noise on image quality negligible. The results indicate that pure Cherenkov PET scanners can have a significant edge over scintillation-based scanners for imaging objects of diameters up to roughly 30 cm. This makes them especially suitable for brain and breast imaging, as well as preclinical imaging. Additionally, the results show that Cherenkov detectors are scalable. The low-cost Cherenkov detectors could therefore become very interesting for LAFOV scanners as their current high cost is limiting their dissemination in hospitals and research clinics.

articleTitle: GAPS: Antarctic Balloon Mission to Search for Dark Matter Signatures in Cosmic-ray Antinuclei
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: The General Antiparticle Spectrometer (GAPS) is an Antarctic balloon mission to search for dark matter by measuring low-energy cosmic-ray antinuclei using a novel detection technique. GAPS is the first experiment optimized to detect cosmic-ray antideuterons below 0.25 GeV/n. Because antideuteron production in this energy range is kinematically suppressed in standard astrophysical processes but expected from a wide range of well-motivated dark matter models, detection of antideuterons by GAPS would be a smoking-gun signature of new physics. Meanwhile, GAPS will also provide a precision cosmic-ray antiproton spectrum in a previously unprobed low-energy range, as well as leading sensitivity to low-energy antihelium-3. The GAPS measurement is possible thanks to a novel particle identification method based on exotic atom formation, de-excitation, and decay. Exotic atoms provide a unique event topology for negatively-charged antinuclei and enable a large sensitive area for detecting rare events within the constraints of a long-duration balloon. The instrument contains two sensitive detector systems. A time-of-flight system, composed of 160 scintillator panels with <400 ps timing resolution, provides the system trigger as well as the GAPS energy scale. Completely enclosed within the time-of-flight, the 2.5 m3 tracker volume is instrumented with 1000 10-cm-diameter silicon sensors which serve as the target, X-ray spectrometer, and particle tracker. An oscillating heat pump thermal system cools the tracker without the need for a bulky cryostat. Calibration of the integrated payload is underway, with the first of several Antarctic flights expected in 2024. This contribution will briefly review the dark matter motivation for a cosmic-ray antinucleus detector. It will then introduce the GAPS instrument and its exotic-atom detection capability before finally reporting the calibration on the sensitive detector systems and the performance of the integrated payload.

articleTitle: ALICE Run 3 at the LHC
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: The ALICE experiment at the CERN LHC has undergone a major upgrade during the second long shutdown of the LHC (2018-2021). This includes the upgrade of several existing detectors like the Time Projection Chamber and the Inner Tracking System, addition of new detectors and a full upgrade of the readout electronics, online and offline systems. The motivation was to improve upon the existing physics measurements, provide insights into new measurements and to fully exploit the scientific potential of the LHC with heavy ions at high luminosity. In Runs 3 and 4, ALICE will record Pb-Pb collisions at the interaction rate of up to 50 kHz and accumulate 13 nb<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">-1</sup> of Pb-Pb collisions, gaining a factor of 100 in statistics for minimum bias triggers and a factor of 10 for calorimeter and muon triggers over the previous programme up to Run 2. After a successful pilot beam program in late 2021, the official restart of the LHC happened with the start of Run 3 in 2022. ALICE, with the new upgrades, successfully participated in the data taking of the pp collisions at √s =13.6 TeV followed by a test run with Pb ions in 2022. In 2023, it is foreseen to take 30 pb<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">-1</sup> of pp collision data and 3.25 nb<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">-1</sup> of Pb-Pb collision data. In this contribution, an overview of the upgraded system will be presented along with a discussion on the performance of ALICE in Run 3.

articleTitle: Investigation of Nanocomposite Scintillators and New Detector Concepts for High Energy Physics
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Particle physics experiments running at future accelerator facilities will rely on fast timing detectors to cope with high event pileup and to enhance particle identification capabilities. Direct band gap engineered semiconductor nanostructures show a high potential for emission of prompt photons due to quantum confinement, standing out in fast timing and high light yield with potential low cost production, thus triggering interest in the high energy physics community. In this contribution, characterization results of the scintillation properties of some promising nanomaterial scintillators will be presented and an overview of possible light-based detector designs based on these nanomaterials will be given, focusing on the NanoCal Blue Sky project of the European project AIDAinnova, a new generation of shashlik calorimeters. First results, obtained during test beam activities, will be presented as well.

articleTitle: A new approach for a quantitative and real-time activity measurement of radiopharmaceuticals inside automatic dose dispensers
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: New technologies in nuclear medicine and PET diagnostics have rapidly increased in recent years for radiopharmaceutical dose preparation based on automatic algorithms. Automatic radiopharmaceutical dose dispensers (ARDDs) reduce radiation levels for technologists and potential infection risk for patients. Ionization chambers are currently the most used detectors to measure the activity of radiopharmaceuticals in ARDDs. This study is part of an international endeavor to develop a new approach for evaluating radiopharmaceutical activity in an ARDD named KARL<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">100</inf>. A preliminary prototype was constructed, consisting of a plastic scintillator (PVT) linked with an array of silicon photomultipliers (SiPMs) and a single channel analyzer (SCA), allowing for the radionuclide's activity concentration to be read out at "run-time." Three widely used medical radioisotopes, <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">18</sup>F, <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">11</sup>C, and <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">68</sup>Ga, were used to evaluate the performance of the detector in terms of linearity and repeatability of the measurements. Half-life and linear response were evaluated over a wide range of activities with different decay schemes. Data analysis was conducted, resulting in half-lives of the <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">18</sup>F, <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">11</sup>C, and <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">68</sup>Ga radioisotopes of 109.75±0.35, 20.62±0.34, and 67.82±0.25 min, respectively, with calculated deviations of 0.0167%, 1.00%, and 0.29% from expected values. The linear response of the detector over the entire range of desired activity concentrations was confirmed after data correction for the detector dead time. Calibration of the detector combined with the dispenser system was carried out in parallel investigations to provide the required device properties for reference applications in nuclear medicine.

articleTitle: Application of Optical Filter for SiPM Crosstalk Reduction
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Correlated noise can be a major limiting factor in the performance of silicon photomultiplier (SiPM)-based detectors operated at high over-voltages (OVs). Utilizing a mismatch between the wavelengths of scintillation and crosstalk photons, we proposed to employ a thin optical bandpass filter between the crystal and SiPM that selectively filters out the external crosstalk produced in the Geiger avalanche. The effect of the filter on noise was investigated on four models, i.e., bare, filter-, crystal-, and filter-crystal-coupled SiPMs. A 4×4 array (AFBR-S4N44P164M) and a single-channel (AFBR-S4N44P014M) 4-mm SiPMs were tested with a 12×12×20 mm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</sup> LYSO and a 3×3×20 mm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</sup> LGSO crystals, respectively. The readout electronics were capable of high-frequency pulse shaping, hence resolving every noise pulse. The noise rate (NR) and crosstalk probability of the array and single channel models were measured under dark conditions from randomly sampled signals. The impact of the filter on coincidence time resolution (CTR) was also investigated using the coincidence measurement of the single channel detectors. The array measurements showed that the filter resulted in a 92% reduction in NR (55 to 4.3 MHz) which was even lower than that of bare SiPM. Crosstalk photon pileup also largely decreased to 1.5%. Large losses in spatial and temporal correlations of the crosstalk caused by inter-channel sharing were explained by high NR but less pileup of the crystal-coupled compared to bare SiPM. The single channel results showed a 63% decrease in crosstalk probability, owing to the suppressed contribution of the external crosstalk on the time delay distribution. The filter degraded CTR at optimum OV by 6 ps but yielded minor degradation in extremely high OV. The results demonstrated a promising effect of the optical filter on the noise reduction, particularly for configurations susceptible to external crosstalk, such as detectors operated at high OVs and at room temperature.

articleTitle: Scintillation Properties of Ti-doped LiGaO2 for Neutron Detection
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: In recent years, a development of neutron scintillators becomes attractive research topic. Up to now, a proportional counter which encloses <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</sup>He gas as a neutron capture element has been mainly used as neutron detectors. However, demands of neutron detectors has increased with growth of security techniques, and shortage of <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</sup>He has been concerned. Therefore, neutron scintillators have been required as replacements to the gas proportional counter. Some <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">6</sup>Li-based neutron scintillators such as Ce-doped Li-glass (GS20) [1], Ag-doped LiF/ZnS [2], and Ce or Eu-doped LiCaAlF<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">6</inf> [3] have been developed. However, there are no materials which meet completely favorable properties. LiAlO<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf>and LiGaO<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf> has been studied as neutron scintillators. Particularly, LiAlO<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf> showed high light yield which was comparable to GS20, and the light yield of Ti-doped LiAlO<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf> were surpass GS20 [4], [5]. Although LiGaO<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf> showed lower light yield than LiAlO<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf>, there is a room for studies on activator-doped LiGaO<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf>. In this study, we synthesized undoped and Ti-doped LiGaO<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf> crystals and evaluated their scintillation properties. The undoped and Ti-doped crystals showed the luminescence due to the host defects and Ti<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">4+</sup> charge transfer, respectively. In the pulse height spectra under neutron irradiation, all the synthesized crystals exhibited thermal neutron peak. The absolute scintillation light yield of the 3% Ti-doped crystal was estimated to be 6710 ph/n ± 10% which was comparable to that of commercial <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">6</sup>Li-glass scintillator.

articleTitle: Cosmo-ArduSiPM: a New Dual-Channel Particle and Light Detector for CubeSat Missions and Earth Applications
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Our INFN Roma1 group has developed a novel architecture of all-in-one scintillator particle detectors, ArduSiPM, utilizing the latest advances in silicon photomultiplier sensors (SiPM) and System on Chip (SoC) technology. By intensively using the internal peripherals of the microcontroller, we have reduced external components to analog parts only, making these devices compact and high-performance. Building on this success, we have now created an even more powerful and compact device, Cosmo ArduSiPM, suitable for space missions. This new detector employs the Microchip SAMV71 320 MHz, 32-Bit ARM® Cortex®-M7, and has two independent channels within a CubeSat form factor weighing only 40 grams. Configurable firmware can be customized to suit various applications and can be seamlessly integrated with different Cubesat On-Board Computers. CosmoArduSiPM can also be operated standalone using its USB interface, which expands its usability for ground-based applications. The analog front-end of Cosmo-ArduSiPM is essentially identical to ArduSiPM, allowing for continued development of the technology. The use of software and SoC capabilities in the ArduSiPM architecture, instead of custom ASICs, provides significant advantages in cost and development time, while upgrades to new commercial SoCs remain easy. We are excited to present our innovative detector technology and its applications at this conference.

articleTitle: Simulation of Particle Paths for Single Cell Tracking in Positron Emission Tomography
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: To validate new reconstruction algorithms in positron emission tomography that are able to track single, radioactively labeled cells, ground truth data that realistically reflect the path of the cells are required. Based on the organ and blood vessel structure of the XCAT phantom, this work aims to simulate these paths in the human body and use them for single cell imaging simulations in GATE. The complex structure of the blood vessels is simplified by considering only certain nodes and assuming that the path between those nodes is linear. Branches of the bloodstream are chosen as the positions of the nodes, as well as places where the blood vessels curve in such a way that the assumption of linearity would lead to a significant spatial error. In addition to the spatial coordinates, each node stores information about which nodes the cell can move to next, the speed at which the cell moves to this node, and the diameter of the blood vessel. If there are several nodes to choose from as the next node, a decision is made based on a given probability as to which node the cell will migrate to. The probabilities can be obtained from measured or simulated concentration distributions of the cells in the body, for example from a physiologically based pharmacokinetic model. As a proof-of-concept, single cell paths are simulated for the kidney arteries showing the potential and feasibility of the proposed method.

articleTitle: Using Diffusion Models for CNN-Based Smoothing Parameter Tuning in Regularized PET Reconstruction
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: In regularized positron emission tomography (PET)reconstruction, it is important to carefully tune the smoothing parameter to achieve a balance between noise reduction and preservation of image features. While efforts have been made to develop automated methods of tuning the smoothing parameter, most of the results have not yet been satisfactory. In this work, we propose a convolutional neural network (CNN)-based smoothing parameter tuning method whose training pairs consist of the sinograms as inputs and the smoothing parameter values as outputs. For a dataset to train the CNN, we generate noiseless sample images and calculate the smoothing parameter for each image using an ML approach. Here, diffusion models, which have proven useful for generating sample images, are used to simulate brain images. Synthetic PET data are then obtained by projecting sample images and adding Poisson noise. To generate large amounts of training pairs, which must be diverse and extensive enough to properly train the CNN, we first train the diffusion model with massive realizations of Gibbs sampling and then retrain with a limited number of conventional digital brain phantoms. The simulation results indicate that our method of using the diffusion model provides an efficient way of generating training datasets for the CNN dedicated to tuning the smoothing parameter in a data-driven manner, and leads to optimized image quality.

articleTitle: On the local geometry of the PET reconstruction problem
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Intrinsic uncertainties related to the ill-posedness of the PET image reconstruction inverse problem are investigated in this work. These uncertainties could lead to instabilities in the reconstructed images in particular when Deep Learning approaches are employed. We propose a framework, based on a Bayesian hypothesis testing, enabling to define various distinguishability measures between PET images and propose a local analysis of such a measure in a neighborhood of a reference image. We test numerically this approach in a synthetic experiment of a Biograph TruePoint TrueV acquisition using a 3D brain PET phantom derived from a [18F]-FDG exam with 100 anatomo-functional regions extracted. Our analysis allows us to highlight the key factors impacting the detectability of variations in a region of interest and to exhibit concrete examples of directions along which variations may not be detectable, and instabilities could appear in PET image reconstruction. In addition, it allows us to conduct a quantitative analysis of the role played by the injected radiotracer dose, and to define thresholds below which clinically significant variations cannot be detected.

articleTitle: Dynamic range enhancement circuit and characterization of non-stationary gain effects in pulsed-reset charge sensitive amplifiers
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: In charge sensitive amplifiers (CSAs), a linear small signal charge-to-voltage conversion gain, is obtained connecting a capacitance Cf in feedback to a high gain voltage amplifier. However, for a sufficiently large input/output signal, the linearity assumption, valid for the neighborhood of the DC operating point (OP), is inevitably lost due to the inherent nonlinearity of internal active and passive elements of the circuit. In pulsed-reset CSA architectures [1], even small charge signals can stack on the feedback capacitance across the integration period, producing an output ramp which effectively moves the DC-OP, and slightly changes the small-signal gain over time up to the output saturation level, or until the reset phase occurs. Using different integrated CSAs, and mapping the small signal gain variations across the different DC-OPs through the integration ramp, we studied and modelled the effect on the spectroscopic resolution of the radiation detection system due to this non-stationary gain behaviour [2]. Experimental results show that, depending on the effective dynamic range selected during the measurement, even small variations in the conversion gain (<1%) for a limited portion of the output CSA voltage ramp can cause significant broadening and peak shift on the 5.9 keV 55Fe line. A circuital solution based on a voltage level shifting on the feedback discharge path to optimize the DC starting point of the CSA integration ramp is presented [3], allowing an increase of the effective linear dynamic range without affecting the spectroscopic resolution of the system.

articleTitle: Effect of post-growth treatment on electrophysical parameters of Hg3In2Te6 crystals
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: The effect of special post-growth treatment (annealing in mercury vapor) on the electro-physical parameters of Hg<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</inf>In<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf>Te<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">6</inf> single crystals was studied. The result of such processing is a 10-100 times decrease in the resistivity of the semiconductor material. Also, the optical transmission coefficient of the semiconductor material in the Urbach area increases significantly. This technological treatment led to a significant improvement in the parameters of the surface-barrier rectifying structures of the Cr/Hg<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</inf>In<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf>Te<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">6</inf>/Cr type, which were manufactured on the basis of this semiconductor material. In particular, a significant decrease in the dark current was observed (approximately 10 times) and the rectification coefficient increased. Diode structures withstood reverse voltages of 200-250 V at moderate values of dark currents. For photodiode structures, the dynamic range of the watt-ampere characteristic increased by 10-100 times. This is an encouraging result for the creation of both rectifying and photosensitive diodes on this semiconductor material, which has high radiation resistance.

articleTitle: Precise measurements of nuclear data using an associated particle imaging system
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Neutron-induced gamma ray reactions including both inelastic scattering (n,n'g) and radiative capture (n,g) are important in several applications of applied nuclear physics that require non-destructive elemental assays of unknown materials.Interpreting these gamma ray measurements requires precise knowledge of the energy and angle dependent reaction probabilities (cross sections, sigma). However, there are large gaps and inconsistencies in public databases for several common elements that are relevant for most applications. These shortcomings can be addressed via a focused effort to benchmark nuclear data libraries and models with experimental datasets to identify and ultimately fix underlying library and model deficiencies. Specifically, we decided to focus on measuring inelastic scattering reactions at 14 MeV incident neutron energy because of the wide use of Deuterium-Tritium (DT) sources. In this work, we present proof-of-concept measurements of (n,n'g) cross sections with an Associated Particle Imaging (API) system that allows a significant reduction in systematic uncertainties via accurate neutron flux measurements.

articleTitle: High performance neutron passive imaging with a self-collimating neutron camera
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Passive imaging of radiative neutron sources plays a crucial role in various industrial applications. However, neutron imaging is challenging due to the strong penetration ability of neutrons and their complex interactions with materials. Current neutron imaging devices, such as coded aperture and scatter cameras, have limitations such as field of view (FOV) size and imaging sensitivity.In this study, we propose a novel neutron camera design that aims to achieve high-performance neutron imaging. Our imaging detector is composed of interspaced plastic scintillators and boron-loaded polyethylene strips, which we term a self-collimating camera. The interactions of neutrons with the scintillators or polyethylene strips create directional-dependent neutron detection sensitivity for the other scintillators, allowing one scintillator or polyethylene strip to play the collimation role for other scintillators. This design enables omnidirectional neutron imaging. We conducted proof-of-concept experiments to validate the feasibility of our approach. Our experimental results demonstrate that our system achieves a positioning accuracy of approximately 5° using a Cf-252 source with an activity of 16.8μCi (neutron emission rate: 7.3×10<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">4</sup> n/s) at a distance of 50 cm during a 900-second scan. Additionally, our system successfully resolved dual sources separated by an angle of 40°. We conclude that the proposed self-collimating neutron imager is portable, has excellent resolution and detection efficiency, and is capable of providing imaging in a 4π field of view (FOV).

articleTitle: High-Resolution Quasi-Hemispherical CdZnTe Detectors for Hard X-ray Spectroscopy of Kaonic Atoms
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: In this work, we will present the potentialities of new quasi-hemispherical CZT detectors, recently developed at IMEM-CNR Parma (Italy), for high-resolution X-ray spectroscopy of kaonic atoms. Kaonic atoms are formed when a K<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">-</sup> is moderated inside a target until it reaches a low enough kinetic energy to be stopped, replacing one of the outer electrons and forming an exotic atom in a highly excited state. Precise and accurate measurements of the radiative X-ray transitions can provide information about the kaon nucleus interaction. In the framework of SIDDHARTA-2 collaboration, we developed new quasi-hemispherical CZT detectors for measurements of hard X rays from kaonic atoms (> 20 keV). The detectors are characterized by good room temperature performance, with energy resolution FWHM of 3 % (3.7 keV) and 1.4 % (9.3 keV) at 122.1 keV and 662 keV, respectively. Preliminary tests at the DAfNE collider in Frascati (Italy) will be presented.

articleTitle: Accelerating Direct Normalization Data Acquisition in PET Imaging with Deep Learning
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Normalization correction is a critical step in image reconstruction for correcting detector efficiency variations and reducing related artifacts in reconstructed positron emission tomography (PET) images. One common approach is direct normalization, which requires a large number of counts per line of response from a known normalization phantom collected within a reasonable time frame. However, this method can be extremely time-consuming due to using a typically relatively low-activity uniform source for collecting a large number of counts. We propose a deep learning framework that leverages synthetic generation of normalization factors and sensitivity maps to normalize images obtained from an MR-compatible brain PET insert. Specifically, we developed an attention-aware image-to-image learning model called AG-Pix2Pix using conditional generative adversarial networks that aims to improve detector efficiencies and remove detector block artifact patterns. We investigated robustness and consistency when normalizing images obtained at varying levels of count statistics, including sensitivity images resampled with rates as low as 1%, 5%, 10%, and 15% of the total acquisition time (4-6 hours). Quantitative evaluation was performed on reconstructed images of a Hoffman brain phantom using high-count, low-count, and synthetic sensitivity maps. The image normalized using a synthetic sensitivity map with 15% count statistics produced the best results, with PSNR, SSIM, and NRMSE (Mean±SE) of 30.68±0.310, 0.95±0.002, and 0.35±0.003, respectively, while for the low count sensitivity data, the PSNR, SSIM, and NRMSE were 15.93±0.426, 0.54±0.013, and 1.84±0.028, respectively. Our findings suggest that realistic correction factors can be obtained using a relatively short scan and deep learning.

articleTitle: Deep Learning-Based High Resolution Imaging in the Second Near-Infrared Window
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Molecular imaging technology of the second near-infrared window (NIR-II) performs well in biological imaging with high sensitivity. In clinical practice, the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) approved fluorescent dye indocyanine green (ICG) has week emission light in NIR-II window and can be used for imaging in a shorter wavelength of NIR-II (1000-1300nm), but imaging in this window is affected by light scattering and autofluorescence, resulting in low imaging resolution. In response to the clinical need for precision imaging, a NIR-II fluorescence imaging method based on cyclic domain conversion generative adversarial network is constructed for resolution enhancement. The proposed method enables single-domain feature extraction and cross-domain feature fusion by using a cyclic training scheme. Moreover, the minimization of Gram matrix difference is introduced to keep texture information while improving the image resolution. Fluorescent images in the shorter wavelength of NIR-II can be converted into high-resolution fluorescent images with imaging characteristics of the longer wavelength of NIR-II (1500-1700 nm). Experimental results show that vascular imaging with proposed method can delineate vasovagal patterns, and enhanced neural imaging can guide the implementation of nerve sparing surgery, which is of great significance to clinical decision-making and practice.

articleTitle: Quality Enhancement of Short-axis PET Scans from Total-body PET Using 3D U-net
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: The axial field of view (FOV) of a positron emission tomography (PET) scanner greatly affects the quality of PET images. The total-body PET scanner (uEXPLORER) is highermore sensitive but more expensive and difficult to widely use. This study used deep learning to utilize high-quality (HQ) images generated by uEXPLORER to optimize the image quality of short-axis PET scanners while controlling costs. The generated HQ PET images of the brain, lungs, and abdomen were quantitatively and qualitatively compatible with the reference images. In particular, the overall mean SSIM between the generated and reference images was greater than 0.9 for all patients who underwent testing. On the other hand, according to the two experienced nuclear medicine experts, the total subjective quality levels of the generated HQ PET images were 3.94±0.23, 3.87±0.34 and 3.64±0.54 (the highest possible score is 5). The findings demonstrate the potential of the proposed technique for improving the image quality of a PET scanner with a 320-mm or even shorter FOV.

articleTitle: Rectal Toxicity Prediction in Prostate Cancer Radiation Therapy Using CT Radiomic and 3D Dose Distribution Dosomic Features
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Radiomics and dosiomics are new and upcoming areas of medical imaging that require extracting numerous quantitative features from medical images and radiation dose data. In this study, we investigated rectum toxicity prediction in prostate cancer by using 3D dose distribution (DD) dosomic and computed tomography (CT) radiomic features. Our study consisted of 60 patients with prostate cancer with CT and DD images. An experienced radiation oncologist segmented the rectum, and radiomic and dosomic features were extracted from CT and DD images. Four different feature selections (FS) and five classifiers were applied to the training dataset and evaluated on the testing dataset. The performance of the model was evaluated with Area Under Curve (AUC), accuracy (ACC), sensitivity (SEN), and specificity (SPE). In DD dosiomics features, the XGB classifier with the MRMR algorithm had the highest performance with ACC=0.84, SEN=0.79, and SPE=0.86. In CT radiomic features, the RF classifier with the ANOVA algorithm is another best-performance model with ACC=0.85, SEN=0.65, and SPE=0.92. Finally, in combining radiomic and dosomic features, the MLP classifier with ANOVA had ACC=0.75, SEN=0.62, and SPE=0.79. The dosiomics and radiomics approach applied to 3D DD and CT images could predict rectal toxicity in prostate cancer.

articleTitle: Updates on the Multi-channel LYRA ASIC for X/γ- ray Detection Instrument onboard HERMES Space Mission
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: The upgraded version of the front-end electronics of the X-/γ-ray detection instrument of the HERMES mission, whose goal is to observe and localize Gamma Ray Bursts (GRBs), through a constellation of more than one hundred nano-satellites, is presented. Since the detection unit is composed of 120 Silicon Drift Detectors (SDDs) coupled to 60 Cesium-doped Gadolinium-Aluminum Gallium Garnet (Ce: GAGG) scintillators, and long connections between the preamplifier and detector must be avoided, the readout ASIC, named LYRA, has been organized in a multi-chip architecture: 30 Front-End (FE-LYRA) chips placed close to the anode of the SDDs send their pre-processed signals, in current mode, to a 32-channel Back-End chip (BE-LYRA). LYRA ASIC has a maximum input charge specification of 5.2 fC (2.2 MeV in GAGG) with a linearity error between ±1.5%. An upgraded version of the LYRA ASIC has been designed and sent for fabrication to ensure uniformity due to process variabilities between channels in terms of parameters and performance. The simulated intrinsic Equivalent Noise Charge is 14 el. rms at 1.6 μs peaking time and 0.6 mW/channel. From Monte Carlo simulations, significant improvements are visible in the dispersion of parameters (offset, gain, channel trigger delay, etc.) between channels. The dispersion of the channel trigger delay was reduced from 42.5% to 11% (±165 ns).

articleTitle: Applications of Novel Fast Photon Counting Detectors in Neutron Scattering Instruments of the SNS Second Target Station
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Novel neutron imaging detectors based on scintillator and Timepix technology, have presented a new opportunity in neutron scattering instrument design. This detector covers a combination of detection area, resolution and rate capability that is not easily reached by more established technologies. Neutron detection tests have been performed in imaging and diffraction modes using pulsed spallation neutron beams. Detection areas between 7x7 mm2 and 200x200 mm2 have been with position granularity of up to 2000x2000 pixels and time resolution up to 2 ns. Counting rate of 5 Mhit/s has been reached. These characteristics make the detector attractive for applications in neutron imaging, reflectometry, SEMSANS and VSANS, and potentially diffraction. Results of the R&D on the detector and its applications on the ORNL Second Target Station instruments are presented.

articleTitle: Polycrystalline CsPbBr3Semiconductor Radiation Detectors
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Solid-state detection of high energy γ-rays is typically limited to single crystal devices, which are expensive to manufacture and limited to small device areas. This work presents the first stages of optimizing the synthesis and processing of polycrystalline CsPbBr<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</inf> devices and evaluating their efficiency in detecting alpha particles and γ-rays. Initial polycrystalline CsPbBr<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</inf> samples were manufactured using Field Assisted Sintering Technology, and demonstrate the importance of manufacturing process parameter optimization on increasing detector performance. The four CsPbBr<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</inf> samples showed that increasing the hold time of the sintering process resulted in larger grain size, as did the use of a boron nitride (BN) liner instead of a Ta foil. Samples with more complete sintering and increased densification demonstrated lower leakage current and improved spectroscopic capability, as only the sample produced using the BN liner showed clear alpha spectra. Further characterization of FAST samples using BN spray will be conducted and compared to furnace- and solution-grown CsPbBr3 crystals. Several oxide materials such as Bi<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">12</inf>SiO<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">20</inf> and Bi<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">12</inf>GeO<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">20</inf> are evaluated as alternatives.

articleTitle: Proof-of-concept of CMOS-based rigid-type laparoscopic system with a coincidence gamma detector for near-infrared fluorescence-guided surgery
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: This study aims to demonstrate the concept of a complementary metal-oxide-semiconductor (CMOS)-based triple imaging system with a coincidence gamma detector for near-infrared fluorescence guided surgery to overcome depth limitation by the scattering and absorption of light in tissues. The triple-imaging system consists of a laparoscopic module, with an optical imaging module and a gamma detector, and a flat detector for the coincidence detection. The color, NIR fluorescence, and gamma images were blended simultaneously with a post-processing algorithm. A sodium-22 point source, a plastic phantom filled with a solution of indocyanine green and dimethyl sulfoxide, and a glass resolution target were used to evaluate performance of the multimodal image. The sensitivity of the coincidence detector was 0.2 cps/kBq. The spatial resolutions in the X-, Y-, and Z-directions were full-width-half-maximum of 6.5, 2.7, and 133 mm, respectively. Three color bars in group 2 and element 6, corresponding to the 7.13 line-pair per mm (lp/mm), were well resolved. Furthermore, the three gray bars in group 2 and element 3 (5.04 lp/mm) were also resolved. Using the proposed triple imaging system, the 511 keV gamma, NIR fluorescence, and color images were obtained and merged simultaneously. A feasibility study will be conducted using preclinical tests to validate the proposed imaging system.

articleTitle: Development of a GAGG prompt gamma camera and simultaneous imaging with prompt X-rays during irradiation by proton beams at clinical dose level
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Prompt gamma photon imaging is a promising method for observing a beam's shape and estimating the range of the beam from outside a subject. However 2 dimensional images of prompt gamma photons during irradiation of protons at clinical dose level were still difficult to measure. To achieve prompt gamma photon imaging, we developed a new gamma camera and imaged prompt gamma photons while irradiating proton beams to a phantom at clinical dose level. We also compared the images with simultaneously measured prompt X-ray images. The developed gamma camera uses a 10 mm thick GAGG block optically coupled to a flat panel photomultiplier tube (FP-PMT), and it is contained in a 20 mm thick tungsten container with a pinhole collimator attached. Proton beams at clinical dose level were irradiated to a poly-methyl-methacrylate (PMMA) block, and the gamma camera imaged prompt gamma photons. The prompt X-rays were simultaneously measured during irradiation of proton beams. For all of the tested beams, we could measure the beam shapes of the prompt gamma photons and the prompt X-rays and the ranges could also be estimated from the images. We confirmed that the prompt gamma photon imaging using our developed gamma camera, as well as prompt X-ray imaging, is promising for beam imaging and range estimation in proton therapy at clinical dose level. In the conference, we will also show the time sequential prompt gamma and X-ray images.

articleTitle: MTD CMS Barrel Timing Layer: Moving from design to production
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Starting in 2029, the High Luminosity Large Hadron Collider (HL-LHC) will deliver an unprecedented instantaneous luminosity that will provide the Compact Muon Solenoid (CMS) collaboration an opportunity to perform precision measurements and search for rare processes in the largest high-energy proton-proton collision dataset ever collected, but these operating conditions will also directly challenge CMS’s ability to correctly associate final state particles with interaction vertices. The CMS Barrel Timing Layer (BTL), which will be installed in the CMS detector before the start of HL-LHC data taking, will aid in particle to interaction vertex association by exploiting the temporal distribution of inelastic collisions within a bunch crossing. Over the course of HL-LHC data taking, BTL will measure charged particle time of arrival with a precision on the order of 30-70 ps, which will allow the identification of primary vertices in four dimensions, aid in charged hadron identification, and provide a powerful new handle to identify potential exotic long-lived particles. The BTL project is currently transitioning from the design and validation phase to the production and installation phase, and this talk focuses on the optimized BTL sensor design that has been validated over the past year and the plans to begin in 2024 the production of the more than 10,000 sensor modules that will comprise BTL.

articleTitle: LUCAS: A Low-Power Ultra-Low Jitter Compact ASIC for SiPM Targetting ToF-CT
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: We present LUCAS (Low power Ultra-low jitter Compact ASIC for SiPM), an analog front-end for Silicon Photomultipliers (SiPM) targeting fast timing detectors in Time-of-Flight Computed Tomography (ToF-CT). LUCAS features a very low input impedance preamplifier followed by a voltage comparator. It is designed in TSMC 65nm low-power CMOS technology with a power supply of 1.2 V. Our first 8-channel prototype has been sent to fabrication and will be received in August 2023.Post-layout simulations predict less than 40 ps FWHM SPTR jitter and an approximate power consumption of 3.2 mW per channel. The front end is suitable for applications with rigorous jitter requirements and high event rates, thanks to its 3.9 GHz unity-gain bandwidth. The front-end compact form factor will facilitate its incorporation into systems demanding high channel densities.

articleTitle: Development of a Time-of-Flight Neutron Emission Spectrometer for General Fusion’s Fusion Demonstration Program
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: General Fusion is developing a Magnetized Target Fusion approach that involves compressing an initial magnetically confined plasma inside a cavity formed in liquid metal. General Fusion has launched a Fusion Demonstration Program to design and construct a large scale, integrated prototype, being built at the Culham Centre for Fusion Energy in the United Kingdom. It is proposed to implement a highly segmented, time-of-flight Neutron Emission Spectrometer to measure the energy distribution of neutrons emitted nominally at 2.45 MeV from deuterium-deuterium fusion. This distribution will be used to extract the ion plasma temperature at the late stages of compression. An incident neutron flux of up to one billion neutrons per second is expected at the spectrometer, resulting in very demanding performance criteria. It is vital that the Fusion Demonstration Program’s prototype machine have a diagnostic system capable of measuring plasma ion temperatures of 10 keV (116 million degrees Celsius) to evaluate the success of a compression and the overall performance. Simulations modeling plasma compression, neutron interactions with the prototype’s apparatus and spectrometer, as well as the development of a prototype time-of-flight spectrometer in partnership with TRIUMF and Simon Fraser University, will be discussed.

articleTitle: Development of a large-area alpha imaging detector capable of measuring the detailed distribution of alpha contaminations on hands and feet
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: This paper describes the development of a large-area imaging detector capable of measuring the detailed distribution of alpha particles on hands and feet for use in entry/exit control monitors in decommissioning sites such as the Fukushima Daiichi Nuclear Power Plant. The detector was developed using a commercially available ZnS(Ag) scintillator and an electron multiplying CCD camera. The effectiveness of the detector was evaluated by measuring several types of radiation sources, and the results showed that it was possible to detect the position of alpha particles in a very short time, and contamination levels of up to 11 Bq/cm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sup> could be visualized. The field of view of the detector was also checked, and it was confirmed that the setup had a field of view that could cover most of the hand and the sole of the shoe. This detector is expected to be useful for preventing internal uptake and decontamination.

articleTitle: Streaming Readout PET Architecture and Development
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Positron emission tomography (PET) is a radionuclide functional diagnostic imaging technique for medical applications such as cancer diagnosis and drug development. Jefferson Lab is developing PET instrumentation using a novel data acquisition system (DAQ) readout methodology referred to as streaming readout (SRO). The SRO-based approach transitions PET DAQ systems from traditional dedicated "triggered" systems to more versatile "triggerless" systems. In this new configuration, the SRO-enabled PET detector modules are interconnected using Ethernet with synchronized external timing circuitry. The SRO-PET system implementation is entirely software-based, encompassing detector calibrations and coincident event sorting. The adoption of SRO technology in PET instrumentation has the potential to simplify system installation and enhance key performance indices, especially for whole-body and total-body PET applications.

articleTitle: Electron tomography limited angular image reconstruction using directional-TV
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Electron tomography (ET) is a powerful method for the characterization of materials at the nanoscale. However, ET reconstructed images often suffer from significant artifacts due to data often covering only a limited angular range, causing disruptive artifacts when using traditional reconstruction algorithms. Previously, the problem of limited angular reconstruction has been formulated as a convex optimization problem and the directional total-variation (DTV) algorithm has shown promising results for image reconstruction from constrained data in X-ray computed tomography (CT). In this work we apply the DTV algorithm to simulated and real ET data over various limited angular ranges. An overview of the DTV algorithm is provided before. The performance of the DTV algorithm is compared to a standard filtered backprojection (FBP) reconstruction. The results show the DTV algorithm is able to accurately recover images at significantly limited angular ranges and considerably reduces artifacts otherwise found in reconstructions using the FBP algorithm.

articleTitle: 16-channel HF readout electronics and pulse discrimination for ultrafast TOF-PET applications
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Ultrafast high-frequency (HF) readout concepts have advanced the performance limits of single-channel time-of-flight positron emission tomography (TOF-PET) detectors to sub-100 ps coincidence time resolution (CTR).We have implemented a 16-channel version of an adapted HF readout concept, including pulse discrimination and a linearized time-over-threshold (TOT) method, fully compatible with a high precision time-to-digital converter (TDC) developed at CERN, the picoTDC. The functionality of the circuit has been initially tested using the TOFPET2 ASIC as back-end electronics, to emulate the TDC. The implemented pulse discrimination has shown the capability to mitigate influences of baseline shifts and noise on the TOFPET2 front end, resulting in a CTR of 105 ps using 2x2x3 mm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</sup> LYSO:Ce,Ca crystals and Broadcom NUV-MT SiPMs and in the absence of side peaks in the coincidence time difference spectra. For a 4x4 matrix of 3.8x3.8x19 mm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</sup> LYSO:Ce,Ca crystals one-to-one coupled to 16 Broadcom NUV-MT SiPMs, the average CTR was improved from 252 ps (FWHM) to 240 ps (FWHM). The ongoing integration with the picoTDC is expected to improve the CTR due to its state-of-the-art resolution of below 10 ps and will further set the path towards a 10 ps readout solution.

articleTitle: Dedicated PET/MRI Research Systems based on the Hyperion III Detector Platform
