publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: The clinical research community demands a variety of dedicated PET and PET/MRI scanners, each tailored to the different needs and research questions. The Hyperion III PET detector platform was thus designed as a flexible and scalable common detector platform from which the desired devices can be constructed. In first projects, different PET/MRI research prototype systems were built: A brain insert for a Siemens 7T MRI Scanner (FZ Juelich), a dedicated breast insert with two simultaneously working PET rings (Hypmed consortium), An MR-Linac radiotherapy planning device (UMU Utrecht, Philips, Futura). The brain PET insert employs 24-mm height, 2-mm pitch, 3-layer DOI crystal arrays. With a total amount of crystals of 196 080, it offers a large FOV of 282 mm × 250 and high sensitivity. The breast PET insert consists of two complete PET rings for the female breasts (1.3-mm crystal pitch, 3-layer DOI crystal arrays). Comparing measurements demonstrate the advantage in spatial resolution over a standard clinical whole-body PET/MRI scanner. The radiotherapy planning PET/MRI scanner is a whole-body installation, that employs a similar split gradient coil with a 20 cm gap for the MRI as the Elekta Unity MR-Linac radiotherapy device. With the with PET ring installed in that gap, a full 70 cm wide-bore system was built, and MRI compatibility was approved by the MRI vendors engineers. The successful scanner implementations demonstrate the flexibility of the Hyperion III detector platform. Currently, more dedicated scanners are built, and the versatility of the platform will be enhanced by adding analog SiPM/ASIC combinations to the portfolio.

articleTitle: Prediction of Drug Sensitivity of HER2-Positive Breast Cancer Cell Line via Graph Neural Network
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: In this study, the drug response prediction (DRP) model based on the graph neural network (GNN) was applied to predict the drug sensitivity of the HER2-positive breast cancer cell lines. GDSC dataset which contains the drug sensitivity of the enormous drug-cell line pairs was used for the training of the model. Drugs in the GDSC library was processed by RDKit software and transformed to the graph structure which composed of nodes, the elements of the molecules, and edges, the chemical bonds. The initial node embedding is set to the chemical properties of the each element. Multi-omics representation of the cancer cell lines were referred from the CCLE library and used as the input. The DRP model was trained with the 197,818 drug-cell line pairs. After training, the accuracy of the model was evaluated for the 7 kinds of HER2-positive breast cancer cell lines with the drugs within the training dataset. It is found that the Pearson correlation coefficient between the label and the predicted value was 0.83, while the R-squared was 0.68. The mean absolute error of log of IC50 was 1.1. In addition, we evaluated whether the HER2-positive cell lines shows similar tendency in drug sensitivity for the several drugs, and which drug is predicted to have high efficacy. It is found that docetaxel has highest efficacy among the drugs we selected. Besides, the boxplots of the predicted drug sensitivity for each drug shows that the HER2-positive breast cancer cell lines shows similar tendency. To sum up, we verified that the GNN-based drug response prediction model is capable of predicting the drug sensitivity of the HER2-positive breast cancer cell lines. We concluded that the GNN-based DRP model is appropriate to predict the efficacy of the unseen drugs according the subtype of the cancer cell lines. Validation of the sensitivity of the unseen drugs for the HER2-positive breast cancer cell lines which is not in the GDSC will be our future work.

articleTitle: Assessment of a hand-held CZT-based gamma-camera for pre-clinical imaging of 177Lu
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: A small CdZnTe-based hand-held gamma-camera has been acquired, intended to be used for preclinical imaging. The camera produces images of size 4 cm x 4 cm with an image-matrix of 16 x 16 pixels and can be equipped with a low-energy high-sensitivity (LEHS) or a high-resolution (LEHR) parallel-hole collimator. Pre-clinical imaging involves scales smaller than what the camera is typically used for, and dedicated assessment of the camera’s performance in this field is thus warranted and the aim of this work. To this end, a mouse-like phantom is developed with the MOBY computer phantom as a basis and manufactured through 3D-printing. The phantom is printed in PLA, with fillable cavities for the liver and a tumour. Additionally, a motorised platform is built enabling SPECT acquisitions by rotating an object in front of the camera. Software is developed in-house for camera operation, SPECT acquisition, and tomographic reconstruction. The camera’s performance for <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">177</sup>Lu imaging is assessed through measurements on the imageuniformity, sensitivity, spatial resolution, as well as planar and SPECT acquisitions on the mouse phantom. Energy windows over the 55 keV, 113 keV, and 208 keV photopeaks are investigated. Obtained sensitivities are around 100 cps/MBq for the LEHS collimator and 20 cps/MBq for the LEHR collimator, meaning that quick acquisitions can be made with <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">177</sup>Lu activity administrations that are typically used pre-clinically. Tomographic reconstructions demonstrates that the camera can be used for SPECT applications. Overall, the camera is found promising for pre-clinical applications, both for planar and SPECT imaging.

articleTitle: Development of novel CsPbBr3-polymer composites for radiation detection
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: The fabrication of perovskite-polymer composites elevates the potential of perovskite-based radiation detectors. Combining the facile production of all-inorganic perovskite materials with the mechanical properties of a polymer can result in the convenient production of large-area, environmentally stable detectors. This work presents the fabrication and characterization of a novel hybrid material that has been created by mixing together the perovskite CsPbBr<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</inf> with a polymer to produce a solid plastic composite. Test samples are polished pellets with metal contacts to enable direct detection via charge collection. IV-characterization data and photocurrent response data has been collected from a composite test device composed of ~8% perovskite material by weight. Bias sweeps have been performed and the dark current measured. X-ray illumination from a 70 kV source across a series of mA values demonstrates the clear linear response of the device over a range of dose-rates. Additionally, microCT and SEM imaging has been used to study the dispersion of CsPbBr<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</inf> through the composite. This work lays the foundation for novel perovskite-polymer radiation detection devices through detector characterization and compositional analysis.

articleTitle: Quantum Yield in Silicon Photomultipliersand the Temperature Dependance
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Incident particles and photons on semiconductor material with energies greater than 2 order of magnitude from the fundamental bandgap tend to produce more than one electron-hole pair referred to as quantum yield. Energy reconstruction of single event detectors such as SiPM requires information on the quantum yield which is measured in this study for the photons in the 140-450 nm wavelength range. Quantum yield for two generations of SiPMs manufactured by Hamamatsu and Fondazione Bruno Kessler has been measured by operating the devices at different biasing schemes where the current modeling can be simplified to extract the parameter of interest. The quantum yield is found to be 1.7 ± 0.15 at -110 °C for LXe applications. Moreover, the temperature dependence of the quantum yield is observed, and shows more than 25% increase over the temperature change of +100°C. This study introduces a transferable method for quantum yield measurement on various p-on-n SiPMs provided by different manufacturer and at different temperatures based on the experiment design.

articleTitle: Enhanced use of contextual data for quantitative Compton imaging
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Contextual sensors can be equipped to radiation detection systems to allow free-moving 3D gamma-ray imaging through scene data fusion. Scene data fusion captures relevant scene information to construct a 3D map of an environment, which can be used to constrain image reconstruction techniques. While developed to enable free-moving imaging measurements, scene data fusion also has applications in cases that require multiple static measurements to generate 3D images, where the scene information can improve results. One way we seek to further leverage contextual scene information is to use the 3D map to automatically identify the radiological object of interest in a scene, and then determine optimal measurement poses around that object for quantitative Compton imaging. We also seek to improve the use of contextual information by identifying materials present in an environment to inform attenuation estimates for intervening materials. We present the approach for further leveraging the contextual information, and the preliminary results of using an SDF-enabled gamma-ray imager to find optimal measurement positions for a distributed source scenario to produce quantitative Compton images with minimization of associated uncertainties.

articleTitle: Firmware design and performance for the ePix HR 2Mega Pixel X-ray Detector for LCLS-II
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: The previously proposed 2 mega pixel x-ray detector at 5,000 frame per second at LCLS-II (ePixHR10k2M) for the tender X-ray beamline is under development. The detector hardware and firmware are constructed with several requirements into consideration: support readout rates higher than 5,000 frames per second, compatible with the matrix of the ePixHR10k sensor/ASIC modules, has a segmented focal plane with an adjustable gap between top and bottom planes that are capable of remote positioning, operate in vacuum and have high quantum efficiency. In this paper we present the ePixHR10k2M overview and subsystem firmware/software co-development accomplishments, a step closer towards having a fully functional and complete detector to measure x-rays in the range of 2 to 4keV. Furthermore, preliminary results are presented, and show reliable communication. Further results will be available at the conference.

articleTitle: Feasibility of Preclinical 225Ac imaging in commercial and a developmental gamma camera
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Actinium-225 (<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">225</sup>Ac) is a very promising radioisotope for targeted alpha theranostics due to its large energy deposition, relatively long half-life of 9.9 days, and its emissions of imageable photons. However, imaging <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">225</sup>Ac with standard single-photon emission computed tomography (SPECT) scanners is challenging due to the low injected doses and the relative high energy of the emitted gamma photons. In this work, we quantify the limitations of a commercial SPECT scanner (VECTor from MILabs) for <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">225</sup>Ac imaging in mice and compare its performance with a dedicated SPECT design equipped with a single-head and high-sensitivity CZT detector and parallel-hole tungsten collimator, using a 3D-printed mouse phantom filled with ~ 30 μCi.A Monte Carlo (MC)-based image reconstruction algorithm was developed to model the scattering and absorption of the gamma-rays of different energies (from the <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">221</sup>Fr and <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">213</sup>Bi daughters) in the collimator. GATE was used to acquire the MC simulations.Additionally, we simulated an animal phantom (MOBY) to validate the model and demonstrate its accuracy in quantify the radioisotope concentration.Results show that the commercial SPECT performance is limited at microcurie activities of <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">225</sup>Ac in a 1.5-hours exposure, whereas the dedicated SPECT system combined with the image reconstruction algorithm produced good quality planar images and contrast in only 1-hour, which could lead to better quantization of <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">225</sup>Ac distributions. The 3D scanner based on the SPECT design shown, using four detector heads to produce <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">225</sup>Ac 3D images, is under development. It has the potential to be used with other challenging theranostics radioisotopes such as <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">177</sup>Lu and <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">227</sup>Th.

articleTitle: Preclinical PET scanner with timing and 3D capabilities based on semi-monolithic crystals
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Semi-monolithic crystals have the potential of combining the timing capabilities of pixelated crystals and the 3D positioning of monolithic crystals. We present here a PET scanner for small animals consisting of 2 rings of 14 semi-monolithic based detectors each. The bore of the scanner is 106 mm, and it covers an axial length of 52 mm. Each semi-monolithic block is composed of an array of 22 slabs with dimensions of 0.97 mm thickness, 12 mm height and 25.6 mm in the monolithic direction. The pixelated lateral surfaces of each slab were unpolished and black painted, and a retroreflector layer was added on the top side, to improve impact position accuracy without compromising timing capabilities.A timestamp averaging method, including time skew and time walk corrections, was applied, achieving a Detector Time Resolution (DTR) as good as 178 ps FWHM.A Neural Network (NN) technique based on two Multilayer Perceptron architectures has been implemented for the prediction of the annihilation photon impact position inside each detector module. An average MAE below 1.5 mm and close to 2 mm, for the monolithic and DOI directions, respectively.Currently, we are optimizing some system acquisition parameters of the data acquisition system, and we will soon carry out a full NEMA protocol evaluation. We will report on these data.

articleTitle: Pharmacokinetic and dosimetry modeling of Radiopharmaceutical Therapy using Spatial Transcriptomics in microenvironment
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: The efficacy of radiopharmaceutical therapy (RPT) relies on the ability to deliver cytotoxic radiation to cancer cells or the surrounding tumor microenvironment (TME) while minimizing normal tissue toxicity. Therefore, dosimetry is essential to understand the factors that influence treatment. The spatial transcriptomics (ST) technique may offer a breakthrough in investigating RPT dosimetry as it enables to spatially profile the diverse gene transcripts that are associated with TME. In this study, we propose a novel approach to combine the pharmacokinetics and dosimetry of RPT with ST maps to elucidate the heterogeneity of RPT dosimetry and its effects. For proof of concept, we focused on modeling 177Lu-and 225Ac-prostate-specific membrane antigen (PSMA), which emit beta and alpha particles, respectively. Specifically, we solved partial differential equations (PDE) of the pharmacokinetic model and applied the dose-voxel kernel (DVK) method using various ST maps. Additionally, assuming hypoxia as one of the influencing factors in RPT, we utilized hypoxia ST to measure the cell survival probability of each 177Lu-and 225Ac- RPT.

articleTitle: System Design and Prototyping for the CMS Level-1 Trigger at the High-Luminosity LHC
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: The High-Luminosity LHC will open an unprecedented window on the weak-scale nature of the universe, providing high-precision measurements of the standard model as well as searches for new physics beyond the standard model. Such precision measurements and searches require information-rich datasets with a statistical power that matches the high-luminosity provided by the Phase-2 upgrade of the LHC. Efficiently collecting those datasets will be a challenging task, given the harsh environment of 200 proton-proton interactions per LHC bunch crossing. For this purpose, the trigger and data acquisition system of the Compact Muon Solenoid (CMS) experiment will be entirely replaced. Novel design choices have been explored, including ATCA prototyping platforms with SoC controllers and newly available interconnect technologies with serial optical links with data rates up to 28 Gb/s. Trigger data analysis will be performed through sophisticated algorithms, including widespread use of Machine Learning, in large FPGAs, such as the Xilinx Ultrascale family. The system will process over 60 Tb/s of detector data with an event rate of 750 kHz. Since the Technical Design Report was approved comprehensive progress has been made in several areas related to prototyping hardware platforms, optical interconnect testing, algorithm development in HLS and VHDL, as well testing between subsystems on real hardware. Recent results in all these areas will be presented.

articleTitle: Simulation Study of Active-Reset ASIC Architecture of Clinical Photon Counting CT
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: This study presents a simulation study of an active reset Application Specific Integrated Circuit (ASIC) architecture for clinical photon counting computed tomography (PCCT). As a critical part of PCCT, one of the key challenges in designing an ASIC is handling the large flux range of clinical CT applications. To address this, a photon counting detector (PCD) with an active reset ASIC architecture was implemented, and its performance was evaluated by investigating the effect of various parameters on ASIC performance. The results showed that the deadtime parameter had a significant impact on ASIC performance in high flux conditions. However, the RC of the high pass filter had less impact on this architecture. Setting the number of energy bins is a trade-off between noise reduction, power and the complexity of processing large amounts of data generated by multiple energy bins.

articleTitle: Dual-Ended Readout PET Detectors with Different SiPM Microcell Sizes and Inter-Crystal Reflector Materials
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: The microcell size of the silicon photomultiplier (SiPM) and the inter-crystal reflector material of the crystal array affect the performance of high-resolution positron emission tomography (PET) detectors. In this study, we compared the performance of dual-ended readout detectors comprised of 24×24 LYSO arrays with the same 1.0 mm pitch but different reflectors (BaSO<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">4</inf> and Toray) and 8×8 SiPM arrays with the same 3.2 mm pitch but different microcell sizes (15, 25, 35, and 50 μm). Our results show that the detector with BaSO<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">4</inf> reflector and SiPMs with 35 μm microcells showed the best performance with energy resolution of 11.31 ± 0.73%, depth of interaction (DOI) resolution of 2.06 ± 0.20 mm, and timing resolution of 759 ± 109 ps.

articleTitle: Non-Invasive Prostate Cancer Diagnosis Using Ultrasound Radiomics and Machine Learning Algorithms
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: One of the most serious diseases affecting male population is prostate cancer (PCa). Mortality rates may be appropriately decreased if PCa can be detected at its early stages. The prostate-specific antigen (PSA) test is the cornerstone of screening. However, PSA is linked to other diseases besides PCa, specifically difficult to identify when the PSA level is in the range of 4 to 10 ng/ml. Ultrasound (US) images have recently emerged as a crucial tool for identifying prostate cancer. The radiomics technique has recently made some observable advancements and can play a significant role in clinical diagnosis. Accordingly, we involved 545 prostate US images with Gleason score and level of PSA in this work. Subsequently, 107 radiomic features were extracted from the prostate region of US images. With the combination of 6 feature selections and 5 classification algorithms, 30 models were created for PCa diagnosis. In this way, 80% of the data were used for the training dataset and 20% for the test dataset. The model adopted in this study was Recursive Feature Elimination (RFE)+ Logistic Regression (LR) with performance metrics of AUC=0.66, Accuracy=0.65, Sensitivity=0.66, and Specificity=0.63. Finally, the findings of this study have also demonstrated that Radiomics non-invasive technique can be useful in identifying PCa, thereby minimizing the need for unnecessary invasive biopsies and the complications they might cause to patients.

articleTitle: Summary and Concluding Remarks
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Concluding Remarks:This meeting has truly presented a special opportunity for us to share knowledge, energy and experience with our colleagues engaged in similar work. Clearly, many challenges remain, but the investigations reported at this meeting and the understanding that has emerged from these studies continue to pave the road to realization of new devices.We would like to invite everyone to the 2024 IEEE NSS MIC RTSD conference at Tampa, Florida, USA on Oct. 26 - Nov. 02, 2024. The symposium co-chairs will be Professor Michael Fiederle and Dr. Ralph James. Before adjourning, I offer a special thanks to all of the speakers, the sponsors, and those who contributed to lively, participative discussions. This concludes the 30th International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Radiation Detectors.

articleTitle: Position Resolution for the Segmented Inverted-Coaxial Germanium detector, SIGMA
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: The position resolution of the novel p-type Segmented Inverted-Coaxial Germanium (SIGMA) detector was investigated using the Pulse Shape Analysis (PSA) technique. The design of this large volume HPGe detector is based on a coaxial geometry and combines the small point contact technology along with the segmentation of the outer contact. The location of the γ-ray interaction points is determined by extracting the digitized signals of the 18 outer segments and of the small point contact electrode, which are characteristic for each point of interaction in the detector.In order to evaluate the position resolution of the SIGMA detector, PSA methods using a figure of merit minimization grid search algorithm are applied, which require a pulse shape database of all possible positions of γ-ray interactions with the detector volume as input. Thus, to determine the γ-ray interaction points, the experimentally measured pulse shapes are compared to the reference signal database. For this reason, the detector response has been simulated using Signal Generation simulation (SigGen) to generate a database of calculated pulse shapes for the SIGMA detector. The simulated pulses were validated against their corresponding average experimental pulses produced on known positions using the University of Liverpool scanning system.The preliminary result of the position resolution shows that the FWHM obtained is between 2.5 mm and 4.6 mm for the radial positions and is around 7 degrees for the azimuthal positions.

articleTitle: Crystal identification for light-sharing Prism-PET detectors
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Prism-PET is a single-ended readout PET detector module featuring a segmented array of prismatoids light guides that enhance the light sharing. We recently constructed a one-ring prototype brain-dedicated scanner using the Prism-PET detectors. However, the employing of light-guide and 4-to-1 crystal-to-SiPM coupling distorts the flood histogram, with the distortion pattern varying across the detector blocks. Although manual segmentation of the flood histogram to create the crystal look-up-table is reliable, it is time consuming as the prototype has 40 detector blocks with 10240 crystals. In this study, we developed an automatic flood histogram segmentation method to identify the crystal boundaries on the flood map. Due to the prismatoid light-guides, the corner, edge, and center crystals exhibit different light-sharing patterns with neighbor SiPM, resulting in different SiPM energy saturation effects and distinguishable energy peaks before saturation correction. For each SiPM, we detected the peaks of the energy histogram and applied energy filters to isolate the events belonging to each energy peak. The coordinates of the filtered events on the flood histograms were calculated using the truncated center of gravity (TCOG) method. A k-means segmentation algorithm was employed to segment the photoelectric spots on the flood map into crystal masks. After obtaining the mask of each crystal, we used the nearest neighbor (NN) method to determine the region and boundary of each crystal on the flood histogram. We applied this method to 40 Prism-PET detectors and the algorithm can reliably identify the boundaries of all crystals, enabling accurate crystal identifications, filtering of inter-crystal scatter events, and crystal-specific corrections. We believe this method can also be extended to segment the floodmap generated from the interleaved multiplexing readout for our next full-ring Prism-PET scanner.

articleTitle: Washout in in-beam PET as a biomarker of tumor vascular condition: a feasibility study in rats
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Positron emission tomography (PET) has been used for treatment verification in charged particle therapy. For accurate dose verification, modeling and correction of the biological washout effect of the positron emitters, which is influenced by the tumor vasculature condition, has been an issue. Conversely, the biological washout effect indicates changes of the tumor vasculature condition, which is known to influence radiation response. At present, blood circulatory changes in a tumor are measured using dynamic contrast-enhanced magnetic resonance imaging (DCE-MRI) to evaluate tumor radiation response. Here, measuring the biological washout rate of the produced positron emitters may also function to evaluate tumor radiation response, in a similar manner to DCE-MRI. Therefore, this study compared the washout rates between in-beam PET during <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">12</sup>C ion beam irradiation and DCE-MRI. Different vascular types of the tumor model were prepared using six nude rats. The tumor of each nude rat was irradiated by a <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">12</sup>C ion beam and scanned by in-beam PET on the first day. On the second day, the DCE-MRI experiment was performed for the same six nude rats. The washout rate of the produced positron emitters (k<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2,1st</inf>) and the MRI contrast agent (k<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2a</inf>) were derived using the single tissue compartment model. A linear correlation was observed between k<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2,1st</inf> and k<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2a</inf>, and they were inversely related to fractional necrotic volume. This is the first study which showed the feasibility of washout in in-beam PET as a biomarker for the tumor vascular condition; a clear correlation was seen between the washout rate of the positron emitters in tumor tissue produced via a nuclear fragmentation reaction and the washout of the MRI contrast agent administrated intravenously.

articleTitle: PyTomography: A GPU-accelerated, Opensource Python Library For Image Reconstruction
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Fast fully-quantitative tomographic image generation opens up new possibilities in research and practice. For different tasks, numerous images may have to be generated, such as for large-scale studies, for dynamic imaging, and/or to select best reconstructions amongst many candidate techniques. As an example, optimal image reconstructions in theranostic imaging as applied to radiopharmaceutical therapies for improved assessments and personalizations remains an important frontier. We introduce PyTomography, a medical imaging tomographic reconstruction framework that generates quantitative Single Photon Emission Computed Tomography (SPECT) and Positron Emission Tomography (PET) images. It is developed in Python and uses the GPUaccelerated functionality of PyTorch to efficiently perform the mathematical operations required for image reconstruction. While the software is straightforward and permits reconstruction from a variety of simulated and real data sources, such as the DICOM format, it also provides the necessary infrastructure and flexibility for the development of novel reconstruction techniques and algorithms. Development in an open-source software framework can enhance reproducibility across vendors and research groups, and may expedite corresponding implementation in a clinical setting. Our research validates PyTomography against vendor-specific reconstructions, explores the incorporation of novel prior functions in SPECT reconstruction, and tests the use of comprehensive resolution modeling in PET imaging.

articleTitle: Saturated Gain Avalanche Diode for charged particle detection
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Next generation particle physics experiments are requiring charged particle detection in 4 dimensions at the micron and picosecond scale. Achieving timing resolution better than 100ps with position resolution better than 100 micron is a major challenge. We are proposing to a concept taking advantage of the high timing resolution capabilities of single photon avalanche diodes (SPAD), developed for single photon, i.e. single charged carrier detection. The main drawback of SPADs compared to other technologies for charged particle detection is the inability to separate the signals from a single carrier, thermally produced in particular, from the signals produced by a charged particle generating more than 100 ionization charge carriers. We are proposing a concept for enhancing the number of SPADs that avalanche at the same time per charged particle such that thermal noise can be effectively rejected. This concept relies on allowing a fraction of the charge carrier to diffuse in the silicon hence reaching neighboring SPADs. We assess the signal and noise including the light emission process in avalanches that can mimic the multi-SPAD signal of a charge particle. We investigate this concept for the detection of Minimum Ionizing Particle that go through the all detector and keV scale electrons that stop very close to the surface. We show that this concept is compelling providing that the average number of photons emitted per avalanche is sufficiently low. Such concept could then be implemented as a modified configuration of back-side illuminated SPAD arrays.

articleTitle: A High Sensitivity Mechanical-collimator-free Magic-brush Brain SPECT
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: The performance and portability of conventional single photon emission tomography (SPECT) systems are limited by heavy metal collimators. In this work, we propose a mechanical-collimator-free detector head for a brain SPECT system. The detector head takes the shape of a paddle-brush: the bristles are slim scintillators, the paddle is a scintillator panel. Because each bristle-scintillator has an orientation dependent projection probability density function (PPDF) due to bristle's slim geometry, each scintillator is a self-collimating detector for gamma imaging; for the scintillators on the paddle, they collect gamma rays collimated by the geometrical formation of the bristle group. We call this detector configuration magic-brush. By eliminating mechanical collimator, this detector promises a significant improvement in resolution and sensitivity. In this work, we evaluate a magic-brush detector brain SPECT scanner using Monte Carlo simulation. The scanner has a 99 mm (Φ) × 51 mm (L) FOV.Our preliminary study shows that the scanner has an average sensitivity of 4.4% over the FOV. In a resolution phantom and a contrast phantom with a total activity of 0.1 mCi and acquisition time of 30 min, 3-mm diameter hot-rods can be clearly resolved. These results are comparable to that on a typical clinical PET system, although the detector gantry has a much smaller footprint.

articleTitle: Direct atomic number reconstruction of dual energy cargo radiographs using a semiempirical transparency model
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Dual energy cargo inspection systems are sensitive to both the area density and the atomic number of an imaged container due to the Z dependence of photon attenuation. The ability to identify cargo contents by their atomic number enables improved detection capabilities of illicit materials. Existing methods typically classify materials into a few material classes using an empirical calibration step. However, such a coarse label discretization limits atomic number selectivity and can yield inaccurate results if a material is near the midpoint of two bins. This work introduces a high resolution atomic number prediction method by minimizing the chi-squared error between measured transparency values and a semiempirical transparency model. Our previous work showed that, through a simple calibration step, the semiempirical transparency model can capture second order effects such as scattering and thus yield more accurate atomic number reconstruction capabilities than a fully analytic model. This method was benchmarked using two simulated radiographic phantoms, demonstrating the ability to obtain accurate material predictions on noisy input images by incorporating an image segmentation step. Furthermore, this approach can be adapted to identify shielded objects if the properties of the shielding are known, taking advantage of the closed-form nature of the transparency model.

articleTitle: Neural Network Based Motion Correction for Freely Moving Animal PET Imaging
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: During PET scanning, motion of animals can result in severe motion artifacts in the image. In this paper, we proposed a novel motion correction method for freely moving animals using PET histo-images and a deblurring neural network. The proposed method was tested on a moving resolution phantom and a cylindrical phantom, both of which obtained good results. The initial results show the promise of performing motion correction on the histo-images and using a neural network to generate high-quality images.

articleTitle: Effect of ring gaps in a Total Body PET: A simulation study
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Total-Body Positron Emission Tomography (PET) systems aim to increase their axial coverage and, thus, their sensitivity compared to earlier generations of shorter conventional scanners. However, the increase in costs and materials makes it necessary to explore configurations that keep such axial coverage while maintaining similar features and sensitivity performance. The goal of this work is to simulate and compare two Total Body PET prototypes with axial coverage > 70 cm but a different number of detector rings (7 vs 5). Thus, the 7-ring scanner (74.7 cm axial length) was fully populated with detectors in the axial direction, whereas the 5-ring scanner (71.4 cm axial length) presented gaps between detector rings of 5 cm. Both prototypes used LYSO semi-monolithic crystals (25×3×20 mm, monolithic × slab × height), combining Depth Of Interaction capabilities and a Detector Time Resolution below 250 ps. NEMA NU 2 2018 sensitivity and spatial resolution protocols were implemented in both prototypes. We also simulated and reconstructed the Jaszczack and Derenzo phantoms, evaluating the contrast-to-noise ratio (CNR) and the valley-to-peak ratio (VPR). Despite the expected decrease in sensitivity, our simulation study shows that adjusting ring numbers is worth allowing to reduce about 30% of the total costs while maintaining image quality and spatial resolution. Our findings emphasize the importance of balancing scanner features and costs when designing an effective and cost-efficient Total Body PET scanner.

articleTitle: Experimental Verification of Prompt Gamma Imaging Technique during Carbon Ion Radiation Therapy
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Prompt Gamma Imaging (PGI) is a technique here considered to verify the range of the particle beams in real-time during Carbon Ion Radiation Therapy (CIRT). In this framework, PGI measurements are strongly affected by the limited number of emitted prompt gammas (PGs) and by the presence of a neutron background. A recent study performed using Monte Carlo simulations demonstrated that, despite these limitations, a prompt-gamma camera based on a knife-edge collimator and a pixelated detector could achieve the required sensitivity to measure a shift of the C-ions range of an energy layer during a clinical treatment. Therefore, a prompt-gamma camera based on this concept was developed in order to experimentally validate the simulation results. The camera is based on a compact scintillation detector composed by a 2"x2" pixelated LYSO crystal (6 mm crystal pitch) coupled 1:1 with an array of SiPMs and by its complete readout electronics, which uses a custom-developed readout ASIC and an FPGA-based DAQ. The spectroscopic and positioning performance of the detector have been characterized, achieving the performance required by the application. An experimental campaign will be carried out in May 2023 at CNAO to demonstrate the system capability to verify the beam range during C-ion treatments. The results of this experimental measurements will be presented at the conference.

articleTitle: Au bump connection technology for 3D stacked sensors and detectors
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: 3D- ICs are effective in reducing the manufacturing cost of advanced 2D LSIs while ensuring equivalent device performance and functionality. In pixel-type detectors, the detector and readout circuits are fabricated in separate chips and stacked in order to increase time-space resolution. In addition, sensor devices that stack compound semiconductor sensors with Si signal processing circuits may break due to the difference in thermal expansion coefficient when returned to room temperature if they are firmly connected at high temperatures for bonding. This is especially true when brittle CdTe is used, and conventionally soft materials such as indium bumps that can be bonded at low temperatures have been used. The author's group has been conducting research and development on gold-cylinder bumps as bumps that can be connected at fine pitch and can alleviate inter-chip shear stress caused by temperature changes. This paper reports on a unique bump connection using an ellipsoidal cylindrical gold bump. These bumps are formed on the upper chip and the lower chip and are connected in a crossed shape. This structure was considered in order to obtain electrical connection even if the position of the upper and lower chips is misaligned in the XY direction.Bumping Characteristic Evaluation Trial production of Daisy Chain TEG with UBM and Au bumps formed on the AL wiring was conducted to evaluate connectivity and yield. Bump pitches of 15 µm, 10 µm, and 6 µm were targeted, and three types of bump chains of 6 x 2 µm, 4 x 2 µm, and 3.5 x 2 µm were fabricated.

articleTitle: TlCl: Be, I: towards a superior Scintillation and Cherenkov emitter for medical imaging
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: The material requirements for gamma-ray detectors for medical imaging applications are multi-fold and sensitivity is often overlooked. High effective atomic number (Z<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">eff</inf>) Cherenkov radiators have raised the attention in the community due to their potential for harvesting prompt photons.A material with one of the highest Z<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">eff</inf> and thus low gamma-ray attenuation length is thallium chloride (TlCl). By doping TlCl with beryllium (Be) or iodine (I), scintillation photons are produced upon gamma-ray interaction on top of the prompt Cherenkov photon signal. We report on the performance of TlCl: Be, I for fast timing applications, in particular time-of-flight positron emission tomography and prompt gamma imaging.Scintillation with a measured effective decay time of about 60 ns can be used for energy discrimination. On top, about 3% of the photons are produced promptly, forming a precise time-tagger. The timing capability of different geometries and readout strategies was investigated utilizing both populations of photons. For instance with silicon photomultiplier readout and absence of energy discrimination, a CTR of about 360 ps FWHM was measured for small (~3x3x3 mm³) TlCl crystals. With energy discrimination and time walk correction this figure improves to 230 ps, while with micro-channel plate photomultiplier tube readout even sub-100ps timing performance is possible.

articleTitle: Application of simultaneous estimation method (SIME) to dynamic 18F-FDG whole-body datasets from a long axial FOV PET scanner
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: When analyzing dynamic PET datasets using kinetic models, it is crucial to have an accurate measurement of the arterial input function (AIF). This often entails collection of multiple blood samples, particularly when tracers with plasma metabolites are used. Simultaneous estimation method (SIME) is a data driven methodology aiming to estimate the AIF by simultaneously modeling time activity curves (TACs) from multiple regions of interest. Initially evaluated with <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">18</sup>F-FDG datasets, SIME-based methods later proved to provide robust volume of distribution (V<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">T</inf>) results for certain PET radiotracers with plasma metabolites. The performance of SIME-based methods depends on the differing TAC shapes. Long axial field-of-view PET systems enable acquisition of dynamic whole-body datasets, allowing us to extract TACs from multiple organs as well as brain structures. In this work, we apply the SIME method to dynamic <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">18</sup>F-FDG datasets from a LAFOV scanner and compare the results against the image derived input function (IDIF). We included TACs from seven volumes-of-interests in the SIME analysis. The SIME cost function included the kinetic parameters used to model each TAC and seven parameters of the function to model the AIF. The SIME estimated input function (SIME-IF) was then used for fitting individual TACs from tumor lesions. To evaluate the effects of blood calibration, the SIME-IFs were also scaled with a single blood concentration from the end of the scan. The K<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">i</inf> of individual tumor lesions were estimated using unscaled and scaled SIME-IF and IDIF. We observed statistically significant differences (P<0.05) between area under curves (AUC) of IDIF and unscaled SIME-IF. However, there were no statistically significant differences between AUCs of IDIFs and the SIME-IF scaled to the terminal blood concentration. Scaled SIME-IF served to calculate tumor lesion K<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">i</inf> with strong correlation (R<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sup>=0.97) and reasonable bias (7%) when compared against K values estimated with IDIF.

articleTitle: Inter-Crystal Scatter in a Novel Brain Dedicated PET Detector with 3D Spatial Information
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: One of the mayor challenges in positron emission tomography (PET) is to increase system efficiency without sacrificing spatial resolution. Including the contribution of inter-crystal scatter (ICS) events during image reconstruction may significantly increase efficiency. However, a method for estimating the primary photon path in such events is required to minimize the degradation of spatial resolution. In this study, we propose a neural network (NN) which utilizes 3D positioning information and energy deposition inside the detector for ICS recovery. The IRIS group (IFIC, Valencia) is investigating the implementation of such an approach for the study of ICS in the 4D-PET brain- dedicated PET scanner, under construction at i3M (Valencia). The semi-monolithic 4D-PET detectors utilize monolithic crystals segmented into slabs in one direction, combining the benefits of pixelated and continuous configurations, including 3D positioning capabilities. The detector achieves the high resolution required for brain imaging by using thin slabs (1.6 mm pitch) in a light- sharing design, whereby pairs of slabs are coupled to a single row of SiPMs. A simulation study of one such detector was carried out in order to investigate the performance of the NN for ICS recovery. For ICS events involving two slabs, a precision of 80% was achieved, assuming exact slab identification as well as exact information regarding the depth of interaction (DOI), position along the length of the slab and energy deposition. When experimental values for spatial and energy resolution were applied the precision was 71%. Future work will investigate a NN-based technique for identifying ICS in slabs-pairs with a light-sharing arrangement, as well as estimating position and energy depositions in individual slabs for such events.

articleTitle: Vibration Correction for Slot-Scanning Dark-Field X-Ray Imaging
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Dark-field x-ray imaging of humans and human sized objects is currently done using slot-scanning to overcome current constraints of grating size and cost. These systems are susceptible to vibrations. Here we propose a new maximum likelihood approach to eliminate vibration induced artifacts. Compared to previous work, we model the effect of grating motion not only between but also during x-ray exposures. The method is evaluated quantitatively and qualitatively using simulations and experimental data.

articleTitle: Triggerless Search of Dark Matter Candidates with DarkSide-20k
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Darkside-20k is a planned experiment at LNGS in Italy, supported by the Global Argon Dark Matter Collaboration. Darkside-20k is a dual phase liquid argon time projection chamber (TPC), readout by SiPM-based cryogenic photosensors and designed to perform direct detection of Weakly Interacting Massive Particles. The scintillation light is collected at the bottom and the top planes of the TPC. This talk focuses on the trigger-less data acquisition system. The detector signals are digitized and processed online in a dedicated computing farm. The implementation of the data acquisition will be presented, along with the preliminary performance estimate.

articleTitle: Personalized Remote Radiation Tracking Portable Organ Dosimetry Device (PRRT PODD): Phantom Testing
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Purpose: The goal of this work is to create a user-friendly, personalized remote radiation tracking portable organ dosimetry device (PRRT PODD) that will enable in home radiation monitoring of a patient’s organs at risk (OAR) after receiving Lu-177 DOTATATE treatment. Remote monitoring will allow personalization based upon dose to a patient’s OAR.Methods: The PRRT PODD is an affordable, portable device designed for at home use. It consists of a light-weight frame; a patient specific registration pad; a set of compact radiation detectors; and electronics. We tested a prototype version of the PRRT PODD using an anthropomorphic phantom. The phantom was placed in the PRRT PODD (without detectors) and a CT scan was acquired. This CT scan registered the PODD with the internal "organs" of the phantom.Proprietary software was used to determine where to place up to 16 small radiation detectors on the frame of the PODD to obtain quantitative radiation activity measurements from the OAR in the phantom. Compact, custom electronics have been built for signal processing, data acquisition and data transfer to a laptop computer. For the phantom experiment, washout rates for the OAR, i.e., liver, spleen, right and left kidneys, were set to 68 hr, 72 hr, 45 hr and 48 hr, respectively.Results: Using data from 14 "daily" measurements, the difference between the true and estimated washout rates for the liver and spleen were 5.0% and 6.9%, respectively. Using data for the first 5 measurements, the difference between the true and estimated washout rates for the right and left kidneys were 5.3% and -2.7%, respectively.Conclusions: The first experimental phantom testing of a prototype PRRT PODD device provided excellent results for OAR washout estimation. Accuracy of results can be further improved by better matching PRRT PODD template size to the object being monitored and by tuning the collimation of the detector probes.

articleTitle: Noise Mitigation for a Short Axial Field of View Brain PET Insert Prototype Using Deep Learning
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: The signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) of positron emission tomography (PET) images is determined by several factors, including the geometry of the scanner. A short axial field of view (FOV) results in low system sensitivity and reduced SNR which can complicate clinical decision-making. To address the low sensitivity issue, a longer FOV is highly desirable. However, this raises the scanner’s cost by requiring many more detectors. We present a deep learning (DL) framework to enhance the image quality of data acquired from a brain-dedicated PET insert system with an axial FOV of 2.8 cm. We collected 28 FDG PET scans from a commercial scanner with a 60 cm diameter and an axial FOV of 25 cm. We reconstructed low-sensitivity images resembling the 2.8 cm axial FOV brain PET prototype by training on data from the 25 cm axial FOV commercial system using a fault-tolerant approach that allowed us to constrain the count statistics from a set of detectors in a single ring of the latter system to match the geometry of the former system. A conditional generative adversarial network (cGAN) was trained and tested using simulated short axial FOV images as input, and long axial FOV image pairs as the target. We compared the DL-enhanced images to the target images using PSNR, MSE, MAE, and SSIM. The DL–enhanced PET images from the 2.8 cm axial FOV system showed promising improvement in all quality metrics compared with the input 2.8 cm axial FOV images. The PSNR and SSIM were improved by 33% and 4% respectively, and the MSE and MAE decreased by 75% and 54%, respectively. The efficacy of cGAN models in enhancing the quality of PET images with a short axial FOV suggests their potential to provide reconstructed SNR equivalent to a large axial FOV system (e.g. a total body geometry), even when acquiring data from a conventional system with a shorter axial FOV.

articleTitle: Optimization of silicon planar lateral p-i-n diodes for NIEL measurements
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: The aim of this research is to investigate the possibility using of a planar p-i-n diode with variable base length as a displacement dose monitor. In the presented study, four planar lateral p-i-n diodes with a different length of i region fabricated on a common substrate were modeled and their response in terms of forward voltage bias change under 1MeV neutron irradiation has been studied theoretically.The I-V characteristics of the planar p-i-n structures taking into account variation of the diode’s parameters such as initial n-Si resistivity, recombination properties of n-Si, and geometry of the planar p-i-n structure have been simulated using the continuity equation. The effect of 1 MeV neutron irradiation on variation in the lifetime and mobility of the charged carriers and the effective doping concentration of the i region has been taken into account in the modeling of the I-V characteristics.The continuity equation was solved numerically under the condition of intermediate and high levels of injection of minor carriers into i region of the diode.The obtained solution allows optimization of the response of the planar lateral p-i-n diode by variation of initial characteristics of silicon, diode geometry and readout current density. For example, for the p-i-n diode with an i region length of 0.5 mm and typical parameters of 1 kOhm×cm n-Si, the diode response is linear up to neutron fluence Φ=10<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">12</sup> cm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">-2</sup> with the sensitivity of S~1×10<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">-9</sup> mV×cm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sup>.The proposed compact planar lateral set of silicon p-i-n diodes which allow easy variation of i-region length in contrast to the bulk p-i-n diode can be attractive as a wide-range displacement damage dose sensor for various applications, including long-term space missions.

articleTitle: 10B12B and 12B14B Line Codes for DC Balanced High Speed Serial Applications
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Modern detector readout ASICs, such as the ePIX line developed at SLAC, feature internal digitization (ADC) and high speed serial readout. Such applications are an ideal target for 8B10B encoding. However, the digitized word sizes of 10 and 12 bits do not fit neatly into the 8-bit words for 8B10B encoding. A common solution for this is to pad each readout word into 16-bits, with zeros at the 4-6 most significant bits. The drawback is that this sacrifices valuable serialization bandwidth, leading to longer readout times and slower trigger rates for the camera or detector system. We present two alternate encoding schemes -- 10B12B and 12B14B -- which are based on the principles of 8B10B and allow for efficient encoding of 10 and 12 bit words for DC balanced serial transmission. These encoding schemes have been utilized in several ASICs and SLAC, which are part of X-Ray camera systems operating on the LCLS beamline. The VHDL implementation is open source, and available as part of the SURF firmware library published by SLAC.

articleTitle: Proton Characterization of FPGA-Embedded Hadron Fluence Sensors
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Hadron fluence monitors based on static random access memories (SRAMs) are in use at particle accelerators for electronics protection and at proton therapy facilities for measuring secondary neutrons. A shortcoming of conventional solutions is that they require the SRAMs to sense radiation-induced single event upsets and additional components to transfer the counts to external systems outside the radiation area. This approach limits the practicality of the sensors due to their power requirements, increased board complexity, larger physical footprint, and reduced total ionizing dose tolerance.In this work, we present proton irradiation test results of a novel hadron fluence sensor we designed. The sensor is fully embedded in an SRAM-based field programmable gate array (FPGA), solving the aforementioned limitations. The FPGA configuration SRAM is used as a sensitive element, and is read via the built-in Joint Test Action Group (JTAG) port. A custom JTAG interface board sits outside of the radiation areas at distances up to 40m from the sensor. We irradiated six sensor units using a variable-energy proton beam at the Trento Institute for Fundamental Physics and Applications (TIFPA, Trento, Italy). We will discuss our results in terms of configuration upset cross section as a function of the proton energy in the range from 70 to 230 MeV, and versus the power supply voltage. Moreover, we will present the variability of the cross section in the set of irradiated samples. As a final note, we will show how we used the device to image the proton beam and measure beam profiles.

articleTitle: Characterizing the Performance of a SiPM Scintillator Detector for Low Radioactivity Measurements
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: A detector that can measure positron emitters at low radioactivity levels is crucial for understanding different molecular processes at the single-cell level. To that end, we have developed a βeta particle detector by coupling a 0.5 mm thick plastic scintillator (EJ-212) to a 3.86 x 3.86 mm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sup> silicon photomultiplier (SiPM). We have characterized the detector in terms of background scintillation rate, absolute detection efficiency, and minimum detectable activity (MDA) at room temperature. The measured background scintillation rate per detector was 6×10<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">-4</sup> bcps/mm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sup> (9×10<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">-3</sup> bcps/detector channel). The absolute detection efficiency using <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">18</sup>F as the positron emitter is 42.5 ± 0.4%, mainly attributed to the hemispheric available solid angle. The MDA of the detector was calculated to be 0.06 Bq for a 10 min acquisition. Using the timing output of BROADCOM’s AFBR-S4E001 evaluation kit, we obtained energy spectra for <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">18</sup>F (EJ-212) and <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">22</sup>Na (LYSO). This makes it possible to eliminate most of the dark counts using energy discrimination. Together, these results show the feasibility of using this detector to measure positron emitters at low radioactivity levels. Work is ongoing to develop an array of many channels with this detector and the aim of measuring the metabolic heterogeneity found within a cell population using different radiotracers.

articleTitle: Multi-Tracer PET Image Synthesis in Prostate Cancer using Generative Deep Learning
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Prostate cancer (PC) is a prevalent malignancy in men worldwide. Early and accurate detection of metastatic disease is critical for treatment planning and outcome in both initial presentation and after biochemical recurrence. Molecular imaging with PET using radiopharmaceuticals that target prostate-specific membrane antigen (PSMA) or gastrin-releasing peptide receptor (GRPR) have shown high sensitivity and specificity for recurrent disease. Due to the high tumor heterogeneity in PC, a single radiopharmaceutical might not be sufficient to show the true extent of the disease. Although performing multiple PET scans with different radiotracers can achieve better disease characterization, it is quite impractical and is thus rarely done. In this study, we employed a conditional generative adversarial network (cGAN) to generate synthetic PET images of a second tracer based on data acquired from a first tracer. A retrospective study was conducted in twenty patients with biochemical recurrence (BCR) of PC after primary treatment, who underwent GRPR and PSMA PET utilizing 68Ga-RM2, and either 68Ga-PSMA11 or 18F-DCFPyL, respectively. The synthetic generation of 68Ga-PSMA11/18F-DCFPyL from 68Ga-RM2 and 68Ga-RM2 from 68Ga-PSMA11/ 18F-DCFPyL yielded PSNR of 26.32 ± 3.24 and 27.53 ± 2.86, mean SSIM of 0.88 ± 0.06 and 0.92 ± 0.042, and MSE of 0.011 ± 0.006 and 0.008 ± 0.005, respectively. These initial results show the feasibility of utilizing cGAN to produce synthetic PET images of just one tracer for the assessment of multiple cancer biomarkers in PC. Additional investigations are examining lesion detectability within the synthetic PET images and how they are affected by biomarker heterogeneity in PC. If successful, this method could revolutionize PC imaging by providing physicians with comprehensive biomarker information from a single-tracer PET study.

articleTitle: Comparison of the radiation damage results from the collision data and the HF Online Radiation Damage Monitoring System
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: The CMS-HF calorimeters are designed to detect and measure the energies of the forward going particles. Detection of such particles may lead to new discoveries. Quartz fibers are the active elements in the HF Calorimeters. These fibers undergo radiation damage during collisions. Determining the amount of damage accurately and independently is important to correct the calibration of the detectors while taking data. The CMS-HF Online Radiation Damage Monitoring system, designed and implemented for this purpose, was upgraded at the end of the LHC Run II period. Results of the commissioning of the online system indicated that the measurements should be taken very close to the collisions, since fibers start recovering immediately after the collisions stop. To alleviate the underestimation of the radiation damage due to the recovery of the fibers, it is proposed that the radiation damage data be taken in the abort gap during collisions. During the first year of Run III period, abort gap data-taking could not be implemented and postponed to the second year. However, comparison between the radiation damage estimates made using the collision data and the online radiation damage monitoring system will be shown for the commissioning data. Data taken outside the collisions during the first year of Run III (2022) and possible abort gap operations will also be discussed.

articleTitle: Improvement of Joint Activity and Attenuation Factors Estimation for PET with TOF and Lu-176 background radiation
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Maximum likelihood activity and attenuation estimation as well as maximum likelihood activity and attenuation correction factors estimation algorithm were developed to reconstruct the activity image in CT-less PET scans. Additional attenuation information can be obtained by background radiation from Lu-176 in LYSO/LSO crystal to overcome the multiple solutions problem. On this basis, reconstructed algorithm joint reconstruction of activity distribution and attenuation correction factors using both TOF emission and background data (MLACF-Tx) was improved. We firstly introduced a complete algorithm workflow based on MLACF-Tx and a set of real combined with simulation data was reconstructed for verification. The results showed that the algorithm performed well, with small deviation compared to the CT-based OSEM algorithm.

articleTitle: Data driven gating and motion correction for low-statistics PET imaging: Application to 90Y SIRT dosimetry
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: The 90Y PET images used for post-treatment dosimetry in SIRT of liver cancer are impacted by respiratory motion. Liver motion due to respiration will result in blurred images and can lead to inaccuracies of the dosimetric measures. Due to the low count statistics in 90Y PET data, the data-driven gating method does not work well, making the deviceless respiratory motion correction method unusable. The purpose of this study was to develop an alternative data-driven gating method to derive triggers directly from the list-mode data in order to produce respiratory motion compensated 90Y PET images and to assess the impact of respiratory motion on 90Y dosimetry. The steps for performing dosimetry have been adapted to improve dosimetry on the motion corrected PET images. Two different motion correction methods called Q.Static and Q.Rigid were investigated and evaluated on both NCAT phantom and patient data. The corrected images were compared to uncorrected respiratory motion PET images. Results demonstrate that both correction techniques lead to an improvement in dosimetry calculation for the liver tumor. Doses delivered to tumor were increased by 18.3% and 37.4% for Q.Static and Q.Rigid respectively for NCAT phantom; tumor doses were increased by 7.12 ± 12.04% and 8.76 ± 12.97% for Q.Static and Q.Rigid respectively, for patient data.

articleTitle: An Edge-on GaAs:Cr Detector for Clinical Photon Counting CT
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: This study proposes the an edge-on Cr-compensated GaAs (GaAs:Cr) detector for clinical photon counting CT applications. Compared to other semiconductors, such as CdZnTe (CZT) and Si, GaAs:Cr offers advantages such as high electron mobility, lower scattering ratio, and lower fabrication cost. The edge-on detector structure provides better detection efficiency compared to conventional horizontal structures. To evaluate the performance, a detector full-response model was developed and compared against edge-on Si and face-on CZT detectors. The results of the noise cloud index analysis demonstrates that the proposed GaAs:Cr detector exhibits a superior mono-energy spectrum and a lower bound of noise, as a potential alternative to photon counting detectors for clinical CT applications.

articleTitle: Data-driven head motion tracking using the lutetium background radiation in the NeuroEXPLORER
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: With the advent of ultra-high-performance dedicated brain PET imaging systems, such as the NeuroEXPLORER (NX), which offer high spatial resolution, high sensitivity, and improved timing resolution, human motion has become a major limiting factor for brain PET quantification. This includes rigid and non-rigid motion in the head and neck regions. Several data-driven methods using PET emission data have been previously proposed and evaluated for motion tracking. However, the accuracy of these methods is susceptible to the early time frames of a dynamic imaging study. Benefiting from the high sensitivity, increased volume of lutetium-based crystal material, as well as improved TOF resolution of the NX scanner, this study investigates the feasibility of utilizing the lutetium background radiation for head motion tracking using experimental data. An image-based centroid-of-distribution (COD) approach and a sinogram-based principal component analysis (PCA) method were applied to the lutetium transmission data acquired with a human subject and their efficacy was validated using a United Imaging Healthcare (UIH) marker-less motion tracking (UMT) camera. The results suggested that both data-driven methods can detect moderate and large motion with a high confidence level, and the sinogram-based PCA approach showed superior sensitivity to the COD method for small-motion detection (<8 mm translation). These results suggest that lutetium background radiation in the NX scanner can be used for motion tracking, and it may provide complementary information to the data obtained with the UMT camera to further improve the sensitivity and stability of motion detection in the future.

articleTitle: High resolution TOF-PET detectors by using dual-ended readout with SiPM arrays of different pixel sizes on each end
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: This study focuses on developing high-resolution depth encoding PET detectors with good timing resolution for organ-specific time-of-flight (TOF) PET scanners. The novel PET detector consists of an LYSO crystal array dual-ended read out with SiPM arrays of different pixel sizes at each end. Three LYSO arrays with crystal size of 1.95×1.95×20, 1.44×1.44×10, and 0.98×0.98×20 mm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</sup> were fabricated. An 8×8 SiPM array with pixel size of 3×3 mm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sup> is used in one end. Row and column summing readout circuits plus 1D position encoding circuits are used to compress the number of signals from 64 to 4 position encoding energy signals. The flood histogram of the detector is calculated by sorely using the four position encoding energy signals of the SiPM array. A 4×4 SiPM array with a pixel size of 6×6 mm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sup> is used at the other end. The timings of the 16 SiPM pixels are obtained using the NINO ASIC and the fastest timing is obtained using an OR circuit and used as the time stamp of the detector. The flood histogram, energy resolution and timing resolution of the detectors were measured. All crystals of the two detectors with large crystal sizes can be clearly resolved. The edge crystals of the detector with the smallest crystal size cannot be resolved. Both energy and timing resolution degrade as crystal size decreases. The detectors provided an average crystal energy resolutions of 11.7%, 15.5%, and 17.6%, and an average crystal coincidence time resolution of 275 ps, 276 ps, and 320 ps. The DOI resolution of the detectors will be measured next. The detectors provided good flood histogram, timing resolution and reduces the number of electronics channels at the same time.

articleTitle: Image-domain Material Decomposition for Photon-counting CT using Neural Attenuation Field
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Photon-counting CT (PCCT) has been widely attracting sustained attention from both academia and industry in recent years. PCCT has the capability to measure the energy of each detected photon and can differentiate between materials/tissues. Although imaging domain material decomposition (IDMD) is widely used, its performance could be degraded in practice due to various reasons, such as noise amplification and beam hardening effects. This paper proposes a novel deep learning model based on neural attenuation field, which can learn an implicit continuous representation of total attenuation in each voxel using measured CT projections, such model allowing reducing the noise and artifacts.

articleTitle: High-resolution Infrared Transient Current Technique for Tellurium Mapping in CdTe material
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: In this study, we investigated the influence of tellurium inclusions on the electrical properties of cadmium telluride (CdTe) semiconductor detectors. Using high-resolution infrared transient current technique (TCT) for tellurium mapping in CdTe material, we conducted a comprehensive raster scan across the entire detector area, focusing on the separation of tellurium inclusions from electrode-induced polarization effects. We analyzed transient currents from different time intervals and calculated the collected charge for each time frame, revealing the temporal dynamics of charge collection and the potential influence of localized defects on the overall charge distribution.Additionally, we employed high-resolution 3D raster scans to obtain a clearer and more detailed understanding of the charging behaviour. By selecting only waveforms that met specific criteria, such as signal timing and amplitude threshold within the observed time period, we isolated relevant waveforms and eliminated potential noise or interference. Our results showed minimal lateral movement of charge within the centres of tellurium inclusions during the time interval of 5-20 ns, suggesting charge localization and accumulation in the central regions of the inclusions.
