This would provide further insights into the charge dynamics in CdTe materials and help optimize the performance of semiconductor detectors under varying conditions, especially as we can control laser settings we can connect laser fluencies to charge accumulation.

articleTitle: Radiation tolerance study of scintillation properties with 6 MeV electron beam on inorganic scintillators
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: The radiation tolerance of several inorganic scintillators was investigated to ensure their reproducibility in electron beam exposure. LuAG:Pr, GPS:Ce, LYSO:Ce, GAGG:Ce single, and GAGG:Ce ceramic scintillators were prepared with all faces polished mechanically and thermally annealed. Electron beam exposures at 50, 100, 500, 1000, and 3000 Gy were conducted using a 6 MeV clinical electron beam from a Varian Novalis Tx linear accelerator with a 270-degree bending magnet. Energy spectra were acquired by exciting a <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">137</sup>Cs source coupled to a photomultiplier tube (PMT) kept in the dark box with a biased high voltage of -900 V. The relative light output of GPS:Ce and LuAG:Pr compared to the baseline decreased steadily after electron beam exposure, recording 66.2% and 56.9%, respectively, at a dose of 3 kGy. The transmittance and photoluminescence of these scintillators also deteriorated with increasing crystallographic defects. In contrast, LYSO:Ce and GAGG:Ce scintillators demonstrated high tolerance to electron beams. Thermal annealing was shown to restore the scintillation properties of the degraded scintillators. These findings provide valuable insights into the radiation tolerance of inorganic scintillators and have implications for the design of radiation detectors for various applications, including radiation therapy and aerospace. Using inorganic scintillators in radiation therapy is particularly critical for estimating radiation exposure. The potential of these scintillators in aerospace applications will also be explored based on the promising results of this study.

articleTitle: Design and initial Measurement Results for the second revision of the High Density Digitizer System on Chip (HDSoCv2): A 64 Channel 1 GSa/s Waveform Digitizer for High Density Detectors
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: This paper presents the design of the second revision of a waveform sampling ASIC (HDSoC), optimized for high density light detectors, such as Silicon Photomultiplier (SiPM) or MA-PMTs, suitable for large and high rate NP experiments such as the Relativistic Heavy Ion Collider and the future Electron Ion Collider. In this paper we cover the improvement of the design, fabrication and preliminary test results for the second revision of the chip.

articleTitle: Design of the digital readout of the prototype SparkPix-RT ASIC with variable data velocity
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: This paper describes the design of the digital readout of the prototype SparkPix-RT ASIC. This joint ANL-SLAC development aims to demonstrate an approach to increase detector frame rates using on-chip compression to reduce the amount of streaming data from a pixel matrix prior to being transmitted off-chip. However, compression can result in variable latency, whereas scientific detectors must operate in real-time (i.e., stall-free) to support continuous streaming of sampled data. We present one solution in the prototype SparkPix-RT ASIC design of the readout block which allows variable rate compressed data to be transmitted off-chip over fixed bandwidth serial channels.

articleTitle: Perspective of a 28nm CMOS Technology for Future Vertex Tracking Applications
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: This work focuses on studying the analog properties of MOSFET transistors belonging to a 28 nm planar CMOS technology. Currently, this node seems to be the more promising in terms of radiation tolerance and density of digital logic for the design of pixel detectors at future particle colliders. Measurements of static and signal parameters have been carried out at different values of gate-to-source and drain-to-source voltages. To estimate the noise performance of a front-end system in the 28 nm node, this work will study the results of noise measurements carried out on NMOS and PMOS devices. The 1/f and white components of the noise voltage spectrum will be experimentally characterized as a function of the polarity, current, and dimensions of the devices in a wide frequency range. Data coming from older CMOS nodes will also be provided in order to evaluate the resolution limits achievable for low-noise analog front-ends.

articleTitle: Building Real Time Edge Machine Learning Systems for High Data Rate Acquisition
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Over the past decade, a developments in radiation and photonic detectors has significantly improved their resolution, pixel density, sensitivity, and sampling rate. The increase in sampling rate corresponds to a considerable increase in generated data, the movement and storage of which requires a large number of storage units with very high bandwidth interconnects to the sensors themselves. The paradigm of edge computing, however, proposes to move the data processing closer to the source, the edge, rather than moving data to processing. Still, the computation resources are limited at the edge and it is necessary to use lean and robust algorithms. Machine learning (ML) is commonly used to identify patterns and relationships in minimally processed data. EdgeML is a combination of ML and edge computing that leverages a combination of benefits from ML algorithms and edge computing. In this paper, we demonstrate a high-speed and configurable ML model in a fully customizable EdgeML flow. Our demonstration focuses on an angular streaking detector developed for the LCLS-II project known as the CookieBox. The flow starts by emulating the CookieBox, digitizing the signals, and passing them to an optimized ML model on the FPGA. By using our ML implementation in this flow, we are able to achieve a 2.7 μs of inference latency. This flow can also be configured for other instrumentation applications that require low-latency solutions.

articleTitle: Highly Compact and Scalable 100 ps CTR + 3D Positioning TOF-PET Detector Sub-Unit
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: We have developed a highly compact design for TOF-PET detector modules employing side-readout of scintillation crystal elements to achieve 100 ps CTR and 3D positioning of 511 keV interactions. Detector modules comprise 16 layers, each containing 4 sub-units. Each detector layer sub-unit is a 2×4 array of 3×3×10 mm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</sup> LGSO elements side-coupled to a 6×4 array of 3×3 mm² SiPMs. To achieve high packing fraction, the electronic readout is implemented with a 4-layer rigid FR4 PCB that is only 0.4 mm thick and has a width matching the 6×4 SiPM array (13.3 mm). Among many features, the circuit multiplexes 24 SiPM timing channels into 1 to reduce the readout complexity. In new configuration reported here, all external connectors have been removed and replaced with 0.4 mm pitch fine connectors for scalable signal routing at the detector module level. The timing performance of this 24:1 multiplexed readout was measured in coincidence with a reference detector, resulting in average 107±1.3 ps FWHM CTR. Thus the proposed side-readout of scintillation crystal elements and readout electronics are now configured in a layer topology and achieve the performance that are scalable to large area detector modules for a ~100 ps CTR TOF-PET system.

articleTitle: Image Reconstruction with DOI Rebinning and PSF Modeling for the Quad-Head PET
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: For positron emission tomography (PET), the quad-head geometry achieves higher system sensitivity, however severe parallax error also deteriorates the image quality. Using depth decoding detectors and considering a more accurate system response matrix (SRM) in iterative reconstruction are two approaches to correct parallax error. In this work, we implemented an image reconstruction method for the quad-head PET with dual-ended readout depth decoding detectors. Firstly, each coincidence event was assigned to multiple rebinned lines of response (LOR) on a compact sinogram defined by a virtual ring located inside the real detection ring. In addition, we applied a spatially invariant point spread function (PSF) model. The performance of the proposed reconstruction method was evaluated by using Monte Carlo (MC) simulation data, including a uniform circular phantom and a Derenzo phantom. Experimental results show that this method provided lower noise and higher peak-to-valley ratios.

articleTitle: A Stable Current Source Based on Ionization Chamber Detector Principles
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Miniature and stable power sources are required for long journeys to the other solar planets. In this work, we present the realization of a current source based on an ionization chamber detector, whose one of its electrodes is coated by Ni-63 beta radioisotope. The beta radiation interacts with the gas atmosphere between the electrodes, ionizes it and creates pairs of positive ions and free electrons. A potential difference is forced between the electrodes intended to produce an electric field. The electric field creates a preferred direction for the movement of the charges within the gas. The "ionization current" flows between the anode and the cathode. That current is measured with an electrometer. The magnitude of the current depends on multiple factors, such as the gas type and pressure, the potential difference between the electrodes, the geometry of the ionization chamber, and the radiation intensity.In this study, the overall efficiency of the ionization chamber as a function of its physical structure, the efficiency of the source and the energy transfer are discussed. An experimental study was conducted to determine the optimal parameters for producing the maximal ionization current from the ionization chamber.

articleTitle: Passive gamma-ray analysis of UO2 fuel rods using SrI2(Eu) scintillators in multi-detector arrangements
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: The use of passive gamma analysis (PGA) to interrogate nuclear fuel rods for quality assurance and non-proliferation purposes has been demonstrated to be as efficient and safer than the more common neutron activation analysis (NAA) for fresh fuel assessment. In this work we will build on existing experimental measurements using a single probe SrI<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf>(Eu), to simulate the response of a multi-probe SrI<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf>(Eu) detector array in the analysis of nuclear fuel rods, containing sintered UO<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf>. The work compares the results to literature studies using bismuth germinate and annulus CsI(Tl) multi-probes to evaluate light water reactor fuel rods. The enhanced scintillation performance of SrI<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf>(Eu) over CsI(Tl) and BGO make it ideally suited for nuclear fuel inspection.

articleTitle: Development of Cosmic Neutron Spectrometer using 3He Proportional Counters with Moderators
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: We developed a neutron spectrometer using <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</sup>He-tube proportional counters with moderators for measurements of the cosmic neutron spectrum on the ground. The design goal is that the spectrometer is portable and carryable by a vehicle to perform measurements at various sites. To measure neutron spectrum in the energy range from meV to hundreds of MeV, we optimized the spectrometer configuration using Monte Carlo N-Particle Transport simulation code. The number of <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</sup>He-tube proportional counters with moderators was determined to cover the entire energy range. In addition, the thickness of moderators and that of moderators with a metal layer were determined as well. The spectrometer consists of 4-atm nine <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</sup>He tube-type thermal neutron detectors with eight high-density polyethylene moderators, including two with an internal copper layer. The data acquisition system for the spectrometer was developed for laboratory measurements. The neutron spectrometer has been operated for months on the ground for stability validation of the data acquisition system. Some measurement data were analyzed, and a neutron spectrum was obtained. We present a preliminary cosmic neutron spectrum obtained from the measured data.

articleTitle: Radiation-Hardened-by-Design Preamplifier with Self-Reset Technique for Radiation Detector
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: This paper presents a radiation-hardened-by-design (RHBD) preamplifier that utilizes a self-reset technique when the preamplifier becomes saturated. The proposed RHBD preamplifier comprises the charge-sensitive amplifier (CSA) part with the self-reset circuit and total ionizing dose (TID) effects compensation part. The CSA part consists of a comparator, a feedback switch, and a trigger circuit. The trigger circuit generates a pulse with sufficient duration to reset the feedback capacitor when the CSA becomes saturated. TID effects compensation part utilizes a binary current source to compensate TID effects in the CSA. The current source control unit detects the operating point of the OPAMP and generates appropriate signals to control the current source switches. The proposed circuit was fabricated using general-purpose 0.18 μm CMOS technology, and verified through an irradiation test up to 231 kGy (SiO<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf>) at a rate of 10.46 kGy/h.

articleTitle: RTS fluctuations in the DCR of 150 nm CMOS SPADs before and after exposure to neutrons
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Random telegraph signal-like fluctuations are investigated in single photon avalanche diodes (SPADs) fabricated in a 150~nm CMOS technology before irradiation and after exposure to neutrons up to a maximum final fluence of about 4.3x10<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">10</sup> 1 MeV equivalent neutrons cm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">-2</sup>. The devices under test (DUTs) consist of two arrays of sensors, belonging to the same chip, with different active area and based on a passive quenching architecture. Pre-screening of the DUTs in search for RTS behavior is performed based on low time resolution measurements by means of a machine learning algorithm, trained with data from previous measurements. DCR measurements performed with much higher time resolution at different temperatures are used to investigate the activation energy of the defects, both those already present in the device before irradiation and those induced by neutrons, at the origin of the RTS behavior.

articleTitle: Imaging Performance of a dedicated Breast-PET-DBT scanner
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: A multi-modality dedicated breast scanner which combines a high spatial resolution dedicated PET scanner (BPET) and DBT has been developed. Phantom measurements demonstrate the BPET scanner to have an in-plane spatial resolution of <2mm and improved quantification of sub-cm lesions in comparison with whole-body PET scanners. Measurements also suggest adequate count-rate capability to support an imaging scan time of 2-5 mins. The scanner will be useful for imaging molecular features in primary breast cancer and will provide intrinsically co-registered anatomic features depicted by DBT. The availability of new PET tracers like <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">18</sup>FES will make the BPET-DBT scanner helpful in a number of areas related to breast cancer treatment and management. Detailed performance characterization and imaging capability assessment of this multi-modality scanner using relevant phantom studies, as well as its application in a pilot clinical research patient imaging will be presented.

articleTitle: Deep Learning for Tritium Detection Using Scientific CCDs
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Utilizing recent advances in image recognition, we explore the possibilities of applying deep learning to to the challenging problem of tritium detection and quantification using thick, fully depleted, highly-pixelated, scientific Charge Coupled Devices (CCDs.) We present a simulation framework developed to study signals from both tritium decay products and background radiation. Simulated particle tracks are used to train a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) to perform track-based particle identification. The importance of thin CCD dead layers are discussed, as 50% of tritium decay particles don't penetrate deeper than 50 nm in silicon.

articleTitle: Projection-based Motion Correction for Shifted-Detector Cone-Beam CT
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Several cone-beam CT (CBCT) application rely on time-resolved (4D) reconstructions that represent organ or patient motion. For that purpose existing approaches typically acquire a motion surrogate signal (e.g. the displacement of a breathing belt) along with the CBCT scan such that different motion phases can be reconstructed independently. However, as this strategy requires additional patient preparation and may fail if there is too little data in a certain motion phase (e.g., due to irregular breathing), we propose a projection-based motion correction to overcome these drawbacks. Instead of operating in image domain, our approach trains an LSTM-based neural network to predict projections in which the patient is frozen in a fixed motion state. Thus, applying the network repeatedly allows to recover any motion state of the CBCT scan. Tested on real patient measurements of a Varian TrueBeam system, the proposed approach provided artifact-free 4D reconstructions that show a good correlation with external motion surrogate signals.

articleTitle: Status of a breast CT phantom dataset from breast MR images for PHENOMENO project
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: This work rises from a framework of the Phenomeno European project and aims at developing a dataset of digital breast models to be used in in-silico tests and anthropomorphic phantom manufacturing for testing and developing apparatuses in x-ray breast imaging. A software was developed for classifying voxels in MRI breast images in air, glandular tissue, adipose tissue, skin or tumoral lesion. Such a software was based on pixel values and determined thresholds. The developed algorithm was tested on MRI breast images taken from an open access database. In order to validate the segmentation process, two approaches were introduced. A first approach is based on a subjective evaluation of an experienced radiologist, meant to evaluate to which extent the glandular tissue distribution and 3D conformation was preserved during the tissue classification as well as to evaluate to which extent fine details contained in the clinical images were preserved in the classified ones. Hence, two evaluation grids were proposed with scores ranging between 1 (lower grade) and 5 (higher grade). Subsequently, an objective analysis was introduced based on the use of dice similarity index (DSI) between images classified by the developed algorithm and images manually segmented by an experienced radiologist. In the two investigated cases, DSI resulted 0.934 and 0.755; when DSI was evaluated for segmented images provided within the database containing the breast MRI images, these values reduced to 0.835 and 0.488, for the same cases. The subjective evaluation is still ongoing.

articleTitle: Quantitative Accuracy Assessment of the NeuroEXPLORER – An Ultra-High Performance Human Brain PET Scanner
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: The NeuroEXPLORER is a recently-developed ultra-high-performance brain-dedicated PET system offering high sensitivity and high spatial resolution with depth-of-interaction estimation. This study evaluates the quantification accuracy and stability of the NeuroEXPLORER for a variety of imaging applications, using a NEMA NU 2 image quality (IQ) phantom and a 3-D Hoffman brain phantom. Each phantom was placed at the center of the field-of-view next to a uniform cylinder. All phantoms were filled with <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">18</sup>F-FDG solution and scanned at multiple delayed timepoints, covering a broad range of activities from 169 MBq to 1.2 MBq in the main phantoms and from 288 MBq to 2.1 MBq in the uniform cylinder. Quantitative accuracy was assessed using contrast recovery coefficient (CRC), background variability, and background bias measurements in the IQ phantom, in addition to recovery coefficient (RC) measurements calculated in reference to the true injected activity concentration for the white matter and six regions of the gray matter in the Hoffman phantom. The results were compared at delayed imaging timepoints, as well as in different reconstruction protocols and dynamic frame durations down to 1 s. Delayed scans of the IQ phantom showed a highly stable performance from 166 MBq to 3 MBq in the phantom, with negligible effects on CRC and mean background bias. Mean background bias ranged from -3.3% to 2.1% in 30-min to 2-s frames of the NEMA IQ scan and increased to 8% in 1-s frames. The Hoffman phantom images exhibited remarkable image quality for activities ranging from 169 MBq to 2 MBq in the phantom, with ±1% RC variations in different segmented regions. Overall, these findings suggest that the NeuroEXPLORER is a reliable tool for quantitative molecular imaging, suitable for a variety of clinical and research imaging applications.

articleTitle: Achieving BSREM image quality at the speed of OSEM reconstruction using the cGAN framework
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Positron emission tomography (PET) is an imaging method for cancer, heart disease, and neurological disorders. PET images are reconstructed from emitted positron data using complex mathematical algorithms, among which ordered subset algorithms, including ordered subset expectation maximization (OSEM) and block sequential regularized expectation maximization (BSREM), are commonly employed. OSEM provides faster image reconstruction but with higher noise, while BSREM offers improved image quality, and reduced noise, albeit at the cost of increased computational complexity. To improve the accuracy and quality of OSEM-reconstructed brain PET images while maintaining time efficiency, we utilized a generative adversarial network (GAN) to enhance OSEM images to a level of quality and accuracy comparable to that of images generated by the BSREM algorithm. We collected 18 FDG PET scans from Alzheimer’s disease patients, which were preprocessed into a list-mode format and reconstructed using OSEM with 2 iterations and 2 subsets, and BSREM with 25 iterations. We trained a cGAN model, consisting of a U-net generator and a discriminator that received OSEM-reconstructed PET images as input, BSREM images as the target, and generated higher quality and accuracy PET images as output. Results were evaluated using PSNR, SSIM, and NRMSE. Using the cGAN model, we improved the SNR and contrast of the OSEM-reconstructed PET images with a 17% enhancement in the PSNR and a 60% decrease in the NRMSE, although the SSIM was not significantly improved. Our findings show that the GAN model can convert low-SNR, low-contrast OSEM images to high-quality, high-accuracy images similar to those generated by the BSREM algorithm. This approach offers potential advantages in achieving the image quality and accuracy of BSREM with the shorter reconstruction time of OSEM.

articleTitle: The ATLAS TRT FastOR Trigger For Heavy Ions in the LHC
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: The ATLAS heavy ion group has made important observations lately including light-by-light scattering and tau lepton pair production in Pb ion runs at the LHC. These analyses are part of the ultra-peripheral physics program, which studies events in which the electromagnetic clouds around the ions interact rather than the Pb ions themselves, giving photon-photon interactions at high energy. In order to further this program of study, higher statistics at low lepton transverse momentum (pT) is needed, but no suitable trigger exists in the ATLAS detector to capture such events. In order to provide such a trigger, the ATLAS Transition Radiation Tracker cosmics trigger known as the FastOR is being adapted for use in Pb-Pb collisions. The Endcap FastOR commissioning procedure and tuning of parameters for the heavy ion physics program are presented, as well as the remaining challenges and considerations that will be addressed between now and the upcoming heavy ion run in October 2023.

articleTitle: LSO Background Radiation-Based Quality Control for Detector Time Offsets During Patient PET/CT Scans
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: LSO background radiation is currently used to monitor scanner detector properties, such as energy spectrum potential drift. However, monitoring time properties remains a challenge because LSO emits photons with lower than 511 keV energies, resulting in different detector responses.An attractive feature is monitoring detector properties through LSO data during patient scans. This can be achieved by acquiring data with two energy windows: one set up for 511 keV emission and another for lower energies of LSO background radiation. In principle, patient data can be self-time aligned, but this is relatively expensive and requires multiple data reconstructions. Moreover, the estimation precision of detector time offsets (TO) can suffer from patient attenuation map misalignment. On the other hand, the LSO background radiation TOF spectrum depends on detector geometry only, and assuming relatively good time alignment can result in a simpler method of TO estimation.Patient data investigations have shown that LSO TOs differ from 511 keV emission TOs. However, due to the simultaneous acquisition of LSO and 511 keV emission data, the LSO footprint can be constantly learned from reliable patient scans, as the true time offsets for 511 keV emission are known from self-time alignment. The learned pattern can be predictive for scanner performance during patient scans.

articleTitle: Multi-energy photon-counting dual-row compound semiconductor x-ray detectors for security screening systems
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: We have fabricated direct conversion cadmium telluride (CdTe) and cadmium zinc telluride (CZT) semiconductor multi-energy x-ray detectors using custom application specific integrated circuits (ASICs). The detectors use a modular two side butt-able geometry and can be tiled into long dualrow one dimensional (1D) panels covering a large field of view (FoV). The CdTe and/or CZT semiconductor sensors have sub-millimeter pixel dimensions perpendicular to the scanning direction for high spatial resolution. Two rows of pixels are used for rapid scanning and to reduce the effect of individual bad pixels in scanned images. The sensors are guard ring free and three millimeters thick for high detective quantum efficiency (DQE). The mixed signal ASICs have six thresholds per pixel for up to six contiguous energy windows across a dynamic range from 20 keV to 160 keV and operate at a fast peaking time for high output count rates of up to 4 million counts per second per square millimeter (Mcps/mm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sup>). Using the guard ring free sensors and geometrically integrated ASICs, multiple two-side butt-able modular detectors, each with ten centimeter FoV, have been tiled together in lengths of up to one meter. We will report the output count rate capability, dynamic range, and the spatial and energy resolution, as well as the uniformity and stability under conditions for baggage inspection in people screening lanes at airports. We will report results of imaging studies performed with a dual-view system using two such tiles of one meter of active FoV. Systems using these detectors may provide better energy separation between low and high energy x-rays as compared to dual layer or dual kVp dual energy systems, potentially leading to improved accuracy of effective atomic number (Z<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">eff</inf>) estimates in image voxels reconstructed from dual views. To see such an improvement, good energy resolution would need to be maintained across the expected output count rates and dynamic range.

articleTitle: Development of PVK-Based Plastic Scintillators Loaded with Bi2O3 Nanoparticles
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: We developed surface-modified Bi<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf>O<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</inf> nanoparticle-loaded plastic scintillators for application in scintillation detectors that have fast response to high-energy X-rays. As the host polymer, poly(9-vinylcarbazole) (PVK) was selected because PVK has a band gap of 3.5 eV, smaller than that of polystyrene (5.4 eV). The scintillation properties of the plastic scintillators with different concentrations of nanoparticles and phosphor (9,10-diphenylantrazene (DPA)) were characterized to optimize concentrations of nanoparticles and DPA. Nanoparticles of 4.5 ± 0.92 nm with high dispersibility in PVK matrix were successfully synthesized by subcritical hydrothermal synthesis. In the X-ray-excited radioluminescence (XRL) spectra, an emission peak around 440 nm was observed in all the samples as well as in the PL emission spectra. The scintillation light yields of the samples were estimated on the basis of the pulse height spectra for 67.41-keV X-rays. Detection efficiencies and light yields significantly larer than those of EJ-256 were achieved for all samples with a nanoparticle concentration of 10 wt%. Among them, the sample with Bi<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf>O<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</inf> nanoparticle concentration of 10 wt% and DPA concentration of 0.25 mol% showed the highest light yield of 10000 photons/MeV for high-energy X-rays of 67.41 keV. Decay time constants of about 6-18 ns were obtained for all samples regardless of nanoparticle concentration. We achieved the fabrication of plastic scintillators with high light yield and high detection efficiency without losing the fast response derived from plastic scintillators.

articleTitle: Fully-organic indirect flexible detector for real-time dose monitoring during proton therapy
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: The development of detectors for protons and heavy particles is a long-lasting research topic not only for fundamental applications but also, more recently, for monitoring energy and flow of particles in ion beam applications. Nowadays, one of the most demanding application of ion beams is hadron therapy of cancer. In this field, ion beams, mostly proton beams, are used for the controlled treatment of cancer by focusing them onto small volumes to deliver energy to the tumor. The effectiveness and safety of the treatment is enhanced by tuning the beam both in intensity and in position to irradiate the tumor in a controlled way, preserving the surrounding healthy tissues. For this reason, there is an increasing demand of systems optimized for the accurate recording and mapping of the dose delivered during a treatment plan in-situ and in realtime. Here, we present the results achieved by a fully-organic indirect detector in which a flexible Organic Photo-Transistor based on DNTT has been coupled with a plastic scintillator based on polysiloxane. The device has been firstly characterized under 5 MeV proton beams provided by LABEC ion beam center (INFN - FI, Italy) to reproduce the energy range that scattered protons deliver on healthy tissues surrounding the tumor during treatments for prostate cancer. The detector exhibits excellent detecting performances even bent down to a curvature radius of 0.5 mm, at low operation voltages (V = -1 V), reaching a limit of detection of 0.0 6 Gy min<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">-1</sup>. Such results confirm its reliability as a personal dosimeter with high comfort and low risk for the user. Finally we tested the detectors in real clinical conditions employing an anthropomorphic phantom and a therapeutic proton beam (energy range [70–00] MeV) provided by TIFPA Proton Therapy Center (TN, Italy).

articleTitle: Piecewise learning-based smoothing model for accurate and sensitive nuclear counting
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Smoothing filters are essential for a radiation monitoring system to measure count rates from stochastic radioactivity. Designing such filters is highly challenging due to inherent trade-off between precise estimation and response time of count rates. While many adaptive filter methods has been recently explored in nuclear counting and show significant performances, they often fail to produce convincing results in numerous radioactive scenarios. This paper first proposes a convolutional neural network based smoothing filter model for accurate and sensitive nuclear counting. In particular, considering to characteristics of natural nuclear counting datas, the two-stage learning framework consisting of (1) change point detection, (2) local regression is designed to approximate space of piecewise continuous and differentiable functions. Experiments demonstrate that the proposed method greatly compromise between response time and precision over the other comparison methods both quantitatively and qualitatively.

articleTitle: Improvement studies of Compton cameras over gamma cameras in nuclear medicine treatments
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: The use of Compton cameras (CCs) for imaging radioisotopes in nuclear medicine can offer benefits over conventional gamma cameras in some aspects, for example in assessment and dosimetry of treatments with radionuclides, in which photon emission is not optimized for gamma camera performance. The IRIS group of IFIC (Valencia) has developed a CC MACACO III, made of LaBr3 crystals coupled to silicon photomultiplier arrays and is evaluating it for nuclear medicine, in different treatments in which its use can be advantageous over gamma cameras. In collaboration with the nuclear medicine department of La Fe Hospital in Valencia, data were taken with phantoms and patients with <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">131</sup>I-NaI. In addition, the necessary conditions for imaging <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">225</sup>Ac and <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">166</sup>Ho are being assessed through Monte Carlo simulations that will be followed by experimental tests. Results will be presented

articleTitle: Estimation of Gamma Source Direction by Multipixel Array Detector based on Convolutional Neural Network Model
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: We proposed a method to estimate gamma-ray incident direction by a multipixel array detector toward radiation source finding based on 4π gamma imaging [1] – [3]. When gamma rays are emitted from a point source incident into the detector, more events occur at pixels closer to the source and fewer events occur at pixels further away from the source. The direction of the source can be estimated by analyzing the spatial distribution of counts in the detector, named a "self-shielding profile". A prediction model based on the self-shielding profile was developed to estimate the direction of the gamma source using a convolutional neural network. Estimation of the direction of a <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">137</sup>Cs point source was demonstrated experimentally using a three dimensional multi-pixel CdTe array detector. The proposed method based on the CNN model has better estimation accuracy at low counts than conventional 4π gamma-ray imaging.

articleTitle: Data-Driven Adaptive Frame Division Motion Correction for Brain PET
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Patient motion during brain PET causes image degradation, and motion correction (MC) is necessary for quantitative imaging. Direct measurement of motion with an external sensor is accurate but not practical for clinical use. Therefore, as a device-less MC method, a data-driven method has been proposed to estimate head motion by image registration between frame images by extracting time periods of low motion from changes in the center of gravity (CoD) of the distribution.However, the purpose of this method is to select continuous frames of 30 s or so with little motion for easy registration, and it is difficult to select such frames in cases where the head is moving intermittently, and many unselected data are discarded.In this work, therefore, based on the CoD, we developed an adaptive frame-division method that can automatically set a narrower time frame for larger motion and a wider time frame for smaller motion by repeating the process of setting the moment when the CoD mutation from the frame start point exceeds a certain threshold as the end point of that frame. The proposed method was validated using clinical study data from Vrain, a dedicated brain PET with a hemispherical detector geometry. This was based on a 10-minute head-fixed PET scan and a 15-minute headmoving PET scan, which were performed on eight healthy male volunteers aged 22 to 45 years, starting 45 minutes after injection of 18F-fluorodeoxyglucose (285 ± 23 MBq). The results from the proposed method were compared with results of a previous data-driven method based on CoD (CoD-based) and with the head-fixation PET images. No difference was observed between the proposed method and the fixed head image. On the other hand, the CoD-based MC images discarded an average of 60% of the events, indicating a statistically significant increase in noise.Visual evaluation also supported the results.

articleTitle: Vision Transformer-based Sinogram Enlarging for Reducing Artifacts in Sparse-view Micro-CT
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Micro-computed tomography (micro-CT) provides three-dimensional (3D) morphological structures at the micrometer scale. Although this modality is expected to contribute to histopathology for analyzing the 3D microstructures of tissue specimens, micro-CT imaging for tissue specimens requires a long scan time. Sparse-view CT, which reduces the number of projections, has great promise for speeding up the scanning process; however, analytical reconstruction from fewer projections causes severe streak artifacts on tomographic images. Convolutional neural network (CNN) based artifact reduction methods have been proposed and outperformed conventional filter processing and compressed sensing approaches. However, CNNs are inefficient for capturing long-range characteristics. Vision Transformer, as an alternative to CNN, has recently appeared, and Swin Transformer achieved state-of-the-art performance on image classification tasks on benchmark datasets. SwinIR based on the Swin Transformer also outperformed the performance of CNN-based networks for image super-resolution tasks. In this paper, we proposed an artifact reduction method for sparse-view micro-CT. We developed a SwinIR-based deep learning network for vertically enlarging sparse-view sinograms to estimate full-view sinograms. Experimental results showed that the proposed method achieved the best performance with the lowest total error among the comparison methods.

articleTitle: 3D Compton Mapping of Point and Distributed Sources with Moving Detectors
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Historically, Compton imagers have primarily been operated as stationary imagers. Recent advances in sensors and computing have enabled imagers to move while collecting measurements, enabling the mapping of gamma-ray radiation onto 3D surfaces and volumes. However, traditional Compton imaging methods do not directly generalize to 3D space due to computational complexity and varying sensitivity of the detector. This study builds on previous 3D imaging algorithms for a method applicable to the range of source distributions from point sources to broad distributed sources. Specifically, we propose a maximum-likelihood method iteratively adding point sources or regions of fully voxelized estimates until the measured events are best explained. Furthermore, we describe validation measurements using 500 point sources of Cu-64 to emulate a broadly distributed source and lessons learned for these algorithms.

articleTitle: Estimation of absorbed fraction for Ac-225 targeted alpha therapy using cortex and medulla geometry
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Kidneys are sensitive to radiation and can develop radiation-induced conditions. Administered radiopharmaceuticals accumulates differently in the kidney, with varying accumulation rate in the cortex and medulla. This study aims to estimate the S-value for different kidney regions (Cortex and medulla) while considering different distribution cases in 225Ac targeted alpha therapy. A comprehensive kidney model was implemented in Gate 9.2 software to generate a 3D dose map. 225Ac (0.3 μCi) and its two daughters 213Bi, 221Fr, and lastly 177Lu with activity of 200 μCi were investigated. Emission spectrum of each source was obtained to confirm the source definition and the Radioactive decay. Dose maps were generated by uniformly distributing the activity once in the cortex or medulla, throughout cortex & medulla, throughout the entire kidney. Finally, S-values were calculated for Cortex, Medulla and whole kidney. The emission spectrums indicated that the sources were well defined. 3D dose map Results showed that the sources were posited within the targeted region and the highest levels of deposited energy were observed in regions where the sources were attached. The Medulla consistently exhibited a higher absorbed fraction (S-value) than the Cortex for all radionuclides tested, with S-value ratios of 2.8:1, 2.7:1, 2.8:1, and 2.6:1 for 225Ac, 213Bi, 221Fr, and 177Lu, respectively. Among the radionuclides studied, Fr-221 had the highest S-value of 3.71 in the whole kidney, while 225Ac, 213Bi, and 177Lu had S-values of 3.41, 0.253, and 0.083, respectively. We concluded that the absorbed fraction varies across different regions of the kidney, and that different radionuclides exhibit varying absorbed fractions. furthermore, francium-221 should be given high priority and consideration, as it had the highest absorbed fraction in the kidney. Overall, our study emphasizes that regional variations in absorbed fraction for different radionuclides should be considered.

articleTitle: PEPT-EC, a location algorithm based on anomaly detection for positron emission particle tracking (PEPT)
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Positron Emission Particle Tracking (PEPT) has provided insights into the dynamical behaviour of mineral processing equipment and many other applications where optical tracking is not possible. Highly precise and frequent measurements are needed in order to measure the location of the tracer particle with time. This work presents a new location algorithm called "PEPT-EC" which is based on anomaly detection methods and tests its performance for tracking a tracer particle in comparison to two existing algorithms, Birmingham and PEPT-ML. The raw data for the measurements were generated from a Monte Carlo based simulation of a tracer particle moving on a circular path of radius 2.0 mm. PEPT-EC produced location data with lower or equivalent uncertainty in the path to the two other algorithms, with a considerable improvement at low activity. It achieved this with lower processing time than PEPT-ML, which is likely related to the reduced complexity of removing outliers compared to finding the centre of a cluster with more data points. PEPT-EC facilitates precise tracking of smaller tracer particles than is routine for PEPT with the potential to measure sub-millimeter flow paths in fine particle flotation in mineral processing and cellular transport in medicine.

articleTitle: A large-size depth-of-interaction encoding BGO detector for low-dose PET imaging
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: We are currently developing a high-sensitivity total-body small animal PET scanner with the specific aim of enabling low-dose PET imaging studies, such as cell tracking using long-lived radionuclides. Bismuth germanate (BGO) scintillator with 20 mm thickness is selected to take advantage of its low intrinsic radiation, high stopping power, and low cost. A large size, 51.2 × 51.2 mm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sup>, dual-ended readout detector module, which incorporates two 16 × 16 SiPM arrays with a 3.2 mm pitch coupled to both ends of a 32 × 32 BGO array with a 1.6 mm pitch is being developed with a multiplexed readout. This detector offers good performance for detecting gamma rays, including position, energy, and depth-of-interaction. The detector is being optimized and is expected to enable a high-sensitivity PET scanner.

articleTitle: Gamma-ray Response of an Optical-fiber-based Neutron Detector Using Small Li Glass Transparent Composite Scintillator
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Boron neutron capture therapy (BNCT) is a binary cancer therapy based on neutron induced <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">10</sup>B(n, α) reactions. It is quite important to measure neutrons in BNCT applications. By combining a small piece of fast Li glass scintillator and a quartz optical fiber with high numerical aperture, we have realized an optical-fiber-based neutron detector having high counting-rate capability and showing a peak corresponding to neutron events in the signal pulse height spectrum. At present, however, since a shape of the scintillator cannot be controlled, it is difficult to accurately evaluate the detector response by using Monte Carlo simulations. Therefore, we proposed a Li glass transparent composite scintillator, in which Li glass powder and UV curable resin are mixed. We fabricated an optical-fiber-based neutron detector using the Li glass transparent composite scintillator, which can spontaneously be formed into semi-spherical shape by surface tension of resin. Although the neutron response of the proposed detector has already been evaluated, the gamma-ray response has never been evaluated. We evaluated the gamma-ray response of the proposed neutron detector. We experimentally confirmed that the proposed detector showed a negligible gamma-ray sensitivity under BNCT irradiation condition.

articleTitle: Towards Real-Time Active Collimation in Monolithic Arrays of Silicon Drift Detectors
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: We propose a study of active collimation for multi-element monolithic Silicon Drift Detectors (SDDs) based on real-time recognition of charge sharing events, exploiting key parameters such as the rise time of voltage step signals at the output of the charge-sensitive preamplifier (CSA), and the occurrence in a specific coincidence window of events generated in adjacent pixels.This method aims to overcome common issues of widely-employed mechanical collimation, especially in small-pixel-size detectors where a large part of the active area is covered by the physical collimator which becomes, moreover, quite complex to be manufactured for small apertures.Firstly, we performed measurements with a pulsed laser system providing a 4 μm spot size beam scanning the SDD surface with 10 μm steps, thanks to a 3-axis manual translating stage, to ensure a precise assessment of the charge sharing region.Afterward, we measured events generated by a <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">55</sup>Fe X-ray source at the CSA output on an uncollimated 16-channel monolithic detector to assess the algorithm's capability of rejecting events with partial charge collection while retaining as many non-charge sharing events as possible. This method paves the way also for the possibility of summing partial events on adjacent pixels in order to recover as useful signals those charge sharing photons that would otherwise be discarded, thus maintaining the advantages of mechanical collimation while maximizing the active area.

articleTitle: An Investigation of Inter-crystal Scatter in Highly Segmented Multiplexed PET Detectors
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)

authors.preferredName: F. E. Enríquez Mier y Terán

abstract: Highly segmented PET detectors are commonly used in ultra-high-resolution preclinical PET systems. Such detectors typically rely on scintillation light sharing across an array of photodetectors. In this case, inter-crystal scattering (ICS) is problematic as the positioning algorithm has no information regarding the multiple interaction positions of the ICS photons. Here, using Monte Carlo simulations of both ionizing radiation and optical photons we evaluate and quantify the effects of ICS events on performance of the Open-Field Mouse Brain PET detector. We then propose a simple and efficient deep learning pipeline for distinguishing single scatter events from other events and discuss the current limitations for correcting such events in highly multiplexed PET detectors.

articleTitle: Design and Development of Advanced Low Power Hybrid Acquisition (ALPHA) ASIC for Antarctic Demonstrator for the Advanced Particle-astrophysics Telescope (ADAPT)
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: This paper discusses the design and development of an Application Specific Integrated Circuit (ASIC) named ALPHA for the Advanced Particle-astrophysics Telescope (APT) sensor elements readout. ALPHA is responsible for scintillating fiber-trackers, and imaging calorimeters to measure gamma-rays and other cosmic-rays. The readout process includes analog sampling, sample conversion with an Analog to Digital Converter (ADC), output-data packet transmission, and collection to Field Programmable Gate Arrays (FPGA). Novel in this architecture is the daisy-chaining of the readout, as well as sharing of clocking resources, all to reduce power. For the readout sequence and the data transmission sequence to work adequately, two data paths, two token paths, and two sampling banks are featured. Two paths can bypass any defective ALPHAs, and a token is used for collision avoidance in the data transmission path. The token and data packet transmit in opposite direction from each other. A token starts from the FPGA initially and loops around the daisy chain until the ADAPT ends its mission. On the other hand, the data packets start from each ALPHA. When a token reaches an ALPHA that has a data packet that is waiting to shift out, the data packet starts shifting through the data path toward the FPGA for collection. The ALPHA was manufactured by TSMC and the functionality of the digital block was tested. In conclusion, the ALPHA functions as expected.

articleTitle: Accurate Attenuation Correction for Self-collimating SPECT Imaging
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Recently, our group proposed a self-collimating SPECT system with multi-layer interspaced mosaic detectors to achieve high resolution and sensitivity simultaneously. In this study, we investigated the effect of attenuation on image quality and applied an accurate attenuation correction during reconstruction for self-collimating SPECT based on a half-ring and a full-ring system, respectively. The attenuation factor was calculated using a fast ray-tracing algorithm. The attenuation correction was performed during OSEM reconstruction by multiplying the attenuation factor by the system matrix. Noise-free and noisy analytical simulations were performed using an XCAT phantom with 1 slice. GATE simulations were performed using an XCAT phantom with 20 slices. The reconstructed image quality was evaluated quantitatively using the absolute relative bias between the reconstructed images and the phantom image. The simulation results showed that attenuation correction greatly improved the image quality qualitatively and quantitatively. The results also showed that the full-ring system was preferable than the half-ring system to avoid attenuation-caused artifact when statistical noise was introduced. The GATE simulation results of the full-ring system showed that the absolute quantification biases were reduced after attenuation correction from 82.0% to 4.2%, from 87.7% to 7.7%, from 24.4% to 2.2%, from 95.0% to 9.5% for 4 ROIs, respectively. In conclusion, attenuation correction is crucial for accurate quantification of the self-collimating SPECT images and the full-ring system is preferable than the half-ring system when both statistical noise and attenuation effect exist in practical applications.

articleTitle: Building a Hybrid Compton Camera System for Improving Proton Therapy Imaging
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: The UCT POLARIS system, a solid-state CZT detector for prompt gamma-ray imaging, has shown potential for improving range verification techniques in proton therapy. However, its limitations in timing resolution and energy range impede its clinical applicability. In this project, we aim to overcome these limitations by combining the POLARIS detector with a fast-timing 2" x 2" LaBr<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</inf>(Ce) detector as a hybrid Compton camera. The LaBr<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</inf>(Ce) detectors have outstanding timing and energy resolution, and a higher maximum energy range, while the POLARIS detectors have high position sensitivity and excellent energy resolution [1]. To investigate the feasibility of the hybrid setup, a pulse selected 66 MeV proton beam experiment was conducted at iThemba LABS.To improve the accurate tracking of double scatter gamma ray events from a POLARIS detector into a LaBr<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</inf>(Ce) detector, effective background reduction is important to minimize unphysical events. The onboard electronics of the POLARIS detector enable the selection of single scatter events within the CZT crystals. For further background reduction, a cyclotron beam radiofrequency time of flight analysis is employed on the fast time data of the LaBr<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</inf>(Ce) detector. This analysis allows for the identification and selection of gamma-ray events originating from interactions between the proton beam and the target. Implementation of these data reduction techniques, along with the intricate time synchronization of the two detector data acquisition systems, facilitates the precise tracking of gamma rays across the two detectors.The development of this Compton camera offers the potential to enhance range verification techniques and facilitate the development of a clinical prompt gamma-ray imaging system.

articleTitle: Fabrication of a Highly Efficent Photodiode Using Black-Silicon Technology
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: We fabricated a highly efficient photodiode using black-silicon (b-Si) technology. We had two kinds of sensors to implement b-Si: one was on bare Si and the other on a regular junction. Both b-Si sensors were fabricated on a high resistivity (HR), n-type Si substrate. The sensor with b-Si on bare Si has higher quantum efficiency especially in the lower wavelength region which is due to following reasons: 1) implementation of a Si nanostructure on the surface of the sensor’s active area prevents the incident light from escaping due to zero surface reflection, thus it has been called b-Si; 2) passivation of Si nanostructure surface by alumina (Al<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf>O<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</inf>) significantly reduces the leakage current. Most importantly, this negatively charged alumina layer also induces an inversion layer beneath b-Si, forming a very thin junction. Notably, this enhanced the collection efficiency of this sensor. The b-Si can be used in all kinds of detectors’ entrance windows that have applications in the wide range of light detection down to UV light.

articleTitle: A Novel Energy-Analysis Reconstruction Algorithm of Compton Back Scatter Imaging Base on Origin Ensemble
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Compton back scatter (CBS) imaging is a tomography method using energy or position information of back forward scattered photons in Compton effect to reconstruct the electron density and is expected to be used in non-destructive testing of large or semi-unbounded objects. CBS imaging can be divided into two kinds based on different principles namely CBS based on accurate collimation and CBS based on energy analysis. CBS based on energy information has the advantages of high efficiency and straightforward scanning process. However, the reconstruction problem of CBS based on energy data is a nonlinear problem if attenuation was taken into consideration, resulting in poor reconstruction results or long reconstruction time. In this study, we present an iterative algorithm of CBS imaging based on the origin ensemble estimation to overcome the disadvantages of the nonlinear reverse problem. To verify the algorithm, Monte Carlo simulation experiments were carried out on various models to get list-mode data and verify the robustness of the algorithm. The proposed Compton back scatter imaging based on origin ensemble (CBS-OE) algorithm avoids the renovation of complex system matrix and simplifies the iteration process. Results show that the algorithm proposed in this study has better performance than the analytical reconstruction algorithm, i.e., circle algebra reconstruction technique (CART), and can reconstruct faster than the list-mode maximum likelihood expectation maximization (LMMLEM) algorithm. The method is also expected to overcome the problem of surface imaging of large objects and has the potential for widespread application in various industries.

articleTitle: Low-Dose CT: Reducing Tube Current, Number of Projections, or Both?
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Due to the harmful nature of X-rays, dose reduction at preserved image quality is always a primary goal of computed tomography research. However, when decreasing the X-ray intensity, the reconstructed image will suffer from increased noise and thus image quality would not be preserved. Similarly, reducing the number of projections, which is another popular means of dose reduction, results in sparseness artifacts. Thus, correction algorithms are required. While the reduction of the tube current followed by algorithmic means of noise reduction is the clinical standard, novel convolutional neural networks have shown great promise in the correction of both noise and sparseness artifacts. We investigate the trade-off between reducing tube current and number of projections, in the context of deep learning-based image post processing. We simulate high-dose and low-dose images from clinical CT scans, and train a residual U-Net for each combination. For analysis, we compare MSE and SSIM. The network successfully corrects all tested combinations, reducing MSE by up to 80% and increasing SSIM up to 23%. However, images from fewer projections yield slightly worse results in both metrics. In addition, some structures are less visible or inconsistent in sparse-view reconstructions. Therefore, dose reduction should preferably be achieved by reducing tube current.

articleTitle: A Low-offset Low-noise Comparator for MVT-SiPM Detector Based on 0.18 μm CMOS Process
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Our group has been dedicated to develop a novel silicon photomultiplier (SiPM) integrated with a multi-voltage threshold (MVT) digitizer for PET detectors to achieve a direct digitization of SiPM output on the chip. This architecture requires a low-offset and low-noise comparator to implement MVT sampling precisely. In this paper, we report a new design of an op-amp comparator with internal positive feedback. A test chip was designed on a 0.18 μm CMOS process. The dimensions of the comparator are 36 μm × 24 μm. Our results show that the comparator achieves a 3.32 mV offset voltage at 1-sigma and a 500 μV temporal noise at 1-sigma. The power consumption is 1.98 mW. These results demonstrate that the proposed comparator is suitable to be applied in the MVT-SiPM detector.

articleTitle: 3D Volume Micro-scale 225Ac Dosimetry in Preclinical Prostate Cancer Models
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Radiopharmaceutical therapy with alpha particle emitters (αRPT) offers an advantage in the treatment of refractory or metastatic cancers, such as metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer (mCRPC), by using a precise targeting strategy to exploit the high therapeutic specificity of short-range (40-80 μm) cytotoxic alpha particles. <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">225</sup>Ac-based radiopharmaceuticals have shown high efficacy in several clinical trials, but off-target toxicity suggests that improvements are needed in radiochemistry and progeny radionuclide management. However, the limited availability of data and technologies that quantify dose distribution on spatial scales relevant to the alpha particle range impairs accurate characterization of novel αRPT agents. Here, we demonstrate that 2D digital autoradiography with an ionizing-radiation quantum imaging detector (iQID) can facilitate 3D volumetric dosimetry of targeted and non-targeted tissues. A series of 10-μm cryosections extracted every 200 μm spanning the organ or tumor is measured with the device. These activity maps are used in a previously developed Monte Carlo dose kernel convolution procedure to obtain dose-rate images, which we digitally register into a 3D volume via intensity-maximization rigid-body transformations. The resulting dose-rate organ or tumor volume has an effective voxel size of 39 x 39 x 210 μm. To permit the measurement of only one slice at each position, we validate a digital duplication approximation with a secondary experiment measuring 10 consecutive 10-μmslices in each tissue. We use this technique to sample dose-rate measurements across whole tumors and kidneys from a murine study of <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">225</sup>Ac-MACROPA-YS5, a novel αRPT agent with specificity to CD46-positive tumors. Renal cortical dose rate is over twice that of the medullary region, which suggests that free progeny <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">213</sup>Bi, which is known to collect in the renal cortex, is the source of nephrotoxicity in <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">225</sup>Ac αRPT.

articleTitle: Development of a tapered TOF-DOI Prism-PET detector module for high-resolution brain PET
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: To provide reliable quantitative PET neuroimaging of small brain nuclei and brain tumors, depth-of-interaction (DOI) is an indispensable capability for high-resolution PET. Meanwhile, DOI estimation has been shown to be correlated with optical photon time-of-flight (TOF) information. In this study, we have developed a next-generation TOF-DOI Prism-PET detector module with tapered scintillator crystals to minimize light leak at the crystal-readout interface and further improve DOI resolution. The tapered Prism-PET module consists of a 16 x 16 array of 1.5 x 1.5 x 20 mm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</sup> lutetium yttrium oxyorthosillicate (LYSO) crystals, which were tapered off down to 1.2 x 1.2 mm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sup> starting 5 mm from the crystal-readout interface. The tapered LYSO array coupled 4-to-1 to an 8 x 8 array of 3 x 3 mm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sup> silicon photomultiplier (SiPM) pixels on one end and to a segmented prismatoid light guide array on the opposite end. The flood histogram result shows that all tapered crystals in the detector module could be clearly resolved. The energy, energy-weighted DOI, and TOF-weighted DOI resolutions of the tapered module are 9.53 ± 1.48%, 2.27 ± 0.19 mm full width at half maximum (FWHM), and 5.57 ± 0.51 mm FWHM, respectively.

articleTitle: mPMT photosensors development for the Water Cherenkov Test Experiment (WCTE)
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: In this work, we will discuss the development of mPMT photosensors for the Water Cherenkov Test Experiment (WCTE), which is set to operate in CERN's East Area T9 beam line. One of the primary objectives of WCTE development is to comprehend the technology and potential obstacles and apply it to Hyper-Kamiokande (Hyper-K) and its Intermediate Water Cherenkov Detector (IWCD). These mPMT modules are built using nineteen 3-inch PMTs, which allow the efficient detection of the Cherenkov radiation produced in the fiducial volume. We report on the novel procedure developed to build the mPMT modules and a concise overview of their mechanical and electronic components. Multiple tests were conducted on both the individual module components and the mPMT as a whole to validate the technology. These tests included optical scanning, pressure testing, and more. The WCTE operation is scheduled to begin in early 2024, with the production of mPMTs set to be completed by November 2023.

articleTitle: Development of a detector array simulation model for the low-dose stationary tomographic Molecular Breast Imaging camera with 3D CZT detectors
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: A novel stationary tomographic Molecular Breast Imaging system (MBI) is being developed by Kromek and University College London. The new system combines the superior energy, position and depth of interaction (DOI) resolution of CZT detectors, wide range angular sampling of MPH collimators and novel de-multiplexing image reconstruction to mitigate the MBI drawbacks (higher than mammography patient dose and long imaging time of 40 min) without compromising diagnostic content.A new detector simulation model is being developed to facilitate the design and optimisation of a large MBI prototype. The existing simulation model, based on the principles described by Prettyman in 1999, has been extended to calculate a time-dependent solution, delivering charge pulse shapes, and using them to simulate the operation of a pulse shaping amplifier. The new model delivers more precise modelling of inter-pixel charge sharing and DOI effects, required for optimisation of the new MBI camera design and creation of large training data sets for machine learning algorithms for data analysis and image reconstruction.

articleTitle: Cascade Gamma Photon Coincidence Imaging System: a Simulation Study
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Cascade radiation refers to radiation from a decaying nuclide via a transition from high to low energy levels occurring in a very short time and producing two or more gamma photons with specific energies. In this article, we proposed a novel idea to develop a time-space coincidence imaging system with high resolution and high sensitivity for using cascade gamma photons. The proposed idea was studied on a simulated system for cascade gamma photon imaging using Monte Carlo simulation via GATE software. We designed a ring detector made of LaBr<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</inf> material, with pinhole-slit collimation which combines the high spatial resolution of pinhole collimation and the high detection efficiency of slit collimation. We simulated a point <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">177</sup>Lu source in the center field of view (CFOV). Then we reconstructed the image and evaluated the potential of determining the position of the decaying nuclide from the temporal and spatial coincidence of cascade gamma photon pairs. The center hole slit efficiency (8581 counts) is 2.49×10<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">-5</sup>, and the center point random coincidence efficiency (1027 counts) is 12.0% of the effective events. The Full Width at Half Maximum (FWHM) resolution is about 1.7 mm. The FWHM in the X direction is 1.69 mm, the FWHM in the Y direction is 1.85 mm, and the FWHM in the Z direction is 2.25 mm. The experimental results show that the cascade gamma photon coincidence imaging ring detector system can produce good-quality images. It is a promising technique for cascade gamma photon coincidence imaging and has great potential in the integration of diagnosis and treatment.

Index Terms: Center Of The Field Of View

articleTitle: 3D Deep-Learning Attenuation Map Generation from Uncorrected Brain PET Images
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Attenuation correction from a synthetic attenuation map generated with deep learning from nonattenuation-corrected images offers several practical benefits in positron emission tomographs not adjoined with another anatomical modality. Yet such current neural network architectures still seem not sufficient for high resolution applications, showing artefacts and inhomogeneities. A more complex setup using internal 3D convolution kernels spanning onto neighboring slices in the encoder stages offers very promising results. We obtain preliminary synthetic maps with errors of lower magnitude (<400 Hounsfield units), less geometric bias, much improved visual quality (less artefacts) and better image metrics (MSE -88%, PSNR +28%, SSIM 0.97). Although more complex to train, the generation time of the new 3D architecture remains practical (21 s per 3D image).

articleTitle: Trap states near the surface in (Cd,Mn)Te crystals
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Laser-induced transient current technique (L-TCT) and photocurrent-voltage characteristics (PC-V) are commonly used in many laboratories to measure the values of μ<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">e</inf>τ<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">e</inf> and τ<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">e</inf>. For both techniques (PC‑V and L-TCT), we observed a significant impact of the surface preparation method for the contacts on the obtained results. Different contact shapes were used on the anode to increase the interaction of light-generated charge at the cathode with near‑surface trap states and near-surface recombination, while a planar cathode was point-illuminated.
