In one experiment, the charge (electrons) generated at the cathode flowed directly to the pixel located vis a vis on the anode, while in another experiment, the charge had to flow first through the near-surface layer at the cathode and then to the lateral pixel on the anode. In the PC-V method, LEDs with photon energy ħω≤E<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">g</inf> or ħω>E<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">g</inf> (E<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">g</inf> is the bandgap energy) were used as the light source with adjustable light intensity. In the L‑TCT method, both contacts (on the cathode and anode) were in the form of pixels. In the L-TCT method, the laser radiation energy ħω was about 2E<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">g</inf>. In some experiments the cathode was additionally illuminated by using LED, with ħω>E<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">g</inf> or ħω≤E<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">g</inf>, in other not. By using the PC-V method for the well prepared surface we obtained μ<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">e</inf>τ<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">e</inf> ~ 10<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">−3</sup> cm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sup>V<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">−1</sup> from fitting with the Hecht formula. For a poorly prepared surface, the results were fitted with the Ridzonova formula. The electron mobility μ<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">e</inf> was obtained from the L-TCT method. The observed results for current waveforms in the L-TCT measurements for unilluminated and LED-illuminated cathodes with different electric fields and light intensity of LEDs were compared with the PC-V results, particularly for ħω of LED≳E<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">g</inf>. In our interpretation we consider two processes: ionization of traps by the electric field, and deionization of traps by recombination with electrons excited by the LED light illuminating the cathode.

articleTitle: Evaluation of Chromium Compensated Gallium Arsenide Sensors Using Timepix1, Timepix3, Medipix3 and Timepix2 Readout Electronics
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: This work summarizes the evaluation results of chromium compensated GaAs sensors manufactured by Advacam Oy and evaluated with four different photon counting readout electronics. Flip chip bonded assemblies were evaluated to study the optimal sensor design and bias voltage; uniformity; sensor stability; energy resolution; Modulation Transfer Function (MTF) and high X-ray flux operation. The presentation summarizes the GaAs performance results received from the contributing authors. It presents analytical comparisons to the other commercially available GaAs sensor material in terms of uniformity and spectral resolution. Advacam's GaAs present better uniformity and similar or better energy resolution. The presentation concludes that it is possible to manufacture radiation sensors of chromium compensated GaAs with high uniformity and a good energy resolution that can operate at high X-ray fluxes.

articleTitle: ePixHRM320k- A Detector System for Soft X-ray Imaging for LCLS-II
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: LCLS-II, a Free Electron Laser (FEL) X-ray light source, operating at SLAC National laboratory, includes experiments with x-rays exploring energies in the soft x-ray regime (250eV to 1600 eV). A full frame detector with 320k pixels capable of sustaining readout rates higher than 5,000 frames per second called ePixHRM has been proposed for this type of application. The ePixHRM is composed of two ASICS, where the sensor includes active pixel circuitry, thinned to 200um and back processed to include a thin entrance window. The sensor is bump bonded to the readout ASIC which includes 4 rows of 192 ADCs, configuration logic using a custom interface called SACI and readout circuitry that transmits data serially to an associated FPGA system. To complete the detector active cooling and mechanics has been designed to enable the detector to be installed in a rotating arm inside a vacuum experimental chamber. Initial results from the prototype sensor/ASIC module are already available they are reported.

articleTitle: Angular Correlation Measurement with Compton-PET for Information on Local Environment
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Positron Emission Tomography (PET) and Single Photon Emission Computed Tomography (SPECT) are two modalities used in nuclear medicine. These modalities are referred to as functional imaging because it provides which part of the body accumulates the medicine with radioisotopes. Many diseases can be diagnosed from many kinds of cancers to brain and heart related diseases using functional imaging. If cascade gamma ray emitting radionuclides are used, additional local environment information can be obtained. Angular correlation between cascade gamma rays is determined spin states of initial, intermediate, and final nuclear spin states of nucleus. If the nucleus is perturbed during intermediate state, the correlation becomes weaker. This information can be chemical state, pH, etc. In this study, the anisotropy of cascade gamma ray directions were measured with a ring type Compton camera structure. Advantage of using ring type Compton camera is that SPECT nuclides and PET nuclides can be measured simultaneously: SPECT nuclides with Compton camera imaging and PET nuclides with PET imaging. This study used <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">111</sup>In source that emits 171 keV and 245 keV cascade gamma rays with 85 ns intermediate state lifetime. Two point-like <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">111</sup>In sources with different pH values, 1.6 and 13.9 each, were measured. The imaging was conducted through Compton camera image reconstruction and anisotropies of the sources were measured on the reconstructed images. The result showed that imaging could find out the positions of radionuclides and the anisotropies of two different pHs could be resolved where the two values were separated by more than two standard deviations.

articleTitle: Fast Reconstruction Enhances Deep Learning PET Head Motion Correction
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Head motion correction poses a major challenge in brain PET imaging because even small-magnitude motion can significantly degrade image quality and introduce artifacts. In this study, we propose a new framework for PET head motion correction that builds upon previous work and takes fast reconstructions as input. The proposed method has three main characteristics: (i) the adoption of a high-resolution short-frame fast reconstruction workflow; (ii) the development of a novel encoder for PET data representation extraction; and (iii) the implementation of data augmentation techniques. Ablation studies are conducted to assess the individual contributions of each of these design choices. Furthermore, we conduct a multi-subject study on an 18F-FPEB dataset and qualitatively and quantitatively evaluate the method performance through comparison of the Motion-compensation OSEM List-mode Algorithm for Resolution-Recovery Reconstruction (MOLAR) reconstruction study and corresponding brain Region of Interest (ROI) Standard Uptake Values (SUV). Additionally, we contrast our method with a conventional intensity-based registration method. Our results demonstrate that the proposed method outperforms other methods on all subjects and can accurately estimate motion for subjects outside of the training set.

articleTitle: Development and Initial Validation of Two Simulation Workflows Using GATE for a Total-Body PET/CT Scanner
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Monte Carlo simulation studies potentially support understanding and characterizing new total-body PET/CT scanners such as the Biograph Vision Quadra (Siemens Healthineers), which enable a broad field of novel applications. This work aims to develop and validate two simulation workflows using the Geant4 Application for Emission Tomography (GATE). Workflow 1 is designed to model the response of the Biograph Vision Quadra as closely as possible by using a custom readout and digitizer modeling tool with an integrated coincidence sorter. Further, the same image reconstruction is performed as for real scan data with the e7 tools (Siemens Healthineers). Workflow 2 is developed for increased flexibility based on open-source software and the Customizable and Advanced Software for Tomographic Reconstruction (CASToR) code for image reconstruction. Phantom simulation studies were performed to validate the workflows against measurement data. Using the normalization matrix of the real scanner with an adapted calibration factor, Workflow 1 demonstrated an excellent quantification accuracy with differences of less than 1% for three different phantoms. Image quality analysis using an IEC phantom simulation with 60 s scan time showed good agreements of contrast recovery coefficients and lung residual error with experimental data. The anthropomorphic XCAT phantom was used for patient-like simulations. The successful NEMA-NU validation of the simulation workflows will enable the investigation of scenarios which practically cannot be tested on patients. Further, the generation of training and validation data sets including simulation ground truth data for machine learning algorithms will be enabled.

articleTitle: Clinical Demonstration of a Hybrid C-arm Scanner for Simultaneous Fluoroscopic (CBCT) and Scintigraphic (SPECT) Imaging
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: The primary methods for imaging in the intervention room have up to now consisted of fluoroscopy to map a patient’s anatomy or using hand-held gamma cameras for localization of radioactivity accumulations. We have developed a hybrid c-arm scanner that combines these modalities in a single device [1],[2]. This new form of imaging may impact a range of procedures [3]. In the current study, we present the results from the first clinical study that has been performed. Twelve patients were successfully imaged during radioembolization: an intervention performed for the treatment of liver cancer. The primary conclusion of the study was that the device is feasible to be used in the intervention room. Secondary, the image guidance capability of the device proved suitable, a comparison with a clinical SPECT/CT scanner demonstrated an accurate dosimetric quality of the device, and the hybrid imaging nature of the device showed potential for motion compensation methods [4]. In the next phase of the device development, the acquisition and reconstruction software will be improved in usability and speed so that the device may be employed in larger planned clinical studies.

articleTitle: Dosimetric properties of LiMgAlF6 activated with Europium
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Undoped, and Eu 0.01, 0.1, 1, 2 and 5% doped LiMgAlF<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">6</inf> ceramics were synthesized by the spark plasma sintering method. After the synthesis, photoluminescence properties were investigated. An intense emission was observed at ~380 nm upon 280 nm excitation, and the decay time was ~2 microseconds. Judging from these characteristics, the emission origin was ascribed to 5d-4f transitions of Eu<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2+</sup>. For dosimetric applications, thermally stimulated luminescence and optically stimulated luminescence properties of Eu:LiMAF were investigated. In TSL glow curves, intense glow peak was observed at ~180 °C in all the samples. When TSL emission spectra were measured, the emission appeared peaking at 380 nm, and the emission origin was also ascribed to 5d-4f transitions of Eu<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2+</sup> since the spectral shape was the same with photoluminescence. A linear relationship between irradiation dose and TSL intensity, namely dose response function, was confirmed from 0.1 to 100 mGy. In OSL, emission was also observed at 380 nm, and the emission origin was same with that in photoluminescence and TSL. Throughout these experiments, Eu:LiMAF was confirmed to have a function of luminescence dosimetry.

articleTitle: Photon-counting CT and deep learning-based tumour segmentation for stereotactic radiosurgery treatment planning
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: The current stereotactic radiosurgery treatment planning pipeline involves manual delineation of tumour volumes and the registration of the MRI and conventional CT scan of the patient, leading to uncertainties in the planning workflow. We propose to alleviate these by introducing photon-counting CT as a single imaging modality in combination with deep-learning based tumour segmentation. We developed an imaging pipeline to simulate and reconstruct photon-counting CT images of the brain. Additionally, we trained and tested the deep learning model DeepMedic on MRI and conventional CT data of glioma patients. We observe a low performance of automatic tumour segmentation on conventional CT data as compared to MRI (Dice similarity coefficient: 0.54 % CT vs. 0.75 % MRI T2), demonstrating the need for an improved imaging quality, as can be achieved by photon-counting CT. Preliminary results of our imaging pipeline show an improved quality of the photon-counting image compared to the traditional energy-integrating image (contrast to noise ratio: 1.43 photon-counting vs. 1.06 energy-integrating). We will train and test DeepMedic on reconstructed photon-counting CT images of multiple patients to evaluate the improvement further and we will discuss the implications of the results for the clinical treatment planning pipeline at the conference.

articleTitle: Validation of a vacuum-ultraviolet sensitive Single Photon Avalanche Diode prototype for deep-UV applications
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: The detection of deep ultraviolet light at cryogenic temperatures using silicon photomultipliers (SiPMs) represents a pioneering area of research in dark matter applications that employ noble gases as both targets and detectors. Scintillation light emitted by the noble gas falls within the vacuum ultraviolet (VUV) range, specifically between 100-200nm. To detect this VUV-sensitive wavelength range, a silicon photon avalanche photosensor has been developed on a 160nm Silicon-on-Insulator (SOI) wafer. The first prototype has been fabricated in various configurations, ranging from a single pixel to 2×2 and 4×4 pixels. Different pixel arrangements featuring guard rings and trenches have been investigated. To assess the prototype's electrical behavior, simulations are initially carried out, followed by measurements to evaluate its operational characteristics. The outcome of these measurements will be presented.

articleTitle: PET-Compton hybrid imaging simulation of a small animal whole-gamma-imaging system
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Whole gamma imaging (WGI) is a new nuclear medicine imaging method that combines PET and Compton imaging. By inserting a scatter detector ring inside a PET detector ring, it is possible to combine two different imaging modalities into one system. <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">89</sup>Zr is one of the PET tracers that is suitable for imaging based on an antigen-antibody reaction. However, the 909 keV single gamma ray emission, which occurs four times more frequently than positron emission, has been a factor to degrade image quality in conventional <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">89</sup>Zr-PET. Since WGI can utilize the single gamma rays for imaging by Compton imaging, WGI is expected to improve the image quality by using image reconstruction from combined PET events and Compton events. On the other hand, it has not been clear how much improvement is expected in image quality by combining data with different characteristics. Therefore, in this work, we modeled a small animal WGI system currently under development and assessed image quality to be achieved by the PET-Compton hybrid imaging. Using GEANT4, we modeled the small animal WGI system employing HR-GAGG crystals as the scatter and LGSO crystals as the absorber. The scatter crystal was 15 mm long, but three-layer depth-of-interaction discrimination was enabled. In a contrast phantom, at the same contrast recovery, the hybrid reconstruction offered 4% lower noise than the PET image reconstruction did. In a Derenzo-like phantom, there was no significant difference observed between the PET reconstruction and the hybrid reconstruction. We concluded the hybrid image reconstruction can improve image quality, but the improvement is limited in the simulated small animal WGI system. We consider this is mainly due to limited energy resolution of the scatterer detector; Compton imaging suffered from degraded spatial resolution, and therefore the effect of an increased number of counts may have been cancelled by the degraded spatial resolution in the Compton events.

articleTitle: Virtual scanner geometry for DOI-TOF Prism-PET brain scanner with compact and conformal geometry
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Accurate PET quantification of tracer uptake in small brain structures is confounded by low sensitivity and partial volume effect (PVE) caused by the limited spatial resolution. To overcome these limitations, we proposed the Prism-PET brain scanner which employs TOF-DOI capable single-ended Prism-PET detector blocks arranged in compact and conformal decagon geometry to stimulatingly achieve ultra-high resolution and high sensitivity. Previously, we have developed a DOI-rebinning method for the Prism-PET that repositions the DOI-based line-of-response (LOR) to the center of the crystal surface. However, this procedure introduced a LOR mispositioning error where the LORs that pass the edge of the crystal are rebinned to the center of the crystal. In this study, to fully exploit the benefits of Prism-PET’s high DOI resolution, we employed a virtual cylindrical (VC) scanner with crystals smaller than the actual crystal size to improve the LOR sampling accuracy. For each event, we defined the endpoints of the LOR using the DOI information. The virtual crystal pairs with the surfaces interacting with the LORs were used to form the list-mode event. We also employed event-by-event motion rebinning on the top of the DOI-VC rebinning: before rebin the event to the virtual crystal, we reposition the LOR based on the motion transformation data acquired from our EMMT motion tracking sensors. We scanned the Phantech hot spot phantom and Hoffman brain phantom using the Prism-PET prototype scanner and applied the VC method to the phantom data. The phantom images were reconstructed using CASToR with list-mode OSEM algorithm. We also applied motions to the Hoffman brain phantom to evaluate the motion correction performance with the virtual cylinder scanner. The presented results indicate that the VC could achieve high spatial resolution and contrast to noise ratio while eliminating the challenge caused by continuous DOI and conformal geometry.

articleTitle: Solution Grown Perovskite Single Crystals for Room Temperature Gamma-ray Spectroscopy
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Metal halide perovskites are promising candidates for room temperature gamma-ray spectrum detectors, however, it is challenging to grow high-quality single crystals under operation conditions to make them performance competitive to existing materials. Here, we report the growth of centimeter-size formamidinium-cesium lead bromide (FACsPbBr<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</inf>) and formamidinium lead bromide (FAPbBr<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</inf>) single crystals at high yield from low purity (98%) precursors using a relatively low-temperature solution method.The FACsPbBr<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</inf> spectrum detectors with an asymmetrical metal electrode configuration have achieved an energy resolution of 2.9% for 662 keV <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">137</sup>Cs γ-rays. I will also present further optimization of perovskite surface to improve the resolution to 1.5% for 662 keV <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">137</sup>Cs γ-rays, and preliminary study of stability of the hybrid perovskite crystals at room and higher temperatures.

articleTitle: Theory and modelling for the design of a selective fast neutron self-powered detector for applications in water pool type reactors
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: As part of a CEA funded PhD thesis work, the Self-Powered Neutron Detector application range seeks to be extended to the fast neutron flux in order to meet the on-line measurement needs for irradiation experiments. This paper describes the design of a new self-powered neutron detector for applications in material testing reactors. First, a theoretical study aiming at a better understanding of signal generation in self-powered detectors is presented. This study facilitates new detector design. Then, prototype development and reactor tests of this new selective self-powered neutron detector are the main objectives of this PhD thesis work.

articleTitle: Count-enhancement PET Imaging using a 0.4 mm Cross-strip 3D CZT Detector
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: This paper investigates a cross-strip Cadmium Zinc Telluride (CZT) positron emission tomography (PET) detector, with anode electrode strip width of 0.3 mm x 16.4 mm and cathode strip width of 0.9 mm x 16.4 mm. By utilizing the design of an orthogonal arrangement of cathode and anode, and the ratio of cathode-to-anode signal amplitudes, three-dimensional positioning of gamma photons can be achieved. A set of three-dimensional position calculation formulas is proposed by analyzing the signal of the CZT detector, which can further improve the positioning accuracy. The 3D gamma-ray interaction coordinates are validatedby the signal waveforms. The energy resolutions of single anode, adjacent anode, and non-adjacent anode events for the 0.4 mm CZT detector were found to be 5.3%, 4.6%, and 8.5%, respectively. PET imaging was performed using the 0.4 mm CZT and 1.0 mm LYSO detector with VP-PET geometry. PET imaging was completed on a rotating platform for a 3 mm diameter Na-22 point source. We reconstructed the PET images using both single-anode events and multiple-anode events. Future work will focus on the PET imaging of high-resolution phantom and mouse.

articleTitle: Optimizing Spatial Resolution and Gamma Discrimination of Neutron Anger Cameras
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Neutron sensitive Anger cameras offer many benefits that make them appealing for diffraction instruments including a spatial resolution < 1mm, uniform 2-dimensional active area, and the ability to cover a 3-dimensional solid angle with minimal gaps. Additionally, using silicon photomultipliers instead of conventional PMTs allows for use in magnetic fields. However, the gamma sensitivity of Li-glass scintillators is a limiting factor for reflectometry and high-background applications. In this work we optimized in-house built SiPM-based Anger cameras by testing a variety of optics configurations (scintillator thickness, glass spacer thickness, optical couplings, etc) as well as operating parameters (SiPM bias, integration times) to deliver the best possible spatial resolution. Additionally, we have designed and tested a new layered scintillator to combat unwanted gamma-ray detection.

articleTitle: Statistical Properties of the Positronium Lifetime Image Reconstruction
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Positronium Lifetime Image (PLI) reconstruction is a technique used in time-of-flight (TOF) Positron emission tomography (PET) imaging that involves measuring the lifespan of positronium, which is a metastable electron-positron pair that arises when a PET molecule releases a positron, prior to its annihilation. In our previous work, we demonstrated that our proposed maximum likelihood (ML) algorithm for PLI reconstruction can generate quantitatively accurate lifetime images for a 570 ps TOF PET system. In this study, we conducted further investigations into the statistical properties of the algorithm, including the variability of the reconstruction results, the sensitivity of the algorithm to the number of acquired PLI events and its robustness to hyperparameter choices. Our findings indicate that the proposed ML method produces sufficiently stable lifetime images to enable reliable distinction of regions of interest and the number of PLI events required to produce quantitatively accurate lifetime images is computationally plausible. These results demonstrate the potential of our ML algorithm for advancing the capabilities of TOF PET imaging.

articleTitle: Cross-Modality Deep Learning-based Striatum Segmentation for Dopamine Transporter SPECT
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Dopamine transporter (DaT) SPECT is a competent imaging method to diagnosis Parkinson’s disease (PD). Striatum segmentation on DaT SPECT is necessary to quantify striatal uptake, but is challenging due to the inferior resolution of SPECT images obtained from current general-purpose scanners. MRI is the preferred image reference for striatum segmentation due to its excellent soft tissue contrast. Deep learning (DL)-based segmentation method has been preliminarily applied on simulated DaT SPECT. This work proposes a cross-modality-DL-based striatum segmentation, estimating MR striatal maps from clinical SPECT images. <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">123</sup>I-Ioflupane DaT SPECT and T1-weighted MR images from 200 anonymized subjects with 152 PD and 48 healthy controls are analyzed from the PPMI database. DaT SPECT and MR images are registered, and 4 striatal compartments are manually segmented from MR images by a radiologist as the label. nnU-Net and standard U-Net are implemented using Pytorch with the Adam optimizer running for 1000 epochs. SPECT and MR striatal label pairs are split into train, validation, and test groups (136:24:40). DL methods are also compared to SPECT thresholding-based segmentation (THR-Seg). Dice and Hausdorff distance (HD) 95%, striatal binding ratio (SBR) and asymmetry index (ASI) are analyzed. Results show that nnU-Net achieves better Dice ([0.667, 0.689] vs [0.595, 0.615]) and HD 95% ([1.719, 1.879] vs [2.359, 2.643]) as compared to U-Net for all striatal compartments, which cannot be resolved by THR-Seg. nnU-Net is superior to U-Net and THR-Seg in SBR consistency (95% confidence interval of [-0.196, 0.203] vs [-0.275, 0.183] vs [-1.185, 0.109]) and ASI correlation (Pearson correlation coefficient, 0.80 vs 0.66 vs 0.37) for the whole striatum, as well as for individual compartments. The proposed cross-modality-DL-based striatum segmentation is feasible for DaT SPECT.

articleTitle: Online Reconstruction of Adaptive Whole-Body SPECT Using Origin Ensembles
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: The advancement of gamma-photon detection technologies, especially Cadmium Zinc Telluride (CZT) detectors, has given rise to adaptive imaging (AIM) single photon emission computed tomography (SPECT) cameras. These cameras can adaptively focus data acquisition on regions of interest, making them highly valuable in theranostic applications. This paper presents an innovative approach for the online tomographic reconstruction of AIM data, with a focus on CZT SPECT systems employing swiveling collimation. Our study develops and evaluates an online reconstruction method using the Origin Ensemble (OE) algorithm, a Bayesian statistical approach that supports online reconstruction and enables complex modeling of imaging system physics. We applied the OE to simulated data from a swiveling detector SPECT system, demonstrating its ability to reconstruct images and improve image quality in specified regions. Our results indicate that OE-based online reconstruction is feasible, and the method can adaptively focus on a specified region of interest during the acquisition process, thereby improving the reconstructed image quality. This is evident in the increased visibility of smaller spheres in our simulations. We plan to increase the complexity of the simulation by incorporating more realistic detection models and using real data. Moreover, we aim to enhance the OE reconstruction by integrating more detailed modeling of the physics, such as Compton scattering and septal penetration, and investigating dual-isotope SPECT. The outcomes of the OE approach will be compared to state-of-the-art methods to evaluate its performance. In conclusion, our study presents a novel approach for online adaptive SPECT reconstruction using the Origin Ensemble technique. The OE method has the potential to serve as an excellent alternative to other statistical methods in theranostic applications and other imaging scenarios that require adaptability and online reconstruction capabilities.

articleTitle: Perovskite-based Low-Noise High-Contrast X-ray PEROXITM Imagers for Medical Imaging
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Digital X-ray radiography using flat panel X-ray imagers is one of the most widely used imaging modalities for many medical and industrial applications. Among these, the imagers based on direct charge collection, thereby circumventing the spatial resolution challenges associated with the scintillator-based imagers, are of particular interest for low-dose and high spatial resolution imaging. Even after decades of research, the only commercial sensor material that is currently used for radiography applications is the low-Z sensor material amorphous selenium (a-Se), which has usable sensitivities of up to only 30keV. In recent years, X-ray detectors fabricated using hybrid perovskites have become the center of direct X-ray detector development due to their excellent charge transport properties. However, all the published X-ray radiography results using this sensor material indicate a common problem of high background noise and large leakage current, resulting in radiographs with inferior contrast. Using our low dark current approach, we have not only demonstrated radiographs with better contrast ratios and high spatial resolution but have also demonstrated the long-term environmental stability of these Perovskite-based X-ray Imagers (PEROXI<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">TM</sup>). These results are the first demonstration of practical applications of these low-cost large-area imagers that hold the potential to revolutionize the field of medical imaging.

articleTitle: Reduction of Motion Artifacts in Head Magnetic Resonance Imaging Using Conditional Generative Adversarial Networks
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Motion artifacts caused by the patient’s head movements affect magnetic resonance imaging accuracy. This study aimed to reveal the accuracy of motion artifacts reduction using a conditional generative adversarial network (CGAN). The training dataset consisted of motion artifacts generated through simulations. To create axial images of fluid-attenuated inversion recovery with simulated motion artifacts, 5,500 head images were used. Of these data, 90% were used for training, while the remainder were used for the evaluation of image quality. The training data were consisted of motion artifacts images, and the effect of artifacts reduction was verified in another simulated motion images and spontaneous motion with volunteer images. The resulting corrected images were evaluated using the structural image similarity (SSIM) and peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR), and the metrics were compared with the images without motion artifacts. The average improvements in the SSIM and PSNR for simulated motion image were observed in 14.3% and 3.3%, respectively. Moreover, in the results of volunteer images, the SSIM and PSNR were improved in 10.9% and 5.2%, respectively. Therefore, the image quality of the corrected images with the CGAN was the closest to that of the original images and demonstrated a high image reproducibility.

articleTitle: Modeling Positronium Lifetime Distribution in Geant4 Monte Carlo Simulation
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: During PET measurement, positronium (Ps), where an electron and a positron are combined, is spontaneously generated inside the patient’s body. As positronium lifetime reflects the surrounding environment, the Ps lifetime is expected to be a new biomarker for such quantities as oxygen density inside cancer tumors. The use of 3γ nuclides, which emit a prompt gamma ray simultaneously as the positron decay, enables the measurement of positronium lifetime, and realization of Ps lifetime imaging is gaining attention. In this work, we modeled Ps lifetime in the Geant4 Monte Carlo toolkit for developing Ps lifetime imaging methods. One of the promising methods is whole gamma imaging (WGI), which we are developing by combining PET and Compton imaging. WGI can detect the position of triple-coincidence events from 3γ nuclides almost as a point. We named Ps lifetime imaging by WGI "quantum PET." In the Geant4, the Ps lifetime was input as an image file and simulated as information independent of the material and radioactivity distributions. The positron lifetime was set based on the Ps production rate and the ortho-Ps (o-Ps) branching ratio, and the fluctuation according to the Poisson distribution was given to the annihilation time. The simulator output was single events, and event selector software performed the coincidence processing in the latter stage. We simulated a Ps lifetime measurement using two time-of-flight PET modules for an initial test. Two simulations were performed assuming o-Ps lifetimes of 1.62 ns and 2.10 ns as uniform lifetime distributions surrounding a <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">22</sup>Na point-like source. Lifetime estimation from the time difference spectra of the coincidence events confirmed that the given lifetimes were reflected in event time stamps. By the time of the conference, we will perform simulations in WGI geometry and imaging simulations of the Ps lifetime.

articleTitle: Experimental Results of an Edgeless PET System for Breast Imaging: DeepBreast
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Breast cancer causes the greatest number of cancer-related deaths among women. Screening programs using X-ray mammography have made possible to increase survival rates, but this technique presents some limitations. Positron Emission Tomography (PET) has demonstrated to be a potential way to overcome these drawbacks, offering more accurate diagnosis at initial staging and the possibility of monitoring the therapy treatment. However, further improvements in PET technology are still required. The proposed PET system, named DeepBreast, has been specifically designed to efficiently scan the breast in prone position. The system is based on a novel edgeless detector ring composed of curved monolithic scintillators glued together using a high-refractive index compound. This design minimizes the physical gaps between modules boosting the system sensitivity. It also improves the image quality since edge effects are reduced. For the x- and y-photon impact estimation, a Neural Network technique has been successfully implemented. The depth of interaction and energy were calibrated using a method based on Voronoi diagrams. The DeepBreast has been fully constructed and calibrated. Experimental data are being acquired following a modified version of the NEMA protocol for this dedicated system. A spatial resolution of 1.8, 2.0 and 1.5 mm FWHM was achieved at the center of the field of view (cFOV) along the radial, tangential and axial directions, respectively. These values remain almost constant over the entire FOV. A sensitivity of 2.3% was measured at the cFOV. Preliminary reconstructed images of phantoms show the ability of the DeepBreast system to provide high-quality images.

articleTitle: Feasibility Study of Optical Imaging of the Boron-dose Distribution by a Liquid Scintillator in a Clinical BNCT field
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Evaluation of the boron dose is essential for boron neutron capture therapy (BNCT). However, a direct evaluation method for boron-dose distribution has not yet been established in the clinical BNCT field. Recently, we successfully performed optical imaging of the boron-dose distribution using a cooled charge-coupled device (CCD) camera and a boron-added liquid scintillator at the E-3 port facility of the Kyoto University research reactor (KUR), which supplies an almost pure thermal neutron beam with very low gamma-ray contamination. However, it was unclear that our method could extract boron dose distribution properly in a clinical BNCT radiation field owing to contaminating fast neutron components and intensive gamma-ray dose. In this study, we experimentally investigated the feasibility of our optical imaging method in a clinical BNCT facility. We prepared a liquid scintillator phantom with <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">10</sup>B by filling a small quartz glass container with a commercial liquid scintillator and boron-containing material; its natural boron concentration was 1 wt%. The luminescence images from the boron-neutron capture reaction were observed in a water tank at several different depths using a CCD camera. The background luminescence mainly owing to gamma rays was removed by subtracting the luminescence images obtained using another sole liquid scintillator phantom (natural boron concentration of 0 wt%) at each corresponding depth. The obtained depth profile of the luminescence distribution from the subtracted images indicated reasonable agreement with the calculated boron-dose distribution and the thermal neutron flux distribution by a Monte Carlo Code (PHITS, ver. 3.28). This method could be implemented in a practical form with further study about the perturbation effect of the boron-containing phantom.

articleTitle: L1 Calorimeter Anomaly Detection Triggering Tests Using the CICADA Algorithm For Run 3 Of The CERN LHC at CMS
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: CICADA (Calorimeter Image Convolutional Anomaly Detection Algorithm) is a fully autonomous AI algorithm that can process LHC event data in real-time and independently pick topologies that are different from the majority of currently recorded collision events from the Large Hadron Collider (LHC). CICADA operates close to the rawest recorded data, i.e. the Compact Muon Soleinoid (CMS) calorimeter energy deposits. In this manner, it has as little human bias as possible. CICADA leverages deep learning-based anomaly detection and methods for efficient neural network deployment in hardware. Validation checks have been performed using past LHC data and correlation checks with traditional trigger algorithms showing a novel and intriguing behavior. Besides this, sensitivity to apparatus failures was investigated. Synthetic samples were produced to mimic common problems, such as noisy channels called hot towers. CICADA did not respond to these with higher anomaly scores. We present here an innovative triggering technique that is being tested within the existing CMS Level-1 Calorimeter Trigger system. The calorimeter pre-processors (CTP7) are equipped with Virtex 7 Xilinx FPGA used as target for these firmware developments. The data is propagated to a copy of the Level-1 Global Trigger of CMS (referred to as the uGT test crate) through 10 Gb/s link, that can be run during collision data taking period in parasitic mode. The goal of the exercise is to experiment these new approaches for the Phase-2 of the LHC already during Run-3. This presentation will detail the complex firmware developments and performance with real data compared to algorithms currently used by CMS.

articleTitle: First steps towards a double-paddle-TOF-PET detector
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Positron Emission Tomography (PET) is a well-known imaging technology for diagnosis, treatment and monitoring of several diseases. Most PET scanners use a Ring-Shaped Detector Configuration (RSDC), which helps obtaining homogeneous image quality taking advantage of the symmetries emerging from this geometry. However, those scanners are restricted to an invariable Field-of-View (FOV) and the detectors are placed far from the target organs, which reduces sensitivity. Alternatively, a few PET systems use an Open Detector Configuration (ODC) to achieve a flexible FOV, that can be adapted to different target geometries optimizing sensitivity. Yet, the lack of angular coverage in ODC provide worse quality compared to the first ones. Yet, new research suggests that enabling Time-of-Flight (TOF) in Biplanar ODC PET, compensate the lack of data. This work presents the considerations that we are following to construct a detector suitable for ODC PET. We present our approach to overcome challenges regarding to scintillator surface treatment and configuration, as well as developing an acquisition system to provide the required Coincidence Time Resolution (CTR), and the reconstruction methods for our specific geometry. We report preliminary results about optimization of the scintillator crystal surface treatment for best CTR, using a new BroadCom SiPM array, a set of LYSO crystal arrays from TACrystal, with different surface treatments and an ASIC-based acquisition system from PETSYS.

articleTitle: Prompt Gamma Imaging of Proton Beam using Modular CdZnTe Compton Camera
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: This paper discusses recent prompt gamma measurements of a 66 MeV proton beam on various targets using a modular Compton camera. The UCT Polaris Imaging system consists of two modular detectors housing CdZnTe position-sensitive crystals. As with any imaging system, the primary challenges are improving the efficiency of detection and the quality of the images. The focus of this work is the modular nature of these detectors to improve prompt gamma imaging. The protons were incident on one of three targets, composed of graphite, water and HDPE, produces the prompt gammas, which were then captured by the CZT detector at one of five angles. This measured data was then combined to form an array of detected Compton scatter interactions that were used to produce images of the prompt gamma production within the targets.These promising results demonstrate the ability to take advantage of modular detectors to improve the both the detection efficient and quality of prompt gamma imaging, moving closer to the development of a clinical prompt gamma-ray imaging system.

articleTitle: Detector upgrade for SENJU neutron diffractometer at J-PARC MLF
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: New detector modules have been developed based on a <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">6</sup>Li:ZnS scintillator and wavelength-shifting fibers technology to upgrade the detectors for SENJU neuron diffractometer at Materials and Life science experimental Facility at J-PARC. The detector upgrade plan includes (1) Thin-type add-in detectors, (2) High efficiency detectors to replace the original ones, (3) a large area detector for installation under the sample vacuum tank (Large area bottom detector), and (4) One detector-bank detectors. As for (1) and (2), the detector modules have been developed with a 1.5-fold improved detection efficiency with a 50-60% smaller detector depth while a pixel size and neutron-sensitive area maintained the same to the original detector. 4 add-in detectors and 6 replacement detectors have been manufactured and installed to the SENJU. The large area bottom detector that has a four-fold larger neutron-sensitive area than the original detector, has also been developed. To increase the light collection efficiency a scintillation light is collected from both ends of the wavelength-shifting fiber. The prototype detector exhibited a count uniformity 5~9% over the detector. In this paper, the detector upgrade plan, present status of the beam line detectors, and experimental results of the new detector modules are presented.

articleTitle: Perovskites- a broad field of radiation detector technologies
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Perovskites are a fascinating and varied class of materials that have great potential in radiation detector technologies. Following their initial development by the PV and solid-state lighting communities, perovskites are being actively developed worldwide as both semiconductor and scintillator radiation detectors. Of particular interest are lead halide perovskites where the presence of high-Z atoms such as Cs and Pb provides high X-ray and gamma ray efficiency, combined with good charge transport. These materials can be relatively easily fabricated using either high temperature or solution processing methods, with CsPbBr<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</inf> currently the leading perovskite material for high resolution gamma spectroscopy applications. Particularly rapid progress has also been made in the development of perovskite X-ray imaging detectors, which have demonstrated excellent X-ray sensitivity, stability, and imaging performance. Through the use of sintered polycrystalline perovskite thick films, large area imaging detectors can be realised that are approaching the performance of traditional imaging detector materials such as a-Se and CdTe.The almost infinite range of perovskite materials means that the field of perovskite radiation detectors continues to expand. Structured 2D and 1D perovskites offer many hybrid organic/inorganic materials that combine high resistivity and low dark currents with excellent radiation sensitivity. ‘Lead free' double perovskites also offer environmentally beneficial materials, many of which combine good semiconductor properties with remarkably high scintillation light yields.In this talk I will present an overview of the latest results from Surrey and our collaborators on perovskite radiation detectors, including semiconductor single crystal detectors for gamma spectroscopy and polycrystalline perovskites for X-ray imaging, plus some recent key results from perovskite scintillators.

articleTitle: Metrics to track dopamine release magnitude using PET: Comparison of Residual Space Detection and linear parametric neurotransmitter PET
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Residual Space Detection (RSD) has been previously shown to improve upon traditional methods for detecting low-magnitude dopamine (DA) release in the human brain by use of [11C]raclopride PET scanning. This work aims to extend this methodology, by examining RSD’s ability to track DA release-induced changes in synaptic DA levels, with the goal of identifying a suitable metric that can be related to behavioural and clinical measures of interest to various research studies. We compare RSD outputs with the traditional metric from linear parametric neurotransmitter PET (lp-ntPET) by means of simulation. Both methods track transient changes in synaptic DA concentration well, exhibiting near-linear scaling of their respective metric with simulated levels of DA release and achieving coefficients of variation between 20-40%. For simulated DA concentration increases from 50 to 275 pmol, RSD’s metric exhibited a 3 to 4x increase compared to lp-ntPET’s 1.5 to 2x increase, along with a y-intercept of close to zero, providing a more sensitive and interpretable measure to track single-task DA release.

articleTitle: The SAFIR-I PET Insert: Performance With Inter-Crystal Scatter Recovery Following NEMA NU 4-2008 Procedures
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: SAFIR-I is a preclinical PET insert to a 7T Bruker BioSpec 70/30 MRI, facilitating truly simultaneous PET/MR imaging in mice and rats at injected activities reaching 500MBq. It features 54.2mm axial FOV, 128.1mm inner radius and a dodecagonal shape. The detector is optimized for high coincidence rates, at a spatial resolution of 2-3 mm. We present key performance parameters of this detector, determined by the NEMA NU 4-2008 standard, and under the application of an inter-crystal scatter recovery (ICSR) algorithm. Using a coincidence time window of 500ps, energy window of 391-601keV, the STIR FBP3DRP image reconstruction algorithm, and an ICSR with three hits per coincidence within a 5mm radius and a single hit E window of 100-601keV, the following results were achieved: The average spatial resolutions at radial offsets of 5mm, 10mm, 15mm, and 25mm from the axial center are 2.61mm, 2.84mm, 3.20mm, and 3.22mm, respectively. At identical transaxial offsets from a point at one quarter of the axial FOV they are 2.59mm, 3.04mm, 3.12mm, and 3.24mm, respectively. None of the count rate curves reaches a peak. The maximal values for the true, and noise-equivalent count rates are 1864.1kcps, and 1477.1, respectively, for the mouse-like phantom, and 754.6kcps, and 447.8kcps, respectively, for the rat-like phantom, all measured at the highest tested activity of 506.1MBq. The peak sensitivity is 2.30%; the average system sensitivity is 1.02%. We conclude that SAFIR-I delivers excellent count rate performance thanks to its high sensitivity compared to its short FOV and large inner diameter. The apparent lack in spatial resolution was expected for this reconstruction algorithm and detector geometry. The image quality under ICSR and MLEM reconstruction remains to be tested.

articleTitle: Dosimetric properties of RE-doped LiF/CaF2 (RE = Gd, Tb, and Dy) eutectics
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Dosimetric properties of non-doped and RE-doped LiF/CaF<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf> (RE = Gd, Tb, and Dy) eutectics have been investigated. Eutectic samples were obtained by melt-solidification of raw powders in a carbon crucible under Ar atmosphere. In X-ray excited spectra, the emission peaks due to both the self-trapped exciton of CaF<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf> and 4f-4f transitions of RE<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3+</sup> ions were observed. Thermoluminescence (TL) spectra of the samples also showed both emissions. TL emissions due to STE were quenched at temperatures above approximately 150 °C, whereas those due to RE<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3+</sup> ions were not quenched. In TL dose response curves, monotonic increases in TL intensities of all the samples against X-ray doses were observed in different dose ranges. The most sensitive sample to X-rays was the Tb-doped LiF/CaF<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf> which showed the monotonic increase in the range from 0.01 to 10 mGy.

articleTitle: Towards Full-body Small Aquatic Animal PET: a Simulation Study of MERMAID-v2
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: The MERMAID (Multi-Emission Radioisotopes-Marine Animal Imaging Device) project aims to make positron emission tomography (PET) for small aquatic animals available, particularly for biomedical research with zebrafish. One limitation of the current prototype, MERMAID-v1, is the lack of depth-of-interaction (DOI) information and the need for module rotation. We are using Monte-Carlo simulation to implement a step-by-step system upgrade towards a cost-effective full-body small animal PET solution. For MERMAID-v2, the next upgrade, we are considering adding two more modules, different from the existing ones. The new modules should provide DOI, extend the axial field-of-view, and reduce the number of rotation steps. This hybrid configuration, unique in its kind, poses several challenges for simulation and reconstruction. We have addressed these challenges through a dedicated reconstruction based on the List-mode Maximum Likelihood Expectation Maximization (LM-MLEM) algorithm with multiray random sampling. The system model also takes into account the geometric efficiency of each detector type and was validated using Monte-Carlo simulated data. The reconstructed images of a simulated modified NEMA-NU4 2004 image quality phantom demonstrate significant improvements in spatial resolution, uniformity, and contrast. Despite only two of the six modules of MERMAID-v2 providing DOI information, the new configuration seems to be capable of achieving sub-millimeter resolution and resolving the shrinkage problem induced by parallax errors. The next steps include the simulation of a fish-like phantom, a more comprehensive image quality assessment, improving the reconstruction, and implementing axial detector motion.

articleTitle: Lead-Free Perovskite FA3Bi2I9Single Crystals: An Innovative Material for Radiation Detection
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Over the past few years, perovskite-based materials have received keen interest as a new class of radiation detector materials thanks to their excellent properties including high attenuation coefficients, attractive charge transport properties, tunable bandgap, and most importantly, costeffective manufacturing. However, most of the previously studied perovskite radiation detector materials contain lead (Pb), which is toxic and poses health concerns to both human-being and environment. To this end, there is a strong need to develop lead-free perovskite materials for enabling next generation radiation detector materials. Here, we report our efforts to develop lead-free perovskite, FA3Bi2I9 (FA=CHNH22) single crystals for ionizing radiation detection and imaging applications. A series of growth, annealing and characterization experiments were exploited to improve the properties of FA3Bi2I9 crystals for enabling radiation detection. Systematic microstructural-, electrical-, optical-, and mechanical-properties, together with detector response testing, will be presented and discussed.

articleTitle: The Development of Novel Hypergraph-Accelerated Signal Analysis Algorithms for the Advanced Gamma Tracking Array (AGATA)
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: In the field of high-resolution gamma-ray spectroscopy the development of large-scale position-sensitive arrays is critical in pushing our understanding of Nuclear Physics. The Advanced Gamma Tracking Array (AGATA) utilises Pulse Shape Analysis (PSA) to localise gamma-ray energy depositions and track photons through the array by matching experimental signals against a simulated basis. Due to the significant crystal size used in AGATA the presence of photons that scatter multiple times within the same segment is non-negligible. Conventional PSA algorithms struggle to properly identify these events, and cannot interpret them in a reasonable timeframe. This negatively affects the quality of the tracking possible with AGATA l.Within this work the development of novel Hypergraph-accelerated algorithms is proposed as a viable alternative, these algorithms utilise complex hierarchical structures to describe the combinations of signals within AGATA and efficiently determine the best explanation for High-Fold experimental signals. These algorithms have been profiled using experimental data against more conventional methods and show substantial improvements to both PSA prediction accuracy and execution rates.

articleTitle: Modeling the Performance of Gamma-ray Source Detection and Identification Algorithms using Spectral Distinctiveness and Similarity Metrics
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Over the last two decades, the widespread deployment of gamma-ray spectrometers for radiological and nuclear security applications has led to the need to develop sophisticated methods for detecting and identifying threat sources and other non-background anomalies. A major challenge has been to achieve a high probability of detection and correct identification for potentially dozens of possible source types while simultaneously maintaining operationally relevant false alarm rates, often in the presence of complex backgrounds that vary due to differing concentrations of naturally occurring radioactive material in the measurement environment. In order to help the community further develop algorithms and compare their performance, synthetic urban search datasets are being generated by the Radiological Anomaly Detection And Identification (RADAI) and RADAI-extended (REX) projects. Along with these datasets, tools are being developed to evaluate and understand the performance of algorithms on the spectral detection and identification task, focusing for now on approaches that examine single spectra rather than time series data. One of these tools is a model algorithm that performs detection and identification via template matching using various approximations and assumptions. Embedded in this model algorithm are two useful quantities that provide insight into the reasons for the absolute and relative difficulty of different source types: a factor that describes how distinguishable a source is from the background, and a factor that describes how distinguishable each source is from all the other source types. In this work we derive the model algorithm and then estimate its detection and identification performance, finally comparing those estimates to the performance of various algorithms, including machine-learning algorithms trained and evaluated using the same RADAI dataset.

articleTitle: High-sensitivity searches for neutron-antineutron conversions at the European Spallation Source
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: The HIBEAM/NNBAR program is a proposed two-stage experiment at the European Spallation Source to search for baryon number violation. The goal of the program is to produce new insights into the origins of baryogenesis and the nature of dark matter by performing high-sensitivity searches for neutron–antineutron oscillations as well as conversions between neutrons and sterile neutrons. For the neutron-antineutron oscillation search, the sensitivity will be increased by three orders of magnitude compared with previous searches. In addition to dealing with unprecedented intensities of slow neutrons, the experiment requires a magnetically shielded beamline and a state-of-the-art detector system to detect the multi-pion final state produced in the annihilation of an antineutron in a carbon target. The current detector design combines silicon detectors and time projection chambers for particle tracking with a scintillator particle range detector and a lead glass calorimeter, as well as a cosmic veto system. A general overview over the HIBEAM/NNBAR program will be given and the current status of the experiment and detector design will be presented.

articleTitle: Development of Tunnel Oxide Passivating Contact for Next-generation Silicon Detectors
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Conventional silicon radiation detectors suffer from severe carrier recombination in the heavily doped p<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">+</sup> and n<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">+</sup> layers or regions, as well as beneath the metal contact areas, especially on the detector side, which is also known as "dead layer". Here we present the tunnel oxide passivating contact with an outstanding carrier selectivity. Its key element is an ultra-thin (~1.5 nm) interfacial oxide layer that can allow an efficient transportation of majority carriers via tunneling, while effectively block the minority carriers. The extraordinarily low saturation current density of 5 ~ 10 fA/cm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sup> even with the metal contact (electrode), which was measured by the quasi-steady-state photoconductance, proves the superiority of tunnel oxide passivating contact. While conventional p-n junction or high-low junction have the saturation current density in the range of 10 ~ 90 fA/cm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sup> for the passivated p<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">+</sup> and n<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">+</sup> layers due to Auger recombination, and 800 ~ 6000 fA/cm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sup> for the metal contact areas because of significant metal-induced recombination at the interface. This demonstrates the potential and supremacy of applying the tunnel oxide passivating contact for silicon radiation detectors to thoroughly collect the generated charge carriers, leading to much higher energy resolution.

articleTitle: Quantification of Volume-of-Distribution of Free-state Radiotracer Using Total-Body PET Kinetic Modeling with Time Delay Correction
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Dynamic PET with tracer kinetic modeling is commonly used for characterizing metabolized or bound radiotracer. The characteristics of free-state radiotracer in tissue, however, have been less explored. In this work, we explore quantification of the volume-of-distribution of free state <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">18</sup>F-FDG, V<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">f</inf>, and demonstrate its potential usefulness in the spleen (a key immune organ) as an example. The evaluation included ten cancer patients who underwent a baseline dynamic FDG scan on the uEXPLORER total-body PET/CT and a follow-up scan after two weeks of immunotherapy. An irreversible two-tissue compartmental model with time delay correction was used for modeling the dynamic FDG PET data. Results show that time delay correction can significantly impact the V<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">f</inf> quantification and its ability to measure subtle changes in response to intervention. With time delay correction, spleen V<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">f</inf> was significantly increased post immunotherapy as compared to the pre-treatment scan, while this change was not observed with other kinetic parameters, including FDG net influx rate Ki and delivery rate K1. The results indicate that characterization of free-state radiotracer has the potential to detect early changes, provide novel insights into the physiology underlying therapy, and likely stimulate new clinical applications.

articleTitle: Hallucination assessment for SPECT attenuation map generation from 177Lu-Dotatate and 99mTc MIP-1404
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: A 3d-UNET based approach is used to generate SPECT emission data only attenuation ("µ" )-map from <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">177</sup>Lu-Dotatate or <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">99m</sup>Tc MIP-1404 acquisitions. Two 3d-UNETs (U<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">1</inf> and U<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf>) are trained using clinical SPECT/CT <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">177</sup>Lu-Dotatate and <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">99m</sup>Tc MIP-1404 data, respectively, and are applied to two test data sets (T<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">1</inf> and T<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf>) consisting of 36 <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">177</sup>Lu-Dotatate and 20 <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">99m</sup>Tc MIP-1404 clinical SPECT/CT studies, respectively. We evaluate the cross-tracer image qualities of the µ-maps using the structural similarity index measure (SSIM) and the line profiles in three different planes. For the SPECT reconstructions using these µ-maps, we also evaluate the quantitative accuracy of the reconstructions by performing statistical testing for the activity concentrations measured on 10 spheres with random locations inside the body and having different volumes from 5mL to 15mL. Cross-tracer SSIM values for µ-maps are: 0.85± 0.05(U<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">1</inf>,T<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">1</inf>), 0.78±0.02(U<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">1</inf>,T<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf>), 0.70±0.04(U<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf>,T<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">1</inf>), 0.84±0.04(U<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf>,T<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf>). The SSIM values for attenuated reconstructions are: 0.99 ± 0.008 for <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">177</sup>LuDotatate tracer, and 0.98 ± 0.009 for <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">99m</sup>Tc MIP-1404 tracer. The Mann-Whitney-Wilcoxon test shows that there is no significant difference between the average activity concentrations measured on 10 random spheres (p-value = 0.9). In conclusion, SPECT alone can generate decent µ-maps using trained 3d-UNETs for <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">177</sup>Lu-Dotatate and <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">99m</sup>Tc MIP-1404 tracer compounds. The reconstructions using these µ-maps show very little differences with that using µ-maps derived from CT, either visually or quantitatively. But the UNET trained on one tracer cannot be used directly to the other tracer, although the images from these two tracers cover similar body parts.

articleTitle: Photon-counting detector spectral calibration enabling iodine quantification for spectral CT
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: Photon-counting detector (PCD) computed tomography (CT) can provide grayscale and spectral images within the same acquisition. To achieve accurate material quantification, PCD-CT requires a pixel-per-pixel calibration. In this work, a novel step-wedge phantom made of various iodine concentrations and water thicknesses was used for such calibration. The phantom allowed for water/iodine material decomposition (MD) and so for a direct quantification of iodine concentration, relevant for CT angiography protocols. The general methodology refines a simulated forward model from measurements of known material thicknesses. However, this technique requires an accurate PCD response model which is difficult to simulate. Here we present a case where this exhaustive methodology led to an inaccurate MD. We tested two alternative models with a reduced number of parameters and a polynomial approach, for spectral accuracy comparison. The reduced parameter methods were compared with real data acquired with a CdZnTe (CZT) PCD with six energy thresholds. The different approaches were evaluated with the calibration measurements taken on the step-wedge phantom and the CT acquisitions of two phantoms: 1) with iodine tubes at different concentrations and 2) an image quality phantom evaluating noise and ring artifacts. The polynomial approach led to the best spectral accuracy but suffered from high noise. The exhaustive model calibration resulted in divergent behavior and inaccurate spectral quantification. Both reduced parameter models achieved iodine quantification accuracy below 0.5 mg/ml and but only the model with two incident energies per bin presented the least noise and ring artifacts. For this last method the impact of the number of energy bins (2-6) was also evaluated. The configuration with 4, 5 or 6 bins provided superior MD, with accurate iodine quantification and reduced ring artifacts.

articleTitle: SCNN-Assisted Fast Image Reconstruction using Small Dataset: Gains and Limitations
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: The emergence of equivariant Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) has shown great promise for image processing in non-Euclidean spaces and symmetrical domains. Equivariant networks shows significant enhancement in image quality and computational efficiency, making them well-suited for medical imaging applications. However, there are several challenges associated with image reconstruction from Monte Carlo simulated data, including computational complexity, statistical noise, and. This study investigates the potential of utilizing equivariant CNNs in augmenting traditional reconstruction algorithms for medical imaging applications. This study aims to explore the use of equivariant spherical CNN (SCNN) in conjunction with maximum likelihood expectation maximization (MLEM) reconstruction to lower computational costs and dependency on the completeness of input data. The approach will be compared with a conventional CNN-based augmentation framework to assess the relative benefits and limitations. Our results show that the computational cost of SCNN is drastically decreased from 2000+ seconds for each iteration of MLEM and 820 seconds for CNN to only 15 seconds for SCNN. The findings of this study have the potential to contribute to the development of more efficient and accurate reconstruction algorithms for medical imaging, ultimately leading to better outcomes and advancements in the field.

articleTitle: Stduy on Induced Signal Compensation and Filtering Methods and Spatial Resolution Ability of Pixel-Type CdZnTe Compton Imaging System
publicationTitle: 2023 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, Medical Imaging Conference and International Symposium on Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (NSS MIC RTSD)
abstract: To realize the application of semiconductor cadmium zinc telluride (CdZnTe) detectors in high-energy ray imaging fields such as nuclear safety monitoring, proton and heavy ion radiotherapy range assessment and verification, the pixel-type CdZnTe imaging detectors were used for Compton imaging research. The 2× 2 Compton imaging system consists 4 CdZnTe pixel detectors with 2 mm pixel size. The spatial resolution of the Compton imaging system was 2 mm× 2 mm× 1 mm. The data used for Compton imaging was corrected for incompletely charge collection according to the depth of interaction (DOI) and the initial gamma energy. The characteristic energy of <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">137</sup>Cs, <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">133</sup>Ba, and <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">152</sup>Eu were used to calculate the energy compensation. The corrected data was filtered by four necessary conditions before imaging reconstruction. The reconstructed events are filtered from the four aspects: the sum of the energy of the two events, the DOI, the calculated scattering angle, and the distance between the two events. The <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">137</sup>Cs dual-source imaging experiment was delivered to verify the imaging ability of the CdZnTe Compton imaging detector.
